period:cambrian.summary: Life was almost entirely in the sea. In a geologically short burst known as the Cambrian explosion, most of the major animal groups alive today appear in the fossil record.
highlights: Trilobites spread through the oceans and became the signature fossil of the era
Anomalocaris, a metre-long predator with grasping limbs, hunted the seafloor
Early chordates such as Pikaia hint at the ancestors of all vertebrates
Exceptional fossil sites like the Burgess Shale (Canada) and Chengjiang (China) preserve soft bodies
period:cambrian.ending: A series of extinction pulses hit trilobites and reef builders hard, closing the period.

period:ordovician.summary: Warm, shallow seas covered much of the continents. Marine diversity multiplied in the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, and the first plants crept onto land.
highlights: Giant straight-shelled nautiloids were the top predators
Jawless fish became more common
Graptolites drifted in huge numbers and are used to date rocks today
Simple plants related to liverworts began colonising land
period:ordovician.ending: An ice age over the southern supercontinent Gondwana drained shallow seas, causing one of the "Big Five" mass extinctions. Around 85% of marine species died out.

period:silurian.tagline: Life gains a foothold on land
period:silurian.summary: Melting ice raised sea levels and life recovered. Reefs flourished, jawed fish spread, and the first vascular plants and land animals appeared.
highlights: Cooksonia, one of the earliest plants with water-carrying tissue, grew a few centimetres tall
Jawed fish diversified, a key step towards all later vertebrates
Sea scorpions (eurypterids) grew to over two metres long
Millipede-like arthropods were among the first animals to live on land
period:silurian.ending: No major extinction marks its end; the boundary is defined by changes in graptolite species.

period:devonian.summary: Fish diversified dramatically, the first forests grew, and four-limbed vertebrates (tetrapods) took their first steps.
highlights: Dunkleosteus, an armoured placoderm fish up to several metres long, had bony blades for jaws
Tiktaalik, a fish with wrist-like fins, shows the transition from water to land
Archaeopteris formed some of the first true forests
Ammonoids appeared and would thrive for over 300 million years
period:devonian.ending: A series of crises, including the Kellwasser and Hangenberg events, collapsed reef ecosystems in another "Big Five" mass extinction.

period:carboniferous.summary: Vast swamp forests covered the tropics. Their buried remains became much of the coal mined today, which gave the period its name.
highlights: Tree-sized club mosses like Lepidodendron grew up to 30 metres tall
High oxygen levels supported giants such as Meganeura, a griffinfly with a 70 cm wingspan
Arthropleura, a millipede relative, grew over two metres long
The first amniotes (animals that lay shelled eggs), such as Hylonomus, appeared
period:carboniferous.ending: As the climate cooled and dried, the rainforests collapsed into isolated patches, and the continents kept merging into Pangaea.

period:permian.tagline: One supercontinent, then the Great Dying
period:permian.summary: All major landmasses were joined as Pangaea, with harsh, dry interiors. Synapsids, the group that later gave rise to mammals, dominated life on land.
highlights: Dimetrodon, a sail-backed synapsid, was a top predator early in the period
Gorgonopsians, sabre-toothed predators, hunted later in the period
Conifers and seed ferns spread across drier landscapes
period:permian.ending: The end-Permian extinction, the worst in Earth’s history, was likely triggered by the Siberian Traps eruptions. Most marine species and around 70% of land vertebrate species vanished.

period:triassic.summary: Life slowly rebuilt after the Great Dying. By the late Triassic the first dinosaurs, pterosaurs and mammal relatives had appeared.
highlights: Lystrosaurus, a stocky plant-eater, was one of the most common land animals early on
Early dinosaurs like Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus appeared around 230 million years ago
Pterosaurs became the first vertebrates to fly
Ichthyosaurs, dolphin-shaped marine reptiles, ruled the seas
period:triassic.ending: Massive volcanism as Pangaea began to split caused the end-Triassic extinction, clearing the way for dinosaurs to dominate.

period:jurassic.summary: Pangaea broke apart and the Atlantic Ocean began to open. Dinosaurs became the dominant land animals, and the first birds took flight.
highlights: Giant sauropods such as Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus were the largest land animals of their time
Stegosaurus and the predator Allosaurus lived in what is now North America
Archaeopteryx, around 150 million years old, links dinosaurs and birds
Plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs hunted in the seas
period:jurassic.ending: No major mass extinction marks the boundary with the Cretaceous.

period:cretaceous.summary: The longest period of the Phanerozoic. Flowering plants appeared and spread, sea levels were high, and dinosaurs reached their greatest variety. Its name comes from the Latin for chalk.
highlights: Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops lived at the very end of the period
Flowering plants spread rapidly alongside pollinating insects
Mosasaurs, huge marine lizards, were the top ocean predators
Tiny plankton shells built the chalk cliffs of Dover
period:cretaceous.ending: An asteroid struck Chicxulub, Mexico, 66 million years ago. About three-quarters of species died out, including all non-bird dinosaurs.

period:paleogene.summary: With the dinosaurs gone, mammals diversified rapidly into the open niches. The climate started hot, then cooled as ice began forming on Antarctica.
highlights: Early primates and the ancestors of horses, elephants and whales appeared
Whales evolved from land mammals: Pakicetus walked, Basilosaurus swam
Giant flightless "terror birds" were top predators in South America
A sudden warming spike 56 million years ago (the PETM) is studied as a guide to climate change
period:paleogene.ending: No mass extinction; the period closed as the climate continued to cool.

period:neogene.summary: Grasslands spread across the continents and many modern mammal groups took shape. In Africa, the human lineage split from that of chimpanzees.
highlights: Megalodon, a shark estimated at 15 metres or more, patrolled the oceans
Horses and other grazers adapted to open grasslands
Early hominins appeared, and Australopithecus ("Lucy") walked upright about 3.2 million years ago
The Isthmus of Panama joined the Americas, triggering the Great American Interchange
period:neogene.ending: Ice sheets began to grow across the Northern Hemisphere, starting the ice ages.

period:quaternary.summary: The current period, defined by repeated glacial cycles. It includes the Pleistocene ice ages and the warmer Holocene, which began 11,700 years ago.
highlights: Woolly mammoths, sabre-toothed cats and giant ground sloths roamed the ice-age world
Homo sapiens appeared in Africa around 300,000 years ago
Humans spread across every continent except Antarctica
Farming began around 12,000 to 10,000 years ago
period:quaternary.ending: Still ongoing. We are living in it.

extinction:end-cambrian.loss: Not well measured: several waves that hit trilobites hardest
summary: Not a single event but a series of extinctions towards the end of the Cambrian, sometimes called the biomere extinctions, in which trilobite faunas were wiped out and replaced several times. Falling oxygen in the oceans and changes in sea temperature are the likeliest causes, but the details are uncertain.
It is not counted among the Big Five, but it cleared the way for the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, when the number of kinds of sea animals multiplied.

lost.name: Many trilobite families
lost.note: Replaced again and again by new ones.

lost.name: Many brachiopods
lost.note: Lamp shells of the Cambrian sea floor.

survived.name: Trilobites as a group
survived.note: They recovered and flourished in the Ordovician.

survived.name: Conodonts
survived.note: Early eel-like vertebrate relatives, known mostly from their tiny teeth.

survived.name: Nautiloid cephalopods
survived.note: Just appearing, they went on to become top predators.

facts.label: When
facts.value: About 487 million years ago, end of the Cambrian

summary: The second-largest mass extinction, when nearly all life was still in the sea. It came in two pulses. First, a short, intense ice age spread from the South Pole across the supercontinent Gondwana, locking up water as ice: sea levels fell by perhaps 100 m, draining the shallow seas where most animals lived, and the water cooled. Then, as the ice melted, the oceans warmed and lost their oxygen, striking again at the survivors.

lost.name: Many trilobites
lost.note: Especially those of the open sea.

lost.name: Many brachiopods
lost.note: The commonest shelled animals of the sea floor.

lost.name: Graptolites
lost.note: Floating colonial animals, nearly wiped out.

lost.name: Giant endocerid nautiloids
lost.note: Never recovered their former size or variety.

survived.name: Jawless fish
survived.note: Armoured fish that flourished in the Silurian.

survived.name: Sea scorpions
survived.note: Reached their greatest size afterwards.

survived.name: Corals and brachiopods
survived.note: Recovered to build the great reefs of the Silurian.

facts.label: When
facts.value: About 445 million years ago, end of the Ordovician

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: Ice age and falling sea levels, then oxygen loss

extinction:kellwasser.loss: The Late Devonian crises together: about 70–75% of species
summary: The first of two great pulses of the Late Devonian extinction, named after dark, oxygen-poor “Kellwasser” limestones in Germany. It devastated the vast reefs of the Devonian, built by stromatoporoid sponges and corals, and tropical sea life suffered most.

Its cause is debated. The oceans lost their oxygen, possibly because the first forests, spreading across the land with deep roots, washed nutrients into the sea and fed huge blooms of algae. Climate swings and volcanic eruptions may also have played a part.

lost.name: Reef builders
lost.note: Stromatoporoid sponges and many corals; reefs took millions of years to return.

lost.name: Many trilobites and brachiopods
lost.note: Tropical forms were hit hardest.

lost.name: Many placoderms
lost.note: Armoured fish, the dominant vertebrates of the Devonian.

survived.name: Some placoderms
survived.note: Including Dunkleosteus, for a few million years more.

survived.name: Sharks
survived.note: Early sharks such as Cladoselache.

survived.name: Lobe-finned fish and early tetrapods
survived.note: The line leading to four-legged animals.

facts.label: Lost
facts.value: Part of about 70–75% of species lost across the Late Devonian

extinction:hangenberg.loss: The Late Devonian crises together: about 70–75% of species
summary: The second great pulse of the Late Devonian extinction, at the very end of the period, named after the Hangenberg black shale in Germany. It hit animals with backbones especially hard: a 2010 study estimated that most vertebrate species disappeared, ending the age of armoured fish.

Oxygen loss in the oceans and a short ice age are the main suspects. A 2020 study found malformed plant spores from this time, suggesting a burst of harmful ultraviolet light as the ozone layer thinned, though this is still being tested.

lost.name: Placoderms
lost.note: The armoured fish died out completely.

lost.name: Many ammonoids and trilobites
lost.note: Only a few lineages of each survived.

survived.name: Sharks and their relatives
survived.note: Flourished in the Carboniferous, “the age of sharks”.

survived.name: Ray-finned fish
survived.note: Went on to become most of the world’s fish.

survived.name: Four-legged animals
survived.note: Survived through a bottleneck; their record is thin afterwards (“Romer’s gap”).

facts.label: When
facts.value: About 359 million years ago, end of the Devonian

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: Ocean oxygen loss and glaciation; ozone loss suggested

extinction:end-permian.loss: About 81% of marine species and about 70% of land vertebrate species
summary: The Great Dying, the largest mass extinction in Earth’s history and the only one to devastate insects. Older estimates of 90–96% of marine species have been revised down to about 81%, still the worst loss of life known.

It was triggered by the Siberian Traps, a vast outpouring of lava in what is now Siberia, which burned through coal and released enormous amounts of carbon dioxide and methane. The world heated rapidly, tropical seas may have reached about 40 °C, the oceans became acidic and lost their oxygen, and some released poisonous hydrogen sulphide. Recovery took about 10 million years.

lost.name: Trilobites
lost.note: The last ones died out, after almost 270 million years.

lost.name: Sea scorpions
lost.note: Gone for good.

lost.name: Gorgonopsians
lost.note: The sabre-toothed top predators of the Permian.

lost.name: Most other synapsids
lost.note: Most dicynodonts and therocephalians; pareiasaurs too.

lost.name: Ancient corals
lost.note: The rugose and tabulate corals of the Palaeozoic.

survived.name: Lystrosaurus and a few other dicynodonts
survived.note: Lystrosaurus became one of the commonest land animals in the world.

survived.name: Cynodonts
survived.note: The relatives of mammals, including their ancestors.

survived.name: Early archosaurs and their relatives
survived.note: Their descendants include dinosaurs, pterosaurs and crocodiles.

survived.name: Ammonoids
survived.note: Just one or two lineages, which rediversified.

survived.name: Temnospondyl amphibians
survived.note: Some thrived in the Triassic.

facts.label: When
facts.value: About 252 million years ago, end of the Permian

facts.label: Lost
facts.value: About 81% of marine species; about 70% of land vertebrate species

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: Siberian Traps eruptions, extreme warming, acid and oxygen-poor oceans

summary: As the supercontinent Pangaea began to split apart, eruptions of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province poured out lava across what are now four continents, releasing carbon dioxide that warmed the climate and acidified the oceans.
It swept away most of the crocodile-line archosaurs that had ruled the Triassic on land, leaving the dinosaurs, until then fairly minor, to dominate the Jurassic.

lost.name: Conodonts
lost.note: Gone after over 300 million years.

lost.name: Phytosaurs
lost.note: Crocodile-like Triassic predators.

lost.name: Aetosaurs
lost.note: Armoured plant-eaters on the crocodile side.

lost.name: Rauisuchians
lost.note: Big crocodile-line predators.

lost.name: Many large amphibians and ammonoids
lost.note: Most big temnospondyls and most ammonoids.

survived.name: Dinosaurs
survived.note: Rose to dominate land for the next 135 million years.

survived.name: Pterosaurs
survived.note: The flying reptiles carried on.

survived.name: Crocodylomorphs
survived.note: The ancestors of crocodiles, then small and nimble.

survived.name: Early mammals and their relatives
survived.note: Small, mostly night-active animals.

survived.name: Turtles, ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs
survived.note: All carried on into the Jurassic.

facts.label: When
facts.value: About 201 million years ago, end of the Triassic

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: Central Atlantic Magmatic Province eruptions as Pangaea split

summary: The best-known mass extinction, at the end of the Cretaceous. An asteroid about 10 km across struck what is now the Yucatán Peninsula of Mexico, leaving the Chicxulub crater, about 180 km wide. It threw up rock, soot and sulphur that blocked sunlight for months to years, causing an “impact winter” that stopped photosynthesis and collapsed food chains on land and at sea.

The enormous Deccan Traps eruptions in India were already under way and may have added to the damage, though the impact is now widely accepted as the main cause. Animals that were small, ate seeds, insects or dead matter, or lived in fresh water fared best.

lost.name: Non-bird dinosaurs
lost.note: All except birds.

lost.name: Pterosaurs
lost.note: Gone after about 160 million years.

lost.name: Mosasaurs
lost.note: The giant sea lizards.

lost.name: Plesiosaurs
lost.note: The last long-necked sea reptiles.

lost.name: Ammonites
lost.note: Gone after over 300 million years.

survived.name: Birds
survived.note: The only dinosaurs to make it, probably small ground-living kinds.

survived.name: Mammals
survived.note: Small and adaptable, they spread into the world the dinosaurs left.

survived.name: Crocodilians
survived.note: Living in rivers helped them through.

survived.name: Turtles, lizards and snakes
survived.note: Many lineages survived.

survived.name: Sharks and ray-finned fish
survived.note: Sharks lost many species but carried on.

survived.name: Nautiluses
survived.note: Their slow-growing eggs may have helped them outlast the ammonites.

facts.label: When
facts.value: About 66 million years ago, end of the Cretaceous

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: The Chicxulub asteroid impact, perhaps helped by the Deccan Traps

clade:vertebrata.description: Animals with a backbone: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

clade:actinopterygii.description: The great majority of living fish, with fins held up by thin bony rays.

clade:acipenseriformes.description: Ancient, mostly cartilage-skeleton fish with long snouts, still living in rivers of North America and Eurasia.

clade:lepisosteidae.description: Long-bodied, needle-jawed predatory fish covered in thick, enamel-like scales; they have barely changed in 100 million years.

clade:batoidea.description: Flattened cartilaginous fish related to sharks, including skates, rays and guitarfish.

clade:caudata.description: Amphibians with long tails and four short legs, living in and around fresh water.

clade:mammalia.description: Warm-blooded, furred animals that feed their young on milk. In the Cretaceous most were small, living in the dinosaurs’ shadow.

clade:multituberculata.description: A long-lived group of rodent-like mammals with many-cusped grinding teeth; they survived the asteroid but died out about 35 million years ago.

clade:metatheria.description: The branch of mammals that includes marsupials. In the Cretaceous they were most diverse in North America.

clade:eutheria.description: The branch of mammals that includes placentals, from shrews to whales.

clade:reptilia.description: Scaly, egg-laying vertebrates: turtles, lizards and snakes, crocodylians, and dinosaurs including birds.

clade:testudines.description: Turtles, tortoises and terrapins: reptiles whose shell grows from ribs and backbone fused to bony plates. About 360 species live today. Hell Creek’s rivers held many kinds, from small baenids to giant softshells.

clade:squamata.description: Lizards and snakes: scaled reptiles that shed their skin. With over 11,000 living species it is the largest group of reptiles. Snakes evolved from lizards, so “lizards” on their own are not a natural group.

clade:choristodera.description: An extinct group of water-living reptiles, some looking much like gharials, that survived the asteroid.

clade:archosauria.description: The “ruling reptiles”: crocodylians, pterosaurs and dinosaurs, including birds.

clade:crocodylia.description: Crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials and their extinct relatives: armoured, water-living ambush predators. The 26 or so living species (counts vary with recent splits) belong to three families, and their closest living relatives are birds.

clade:dinosauria.description: Reptiles with an upright, pillar-like stance that dominated land life for over 150 million years. Birds are their living descendants.

clade:theropoda.description: Two-legged, mostly meat-eating dinosaurs with hollow bones and three main toes. The group includes birds.

clade:coelurosauria.description: Theropods closer to birds than to Allosaurus, including tyrannosaurs, ostrich-mimics, raptors and birds. Many were feathered.

clade:tyrannosauroidea.description: The tyrant dinosaurs. They began in the Jurassic as small, often crested and feathered hunters, and ended as the giant top predators of Late Cretaceous Asia and North America.

clade:tyrannosauridae.description: The large, deep-skulled tyrannosaurs of the last 20 million years of the Cretaceous, with tiny two-fingered arms and bone-crushing bites.

clade:albertosaurinae.description: Lighter, longer-legged tyrannosaurids from western North America.

clade:tyrannosaurinae.description: The heavier tyrannosaurids, from Daspletosaurus to Tyrannosaurus, plus the long-snouted alioramins of Asia.

clade:maniraptora.description: Feathered, bird-like theropods with long arms and hands: alvarezsaurs, therizinosaurs, oviraptorosaurs, raptors, troodontids and birds.

clade:dromaeosauridae.description: Feathered, sickle-clawed hunters such as Velociraptor and Deinonychus.
clade:dromaeosauridae.akaNote: Popularly called “raptors”, a name made famous by Jurassic Park. Birds of prey are also called raptors; the two are not the same group.

clade:caenagnathidae.description: Toothless, beaked, crested oviraptorosaurs of North America and Asia, built like large flightless birds.

clade:aves.description: Modern birds in the strict sense (the crown group): the last common ancestor of all living birds and every descendant. A few lineages, such as early waterfowl and gamebird relatives, appear before the asteroid; they were the only birds to survive it.

clade:ornithischia.description: The “bird-hipped” plant-eating dinosaurs: horned, duck-billed, dome-headed and armoured dinosaurs and their relatives.

clade:ceratopsidae.description: Large, four-legged plant-eaters with horns and bony neck frills.

clade:hadrosauridae.description: Plant-eaters with broad, duck-like beaks and batteries of hundreds of grinding teeth.

clade:pachycephalosauridae.description: Two-legged plant-eaters with thick, domed skulls ringed with bony knobs.

clade:thescelosauridae.description: Small to medium, two-legged plant-eaters, quick on their feet.

clade:ankylosauria.description: Low, broad plant-eaters covered in bony plates, some with tail clubs.

clade:pterosauria.description: Flying reptiles, close cousins of dinosaurs, with wings of skin stretched from a hugely long fourth finger. They were the first vertebrates to fly and died out at the asteroid impact.
clade:pterosauria.akaNote: Popularly called “pterodactyls”, which strictly is one genus, Pterodactylus. Pterosaurs were flying reptiles, close relatives of dinosaurs but not dinosaurs.

clade:azhdarchidae.description: The last and largest pterosaurs: toothless, long-necked giants that stalked the ground like storks, some with wingspans over 10 m.

clade:myllokunmingiidae.description: Small, fish-shaped animals from the Cambrian with a head, gills and zig-zag muscles: the oldest known vertebrates.

clade:conodonta.description: Eel-like early vertebrates with complex sets of tiny teeth. Their teeth are so common they are used to date rocks.

clade:pteraspidomorphi.description: Jawless fish covered in plates of bone, common in Ordovician to Devonian seas.

clade:placodermi.description: Armoured jawed fish of the Silurian and Devonian, from small bottom-dwellers to giant predators. They were the first fish with jaws, and some gave birth to live young.

clade:chondrichthyes.description: Fish with skeletons of cartilage rather than bone: sharks, rays and chimaeras.

clade:cladoselachidae.description: Some of the earliest well-known sharks, sleek Devonian predators.

clade:sarcopterygii.description: Fish with fleshy, bony fins, like coelacanths and lungfish, and the group that gave rise to four-legged animals.

clade:tetrapodomorpha.description: Lobe-finned fish on the line to four-legged animals, and the first animals with legs.

clade:temnospondyli.description: Early amphibians, from salamander-sized to crocodile-sized, common from the Carboniferous to the Triassic. Living frogs and salamanders may descend from them.

clade:lepospondyli.description: Small Carboniferous and Permian amphibian-like animals, some snake-like, some with boomerang-shaped heads.

clade:reptiliomorpha.description: Four-legged animals close to the ancestry of amniotes, the egg-laying group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals.

clade:eureptilia.description: The first reptiles: small, lizard-like insect eaters of the Carboniferous coal forests.

clade:synapsida.description: Mammals and their extinct relatives, once called “mammal-like reptiles”, recognised by a single opening in the skull behind the eye.
clade:synapsida.akaNote: Once called “mammal-like reptiles”, an outdated term: synapsids are the group that includes mammals, and were never reptiles.

clade:sphenacodontidae.description: Early Permian meat-eating synapsids, many with tall sails on their backs, and the group from which mammals’ ancestors came.

clade:edaphosauridae.description: Plant-eating early synapsids with small heads and knobbly sails.

clade:dicynodontia.description: Plant-eating synapsids with a turtle-like beak and, often, two tusks. They were the most common plant-eaters of the late Permian and Triassic.

clade:cynodontia.description: The synapsids closest to mammals, with dog-like teeth. Mammals evolved from cynodonts in the Late Triassic.

clade:proterosuchidae.description: Sprawling, crocodile-like reptiles close to the ancestry of archosaurs (crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds).

clade:ichthyosauria.description: Dolphin-shaped sea reptiles that gave birth to live young, from the Triassic to the middle of the Cretaceous.

clade:tanystropheidae.description: Triassic reptiles with extremely long necks, some living along coasts and catching fish.

clade:sauropterygia.description: Sea reptiles with paddle limbs: Triassic nothosaurs and placodonts, and the plesiosaurs and pliosaurs of the Jurassic and Cretaceous.

clade:rauisuchidae.description: Big Triassic predators on the crocodile side of the archosaur family tree, walking upright on pillar-like legs.

clade:thalattosuchia.description: Jurassic and Early Cretaceous crocodile relatives that lived in the sea, some with flippers and a tail fin.

clade:herrerasauridae.description: Some of the earliest dinosaurs, Late Triassic predators from South America and elsewhere.

clade:sauropodomorpha.description: Long-necked plant-eating dinosaurs, from small Triassic ancestors to the largest animals ever to walk the Earth.

clade:mamenchisauridae.description: Asian sauropods with some of the longest necks of any animal.

clade:diplodocidae.description: Long, low sauropods with whip-like tails and peg-like teeth, such as Diplodocus and Apatosaurus.

clade:macronaria.description: Sauropods with large nasal openings and spoon-shaped teeth, including Brachiosaurus, Camarasaurus and the titanosaurs.

clade:coelophysidae.description: Slender, early theropods of the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic.

clade:ceratosauria.description: A branch of theropods including horned Ceratosaurus, the abelisaurs of the southern continents, and the toothless Limusaurus.

clade:megalosauroidea.description: Large theropods including Megalosaurus, the first dinosaur ever named, and the fish-eating spinosaurs.

clade:allosauroidea.description: Big predatory theropods with narrow, blade-toothed skulls: Allosaurus, Sinraptor and the giant carcharodontosaurs.

clade:compsognathidae.description: Small, long-legged predatory coelurosaurs of Late Jurassic Europe, such as Compsognathus.

clade:archaeopterygidae.description: Feathered, winged dinosaurs from the Late Jurassic of Germany, close to the origin of birds.

clade:stegosauria.description: Plant-eating dinosaurs with rows of plates and spikes along their backs and tails.

clade:scelidosauridae.description: Early Jurassic plant-eaters covered in bony studs, close to the ancestry of stegosaurs and ankylosaurs.

clade:dimorphodontidae.description: Early Jurassic pterosaurs with huge, deep heads.

clade:rhamphorhynchidae.description: Long-tailed Jurassic pterosaurs with a diamond-shaped vane at the tail tip and forward-pointing teeth for catching fish.

clade:pterodactylidae.description: Short-tailed Late Jurassic pterosaurs, early members of the group that later included the giants.

clade:eugeneodontida.description: Shark-like fish related to living ratfish, with whorls of teeth in their lower jaws.

clade:mesosauridae.description: Small early Permian reptiles that went back to the water, from the inland seas of Gondwana.

clade:pareiasauria.description: Bulky, armoured plant-eating reptiles of the middle and late Permian.

clade:weigeltisauridae.description: Late Permian reptiles with skin wings, the first vertebrates to glide.

clade:dinocephalia.description: Large middle Permian synapsids with thick-boned, heavy heads, both plant-eaters and predators.

clade:gorgonopsia.description: Sabre-toothed predatory synapsids, the top predators of the late Permian.

clade:plateosauridae.description: Late Triassic sauropodomorphs, the first large plant-eating dinosaurs.

clade:dicraeosauridae.description: Short-necked sauropods with tall, often forked spines on their necks and backs. The spines were most likely covered in skin, forming ridges or sails, rather than bare or sheathed in horn.

clade:dilophosauridae.description: Early Jurassic theropods with paired crests on their heads.

clade:anchiornithidae.description: Small, four-winged feathered dinosaurs of the Jurassic, close to the origin of birds.

clade:scansoriopterygidae.description: Tiny, tree-dwelling theropods with very long fingers, some with bat-like wings of skin.

clade:wukongopteridae.description: Jurassic pterosaurs mixing long tails with advanced, pterodactyl-like heads.

clade:pachycormidae.description: Jurassic and Cretaceous bony fish, including giant filter-feeders like Leedsichthys.

clade:iguanodontia.description: Plant-eaters with thumb spikes and beaks, ancestors of the duck-billed hadrosaurs.

clade:psittacosauridae.description: Early horned-dinosaur relatives from Asia, with parrot-like beaks.

clade:protoceratopsidae.description: Sheep-sized frilled dinosaurs without big horns, close relatives of the horned dinosaurs.

clade:titanosauria.description: The last sauropods, found worldwide in the Cretaceous, including the largest land animals ever.

clade:sinosauropterygidae.description: Small, long-tailed feathered predators of the Early Cretaceous Jehol Biota of China. Once grouped with Compsognathus, they were placed in their own family in 2025.

clade:ornithomimosauria.description: Long-legged, beaked, ostrich-like theropods, some of the fastest dinosaurs.

clade:therizinosauria.description: Pot-bellied, plant-eating theropods with huge claws on their hands.

clade:oviraptoridae.description: Toothless, crested, parrot-headed theropods of Asia, known for sitting on their nests like birds.

clade:confuciusornithidae.description: Early Cretaceous birds from China with the first toothless beaks, some with long tail streamers.

clade:hesperornithes.description: Flightless Cretaceous sea birds with teeth that swam with their feet, like loons.

clade:gobiconodontidae.description: Early Cretaceous meat-eating mammals, some big enough to eat baby dinosaurs.

clade:mosasauridae.description: Giant sea lizards related to monitor lizards and snakes, the top predators of Late Cretaceous seas.

clade:pteranodontidae.description: Big, toothless, crested pterosaurs that soared over the sea.

clade:ichthyodectidae.description: Large, fast predatory fish of Cretaceous seas, with upturned, fanged jaws.

clade:lamniformes.description: Sharks such as the great white, mako and megalodon, and their Cretaceous relatives.

clade:pholidosauridae.description: Long-snouted crocodile relatives, including the giant Sarcosuchus.

clade:mahajangasuchidae.description: Short-snouted, land-dwelling crocodile relatives of Cretaceous Africa and Madagascar.

clade:rebbachisauridae.description: Diplodocid relatives with broad, square muzzles for grazing low plants.

clade:anhangueridae.description: Big fish-eating pterosaurs with crests on their snouts and interlocking teeth.

clade:tapejaridae.description: Toothless pterosaurs with short beaks and huge, sail-like head crests.

clade:actinistia.description: Lobe-finned fish once thought extinct with the dinosaurs, until a living one was caught in 1938.

clade:parankylosauria.description: Small, early-branching armoured dinosaurs from the southern continents, named in 2021: Stegouros from Chile, Kunbarrasaurus from Australia and probably Antarctopelta from Antarctica. Their lineage must have split from other ankylosaurs by the Jurassic. Stegouros had a flat, bladed tail weapon, and Antarctopelta may have too.

clade:protostegidae.description: Cretaceous sea turtles, including the largest turtle ever, Archelon.

clade:anura.description: Frogs and toads, amphibians with long back legs for jumping and no tail as adults.

clade:troodontidae.description: Small, large-brained, big-eyed feathered dinosaurs, close relatives of birds.

clade:alvarezsauridae.description: Small, long-legged feathered dinosaurs with stubby arms ending in a single big claw, probably for breaking into insect nests.

clade:primates.description: Lemurs, monkeys, apes and humans: mammals with grasping hands, forward-facing eyes and large brains.

clade:adapiformes.description: Early lemur-like primates of the Eocene of Europe, North America, Asia and Africa.

clade:chiroptera.description: The only mammals that truly fly. By the early Eocene bats were already widespread.

clade:clupeiformes.description: Silvery schooling fish such as herrings, sardines and anchovies.

clade:monotremata.description: Egg-laying mammals: the platypus and echidnas of Australia and New Guinea.

clade:thylacoleonidae.description: Australian meat-eating marsupials related to wombats and koalas, with blade-like cheek teeth.

clade:rhinocerotidae.description: Rhinoceroses, once far more varied and widespread, including in North America.

clade:felidae.description: Cats, from house cats to lions, and extinct sabre-toothed cats.

clade:canidae.description: Wolves, foxes, jackals and their extinct relatives.

clade:pilosa.description: Tree sloths, anteaters and the extinct giant ground sloths of the Americas.

clade:madtsoiidae.description: An extinct family of probably constricting snakes, mostly from the southern continents, from the Late Cretaceous to about 50,000 years ago in Australia. It included giants such as Vasuki of India and Gigantophis of Egypt; Sanajeh of India ate dinosaur hatchlings.

clade:gastornithidae.description: Giant flightless birds of the Paleocene and Eocene, relatives of ducks and geese.

clade:phorusrhacidae.description: Big, flightless predatory birds with hooked beaks, the top predators of South America for millions of years.

clade:teratornithidae.description: Giant soaring birds of the Americas, related to storks and vultures.

clade:cetacea.description: Whales, dolphins and porpoises, which evolved from four-legged hoofed mammals on land about 50 million years ago. Early forms such as Pakicetus and Basilosaurus sit outside the two living groups: baleen whales and toothed whales.

clade:entelodontidae.description: Pig-like hoofed mammals with huge heads, nicknamed “hell pigs”.
clade:entelodontidae.akaNote: Despite the nicknames, entelodonts were not pigs; some studies place them closer to hippos and whales.

clade:chalicotheriidae.description: Odd relatives of horses and rhinos with claws instead of hooves, used to pull down branches.

clade:castoridae.description: Beavers, including burrowing early kinds and the Ice Age giant beaver.

clade:camelidae.description: Camels and llamas, a family that evolved in North America.

clade:sparassodonta.description: Meat-eating relatives of marsupials that were South America’s main mammal predators, including a sabre-tooth.

clade:hominidae.description: Orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos, and humans with our extinct relatives.

clade:proboscidea.description: Trunked mammals: today’s three elephant species and their many extinct relatives. They began in Africa about 60 million years ago as fox-sized animals like Eritherium, grew trunks and tusks, and branched into deinotheres, mastodons, gomphotheres, shovel-tuskers, stegodons and true elephants and mammoths, spreading to every continent except Australia and Antarctica. Many island forms shrank into dwarfs.

clade:sirenia.description: Slow, plant-eating sea mammals: manatees and the dugong, close relatives of elephants and hyraxes.

clade:bovidae.description: Hoofed, cud-chewing mammals with permanent horns: cattle, bison, sheep, goats and antelopes.

clade:equidae.description: Horses, asses and zebras, the last survivors of a family that evolved mostly in North America.

clade:thylacinidae.description: Wolf-like meat-eating marsupials of Australia and New Guinea; the last species died out in 1936.

clade:columbidae.description: Plump, small-headed seed and fruit eaters found worldwide, including the flightless dodo.

clade:alcidae.description: Black-and-white diving seabirds of northern seas, such as puffins, guillemots and razorbills.

clade:dinornithiformes.description: Giant flightless birds of New Zealand with no wings at all. All nine species were gone by about 1445.

clade:ursidae.description: Bears, living and extinct, including the Ice Age cave bear and short-faced bear.

clade:cervidae.description: Deer, whose males grow and shed antlers every year.

clade:glyptodontidae.description: Giant armadillo relatives covered in a domed shell of bone, some with clubbed tails.
clade:glyptodontidae.akaNote: Relatives of armadillos rather than true armadillos.

clade:litopterna.description: South American hoofed mammals, some looking like horses or camels; distant relatives of horses and rhinos.

clade:notoungulata.description: A large group of South American hoofed mammals, from rabbit-sized to rhino-sized.

clade:diprotodontidae.description: Giant plant-eating marsupials related to wombats.

clade:macropodidae.description: Kangaroos and wallabies, including giant short-faced kangaroos of the Ice Age.

clade:varanidae.description: Monitor lizards, from small goannas to the Komodo dragon and the extinct giant Megalania.

clade:dromornithidae.description: Giant flightless Australian birds, the mihirungs, related to ducks and geese.
clade:dromornithidae.akaNote: Nicknamed “demon ducks”: they were distant relatives of waterfowl.

clade:accipitridae.description: Eagles, hawks, kites and Old World vultures.

clade:aspidorhynchidae.description: Slender, long-snouted predatory fish of Jurassic and Cretaceous seas, like Mesozoic needlefish.

clade:dinocerata.description: Large, heavy plant-eating mammals of the Paleocene and Eocene, many with knobbly horns and tusks.

clade:phytosauria.description: Long-snouted Triassic reptiles that looked and lived like crocodiles, but with their nostrils near their eyes.

clade:aetosauria.description: Armoured, plant-eating Triassic reptiles on the crocodile side of the archosaur tree, some with long spikes.

clade:rhynchosauria.description: Stocky, beaked plant-eating reptiles that were among the most common animals of the Triassic.

clade:dipnoi.description: Lobe-finned fish that breathe air with lungs; six species survive in Australia, Africa and South America.

clade:spheniscidae.description: Flightless diving seabirds of the southern hemisphere.

clade:oviraptorosauria.description: Feathered, mostly beaked theropods with short skulls, from turkey-sized to the giant Gigantoraptor.

clade:nyctosauridae.description: Toothless ocean-going pterosaurs that had lost the three small clawed fingers, keeping only the long finger that held the wing.

clade:anurognathidae.description: Small, frog-faced pterosaurs with wide mouths and big eyes, probably catching insects in flight.

clade:ctenochasmatoidea.description: A widespread group of short-tailed pterosaurs from the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous, many with long, slender jaws. The best known are the comb-jawed ctenochasmatids, which strained small animals from water with hundreds of needle-like teeth; the group is known from Europe, Asia, the Americas and possibly Australia.

clade:ctenochasmatidae.description: Pterosaurs with long jaws full of fine, comb-like teeth for filtering food from water.

clade:germanodactylidae.description: Small crested pterosaurs from the Late Jurassic of Europe.

clade:heterodontosauridae.description: Small, early bird-hipped dinosaurs with tusk-like canines as well as grinding cheek teeth.

clade:leptoceratopsidae.description: Small, hornless relatives of the horned dinosaurs with deep jaws for chewing.

clade:docodonta.description: Early mammal relatives of the Jurassic with complex grinding teeth; some swam, dug or glided.

clade:osteoglossiformes.description: Fish with toothed tongues, such as the arowana and arapaima.

clade:perciformes.description: Spiny-finned fish such as perch and bass, one of the largest groups of vertebrates.

clade:shuvosauridae.description: Toothless, two-legged Triassic reptiles on the crocodile side of the family tree that looked remarkably like ostrich dinosaurs.

clade:therocephalia.description: Permian and Triassic mammal relatives, close cousins of the cynodonts; some survived the end-Permian extinction.

clade:amphicyonidae.description: Extinct meat-eaters with features of both bears and dogs. Despite the name, they were a separate branch of carnivorans, not a link between the two.

clade:astrapotheria.description: Large South American hoofed mammals with tusks, probably with a short trunk or mobile lip.

clade:dyrosauridae.description: Long-snouted crocodile relatives that survived the end-Cretaceous extinction and spread through coasts and rivers.

clade:spinosauridae.description: Large theropods with long, crocodile-like snouts and cone-shaped teeth, many of which ate fish. They lived from at least about 130 to 95 million years ago.

clade:baryonychinae.description: Spinosaurids with finely serrated teeth and many teeth in the jaw, such as Baryonyx and Suchomimus.

clade:spinosaurinae.description: Spinosaurids with unserrated, straighter teeth, such as Spinosaurus and Irritator.

clade:megaraptora.description: Lightly built predators with long arms and huge claws on the first two fingers, from about 125 to 66 million years ago. Where they belong on the theropod tree is still debated: some studies make them allosauroids, others early tyrannosauroids or other coelurosaurs.

clade:megaraptoridae.description: Later megaraptorans of South America and Australia, including the largest, such as Maip.

clade:abelisauridae.description: Short-faced predators with tiny arms, the top predators of much of the southern continents in the Late Cretaceous.

clade:notosuchia.description: Land-living crocodile relatives of the southern continents, some with mammal-like teeth for chewing.

clade:elasmaria.description: Small, fast two-legged plant-eaters of the southern continents. Their exact place among the ornithopods is debated.

clade:pampatheriidae.description: Large armadillo relatives with flexible armour bands, close to the glyptodonts.

clade:procyonidae.description: Raccoons, coatis and their relatives, which reached South America before the Panama land bridge was complete.

clade:chordata.description: Animals with a stiff rod (notochord) along the back at some stage of life, including the vertebrates and small relatives such as lancelets and sea squirts.

clade:osteostraci.description: Jawless fish with a horseshoe-shaped bony head shield, the closest jawless relatives of jawed vertebrates.

clade:hybodontiformes.description: Sharks with a spine in front of each back fin, common from the Permian to the end of the Cretaceous.

clade:symmoriiformes.description: Palaeozoic sharks, many of whose males carried strange spines or brushes on their heads or backs.

clade:holocephali.description: The group of today’s chimaeras or ratfish, which was far more varied in the Carboniferous.

clade:saurichthyidae.description: Long, slim predatory fish with long snouts, like Triassic barracudas or garfish.

clade:amiiformes.description: The group of the living bowfin, once far more varied.

clade:gonorynchiformes.description: The group of the living milkfish, with small toothless mouths.

clade:aulopiformes.description: Lizardfish and their relatives, including the fanged Cretaceous Enchodus.

clade:gymnophiona.description: Legless, burrowing amphibians. The earliest fossil ones still had small legs.

clade:cryptobranchidae.description: The largest amphibians alive today, the Chinese, Japanese and American giant salamanders, and their fossil relatives.

clade:procolophonidae.description: Small, stocky, lizard-like reptiles with broad heads, among the few groups to thrive just after the end-Permian extinction.

clade:rhynchocephalia.description: The group of the living tuatara of New Zealand, which was widespread and varied in the Jurassic.

clade:pleurodira.description: Turtles that fold their necks sideways under the shell rather than pulling them straight back.

clade:polycotylidae.description: Short-necked plesiosaurs with long, slim jaws, fast swimmers of the Cretaceous seas.

clade:lagerpetidae.description: Small, long-legged Triassic reptiles. A 2020 study of their skulls and ears found them to be the closest known relatives of pterosaurs.

clade:silesauridae.description: Slender, four-legged Triassic relatives of dinosaurs. Some studies place them among the earliest ornithischian dinosaurs.

clade:ornithosuchidae.description: Triassic predators on the crocodile side of the family tree with distinctive, down-turned snouts.

clade:istiodactylidae.description: Pterosaurs with broad, rounded snouts and interlocking triangular teeth, possibly for cutting flesh from carcasses.

clade:poposauroidea.description: Crocodile-line Triassic reptiles, some of which walked on two legs.

clade:enantiornithes.description: The most varied birds of the Cretaceous, most with teeth and clawed wings, which died out with the dinosaurs.

clade:ophiacodontidae.description: Early synapsids with long, deep skulls, among the first large land predators.

clade:varanopidae.description: Lightly built, monitor-lizard-like early synapsid predators.

clade:brontotheriidae.description: Rhino-like relatives of horses, some as big as elephants, with forked horns on their noses.

clade:nimravidae.description: Cat-like carnivores, many with sabre teeth, that evolved this shape separately from true cats.
clade:nimravidae.akaNote: Cat-like predators, many with sabre teeth, that were not true cats.

clade:hyaenodonta.description: Meat-eating mammals outside the true carnivorans, with shearing teeth further back in the jaw.

clade:merycoidodontidae.description: Sheep- to pig-sized plant-eaters, extremely common in North America; their nearest living relatives are probably camels.

clade:lagomorpha.description: Rabbits, hares and pikas and their fossil relatives.

clade:embrithopoda.description: Heavy plant-eaters from Africa and nearby lands, relatives of elephants and sea cows.

clade:cingulata.description: Armadillos and their extinct relatives, protected by bony armour.

clade:animalia.description: Many-celled organisms that eat other living things and, at least at some stage, can move. All the life in PaleoDex belongs here.

clade:porifera.description: Simple filter-feeding animals without true tissues or organs, among the earliest animal groups.

clade:cnidaria.description: Animals with stinging cells and a single body opening, from jellyfish to corals and sea anemones.

clade:chaetognatha.description: Small, dart-shaped predators of the plankton today, with grasping spines around the mouth. Some early ones were giants.

clade:priapulida.description: Burrowing worms with a spiny, turn-out proboscis, common in Cambrian seas and still alive today.

clade:mollusca.description: Snails, clams, squid and their relatives, plus early armoured forms whose links to the living groups are debated.

clade:lobopodia.description: Worm-like animals walking on soft, stubby legs. Their relatives gave rise to velvet worms, water bears and arthropods.

clade:arthropoda.description: Animals with jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton, the most varied animals on Earth: insects, spiders, crustaceans, millipedes and many extinct groups. Some early forms here sit just outside the living groups.

clade:radiodonta.description: Swimming early relatives of the arthropods with a pair of spiny head limbs, a ring-like mouth and flaps along the body. Anomalocaris is the best known.

clade:trilobita.description: Sea-living arthropods with a three-lobed body, over 20,000 species, from the Cambrian to the end of the Permian.

clade:chelicerata.description: Spiders, scorpions, mites, horseshoe crabs and the extinct sea scorpions, with pincer-like mouthparts (chelicerae).

clade:eurypterida.description: Aquatic relatives of scorpions and horseshoe crabs, from palm-sized to over 2 m long, among the largest arthropods ever.

clade:myriapoda.description: Many-legged land arthropods, among the first animals to live on land.

clade:hexapoda.description: Six-legged arthropods: insects, springtails and their relatives.

clade:cephalopoda.description: Squid, octopus, cuttlefish, nautilus and the extinct ammonites and belemnites: molluscs with arms and, usually, beak-like jaws.

clade:ammonoidea.description: Shelled cephalopods with coiled, chambered shells, so common and fast-changing that they are used to date rocks. They died out with the dinosaurs.

clade:bivalvia.description: Molluscs with two hinged shells: clams, oysters, mussels and scallops.

clade:echinodermata.description: Starfish, sea urchins, sea lilies and their relatives, with five-part symmetry and skeletons of calcite plates.

clade:crustacea.description: Crabs, lobsters, shrimp, crayfish and many small relatives.

clade:hymenoptera.description: Bees, ants, wasps and sawflies. Bees and ants arose in the Cretaceous as flowering plants spread.

clade:cetiosauridae.description: Early long-necked sauropods of the Middle Jurassic, outside the later diplodocoids and macronarians. Whether they form a true family or just a grade of early sauropods is debated.

clade:pennaraptora.description: Maniraptorans with large pennaceous (vaned) feathers on the arms and tail: oviraptorosaurs, scansoriopterygids and paravians. Where scansoriopterygids belong within it is debated.

clade:paraves.description: Dromaeosaurs (popularly “raptors”), troodontids and avialans, many with an enlarged second toe claw. Anchiornithids and Rahonavis sit near the base; whether they are early birds, troodontids or dromaeosaur relatives is debated.

clade:avialae.description: Birds in the broad sense: Archaeopteryx, modern birds and every dinosaur closer to modern birds than to dromaeosaurs or troodontids, including toothed and long-tailed early birds.

clade:ornithuromorpha.description: Avialans with modern-style bodies, such as a short tail ending in a ploughshare bone and a deep breastbone: Ichthyornis, the toothed diving hesperornithines and the crown birds.

clade:unenlagiinae.description: Long-snouted, lightly built raptor relatives from the Cretaceous of South America, from the 1.5 m Buitreraptor to the 5 m Austroraptor. Many had small, simple teeth, perhaps for catching fish and other small prey. They are usually placed within the dromaeosaurs, but some studies put them just outside, closer to birds, as a family of their own (Unenlagiidae). Rahonavis of Madagascar is sometimes counted among them.

clade:halszkaraptorinae.description: Small raptor relatives from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia, several of them long-necked and duck-like: Halszkaraptor, Mahakala, Hulsanpes and Natovenator. They are usually treated as early-branching dromaeosaurs, but a 2025 study placed them among the avialans, closer to birds. Whether they swam is debated.

clade:strepsirrhini.description: Primates with a wet nose, a grooming claw on the second toe and, in most, a “toothcomb” of forward-pointing lower front teeth. Lemurs live only on Madagascar; lorises and galagos in Africa and Asia.

clade:lemuridae.description: Ring-tailed, brown, bamboo and ruffed lemurs of Madagascar.

clade:cheirogaleidae.description: Small, nocturnal lemurs, including the smallest primates alive. Some hibernate or go torpid to survive the dry season.

clade:lepilemuridae.description: Nocturnal, leaf-eating lemurs that cling upright to tree trunks and leap between them.

clade:indriidae.description: Long-legged leaping lemurs that eat leaves, fruit and flowers, including the largest living lemur.

clade:daubentoniidae.description: One living species, the aye-aye; a larger relative died out within the last thousand years.

clade:lorisidae.description: Slow-moving, nocturnal climbers of African and Asian forests with a powerful grip.

clade:galagidae.description: Small, nocturnal, big-eyed leapers of Africa, named bushbabies for their child-like calls.

clade:haplorhini.description: Dry-nosed primates: tarsiers and the monkeys and apes (including humans).

clade:tarsiidae.description: Small, nocturnal, wholly carnivorous primates of Southeast Asian islands, with enormous eyes and very long ankle bones.

clade:platyrrhini.description: Monkeys of Central and South America, with flat noses and outward-facing nostrils. Their ancestors probably rafted across the young Atlantic from Africa over 30 million years ago.

clade:callitrichidae.description: Small monkeys with claw-like nails, which usually give birth to twins; fathers and older siblings help carry the young.

clade:cebidae.description: Clever, active monkeys; some capuchins use stone tools.

clade:aotidae.description: The only nocturnal monkeys, with large eyes.

clade:pitheciidae.description: South American monkeys, many of them specialists in cracking hard unripe fruit and seeds.

clade:atelidae.description: The largest New World monkeys, with grasping prehensile tails.

clade:catarrhini.description: Monkeys and apes of Africa and Asia (and humans), with narrow, downward-facing nostrils.

clade:cercopithecidae.description: Baboons, macaques, guenons, colobus monkeys, langurs and their relatives, the most diverse primate family.

clade:hylobatidae.description: The lesser apes: small, tailless apes that swing arm over arm through the canopy and sing loud duets.

clade:carnivora.description: Cats, dogs, bears, seals, weasels, mongooses, hyenas and their relatives, united by carnassial teeth: a pair of blade-like cheek teeth for slicing meat (lost or changed in some, such as pandas and seals). Not all are meat-eaters.

clade:feliformia.description: Cats, civets, genets, linsangs, mongooses, hyenas and the carnivorans of Madagascar.

clade:caniformia.description: Dogs, bears, the red panda, skunks, weasels, raccoons and the seals, sea lions and walrus.

clade:prionodontidae.description: Two slender, spotted Asian species, now known to be the closest living relatives of cats.

clade:nandiniidae.description: One species, the earliest-branching living cat-like carnivoran.

clade:viverridae.description: Long-bodied, short-legged carnivorans of Africa and Asia, many with scent glands whose musk was once used in perfume.

clade:eupleridae.description: The carnivorans of Madagascar, descended from a single mongoose-like ancestor that crossed from Africa about 20 million years ago.

clade:herpestidae.description: Small, agile carnivorans of Africa and Asia; some live in large cooperative groups, and some take on venomous snakes.

clade:hyaenidae.description: Four living species, though the family was far more diverse in the past. Despite their dog-like looks, hyenas are cat-like carnivorans.

clade:ailuridae.description: One living genus, the red panda; not closely related to the giant panda, which is a bear.

clade:mephitidae.description: Boldly marked carnivorans that defend themselves by spraying foul-smelling musk from glands beside the tail.

clade:mustelidae.description: The largest carnivoran family: weasels, martens, polecats, badgers, wolverines and otters.

clade:otariidae.description: Eared seals, which swim with their front flippers and can turn their hind flippers forward to walk on land.

clade:odobenidae.description: One living species, the walrus; the family was more diverse in the Miocene.

clade:phocidae.description: Earless seals, which swim with their hind flippers and wriggle on their bellies on land.

clade:perissodactyla.description: Hoofed mammals that bear their weight on the middle toe: horses, rhinos and tapirs, and extinct groups such as brontotheres and chalicotheres.

clade:artiodactyla.description: Hoofed mammals that bear their weight on the third and fourth toes: pigs, camels, deer, giraffes, cattle and antelopes, plus the whales and dolphins, which DNA and fossil ankle bones show evolved from within this group, closest to hippos.

clade:tapiridae.description: Forest browsers with a short, flexible trunk, little changed for millions of years.

clade:suidae.description: Wild pigs, hogs and babirusas of Africa, Asia and Europe, with a flat-ended snout for rooting.

clade:tayassuidae.description: Pig-like animals of the Americas that live in herds and have straight, interlocking tusks.

clade:hippopotamidae.description: Two living species of semi-aquatic African giants, the closest living relatives of whales.

clade:tragulidae.description: Tiny, hornless ruminants with tusk-like canines, among the most primitive living ruminants.

clade:antilocapridae.description: One living species, the last survivor of a once-diverse North American family.

clade:giraffidae.description: African ruminants with skin-covered horn-like ossicones and long, dark, grasping tongues.

clade:moschidae.description: Small, antlerless Asian ruminants whose males have long, tusk-like upper canines and a musk gland.

clade:mysticeti.description: Toothless whales that filter krill and small fish from huge mouthfuls of water through plates of baleen, made of keratin like our fingernails. They include the largest animals that have ever lived.

clade:odontoceti.description: Dolphins, porpoises, sperm whales, beaked whales and their relatives, which hunt with echolocation: clicks focused through the fatty “melon” in the forehead.

clade:balaenidae.description: Stocky, slow baleen whales with arched jaws and the longest baleen; “right whales” were the right ones to hunt because they float when killed.

clade:neobalaenidae.description: One species, the smallest and least-known baleen whale, possibly the last of an ancient lineage.

clade:eschrichtiidae.description: One species, the grey whale, which feeds on the seabed.

clade:balaenopteridae.description: Streamlined baleen whales with throat pleats that balloon out as they gulp huge mouthfuls of water and prey.

clade:physeteridae.description: One living species, the largest toothed predator alive.

clade:kogiidae.description: Two small, shy relatives of the sperm whale that can release a cloud of reddish-brown fluid to escape predators.

clade:ziphiidae.description: Deep-diving, rarely seen whales; some species are known only from a few stranded animals. Most males have just one or two pairs of teeth.

clade:platanistidae.description: Nearly blind river dolphins of the Ganges and Indus, the last of an ancient lineage.

clade:iniidae.description: River dolphins of the Amazon and Orinoco.

clade:pontoporiidae.description: One species, a small, long-beaked dolphin of South American coasts and estuaries.

clade:lipotidae.description: One species, the baiji of the Yangtze, probably extinct.

clade:monodontidae.description: Two Arctic whales without a dorsal fin, which lets them swim under sea ice.

clade:phocoenidae.description: Small, blunt-faced toothed whales with spade-shaped teeth.

clade:delphinidae.description: The largest cetacean family, from small dolphins to pilot whales and the orca, the largest dolphin.

clade:rodentia.description: The largest order of mammals, with about 2,500 species, roughly 40% of all mammals. All have a single pair of ever-growing incisors in each jaw, kept sharp by gnawing. Only a few well-known species are included here.

clade:caviidae.description: South American rodents including guinea pigs, maras and the capybara.

clade:muridae.description: The largest mammal family, with over 800 species, including house mice, rats and gerbils.

clade:sciuridae.description: Tree squirrels, ground squirrels, chipmunks, marmots, prairie dogs and flying squirrels.

clade:leporidae.description: About 65 species of rabbits and hares in 11 genera, on every continent except Antarctica (in Australia only as introduced animals). Hares are born furred with open eyes and live above ground; most rabbits are born naked and blind in burrows or nests.

clade:ochotonidae.description: Small, round-eared, tailless relatives of rabbits, with about 34 living species in one genus, Ochotona, mostly in the mountains and steppes of Asia. Many more genera lived in the past, including the Sardinian pika, which survived until historical times.

clade:cricetidae.common: Hamsters, voles and New World mice
clade:cricetidae.description: A huge rodent family of about 800 species, including hamsters, voles, lemmings, muskrats, gerbils and most American mice and rats.

clade:chinchillidae.description: South American rodents with dense, soft fur, related to guinea pigs: the two chinchillas and the viscachas.

clade:erinaceidae.description: Spiny hedgehogs of Europe, Asia and Africa, and their spineless relatives, the gymnures or moonrats of South-east Asia. The family has a fossil record going back about 55 million years.

clade:psittaculidae.description: Parrots of Australia, Asia and Africa, including budgerigars, lovebirds, lorikeets, rosellas and ring-necked parakeets.

clade:estrildidae.description: Small, seed-eating songbirds of Africa, Asia and Australia, including zebra finches, Gouldian finches, munias and waxbills.

clade:eublepharidae.description: Ground-living geckos that, unlike most geckos, have movable eyelids and no sticky toe pads.

clade:poeciliidae.description: Small fish of the Americas, most of which give birth to live young: guppies, mollies, platies, swordtails and mosquitofish.

clade:characidae.description: A large family of mostly small, often colourful freshwater fish of Central and South America, including many aquarium tetras.

clade:danionidae.description: Small carp-like freshwater fish of South and South-east Asia, separated from the carp family in 2018, including danios, rasboras and the zebrafish.

clade:afrotheria.description: One of the four great branches of placental mammals, which evolved in Africa when it was an island continent. DNA studies in the late 1990s showed that animals as different as elephants, sea cows, hyraxes, the aardvark, tenrecs, golden moles and sengis are each other’s closest relatives.

clade:paenungulata.description: The afrotherian branch containing elephants and their relatives, sea cows, hyraxes and the extinct embrithopods.

clade:elephantidae.description: True elephants: the three living species and extinct relatives such as mammoths and straight-tusked elephants.

clade:trichechidae.description: Three living manatees of the Atlantic coasts and the rivers of the Americas and West Africa, with rounded, paddle-shaped tails.

clade:dugongidae.description: Sea cows with whale-like, notched tail flukes: the living dugong and the giant Steller’s sea cow, hunted to extinction in the 1760s.

clade:hyracoidea.description: Small, rabbit-sized plant-eaters of Africa and the Middle East, despite appearances close relatives of elephants and sea cows. About 35 million years ago hyraxes were the main plant-eaters of Africa, and some were as big as horses.

clade:procaviidae.description: The only living hyrax family, with five species in three genera: rock, bush and tree hyraxes.

clade:tubulidentata.description: An order with a single living species, the aardvark. Its name means “tube-toothed”: its teeth have no enamel and are made of many fine tubes.

clade:afrosoricida.description: Small insect-eaters of Africa and Madagascar that look like shrews, hedgehogs, otters or moles, but are afrotherians that evolved those shapes independently.

clade:tenrecidae.description: About 30 species found only on Madagascar, all descended from a single ancestor that crossed from Africa, probably on floating vegetation. They have evolved into hedgehog-like, shrew-like, mole-like and otter-like forms.

clade:potamogalidae.description: Three species of semi-aquatic insectivores in the rivers and streams of central Africa.

clade:chrysochloridae.description: About 21 species of blind, burrowing insectivores of southern Africa, with eyes covered by skin and shiny, often iridescent fur. They look like the moles of Europe and North America but are not related.

clade:macroscelidea.description: About 20 species of small, fast-running insect-eaters of Africa with long, flexible, trunk-like snouts. Long called elephant shrews, they are not shrews but relatives of elephants, and are now often called by their African name, sengi.

clade:ornithorhynchidae.description: The platypus and its fossil relatives, such as the toothed Obdurodon from Australia and Patagorhynchus from Patagonia, which shows the family once lived in South America too.

clade:tachyglossidae.description: Spiny, toothless, ant- and worm-eating monotremes of Australia and New Guinea: the short-beaked echidna and three long-beaked echidnas.

clade:marsupialia.description: Mammals whose young are born tiny and finish developing attached to a teat, usually inside a pouch. About 380 living species: about 120 in the Americas and the rest in Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands, where they evolved into kangaroos, koalas, wombats, gliders and meat-eaters.

clade:didelphimorphia.description: About 120 species of opossums from Canada to Argentina, the largest group of American marsupials.

clade:didelphidae.description: Opossums, from the large Virginia opossum to tiny mouse opossums; many have no proper pouch.

clade:paucituberculata.description: Seven small, shrew-like marsupials of the cool, wet forests of the Andes, survivors of a group that was varied in South America about 20 million years ago.

clade:caenolestidae.description: The only living family of shrew opossums.

clade:microbiotheria.description: A South American order now down to the monito del monte, which is more closely related to Australian marsupials than to other American ones, a clue that marsupials crossed between South America and Australia through Antarctica.

clade:microbiotheriidae.description: The monito del monte and its fossil relatives.

clade:dasyuromorphia.description: Meat- and insect-eating marsupials of Australia and New Guinea: the Tasmanian devil, quolls, dunnarts, antechinuses and planigales, the numbat, and the extinct thylacine.

clade:dasyuridae.description: About 75 species of carnivorous marsupials, from the 4 g planigales to the Tasmanian devil.

clade:myrmecobiidae.description: A family with a single living species, the termite-eating numbat.

clade:peramelemorphia.description: Long-snouted, omnivorous marsupials of Australia and New Guinea that dig for insects, roots and fungi. They have been hit harder than almost any other group by introduced foxes and cats.

clade:thylacomyidae.description: Rabbit-eared, burrowing bilbies: the living greater bilby and the extinct lesser bilby.

clade:chaeropodidae.description: Long-legged, hoof-footed bandicoots of the Australian deserts, all extinct by the mid-1900s.

clade:notoryctemorphia.description: Two species of blind, burrowing marsupial moles of Australia’s sandy deserts.

clade:diprotodontia.description: The largest marsupial order, with about 155 living species, all with two forward-pointing lower incisors (the name means “two front teeth”). It includes kangaroos, koalas, wombats, possums and gliders, and extinct giants such as Diprotodon and the marsupial lion.

clade:vombatidae.description: Three species of stocky, burrowing, grass-eating wombats.

clade:phascolarctidae.description: The koala, the only living member of a family that once had many species.

clade:potoroidae.description: Small, rabbit-sized relatives of kangaroos that dig for fungi, roots and bulbs, spreading fungal spores that help trees grow.

clade:hypsiprymnodontidae.description: The musky rat-kangaroo, the last of a family that also included the extinct meat-eating “killer kangaroos”.

clade:phalangeridae.description: About 30 species of possums and cuscuses of Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands.

clade:petauridae.description: Sugar gliders and their relatives, Leadbeater’s possum and the striped possums.

clade:pseudocheiridae.description: Leaf-eating possums with gripping tails, and the greater gliders.

clade:acrobatidae.description: Tiny possums with feather-like tails fringed by stiff hairs.

clade:tarsipedidae.description: The honey possum, a single species with no close living relatives.

clade:burramyidae.description: Five species of tiny, mouse-sized possums.

clade:palaeognathae.description: One of the two main branches of living birds: the flightless ratites (ostriches, rheas, emu, cassowaries, kiwis and the extinct moa and elephant birds) and the flying tinamous of the Americas. DNA shows flight was lost several times among them, so ratites are not one natural group. All other living birds are neognaths.

clade:struthionidae.description: Two African species, the largest living birds.

clade:rheidae.description: Two large flightless birds of South American grasslands.

clade:casuariidae.description: Large flightless birds of Australia and New Guinea.

clade:apterygidae.description: Small, nocturnal, flightless birds of New Zealand. DNA shows their closest relatives are the extinct elephant birds of Madagascar, not the moa they lived beside.

clade:pandionidae.description: One species (some split it into two), a fish-hunting raptor found on every continent but Antarctica.

clade:cathartidae.description: Vultures and condors of the Americas, which evolved their scavenging lifestyle separately from Old World vultures.

clade:sagittariidae.description: One species, a long-legged African raptor that hunts on foot.

clade:falconidae.description: Fast, pointed-winged raptors that kill with a bite to the neck. DNA shows they are closer to parrots than to eagles.

clade:strigidae.description: Most of the world’s owls, from tiny pygmy owls to eagle-owls, hunting by sight and by superb hearing.

clade:tytonidae.description: Owls with heart-shaped facial discs that funnel sound to their ears.

clade:psittacidae.description: Macaws, amazons, conures and the African grey: intelligent, long-lived birds with strong curved bills and grasping feet.

clade:cacatuidae.description: Crested parrots of Australia and nearby islands, including the cockatiel.

clade:strigopidae.description: The kākāpō, kea and kākā, an ancient branch of the parrots.

clade:trochilidae.description: About 360 species of tiny nectar-feeders of the Americas, the only birds that can fly backwards and hover for long periods.

clade:apodidae.description: Supremely aerial birds that feed, drink, sleep and mate on the wing, related to hummingbirds.

clade:corvidae.description: Crows, ravens, magpies, jays and nutcrackers: among the most intelligent animals, able to make tools, plan ahead and recognise human faces.

clade:paradisaeidae.description: Birds of New Guinea and nearby, whose males have evolved some of the most extravagant plumes and courtship dances of any animal.

clade:menuridae.description: Two Australian ground birds famous for mimicry, from one of the oldest songbird lineages.

clade:hirundinidae.description: Agile aerial insect-hunters, many of them long-distance migrants.

clade:turdidae.description: Songbirds including the blackbird, song thrush and American robin.

clade:muscicapidae.description: Flycatchers, chats, wheatears, the nightingale and the European robin.

clade:fringillidae.description: Seed-eating songbirds such as chaffinches, goldfinches and canaries, and the Hawaiian honeycreepers, which evolved into dozens of forms on Hawaii.

clade:thraupidae.description: A huge, varied family of the Americas that, DNA shows, includes Darwin’s finches of the Galápagos.

clade:passeridae.description: Small seed-eaters, including the house sparrow, which has followed people around the world.

clade:sturnidae.description: Noisy, sociable songbirds, many of them skilled mimics.

clade:mimidae.description: American songbirds known for copying other birds’ songs and other sounds.

clade:cardinalidae.description: Thick-billed songbirds of the Americas, many brightly coloured.

clade:ptilonorhynchidae.description: Birds of Australia and New Guinea whose males build and decorate elaborate structures, bowers, to attract mates.

clade:phoenicopteridae.description: Six species of filter-feeding wading birds, closest related to grebes.

clade:diomedeidae.description: Great ocean wanderers that glide for hours without flapping, many threatened by longline fishing.

clade:procellariidae.description: Tube-nosed seabirds with a keen sense of smell for finding food at sea.

clade:pelecanidae.description: Eight species of large water birds with a throat pouch for scooping up fish.

clade:balaenicipitidae.description: One species, a huge stork-like bird of African swamps, related to pelicans.

clade:ardeidae.description: Long-legged wading birds that stalk fish and frogs, flying with their necks pulled in.

clade:ciconiidae.description: Large, long-legged birds that soar on thermals, flying with their necks outstretched.

clade:threskiornithidae.description: Wading birds with long down-curved or spoon-shaped bills.

clade:gruidae.description: Tall, long-legged birds famous for loud calls and dancing courtship displays.

clade:rallidae.description: Rails, crakes, coots and moorhens; many island rails became flightless, and many of those are now extinct.

clade:anatidae.description: Waterfowl with webbed feet and flattened bills. Vegavis, from the last days of the dinosaurs, may be an early relative.

clade:phasianidae.description: Ground-dwelling birds including partridges, quail, peafowl, turkeys and the chicken.

clade:megapodiidae.description: Birds of Australasia that bury their eggs in mounds of rotting vegetation or warm soil instead of sitting on them.

clade:picidae.description: Birds that chisel into wood with strong bills, using long tongues to pull out grubs, with skulls adapted to repeated impacts.

clade:ramphastidae.description: Fruit-eating birds of tropical America with huge, light, colourful bills.

clade:bucerotidae.description: Birds of Africa and Asia with large bills, often topped by a casque. Most nesting females seal themselves into a tree hole.

clade:alcedinidae.description: Brightly coloured birds that dive for fish; the family also includes the kookaburras.

clade:laridae.description: Seabirds of coasts and oceans worldwide, including skimmers and noddies.

clade:sulidae.description: Seabirds that plunge-dive from height to catch fish.

clade:fregatidae.description: Seabirds with the largest wingspan for their weight of any bird, which steal food from other seabirds.

clade:phalacrocoracidae.description: Diving seabirds and waterbirds whose feathers soak up some water, helping them dive.

clade:cuculidae.description: Cuckoos, roadrunners and coucals; many cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds’ nests.

clade:otididae.description: Heavy, long-legged birds of open grassland in Africa, Europe, Asia and Australia.

clade:tinamidae.description: Ground birds of Central and South America, the only palaeognaths that can fly.

clade:gaviidae.description: Five species of diving birds of northern lakes and coasts.

clade:podicipedidae.description: Diving water birds with lobed toes, closely related to flamingos.

clade:upupidae.description: Crested, striped birds of Europe, Africa and Asia.

clade:scolopacidae.description: Shorebirds including sandpipers, godwits, curlews, snipe and woodcocks, among the greatest migrants.

clade:charadriidae.description: About 70 species of short-billed shorebirds that run and stop to pick food from the ground, found on every continent but Antarctica.

clade:haematopodidae.description: About 12 species of black or black-and-white shorebirds with long, bright orange bills for prising open shellfish.

clade:recurvirostridae.description: Long-legged wading birds with slender bills; avocets’ bills curve upwards.

clade:odontophoridae.description: About 35 species of plump, ground-living quails of the Americas, not closely related to Old World quails.

clade:numididae.description: Six species of African gamebirds with bare heads and spotted plumage; the helmeted guineafowl was domesticated.

clade:cracidae.description: About 55 species of large, turkey-like forest birds of the Americas, from Texas to Argentina.

clade:caprimulgidae.description: About 95 species of camouflaged, night-flying birds with tiny bills and huge mouths for catching insects in flight.

clade:steatornithidae.description: A single species, a fruit-eating, cave-nesting relative of nightjars.

clade:podargidae.description: About 16 species of big-headed, night-hunting birds of southern Asia and Australia that pass the day disguised as broken branches.

clade:coraciidae.description: About 13 species of brightly coloured, crow-sized birds of Africa, Europe, Asia and Australia, named for their rolling, tumbling display flights.

clade:meropidae.description: About 30 species of slender, colourful birds of warm parts of the Old World that catch bees and other insects in flight.

clade:trogonidae.description: About 45 species of brightly coloured forest birds of the tropics of the Americas, Africa and Asia.

clade:musophagidae.description: About 23 species of African birds, many with green and red pigments found in no other birds.

clade:opisthocomidae.description: A single, strange South American species whose relationships to other birds are still debated.

clade:pteroclidae.description: About 16 species of pigeon-like desert birds of Africa and Asia.

clade:rhynochetidae.description: A single species found only on New Caledonia, related to the sunbittern of South America.

clade:indicatoridae.description: About 17 species of African and Asian birds that eat beeswax; most lay their eggs in other birds’ nests.

clade:tyrannidae.description: The largest bird family in the Americas, with over 400 species, from tiny tody-tyrants to kingbirds, most catching insects in flight.

clade:furnariidae.description: About 300 species of mostly brown South and Central American birds, famous for their elaborate nests.

clade:thamnophilidae.description: About 240 species of tropical American forest birds; some follow army ant swarms to catch the insects they flush.

clade:pipridae.description: About 50 species of small, colourful tropical American birds whose males perform elaborate courtship dances and sounds.

clade:cotingidae.description: About 65 species of tropical American fruit-eating birds, including the cocks-of-the-rock, umbrellabirds and bellbirds.

clade:parulidae.description: About 120 species of small, often brightly coloured insect-eating songbirds of the Americas.
