clade:icteridae.description: About 110 species including blackbirds, orioles, meadowlarks, grackles, cowbirds and oropendolas.

clade:passerellidae.description: About 140 species of sparrows, juncos and towhees of the Americas, not closely related to Old World sparrows.

clade:vireonidae.description: About 60 species of small, green or grey songbirds of the Americas.

clade:meliphagidae.description: About 190 species of nectar-feeding songbirds of Australia, New Guinea and the Pacific, with brush-tipped tongues.

clade:maluridae.description: About 30 species of small Australian and New Guinean songbirds with cocked tails.

clade:callaeidae.description: An ancient New Zealand family with fleshy wattles at the base of the bill: the kōkako, the saddlebacks and the extinct huia.

clade:acanthisittidae.description: Tiny New Zealand birds that form the oldest branch of the songbird order: the rifleman, the rock wren and several extinct species.

clade:mohoidae.description: The ʻōʻō and kioea of Hawaii, all extinct since 1987; DNA showed they were not true honeyeaters but a separate family.

clade:artamidae.description: About 24 species of Australasian birds, including butcherbirds, currawongs, woodswallows and the Australian magpie.

clade:rhipiduridae.description: About 50 species of small, insect-eating birds of Australasia and Asia that fan their tails.

clade:paridae.description: About 60 species of small, acrobatic songbirds of Europe, Asia, Africa and North America that nest in holes.

clade:aegithalidae.description: About 13 species of tiny, long-tailed birds that live in flocks and build domed nests.

clade:sittidae.description: About 29 species of short-tailed birds that climb down tree trunks head first.

clade:troglodytidae.description: About 90 species of small, loud-voiced, mostly brown songbirds, nearly all in the Americas.

clade:regulidae.description: Six species of tiny, crested songbirds of northern forests, the smallest songbirds in Europe and North America.

clade:phylloscopidae.description: About 80 species of small, greenish warblers of Eurasia and Africa, many of them long-distance migrants.

clade:acrocephalidae.description: About 60 species of brown warblers of reedbeds and thickets in Europe, Asia, Africa and the Pacific.

clade:sylviidae.description: About 70 species of warblers and babblers of Europe, Africa and Asia, including the blackcap and whitethroats.

clade:pycnonotidae.description: About 150 species of noisy, fruit-eating songbirds of Africa and tropical Asia.

clade:zosteropidae.description: About 140 species of small, green songbirds with white eye-rings, among the fastest-evolving bird families.

clade:alaudidae.description: About 100 species of ground-living songbirds of open country, famous for singing in flight.

clade:motacillidae.description: About 70 species of slender, ground-feeding songbirds found worldwide.

clade:laniidae.description: About 34 species of predatory songbirds that impale prey on thorns.

clade:bombycillidae.description: Three species of crested, fruit-eating songbirds with red, wax-like tips on their wing feathers.

clade:cinclidae.description: Five species of stocky songbirds that walk and swim underwater in fast streams.

clade:prunellidae.description: About 13 species of small, brown songbirds of Europe and Asia, many in high mountains.

clade:emberizidae.description: About 45 species of seed-eating songbirds of Europe, Asia and Africa.

clade:oriolidae.description: About 40 species of yellow and black songbirds of Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia, unrelated to American orioles.

clade:dicruridae.description: About 30 species of glossy black, fork-tailed songbirds of Africa, Asia and Australia, bold mobbers and skilled mimics.

clade:pittidae.description: About 40 species of brightly coloured, short-tailed ground birds of tropical Asian, African and Australian forests.

clade:ploceidae.description: About 115 species of seed-eating songbirds, mostly African, many of which weave elaborate nests.

clade:nectariniidae.description: About 145 species of small, glittering nectar-feeding songbirds of Africa, Asia and Australia, the Old World’s answer to hummingbirds.

clade:alligatoridae.description: Broad-snouted crocodylians whose lower teeth fit inside the upper jaw when the mouth is closed. Two alligators and six caimans live today, mostly in the Americas.

clade:crocodylidae.description: Crocodiles of the tropics worldwide, whose fourth lower tooth shows when the mouth is closed. Many tolerate salt water thanks to salt glands on the tongue.

clade:gavialidae.description: The gharial and the false gharial (tomistoma), slender-snouted fish-eaters of South and Southeast Asia; DNA shows the two are close relatives.

clade:testudinidae.description: Land turtles with domed shells and stumpy, elephant-like hind legs, about 50 species, including the giant tortoises of the Galápagos and Aldabra and the familiar Mediterranean tortoises kept as pets.

clade:cheloniidae.description: Six sea turtles with flipper limbs and hard, scaly shells: green, loggerhead, hawksbill, flatback, olive ridley and Kemp’s ridley. Females return to beaches to lay eggs, often near where they hatched.

clade:dermochelyidae.description: A family with one living species, the leatherback, whose shell is a mosaic of small bones under leathery skin.

clade:chelydridae.description: Big-headed American freshwater turtles with powerful jaws, small shells and long tails.

clade:emydidae.description: About 50 species of mostly American freshwater and land turtles, including sliders, painted turtles, box turtles and the European pond turtle.

clade:iguanidae.description: Large, mostly plant-eating lizards of the Americas, Caribbean, Galápagos and Fiji, including green, marine, land and rock iguanas.

clade:helodermatidae.description: The Gila monster and the beaded lizards of Mexico and Guatemala: heavy, venomous lizards covered in bead-like bony scales.

clade:chamaeleonidae.description: Over 200 species of slow-moving tree lizards with grasping feet, independently swivelling eyes and a tongue that shoots out faster than the eye can follow. Nearly half live in Madagascar.

clade:gekkonidae.description: About 1,500 species of mostly night-active lizards, many of which climb walls and glass with millions of microscopic hairs on their toes. Most cannot blink and lick their eyes clean instead.

clade:agamidae.description: About 500 species of Old World lizards including bearded dragons, frilled lizards, thorny devils, water dragons and gliding flying dragons.

clade:corytophanidae.description: Basilisks and their relatives, slender tree lizards of Central and South America with crests on the head.

clade:phrynosomatidae.description: North American lizards including horned lizards, spiny lizards, fence lizards and side-blotched lizards.

clade:scincidae.description: The largest lizard family, with about 1,700 species, mostly smooth, shiny-scaled ground lizards. Many have tiny legs or none, and many give birth to live young.

clade:serpentes.description: Legless squamates that swallow prey whole using loosely connected jaws. Snakes evolved from lizards over 100 million years ago; about 4,000 species live today, on every continent except Antarctica.

clade:pythonidae.description: About 40 egg-laying constrictors of Africa, Asia and Australia. Females coil around their eggs and some warm them by shivering.

clade:boidae.description: Constricting snakes, mostly of the Americas, that give birth to live young; they include the anacondas and the boa constrictor.

clade:elapidae.description: About 400 venomous snakes with short, fixed front fangs: cobras, mambas, kraits, coral snakes, taipans and the sea snakes. Most Australian snakes belong here.

clade:viperidae.description: About 400 venomous snakes with long, hinged fangs that fold back when the mouth closes, including rattlesnakes, adders and pit vipers. Pit vipers sense the body heat of prey with pits between the eye and nostril.

clade:colubridae.description: The largest snake family in the traditional sense, with about 2,000 species including rat snakes, kingsnakes, garter snakes and grass snakes; some scientists now split garter and water snakes into their own family, Natricidae. Most are harmless to people.

clade:phyllomedusidae.description: Slow-climbing tree frogs of Central and South America that walk rather than leap and lay their eggs on leaves over water.

clade:dendrobatidae.description: About 200 small, often brilliantly coloured frogs of Central and South American rainforests. Many carry poisons they get from eating ants and mites, and their bright colours warn predators. Parents carry tadpoles on their backs to pools.

clade:ranidae.description: Over 400 species of long-legged, smooth-skinned frogs found on every continent except Antarctica, including the common frog and the bullfrog.

clade:bufonidae.description: About 650 species of mostly warty, short-legged toads with poison glands behind the eyes, native to every continent except Australia and Antarctica.

clade:conrauidae.description: African river frogs, including the goliath frog, the largest frog alive.

clade:pipidae.description: Flat, fully aquatic frogs of Africa and South America with no tongue, including clawed frogs and the Surinam toad, whose young develop in pockets on the mother’s back.

clade:microhylidae.description: About 700 species of mostly small frogs found across the tropics, including some of the smallest vertebrates known.

clade:ambystomatidae.description: About 30 North American salamanders that live in burrows as adults, including the tiger salamander and the axolotl.

clade:salamandridae.description: About 130 species across Europe, Asia, North Africa and North America, most with poisonous skin, including fire salamanders and newts.

clade:proteidae.description: Salamanders that keep their feathery gills all their lives: the North American mudpuppies and the blind olm of European caves.

clade:rhincodontidae.description: A family with a single species, the whale shark, a giant filter-feeding relative of carpet sharks and nurse sharks.

clade:carcharhiniformes.description: The largest group of sharks, with nearly 300 species, including requiem sharks such as tiger and bull sharks, hammerheads and catsharks. They have a protective third eyelid.

clade:squaliformes.description: About 130 species of sharks without an anal fin, including spiny dogfish, sleeper sharks such as the Greenland shark, and tiny glowing lanternsharks.

clade:petromyzontiformes.description: Jawless, eel-shaped fish with a round, sucker-like mouth full of horny teeth. About 40 species live today; fossil lampreys over 300 million years old look much like them.

clade:salmonidae.description: Salmon, trout, char, grayling and whitefish of cold northern waters. Many hatch in rivers, grow at sea and return to spawn.

clade:cyprinidae.description: One of the largest fish families, with over 1,500 species including carp, goldfish, barbs and minnows. They have no teeth in their jaws but grind food with teeth in their throats.

clade:gadidae.description: Cod, haddock, pollock and their relatives, mostly of cold northern seas, many with a chin barbel.

clade:scombridae.description: Fast, streamlined ocean fish including tunas, mackerels and bonitos. Larger tunas keep their muscles warmer than the water.

clade:xiphiidae.description: A family with a single species, the swordfish. Marlins and sailfish, also billfish, form a separate family.

clade:serrasalmidae.description: Deep-bodied South American river fish: the meat-eating piranhas and their mostly fruit- and seed-eating relatives the pacus.

clade:pomacentridae.description: About 400 species of small, often colourful reef fish, including clownfish (anemonefish) and sergeant majors.

clade:tetraodontidae.description: About 200 species of fish that inflate with water when threatened. Most carry tetrodotoxin, a deadly nerve poison made by bacteria they live with.

clade:syngnathidae.description: Seahorses, pipefish and seadragons, armoured fish with tube snouts in which the male carries the eggs.

clade:molidae.description: Giant, disc-shaped ocean fish with no true tail, related to pufferfish.

clade:regalecidae.description: Long, ribbon-like deep-sea fish with a red crest along the back.

clade:anguillidae.description: About 20 species of eels that grow up in rivers and lakes and migrate to the ocean to spawn once and die.

clade:gymnotidae.description: South American knifefishes that sense and communicate with electric fields; they include the electric eels.

clade:melanocetidae.description: Deep-sea anglerfish whose females dangle a glowing lure in front of a huge, toothy mouth.

clade:esocidae.description: Long-bodied ambush predators of northern fresh waters: pikes and pickerels.

clade:siluridae.description: Old World catfishes of Europe and Asia, including the giant wels catfish.

clade:osphronemidae.description: Asian freshwater fish that can breathe air using a maze-like labyrinth organ above the gills, including bettas and gouramis.

clade:nautilida.description: Cephalopods with a coiled outer shell divided into gas-filled chambers. Only the nautiluses survive, the last of the shelled nautiloids that once filled the seas.

clade:coleoidea.description: Cephalopods whose shell is inside the body, reduced or lost. They include squid, cuttlefish, octopuses, the vampire squid and the extinct belemnites, and are among the most intelligent invertebrates.

clade:decapodiformes.description: Coleoids with eight arms and two longer feeding tentacles: squid, cuttlefish, bobtail squid and the ram’s horn squid.

clade:octopoda.description: Eight-armed coleoids with no tentacles and, in most, no trace of a shell. About 300 species live today, from the shallows to the deep sea.

clade:vampyromorpha.description: A single living species, the vampire squid of the deep sea, the last of an old group closer to octopuses than to squid.

clade:apidae.description: The largest bee family, including honey bees, bumblebees, stingless bees and carpenter bees.

clade:crocodylomorpha.description: Crocodiles and all their extinct relatives. The earliest, in the Late Triassic and Jurassic, were small, long-legged, fast-running land animals; later ones took to rivers and seas.

clade:dryolestida.description: Small, shrew-like Mesozoic mammals with sharp, many-cusped teeth for crushing insects. They were common in the Jurassic of North America and Europe and survived in South America into the age of mammals.

clade:eutriconodonta.description: Mesozoic mammals whose cheek teeth had three cusps in a row. Most were small, but some, like Repenomamus, were big enough to eat baby dinosaurs.

clade:ceratopsia.description: The horned dinosaurs and their early relatives: plant-eaters with a parrot-like beak and a unique bone, the rostral, at the tip of the upper jaw. The earliest, in the Late Jurassic of China, were small and ran on two legs; the giant horned and frilled ceratopsids came much later.

clade:brachiopoda.description: Sea animals with two shells, like clams, but built differently: the shells cover the top and bottom of the body rather than the sides, and they feed with a coiled fan of tentacles. They were among the commonest shelled animals of the Palaeozoic seas; a few hundred kinds survive today.

clade:annelida.description: Worms whose bodies are made of many similar ring-like segments: earthworms, leeches and the bristly sea worms (polychaetes). Soft-bodied, they are rare as fossils except in places like the Burgess Shale.

clade:plagiosauridae.description: Very flat, broad-headed temnospondyl amphibians of the Triassic, often armoured, that lay on the bottom of rivers, lakes and, it now seems, the sea.

clade:thalattosauria.description: Long-bodied, long-tailed sea reptiles of the Triassic that swam by waving their tails, many with odd, pointed or down-turned snouts. Not close to lizards or ichthyosaurs.

clade:omphalosauridae.description: Early Triassic sea reptiles with batteries of rounded, crushing teeth for grinding shelled prey. Usually thought to be early relatives of ichthyosaurs, though some researchers dispute this.

clade:endocerida.description: Ordovician nautiloids with long, straight shells, some the largest shelled animals of their time. Cone-shaped deposits filled the narrow end of the shell, probably weighting it so the animal swam level.

clade:orthocerida.description: Nautiloids with slender, straight shells divided into gas-filled chambers, common from the Ordovician to the Triassic. Their shells are among the most common fossils sold in rock shops, often labelled “Orthoceras”.

clade:sylviornithidae.description: Giant flightless ground birds of New Caledonia and Fiji, early relatives of megapodes and the other fowl-like birds, all now extinct.

clade:deinotheriidae.description: An early branch of proboscideans with no upper tusks and a pair of lower tusks curving down and back, like hooks. Some were among the largest land mammals ever.

clade:mammutidae.description: Browsing proboscideans with cone-cusped molars for leaves and twigs, a separate branch from mammoths and elephants despite the similar names. The American mastodon lasted until the end of the last Ice Age.

clade:gomphotheriidae.description: A large, varied group of proboscideans, many with tusks in both jaws, that spread from Africa across Eurasia and into the Americas. They were the only proboscideans to reach South America, where some survived until people arrived.

clade:amebelodontidae.description: Gomphothere relatives of the Miocene whose lower tusks were flattened into broad, shovel- or spoon-shaped blades. Some researchers include them in the gomphotheres.

clade:stegodontidae.description: Elephant-like proboscideans of Asia and Africa with low, ridged, roof-like molars, close relatives of true elephants. Most were as big as elephants or bigger, but some island forms became dwarfs.

clade:marginocephalia.description: The ornithischian dinosaurs with a bony shelf or frill at the back of the skull: the ceratopsians, from small parrot-beaked forms to Triceratops, and the dome-headed pachycephalosaurs. The two lines probably split in the Jurassic, in Asia.

species:tyrannosaurus-rex.ageText: About 68 to 66 million years ago (latest Cretaceous)
summary: Tyrannosaurus rex, the “tyrant lizard king”, was one of the largest meat-eating land animals ever. It was the top predator of western North America in the last two million years before the asteroid impact, living alongside Triceratops and Edmontosaurus.

Adults reached about 12 m long and around 8 tonnes. A 1.5 m skull, teeth up to about 30 cm long including the root, and one of the strongest bites measured for any land animal let it crush bone. Its arms were short but muscular, with two fingers.

Growth rings in its bones show it grew slowly as a juvenile, then put on hundreds of kilograms a year as a teenager, reaching full size at around 20 and living to about 30. Some of the small skeletons once used in these studies, such as “Jane”, are now known to be Nanotyrannus, so the picture of how young T. rex looked and grew is being redrawn. Its brain had large smell centres, and its forward-facing eyes gave it good depth perception.

Skin impressions show small scales on its body; its smaller, earlier relatives such as Yutyrannus had feathers. A 2023 study of tooth wear and living reptiles suggests it had lips covering its teeth, unlike most older reconstructions.

Its family tree is still debated. A 2022 proposal to split it into three species was widely rejected. In 2024 an older, closely related species, Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis, was named from about 72-million-year-old rocks in New Mexico. And in 2025 two studies showed that small Hell Creek tyrannosaurs long thought to be young T. rex belong to a separate genus, Nanotyrannus, which lived alongside it.

species:nanotyrannus-lancensis.placeText: Montana, Wyoming and the Dakotas, USA
summary: Nanotyrannus, the “dwarf tyrant”, was a slender, long-legged tyrannosaur about 5 to 6 m long and around 700 kg that lived alongside T. rex at the very end of the Cretaceous. It had a long, narrow skull, bladelike teeth and relatively long, strong arms: a fast pursuit predator, about a tenth the weight of an adult T. rex.

For decades many experts treated its fossils as teenage T. rex. Two studies in 2025 settled the question. Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli showed that the small tyrannosaur in the “Dueling Dinosaurs” fossil, found with a Triceratops in Montana, was about 20 years old and fully grown, with growth rings, fused vertebrae and anatomy that T. rex never has at any age. Christopher Griffin and colleagues independently found, from growth layers in its throat (hyoid) bone, that the original 1942 skull was also from a near-adult animal.

So Hell Creek had at least two kinds of tyrannosaur, and some fossils once used to describe how T. rex grew up actually belong to Nanotyrannus. Exactly where Nanotyrannus sits in the tyrannosaur family tree is still being worked out.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Robert Bakker, Michael Williams and Philip Currie, 1988 (first as Gorgosaurus lancensis by Charles Gilmore, 1946)

facts.label: Holotype
facts.value: A skull found in Hell Creek rocks of Montana in 1942 (Cleveland Museum of Natural History)

facts.label: Shown valid by
facts.value: Zanno and Napoli (Nature, 2025); Griffin and colleagues (Science, 2025)

summary: A second, larger species of Nanotyrannus, named in 2025 from “Jane”, a skeleton more than half complete found by a Burpee Museum expedition in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana in 2001. For two decades Jane was the best-known “teenage T. rex”, used in many studies of how T. rex grew up.

Zanno and Napoli’s 2025 study found that Jane differs from both T. rex and Nanotyrannus lancensis, and named it Nanotyrannus lethaeus, after Lethe, the river of forgetfulness in Greek myth. Only one skeleton is known, so its full adult size is uncertain; estimates suggest about 1,200 kg.

facts.label: Holotype
facts.value: “Jane” (BMRP 2002.4.1), Burpee Museum of Natural History, Rockford, Illinois

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Perhaps about 1,200 kg as an adult (estimate from one skeleton)

summary: A Tyrannosaurus species named in 2024 from a partial skull found in New Mexico, several million years older than T. rex, with a lower jaw of a different shape. If it is a separate species, Tyrannosaurus first evolved in the south of Laramidia. Not all researchers accept it as distinct: some think the skull is a T. rex, or the dating has been questioned.

Tarbosaurus, the “alarming lizard”, was the giant tyrannosaurid of Late Cretaceous Asia and the top predator of the Nemegt river plains in what is now the Gobi Desert. It is one of the closest relatives of Tyrannosaurus; some researchers even place it in the same genus, as Tyrannosaurus bataar.

It grew to about 10 m long and 4 to 5 tonnes, a little smaller and more lightly built than T. rex. Its skull was narrower, so its eyes faced less forwards, and its lower jaw had a bony lock that stiffened it for biting. Its arms were the smallest, for its size, of any tyrannosaurid.

It is known from dozens of skeletons, from hatchling-sized juveniles to adults, making it one of the best-understood tyrannosaurs. Young ones had slimmer skulls and probably hunted smaller prey than adults. Tooth marks on bones show it fed on the duck-billed Saurolophus and on the giant, long-armed Deinocheirus.
Its fossils are prized by collectors. In 2012 a smuggled skeleton was seized in the United States before it could be sold, and returned to Mongolia in 2013.

A heavily built tyrannosaur about 9 m long with a deep skull, large teeth and small horns over its eyes, one of the earlier relatives on the line to Tyrannosaurus. It was rarer and bulkier than Gorgosaurus, which shared its world, and may have hunted bigger prey such as horned dinosaurs. Its name means “frightful lizard”.

A tyrannosaur about 8 m long with a short, broad skull and forward-facing eyes, like T. rex, but more than 10 million years older. It showed that the T. rex branch first evolved in the south of Laramidia. Its name means “gore king from the south-west”.

A tyrannosaur about 8 m long with a short, deep skull. Several individuals found together at one site in 2014 add to the evidence that tyrannosaurs sometimes lived in groups. Its name means “monstrous murderer”.

A lightly built, long-snouted tyrannosaur about 5–6 m long with a row of small bony bumps along the top of its nose. It lived alongside the much bigger Tarbosaurus, probably hunting smaller, faster prey, and belongs to the same slender-snouted group as Qianzhousaurus.

A long-snouted tyrannosaur about 9 m long nicknamed “Pinocchio rex”, found by construction workers in Ganzhou. Its narrow snout and small teeth show that not all late tyrannosaurs were bone-crushers; it belongs to a group of slender-snouted tyrannosaurs that included Alioramus.

A tyrannosaur about 9 m long, lighter and faster than T. rex. In 1910 Barnum Brown found a bonebed at Dry Island with at least 26 individuals of all ages, from youngsters to old adults, suggesting it lived and maybe hunted in groups. Its name means “flesh-eating lizard from Alberta”.

species:gorgosaurus-libratus.placeText: Alberta, Canada and Montana, USA (Dinosaur Park Formation)
summary: The most common big predator of the Dinosaur Park Formation, about 8–9 m long, a slender, long-legged relative of Albertosaurus. More than 20 skeletons are known, from juveniles to adults, some with healed injuries and infections. A young one was found in 2023 with two baby Citipes in its stomach.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Hadrosaurs, horned dinosaurs; young ones ate small dinosaurs

summary: A tyrannosaur about 6–7 m long from Appalachia, the eastern island of Late Cretaceous North America, cut off from the giants of the west by the Western Interior Seaway. Its carcass washed out to sea and was buried in chalk. It had longer arms than western tyrannosaurs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Thomas Carr, Thomas Williamson and David Schwimmer, 2005

summary: An eastern tyrannosaur about 7.5 m long with long arms and big, eagle-like hand claws, which gave it its name, “tearing lizard with eagle’s claws”. Found in New Jersey in 1866, it was one of the first theropods known from good remains. Cope called it Laelaps, but the name was taken, and Marsh renamed it.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Edward Drinker Cope, 1866 (as Laelaps); genus by Othniel Marsh, 1877

summary: A horse-sized tyrannosaur about 3–4 m long. Its braincase shows it already had the large brain and the ears tuned to low-pitched sounds of its giant later relatives, suggesting these were in place before tyrannosaurs grew big. Named after Timur (Tamerlane), the 14th-century Central Asian conqueror.

A small, swift tyrannosaur about 3 m long and 78 kg, with long, slender legs built for running. It is the oldest Cretaceous tyrannosaur known from North America, showing that the family arrived from Asia and stayed small for millions of years before becoming giants. Its name means “harbinger of doom”.

A big early tyrannosaur about 9 m long and weighing over a tonne, covered in long, simple, filament-like feathers up to 20 cm long: the largest known feathered animal. Three skeletons were found together. Its feathers may have kept it warm in Liaoning’s cool climate. Its name means “beautiful feathered tyrant”.
A small, early tyrannosaur about 1.6 m long, the first tyrannosaur found with feathers, in 2004: simple, hair-like filaments on its jaw and tail. Its name means “emperor dragon”.

An early tyrannosaur about 4–5 m long from the Isle of Wight, with long arms and grasping three-fingered hands, unlike its giant later relatives. It was found in 1995 by Gavin Leng, a local collector, after whom it is named.

An early tyrannosaur about 3 m long with a tall, thin, perforated crest running along its snout, probably for display. It had three long-clawed fingers, unlike the two short ones of later tyrannosaurs.
Two skeletons, an adult and a youngster, were found in a sauropod footprint pit, one on top of the other. Its name means “crowned dragon of the five colours”, after the colourful rocks of Wucaiwan.

One of the oldest known tyrannosaurs, about 3 m long, known from a single skull found in 1910 while digging a reservoir at Minchinhampton. The base of a crest on its snout led to its name, “before Ceratosaurus”, as it was first thought to be related to that horned dinosaur.
A 2010 study showed it was an early tyrannosauroid, a close relative of Guanlong, which had a similar crest. It shows the tyrannosaur family was already around 100 million years before T. rex.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Arthur Smith Woodward, 1910 (as Megalosaurus bradleyi); genus by Friedrich von Huene, 1926

summary: Triceratops, the “three-horned face”, was the most common large dinosaur of Hell Creek: surveys find it makes up around 40 percent of big dinosaur fossils. It was a heavy, four-legged plant-eater about 8 to 9 m long with two long brow horns, a short nose horn and a solid bony frill.

Its beak and shearing tooth batteries sliced tough plants. Healed wounds on frills and horns show it was attacked by Tyrannosaurus, and fought its own kind. T. horridus is the earlier of the two species, found in the lower part of Hell Creek; it was replaced by T. prorsus higher up, possibly by evolving into it.
The later of the two Triceratops species, found in the upper part of Hell Creek right up to the asteroid impact. It differs from T. horridus mainly in the shape of its snout and nose horn.

Because the two species sit at different levels in the rock, with in-between forms in the middle, some researchers think T. horridus gradually evolved into T. prorsus: a rare view of evolution happening within one lineage.

A horned dinosaur close to Triceratops in size, which lived alongside it, but with a longer, thinner frill pierced by two large openings and edged with small bony points. Its skull, up to about 2.7 m long including the frill, is one of the largest of any land animal.
It is much rarer than Triceratops in Hell Creek and Lance rocks, and is also known from Saskatchewan to New Mexico.

Edmontosaurus was a large duck-billed dinosaur, about 12 m long, that walked on two or four legs and grazed on low plants with a broad, toothless beak backed by hundreds of tightly packed grinding teeth.

Several “mummies” preserve its skin, showing pebbly scales and a fleshy crest on top of its head. One specimen from Hell Creek has a healed bite in its tail made by Tyrannosaurus, proof that T. rex attacked live prey and that this one escaped.

A stocky, two-legged plant-eater about 3 to 4 m long, and one of the most common small-to-medium dinosaurs in Hell Creek. It had a narrow beak, leaf-shaped cheek teeth and probably lived in thick undergrowth near rivers.
A skeleton from South Dakota nicknamed “Willo” was once claimed to contain a fossilised heart; later studies concluded the structure was an ironstone concretion.
The largest dome-headed dinosaur, about 4.5 m long, with a skull roof up to 25 cm thick fringed by bony knobs and spikes.
Whether it head-butted is debated, but healed injuries on many domes suggest they did fight with their heads.

It shared Hell Creek with two other spiky-headed pachycephalosaurs: Stygimoloch, with a narrow dome ringed by long horns, and the flat-headed Dracorex. Dracorex may be a juvenile, or the other sex, of Pachycephalosaurus, of Stygimoloch, or of both.

related.note: A spiky, narrow-domed pachycephalosaur from the same rocks
Flat-headed and spiky: possibly a juvenile or the other sex of Pachycephalosaurus, Stygimoloch or both

summary: A small dome-headed dinosaur known from skull domes. It shared Hell Creek with the much larger Pachycephalosaurus.
The largest armoured dinosaur, about 6 to 8 m long, with a broad, low body covered in bony plates and a heavy tail club made of fused bones.
It was first found in Hell Creek by Barnum Brown in 1906. Despite its fame it is known only from a few partial skeletons, and seems to have been rare.
A nodosaurid, an armoured dinosaur without a tail club but with spikes on its shoulders, about 5 to 6 m long. It is one of the last nodosaurids known anywhere.

A feathered, sickle-clawed raptor about 3 m long, known from jaws and teeth. Its name means “underworld plunderer”, after the river Acheron of Greek myth and Hell Creek. Its closest relatives appear to be Asian raptors such as Velociraptor.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: David Evans, Derek Larson and Philip Currie, 2013

summary: A large raptor, around 5 m long, described in 2015 with bumps on its forearm thought to anchor big feathers. Soon after, part of the original skeleton turned out to be turtle shell, and some researchers suspect other bones belong to other animals, so its size and features are still being checked.
A toothless, beaked oviraptorosaur about 3.5 m long and 200 to 300 kg, with a tall crest, long legs and clawed arms: nicknamed “the chicken from hell”. It probably ate plants, small animals and eggs.
A bird known from its foot bones, belonging to the enantiornithines, the most common birds of the Cretaceous. They had teeth and clawed wings, and all of them died out at the asteroid impact.

An otter-sized relative of marsupials, about 5 kg, with powerful jaws and blunt teeth that could crack snails and bones: for its size, one of the strongest bites of any mammal. It may have hunted in and around water.
One of the largest Cretaceous multituberculates, roughly the size of a big squirrel. Its rows of cusped teeth ground up seeds, fruit and other plant food, rather like a rodent’s.
A small, opossum-like relative of marsupials, known mostly from teeth. Mammals like it scurried through the undergrowth eating insects and fruit.
A small, shrew- to weasel-sized relative of placental mammals with sharp teeth for eating insects and small animals.
A broad-snouted relative of alligators, a few metres long, with blunt back teeth suited to crushing turtles and shellfish.
A crocodylian about 3 to 4 m long with a longer, slimmer snout than Brachychampsa, suited to catching fish. Its family survived the asteroid impact.

species:champsosaurus.ageText: About 68 to 66 million years ago, surviving into the Paleocene
summary: A water-living reptile about 1.5 m long that looked like a small gharial, with a long, thin snout full of small teeth for catching fish. Several species are known; Hell Creek fossils are usually identified only to the genus.
Champsosaurus survived the asteroid impact and lived on for millions of years afterwards.
A large land turtle with a broad, high shell up to about 1 m long, covered in a textured pattern. It belonged to an Asian-origin family, the nanhsiungchelyids, and ate plants.
A small freshwater turtle of the baenid family, which lived only in North America. It had a broad crushing palate, probably for eating snails and clams. Baenids survived the asteroid impact.
A large monitor-like lizard, perhaps 2 m long, with serrated teeth like a Komodo dragon’s. It may have eaten eggs, baby dinosaurs and small animals.
A small lizard with comb-like teeth, named in 2012 after Barack Obama. It belonged to a group of lizards that was hit very hard by the asteroid, with most species dying out.

One of the most primitive snakes known. It had a snake’s long body but a lizard-like head, suggesting snakes evolved their body shape before their flexible jaws. It probably burrowed and ate small prey.
A large aquatic salamander, one of the most common amphibians in Hell Creek’s rivers and ponds. Its vertebrae are found by the hundred in screen-washed sediment.
A freshwater ray related to guitarfish, perhaps 1 to 2 m long, known mostly from its flat, ridged crushing teeth. It lived on river bottoms, crunching shellfish.
A paddlefish, a relative of the living American paddlefish, with a long flat snout. Paddlefish strain tiny food from the water as they swim.
A sturgeon related to today’s shovelnose sturgeons of the Mississippi basin, feeling along river beds for food with its sensitive snout.
A gar, a long, needle-jawed fish covered in thick, shiny, diamond-shaped scales; its scales are among the most common Hell Creek fossils. Gars like it still live in North American rivers today.

Infernodrakon, the “dragon from hell”, is the first pterosaur named from Hell Creek. It was an azhdarchid with a wingspan of about 4 m, a medium-sized member of the family of giant, long-necked pterosaurs that included Quetzalcoatlus.

It is known from a single neck vertebra found in Montana in 2002, first thought to belong to Quetzalcoatlus. A 2025 study found its shape was different enough to make it a new species, more closely related to Arambourgiania from the Middle East than to Quetzalcoatlus. Like its relatives it probably walked on all fours, picking off small animals on the ground.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Henry Thomas, David Hone, Timothy Gomes and Joseph Peterson, 2025

summary: One of the two oldest known vertebrates, about 3 cm long. It had a distinct head, five or six gill pouches, a fin along its back, and V-shaped blocks of muscle along its body like a fish today, but no jaws, bone or scales.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Shu Degan, Zhang Xingliang and Han Jian, 1999

summary: A tiny early vertebrate, 2–3 cm long, known from hundreds of fossils. Some show eyes, a nose and ear capsules, and a series of supports along its fin: the beginnings of a vertebrate head and skeleton, in an animal with no jaws or bone.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Luo Huilin, Hu Shixue and Shu Degan, 1999

summary: A small jawless fish about 6 cm long with large eyes and a pair of nostrils. A 2014 study of new specimens showed it had seven pairs of gill arches, the first of which is the kind that later evolved into jaws.

facts.label: Redescribed
facts.value: Simon Conway Morris and Jean-Bernard Caron, 2014

summary: A jawless fish about 15 cm long, its head and chest covered by a shield of star-patterned bony plates, with eyes at the sides of its head. It probably fed by sucking up food particles from the sea floor.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Food particles from the sea floor

summary: A giant among conodonts, perhaps 40 cm long. Fossils from the Soom Shale preserve its eyes, muscles and its full set of nineteen teeth in place, helping to show how conodonts used their teeth to grasp and slice food.

The oldest known complete bony fish, about 33 cm long. It mixes features of the two great branches of bony fish, ray-finned and lobe-finned, and is placed at the base of the lobe-finned fish, the branch that would lead to land animals. Its name means “ghost fish”.

An armoured placoderm with a surprise: the same set of jaw bones (maxilla, premaxilla and dentary) that bony fish, and humans, have. It suggests that our jaw bones evolved from the armour of placoderms. Its name means “primordial complete jaw”.

A small ptyctodont placoderm, about 25 cm long, found with an embryo inside it still connected by a mineralised umbilical cord: the oldest known example of live birth, and evidence of internal fertilisation. Its name means “Attenborough’s mother fish”, after David Attenborough, who had filmed at Gogo.

A small arthrodire placoderm about 25 cm long, a fast predator of the reef. It is the state fossil emblem of Western Australia. Gogo arthrodires are so well preserved that their hearts have been found, the oldest known.

A lobe-finned fish about 30–40 cm long on the line to land animals. A perfect 3D skull showed a large opening on top (a spiracle) used for breathing air, and its front fin bones are arranged like those of a tetrapod’s arm.

The famous “fishapod”: a fish with scales, fins and gills, but also a flat, crocodile-like head, a neck, lungs, strong ribs and front fins with shoulder, elbow and wrist bones. It probably lived in shallow streams, propping itself up on its fins and snapping at prey. It was up to about 2.7 m long.
Its name means “large freshwater fish” in Inuktitut, chosen by the elders of Nunavut.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Ted Daeschler, Neil Shubin and Farish Jenkins, 2006

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Fish and other prey in the shallows

summary: One of the earliest animals with legs, about 60 cm long, with eight fingers on each hand. It still had internal gills and a fish-like tail fin, and its weak wrists could not have held it up on land. It showed that legs evolved in the water, before animals walked on land.

An early tetrapod about 1–1.5 m long with a broad chest of overlapping ribs and powerful front legs, and seven toes on its back feet. It may have heaved itself over land rather like a seal, though it spent much of its time in water.

species:dunkleosteus-terrelli.placeText: Ohio, USA, and elsewhere in North America
summary: A giant arthrodire placoderm and one of the first big vertebrate predators. Instead of teeth it had sharp-edged bony plates that sharpened each other as its jaws closed, and it could open its mouth extremely fast to suck in prey.
Only its armoured head and shoulders are known, so its length is uncertain: older estimates of 6–10 m have been revised to about 3.5–4 m in a 2023 study.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: About 3.5–4 m (older estimates up to 10 m)

summary: A sleek early shark about 1–1.8 m long with large triangular fins and a crescent tail, built for speed. Specimens from the Cleveland Shale are so well preserved that they show muscle fibres and kidneys, and some have whole small fish in their stomachs, swallowed tail first.

A small, long-bodied animal about 20 cm long, nicknamed “Lizzie the lizard” when Stan Wood found it in 1988. It is not a lizard, but it is close to the ancestry of amniotes, the egg-laying group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals.
A small temnospondyl amphibian, about 50 cm long, one of the earliest vertebrates adapted to life on land. It had an eardrum for hearing sounds in air, an early example of this.

The oldest known reptile, about 20–25 cm long, looking much like a modern lizard. It probably hunted insects and millipedes on the forest floor. Reptiles like it were among the first animals to lay shelled eggs on land, freeing them from water.
A salamander-like temnospondyl about 1 m long, the most common animal found in the Joggins tree stumps. It probably lived on the forest floor and in pools, hunting small animals.
A small temnospondyl only about 10 cm long, with big eyes and a broad head. It belongs to a group, the amphibamiforms, thought by many to include the ancestors of living frogs and salamanders.

A shark with an extremely long, spoon-like snout covered in sensory organs, used to find prey hidden in mud. Young ones are found in the delta’s brackish water and adults in rivers, suggesting the oldest known shark nursery: adults swam down to lay egg cases near the coast.

Often mistaken for a dinosaur, Dimetrodon is a synapsid, closer to mammals than to reptiles, and lived 40 million years before the first dinosaurs. It was the top predator of its world, up to about 3 m long, with a tall sail of skin stretched over spines along its back.
Its name means “two measures of teeth”: it had sharp teeth of different sizes, an early step towards the different tooth types of mammals.

One of the first large plant-eating land animals, about 3 m long, with a small head and a sail whose spines carried short crossbars like the yards of a ship’s mast. Its sail evolved separately from Dimetrodon’s.

species:eryops-megacephalus.placeText: Texas, New Mexico and elsewhere, USA
summary: A heavily built temnospondyl about 2 m long with a broad, flat head full of sharp teeth, rather like an alligator. It hunted fish and other animals in and around rivers and ponds.

A salamander-like lepospondyl about 1 m long with a boomerang-shaped head, its “horns” growing wider as it aged. The head may have worked like a hydrofoil when swimming, or made it too wide for predators to swallow.

species:nothosaurus-mirabilis.ageText: About 243 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic)
species:nothosaurus-mirabilis.placeText: Germany (Muschelkalk); relatives across Europe, the Middle East and China
summary: A long-necked marine reptile about 3 to 4 m long, with a flat skull and a mouth full of long, interlocking, fang-like teeth for snagging fish. It had webbed, paddle-like limbs and probably lived much like a seal, hunting at sea and hauling out on shores to rest. It was named in 1834 and its name means “false lizard”.

Nothosaurs were relatives of the later plesiosaurs, from the early wave of reptiles that returned to the sea after the end-Permian mass extinction. Nearly a dozen Nothosaurus species are known from Europe to China; the biggest, Nothosaurus giganteus, reached perhaps 7 m.

species:placodus-gigas.ageText: About 247 to 240 million years ago (Middle Triassic)
summary: A stout, barrel-bodied marine reptile about 2 m long that fed on shellfish. Its forward-pointing front teeth plucked clams and brachiopods off the sea floor, and broad, flat teeth on its jaws and palate crushed them like a nutcracker. A row of bony knobs ran down its back. It was a placodont, a relative of nothosaurs and plesiosaurs, and lived in the shallow Muschelkalk sea.

species:spicomellus-afer.ageText: About 168 to 165 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: The oldest known ankylosaur, and one of the strangest. It was named in 2021 from a single rib with spikes fused directly to the bone, something never seen in any other animal. A 2025 study of new fossils showed a bony collar around its neck with long spikes, the best-preserved one 87 cm long, plus spiked ribs and a spiky hip shield.

Its fused tail vertebrae form a “handle” like that of club-tailed ankylosaurs, so it probably had a tail weapon over 30 million years before any other known ankylosaur, though the tail tip has not been found. The neck spikes are so long that they may have been more for display than defence. Its name means “spiny collar” and afer refers to Africa.

One of the oldest definite stegosaurs, known from a back vertebra and other bones, named in 2019. Surprisingly it was more closely related to European stegosaurs such as Dacentrurus than to the African Kentrosaurus. Its name combines the Berber words for mountain and lizard.

species:lystrosaurus-murrayi.ageText: About 252 to 250 million years ago (Early Triassic)
species:lystrosaurus-murrayi.placeText: South Africa; relatives across Pangaea, from India to Antarctica
summary: A stocky, pig-sized plant-eater with a beak and two tusks, the great survivor of the end-Permian extinction. In the first million years of the Triassic, Lystrosaurus made up most of the land animals in the Karoo. Its relatives are found in India, China, Russia and Antarctica, early evidence that the continents were once joined.
Survivors grew fast and bred young, and a burrowing lifestyle may have helped them through the heat.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Tough plants, cropped with its beak

species:proterosuchus-fergusi.ageText: About 252 to 250 million years ago (Early Triassic)
summary: A crocodile-like predator up to about 3.5 m long with a hooked upper jaw, one of the first animals on the line to archosaurs. It appeared just after the end-Permian extinction, when the archosaur family that would later include dinosaurs and crocodiles began to spread.

species:thrinaxodon-liorhinus.ageText: About 251 to 249 million years ago (Early Triassic)
summary: A cat-sized cynodont, a close relative of the ancestors of mammals. It had a bony shelf separating its nose from its mouth (so it could breathe while chewing) and may have had whiskers. Skeletons are often found curled up in burrows, sometimes sharing them with injured amphibians.

A reptile whose stiff neck was as long as its body and tail together, built from just 13 very long vertebrae. This is the small species, under about 2 m long, which probably hunted shrimp-like prey in shallow water.

Its fossils were long taken for juveniles of the large Tanystropheus. Growth rings in its bones, studied in 2020, show they are adults of a separate, smaller species; the large one is now T. hydroides.

related.note: The large species, up to about 6 m, a fish-eater living alongside it.

summary: A small early ichthyosaur about 1 m long, with a long snout and a tail fin only half-developed compared with later ichthyosaurs. Hundreds of specimens are known from Monte San Giorgio, some with embryos.

A nothosaur up to about 4 m long, an early relative of the plesiosaurs. It had a long neck, a long tail and limbs turning into paddles, and probably swam with side-to-side sweeps of its body, catching fish in its needle-like teeth.

A land predator about 2.5 m long on the crocodile side of the archosaur family, with legs held under its body and bony plates along its back. Its skeleton washed out into the Monte San Giorgio lagoon from nearby land.

One of the earliest known dinosaurs, about 1 m long and lightly built, running on its hind legs. It was first thought to be an early theropod, but its leaf-shaped teeth suggest it was an early sauropodomorph, on the line to the giant long-necked dinosaurs. It probably ate both plants and small animals.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Paul Sereno, Catherine Forster, Raymond Rogers and Alfredo Monetta, 1993

summary: One of the first big predatory dinosaurs, up to about 6 m long, with a long skull, curved, serrated teeth and grasping hands. Named after Victorino Herrera, the local goat farmer who found it in 1959.
A slender, fox-sized early theropod about 1.2 m long, with blade-like teeth: one of the first members of the meat-eating dinosaur line that would lead to T. rex and to birds.
A huge, tuskless dicynodont about 3.5 m long, one of the biggest plant-eaters of its time, cropping tough plants with its broad beak.

species:coelophysis-bauri.ageText: About 215 to 208 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: A slender early theropod about 3 m long, lightly built with hollow bones, a long neck and a narrow head full of small, serrated teeth. Hundreds of skeletons, young and old, were found together at Ghost Ranch in 1947.
In 1998 a Coelophysis skull went into space aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavour, making it the second dinosaur in space.

species:postosuchus-kirkpatricki.ageText: About 225 to 205 million years ago (Late Triassic)
species:postosuchus-kirkpatricki.placeText: Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, USA
summary: The top predator of its world, about 4–5 m long, with a deep skull and dagger-like teeth. Though it looked like a predatory dinosaur, it was on the crocodile side of the family tree. It may have walked partly on its hind legs.

species:placerias-hesternus.ageText: About 221 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: One of the last and largest dicynodonts, about 3.5 m long and weighing up to a tonne, with a pair of short tusks. Remains of about 40 animals were found together in the Placerias Quarry in Arizona.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Plants, dug up and cropped with its tusks and beak

species:ichthyosaurus-communis.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A dolphin-shaped sea reptile about 2 m long with huge eyes, a long, toothy snout, and a crescent-shaped tail fin. It gave birth to live young at sea. The first skeleton to be recognised as an ichthyosaur was found by Joseph and Mary Anning around 1811–1812.

species:plesiosaurus-dolichodeirus.ageText: About 199 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A sea reptile about 3.5 m long with a small head, a long neck, a broad body and four big flippers, which it “flew” through the water with. Mary Anning found the first complete skeleton in 1823; it looked so odd that Georges Cuvier at first suspected it was a fake.

species:dimorphodon-macronyx.ageText: About 195 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A pterosaur with a wingspan of about 1.4 m and a large, deep, lightly built head with two kinds of teeth. It may have been better at climbing and short flights than long-distance soaring. Mary Anning found the first skeleton in 1828.

species:sarcosaurus-woodi.ageText: About 200 to 195 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
species:sarcosaurus-woodi.placeText: Leicestershire and Warwickshire, England; a similar bone from Northern Ireland
summary: An early meat-eating dinosaur, perhaps 3.5 to 5 m long, known from partial skeletons from central England. A 2020 study showed the three English specimens are one species and placed it among the closest relatives of the averostrans, the group that later produced Allosaurus, tyrannosaurs and birds.

A slender shin bone from Islandmagee, Northern Ireland, described the same year, is very like that of Sarcosaurus and is one of Ireland’s only two dinosaur bones; it may be Sarcosaurus or a close relative.

related.note: The armoured plant-eater whose thigh bone was found with it in Northern Ireland.

summary: An early armoured dinosaur about 4 m long, covered in rows of bony studs, close to the ancestry of stegosaurs and ankylosaurs. It was the first fairly complete dinosaur skeleton ever found. Its carcass probably washed out to sea from nearby land.
A thigh bone from Islandmagee in County Antrim, described in 2020, is one of the only two dinosaur bones known from Ireland. Its relative Scutellosaurus lived in Arizona at about the same time.

species:stenopterygius-quadriscissus.ageText: About 183 to 180 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A fast, tuna-like ichthyosaur about 3–4 m long. Specimens from Holzmaden show its body outline, with a fleshy dorsal fin and a crescent tail, and some are mothers that died giving birth, babies emerging tail first, as in dolphins. Skin pigments show it was dark on top and pale underneath.
A long-snouted sea crocodile about 4–5 m long, rather like a modern gharial, that hunted fish in coastal waters. It was long known as Steneosaurus bollensis.
The first dinosaur ever named. William Buckland described its jaw and bones from Stonesfield in 1824, years before the word “dinosaur” existed. It was a big, two-legged predator about 6 m long.
For a century, almost any large theropod bone was called Megalosaurus, and it is the “Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so” that Dickens imagined waddling up Holborn Hill in Bleak House.

A small ceratosaur about 2 m long whose young had teeth but whose adults lost them all and grew a beak, a change not known in any other animal with a backbone. Adults seem to have become plant-eaters. Its name means “mud lizard that could not escape”: skeletons were found stacked in a sauropod footprint pit.

A giant sauropod with one of the longest necks of any animal, estimated at about 15 m, probably used to reach a wide area of plants without moving its huge body. It was named for the joint China–Canada Dinosaur Project that found it.
A big allosaur-like predator about 7.5 m long. Its skull carries tooth marks from another Sinraptor, suggesting fights between them.

species:allosaurus-fragilis.ageText: About 155 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: The most common big predator of the Morrison, about 8.5 m long, with short horns over its eyes, strong arms with three large claws, and a skull that worked like a hatchet, slashing at prey with its upper teeth.
Over 40 individuals were found in the Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry in Utah. “Big Al”, a young adult found in Wyoming, had broken ribs, infected toes and other injuries, showing a hard life.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Meat, including stegosaurs and young sauropods

species:allosaurus-fragilis.akaNote: Antrodemus valens, named from part of a tail bone in 1870, was long used as the name for Allosaurus. It is now treated as a doubtful name, probably the same animal.

species:ceratosaurus-nasicornis.ageText: About 153 to 148 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A predator about 6 m long with a blade-like horn on its nose, two hornlets over its eyes, very long upper teeth and a row of bony studs down its back. It may have hunted in and near water, taking fish and crocodiles as well as dinosaurs.

species:stegosaurus-stenops.ageText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A plant-eater about 7–9 m long with two alternating rows of tall bony plates along its back and four tail spikes, nicknamed the “thagomizer”. Its plates were probably for display. Allosaurus bones have been found with wounds matching its tail spikes.
Its brain was small for its size, weighing perhaps 80 g. The most complete specimen, “Sophie”, is in the Natural History Museum, London.

species:diplodocus-carnegii.ageText: About 154 to 152 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A long, slender sauropod about 25 m long, most of it neck and whip-like tail. It stripped leaves from branches with its peg-like front teeth.
Named after the steel magnate Andrew Carnegie, who funded the dig. He gave casts of the skeleton, “Dippy”, to museums around the world, making Diplodocus one of the best-known dinosaurs.

species:apatosaurus-ajax.ageText: About 152 to 151 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A massive diplodocid about 22 m long, with a thick, heavily built neck that may have been used in fights between rivals. Marsh named it in 1877, and two years later named Brontosaurus, which was long thought to be the same animal.
species:apatosaurus-ajax.akaNote: For about a century Brontosaurus was treated as a synonym of Apatosaurus. A 2015 study revived Brontosaurus as its own genus, which PaleoDex follows.

species:brontosaurus-excelsus.ageText: About 156 to 146 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: The “thunder lizard”, a huge diplodocid about 22 m long. In 1903 it was declared the same as Apatosaurus and the name officially dropped, though the public never gave it up. A 2015 study of diplodocid skeletons found enough differences to bring Brontosaurus back as its own genus.

facts.label: Revived
facts.value: Emanuel Tschopp, Octávio Mateus and Roger Benson, 2015

species:brachiosaurus-altithorax.ageText: About 154 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A giraffe-shaped sauropod with front legs longer than its hind legs, holding its neck high to browse the treetops up to about 9 m above the ground. It was about 22 m long. The better-known mounted skeleton in Berlin is a separate African genus, Giraffatitan.

species:camarasaurus-supremus.ageText: About 155 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: The most common sauropod of the Morrison, about 18–23 m long, with a short, boxy skull, large nostrils and spoon-shaped teeth for tough plants. Its vertebrae were full of air-filled chambers, which gave it its name, “chambered lizard”.

The famous “first bird”: a raven-sized animal with feathered wings and tail, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like a small dinosaur. Found in 1861, it was soon held up as a link between reptiles and birds, supporting Darwin’s theory of evolution.
Many feathered dinosaurs are now known, and Archaeopteryx sits near the base of the bird line. It could probably fly in short bursts. One of its feathers preserves pigment cells showing it was black.

facts.label: Specimens
facts.value: About a dozen skeletons and a single feather

summary: A small, long-legged predatory dinosaur about 1 m long, most of it tail. For more than a century it was the smallest dinosaur known. The German specimen has a lizard in its stomach, showing what it hunted.

A long-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan up to about 1.8 m, a diamond-shaped vane at the end of its tail and forward-pointing teeth for spearing fish. One specimen was caught in the jaws of the big fish Aspidorhynchus as it swallowed a fish of its own.

The first pterosaur ever described, from a Solnhofen skeleton studied in 1784. At first it was thought to be a sea creature using its wings as flippers. A short-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about 1 m, it gave its name to the popular word “pterodactyl”.
One of the earliest tetrapods from North America, known from a shoulder girdle with strong muscle attachments, suggesting it could push itself up on its front legs. It was about 1 m long.

A giant predatory lobe-finned fish up to about 2.5–3 m long, a tristichopterid with big fangs, which hunted in the shallow streams of the Catskill delta. It is a distant relative of the tetrapods it may have eaten.
A small, armoured placoderm with a tall, tent-shaped shield over its back. Groenlandaspis species are found from Greenland to Antarctica, showing how widespread placoderms were.

species:mesosaurus-tenuidens.placeText: Brazil, Uruguay, South Africa and Namibia
summary: A slender reptile about 1 m long with a long tail flattened for swimming and very long, thin teeth for straining small crustaceans from the water. One of the first reptiles to return to the water, and one of the first fossils used to argue for continental drift.
A mesosaur close to Mesosaurus, with shorter, stouter teeth, that swam in the same inland sea.

The “buzz-saw shark”, known mostly from its spiral whorl of teeth. A 2013 CT scan showed the whorl sat in the middle of its lower jaw, with no teeth on the sides; as the jaw closed, the whorl rolled backwards, slicing soft prey such as squid-like animals. It was a relative of ratfish rather than a true shark, perhaps 5–8 m long.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Soft-bodied prey such as squid-like animals

summary: A heavy plant-eater about 2.5–3 m long with a short, broad head and a skull roof of bone up to 10 cm thick, probably for head-butting contests. It was made famous by the 1980s children’s show “Moschops”.

The largest meat-eater of the middle Permian, about 5–6 m long, with a massive, thick-boned skull and long canines. A 2022 study of its inner ear suggests it was more agile than its bulky build suggests.
An early, bulky pareiasaur about 2.5 m long with a knobbly skull and leaf-shaped teeth for chewing tough plants.

species:coelurosauravus-elivensis.ageText: About 258 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
summary: One of the oldest known gliding vertebrates, about 40 cm long, with wings of skin stretched over long, rod-like bones growing out from its body, and a frill of spikes on the back of its head. It probably glided between trees.
The German gliders once called Coelurosauravus jaekeli are now placed in their own genus, Weigeltisaurus; Coelurosauravus itself is known from Madagascar.

A lizard-like reptile about 2 m long with a long neck, an early relative of the archosaurs. Described in 1710, it was the first fossil reptile ever described scientifically, though it was at first thought to be a crocodile.

A wolf-sized predator about 2 m long with long sabre-like canines and a jaw that opened very wide to drive them into prey. Gorgonopsians were the top predators of the late Permian, until the end-Permian extinction wiped them out.
A small dicynodont about 45 cm long, the most common animal of the late Permian Karoo. It dug corkscrew-shaped burrows, some found with pairs of adults inside. Only some had tusks, perhaps the males.

The largest gorgonopsian, about 3.5 m long, with canines up to 15 cm. In 2023 it was also found in South Africa, where it seems to have moved in to fill the gap left by local predators dying out shortly before the end-Permian extinction.
A barrel-shaped, armoured plant-eater about 2.5–3 m long, studded with bony plates and with spiky cheek flanges on its head. It probably lived in herds near rivers.
A water-dwelling temnospondyl about 1 m long that kept its gills as an adult, like a modern axolotl.

One of the first large dinosaurs, 5–10 m long, a long-necked plant-eater that walked on its hind legs, an early relative of the giant sauropods. Its growth rings show that adults could be very different sizes, so growth depended on conditions, as in reptiles.
One of the oldest turtles with a complete shell, about 1 m long, with spiky armour on its neck and a club on its tail. It could not pull its head into its shell.

The largest land predator of its time, about 6–7 m long, with a pair of thin, arched crests on its head. Despite Jurassic Park, there is no evidence it spat venom or had a neck frill, and it was much bigger than the film version. A 2020 study showed it was strongly built, with a powerful bite.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Jurassic World Dominion (2022), Jurassic World Rebirth (2025), Camp Cretaceous

summary: One of the earliest armoured dinosaurs, about 1.2 m long, with hundreds of small bony studs and a long tail. It could probably run on two legs.
An early sauropodomorph about 4 m long with strong hands and large claws, a relative of the ancestors of the giant sauropods.
A beaver-sized plant-eating tritylodont, a close relative of mammals. A mother was found with 38 tiny babies, far more than any mammal, suggesting a reptile-like way of raising young.

The first meat-eating dinosaur found in Antarctica, about 6–7 m long, with a strange crest running sideways across its head like a fan, nicknamed “Elvisaurus”. It was among the largest predators of its time.
A large early sauropodomorph, perhaps 6 m long, known from feet and leg bones, living alongside early true sauropods.

A big pliosaur, a short-necked, big-headed plesiosaur relative, about 6–7 m long, with a powerful bite and four big flippers. Walking with Dinosaurs (1999) made it famous at 25 m, but no specimen supports that size.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Fish, squid and other marine reptiles

summary: A long-necked plesiosaur about 4 m long, with a mesh of thin, interlocking teeth for trapping small fish and shrimp.
An ichthyosaur about 4 m long with enormous eyes, up to 22 cm across, among the largest of any vertebrate for its body size, suggesting it hunted squid in deep, dim water.

The largest bony fish ever, a gentle filter-feeder perhaps up to about 16 m long, sieving plankton with huge gill rakers like a basking shark. Its skeleton was mostly cartilage, so only fragments survive, which is why it is “problematicus”.
A sea crocodile about 3 m long that had given up armour and legs for flippers and a shark-like tail fin. It probably came ashore only rarely, if ever, and may have given birth at sea.

A crow-sized, four-winged feathered dinosaur. In 2010 its fossil pigment cells revealed its colours: grey and black, with white-banded wings and a reddish crest, making it the first dinosaur whose whole colour pattern was known. Named after Thomas Huxley, who first argued birds came from dinosaurs.

A pigeon-sized dinosaur with bat-like wings of skin, held out by a long rod-like bone on each wrist. It probably glided rather than flew. Its name, meaning “strange wing”, is the shortest of any dinosaur.

A pterosaur mixing a primitive long tail with an advanced, long-snouted head, showing that pterosaurs evolved in “modules”. One female was found with an egg, revealing which individuals were males (with crests) and females.
A dwarf sauropod only about 6 m long, a relative of Brachiosaurus that shrank on a small island. Bones of at least 20 individuals, from babies to adults, show adults really were small.

A giant, giraffe-like sauropod about 22–23 m long, long known as Brachiosaurus brancai. Its mounted skeleton in Berlin’s Museum für Naturkunde, 13.27 m tall, is the tallest mounted dinosaur skeleton in the world.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Werner Janensch, 1914; genus by Gregory Paul, 1988

summary: A stegosaur about 4.5 m long with small plates on its neck and back that turned into long spikes along its hips and tail, plus a spike on each shoulder. Computer models show its spiked tail could swing fast enough to crack bone.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Jurassic World: Camp Cretaceous (2020), Jurassic World Evolution

summary: A short-necked sauropod about 12–13 m long with tall, forked spines along its neck and back, probably feeding on low plants.

A 2022 study of its relative Amargasaurus found that dicraeosaur spines were most likely covered in skin rather than bare or sheathed in horn, so in life the spines probably formed a ridge or low sail.
A slender, long-bodied, short-armed ceratosaur about 6 m long, related to the toothless Limusaurus.
A giant brachiosaurid, perhaps about 25 m long, the largest dinosaur known from Portugal, a close relative of Brachiosaurus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Albert-Félix de Lapparent and Georges Zbyszewski, 1957; genus by Miguel Antunes and Octávio Mateus, 2003

summary: The largest land predator of Jurassic Europe, about 10 m long, a megalosaur with a deep skull and blade-like teeth up to 10 cm. Nests of Torvosaurus eggs with embryos have also been found in Portugal. It is named after James Gurney, creator of Dinotopia.
A medium-sized predator about 4.5 m long. A clutch of over 100 eggs from Paimogo, some with embryos inside, may belong to it.
A stegosaur with an unusually long neck of 17 vertebrae, longer than some early sauropods, perhaps for browsing higher than other stegosaurs.
A European Allosaurus, very close to A. fragilis of the Morrison, a sign that Iberia and North America were still linked.

A giant pliosaur, a short-necked, big-headed relative of plesiosaurs, from the Late Jurassic seas of Svalbard. It was formally named in 2012 from two partial skeletons. That study estimated a length of roughly 10–13 m, but the skulls are incomplete, so its true size is uncertain.

Before it was named, it was publicised as “Predator X”, the subject of a 2009 documentary. Claims made then, such as a bite four times stronger than T. rex’s, came from the documentary and press coverage, not from the scientific description.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Espen Knutsen, Patrick Druckenmiller and Jørn Hurum, 2012

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably marine reptiles and big fish

species:pliosaurus-funkei.akaNote: “Predator X” was its nickname before it was formally named in 2012.

summary: A small ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur with very large eyes and a short snout, from the cool northern sea.
A predator about 5–6 m long with a single bony crest running along the top of its snout, probably for display.
The North American Torvosaurus, about 9–10 m long, the largest predator of the Morrison along with the biggest allosaurs.

The largest known raptor, about 6–7 m long and weighing up to half a tonne, with a 23 cm sickle claw on each foot. It was heavily built, more a powerful grappler than a sprinter, and like its relatives it was almost certainly feathered.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: James Kirkland, Robert Gaston and Donald Burge, 1993

species:falcarius-utahensis.ageText: About 139 to 130 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: An early therizinosaur about 4 m long, caught midway in the change from meat-eater to plant-eater: it had leaf-shaped teeth and a widening belly, but still ran on long legs. Thousands of its bones were found in a single bonebed.

species:gastonia-burgei.ageText: About 135 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A spiky ankylosaur about 5 m long, covered in bony plates with large spikes along its sides and a shield of fused armour over its hips. It was found in the same quarry as Utahraptor, which probably hunted it.

The top predator of the Isle of Wight, about 7.5 m long, a relative of Allosaurus. Its snout was full of nerve channels, suggesting a sensitive face, perhaps used to feel for food or in courtship. It was found in 1978 after a cliff fall.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Stephen Hutt, David Martill and Michael Barker, 1996

summary: A small, nimble plant-eater about 1.5–2 m long that ran on its hind legs. It was once wrongly thought to climb trees like a kangaroo. Many skeletons have been found together on the Isle of Wight, perhaps a herd overwhelmed by a flood.

species:mantellisaurus-atherfieldensis.ageText: About 126 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
species:mantellisaurus-atherfieldensis.placeText: Isle of Wight and south-east England, Belgium and Germany
summary: A lighter relative of Iguanodon, about 7 m long, with a thumb spike and a horny beak, able to walk on two or four legs. It is named after Gideon Mantell, who discovered Iguanodon in 1822, and it is the most common iguanodont on the Isle of Wight.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Reginald Hooley, 1925 (as Iguanodon atherfieldensis); genus by Gregory Paul, 2007

species:polacanthus-foxii.ageText: About 130 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
species:polacanthus-foxii.placeText: Isle of Wight and southern England
summary: An armoured dinosaur about 5 m long with tall spikes over its shoulders and a solid shield of bone over its hips. Like Hypsilophodon, it is named after the Reverend William Fox, a pioneering Isle of Wight collector.

The first non-bird dinosaur found with feathers, in 1996: a small predator about 1 m long covered in simple, hair-like filaments. Pigment cells show it was ginger-brown with a pale belly and a striped tail, and dark around the eyes, like a racoon’s mask.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Lizards and small mammals (found in its stomach)

summary: A second species of Sinosauropteryx, named in 2025 from the Jehol Biota near Lingyuan, Liaoning. Its describers found that it and its relatives ate different prey, a sign that several small feathered predators shared the Jehol forests by hunting in different ways.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Qiu Rui, Wang Xiaolin, Jiang Shunxing, Meng Jin and Zhou Zhonghe, 2025

summary: A small feathered predator named in 2025 from a nearly complete skeleton that had long been identified as Sinosauropteryx. The skeleton is probably of a young animal.
Its stomach held two small mammals, apparently swallowed whole. Its robust jaws and strong neck muscles suggest it killed with a powerful bite, unlike Sinosauropteryx, which mostly ate lizards.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Qiu Rui, Wang Xiaolin, Jiang Shunxing, Meng Jin and Zhou Zhonghe, 2025

species:confuciusornis-sanctus.ageText: About 125 to 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A crow-sized early bird with the first known toothless, horny beak, but still with large claws on its wings. Thousands of specimens are known. Some have a pair of long tail streamers, probably males, used for display like a bird of paradise.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Hou Lianhai, Zhou Zhonghe, Gu Yucai and Zhang He, 1995

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably fish and other small animals

summary: A badger-sized mammal, about 1 m long including its tail, far bigger than the usual picture of mouse-sized Mesozoic mammals. One skeleton has a baby Psittacosaurus in its stomach, proof that some mammals ate dinosaurs. A 2023 fossil shows one attacking an adult Psittacosaurus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Li Jinling, Wang Yuan, Wang Yuanqing and Li Chuankui, 2000

summary: A dog-sized, parrot-beaked plant-eater about 1–1.5 m long, an early relative of the horned dinosaurs. Psittacosaurus is one of the best-known dinosaurs, with hundreds of specimens; one from Liaoning preserves bristles along its tail and colour patterns showing it was countershaded, dark above and pale below. Groups of young have been found buried together.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Plants, with gizzard stones to grind them

summary: A therizinosaur about 2 m long, covered in downy feathers with longer, stiff, quill-like feathers along its neck and back. It showed that feathers were widespread among theropods, not just in the ancestors of birds.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Xu Xing, Tang Zhilu and Wang Xiaolin, 1999

summary: A turkey-sized raptor about 1 m long covered in feathers, including branched ones like those of birds. Some have suggested it had venom grooves in its teeth, but most researchers now doubt it.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Xu Xing, Wang Xiaolin and Wu Xiaochun, 1999

species:spinosaurus-aegyptiacus.ageText: About 100 to 94 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: Perhaps the longest predatory dinosaur, about 14 m, with a crocodile-like snout, cone-shaped teeth for gripping fish, and a sail up to about 2 m tall on its back. Ernst Stromer named it from Egyptian bones in 1915; they were destroyed in a 1944 bombing raid on Munich.

New skeletons from the Kem Kem show short hind legs, dense bones and a paddle-like tail, so it spent much of its life in rivers. Whether it actively swam after fish or waded like a giant heron is still debated.

related.note: A second species named in 2026 from inland river deposits in Niger, with a tall, scimitar-shaped head crest.
Kem Kem vertebrae that may belong to Spinosaurus or to a second spinosaurine; studies disagree.
A Brazilian spinosaurine once proposed to be the same animal; later studies keep it separate.

species:carcharodontosaurus-saharicus.ageText: About 100 to 94 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A giant predator about 12 m long, as big as T. rex, with a long skull and blade-like teeth like a great white shark’s, which gave it its name, “shark-toothed lizard”. It hunted the big plant-eaters of North Africa.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Charles Depéret and Justin Savornin, 1925; genus by Ernst Stromer, 1931

species:deltadromeus-agilis.ageText: About 97 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A slender, long-legged theropod about 8 m long, built for speed; its name means “agile delta runner”. Its relationships are uncertain, but it is usually thought to be a ceratosaur.

species:onchopristis-numida.ageText: About 100 to 95 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A giant sawskate, a ray with a long, saw-like snout edged with barbed teeth, perhaps 8 m long. It slashed through shoals of fish in the Kem Kem rivers and may have been prey for Spinosaurus.

species:alanqa-saharica.ageText: About 97 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A long-necked, toothless pterosaur with a wingspan of about 4–6 m, known from its jaws. Its lower jaw had a bump inside, perhaps for crushing shellfish. It is one of the oldest members of the azhdarchoid group that later produced Quetzalcoatlus.

species:siats-meekerorum.ageText: About 98 to 96 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A giant predator about 9–10 m long, named after a man-eating monster of Ute legend. It belongs to the megaraptorans, a group with huge hand claws, and was the top predator of its time in North America, when tyrannosaurs were still small.

species:eolambia-caroljonesa.ageText: About 96 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A plant-eater about 6 m long close to the origin of the duck-billed hadrosaurs, the most common large dinosaur of the Mussentuchit.
A close relative of the duck-billed hadrosaurs, named after the palaeontologist Lev Nessov, who explored the Bissekty Formation for decades.

An Asian horned dinosaur with brow horns, very close to the true horned dinosaurs (ceratopsids), which are otherwise known only from North America. It suggests their ancestors lived in Asia before crossing to North America.

species:tylosaurus-proriger.ageText: About 86 to 80 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A giant mosasaur with a bony, pointed snout, perhaps used to ram prey or rivals. Stomach contents show it ate almost anything: fish, sharks, plesiosaurs, other mosasaurs, even a flightless bird.
