In 2026 several of the largest skeletons long counted as Tylosaurus proriger, up to about 13 m long, were found to belong to a new species with serrated teeth, Tylosaurus rex, so the biggest “Tylosaurus” in many books is now T. rex.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Large; its biggest specimens were reassigned to T. rex in 2026

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Fish, sharks, sea reptiles and diving birds

related.note: A larger relative with serrated teeth, named in 2026 from specimens once counted as this species.

species:pteranodon-sternbergi.ageText: About 88 to 85 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: The earlier of the two Pteranodon species, from the lower layers of Kansas’s Smoky Hill Chalk, laid down in the Western Interior Seaway. Like its later relative Pteranodon longiceps it was a toothless, long-beaked ocean glider that caught fish far from shore, with males reaching wingspans of around 6 m.

Adult males had a tall, broad, upright head crest, quite unlike the long, backward-pointing crest of Pteranodon longiceps; females and young had much smaller crests, so the crest was probably for display. It was named in 1966 after George F. Sternberg, who found the first skull. Because its crest and age differ, Alexander Kellner gave it its own genus, Geosternbergia, in 2010, but most researchers still treat it as a species of Pteranodon, perhaps the ancestor of P. longiceps.

facts.label: Crest
facts.value: Tall and upright in adult males

species:pteranodon-sternbergi.akaNote: In 2010 Alexander Kellner moved it to its own genus, Geosternbergia, and named a long-snouted specimen Dawndraco; most pterosaur researchers keep both in Pteranodon sternbergi.

related.note: The later species, with a long, backward-pointing crest; P. sternbergi may be its ancestor.

species:pteranodon-longiceps.ageText: About 86 to 84 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A large, toothless pterosaur with a wingspan of up to about 7 m and a long backward-pointing crest, bigger in males. It soared over the open sea like an albatross and caught fish. More than a thousand specimens are known from the Smoky Hill Chalk.

species:xiphactinus-audax.ageText: About 90 to 80 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:xiphactinus-audax.placeText: Kansas and elsewhere in North America
summary: A huge, fanged bony fish up to about 5–6 m long, like a giant, bulldog-faced tarpon. The famous “fish within a fish” in Hays, Kansas, is a Xiphactinus with a 2 m Gillicus inside it; it seems to have died soon after swallowing its oversized meal.
A flightless, toothed sea bird about 1.5 m long that dived for fish, propelled by powerful feet set far back on its body, like a giant loon. Its wings were reduced to tiny stubs.

species:cretoxyrhina-mantelli.ageText: About 100 to 73 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:cretoxyrhina-mantelli.placeText: Worldwide; best known from Kansas, USA
summary: The “Ginsu shark”, a fast, powerful mackerel shark up to about 7–8 m long with smooth, knife-like teeth, a Cretaceous equivalent of the great white. It attacked mosasaurs, plesiosaurs and big fish.
An early horned dinosaur about 5.5 m long with two long, curving spikes at the top of its frill, giving it a devilish look, hence its name.
A duck-billed dinosaur with no crest at all, an early relative of crested Brachylophosaurus and Maiasaura. Its name means “crestless grandfather”.

species:brachylophosaurus-canadensis.ageText: About 78 to 76 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A duck-billed dinosaur about 9 m long with a short, flat, paddle-like crest over its head. “Leonardo”, a young adult found in Montana in 2000, is one of the best-preserved dinosaurs ever, mummified with skin, muscle and possibly its last meal.

species:clidastes-propython.ageText: About 86 to 79 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, slender, agile mosasaur about 3–4 m long, among the most streamlined of its family, with a tail fin like a shark’s. It hunted fish in shallow coastal seas.

species:corythosaurus-casuarius.ageText: About 77 to 75.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A duck-billed dinosaur about 9 m long with a tall, rounded, hollow crest like a Corinthian helmet. Air passages looped through the crest, which may have worked as a resonating chamber to make deep, honking calls.

species:parasaurolophus-walkeri.ageText: About 76.5 to 75.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A duck-billed dinosaur about 9.5 m long with a long, curved, tube-like crest sweeping back from its head, containing looping air passages. Computer models suggest it could make deep, trombone-like sounds.

species:styracosaurus-albertensis.ageText: About 75.5 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A horned dinosaur about 5.5 m long with a single long nose horn and a frill crowned with four to six long spikes, a spectacular display for rivals and mates. Bonebeds suggest it lived in herds.

species:chasmosaurus-belli.ageText: About 76.5 to 75.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A horned dinosaur about 5 m long with a huge, rectangular frill pierced by two large openings, so it was light and probably covered in skin for display rather than protection. A baby skeleton was found in 2010.

species:euoplocephalus-tutus.ageText: About 76.5 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A tank-like ankylosaur about 5.5 m long, covered in bony plates (even its eyelids were armoured), with a heavy tail club that could break the bones of an attacker.

species:dromaeosaurus-albertensis.ageText: About 76.5 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: The raptor that gave its family its name, about 2 m long, with a deep, strong skull and a sickle claw on each foot. Its bite was strong for its size, so it may have relied more on its jaws than its claws.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: William Diller Matthew and Barnum Brown, 1922

summary: A large horned dinosaur about 7 m long with short, sideways-pointing brow horns, a stubby nose horn and a big, heart-shaped frill.
The most ornate horned dinosaur known, with 15 horns: one on its nose, one over each eye, one on each cheek, and ten curling forward over the top of its frill like a fringe.
A robust duck-billed dinosaur about 8 m long with a big, arched, hook-shaped nose and a powerful jaw with about 300 teeth in use at a time, backed by hundreds more waiting to replace them.

species:velociraptor-mongoliensis.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A turkey-sized raptor, about 2 m long including its long tail and up to about 15 kg: much smaller than the ones in Jurassic Park, and covered in feathers, as quill knobs on its forearm show. It had a long, low snout and a sickle claw on each foot.
The famous “Fighting Dinosaurs” fossil shows a Velociraptor with its claw in a Protoceratops’ neck while the Protoceratops bites its arm, both buried by collapsing sand.

species:protoceratops-andrewsi.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A sheep-sized plant-eater about 2 m long with a parrot beak and a bony frill, but no real horns. It is known from hundreds of skeletons, from hatchlings to adults, and nests of babies have been found. Its skulls, found by ancient prospectors, may have inspired the legend of the griffin.

A toothless, beaked theropod about 1.6 m long found on top of a nest of eggs in 1923. The eggs were thought to be Protoceratops eggs, so it was named “egg thief, fond of ceratopsians”. In the 1990s, embryos showed the eggs were its own: it was brooding them like a bird, not stealing them.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably plants, eggs and small animals

summary: A lightly built ankylosaur about 5 m long with a tail club. Groups of young ones have been found buried together, still upright, suggesting juveniles lived in groups and were caught by sandstorms.
A horned dinosaur about 4.5 m long with long brow horns and a frill with triangular, scalloped edges. Named in 2022, it belongs to a group of southern horned dinosaurs distinct from those of Canada.

species:edmontosaurus-regalis.ageText: About 73 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A huge duck-billed dinosaur up to about 12 m long, the older relative of Edmontosaurus annectens of Hell Creek. One “mummy” from Alberta shows it had a fleshy, rooster-like comb on its head. Bonebeds suggest it lived in herds.

A crested duck-billed dinosaur about 9 m long with a helmet-shaped crest and a ridge of tall spines along its back. Nests, eggs and embryos of its relatives are known, showing how fast these dinosaurs grew.

species:anchiceratops-ornatus.ageText: About 72 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A horned dinosaur about 5 m long with a long, rectangular frill edged with bony knobs, often found in rocks laid down near the coast, so it may have lived in salt marshes.

species:pachyrhinosaurus-canadensis.ageText: About 71 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A horned dinosaur about 6 m long without a nose horn: instead it had a huge, flat, rough boss of bone over its nose and eyes, perhaps for head-butting. Bonebeds of its relatives in Alberta and Alaska suggest it lived in herds, even in the Arctic.

An ostrich-like dinosaur about 3.5 m long with a toothless beak, long legs and a fast stride. Fossils from Alberta show it was feathered, and only adults had wing-like arms, suggesting these were for display or brooding rather than flight.
An oviraptorid about 1.5 m long with a tall, rounded crest, one of many found by construction workers in Ganzhou.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably plants, eggs and small animals

summary: An oviraptorid about 1.6 m tall with a tall, helmet-like crest very like that of a living cassowary, probably used for display.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably plants, eggs and small animals

summary: A second species of Alioramus, named in 2009 from a much more complete skeleton than A. remotus, found at Tsagan Khushu in the Nemegt Formation. It had a long, shallow snout topped by a row of small bony horns. Its skeleton is of a young animal, about 9 years old when it died, so its adult size is not known.

For almost 50 years known only from a pair of huge arms 2.4 m long. Skeletons found in 2006 and 2009 revealed a giant, 11 m ostrich dinosaur with a hump or sail on its back, a duck-like beak and broad hooves. Its stomach held fish scales and gizzard stones.
A duck-billed dinosaur up to about 13 m long with a spike-like crest pointing back from its head. It is the most common large dinosaur in the Nemegt and was a main prey of Tarbosaurus.

A giant, pot-bellied, plant-eating theropod about 9–10 m long with the longest claws of any known animal, up to about 50 cm along the curve. It was first thought to be a giant turtle; its claws were probably used to pull down branches and to defend itself.

A titanosaur about 11–13 m long known from a headless skeleton found in 1965, with Tarbosaurus tooth marks on its bones. Its tail vertebrae suggest it could rear up on its hind legs, propped on its tail.

species:austrosaurus-mckillopi.placeText: Clutha Station, near Richmond, Queensland, Australia (found in marine rocks)
summary: The first sauropod named from Australia. Its bones were found in 1932 on Clutha sheep station, west of Richmond; the local doctor, Dr McKillop, sent a sketch to Heber Longman of the Queensland Museum, who named it in 1933 and estimated it at about 15 m long. Like other Allaru dinosaurs, its carcass ended up in the sea.

The site was lost for decades until it was found again and re-excavated, and a 2017 restudy added more bones and showed it was a somphospondylan, a relative of the titanosaurs, like Wintonotitan from the younger Winton Formation.

species:notochelone-costata.ageText: About 110 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A small sea turtle, under 1 m long, with a low ridge along the middle of its shell, related to the giant Archelon and Protostega. It is one of the most common turtles in the rocks of the old Eromanga Sea, and baby sea turtles like it turn up in the stomachs of the ichthyosaur Platypterygius. Richard Owen first described it in 1882.

species:cooyoo-australis.ageText: About 110 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A large predatory bony fish of the Eromanga Sea, an ichthyodectid related to the North American Xiphactinus and Ichthyodectes. Like them it had a deep, upturned jaw lined with fang-like teeth for seizing other fish.

species:kunbarrasaurus-ieversi.placeText: Marathon Station, near Richmond, Queensland, Australia (found in marine rocks; it lived on land)
summary: A small, early armoured dinosaur about 2.5 to 3.5 m long, covered in bony plates and studs. Station manager Ian Ievers found it in 1989. It is the most complete dinosaur skeleton known from Australia and the most complete ankylosaur from any of the southern continents: skull, much of the backbone, hips, legs and most of the armour, much of it still in place. It was a land animal; its body floated out to sea and sank into the mud of the Eromanga Sea.

Its last meal survives in its belly: chopped-up stems and leaves, fern spore cases, and whole seeds and fruit-like bodies, including some from early flowering plants. CT scans showed a very large inner ear for its size and a braincase made largely of cartilage. It was first thought to be a specimen of Minmi, but in 2015 it was named as a genus of its own, from kunbarra, the word for “shield” in the Mayi language of the local Wunumara people.

related.note: Its Chilean relative in the parankylosaurs, with a bladed tail weapon.

species:haliskia-peterseni.ageText: About 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, late Albian)
summary: A fish-eating pterosaur with a wingspan of about 4.6 m, named in 2024. About 22% of its skeleton survives, including a complete lower jaw with teeth, making it the most complete pterosaur ever found in Australia. Its name means “sea phantom”.

It belonged to the anhanguerians, pterosaurs with crests on the tips of their jaws and interlocking, spiky teeth for snatching slippery prey from the water, and it hunted over the Eromanga Sea that then covered inland Queensland. Its throat bones survive too, and its describers think they anchored a strong, muscular tongue that helped it swallow prey. Kevin Petersen, a curator at the Kronosaurus Korner museum, found it in 2021, and it is named after him.

species:mackunda-ctenochasmatoid.placeText: Vellum Downs, south-west of Hughenden, Queensland, Australia
summary: An unnamed pterosaur known from a single upper arm bone (humerus) found in the Mackunda Formation and described in 2010 by Timothy Fletcher and Steven Salisbury. Its shape suggested it may belong to the ctenochasmatoids, a group of pterosaurs with long jaws that in many species were lined with fine, comb-like teeth for straining small animals from water.

If the identification is right, it is the only ctenochasmatoid known from Australia; most Queensland pterosaurs belong to other groups, such as the toothed anhanguerians like Ferrodraco. One bone is not enough to name a species, so it is known simply as an indeterminate ctenochasmatoid, and the identification is tentative. It would have flown over the shores of the shrinking Eromanga Sea.

facts.label: Name
facts.value: None: too incomplete to name a species

summary: A large plant-eating ornithopod, around 7 to 8 m long, best known for the big, hollow bump on top of its snout. Grazier Doug Langdon found the skeleton by a creek near Muttaburra in 1963, and it was named in 1981. It is one of the most complete dinosaurs from Australia.

A 2026 study CT-scanned its skull. It found that the bulbous nose is built from bones not seen in other dinosaurs rather than from the usual nasal bones, and that it had teeth at the front of its snout, unexpected in its group. Its brain had a large region for smell, which the researchers suggest helped it pick out particular plants. Whether it is closest to Iguanodon and its relatives or to the European rhabdodontids is still debated.

The last known temnospondyl, a group of big, flat-headed amphibians that had thrived since the Carboniferous but had died out almost everywhere else by the Jurassic. It was a chigutisaurid with a broad, flat skull about 65 cm long and is estimated at roughly 3 to 5 m long, an ambush hunter that probably lay on the beds of rivers and lakes waiting for fish and other prey.

It lived in a polar rift valley inside the Antarctic Circle, where winters were dark and the ground froze. One idea is that the cold kept out crocodylians, which elsewhere may have taken over its way of life, letting this ancient group hang on. It is known only from fragments: jaw pieces, part of the skull roof, vertebrae, ribs and shoulder bones. It is named after Lesley Kool and Mike Cleeland, who helped find it.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Anne Warren, Tom Rich and Patricia Vickers-Rich, 1997

summary: A small, two-legged plant-eating dinosaur, perhaps about 2 m long, known from short, deep lower jaws with teeth. It lived through polar winters inside the Antarctic Circle. It is named after the airline Qantas, which helped the dig by flying fossils and exhibitions around the world.

A small, two-legged plant-eater known from upper jaws, named in 2019. Its upper jaw bone looks like the upturned hull of a galleon, giving the name. It lived alongside Qantassaurus, showing that several kinds of small plant-eating dinosaurs shared the polar forests.

A tiny mammal known from a jaw with teeth. When it was named in 1997 its complex molars looked so like those of placental mammals that it was claimed as an early placental in Australia, a surprise that was widely debated. Most researchers now place it among the australosphenidans, a southern group whose molars evolved separately and which may include the ancestors of the platypus and echidnas.

The first multituberculate found in Australia, named in 2009 from a scrap of jaw with a single blade-like tooth. Multituberculates were rodent-like mammals that were common on the northern continents; this find showed they had also reached the far south.

species:borealopelta-markmitchelli.placeText: Fort McMurray, Alberta, Canada (found in marine rocks; it lived on nearby land)
summary: A nodosaur, an armoured dinosaur without a tail club, about 5.5 m long and around 1,300 kg, with long spikes over its shoulders. It lived on land near the coast; it is known only because its body washed out to sea and was buried on the sea floor, in rocks that otherwise hold marine life. In 2011 Shawn Funk, a machine operator at an oil sands mine, struck it while digging. It is one of the best-preserved dinosaurs known: the front half of the body survives in three dimensions with its armour plates and their horny coverings, and skin, still in place, so it looks more like a statue than a skeleton. Preparing it took technician Mark Mitchell, its namesake, more than 7,000 hours.

Traces of pigment in its skin, described in 2017, show it was reddish-brown and countershaded, darker on its back and paler underneath. Such camouflage suggests that even a 1.3-tonne armoured animal had to hide from big predators.

Its stomach contents, described in 2020, are mostly ferns, picked out over other plants, with bits of charcoal suggesting it browsed regrowth after a wildfire. A twig in the gut shows it died in late spring or summer. Its carcass then floated out to sea, bloated, before sinking on its back.

A spinosaur about 7.5–10 m long with a long, crocodile-like snout, cone-shaped teeth and a huge 31 cm thumb claw, which gave it its name, “heavy claw”. Its stomach held fish scales and the bones of a young iguanodont.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom (2018), Jurassic World: Camp Cretaceous

summary: A carcharodontosaur about 6 m long with a strange, pointed hump over its hips made by two very tall vertebrae. Bumps on its arm bones may be quill knobs, though this is debated. Its name means “hunchback hunter from Cuenca”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Francisco Ortega, Fernando Escaso and José Luis Sanz, 2010

summary: An early ostrich dinosaur about 2 m long with about 220 tiny teeth, more than any other theropod, and a soft throat pouch like a pelican’s, preserved in the fossil.

A heavy plant-eater about 9–10 m long with a beak, cheek teeth and a large thumb spike, able to walk on two or four legs. Gideon Mantell named Iguanodon from teeth in 1825, the second dinosaur ever named. The spike was first put on its nose, until the Bernissart skeletons showed it belonged on the thumb.
A tiny crocodile relative about 60 cm long with blunt back teeth for crushing snails and crustaceans.
A short-necked sauropod about 10 m long with two parallel rows of tall, backward-pointing spines along its neck, the longest about 60 cm.

The spines were once shown bare, as rattling display structures, or sheathed in horn as defensive spikes. A 2022 study of their bone structure and surface found no sign of a horn sheath. Instead the spines were most likely covered in skin and tied together by ligaments, forming a double “sail” along the neck. What the sail was for is not known; display is the most common suggestion.

A crow-sized raptor with long flight feathers on its arms and its legs: four wings. It could glide and probably fly. Fossil pigment shows its feathers were glossy black with a blue-green sheen, like a crow’s. Stomach contents include a bird, a fish, a lizard and a mammal.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Xu Xing, Zhou Zhonghe and Wang Xiaolin, 2000

summary: A turkey-sized early bird with a long bony tail like Archaeopteryx. Its stomachs are packed with seeds, the first evidence of a bird eating seeds.
A pterosaur with a crest under its lower jaw, named after the flying ikran of the film Avatar. It may have skimmed fish from the water surface.

One of the largest crocodile relatives ever, about 9–9.5 m long and up to 8 tonnes, with a long snout ending in a bulbous bulla. Its diet is inferred from its size and skull: probably big fish and other animals, perhaps including dinosaurs at the water’s edge. Paul Sereno’s 2000 expedition and the documentary that followed nicknamed it “SuperCroc”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: France de Broin and Philippe Taquet, 1966

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably fish and other large animals

summary: An iguanodont about 7–8 m long with tall spines along its back, making a sail or a hump, and a long, flat, duck-like snout. The sail may have been for display or for controlling body heat.

A spinosaur about 9.5–11 m long, a close relative of Baryonyx, with a long, narrow, crocodile-like snout (its name means “crocodile mimic”) and a low ridge along its back. It probably fished in the rivers like a giant heron.
species:suchomimus-tenerensis.akaNote: Cristatusaurus lapparenti, named in 1998 from jaw scraps from the same rocks, may be the same animal; it is usually treated as a doubtful name.

summary: A sauropod about 9 m long with a straight-edged, vacuum-cleaner-shaped muzzle lined with over 500 slender teeth, replaced as often as every 14 days. It grazed low plants with its head held down.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Ferns, horsetails and other low plants

summary: An early abelisaur about 6–7 m long with a short, rough-textured face, perhaps covered in horn.

A wolf-sized raptor about 3.4 m long with a 12 cm sickle claw on each foot. John Ostrom’s study of it in 1969 started the “Dinosaur Renaissance”, picturing dinosaurs as active, warm-blooded animals related to birds. Jurassic Park’s “Velociraptors” are really modelled on Deinonychus.
A plant-eater about 6.5–8 m long with a very long, stiffened tail, the most common large dinosaur of the Cloverly and a frequent victim of Deinonychus.
A nodosaur about 5 m long covered in bony plates, with big spikes along its neck and shoulders but no tail club.
A giant carcharodontosaur about 11–11.5 m long with a tall, muscular ridge along its neck, back and tail, held up by spines up to 30 cm. Trackways in Texas may show one following a sauropod.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston Jr, 1950

summary: One of the tallest dinosaurs, perhaps 17 m tall with its neck raised, known from neck vertebrae over 1.2 m long. Its name means “earthquake god lizard”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Mathew Wedel, Richard Cifelli and Kent Sanders, 2000

summary: A spinosaur about 6.5 m long known from a beautiful skull. Its name comes from the irritation its describers felt on finding that commercial collectors had faked its snout with plaster. It is named after Professor Challenger of Conan Doyle’s The Lost World.

related.note: Possibly the same animal; the known fossils barely overlap.

summary: A big fish-eating pterosaur with a wingspan of up to about 8 m and keel-shaped crests on both jaws. It was the giant “Ornithocheirus” of Walking with Dinosaurs (1999), though shown far too big.
A small, toothless pterosaur with a short, down-turned beak and a tall crest of bone and soft tissue on its head. It may have eaten fruit.
A pterosaur with a wingspan of about 4.5 m and an enormous crest making up three-quarters of its skull. Its name, “sea runner”, comes from the idea that it skimmed fish like a skimmer bird.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos, 2002

summary: A coelacanth up to about 2 m long, a relative of the living coelacanth, preserved in 3D in Santana nodules, some with a fossilised lung.

A giant pliosaur about 9–10 m long with a huge head and teeth up to 30 cm long including roots. Its famous Harvard skeleton was reconstructed too long, at 12.8 m. Stomach contents show it ate turtles and plesiosaurs.

One of the last ichthyosaurs, about 6 to 7 m long, from the Eromanga Sea that covered inland Queensland. One pregnant female’s stomach held baby sea turtles and a bird, the first evidence that ichthyosaurs ate either; the turtles were probably easy prey and the bird perhaps scavenged. Specimens once named Platypterygius longmani are now treated as the same species.

One of the largest animals ever, about 31–37 m long and weighing perhaps 50–60 tonnes, known from six individuals. A cast of its skeleton is so long its head pokes out of the gallery at the American Museum of Natural History.
A giant carcharodontosaur about 12 m long, one of the largest predators of its time. Its teeth were found with Patagotitan bones.

species:giganotosaurus-carolinii.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: One of the largest meat-eating dinosaurs, about 12–13 m long, as long as T. rex but more lightly built, with a long, narrow skull and blade-like teeth for slicing flesh rather than crushing bone. Its name means “giant southern lizard”.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Jurassic World Dominion (2022), ARK: Survival Evolved

species:andesaurus-delgadoi.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: An early titanosaur about 15–18 m long, known from back and tail bones, close to the base of the titanosaur family tree.

species:limaysaurus-tessonei.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A rebbachisaurid sauropod about 15 m long with tall spines on its back, a likely prey of Giganotosaurus.

species:buitreraptor-gonzalezorum.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A small, long-snouted, raptor-like dinosaur about 1.5 m long with many small teeth, probably for catching small prey such as lizards, snakes or fish.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Peter Makovicky, Sebastián Apesteguía and Federico Agnolín, 2005

species:ekrixinatosaurus-novasi.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A big abelisaur about 7 m long whose bones were found during blasting for road works, hence its name, “explosion-born lizard”.

species:najash-rionegrina.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: An early snake about 1–2 m long with small but complete back legs and a hip girdle. It lived on land and shows how snakes lost their legs.
A giant titanosaur, perhaps 26–30 m long, found in 2000 in what was once a mangrove swamp. Its name means “tidal titan”. Its bones show tooth marks, probably from scavengers.
A titanosaur about 15 m long found by Stromer’s team; its bones were destroyed in Munich in 1944.
A big theropod, perhaps 11–12 m long, of uncertain relationships, known only from bones destroyed in 1944.

A land-dwelling crocodile relative about 6 m long with three sets of tusk-like teeth sticking up and down, which led to the nickname “BoarCroc”. It is known from a single skull; its long-legged, running build is inferred from relatives.

An abelisaur about 6 m long with a short, wrinkled face (its name means “wrinkle face”) lined with blood vessels, perhaps covered in horn or skin for display. Its weak skull suggests it may have scavenged.
A second species of Carcharodontosaurus, about as large as C. saharicus, known from skull bones found in Niger.

species:argentinosaurus-huinculensis.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: Perhaps the largest land animal ever, estimated at about 30–35 m long and 65–75 tonnes, though it is known from only a few bones, including vertebrae 1.6 m tall.

species:mapusaurus-roseae.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A giant carcharodontosaur about 10–12 m long. A bonebed of at least seven individuals of different ages suggests they lived in groups, perhaps hunting giant titanosaurs together.

species:meraxes-gigas.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A huge carcharodontosaur about 11 m long with tiny arms, showing that short arms evolved separately in carcharodontosaurs and tyrannosaurs. Named after a dragon in A Song of Ice and Fire.

species:skorpiovenator-bustingorryi.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: An abelisaur about 6–7 m long with a short, bumpy skull. Its name, “scorpion hunter”, comes from the many scorpions around the dig site.

A giant oviraptorosaur about 8 m long and 2 tonnes, a toothless, beaked, feathered relative of birds 35 times heavier than its closest relatives. Giant eggs and nests found in China may belong to animals like it.
A mid-sized tyrannosaur about 5 m long, a step between the small early tyrannosaurs and the giants of the latest Cretaceous.
An ostrich dinosaur about 3.4 m long, known from many bones collected by the 1920s American expeditions.
An early duck-billed dinosaur about 6 m long, the most common dinosaur in Iren Dabasu bonebeds. One specimen has a tumour in its tail bones.

A small armoured dinosaur about 2 m long, known from an almost complete skeleton named in 2021. Its tail ended in a flat, frond-like weapon made of seven pairs of bony blades fused together, unlike the club of Ankylosaurus or the spikes of Stegosaurus. Its describers called it a macuahuitl, after an Aztec war club edged with blades.

Its mix of features at first suggested a stegosaur, hence the name, which means “roof tail”, but it turned out to be an early ankylosaur. It founded a new southern group, the parankylosaurs, with Kunbarrasaurus from Australia and probably Antarctopelta from Antarctica. Elengassen is an armoured beast from the legends of the Aónik’enk people of Patagonia.

facts.label: Tail
facts.value: Flat, bladed weapon of seven pairs of fused osteoderms

related.note: Its Australian relative in the parankylosaurs.

species:deinosuchus-riograndensis.placeText: Texas and across southern North America
summary: A giant alligator relative about 8–10 m long with a skull up to 1.5 m long and thick, blunt back teeth suited to crushing turtles. Bite marks on hadrosaur and tyrannosaur bones show it ambushed dinosaurs at the water’s edge. Its name means “terrible crocodile”.
A horned dinosaur about 4–5 m long with short brow horns, related to Chasmosaurus, known from a bonebed of several animals.

The largest turtle ever, about 4.6 m long and 4 m across the flippers, with a leathery shell over a framework of bone and a hooked beak for crushing jellyfish and shellfish. The best specimen is missing a back flipper, perhaps bitten off by a mosasaur.

A plesiosaur about 10 m long, more than half of it neck, with 72 neck vertebrae, more than any other animal. In 1868 Cope put its head on the wrong end, on its tail; Othniel Marsh’s mockery helped start their bitter Bone Wars.

A giant titanosaur about 26 m long, with about 70% of its skeleton (excluding the head) known, making it the most complete giant sauropod. Its describers estimated about 59 tonnes, though later work suggests 30–50. The type specimen was still growing. Named after dreadnought battleships, it “dreaded nothing”.
A raptor about 1.6–2.5 m long known from a few bones, including a sickle claw, found after a forest fire in 1992, which gave it its name, “fire thief”.
A stocky plant-eater about 4–6 m long, an iguanodont relative with grinding teeth, common on the islands of Late Cretaceous Europe.
A small titanosaur about 8–12 m long from the islands of Late Cretaceous Europe. Its name means “gypsy lizard”, because its relatives wandered across Europe.

An abelisaur about 7.5–8 m long with two thick horns over its eyes, a short, deep skull and tiny, almost useless arms. Its skin was covered in small scales with rows of larger bumps. Powerful tail muscles may have made it one of the fastest large theropods. Its name means “meat-eating bull”.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom (2018), Camp Cretaceous, Prehistoric Planet (2022)

summary: The Arctic Pachyrhinosaurus, about 6–8 m long, with a big bony boss over its nose and spikes on its frill. Huge bonebeds show herds lived on the North Slope, perhaps all year round.

An Arctic tyrannosaur, perhaps 6 m long, known from skull fragments. It was first thought to be a dwarf, but later finds suggest it may have been larger. Its name means “polar bear lizard” in Iñupiaq. Whether it had feathers is not known from its fossils.

A duck-billed dinosaur from Alaska’s North Slope, a close relative of Edmontosaurus, known from thousands of bones in the Liscomb bonebed, mostly of young animals that died together. It lived far north of any other hadrosaur, through months of polar darkness. Its name means “ancient grazer” in Iñupiaq.

A giant azhdarchid pterosaur with a wingspan of about 10–12 m and an unusually short, thick, heavily built neck and broad skull. No big theropods are known from its island, and a 2017 study suggested it may have been the top predator, hunting dwarf dinosaurs on the ground.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Eric Buffetaut, Dan Grigorescu and Zoltán Csiki, 2002

summary: A dwarf titanosaur only about 6 m long and under a tonne, one of the smallest sauropods known, shrunk by island life.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Franz Nopcsa, 1915 (genus by Friedrich von Huene, 1932)

summary: A small, primitive duck-billed dinosaur about 5 m long, an island dwarf. Its eggs and hatchlings have been found at Hațeg.
A small, stocky plant-eater about 2.5 m long with a big head, a relative of Rhabdodon living on the Hațeg island.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Franz Nopcsa, 1899 (genus by David Weishampel and colleagues, 2003)

summary: A stocky, short-legged theropod about 2 m long with two big claws on each foot instead of one. First described as a raptor, it may instead be an early flightless bird. Its name means “stocky dragon”.

An abelisaur about 6–7 m long with a short, broad snout, a single knob-like horn on its head and tiny arms. Majungasaurus bones carry tooth marks from other Majungasaurus, showing it was a cannibal. It was the top predator of Madagascar.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Sauropods and other dinosaurs, including its own kind

summary: A titanosaur about 15 m long and the first known from a nearly complete skull and skeleton. A baby found in 2016 was only about 40 kg, and probably independent soon after hatching.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Kristina Curry Rogers and Catherine Forster, 2001

summary: A small noasaurid about 2 m long with forward-jutting front teeth, perhaps for snatching fish or small animals. It is named after Mark Knopfler of Dire Straits, whose music was playing at the dig.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Scott Sampson, Matthew Carrano and Catherine Forster, 2001

summary: One of the largest frogs ever, about 40 cm long and perhaps 4.5 kg, with a huge, armoured head and wide mouth. It probably ambushed small animals, maybe even baby dinosaurs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Susan Evans, Marc Jones and David Krause, 2008

summary: A pug-nosed, plant-eating crocodile relative about 1.2 m long, with clover-shaped teeth and heavy armour, living on land.
A heavy, blunt-snouted crocodile relative about 4 m long, a close cousin of Kaprosuchus.
A raven-sized bird-like dinosaur with quill knobs for flight feathers and a sickle claw on its foot. Whether it is an early bird or a flying relative of raptors is debated.
A cat-sized gondwanatherian mammal, very large for the Mesozoic, with a strange mix of features. Its name means “crazy beast”.
An elasmosaur, a long-necked plesiosaur, about 8 m long, from the southern seas around Zealandia.
A mosasaur about 8–9 m long named after the taniwha, a water monster of Māori legend.
The only true horned dinosaur (ceratopsid) known from outside North America, about 6–7 m long, with a short nose horn and a ring of curling hornlets on its frill.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom (2018), Jurassic World Dominion (2022), Camp Cretaceous

summary: A giant tyrannosaur about 11 m long, close to Tarbosaurus and T. rex, known from jaw bones found in the Zhucheng bonebed.
The largest duck-billed dinosaur, about 15 m long and perhaps 13–16 tonnes, as heavy as many sauropods, with around 1,500 teeth in its jaws.

species:rajasaurus-narmadensis.placeText: Rahioli, near Balasinor, Gujarat; also near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, India
summary: A large abelisaur with a low, rounded horn on its forehead, formed from the nasal and frontal bones and probably used for display or head-butting. Like other abelisaurs it had a short, deep skull and tiny arms, and was probably an ambush predator; titanosaurs nested in its habitat by the thousand. Its name means “king lizard of the Narmada”.

Its bones were dug up in 1982–84 by Suresh Srivastava of the Geological Survey of India at Rahioli, a quarry rich in dinosaur eggs, and named in 2003. It is the first Indian theropod known from both skull and body bones. It was a close relative of Majungasaurus of Madagascar, showing that India and Madagascar shared animals after they separated. The fragmentary Lametasaurus and Indosaurus, named earlier, may be the same animal, but their remains are too poor (and Lametasaurus is lost) to tell.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: About 6.6 m (2016 estimate); older estimates up to 11 m

related.note: Its close relative in Madagascar, with a similar skull and a single horn-like bump.

summary: A titanosaur about 18 m long with unusually long front legs and a short neck. Fossil dung linked to titanosaurs in India contains grass, showing grasses already existed.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Sohan Lal Jain and Saswati Bandyopadhyay, 1997

summary: The first titanosaur named, by Richard Lydekker in 1877 from two tail vertebrae found near Jabalpur, and the namesake of the whole group. The bones are too incomplete to tell it apart from other titanosaurs, so the name is now considered doubtful. The giant “Titanosaurus” of Jurassic World Rebirth is a generic film sauropod: nothing is known of the real animal’s size or appearance beyond those vertebrae.
A snake about 3.5 m long found coiled around a crushed titanosaur egg next to a hatchling in a nest, a rare snapshot of a snake preying on baby dinosaurs.

A nyctosaurid pterosaur with a wingspan of about 4–5 m, one of several pterosaurs from the last years of the Cretaceous that show pterosaurs were still diverse before the asteroid. Some specimens have bigger crests than others, which may reflect differences between the sexes.

A giant mosasaur about 9–10 m long with a short, broad skull and conical teeth like an orca’s, often broken from biting bone. Partly digested remains of plesiosaurs and other mosasaurs found nearby may be its meals.
An elasmosaur, a long-necked plesiosaur, about 7 m long. Its name means “giraffe lizard” in Arabic.

species:mosasaurus-hoffmannii.placeText: Netherlands, Belgium, and around the North Atlantic
summary: One of the largest mosasaurs, about 12–13 m long (nowhere near the size shown in Jurassic World), with a massive skull and big conical teeth, the top predator of the latest Cretaceous seas. Its jaw, found near Maastricht around 1780, was one of the first fossils recognised as an extinct animal.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Fish, turtles, plesiosaurs and other mosasaurs

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Jurassic World (2015), Fallen Kingdom (2018), Dominion (2022), Rebirth (2025), Prehistoric Planet (2022)

summary: A massive-jawed mosasaur about 12 m long with thick teeth for crushing turtles and other hard-shelled prey.
A large sea turtle about 1.5 m long, the most common reptile in the Maastricht limestone.

One of the largest flying animals ever, with a wingspan of about 10–11 m and, standing, as tall as a giraffe. It probably walked on all fours and hunted small animals on the ground like a giant stork, and could launch itself into the air with its powerful arms. Named after the Aztec feathered-serpent god.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Prehistoric Planet (2022), Jurassic World Dominion (2022), Jurassic World Rebirth (2025)

species:alamosaurus-sanjuanensis.placeText: Texas, New Mexico and Utah, USA
summary: The last giant sauropod of North America, perhaps 26–30 m long, which lived alongside T. rex in the south-west, and may have been its prey.
A duck-like diving bird and one of the oldest members of the modern bird groups, living alongside non-bird dinosaurs. Its fossil voice box (syrinx), found in 2016, suggests it honked like a goose.
An elasmosaur with a short neck for its group and interlocking teeth that may have worked like a sieve for filter-feeding, like a baleen whale.
A giant mosasaur, perhaps 10 m long, the top predator of the Antarctic seas, named after a sea serpent of Mapuche legend.

species:stygimoloch-spinifer.placeText: Montana, Wyoming and South Dakota, USA
summary: A dome-headed dinosaur about 3 m long with a tall, narrow dome ringed by long horns, living in Hell Creek alongside the larger Pachycephalosaurus. Its name means “horned devil from the River Styx”.
The flat-headed Dracorex, from the same rocks, may be a juvenile, or the other sex, of Stygimoloch, of Pachycephalosaurus, or of both.

related.note: The larger dome-headed dinosaur of the same rocks
Flat-headed and spiky: possibly a juvenile or the other sex of Stygimoloch, Pachycephalosaurus or both

summary: A pachycephalosaur with a flat, undomed skull covered in knobs and spikes, known from one skull. Its name, “dragon king of Hogwarts”, was chosen with children at the Children’s Museum of Indianapolis.

Its flat head has led some researchers to interpret it as a juvenile of Stygimoloch or Pachycephalosaurus, with the dome growing later; differences in head ornaments could also be differences between the sexes. It may relate to either or both.

related.note: Possibly the adult, or the other sex, of Dracorex
Possibly the adult, or the other sex, of Dracorex

species:pectinodon-bakkeri.placeText: Wyoming, Montana and South Dakota, USA
summary: A troodontid known mostly from small, finely serrated teeth, one of the last members of the family.
A goat-sized dome-headed dinosaur about 2 m long, with a thick, smooth dome fringed by small knobs, probably used for head-butting or flank-butting rivals.
A horned dinosaur about 5.5 m long with a big nose horn and hooks on its frill. Bonebeds with thousands of animals suggest huge herds, some drowned crossing flooded rivers.
A duck-billed dinosaur about 9 m long with a hatchet-shaped hollow crest, named after Lawrence Lambe, the pioneer of Alberta palaeontology.
A troodontid about 2–2.5 m long with large forward-facing eyes and one of the biggest brains for its size of any dinosaur. Long known as Troodon, the name famous from documentaries and books.
species:stenonychosaurus-inequalis.akaNote: Troodon was named in 1856 from a single tooth from Montana and is now usually treated as a doubtful name; the skeletons long called Troodon belong to Stenonychosaurus. Latenivenatrix, named in 2017 for some of those skeletons, was found in 2021 to be the same species.

summary: A horned dinosaur about 4.5 m long with a huge nose and long, forward-curving brow horns like a bull’s.
One of the largest ostrich dinosaurs, about 6 m long, with a small, toothless beak, long neck and long legs for running. The flock fleeing the T. rex in Jurassic Park (1993) made it famous.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Halszka Osmólska, Ewa Roniewicz and Rinchen Barsbold, 1972

summary: A turkey-sized, long-legged alvarezsaur with short, powerful arms ending in a single big claw, probably for breaking into insect nests.
A dome-headed dinosaur about 2.5 m long with a rounded dome edged by small knobs.

An oviraptorid about 2.5–3 m long, famous for skeletons found sitting on their nests with arms spread over the eggs, brooding like birds when they were buried by sand. Named after funeral-dancing skeletons of Tibetan Buddhist legend.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: James Clark, Mark Norell and Rinchen Barsbold, 2001

summary: A tiny alvarezsaur about 60 cm long with huge eyes and owl-like ears, probably hunting insects at night. Some of its feathers kept traces of keratin.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Luis Chiappe, Mark Norell and James Clark, 1998

summary: A raptor about 2 m long with a short, deep snout and big teeth, known from a partial skull. Its name means “savage robber”.

species:ichthyornis-dispar.placeText: Kansas, Texas and elsewhere in North America
summary: A tern-sized seabird with teeth and strong flight muscles, one of the closest relatives of modern birds. 3D skulls described in 2018 showed it had a beak tip as well as teeth.
An elasmosaur about 11 m long with a neck over 5 m long. One skeleton has gastroliths, stones swallowed perhaps for grinding food or for buoyancy.
A medium-sized mosasaur about 5–6 m long, the most common in the Smoky Hill Chalk. A specimen with soft tissue showed mosasaurs had a shark-like tail fin.

A small herring about 10–15 cm long that swam in huge shoals in the Green River lakes. It is probably the most common vertebrate fossil in the world, and the state fossil of Wyoming. Many were eaten by bigger fish such as Diplomystus.
A herring relative up to about 65 cm long with an upturned mouth. Some fossils have a Knightia stuck in their mouths, apparently choked while swallowing it.

A freshwater stingray about 30 cm long, round like a sun (hence its name), with a barbed tail spine. It lay in the mud of the lake bottom, feeding on shrimp and insect larvae. Its discovery was fought over in the Bone Wars.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Shrimp, insect larvae and small fish

summary: One of the oldest complete bats, with a wingspan of about 37 cm. It already looked much like a modern bat and could probably echolocate, finding moths and other insects by sound.

The most primitive bat known. It had claws on all five fingers, and its ear bones suggest it could not echolocate, so bats probably learned to fly before they learned to hunt by sound. It may have climbed trees and flown with a mix of flapping and gliding.
“Ida”, a young lemur-like primate about 58 cm long including its long tail, is one of the most complete fossil primates ever found, with fur, skin outline and her last meal of fruit and leaves.
Unveiled in 2009 with claims that she was a “missing link” close to the ancestry of monkeys, apes and humans, she is now thought to be an adapiform, closer to lemurs and lorises.

A tiny early horse about the size of a fox terrier, with four toes on its front feet and three on its back, browsing on leaves in the forest. One Messel mare was found with a foal still inside her, positioned for birth.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Otto Haupt, 1925; genus by Jens Franzen, 2006

summary: A small bat with a wingspan of about 30 cm, the most common mammal at Messel. Stomach contents show it ate moths and caddisflies, and pigments show it was reddish-brown. Its short, broad wings suit low flight among trees and over the lake.

An extinct platypus about 60 cm long, with a broad, flat bill. Unlike the living platypus, adults kept their teeth. A complete skull from Riversleigh shows its bill was even wider than the living platypus’s.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Crayfish, frogs and other water animals

species:nimbacinus-dicksoni.ageText: About 16 to 12 million years ago (middle Miocene)
species:nimbacinus-dicksoni.placeText: Queensland and the Northern Territory, Australia
summary: A fox-sized relative of the thylacine, about 5 kg. A complete skull from Riversleigh shows it had a relatively strong bite for its size and could take prey as big as itself.

species:wakaleo-schouteni.ageText: About 23 to 18 million years ago (late Oligocene to early Miocene)
summary: A dog-sized marsupial lion of the Riversleigh rainforest, about 20 kg, with blade-like cheek teeth for slicing meat. Marsupial lions were related to wombats and koalas, and later reached the size of a leopard with Thylacoleo.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Anna Gillespie, Michael Archer and Suzanne Hand, 2017

species:teleoceras-major.placeText: Nebraska and the Great Plains, USA
summary: A barrel-bodied, short-legged rhino about 4 m long with a single small horn on its nose, shaped rather like a hippo. It was long thought to live partly in water like one, but chemical studies of its teeth suggest it grazed on land. More than 100 skeletons lie in the Ashfall “rhino barn”, including mothers with calves, some still suckling.

species:cormohipparion-occidentale.placeText: Nebraska and the Great Plains, USA
summary: A three-toed, pony-sized grazing horse, one of several kinds of horse at Ashfall. Horses evolved mostly in North America, spreading to Asia across the Bering land bridge, and this group of three-toed grazers reached Eurasia and Africa.

One of the best-known early humans. It walked upright on two legs, as the footprints at Laetoli in Tanzania show, but kept long arms and curved fingers for climbing, and had a brain about a third the size of ours. Adults stood about 1–1.5 m tall.
Lucy, found at Hadar in 1974, was named after the Beatles song “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds”, which was playing in camp that night. In Amharic she is Dinkinesh, “you are marvellous”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Donald Johanson, Tim White and Yves Coppens, 1978

species:paranthropus-boisei.placeText: East Africa: Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania and Malawi
summary: A “robust” relative of humans with a huge jaw, cheek teeth about four times the size of ours, very thick enamel, and a crest along the top of its skull for enormous chewing muscles. Its brain was about 500–550 cm³, a little larger than a chimpanzee’s. Mary Leakey found the first skull at Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, in 1959, and it was nicknamed “Nutcracker Man”.
The nickname is misleading: chemical signatures in its tooth enamel show it ate mostly grasses and sedges, and its teeth lack the wear of a nut-cracker; it was a heavy-duty grinder of tough plants.

It lived alongside early Homo, including Homo erectus, for about a million years. Footprints at Ileret in Kenya, about 1.5 million years old, show the two walking the same lakeshore within hours or days of each other. In 2025 the first hand bones confidently linked to it showed a powerful, gorilla-like grip with a long thumb able to make precise grips, reopening the question of whether it made stone tools. The older Paranthropus aethiopicus (the “Black Skull”, about 2.5 million years old) and Paranthropus robustus of South Africa were its relatives.

species:paranthropus-robustus.placeText: Swartkrans, Kromdraai and Drimolen caves, South Africa
summary: The southern African “robust” hominin, with big cheek teeth and a crested skull, though less extreme than its East African relative Paranthropus boisei. Robert Broom named it in 1938 from a skull found at Kromdraai by a schoolboy, Gert Terblanche; hundreds of fossils have since come from the caves of the Cradle of Humankind. Its diet was more varied than boisei’s, including harder foods.

A 2-million-year-old skull from Drimolen, described in 2020, lies in the same cave deposits as an early Homo erectus skull, showing the two lived side by side. Worn bone tools from Swartkrans, perhaps used to dig into termite mounds, may have been used by either. In 2025 proteins read from its 2-million-year-old tooth enamel revealed the sex of individuals and hinted the group was more varied than its bones suggest.

related.note: Its larger-toothed East African relative.

species:homo-naledi.placeText: Rising Star Cave, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa
summary: In 2013 cavers Rick Hunter and Steven Tucker squeezed through an 18 cm-wide crack deep in the Rising Star Cave and found bones covering the floor of a chamber. Lee Berger’s team recruited slim scientists to go in, and recovered over 1,500 bones from at least 15 individuals, the richest find of any human relative in Africa, named in 2015. More, including a partial skeleton called “Neo” and a child’s skull called “Leti”, came from nearby chambers.

It mixes old and new features: a brain of only about 465–610 cm³, about a third the size of ours, curved fingers for climbing and ape-like shoulders, but human-like feet, wrists and hands. People expected it to be about 2 million years old, so the 2017 dates of about 335,000 to 236,000 years were a shock: small-brained humans were living in southern Africa when Homo sapiens was appearing.

How the bodies got so deep into the cave is debated. Berger’s team argues Homo naledi carried its dead there on purpose, and in 2023 claimed it buried them in pits, used fire and engraved marks on the walls. Most specialists who reviewed this found the evidence too weak to show deliberate burial or engravings, and the claims remain unproven.

species:homo-erectus.placeText: Africa and Asia, from Georgia to China and Java
summary: The first human species with a body much like ours: tall, long-legged and built for walking and running long distances, with a brain that grew over its history from about 600 to over 1,000 cm³. It was the first to spread out of Africa, reaching Dmanisi in Georgia about 1.8 million years ago and China and Java soon after. It made teardrop-shaped Acheulean hand axes for over a million years, and probably used fire.

Eugène Dubois found the first fossil, “Java Man”, in 1891, and “Peking Man” followed in China in the 1920s–30s, though those fossils were lost in 1941. The most complete skeleton is the “Turkana Boy” from Kenya, about 1.5 million years old. Its oldest known skull, from Drimolen in South Africa, is about 2 million years old, and the last known Homo erectus lived at Ngandong, Java, about 117,000 to 108,000 years ago, making it the longest-lasting human species known.

Early African fossils are sometimes called Homo ergaster. It lived alongside Paranthropus for about a million years; footprints at Ileret in Kenya show the two on the same lakeshore. A shell from Trinil, Java, about 500,000 years old, carries a zigzag engraving that may be its work.

related.note: Lived alongside it in East Africa for about a million years.

species:smilodon-fatalis.placeText: North America and western South America
summary: The famous sabre-toothed cat, about the size of a lion but more heavily built, with 18 cm upper canines. It probably wrestled prey to the ground with its powerful forelimbs, then bit its throat. Over 2,000 have come from La Brea, the most common big mammal there, and many have healed injuries, which some researchers take as a sign that it lived in groups. This is debated.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Bison, horses, camels and ground sloths

species:smilodon-fatalis.akaNote: Often called a sabre-toothed tiger, but it was not closely related to tigers.

species:panthera-atrox.placeText: North America, from Alaska to Mexico
summary: A huge lion-like cat, about 25% bigger than an African lion, that hunted horses, bison and camels across North America. It is much rarer than Smilodon at La Brea.

A wolf bigger and heavier than a grey wolf, with a powerful bite. It is the most common mammal at La Brea: over 4,000 individuals, probably packs drawn in by trapped animals. DNA shows it was not a close relative of the grey wolf, but the last of a separate lineage that evolved in the Americas.
In 2025 a company announced wolf pups gene-edited to look like dire wolves; they are grey wolves with a handful of changes, not true dire wolves.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Horses, bison and other large animals

species:aenocyon-dirus.akaNote: Long placed in Canis with wolves; a 2021 DNA study moved it to its own genus, Aenocyon.

species:mammuthus-columbi.placeText: North America, from Canada to Central America
summary: A giant mammoth of warmer, more southern North America, up to about 4 m tall at the shoulder, bigger than the woolly mammoth and with less hair. DNA suggests it arose from interbreeding between woolly mammoths and an older lineage. “Zed”, a near-complete skeleton, was found at La Brea in 2006.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: Up to about 4 m at the shoulder

species:paramylodon-harlani.ageText: Pliocene and Pleistocene, until about 11,000 years ago
summary: A giant ground sloth about 3 m long and over a tonne, with huge claws and small bones (osteoderms) studding its skin like chain mail. It probably dug for roots and grazed, and is one of the most common plant-eaters at La Brea.

One of the two largest snakes known, about 13 m long and over a tonne, a member of the boa family and a relative of anacondas. Vasuki of India, named in 2024, may have been as long or longer, but both sizes are estimated from backbones alone. Its size shows the tropics were much hotter than today, since cold-blooded animals can only grow that big in great heat. It probably ate fish and crocodile relatives in the swamps.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Titanoboa: Monster Snake (2012), ARK: Survival Evolved

summary: A giant side-necked turtle with a shell about 1.7 m long and powerful jaws, big enough to eat crocodiles. Its name means “coal turtle”.
A small, short-snouted dyrosaurid, a crocodile relative about 2 m long, and probably prey for Titanoboa.

species:gastornis-giganteus.placeText: Wyoming and New Mexico, USA; relatives in Europe and Asia
summary: A flightless bird about 2 m tall with a huge, deep beak. It was long pictured as a predator of tiny horses, but its beak lacks a hook and chemical studies of its bones suggest it ate plants, seeds and nuts. Long known in North America as Diatryma.
species:gastornis-giganteus.akaNote: North American fossils were long called Diatryma; they are now placed in Gastornis.

summary: The “dawn horse”, about the size of a small dog, with four toes on its front feet and three on its back, browsing leaves in the forest. It is one of the first members of the horse family, which evolved over 50 million years into today’s single-toed grazers.
species:eohippus-angustidens.akaNote: Often called Hyracotherium, a name now usually kept for a European animal outside the horse family.

summary: A hippo-like pantodont about 2.25 m long with short legs and tusk-like canines, one of the first large mammals, living in swamps and along rivers. It had one of the smallest brains for its size of any mammal.
One of the earliest whales, a wolf-sized, long-tailed, four-legged land animal that waded in streams for food. Only its ear bones, thick-walled like a whale’s, give away its relationships.
The “walking, swimming whale”, about 3 m long, built like a crocodile with big webbed feet. It probably ambushed animals at the water’s edge and could move on land and swim by flexing its back.

Known only from a single skull 83 cm long, the largest skull of any land mammal meat-eater. It was long pictured as a giant wolf-like predator, but it was an even-toed hoofed mammal, part of the group that includes pigs, hippos and whales; its exact relatives and diet are debated.

species:basilosaurus-isis.placeText: Egypt and elsewhere around the Tethys
summary: A long, eel-like early whale up to about 18 m long, with tiny back legs about 60 cm long, useless for walking. It was the top predator of its seas.
A dolphin-shaped early whale about 5 m long with small hind legs. It may have come into the bay to give birth, where its young were hunted by Basilosaurus.

The largest land mammal ever, a hornless rhino relative about 4.8 m tall at the shoulder and 15–20 tonnes, with a long neck for browsing treetops like a giraffe. Its relatives, sometimes called Indricotherium, roamed from China to eastern Europe.
species:paraceratherium-bugtiense.akaNote: Indricotherium and Baluchitherium are often treated as synonyms of Paraceratherium, though some researchers keep Indricotherium separate.

species:daeodon-shoshonensis.placeText: Nebraska, Oregon and the western USA
summary: The largest entelodont, or “hell pig”, about 1.8 m tall at the shoulder, with a huge head, bony cheek flanges and teeth for crushing bone. It probably scavenged and hunted, eating almost anything.
species:daeodon-shoshonensis.akaNote: Dinohyus is a synonym. Despite the nickname, entelodonts were not pigs.

species:menoceras-arikarense.placeText: Nebraska and the Great Plains, USA
summary: A pig-sized rhino with a pair of small horns side by side on its nose, worn only by males. Thousands died together around the Agate waterhole in a drought.
A horse-like chalicothere about 2.4 m tall at the shoulder with big claws instead of hooves on its front feet, used to pull down branches. It walked on the sides of its clawed hands.
A small burrowing beaver that dug spiral burrows 2–3 m deep with its teeth, the “Devil’s corkscrews”. They puzzled scientists until beaver skeletons were found inside them.
A small, slender, gazelle-like camel about 60 cm tall at the shoulder, found in a quarry full of skeletons, perhaps a herd.
A flightless predatory bird about 2.5 m tall with a huge, hooked, axe-like beak. Terror birds ran down prey and struck with their beaks, and were South America’s top predators for millions of years.
An early New World monkey, about the size of a capuchin, living in the forests of Miocene Patagonia, far south of any monkey today.

A giant elephant relative about 4 m tall at the shoulder with tusks on its lower jaw curving down and back, perhaps for stripping bark or pulling down branches. Its family survived in Africa until about 1 million years ago.
A three-toed, pony-sized horse that spread from North America into Europe, part of the Hipparion group. Skeletons from Höwenegg, Germany, include a mare with a foal inside her.
A gorilla-shaped chalicothere about 2.6 m tall with long, hooked front claws, which it walked on its knuckles to protect.

The largest shark ever, with teeth up to 18 cm long. Estimates of its size range from about 14 to over 20 m; recent studies suggest it was more slender than a scaled-up great white. Bite marks on fossil whale bones show it ate whales. It died out about 3.6 million years ago, perhaps outcompeted by the great white as the oceans cooled.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: The Meg (2018), Meg 2: The Trench (2023), ARK: Survival Evolved

species:otodus-megalodon.akaNote: Once placed in Carcharodon (with the great white) or Carcharocles; most researchers now put it in Otodus.

summary: A giant sperm whale about 14–17 m long with the biggest teeth of any animal (excluding tusks), up to 36 cm. Unlike today’s sperm whales it had teeth in both jaws and hunted big prey, probably other whales. It is named after the Leviathan and Herman Melville, author of Moby-Dick.
species:livyatan-melvillei.akaNote: First named Leviathan in 2010, then renamed Livyatan because the name Leviathan was already taken.

summary: A ground sloth that took to the sea, grazing on seagrass and seaweed along the coast. Later species grew denser bones and became more aquatic over 4 million years.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Christian de Muizon and H. Gregory McDonald, 1995

summary: A slender seal with a long neck and snout, once thought to be an ancestor of the leopard seal.

A sabre-toothed predator about the size of a jaguar, but a relative of marsupials rather than a cat: a famous case of convergent evolution. Its sabres grew throughout life, protected by a bony flange on the chin. Its eyes faced sideways, unlike most predators’.
species:thylacosmilus-atrox.akaNote: Not a cat: a sparassodont, related to marsupials, that evolved sabre teeth independently.

summary: The heaviest flying bird known, about 70 kg, with a wingspan of about 6–7 m. Like a condor, it soared on rising air currents over the Andes foothills and pampas.

Probably the largest ape ever, a relative of the orangutan. It is known only from four jaws and about 2,000 teeth, so its size is a guess from those: estimates of up to about 3 m tall and 200–300 kg are very uncertain. The teeth were first recognised by Ralph von Koenigswald in 1935 among “dragon teeth” sold in a Hong Kong pharmacy. It ate fruit and plants in the forest, and died out when the forests changed.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: Unknown; estimates up to about 3 m and 200–300 kg

summary: A giant madtsoiid snake known from 27 vertebrae, some found still joined, in a lignite mine in western India. From the size of its vertebrae its describers estimated a length of about 11 to 15 m, a match for Titanoboa, though with no skull or tail bones the figure is uncertain. Its broad, cylindrical body suggests a slow ambush hunter, like today’s anacondas.

It lived in coastal swamps in a much warmer world than today, which allowed cold-blooded animals to grow huge. Its closest relatives were Madtsoia of Late Cretaceous India and Gigantophis of Eocene Egypt, which suggests its lineage began in India and spread to Africa after India joined Asia. It is named after Vasuki, the serpent king coiled around the neck of the Hindu god Shiva.

The largest otter known, estimated from its teeth and thighbone at around 200 kg, about the size of a lion. It is known only from teeth and parts of the skeleton, so its size and shape in life are uncertain. Its broad, blunt cheek teeth were built for crushing rather than slicing, like those of the modern sea otter.

A 2022 study of its tooth enamel found chemical signatures like those of the big cats and hyenas it lived with, not of water-living animals such as hippos. This suggests it spent much of its time on land and hunted or scavenged land animals, unlike any living otter, though it may still have taken fish, shellfish and other water prey.

It shared the Omo Valley with early humans and their relatives. Its genus, whose name means “otter tooth”, lived in Africa and South Asia from about 7 million to 2 million years ago; another giant, Enhydriodon dikikae, lived in the Hadar region of Ethiopia in Lucy’s time.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Camille Grohé, Kevin Uno and Jean-Renaud Boisserie, 2022

species:homo-sapiens.placeText: Every continent (Antarctica only in research stations)
summary: Our species. The oldest fossils that look like early Homo sapiens come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco and are about 300,000 years old. For most of our history we lived only in Africa.

From about 60,000 years ago people spread out of Africa across Asia and Europe, meeting and interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans. They crossed the sea to Australia by about 50,000 years ago, reached the Americas by at least 16,000 years ago (footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, may be 21,000 to 23,000 years old), and settled New Zealand, the last large land mass, around 1280 CE.
In 1969 two members of the species walked on the Moon.

facts.label: Oldest fossils
facts.value: Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, about 300,000 years old

species:homo-neanderthalensis.placeText: Europe and western and central Asia
summary: Our closest extinct relatives: stocky, strong, big-brained humans adapted to the cold of Ice Age Europe. They made fine stone tools, controlled fire, hunted large animals, buried some of their dead and made simple ornaments and cave markings.

Modern humans arrived in Europe from about 45,000 years ago, and within a few thousand years the Neanderthals were gone. The two interbred: most people with ancestry from outside Africa carry about 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA.

facts.label: Brain
facts.value: About 1,400–1,500 cm³, as big as ours or bigger

facts.label: Legacy
facts.value: About 1–2% of the DNA of people outside Africa

species:homo-floresiensis.placeText: Liang Bua cave and the Soa Basin, Flores, Indonesia
summary: A tiny human found in 2003 in Liang Bua cave on the island of Flores and nicknamed the “hobbit”. The best skeleton, a woman known as LB1, stood about 1.06 m tall and had a brain of about 420 cm³, about the size of a chimpanzee’s, yet her species made stone tools. It had long, flat feet, short legs and a wrist built like an ape’s.

At first its bones were thought to be as young as 12,000 years, but redating in 2016 showed they are about 100,000 to 60,000 years old, with its stone tools from about 190,000 to 50,000 years ago. It disappeared around the time modern humans reached the region, though whether they were the cause is not known. Even older, 700,000-year-old fossils from the Soa Basin, described in 2016 and 2024, come from people just as small.

Most researchers think it descended from Homo erectus that reached Flores and shrank over many generations, as large animals often do on islands (island dwarfism); others argue for an older, smaller-bodied ancestor. Early claims that LB1 was a modern human with a disorder such as microcephaly have been largely rejected. It shared Flores with dwarf elephant relatives (Stegodon), Komodo dragons, giant rats and a giant marabou stork.

facts.label: Brain
facts.value: About 420 cm³, roughly a third of ours

species:homo-longi.ageText: About 220,000 to 50,000 years ago, perhaps later
species:homo-longi.placeText: Asia, from Siberia and the Tibetan Plateau to China and Taiwan
summary: An extinct group of humans first discovered from DNA alone. In 2010 the genome from a tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave, in Siberia’s Altai Mountains, revealed a kind of human no one knew existed, the closest relatives of the Neanderthals. For years they were known only from a few teeth and bone scraps.

Proteins later identified a jaw from a cave on the Tibetan Plateau (2019), at least 160,000 years old, and a jaw dredged from the sea off Taiwan (2025). In 2025, proteins and DNA from the Harbin “Dragon Man” skull, at least 146,000 years old, showed it was Denisovan, giving the first look at a face: a big brain, a heavy brow and very large teeth. Because that skull had been named Homo longi in 2021, many researchers now use that name for Denisovans, though others prefer not to give them a species name. In 2026, teeth, bones and over 1,300 stone tools from Bianfu Cave in Yunnan, about 167,000 to 134,000 years old, and proteins from fossils at Xujiayao in northern China added more.

They interbred with Neanderthals: “Denny”, a girl from Denisova Cave, had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. They also interbred with modern humans. People of New Guinea, Aboriginal Australians and the Ayta of the Philippines carry several per cent Denisovan DNA, so Denisovans probably lived in Southeast Asia too, and a gene variant that helps Tibetans live at high altitude came from them.

facts.label: First found
facts.value: Denisova Cave, Russia; identified from DNA in 2010

facts.label: Named Homo longi
facts.value: Ji Qiang and colleagues, 2021, from the Harbin skull

facts.label: Legacy
facts.value: Several per cent of the DNA of some Oceanian and Southeast Asian peoples

species:mammuthus-primigenius.placeText: Northern Eurasia and North America; last on Wrangel Island, Russia
summary: An elephant built for the Ice Age, about the size of an African elephant, with a coat of long hair, small ears, a short tail, a fatty hump and long, curving tusks. It grazed the vast, dry “mammoth steppe” that stretched from Spain to Canada.

As the Ice Age ended the steppe shrank and people hunted mammoths, and most populations were gone by about 10,000 years ago. A small population hung on, cut off on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean, until about 4,000 years ago, when the pyramids of Giza were already standing.

species:thylacinus-cynocephalus.placeText: Australia and New Guinea; finally only Tasmania
summary: The “Tasmanian tiger”, a dog-sized meat-eating marsupial with stripes across its back and a stiff tail. Females carried their young in a backward-facing pouch. It looked so much like a dog because it evolved to fill the same role.

It died out on mainland Australia about 3,200 years ago, perhaps because of people and the arrival of the dingo, and survived only in Tasmania. European settlers paid bounties for killing them, and the last known thylacine died at Hobart’s Beaumaris Zoo on 7 September 1936. The name “Benjamin” often given to it first appeared decades later and is not recorded from the time.
species:thylacinus-cynocephalus.akaNote: A marsupial, neither a tiger nor a wolf.

summary: A flightless pigeon about a metre tall, found only on the island of Mauritius. Its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon. With no predators on the island, it had no need to fly and no fear of people.

Dutch sailors settled Mauritius from 1598. Hunting, and the rats, pigs, monkeys and dogs they brought, which ate the dodos’ ground nests, wiped it out in under a century. The last widely accepted sighting was in 1662.

Possibly once the most numerous bird on Earth, with an estimated 3 to 5 billion birds. Flocks a kilometre wide took hours to pass overhead, and they nested in colonies covering hundreds of square kilometres of forest.

Commercial hunting, made easy by the telegraph and railways, and the clearing of the eastern forests destroyed it within a few decades. The last one, Martha, died at Cincinnati Zoo on 1 September 1914.

species:pinguinus-impennis.placeText: Rocky islands of the North Atlantic
summary: A large flightless seabird, black above and white below, that swam after fish like a penguin. It was the original “penguin”: the name was given to the southern birds later, because they looked like it.

It came ashore to breed on just a few remote islands, where sailors killed vast numbers for meat, oil and feathers. As it became rare, collectors paid for specimens. The last breeding pair was killed on Eldey, off Iceland, in June 1844.

species:hydrodamalis-gigas.placeText: North Pacific; last around the Commander Islands, Russia
summary: A giant relative of the manatee, up to about 8 m long, that grazed on kelp in cold coastal waters. Fossils show it once lived all around the North Pacific rim, from Japan to California.

By the time Europeans found it, only a small population was left around the Commander Islands in the Bering Sea. The naturalist Georg Steller described it in 1741, after Vitus Bering’s expedition was shipwrecked there. Fur hunters killed the slow animals for meat, and within 27 years they were gone.

One of the tallest birds that ever lived: with its neck stretched up, a female could reach about 3.6 m. Females were much bigger than males. Moa had no wings at all, not even the small bones other flightless birds keep. Their only predator was Haast’s eagle.
Polynesian settlers reached New Zealand around 1280 CE. Moa had never met people, and hunting and forest burning wiped out all nine species within about 150 years.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: Up to about 3.6 m with neck raised (females)

species:bos-primigenius.placeText: Europe, North Africa and Asia; last in Poland
summary: The wild ancestor of domestic cattle: huge, long-horned and fierce, with bulls standing about 1.8 m at the shoulder. Aurochs are painted on the walls of Lascaux cave, and cattle were domesticated from them about 10,500 years ago in the Middle East and separately in South Asia.
Hunting and the loss of forests to farming pushed them back to central Europe. The last herd was protected as royal game in the Jaktorów Forest in Poland, where the last aurochs, a cow, died in 1627.
A zebra striped only on its head and neck, fading to plain brown behind. DNA shows it was a southern form of the plains zebra rather than a separate species. Its name copies its call.

Settlers shot quaggas for meat and hides and to keep the grass for their livestock, and the last wild ones were killed in the 1870s. The last quagga died at Artis Zoo in Amsterdam on 12 August 1883. The Quagga Project in South Africa is breeding plains zebras to bring back its look.

A shaggy, cold-adapted rhino about 3.5 m long with a flattened front horn over 1 m long, worn on its underside, probably from sweeping snow aside to reach grass. Frozen carcasses from Siberia preserve its fur and stomach contents, and it was painted on the walls of Chauvet cave in France more than 30,000 years ago.
Its decline seems to have followed the warming at the end of the last glacial period more than human hunting.

facts.label: On screen
facts.value: Prehistoric Planet: Ice Age (2023), ARK: Survival Evolved

species:panthera-spelaea.placeText: Europe, northern Asia, Alaska and the Yukon
summary: A lion about 10% bigger than today’s, closely related but separate, which hunted reindeer, horses and young mammoths across the mammoth steppe. Cave paintings at Chauvet show lions without manes. Frozen cubs, Boris and Sparta, were found in the Siberian permafrost in 2017–2018.

A huge bear, males up to about 500 kg, that hibernated in caves, where many died over the winters, leaving thousands of skeletons: over 30,000 in the Drachenhöhle in Austria alone. Its teeth show it ate mostly plants. It may have declined as people competed with it for caves and climate cooled.

A giant deer, not an elk and not only Irish, standing about 2.1 m at the shoulder with antlers up to 3.6 m across, the largest of any deer. Many have been dug from Irish peat bogs. It survived longest in western Siberia, until about 7,700 years ago.
species:megaloceros-giganteus.akaNote: Called the Irish elk, but it lived across Eurasia and was not an elk: its closest living relative is the fallow deer.

species:elasmotherium-sibiricum.placeText: Steppes of Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan
summary: A giant rhino about 4.5 m long and 3.5–4 tonnes with a huge bony dome on its forehead that supported a horn. The horn itself, made of keratin, has never been found, so its size is unknown, despite popular pictures of a long “Siberian unicorn” horn. Dating in 2018 showed it survived until about 39,000 years ago, overlapping with modern humans.
