A lion-sized cat with long legs, a sloping back and shorter, serrated “scimitar” sabres, built for chasing prey across open country, perhaps in groups. A jaw trawled from the North Sea floor, then dry land, is about 28,000 years old. A mummified cub was found in Siberian permafrost in 2024.

One of the largest meat-eating land mammals ever, standing about 3.4 m on its hind legs, with long legs and a short face. Its bones suggest it ate a lot of meat, perhaps driving other predators off kills, though it may also have eaten plants.

A shaggy, stocky elephant relative about 2.5–3 m tall, a browser of forests and swamps with cone-cusped teeth for chewing twigs and leaves (its name means “nipple tooth”). Thomas Jefferson hoped explorers would find living mastodons in the American West.
A beaver the size of a black bear, about 2 m long and 100 kg, with incisors up to 15 cm long. Its teeth were not suited for felling trees: it ate water plants and probably did not build dams.
“Yesterday’s camel”, a tall camel about 2.2 m at the shoulder, closer to llamas than to Old World camels, common at La Brea and across western North America.

species:glyptotherium-texanum.placeText: Southern North America to northern South America
summary: The North American glyptodont, a giant armadillo relative about 2.5 m long under a domed shell of more than 1,000 bony plates. Glyptodonts crossed from South America over the new Panama land bridge.
The largest glyptodont, about 3.6 m long and 1.4 tonnes, with a tail ending in a spiked club like a medieval mace. Dents in glyptodont shells suggest males fought each other with their tails.

An elephant-sized ground sloth about 6 m long and 4 tonnes that could rear up on its hind legs to pull down branches with its huge claws. Georges Cuvier named it in 1796 from a skeleton sent to Madrid, one of the first extinct animals to be recognised.

A long-necked, camel-like hoofed mammal about 3 m long, with nostrils high on its head that may mean a short trunk. Charles Darwin found the first bones in 1834 at Puerto San Julián. Proteins from its bones showed in 2015 that litopterns were distant relatives of horses and rhinos.

A rhino-sized hoofed mammal about 2.7 m long with curved, ever-growing teeth. Darwin bought a skull from a farmer in Uruguay for eighteen pence in 1833 and called it “perhaps one of the strangest animals ever discovered”.

species:smilodon-populator.placeText: South America east of the Andes
summary: The largest sabre-toothed cat, up to about 220–400 kg, with canines up to 28 cm including roots. It moved into South America over the Panama land bridge and hunted the giant ground sloths and toxodonts there.

The largest marsupial ever, a wombat relative the size of a hippo, about 3–4 m long and up to 2.7 tonnes. Females carried young in a pouch. Trackways show it roamed in herds, and it may have migrated seasonally. It disappeared soon after people reached Australia.
species:diprotodon-optatum.akaNote: A relative of wombats, not a wombat itself.

summary: A leopard-sized marsupial predator, about 100–160 kg, with one of the strongest bites for its size of any known mammal predator, slicing cheek teeth, and a huge thumb claw. Scratch marks in caves show it could climb, perhaps raising young in caves and dragging prey into trees.

A giant monitor lizard, a relative of the Komodo dragon, perhaps 3.5–7 m long (estimates vary widely). It was probably Australia’s top land predator, possibly with a venomous bite like its living relatives.
species:varanus-priscus.akaNote: Long known as Megalania prisca; it is now placed in Varanus with living monitor lizards.

summary: The largest kangaroo ever, about 2 m tall and 230 kg, with a short, flat face and a single big toe on each foot. It probably walked on its hind legs rather than hopping, browsing leaves from trees with its long-clawed arms.
A flightless “thunder bird” about 2 m tall and over 200 kg, related to ducks and geese. Burnt eggshells may show people cooking its eggs, though whose eggs they are is debated.

The largest eagle ever, females weighing 10–15 kg with a wingspan of 2.6–3 m and massive talons. It hunted moa, many times its own weight. When people wiped out the moa it lost its prey and died out too. Māori tradition remembers it as Pouākai or Te Hōkioi. DNA shows its closest relative is the small little eagle of Australia.
species:hieraaetus-moorei.akaNote: First named Harpagornis; DNA shows it belongs in Hieraaetus with much smaller living eagles.

summary: One of the largest elephants ever, males about 4 m tall and up to 13 tonnes, with long, nearly straight tusks. It lived in the forests of Europe in warm interglacials. Neanderthals butchered them: a 125,000-year-old site in Germany shows dozens processed for meat and fat.
A dwarf elephant only about 1.4 m tall and 200 kg, a tenth the size of its straight-tusked ancestor, which shrank after reaching Cyprus. It died out soon after people arrived on the island.

A small, long-legged caenagnathid, a toothless, beaked relative of Anzu. Its foot bones were moved between several genera for nearly 90 years before it got its own name in 2020. The legs of two young Citipes were found in the stomach of a young Gorgosaurus, showing young tyrannosaurs hunted small, fast dinosaurs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: William Parks, 1933 (as Ornithomimus elegans); genus by Gregory Funston, 2020

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably plants, small animals and eggs

species:gillicus-arcuatus.placeText: Kansas and the Western Interior, USA
summary: An ichthyodectid fish about 2 m long with small teeth, a smaller relative of Xiphactinus that probably fed on small fish and plankton. The famous “fish within a fish” in Hays, Kansas, is a Gillicus swallowed whole by a Xiphactinus.

A slender, needle-snouted predatory fish up to about 1 m long. Several Solnhofen slabs show an Aspidorhynchus with its teeth tangled in the wing of a Rhamphorhynchus, probably snapping at the pterosaur as it fished, and both dying together.
An Asian uintathere about the size of a cow, with a strange, swollen, bulbous snout but none of the horns or tusks of its North American relatives.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Henry Fairfield Osborn and Walter Granger, 1932

summary: A crocodile relative about 6 m long with a long, flat, wide head and slender teeth. It probably lay still in the water with its jaws open, snapping them shut on passing fish.

A duck-billed dinosaur about 9 m long whose name means “good mother lizard”. Nesting grounds at Egg Mountain hold mud nests of eggs and babies too large to be newly hatched but still in the nest, evidence that parents fed and protected their young. A bonebed of thousands of individuals shows they lived in huge herds.

A horned dinosaur about 4.5 m long with a nose horn that curved forwards and down like a bottle opener, and two long spikes on its frill. It is known from bonebeds of many animals that died together, perhaps in droughts.

A second species of Daspletosaurus, about 9 m long, younger than D. torosus. Its describers argued that it evolved directly from D. torosus, and that the rough bone texture of its face shows it had a scaly, sensitive snout like a crocodile’s. Both ideas have been debated.

A giant azhdarchid pterosaur known mainly from a neck vertebra that would have been about 78 cm long when complete, suggesting a wingspan of roughly 7–10 m. It was first named Titanopteryx in 1959, but that name was already taken, so it was renamed after its describer, Camille Arambourg. The species name comes from Philadelphia, the ancient name of Amman.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Camille Arambourg, 1959 (as Titanopteryx); genus by Lev Nessov, 1984

summary: A big predator about 10 m long, collected at Bahariya in 1914 and long counted as Carcharodontosaurus. The bones were destroyed in a bombing raid on Munich in 1944, but a 2025 study of old photographs found enough differences to give it its own name. The name means “thief from the beloved land”, from Ta-mery, an ancient name for Egypt, and honours the collector Richard Markgraf.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Maximilian Kellermann, Elena Cuesta and Oliver Rauhut, 2025

facts.label: Known from
facts.value: Photographs and drawings of bones destroyed in 1944

summary: An ankylosaur with a broad, armoured skull and a heavy tail club, named in 2021 from a partial skeleton found at Hermiin Tsav in the Nemegt Formation. Other Tarchia species are known from slightly older Gobi rocks.

species:typothorax-coccinarum.placeText: New Mexico, Arizona and Texas, USA
summary: An aetosaur about 3 m long with a very wide, flat body covered in bony plates, and a small, pig-like snout for rooting for plants.

species:desmatosuchus-spurensis.placeText: Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, USA
summary: An aetosaur about 4.5 m long armoured with bony plates and a pair of long, curved spikes on each shoulder, probably for defence against predators such as Postosuchus.

One of the largest phytosaurs, perhaps 7 m long, a crocodile look-alike with a long, heavy snout, hunting along the Chinle rivers. Its nostrils sat on a mound just in front of its eyes, not at the tip of its snout.

A stocky, beaked rhynchosaur about 1.5 m long that sheared tough plants with rows of teeth on its palate. In the lower Ischigualasto it is by far the most common animal, outnumbering the early dinosaurs.
A large, plant-eating cynodont about 1.8 m long with broad grinding cheek teeth, a relative of the ancestors of mammals.

The top predator of the Ischigualasto, about 6–7 m long, with a deep skull and large blade-like teeth, on the crocodile side of the archosaur family. It was bigger than any of the early dinosaurs around it.

A small plant-eater about 1 m long, known from a partial skeleton. It was long thought to be the oldest ornithischian dinosaur, but a 2017 study suggested it is a silesaurid, a close relative of dinosaurs rather than a dinosaur.
A lungfish with a long, duck-billed snout covered in tiny tooth-like denticles, perhaps for crushing small shelled animals. Gogo specimens preserve its skull in perfect 3D.
A predatory lobe-finned fish with a whorl of large, curved fangs at the front of its lower jaw. Gogo specimens preserve its skull in such detail that its jaw mechanism could be reconstructed.

A giant coelacanth, relatives of which reached perhaps 5 m, living in the rivers of the Kem Kem. Coelacanths like it were once thought to have died out with the dinosaurs, until a living one was caught off South Africa in 1938.
A lungfish known from its big crushing tooth plates, common in the Kem Kem. It is placed in the same genus as the living Queensland lungfish, one of the longest-lived genera of vertebrates.
A large, long-snouted crocodile relative of the Kem Kem rivers, a fish-eater related to Sarcosuchus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: René Lavocat, 1955 (genus by France de Broin, 2002)

summary: A toothless, ant-eating mammal about 90 cm long with powerful digging claws and a gripping tail. It was first described as an anteater, which would mean anteaters once lived in Europe, but most researchers now think it is a relative of pangolins that evolved a similar body.

A small insect-eating mammal about 75 cm long, most of it tail, with long hind legs, short arms and a long, mobile nose. It may have run or hopped on its hind legs. Stomach contents include insects, lizards and small mammals.
A tree-climbing mammal about 1.15 m long with a long, bushy tail, preserved with its fur outline. Its strong canines and teeth suggest it ate fruit, seeds and nuts.
The most common bird at Messel, a long-legged, rail-like ground bird about 30 cm long, distantly related to today’s sunbittern and kagu.
A medium-sized alligator relative, the most common crocodylian at Messel. Its family lived in Europe for over 40 million years.
A long-legged wading bird with a duck-like bill, an early relative of ducks and geese. It nested in huge colonies on the lake shores: whole beds of its bones and eggshells are found.
A crocodylian of the Green River lakes, a later relative of Borealosuchus sternbergii of Hell Creek, showing its family survived the asteroid.
A kangaroo relative with large, blade-like premolars. It is sometimes called a “killer kangaroo”, but whether it ate meat or tough plants is debated.
A small, short-snouted crocodile about 1 m long that seems to have lived on land. The popular idea that its relatives dropped on prey from trees is speculation without fossil support.
A sheep-sized relative of Diprotodon that climbed trees, with long, strong arms and big claws. Dozens of skeletons, from babies to adults, were found together in an ancient cave.
One of the earliest primates of North America, a small, lemur-like tree-dweller about 2 kg, which arrived as the world warmed at the start of the Eocene.

species:pseudhipparion-gratum.placeText: Nebraska and the Great Plains, USA
summary: A small, three-toed grazing horse, about the size of a goat, one of several kinds of horse buried at Ashfall.
A wolf-sized meat-eating sparassodont, a relative of marsupials, and one of the main mammal predators of Miocene Patagonia.
An early glyptodont about 1 m long, small compared with its Ice Age relatives, already covered in a domed shell of bony plates.
A fossil penguin of the same genus as today’s Humboldt and African penguins, larger than its living relatives, which fished the cold, rich coastal waters off Peru.
A small, fast, two-legged plant-eater about 3 m long with long legs and a horny beak. Fossils of very young animals are known as well as adults.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Othniel Marsh, 1878 (as Laosaurus altus); genus Dryosaurus 1894

summary: A bulky plant-eater about 5–7 m long, an early relative of Iguanodon that could walk on two or four legs.

A small coelurosaur about 2 m long with grasping hands, known from one partial skeleton found at Bone Cabin Quarry in 1900. Its name, “bird robber”, reflects an old guess about its diet; it probably ate small animals of many kinds.

species:barosaurus-lentus.placeText: Utah, South Dakota and Wyoming, USA
summary: A diplodocid about 26 m long with an even longer neck than Diplodocus. The American Museum of Natural History mounts one rearing up to defend its young from an Allosaurus, a pose that is possible but debated.

One of the longest dinosaurs known, a diplodocid usually estimated at about 33–35 m. Some newer estimates based on single neck bones are much higher, but they are disputed. A more complete skeleton from Wyoming, nicknamed “Jimbo”, is still being studied.
A medium-sized sauropod about 15 m long, more primitive than the Morrison’s diplodocids and macronarians.
A stegosaur about 6 m long with longer, lower plates than Stegosaurus. One specimen preserves impressions of the horny sheath that covered a plate in life.
One of the earliest ankylosaurs known from a good skull, about 3–4 m long, with bony armour over its body.
One of the smallest known plant-eating dinosaurs, about 70 cm long and under 1 kg, with small tusk-like teeth. Its teeth suggest it ate both plants and small animals such as insects.
A small mammal relative with complex grinding teeth, known mostly from jaws, one of the commonest mammals of the Morrison.

A turkey-sized oviraptorosaur with a short, toothy beak, short arms with fans of long feathers, and a fan of feathers on its tail, probably for display. Gizzard stones found with its skeletons suggest it ate mostly plants.
A small oviraptorosaur with a pair of large, rodent-like front teeth, suggesting it ate plants.
A turkey-sized feathered dinosaur with symmetrical feathers on its arms and tail, probably an early oviraptorosaur. It could not fly.
A duck-sized troodontid found curled up with its head tucked under its arm, just like a sleeping bird, buried by volcanic ash. Its name means “soundly sleeping dragon”.

A mouse-sized early mammal preserved with traces of fur. It was described as an early eutherian, on the branch leading to placental mammals, though some later studies place it just outside that branch. Its feet suggest it could climb. Its name means “dawn mother”.
A small, early mammal with a spur on its ankle like a male platypus’s, preserved as a complete skeleton.
An iguanodont about 7 m long, one of the larger plant-eaters of the Yixian, known from a nearly complete skeleton.

A tiny pterosaur with a wingspan of about 50 cm, a short, wide, frog-like head and large eyes. Its teeth suggest it ate insects, and its eyes suggest it hunted in dim light, perhaps at dusk or night, though this is an inference.
A small pterosaur with long jaws lined with hundreds of fine, comb-like teeth, used to strain small animals from shallow water like a flamingo.
A short-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about 1 m and a low bony crest along the top of its skull.
A coyote-sized raptor about 1.8 m long, the most common dromaeosaur of the Dinosaur Park Formation. A pterosaur bone with one of its teeth embedded shows it ate, or scavenged, pterosaurs.
One of the smallest known non-bird dinosaurs of North America, about 1 m long and perhaps 2 kg, a relative of Microraptor.
A medium-sized caenagnathid about 2.5 m long with long, slender fingers, perhaps for probing for food.
The largest caenagnathid of the Dinosaur Park Formation, known mainly from a toothless lower jaw, which gave its family its name, “recent jaw”.
An ostrich-like dinosaur about 4 m long with a toothless beak and long legs, built for speed. Later Struthiomimus fossils from Hell Creek are usually given a separate species, S. sedens.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Lawrence Lambe, 1902 (genus by Henry Fairfield Osborn, 1917)

summary: A nodosaur about 6 m long with big forward-pointing spikes on its shoulders, possibly used in shoving contests or for defence. It had no tail club.
A duck-billed dinosaur about 8.5 m long with a small, solid crest in front of its eyes, a possible ancestor of Saurolophus.
A horned dinosaur about 4.5 m long with short horns and a broad frill topped by a row of curling hooks, close to Kosmoceratops of Utah.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Holmes and colleagues, 2001 (as Chasmosaurus irvinensis); genus by Scott Sampson and colleagues, 2010

summary: An ankylosaur about 5.5 m long known from a headless skeleton preserved lying on its back with much of its armour still in place.

A small raptor known mainly from a young animal about 1 m long, found in 1993 by 14-year-old Wes Linster near Glacier National Park. It is one of the most complete small raptors from North America and had a large brain for its size.
A crested duck-billed dinosaur known from nests of eggs with embryos and hatchlings, from which scientists have studied how fast baby dinosaurs grew.
A troodontid about 2 m long with large eyes and a long, low snout, found by the Central Asiatic Expeditions in 1923.
A small troodontid with many needle-like, unserrated teeth, perhaps for catching small animals. Tiny skulls of its hatchlings were found in an oviraptorid nest.
A small, rodent-like multituberculate mammal, the most common mammal of the Djadochta dunes, known from many complete skulls.
A small, long-snouted eutherian mammal about 20 cm long with long hind legs, perhaps hopping like an elephant shrew.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: William Gregory and George Gaylord Simpson, 1926

summary: A large predatory lizard about 1.5–2 m long, a relative of the venomous Gila monster. Grooves on its teeth suggest it may have been venomous too.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Mark Norell, Malcolm McKenna and Michael Novacek, 1992

summary: A titanosaur known only from a skull with peg-like teeth. It may be the same animal as Opisthocoelicaudia, which is known only from a headless body.
An oviraptorid about 2 m long with a tall crest. One skeleton was found sitting on a nest of eggs, its arms spread over them.
A raptor about 2 m long with an unusually small sickle claw on each foot.
The sauropod that gave its family its name, with very tall spines along its back. It is known from only part of one skeleton, so its size is uncertain.
An iguanodont about 8 m long with a bulbous, swollen nose, named in 2021 from a skeleton collected on the Isle of Wight in 1978.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Jeremy Lockwood, David Martill and Susannah Maidment, 2021

summary: A toothless, beaked reptile about 2–3 m long that walked on two legs and looked like an ostrich dinosaur, though it was on the crocodile side of the family tree. It was found in a block collected at Ghost Ranch in 1947 and named in 2006 after the painter Georgia O’Keeffe, who lived there.

Named from leaf-shaped teeth thought to belong to an early plant-eating dinosaur. Skeletons found later at Petrified Forest showed it was an armoured relative of the aetosaurs, a reminder that teeth alone can mislead.
A small coelophysid theropod about 2 m long with a pair of low crests on its snout. Some researchers place it in Coelophysis.
A large predatory bonytongue fish, a relative of the living arowana, with a deep body and sharp teeth.
A perch-like predatory fish. Some fossils have a Knightia stuck in the mouth, apparently prey too large to swallow.

An Ice Age horse of western North America, common at La Brea. How many species of Ice Age American horse there were is still debated. Horse fossils in the Americas end about 11,000 years ago, though ancient DNA in soil suggests a few may have survived somewhat later; horses returned with Europeans.
A bison about 15–25% larger than the living American bison, with bigger horns, the most common large plant-eater at La Brea. It is thought to have evolved into today’s bison.

A huge soaring bird with a wingspan of about 3.5 m, a relative of Argentavis. More than 100 specimens have come from La Brea. Its beak and jaws suggest it caught small prey and swallowed it whole, rather than only scavenging.
A fast, swordfish-like predatory fish about 2–3 m long with a bony rostrum and blade-like pectoral fins, a late relative of Leedsichthys.

A pterosaur with a wingspan of about 2 m that had lost all its clawed fingers. Some adults had a huge, antler-like crest nearly three times the length of the skull. Whether it carried a skin sail is unknown.

species:toxochelys-latiremis.placeText: Kansas and the Western Interior, USA
summary: A sea turtle about 1 m long, an early relative of living sea turtles, common in the Smoky Hill Chalk.
A small, hornless relative of the horned dinosaurs about 2 m long, with powerful jaws for chewing tough plants. It lived alongside Triceratops at the very end of the Cretaceous.
A small early tetrapod with a mix of features from several early tetrapod groups, which makes it hard to place on the family tree. Its name means “creature from the black lagoon”.
A long-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about 1 m and long, curved front teeth for catching fish.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Theodori, 1830 (as Ornithocephalus banthensis); genus by Johann Andreas Wagner, 1860

summary: A short-necked pliosaur about 3.5–4 m long with a long, narrow snout, probably for catching fish and squid-like animals.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Harry Seeley, 1869 (as Plesiosaurus philarchus); genus by Richard Lydekker, 1889

summary: A pliosaur with an unusually short, broad skull and strong teeth, a different hunting style from its long-snouted neighbour Peloneustes.
A long-necked plesiosaur about 5 m long with a small head, named after Alfred Leeds, who collected much of the Oxford Clay’s marine reptiles.
A small, fast plant-eater close to Dryosaurus, known from thousands of bones from a single site. Some of its bones show signs of Paget’s disease, a bone disorder also found in people.
A diplodocid sauropod from Tendaguru, the best evidence that diplodocids reached Africa.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Eberhard Fraas, 1908 (as Gigantosaurus africanus); genus by Richard Sternfeld, 1911

summary: A slender, eel-like marine reptile about 2 m long, a thalattosaur that swam by waving its long body and tail.
A small pachypleurosaur, an early relative of plesiosaurs, with a long body and paddle-like limbs, common in the Monte San Giorgio shales.
The earliest known alvarezsaur, about 2 m long, with a long snout and three-fingered hands whose thumb was already enlarged, long before later alvarezsaurs reduced their arms to one stout claw.
An early coelurosaur about 3 m long. Its name honours General Zuo Zongtang, after whom the dish “General Tso’s chicken” is named.
A small coelurosaur known from a young animal about 1 m long, named after a dragon king of Chinese legend.
A diplodocid sauropod from Portugal. A 2015 study suggested it may belong in Supersaurus, which would show the same kind of sauropod lived on both sides of the young North Atlantic.
A large turiasaur sauropod with spoon-shaped teeth, named after the geologist Georges Zbyszewski.
A plant-eater about 6 m long, a relative of Camptosaurus, known from a partial skeleton.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Octávio Mateus and Miguel Telles Antunes, 2001

summary: A troodontid about 2 m long. The only known specimen had an injured second toe, the one bearing the enlarged claw, which had partly healed, so it lived for some time after the injury.
A large caenagnathid known from a partial hand and foot. It is one of the larger North American members of its family.
An ankylosaurid with a head covered in spiky bony knobs. It was more closely related to Asian ankylosaurs than to its North American neighbours, suggesting several crossings between the continents.
A heavily built iguanodont about 9 m long with a low, wide body, short limbs and a large thumb spike. Its name means “heavy lizard”.
An early carcharodontosaurid, an older relative of Carcharodontosaurus, with a thick, swollen bony brow over each eye.
A long, slim fish with a pointed snout and rows of deep scales along its sides, one of the most common fish in the Santana concretions.
A predatory ichthyodectid fish up to about 1 m long, a smaller relative of Xiphactinus.
A small coelurosaur, possibly an early tyrannosauroid, known from a young animal’s hips and legs. Remains of muscle fibres and skin were preserved in its concretion.
A small compsognathid about 2 m long whose hip bones differ between its left and right sides. A structure in its pelvis may be an air sac like those of birds.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Darren Naish, David Martill and Eberhard Frey, 2004

species:ilokelesia-aguadagrandensis.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A medium-sized abelisauroid theropod known from a partial skeleton, a smaller neighbour of Skorpiovenator.

A wolf-sized bear-dog. A complex of burrows at Agate held at least nine of its skeletons, including an adult female with her young, and is one of the oldest known records of large meat-eating mammals using dens.
A toothed whale, a relative of the narwhal, that looked strikingly like a walrus, with a short blunt snout and backward-pointing tusks. It probably sucked up shellfish from the seabed as walruses do.
A horned dinosaur with a short face and a broad frill. Its name means “no nose-horn face”, though it did have a small nose horn.
A close relative of Triceratops with one of the largest skulls of any land animal, estimated at about 3 m long.
A troodontid named in 2017 from a skull bone once thought to belong to Troodon; the differences showed it was a separate animal.
A small oviraptorosaur known from a young animal about 1.2 m long, one of the earliest of its group in North America.
One of the largest birds of its time, with long wings and a short tail. Some specimens have seeds preserved in their crops.
A small dicynodont with a wedge-shaped head and strong forelimbs, adapted for digging and probably living underground like a mole. The Cistecephalus Assemblage Zone of the Karoo is named after it.
One of the largest gorgonopsians, with a broad skull about 45 cm long and long sabre-like canines.

A large predatory therocephalian with a broad, short snout. It is one of the few top predators to survive the end-Permian extinction, though only briefly, and survivors were smaller than their Permian ancestors.
A long-snouted dyrosaurid crocodile relative that hunted fish in the rivers of the Cerrejón rainforest alongside Titanoboa.
One of the earliest horses, about the size of a house cat. Its teeth show that it shrank by about a third during the hot spell at the start of the Eocene and grew again as it cooled.
A wolf-sized meat-eater with a heavy skull, a relative of marsupials rather than of dogs, one of the top mammal predators of Miocene Patagonia.
A large hoofed mammal about 3 m long with tusks. Its skull suggests a short trunk or mobile upper lip.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Richard Owen, 1853 (as Nesodon magnus); genus by Hermann Burmeister, 1879

summary: A sheep- to tapir-sized notoungulate, an earlier relative of Toxodon and one of the commonest large plant-eaters of the Santa Cruz.

The second known species of Spinosaurus, named in 2026, the first new species of the genus in more than a century. Its skeleton is very like that of S. aegyptiacus, but its skull carried a much taller, curved, scimitar-shaped bony crest, one of the tallest head crests of any meat-eating dinosaur. Its interlocking front teeth suited gripping slippery fish.

All the known specimens are from young animals; the type specimen was roughly 8 m long, and adult size is unknown. Its describers argue it waded in shallow water to hunt, like a giant heron, and nicknamed it the “hell heron”. Whether Spinosaurus waded or swam is still debated. Its name means “wonderful” or “astonishing”.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: About 8 m (young animal; adult size unknown)

facts.label: Collected
facts.value: Expeditions in 2000, 2019 and 2022, mostly at Jenguebi

related.note: The type species, from Egypt and Morocco, with a much lower head crest.

summary: A giant terror bird with a skull 71.6 cm long, the largest bird skull known, with a tall, hooked beak. It is known from that skull and part of one leg, so estimates of its height and weight are rough: it may have stood about 3 m tall.

A medium-sized, lightly built terror bird, probably a fast pursuit hunter, that lived alongside the larger Phorusrhacos. Some researchers argue it should take an older name, Tolmodus inflatus; this is not settled.

The smallest known terror bird, about 70–80 cm tall with its head raised and about 5 kg. Terror birds were not all giants: the genus Psilopterus, small and long-legged, lasted from the Oligocene into the Pleistocene.

A terror bird about 1.4 m tall. A 2010 CT and computer-modelling study found its skull was strong when striking up and down but weak against sideways twisting, suggesting it hunted with repeated, accurate beak strikes rather than struggling with large prey.

A terror bird about 1.2 m tall, known from the most complete terror bird skeleton yet found, with over 90% of its bones. Its inner ear suggests it heard low-frequency sounds best, which may have helped it detect prey, and its describers suggested it had a low-pitched call; both are inferences from its anatomy.

The only terror bird known from North America, perhaps about 1.8–2 m tall and 150 kg, though it is known only from scattered bones. Dating published in 2007 suggested its Texas fossils are about 5 million years old, earlier than the Panama land bridge is usually thought to have been complete; how it crossed is still debated.

One of the largest alvarezsaurids, about 2.5 m long, and one of the last of its group in South America. Its partial skeleton was found with two eggs and pieces of eggshell. Its describers thought the eggs may still have been inside the female when she died, as no nest was found; others have argued they were being incubated.
Its eggshell has three layers, which is unusual for non-bird dinosaurs, and was given its own egg name, Arriagadoolithus. Bonapartenykus is named after the Argentine palaeontologist José Bonaparte.

One of the largest raptors, about 5 m long, with a long, low skull, many small cone-shaped teeth and very short arms. Its teeth are like those of fish-eaters, so it may have hunted fish and other small prey, though this is an inference.

A baryonychine about 9 m long, known from parts of the skull and some vertebrae found at Chilton Chine, with low bumps and ridges above its eyes. Its name means “horned crocodile face, hell heron”: the “hell heron” nickname started with this species, not with Spinosaurus mirabilis.

A baryonychine about 9 m long from the same rocks as Ceratosuchops, named “riverbank hunter”. It honours Angela Milner, who described Baryonyx. Two spinosaurids living side by side suggests they divided up food or habitat between them.
A baryonychine about 7–8 m long, one of the youngest known, from a partial skeleton once thought to be Baryonyx.

Named in 2023 from part of an upper jaw and five tail vertebrae, and described as an early baryonychine. A later review doubted that the bones all came from one animal and treated the name as probably not valid, so its status is uncertain. Its name, “champion”, celebrates the Villarreal football club’s Europa League win.
A spinosaurid known from a partial skeleton without a skull. Analyses place it among the spinosaurines, showing that both branches of the family lived in Europe.

A spinosaurid known from a single partial skeleton, described as Baryonyx in 2011 and given its own name in 2022 after more bones were dug out of the cliff. Later analyses place it among the spinosaurines.
Named in 2014 as a ceratosaur, from a partial skeleton. Restudies in 2021 and 2025 showed it is a spinosaurid, different from the other Iberian ones, probably a spinosaurine.

facts.label: Reidentified
facts.value: As a spinosaurid: Samathi and colleagues, 2021; Rauhut and colleagues, 2025

summary: A spinosaurid known from a partial skeleton without a skull or limbs, found in 2010. Its back carried a low, wavy sail. Its name means “fish hunter”, from the diet assumed for spinosaurids.
The first spinosaurid reported from Asia, known for certain only from its fluted, cone-shaped teeth. Teeth from China named “Sinopliosaurus” fusuiensis may belong to the same animal.

Named from the tip of a snout found in the same rocks as Irritator, in the same year. Some researchers think both names belong to one animal; others keep them separate. More overlapping fossils are needed to tell.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos, 1996

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Possibly the same animal as Irritator

related.note: Possibly the same animal; the known fossils barely overlap.

summary: A large spinosaurine known from the front of a snout and part of an upper jaw, found on Cajual Island in 1999. One study suggested it is the same as Spinosaurus; later studies keep it separate.

related.note: Proposed by one study to be the same animal; later studies disagree.

summary: Named from short, broad vertebrae from the Kem Kem. Whether it is a separate animal or part of Spinosaurus is one of the longest-running debates about spinosaurs: a 2014 study merged them, while restudies in 2015 and 2018 found clear differences and kept it separate, which would mean two large spinosaurines shared the Kem Kem rivers.

related.note: Possibly the same animal; studies disagree.

summary: One of the earliest and smallest megaraptorans, about 4–5 m long. Its type specimen was first thought to be a young animal, but smaller individuals found later make that less certain. As with Megaraptor, its large hand claw was at first mistaken for a foot claw. It shows the group was in Asia early in its history.
A megaraptoran known from a partial skeleton without a skull. With Fukuiraptor, it suggests the group may have started in Asia before spreading south.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Adun Samathi, Phornphen Chanthasit and Martin Sander, 2019

summary: Known only from leg bones. Its describers placed it among early coelurosaurs and thought it was probably a megaraptoran, but its position is not settled.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Adun Samathi, Phornphen Chanthasit and Martin Sander, 2019

summary: The first megaraptoran known from Europe, named in 2026 from a partial braincase found at the foot of a cliff at Sudmoor Point, near Brook. The Natural History Museum in London bought it in 1924, and it sat unstudied for about a century. Features of the back of the skull place it as an early member of the group.

Its braincase is about the size of Timurlengia’s, so it was probably a smaller predator, perhaps 3–4 m long; this is estimated from its relatives, as no other bones are known. Its describers argue it shows megaraptorans spread through Europe on their way to the southern continents. Its name means “unconquered warrior”, and amberina refers to the amber found in the same rocks.

A lightly built megaraptorid about 6 m long, nicknamed “Banjo”, and the most complete large predatory dinosaur from Australia. Its well-preserved arms and hands show the large, curved claws typical of the group. It was found with the sauropod Diamantinasaurus.

A stocky titanosaur, found mixed together with Australovenator at the “Matilda” site near Winton. Its genus is named after the nearby Diamantina River and its species after the song “Waltzing Matilda”, which the site is also named after.

A predator about 8 m long. It was named in 1998 from a huge claw thought to come from the foot, like a giant raptor’s sickle claw, which is where the names Megaraptor (“giant thief”) and namunhuaiquii (Mapuche for “foot lance”) come from. A hand found in 2004 showed the claw was on its first finger, and it is not a raptor at all.
A skeleton of a young Megaraptor described in 2014 had a skull with features like early tyrannosauroids, one reason the group’s place on the family tree is debated.
A megaraptorid whose skeleton includes much of the braincase, rare for the group. Its name, “wall thief”, refers to the canyon wall it was found in.
A megaraptorid known from a row of back and hip vertebrae and part of the hip, the first megaraptoran with the whole hip section of the backbone preserved.

A megaraptorid about 9 m long whose name means “air bone”. Many of its bones, including the hips, ribs and wishbone, were hollowed by air sacs connected to the lungs, evidence that it breathed with a bird-like system of air sacs.

species:orkoraptor-burkei.ageText: About 77 to 69 million years ago (dating debated)
summary: A megaraptorid known from fragments of the skull, teeth, vertebrae and legs, one of the southernmost large predators of its time. It was first thought to be the youngest megaraptoran, but the age of its rocks has since been disputed. Its name comes from “Orr-korr”, the Tehuelche name for the Santa Cruz River.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Fernando Novas, Martín Ezcurra and Agustín Lecuona, 2008

summary: One of the largest megaraptorids, about 9–10 m long, known from a partial skeleton with a huge rib cage, which gave it its species name, “large chest”. Its genus name comes from Maip, an evil spirit of Patagonian legend, “the shadow of death” that kills with the cold wind.

The youngest definite megaraptoran, about 7 m long and around 1 tonne, from just before the end-Cretaceous extinction. It is only the second megaraptorid with much of its skull. An arm bone of a crocodile relative, with tooth marks, was found between its jaws: perhaps its last meal, though the bone may also have washed in after death.

An unenlagiine, a long-snouted South American relative of the raptors, about 2.5–3 m long. Its upper arm bone has two puncture marks, and a megaraptorid tooth was found a few metres away: possibly a megaraptorid fed on it, though this is uncertain.

A horned dinosaur with rough bony bosses on its nose and over its eyes instead of horns, and a pair of spikes on its frill. It was once proposed as a step in a single line of descent from Einiosaurus to Pachyrhinosaurus; later finds show it is a close relative of Pachyrhinosaurus, and the straight-line idea is doubted.
A small, hornless leptoceratopsid known from a bonebed of many individuals, close to Leptoceratops.

A small, fast plant-eater about 2.5 m long from Egg Mountain. Eggs with embryos found there were first thought to be its own, but study of the embryos showed they belong to a troodontid. Orodromeus bones found near the troodontid nests may even be the remains of their meals.
A small New World monkey related to the living sakis and uakaris, showing monkeys lived as far south as northern Patagonia in the Middle Miocene, when it was warmer and more wooded.
A small saltasaurine titanosaur, a relative of Saltasaurus, from Salitral Moreno.
A small titanosaur known from braincases, tail vertebrae and limb bones of more than one individual.
An aeolosaurine titanosaur known from a partial skeleton, named after the energy company that supported the excavation.

A duck-billed dinosaur, one of the hadrosaurs that crossed from North America into South America near the end of the Cretaceous. Some bones once given the name Willinakaqe, now considered too poorly founded to use, were moved to it.
A hadrosaur known from backbone and limb bones of a subadult from La Pampa province.
A small elasmosaurid plesiosaur from the shallow sea that flooded into Patagonia at the end of the Cretaceous.

species:glyptotherium-arizonae.placeText: Florida, Arizona and the southern USA
summary: An early North American glyptodont, one of the animals that crossed north from South America during the Great American Interchange. Some researchers think it is the same species as the later Glyptotherium texanum.

related.note: The later species; some studies treat both as one.

summary: A pampathere, a giant armadillo relative with flexible bands of armour, another South American immigrant to North America.
A giant relative of raccoons and coatis, roughly 125–180 kg, first mistaken for a bear. Its ancestors reached South America from the north before the Panama land bridge was complete.
An iguanodont about 6 m long with tall spines along its back that probably supported a low ridge or sail. What the sail was for is unknown; display and heat control have both been suggested.
A large somphospondylan sauropod, related to the ancestors of the titanosaurs, named in 2024 from fossils found near Morella.

An Iguanodon known from every stage of life: embryos, more than a dozen hatchlings found together, juveniles and adults up to about 10 m long. The cluster of babies suggests a nesting or nursery site.
Whether it belongs in Iguanodon is disputed. In 2025 one team gave it its own genus, Paulodon; other researchers objected, and the new name is not yet widely used.

related.note: The type species of Iguanodon, from slightly younger rocks.

summary: A sauropod about 15 m long known from two or three individuals, named after the village of Tang Vay and the geologist Josué-Heilmann Hoffet. It may be close to Phuwiangosaurus of Thailand; a recent review keeps them separate.
The most common sauropod of Thailand, about 15–20 m long, known from many individuals of different sizes. It is named after Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Valérie Martin, Eric Buffetaut and Varavudh Suteethorn, 1994

summary: A large theropod known from hips, part of the tail and backbone. It was named in 1996 as an early tyrannosaur, which gave it its name, but later studies disagree: it has been placed among allosauroids, carcharodontosaurs and, most recently, early coelurosaurs. It is probably not a tyrannosaur.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Eric Buffetaut, Varavudh Suteethorn and Haiyan Tong, 1996

summary: An early ostrich-dinosaur known from leg and back bones, among the oldest of its group.
A lungfish known from tooth plates. Unlike most of the Alcântara fauna, which closely matches that of North Africa, it has no close African counterpart.
A sclerorhynchoid, a ray with a long, toothed saw on its snout like a sawfish, though not closely related to living sawfish. It is known from its rostral teeth.
An iguanodont about 4.5 m long whose skull lacked the joint that let some relatives flex their upper jaws outwards while chewing.
An early hadrosauroid, a forerunner of the duck-billed dinosaurs, known from part of the upper jaw and teeth of a young animal. It was the first hadrosauroid named from Japan.
A titanosauriform sauropod known from limb bones and teeth, the first sauropod named from Japan.
A small feathered-dinosaur relative with a puzzling mix of features, hence “paradoxus”. Studies have placed it among early maniraptoriforms or as an early therizinosaur.
An early bird whose bones are preserved in three dimensions rather than flattened, which is rare for birds of its age.

A wide-bodied titanosaur found in 2005 on a sheep station and named in 2016. With Diamantinasaurus, Wintonotitan and Australotitan it belongs to a group of Australian sauropods whose place on the family tree is still debated.
A titanosauriform sauropod known from part of a skeleton first found in 1974 and named in 2009.
A small crocodile relative about 1 m long, close to the origin of modern crocodilians, known from a nearly complete skeleton from the lower Winton Formation near Isisford.
One of the largest and most complete giant titanosaurs, perhaps 24–28 m long, with a deep, sail-like row of spines on its neck. Leaves, fish and other fossils were found with it.
A long-legged unenlagiine about 2–3.5 m long with a shoulder that let it raise its arms like a bird’s wings. It was too large to fly; why it had this ability is unknown.
A small unenlagiine known from leg and foot bones, including the sickle claw. Its feet resemble Unenlagia’s, and some researchers think the two are the same animal.

related.note: Possibly the same animal; the known bones barely overlap.

summary: An alvarezsaurid about 2 m long, known from an incomplete but well-preserved skeleton including the stout, single-clawed hand typical of the group.
A titanosaur with bony armour plates, known from several partial skeletons at a single site in southern Mendoza.
The alvarezsaur that gave the group its name, a small, long-legged runner known from part of a skeleton.
A chicken-sized bird with small wings, one of the oldest known birds to have lost the ability to fly.
An enantiornithine, one of the “opposite birds” that died out with the dinosaurs. Small eggs, some with embryos, found nearby probably belong to it.
A small land-living crocodile relative with a short snout and cheek teeth that worked somewhat like a mammal’s, probably eating plants as well as small animals.
An early snake about 2 m long, known from well-preserved skulls, important for working out how snakes evolved from lizards.
An abelisaurid known from a partial skeleton and braincase, an early member of the branch that includes Carnotaurus.
A nearly complete abelisaurid about 5.5 m long, a close relative of Carnotaurus, found at the Auca Mahuevo titanosaur nesting site.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Rodolfo Coria, Luis Chiappe and Lowell Dingus, 2002

summary: The predator that gave abelisaurids their name, known only from a skull about 85 cm long. It honours Roberto Abel, who found it.
A small, two-legged plant-eater about 1 m long, known from several individuals, some with gizzard stones.
A titanosaur named in 2019 in honour of the geologist Francisco Nullo, one of the southernmost sauropods of the latest Cretaceous.
A small, fast elasmarian plant-eater named after the technician Marcelo Isasi, who found its bones near mosasaur teeth.
The first hadrosaur named from South America, in 1979, known from part of a skeleton. It descends from hadrosaurs that crossed from North America.
A titanosaur known from a partial skeleton, with tail vertebrae whose spines lean forward, a feature of its group.
An elasmarian plant-eater known from a partial skeleton, living alongside the hadrosaur Secernosaurus.

species:puertasaurus-reuili.ageText: About 77 to 69 million years ago (dating debated)
summary: A giant titanosaur known from only four vertebrae, including enormous neck and back vertebrae. Size estimates of 30 m or more are based on comparing those few bones with other titanosaurs, so they are uncertain.

species:talenkauen-santacrucensis.ageText: About 77 to 69 million years ago (dating debated)
summary: A plant-eater about 4 m long with thin bony plates along its ribs, whose purpose is unknown; similar plates are found in Thescelosaurus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Fernando Novas, Andrea Cambiaso and Alfredo Ambrosio, 2004

summary: An early jawless fish known from fragments of bony armour and, from a 2023 CT study, part of a head that suggests an early stage in the evolution of the vertebrate skull.
One of the last osteostracans, a jawless fish with a broad, flat bony head shield, living on the estuary floor.
An antiarch placoderm with a boxy armoured body and jointed, arm-like bony fins. It is the commonest fish at Miguasha, with thousands of specimens. Bothriolepis as a genus lived worldwide.
A small arthrodire placoderm. A specimen described in 2009 contains an embryo, evidence with Materpiscis that some placoderms gave birth to live young after internal fertilisation.
A small arthrodire placoderm preserved in three dimensions in Gogo limestone nodules. CT scans of specimens have shown details of its teeth and jaw joints.

A giant arthrodire as large as Dunkleosteus or larger, but with weak, toothless jaws. A 2020 study of its jaw found it was poor at biting and suggested it fed by filtering small prey, like a basking shark.

A small shark about 25–30 cm long. Mature males carried a long, sword-like spine curving forward over the head, probably for display or mating. A male and female found together have been interpreted as a possible courting pair.
A small, eel-shaped ratfish relative whose males had a pair of branched claspers on their heads.
An early ratfish relative with spines on its back and, in males, rows of spiny scales, known from complete bodies.
A hybodont shark about 2 m long. One famous specimen from Holzmaden has the hard guards of over 200 belemnites (squid-like animals) in its stomach.

species:squalicorax-falcatus.placeText: Western Interior Seaway, North America, and worldwide
summary: A shark about 2–3 m long with serrated teeth like a tiger shark’s. Squalicorax teeth embedded in, and bite marks on, bones of mosasaurs, turtles and even a hadrosaur washed out to sea show these sharks scavenged as well as hunted.
A large shark with pavements of flat, ridged crushing teeth, probably for cracking shellfish such as giant clams. Its teeth are common; its skeleton is rarely found.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Usually credited to Louis Agassiz, 1843; a recent review argues for Gideon Mantell, 1836

summary: A large mako-like shark with broad, smooth-edged teeth. Its line is thought to have given rise to the great white shark, though which species was the direct ancestor is debated. A young one from the Pisco Formation was found with sardines in its belly, the first proof that juveniles ate fish.
One of the earliest well-known ray-finned fish, small and preserved in three dimensions, used to work out the anatomy of the ancestors of most living fish.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Gardiner and Bartram, 1977 (as Mimia toombsi); renamed Mimipiscis by Brian Choo, 2011

summary: A small early ray-finned fish from Gogo with diamond-shaped scales, preserved in three dimensions like Mimipiscis.
A common early ray-finned fish of the Zechstein Sea, with thick, shiny scales, often found complete in the copper shale.
A slim, long-snouted predatory fish. Embryos found inside Saurichthys females show it gave birth to live young, one of the earliest ray-finned fish known to do so.
A large predatory fish with big jaws and few scales, a fast open-water hunter of the Triassic seas.
A deep-bodied fish up to about 1 m long covered in thick, shiny, enamel-coated scales, with peg-like teeth for crushing shellfish. It is a relative of the gars.
A fast predatory fish about 1 m long with a deep tail and sickle-shaped pectoral fins, an early member of the family that later produced the giant Leedsichthys.
A small, sprat-like early teleost, the commonest fish at Solnhofen, sometimes found in mass deaths of thousands.
One of the commonest Santana fish, often preserved in three dimensions with soft tissues such as muscle and gill structures.
A large bowfin relative up to about 1 m long, a top fish predator of the Santana lagoon. Some specimens have other fish inside them.
A milkfish relative, common in the Santana concretions, with a small, toothless mouth.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: David Starr Jordan and John Casper Branner, 1908

species:ichthyodectes-ctenodon.placeText: Kansas and the Western Interior, USA
summary: A predatory fish about 2 m long, a smaller relative of Xiphactinus, with a row of sharp teeth.

species:pachyrhizodus-caninus.placeText: Kansas and the Western Interior, USA
summary: A fast predatory fish about 2 m long with a deeply forked tail.

A predatory fish about 1.5 m long with long fangs at the front of its jaws. It is often called the “sabre-toothed herring”, but it is a relative of lizardfish, not herring. It was itself common prey for larger fish, mosasaurs and seabirds.
A paddlefish with a shorter snout than the living American paddlefish, rare in the Green River lake deposits.
A bottom-feeding fish with a pointed snout and an underslung mouth, related to the milkfish.
A small, deep-bodied spiny-finned fish, sunfish-like in shape, common in the Green River lake beds. A similar Green River species once placed in Priscacara is now in its own genus, Cockerellites.
A gar from the Messel lake, a relative of the living alligator gar, known from complete skeletons.
A bowfin relative, one of the commonest fish of the Messel lake.

A lobe-finned predatory fish up to about 1.5 m long whose fin bones match the upper arm, forearm and thigh bones of tetrapods. Thousands of specimens, some sectioned layer by layer in the 20th century, made it one of the best-known fossil fish.

A close relative of Tiktaalik and of the first tetrapods. A complete 1.6 m skeleton described in 2020 has a fin with rows of small bones like finger bones, the closest a fish fin is known to come to a hand.
A broad-headed lobe-finned fish about 1.5 m long from the same rocks as Tiktaalik, probably an ambush predator on the river bottom.
An early tetrapod known from a heavy lower jaw, found at Red Hill alongside Hynerpeton.
One of the earliest coelacanths, with a tail fin more like other fish’s than the three-lobed tail of later coelacanths.
The coelacanth that gave the group its name, “hollow spine”, after its hollow fin rays.
A small coelacanth from the Mazon Creek nodules, where young individuals are also found.
An unusual coelacanth with a deep body and a long, tapering tail, quite unlike the living coelacanth in shape.
A lungfish with crushing tooth plates, preserved in three dimensions at Gogo, one of several lungfish living on the reef.
A lungfish about 30–50 cm long, common at Miguasha, with two back fins rather than the single long fin of later lungfish.
A lungfish found inside fossil burrows, evidence that, like living African lungfish, it survived dry seasons sealed in mud.
A stocky temnospondyl about 40 cm long with a row of bony plates along its back and a large ear notch, adapted to life on land.
A flat-headed, mostly aquatic temnospondyl, common in the Texas red beds, where it lived in ponds and streams.

A metoposaurid, a big, flat-headed amphibian about 3 m long that lay in wait in rivers and lakes. It was long known as Koskinonodon (and before that Buettneria), but a 2019 study showed the older name Anaschisma applies, and several species once kept apart turned out to be one.
A seymouriamorph, one of the amphibian-like relatives of the earliest reptiles, living along the rivers of Permian Russia.
A sturdy animal about 60 cm long, once taken for an early reptile. Larvae of its relatives with gill traces showed it was still amphibian-like and bred in water.
One of the first large plant-eating land vertebrates, about 3 m long, with broad cheek teeth. It is close to, but not quite, the first reptiles.
One of the earliest true frogs, with hips and long hind legs already built for jumping.
The earliest known caecilian, a burrowing amphibian that, unlike living caecilians, still had small legs.
A giant salamander about 1 m long, close to the living Chinese and Japanese giant salamanders, which lived in Europe until the Pliocene.

Its first skeleton was described in 1726 as the remains of a man drowned in Noah’s Flood. Cuvier showed in 1811 that it was a salamander, and it was later named after the man who had misidentified it.

A small, lizard-like early reptile about 20 cm long with several rows of teeth, which may have helped it eat tough plants as well as insects. Some tails show it could shed them to escape, like many lizards.

A small reptile with very broad, flattened ribs that formed a wide body. Many researchers see it as an early turtle relative showing how the shell began, possibly as an adaptation for digging; others doubt the link.
A heavy, armoured plant-eater about 2.5 m long with leaf-shaped teeth, the animal that gave the pareiasaurs their name.
A small, stocky reptile about 35 cm long with a wide, triangular head and spikes at the back of the skull. It is common in the earliest Triassic, and some are found in burrows.
One of the earliest gliding vertebrates, about 40 cm long, with a wide wing of skin stretched over long bony rods along its sides and a frill of spikes on its head.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Johannes Weigelt, 1930 (as Palaechamaeleo jaekeli); genus by Oskar Kuhn, 1939

species:weigeltisaurus-jaekeli.akaNote: Long called Coelurosauravus jaekeli; given its own genus again in 2021, as Coelurosauravus itself is from Madagascar.

summary: The large species of Tanystropheus, up to about 6 m long, half of it neck. Its skull, rebuilt from scans, has nostrils on top of the snout and long, interlocking fangs for trapping fish, so it lived in the water. Large Tanystropheus fossils were long thought to be adults of the same species as the small ones, until a 2020 study separated them.

related.note: The small species, under 2 m, living alongside it; its adults were long mistaken for young of this one.

summary: A small aquatic reptile about 1 m long with a very long neck, known from hundreds of skeletons. A female with 18 embryos inside shows it gave birth to live young, and one embryo had two heads.
A small, lizard-like relative of the living tuatara, about 20 cm long, preserved complete at Solnhofen.
A long, slender, eel-like relative of the tuatara, about 60 cm long, with small limbs, adapted to swimming in the sea.
An early, long-bodied ichthyosaur with a long tail but no tall tail fin. Other species of Cymbospondylus, from Nevada, grew to over 15 m, among the first giant animals of the seas.
A slender ichthyosaur up to about 8 m long with a long, thin snout. The first skeleton held embryos, so it gave birth to live young.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Cristiano Dal Sasso and Giovanni Pinna, 1996

summary: A large ichthyosaur, perhaps 9 m or more, with very large eyes, among the largest of any vertebrate, and big teeth. It probably ate large prey, including other marine reptiles. Mary Anning’s brother Joseph found the first skull at Lyme Regis around 1811.
A slender ichthyosaur about 3–4 m long with a long, thin snout, probably for catching small, fast prey.
An ichthyosaur whose upper jaw stuck out far beyond its lower jaw, like a swordfish’s bill, perhaps to slash at fish.
An ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur from Solnhofen preserved with outlines of its skin and fins.

An ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur about 5 m long from the Arctic seas of Svalbard, known from a nearly complete skeleton. A 2019 study argued it is the same as the Russian Undorosaurus, which would make that the correct name.
An early placodont with strong, peg-like front teeth and crushing back teeth, probably eating shellfish.
A placodont with a turtle-like shell of bony plates and large, flat crushing teeth on its palate for breaking shellfish.
A tiny pachypleurosaur about 20 cm long, known from hundreds of skeletons, including young ones, which make it possible to study its growth.

A plesiosaur with a fairly large head and moderate neck, between the long-necked and short-necked types. The original skeleton was destroyed in a 1940 bombing raid on Bristol; casts survive. It is named after David Attenborough.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: William Sollas, 1881 (as Plesiosaurus conybeari); genus by Robert Bakker, 1993

summary: A long-necked plesiosaur from Holzmaden, preserved with outlines of its soft tissues, including a tail fin. Its species name honours Kaiser Wilhelm II.
An early pliosaur with a longer neck than later pliosaurs, named after Bernhard Hauff of the Holzmaden fossil family.

species:dolichorhynchops-osborni.placeText: Kansas and the Western Interior, USA
summary: A polycotylid plesiosaur about 4–5 m long with a long, narrow snout full of small teeth for catching fish and squid.
A polycotylid plesiosaur. A 4.7 m adult found with a single large fetus inside, described in 2011, showed that plesiosaurs gave birth to live young, probably one big baby at a time.
An elasmosaurid plesiosaur from the inland Eromanga Sea that once covered much of Australia, known from a skull and neck.
A mosasaur with a long, slim snout, known from only a few specimens from the Smoky Hill Chalk.

species:globidens-dakotensis.placeText: South Dakota and the Western Interior, USA
summary: A mosasaur with rounded, ball-shaped teeth for crushing shellfish such as clams and ammonites, very different from the pointed teeth of most mosasaurs.
A small, slender mosasaur about 4 m long from a more primitive branch of the family.

A long, slim halisaurine mosasaur, perhaps 5–10 m long, with small eyes and many small teeth. Its describers suggested it hunted in dim light or deep water, by touch or other senses; this is an inference.

species:protostega-gigas.placeText: Kansas and the Western Interior, USA
summary: A large sea turtle about 3 m long with a reduced, lightweight shell, a slightly older relative of Archelon.

A giant sea turtle known from a skull about 70 cm long, with a long tube-like snout ending in a round mouth. Its describers suggested it sucked in prey like a pipefish; this is an inference from the skull.

A small freshwater turtle, a relative of the pig-nosed turtle. Several pairs have been found preserved together, male and female, apparently in the act of mating. They seem to have sunk into poisonous deep water of the lake while mating.

One of the largest turtles ever, a side-necked freshwater turtle with a shell up to about 2.4 m long. Some males had forward-pointing horns on the front of the shell, probably used in fights. Bite marks and a caiman tooth in one shell suggest giant caimans attacked it.
A monitor lizard relative about 1.3 m long. A 2018 study found it had a fourth eye, a light-sensing organ on top of the head beside the pineal eye, the only jawed vertebrate known to have had both.
A boa relative about 2 m long. One young specimen has a lizard, Geiseltaliellus, inside it, and the lizard has an insect in its own stomach, a three-level food chain in one fossil.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Stephan Schaal, 2004 (as Palaeopython fischeri); genus by Agustín Scanferla and Krister Smith, 2020

summary: A lizard about 35 cm long. One female contains 15 well-developed embryos, among the oldest evidence of live birth in lizards.
A giant caiman with a broad skull. Its relative Purussaurus brasiliensis may have reached 10–12 m, among the largest crocodylians ever.
A small, agile reptile about 60 cm long, very close to the common ancestor of crocodiles, pterosaurs and dinosaurs. It probably walked on four legs but may have been able to run on two.
A large-headed predator up to about 5 m long, one of the biggest land animals of its time and an early relative of the archosaurs.

A small, long-legged reptile known mostly from its hindlimbs. Long treated as an early dinosaur relative, it is now thought, with its family, to be closest to the pterosaurs, showing what their ground-living ancestors may have been like.

A rabbit-sized, long-legged, lightly built reptile close to the ancestry of dinosaurs. Larger specimens were split off as Marasuchus in 1994; other researchers think they all belong to Lagosuchus, so whether there are one or two animals is debated.
species:lagosuchus-talampayensis.akaNote: Better fossils from the same rocks were named Marasuchus lilloensis in 1994. Some researchers think they belong to Lagosuchus, others keep Marasuchus separate.

summary: A silesaurid with sharp, flesh-eating teeth, one of the oldest members of the dinosaur line. Bones named Pseudolagosuchus may belong to it.
A proterochampsid, a low, crocodile-like reptile with eyes on top of its head, probably living in and around water.
A flat-skulled, crocodile-like proterochampsid about 1–2 m long, an ambush predator in Ischigualasto rivers.
An ornithosuchid predator known from a skull with the group’s typical hooked snout tip.
An armoured, plant-eating aetosaur about 2 m long, one of the earliest of its group.
An aetosaur with broad, flat back armour and no big spikes, one of the commonest in the lower Chinle.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Robert Long and Karen Ballew, 1985 (as Stagonolepis wellesi)

species:poposaurus-gracilis.placeText: Wyoming, Arizona, Utah and Texas, USA
summary: A crocodile-line reptile about 4 m long that walked on two legs, with short arms and long hind legs, looking strikingly like a theropod dinosaur.
A small, long-legged early crocodylomorph about 1.2 m long, an agile land predator quite unlike living crocodiles.
A small, land-living early crocodylomorph known from a partial skeleton.
A small, slender-snouted marine crocodile relative about 1 m long, probably catching fish in shallow seas.

A small, long-legged land-living crocodile relative about 1 m long. Its relatives lived in South America and Madagascar too. Press coverage nicknamed it “DogCroc”, after its dog-like build; the name is not scientific.
A small notosuchian with a short, broad snout and few teeth, living on land alongside Notosuchus.
A medium-sized crocodylian about 2–3 m long, an early relative of alligators, common in the rivers of the Dinosaur Park Formation.
A long-snouted, gharial-like crocodylian of coastal seas that survived the end-Cretaceous extinction.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: James De Kay, 1842 (as Gavialis neocesariensis); genus by Joseph Leidy, 1852

summary: A giant gharial, perhaps around 10 m long, one of the largest gharials known, from the rivers and estuaries of northern South America.
A strange caiman with a long, wide, flat, duck-bill-like snout and small teeth. It has been suggested it filtered or gulped small prey from the water; whether it really filter-fed is debated.
A land-living mekosuchine crocodile with a deep snout and blade-like, serrated teeth, unlike the cone-shaped teeth of water-hunting crocodiles. Later species of Quinkana lived into the Pleistocene.
A long-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about 1 m, large eyes and a short, rounded snout.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Quenstedt, 1858 (as Pterodactylus liasicus); genus by Embrik Strand, 1928

summary: A long-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about 90 cm and a short, blunt snout. The first specimen, described in 1831, was one of the first pterosaurs studied, and Goldfuss reported traces of hair-like covering on it.
A short-tailed pterosaur with jaws that met only at the tips, leaving a gap with teeth at the front, perhaps for grabbing hard-shelled prey.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Friedrich Quenstedt, 1855 (as Pterodactylus suevicus); genus by Harry Seeley, 1870

summary: A pterosaur with a long neck like later pterodactyloids but a long tail like earlier pterosaurs, a mosaic named after the Monkey King, Sun Wukong.
A small wukongopterid known from a nearly complete skeleton, the earliest-branching member of its family in some analyses.

A pterosaur with a wingspan of about 4–5 m and a broad, rounded snout lined with small, triangular, interlocking teeth. It may have scavenged, cutting chunks from carcasses; this is an inference from its teeth.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Harry Seeley, 1901 (as Ornithodesmus latidens); genus by Christopher Howse and colleagues, 2001

summary: A fish-eating pterosaur with a wingspan of about 4 m, rounded crests on the tips of both jaws and long, interlocking front teeth. Three-dimensional Santana skulls of anhanguerids have been used to study pterosaur brains.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Diogenes de Almeida Campos and Alexander Kellner, 1985

summary: A toothless pterosaur with a wingspan of about 4–5 m and a tall, rounded crest on its head, a close relative of Thalassodromeus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos, 1988

summary: A small, toothless tapejarid with a crest on its snout. One specimen has the remains of a fish in its stomach, so it was not only eating fruit and seeds, as some had suggested for its family.

A stegosaur about 4.2 to 4.5 m long with small back plates but enormous spines growing from its shoulders, each about twice the length of the shoulder blade beneath it. How the spines were angled in life is still debated; they may have pointed out sideways or backwards, for defence or display.

The holotype preserves patches of skin on its left shoulder, described in 2008, among the first skin impressions known from any stegosaur, showing small, many-sided scales. Its relationships are uncertain: some studies find it one of the earliest-branching stegosaurs, others closer to Huayangosaurus. It was first named in an unpublished thesis in 1992 and formally described later.

facts.label: Shoulder spines
facts.value: About twice the length of the shoulder blade

summary: A stegosaur about 6.5 m long with two rows of tall, pointed plates down its back and two pairs of spikes on its tail. Named in 1977, it was the first nearly complete stegosaur skeleton found in Asia, and casts of it have stood in museums around the world. It is named after the Tuo River.

The top predator of Late Jurassic Sichuan, a big allosaur relative about 8 to 10 m long with a deep skull, a low ridge on its snout and bony bumps over its eyes. Workers building a dam reservoir in Yongchuan found a nearly complete skeleton in 1977. It belongs to the metriacanthosaurids, Asian cousins of Allosaurus, and would have hunted the stegosaurs and sauropods it lived with.

A small plant-eater about 1–1.75 m long with three kinds of teeth: cutting front teeth, a pair of tusks and chisel-like cheek teeth. Its strong hands may have been used for digging. Whether the tusks were for fighting, display or eating is not known.

A small, fast, two-legged plant-eater about 1 m long, one of the earliest well-known ornithischians. Some researchers think the larger Stormbergia, from the same rocks, is simply the adult form of Lesothosaurus.
species:lesothosaurus-diagnosticus.akaNote: Fabrosaurus australis, named in 1964 from a piece of jaw from the same rocks, may be the same animal; it is usually treated as a doubtful name.

summary: A long-necked early sauropodomorph about 4–6 m long, walking on two legs. Embryos in its eggs had big heads and walked on all fours, so the young changed posture as they grew. Its nesting site shows it returned to lay clutches in the same place.
A sauropodomorph about 6–7 m long that walked mainly on two legs but showed the first steps towards the four-legged walking of later sauropods.

One of the earliest large sauropods or near-sauropods, about 8–10 m long, walking on four legs in the Late Triassic. Its name means “before the thunder”, as it came before the Brontosaurus-type giants.
A medium-sized predator known from parts of the skull, a relative of Dilophosaurus.
A sauropod about 9–10 m long with a fairly short neck and a small bony club with spikes at the end of its tail. It is known from many complete skeletons.
A sauropod about 15–20 m long with a very long neck, an early relative of Mamenchisaurus.
One of the earliest and smallest stegosaurs, about 4 m long, with small plates and spines, shoulder spikes and teeth at the front of its upper jaw, which later stegosaurs lost.
A medium-sized predator about 4 m long known from a partial skeleton. It is named after the gas-mining company whose construction work uncovered the site.

A small heterodontosaur with long, stiff filaments along its back and tail. Whether these are related to the feathers of theropods is debated, but they suggest body coverings were widespread among dinosaurs.
The earliest known ceratopsian, about 1.2 m long and two-legged, with the beak-like rostral bone that all horned dinosaurs share, but no horns or frill.
A small early ceratopsian with a small frill and small horns below its eyes, close to the split between psittacosaurs and later horned dinosaurs.
A small early neoceratopsian known from a skull about 8 cm long, one of the earliest horned-dinosaur relatives in North America, related to Asian forms.
A small, two-legged plant-eater about 1 m long, known from several skulls, some from young animals.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Xu Xing, Wang Xiaolin and You Hailu, 2000

summary: A small plant-eater known from a partial skull and skeleton. Burrows of similar animals suggest its relatives may have dug dens.
A small, two-legged plant-eater about 2.5 m long, a close relative of Thescelosaurus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: William Parks, 1926 (as Thescelosaurus warreni); genus by Charles Sternberg, 1937

summary: A pachycephalosaur with a flat, thickened skull roof instead of a dome. Some researchers think it is a juvenile of the domed Prenocephale, as with Dracorex and Pachycephalosaurus; others keep it separate.

related.note: Possibly the adult form.

summary: A large stegosaur, perhaps 7–8 m long, the first stegosaur named, in 1875. It had small plates and long spines.
A stegosaur known from a skull and neck, living alongside Guanlong and Limusaurus.
A stegosaur from the Oxford Clay, known from limb and armour bones. Its remains were once placed in Lexovisaurus, until a 2008 restudy gave them their own name.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Franz Nopcsa, 1911 (as Stegosaurus priscus); genus by Susannah Maidment and colleagues, 2008

summary: A herrerasaurid predator about 3 m long, a smaller relative of Herrerasaurus.
One of the earliest sauropodomorphs, a small, two-legged animal about 1.3 m long. Its teeth suggest it ate both plants and small animals, hence its name, “eats everything”.
A brachiosaurid sauropod, a smaller relative of Brachiosaurus. Over 100 gizzard stones were found with one skeleton.

species:cathartesaura-anaerobica.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A rebbachisaurid sauropod about 15 m long. Its name refers to the vultures nesting at the site and to the energy company Anaeróbicos S.A. that supported the work.
An earlier Allosaurus species from the lower Morrison, with a narrower skull and low crests. “Big Al”, a famous skeleton with many injuries and infections, belongs to it.

related.note: The later, better-known species.

summary: A very large Allosaurus from Oklahoma, named in 2024. Its bones were previously part of “Saurophaganax”, a giant predator named in 1995. Restudy found that material was a mix of theropod and sauropod bones, with a name-bearing bone too poor to identify, so Saurophaganax is now treated as a doubtful name and the theropod bones were given this name.

facts.label: Formerly
facts.value: Part of “Saurophaganax maximus” (now a doubtful name)

related.note: Its smaller, better-known relative.

summary: A megalosauroid known from one of the most complete large predatory dinosaur skeletons from Europe, found in 1870 near Oxford. The skeleton is of a young animal, about 4.5–5 m long, so adults were larger. It was found in marine rocks, so the body probably washed out to sea.
A medium-sized predator about 4.5 m long from the Morrison. Its species name marks the US bicentennial, 1976, the year it was named.
A small early tyrannosauroid, about 3–4 m long, known mainly from hip bones. It shows tyrannosaur relatives lived alongside Allosaurus long before they became giants.

A large compsognathid about 2.4 m long covered in simple feathers. One specimen has the leg of the raptor Sinornithosaurus in its belly, another the remains of at least two Confuciusornis birds, eaten in quick succession. Whether it hunted or scavenged them cannot be told.
A compsognathid about 1.6–1.8 m long with large, grasping hands, known from a nearly complete skeleton.
A small feathered dinosaur close to Anchiornis. Its 2011 description briefly moved Archaeopteryx out of the birds; later analyses mostly put it back.
A small feathered dinosaur about 30 cm long with short feathers on its tail and legs and few on its lower legs, suggesting it ran on the ground rather than gliding.
An early troodontid about 1 m long, with features shared with early dromaeosaurs, helping show how the two raptor groups split.
An early therizinosaur known from a nearly complete young skeleton with feathers, showing early stages of the group’s plant-eating adaptations.
A medium-sized therizinosaur known from a partial skeleton with long, slender arms.
A therizinosaur about 2–3 m long known from two partial skeletons and a braincase.
A small, crestless oviraptorid about 1.2 m long, known from several fine skeletons from Ukhaa Tolgod. Two found together have been nicknamed “Romeo and Juliet”, and may differ by sex.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: James Clark, Mark Norell and Rinchen Barsbold, 2001

summary: An oviraptorid with a tall, domed crest, first described as a species of Oviraptor and later given its own genus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Rinchen Barsbold, 1986 (as Oviraptor mongoliensis); genus by Barsbold, 1997

summary: An ostrich-dinosaur with strong arms and flat, straight hand claws, perhaps used for digging.
A small noasaurid known from a slender leg and foot built for running, with the weight carried mainly on the middle toe.
A sparrow-sized enantiornithine, one of the first well-preserved Cretaceous birds found in Europe.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: José Luis Sanz and José Bonaparte, 1992

summary: A small enantiornithine whose wing preserves an alula, the small tuft of feathers birds use to fly slowly without stalling, the earliest known. One specimen held crustacean remains in its stomach.
An enantiornithine with a long snout and a few large teeth only at its tip, long wings and short legs, perhaps catching fish or other prey near water like a kingfisher; this is an inference.
A toothed bird on the line to modern birds, with fish remains preserved in the throat or stomach of some specimens, showing it ate fish.
A small, toothless bird on the line to modern birds, preserved in three dimensions in the Gobi sandstones of Ukhaa Tolgod.
A flightless, foot-propelled diving bird about 1 m long, a smaller relative of Hesperornis. Fossil droppings with fish bones have been linked to it.
