A small bird with a skull combining features of landfowl and waterfowl, among the oldest fossils clearly belonging to a modern bird group, from less than a million years before the asteroid impact. The press nicknamed it “Wonderchicken”; it was not a chicken, but may be close to the ancestor of chickens and ducks.
A large early synapsid about 2–3 m long with a deep, long skull and many sharp teeth, probably catching fish and land animals near water.
A slender early synapsid predator about 1.2 m long, shaped like a monitor lizard. One skeleton shows tooth marks from a scavenger.
A wolf-sized gorgonopsian about 1 m long with long canines, a lightly built hunter.

A small therocephalian with a large pit in front of each eye and grooved canines. It has been suggested it was venomous, with the pit holding a venom gland. A 2017 CT study looked at the pit and canals in detail, but whether it was venomous is still debated, as soft tissue is not preserved.
A large dicynodont about 3 m long with a toothless beak and two tusks, one of the main plant-eaters of the Middle Triassic.

species:cynognathus-crateronotus.placeText: South Africa, Argentina, China and Antarctica
summary: A wolf-sized cynodont predator about 1–1.2 m long with a big head and strong bite. Its fossils on several southern continents were early evidence that they had once been joined.
A cynodont about 2 m long with broad, grinding cheek teeth, probably eating plants as well as small animals.
A plant-eating cynodont about 50 cm long, the commonest animal in the Chañares concretions.
A small cynodont close to the ancestry of mammals, with an early contact between the bones that form the mammal jaw joint.
A shrew-sized early mammal relative about 10 cm long, probably active at night and eating insects.
A mouse-sized multituberculate, one of the commonest mammals of the latest Cretaceous, and one of the few that survived the extinction.
A small climbing mammal named in 2003 as the oldest known relative of marsupials. A 2018 restudy found it was more likely an early eutherian, on the placental side, so its place is disputed.
One of the last and largest brontotheres, about 2.5 m tall at the shoulder, with a forked, blunt horn on its nose, larger in males. A rib with a healed wound may record a fight between males.
species:megacerops-coloradensis.akaNote: Brontotherium is a synonym of Megacerops.

summary: An entelodont about 1.2 m tall at the shoulder with bony knobs on its jaws. Bite marks and a possible meat cache of early camels suggest it ate meat as well as plants.
A three-toed horse about the size of a sheep, larger than Eohippus, with longer legs suited to more open woodland.
A hornless rhino about the size of a cow, common in the White River badlands.
A small, slender early camel about the size of a sheep, with two-toed feet still bearing hooves rather than the padded feet of modern camels.
An oreodont about 1.4 m long, one of the commonest fossil mammals in North America, known from thousands of skulls. It was the first oreodont named.
A leopard-sized nimravid with long upper sabre teeth and a bony flange on the lower jaw to protect them, a “false sabre-tooth cat” that evolved this shape separately from true cats.
A wolf-sized hyaenodont with a long skull and shearing teeth. Despite the name, it was not related to hyenas.
One of the earliest members of the dog family, about 80 cm long including its long tail, more like a mongoose or civet in shape than a dog.
An early rabbit relative with shorter hind legs than living rabbits, very common in the White River badlands.
A cat-sized tree-dwelling primate close to the common ancestor of Old World monkeys and apes. Its skull shows a small brain for its size compared with living monkeys.
A small, squirrel-sized early anthropoid primate, probably a good leaper, eating fruit and seeds.

species:arsinoitherium-zitteli.placeText: Egypt and northern and eastern Africa
summary: A rhino-sized plant-eater about 3 m long with two huge, hollow, side-by-side horns over its nose. Despite its look, it was related to elephants and sea cows, not rhinos.
An early elephant relative about 1–2 m tall at the shoulder, with short tusks in both jaws and probably a short trunk.
A lion-sized early sabre-toothed cat, named from teeth found at Eppelsheim, the genus that gave the machairodont cats their name.
A “bone-crushing dog” with a short, powerful muzzle and broad teeth for cracking bones, like a hyena. It was one of the last of its subfamily.
An early species of Megalonyx, the ground sloth genus first described by Thomas Jefferson; this one was smaller than the later Ice Age Jefferson’s ground sloth.
A small baleen whale, one of the commonest whales at Pisco, a relative of the living pygmy right whale or of extinct cetotheres.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Giorgio Pilleri and Hans Jakob Siber, 1989

summary: A beaked whale known from many skulls at Cerro Colorado. Males had tusks, probably used in fights. One skull lies among the remains of sardines, perhaps its stomach contents.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Giovanni Bianucci, Olivier Lambert and Klaas Post, 2010

summary: A true seal with a short, robust skull and strong teeth, probably crushing hard-shelled prey, living alongside Acrophoca.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Eli Amson and Christian de Muizon, 2014

summary: A rabbit- to hare-sized notoungulate, one of the commonest small plant-eaters of the Santa Cruz, with ever-growing teeth.
A notoungulate about 2 m long with claws instead of hooves on its front feet, perhaps rearing up to pull down branches like a chalicothere.
A small, horse-like litoptern that walked on a single toe on each foot, with its side toes reduced even more than in modern horses, which it was not related to.
An armadillo about 1 m long with a pair of horn-like scutes on its snout. Its teeth suggest it may have eaten meat as well as plants, which is debated.

A jawless fish about 25–35 cm long with a bony head shield, a small, always-open mouth and eyes set at the very front of the head. It probably fed by sucking up small food particles. A cheerful-looking reconstruction became an internet meme in 2023.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Pierre-Yves Gagnier, Alain Blieck and Gabriela Rodrigo, 1986

summary: A flat, broad jawless fish about 35 cm long covered in bony plates, with an upturned mouth, probably living on the sea floor.
A flattened placoderm about 25 cm long with wide, wing-like pectoral fins, looking remarkably like a skate or ray, though not related to them.
An early lungfish about 35 cm long, with tooth plates for crushing food like living lungfish but two back fins rather than one long fin.
An arthrodire placoderm about 40 cm long, a small relative of Dunkleosteus, with bony blades for teeth.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Louis Agassiz, 1841, from Hugh Miller’s material

summary: A boxy antiarch placoderm about 20 cm long with jointed, arm-like fins, named after Hugh Miller, who thought it looked like a winged creature.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Hugh Miller, 1841 (as Pterichthys); genus by Bleeker, 1859

summary: A lobe-finned fish about 20 cm long covered in shiny, enamel-coated scales, an early member of the line that led to tetrapods.
One of the earliest well-known ray-finned fish, about 25–50 cm long with small, diamond-shaped scales and a large mouth, a predator that could swallow fish a good fraction of its own size.

species:cimolichthys-nepaholica.placeText: Kansas and the Western Interior, USA
summary: A long, slim predatory fish about 1.5–2 m long with rows of bony scutes along its body, a relative of Enchodus.
A hybodont shark about 1 m long with crushing teeth, known from three-dimensional skeletons in the Santana concretions.
An aquatic batrachosauroidid salamander, known from vertebrae and jaws, common in latest Cretaceous rivers and ponds alongside Scapherpeton.
A small, eel-like amphibian with tiny limbs, often found coiled inside fossil burrows, probably sitting out dry seasons in the mud.
A side-necked turtle with an unusually round, high shell about 1.5 m across, perhaps to resist the jaws of large crocodile relatives and Titanoboa.
A lizard-like tanystropheid about 1 m long with a long neck, but nothing like as long as Tanystropheus. It probably lived on land near the shore.
A small, early rhynchosaur about 1 m long, before the group developed its broad, beaked skulls and grinding tooth plates.
An early rhynchosaur about 50 cm long with several rows of teeth on its palate, a step towards the tooth plates of later rhynchosaurs.
A late phytosaur with a long snout ending in a raised crest. These phytosaurs were long called Pseudopalatus; a 2013 study showed Machaeroprosopus is the correct, older name.

A small lagerpetid found at the Hayden Quarry at Ghost Ranch alongside early dinosaurs, showing that close dinosaur and pterosaur relatives still lived alongside true dinosaurs millions of years after dinosaurs appeared.
Named as a small theropod dinosaur, but later recognised as a silesaurid, a close dinosaur relative.
A comb-jawed pterosaur with a spoon-shaped jaw tip lined with long, needle-like teeth. Its jaw was first described in 1832 as that of a crocodile.
An istiodactylid pterosaur with a wingspan of about 2.5 m and triangular teeth, known from a skull and neck.
A small, short-tailed anurognathid with a broad, short skull, one of the youngest of its family.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Ji Shu’an and Ji Qiang, 1998 (as Dendrorhynchus; renamed 1999)

summary: A small horned dinosaur about 1 m long with a short frill and a small nose horn, the commonest dinosaur of the Barun Goyot, known from young and adult skulls. Several other names, such as Breviceratops, have been shown to be growth stages of it.
A heavily armoured ankylosaur about 5–6 m long with a tail club. Its name means “beautiful”, after its well-preserved skull and armour.
A small, crestless oviraptorid about 1.5 m long. Its name, “shell thief”, comes from the idea that it crushed molluscs with its beak; this is a guess.
A small toothless bird related to Confuciusornis, with a curved beak and long tail feathers.
A small dromornithid (“thunder bird”) about the size of a cassowary, a relative of the giant Dromornis and Genyornis.
A cat-sized carnivorous mammal relative of Repenomamus, with large front teeth like canines. Its relatives may have eaten small dinosaurs.
An early sea cow with small hind legs, mostly or entirely aquatic, living alongside early whales in the Eocene sea.
A lynx-sized nimravid, a “false sabre-tooth cat” with moderately long upper canines.
A small oreodont with eyes and nostrils set high on its head. It was once thought to be aquatic, but the rocks it is found in formed in dry, open country.
An armadillo with a long, slender snout and tiny, peg-like teeth, probably eating ants and termites like a living anteater.

A coati-like member of the raccoon family about the size of a medium-sized dog, among the first North American mammals to reach South America, before the Panama land bridge was complete. It was probably the ancestor of the giant Chapalmalania.

A shrimp-like early arthropod about 10 cm long, preserved with its brain and nerves. They show that a complex, three-part brain like those of insects and crustaceans had already evolved. One find of several adults with a juvenile has been suggested to show parental care.
A radiodont predator, a relative of Anomalocaris, with grasping head limbs that had a large, pincer-like spine near the base.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Hou Xianguang, Jan Bergström and Per Ahlberg, 1995

summary: A Chinese species of Hallucigenia. Its fossils, described in 1991, showed which way up Hallucigenia went: the spines were on its back and the “tentacles” were legs.

related.note: The Burgess Shale species, first drawn upside down.

summary: A worm-like lobopodian with pairs of net-like plates along its body above each pair of legs. The tiny plates are found as separate microfossils worldwide.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Chen Junyuan, Hou Xianguang and Lu Haozhi, 1989

summary: A small lobopodian with long, slender legs bearing fine bristles, probably used to filter food from the water.
One of the earliest trilobites, preserved at Chengjiang with its legs and antennae, which are almost never found.

A swimming predator over 30 cm long with fins and jaws inside its head, a giant relative of today’s tiny arrow worms. Its gut holds the spiny arthropod Isoxys, and it was among the largest swimming predators of its time. Its name means “terror beast”.
A slug-like animal a few centimetres long covered in rows of small scales, with a shell at each end. Whether it was closer to molluscs or to brachiopods is still debated.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Simon Conway Morris and John Peel, 1990

summary: A “gilled lobopodian” with flaps along its sides for swimming and long, spiny front limbs, a step between walking lobopodians and swimming radiodonts. It is named after the philosopher Søren Kierkegaard.
A large gilled lobopodian up to about 50 cm long with flaps and stubby legs, and a mouth ringed with plates, probably a predator or scavenger.
The commonest trilobite at Sirius Passet, one of the oldest trilobites known from ancient North America (Laurentia).
A large trilobite up to about 15 cm long with spiny legs. Injured trilobites in the same rocks suggest it attacked other trilobites, perhaps even its own kind.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: James Holmes, John Paterson and Diego García-Bellido, 2020

summary: Probably the most collected trilobite in the world, a small, flat trilobite about 2–4 cm long quarried by the hundreds of thousands from the Wheeler Shale.
A radiodont up to about 40 cm long or more, one of the largest animals of its time and one of the first big predators, with spiny grasping limbs, big stalked eyes and flaps along its sides.

Its pieces were first described as different animals: its limbs as the tail of a shrimp-like creature (its name means “odd shrimp”). Whittington and Briggs put the whole animal together in 1985. Whether it could crunch hard trilobites is debated; its mouth may have been better at softer prey.

A small, ribbon-shaped swimmer about 4–5 cm long with a stiff rod along its back and blocks of muscle, an early chordate: not a vertebrate itself, but a member of the larger group vertebrates belong to.

The commonest animal in the Burgess Shale, with tens of thousands of specimens: a small arthropod about 2 cm long with long, sweeping spines on its head. It was the first Burgess Shale fossil Walcott found, and is nicknamed the “lace crab”.
A trilobite preserved with its legs and antennae, which showed how trilobite limbs worked. Spines on its legs may have helped it tear up food.
A large-eyed trilobite up to about 10 cm long, common in the shales of Mount Stephen near the Burgess Shale.
A lobopodian up to about 3.5 cm long that walked on slender, clawed legs, with two rows of stiff spines along its back.

It was first reconstructed upside down, walking on its spines with its legs taken for tentacles, and also back to front. Chinese relatives showed which way up it went in 1991, and in 2015 its true head was found, with simple eyes and a ring of teeth around its mouth. Its relatives include today’s velvet worms.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Charles Walcott, 1911 (as Canadia sparsa); genus by Simon Conway Morris, 1977

related.note: The Chinese species that showed which way up it went.

summary: An animal about 7 cm long with five eyes on stalks and a long, flexible proboscis ending in a grasping claw. When it was shown at a scientific meeting in the 1970s the audience reportedly laughed. It is an early relative of the arthropods.

A slug-like animal up to about 5 cm long covered in overlapping scales and two rows of tall spines, grazing on the sea floor with a tooth-bearing feeding organ. Most researchers see it as an early mollusc; some link it to bristle worms.
A burrowing priapulid worm about 8 cm long with a spiny proboscis. Its gut contents include small shelled animals and even other Ottoia, so it was a predator and sometimes a cannibal.
A branching sponge, one of the commonest sponges in the Burgess Shale, with a skeleton of a tough, organic fibre rather than glassy spicules.

The largest radiodont known, over 2 m long. Its head limbs were fringed with fine spines for filtering plankton, like a baleen whale, and its body had two rows of flaps on each side, clues to how arthropod limbs evolved. It is named after Mohamed Ben Moula, who found it.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Peter Van Roy, Allison Daley and Derek Briggs, 2015

summary: A small trilobite preserved in pyrite with its legs, gills and antennae. These fossils showed for the first time how trilobite limbs were arranged, and some females preserve eggs.
A sea scorpion preserved with its legs, gills and even muscles, showing how it swam with its paddle-shaped back legs. It lived in cold water during the end-Ordovician ice age.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Simon Braddy, Richard Aldridge and Johannes Theron, 1995

summary: A cold-water trilobite that spread worldwide during the end-Ordovician ice age, one of the survivors of the first wave of that mass extinction.

A tiny arthropod about 1 cm long with smaller animals attached to its body by long threads, like kites on strings. They are probably its young, an unusual form of parental care. Its name means “kite bearer”.
A tiny early chelicerate, a relative of horseshoe crabs, preserved in three dimensions with its limbs.

species:eurypterus-remipes.placeText: New York, USA, and Ontario, Canada
summary: A sea scorpion about 20 cm long, one of the most common eurypterid fossils, with paddle-shaped back legs for swimming. It has been the state fossil of New York since 1984.
A large pterygotid sea scorpion, perhaps up to about 2 m long, with long claws.

Known only from a tiny head with jaws, it was long called the oldest insect, possibly even a winged one. A 2017 restudy found it is more likely a centipede-like myriapod. The question is not fully settled.
The oldest known harvestman (daddy-long-legs), preserved in such detail that its reproductive organs survive. It looks very much like living harvestmen.
A springtail about 1–2 mm long, one of the oldest six-legged animals known.

A radiodont about 10 cm long, known from one specimen, living about 100 million years after the Cambrian. It shows that relatives of Anomalocaris survived far longer than once thought. It is named after a famous local outlaw.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Gabriele Kühl, Derek Briggs and Jes Rust, 2009

summary: One of the largest scorpions ever, up to about 70 cm long. It breathed air with book lungs, like living scorpions, and was one of the top predators on land when vertebrates were only just arriving there.

A millipede relative up to about 2.6 m long, the largest land invertebrate known. Its wide trackways cross the Joggins rocks. Head fossils described in 2024 confirmed it was a myriapod. High oxygen in the Carboniferous air has been suggested to explain its size, but this is debated.
A tiny snail found by John William Dawson inside fossil tree stumps at Joggins, one of the oldest known snails to live on land.
A soft-bodied swimmer up to about 35 cm long with eyes on a crossbar and a long proboscis ending in toothed jaws, found by Francis Tully in 1955.
What it was is still debated. Studies in 2016 argued it was a vertebrate, a relative of lampreys; later studies of its eyes and body argued it was an invertebrate. It is the state fossil of Illinois.
A small, spiny horseshoe crab, a common Mazon Creek fossil. It may have climbed among plants rather than living only in water.
A jellyfish, the commonest fossil of the marine part of Mazon Creek, preserved as bell-shaped impressions in ironstone nodules.

A griffinfly, an early relative of dragonflies, with a wingspan of about 65–70 cm, one of the largest insects that ever lived. It hunted other insects on the wing. High oxygen in the air is often suggested to explain its size; this is debated. A slightly later Permian relative, Meganeuropsis, was about as big or a little bigger.
species:meganeura-monyi.akaNote: Not a true dragonfly: a griffinfly, from an older related group.

summary: An oyster with one thick, curled shell and a small flat lid, lying on the soft sea floor. Its shape earned it the folk name “devil’s toenail”.
A small, strongly ribbed ammonite a few centimetres across, found in huge numbers in the Lower Lias around Lyme Regis.
A small, flat ammonite with straight ribs and a keel along its outer edge, common in the Blue Lias.

A sea lily whose colonies hung upside down from floating driftwood logs, with stems up to about 20 m long, among the longest of any animal. Whole rafts sank intact to the poisonous sea floor and were preserved together.
A common, finely ribbed ammonite. In Whitby, England, such ammonites were once carved with snake heads and sold as “snakestones”, said to be snakes turned to stone by St Hilda.
A flattened, sickle-ribbed ammonite used to date the Posidonia Shale. Some are preserved with their jaws.
A small, thin, flat clam whose shells cover bedding planes of the shale. It was formerly called Posidonia, and gave the Posidonia Shale its name.

A small, ornate ammonite so common it is used to divide the Oxford Clay into zones. Its males and females were so different in size and shape, the larger with a plain mouth and the smaller with long lappets, that they were long classed as separate species.
A squid-like relative of the belemnites, preserved at Christian Malford with its arms, hooks, ink sac and even muscle tissue.
A horseshoe crab very like living ones, sometimes found at the end of a long, winding trackway: its “death march” across the poisonous lagoon floor.
A small, stemless, free-living sea lily with feathery arms, so common that some Solnhofen layers are crowded with it. Whether it floated or rested on the bottom is debated.
A large prawn with long, spiny front legs, perhaps for catching prey, one of the commonest Solnhofen crustaceans.

species:platyceramus-platinus.placeText: Kansas and the Western Interior, USA
summary: A giant, thin-shelled clam over 2 m across, lying flat on the soft chalk sea floor. Small fish sheltered inside its shells and some were preserved there.
A stemless sea lily with arms up to about 1 m long, found in slabs packed with hundreds of individuals. How it lived, floating at the surface or resting on the bottom, is debated.

species:enchoteuthis-melanae.placeText: Kansas and the Western Interior, USA
summary: A giant relative of octopuses and vampire squid from the Western Interior Seaway, known from its pens (gladii), the stiff internal supports of its body, some over 1 m long. Bite marks on pens show fish and mosasaurs ate these animals. Much of the giant “Tusoteuthis” material belongs here, as Tusoteuthis itself is now thought to be based on too poor a specimen.
An ammonite with a straight shell like a walking stick, up to about 1 m long, so common and fast-changing that its species are used to date the Pierre Shale in fine detail.
A large, flat, smooth ammonite up to about 60 cm across whose iridescent shell layer is mined as the gemstone ammolite.

Some shells have rows of round holes that a 1960 study took to be mosasaur bites. In 1998 other researchers argued they are scars left by limpets, small snails that clamped onto the shell. Both views still have supporters.

The oldest known sepioid, a small cuttlefish-like squid relative, named in 2026 from two lower beaks. They were found hidden inside rock concretions by an AI-assisted method that digitally slices the rock and picks out fossils. Its beak is intermediate between those of cuttlefish and bobtail squid.

species:nanaimoteuthis-haggarti.placeText: Vancouver Island, Canada, and Hokkaido, Japan
summary: A giant octopus known only from large jaws. A 2026 study estimated it at about 7–19 m long, which would make it one of the largest invertebrates ever, and found worn jaws suggesting it crushed shells and bones. Size estimates from jaws alone are uncertain, and some researchers think it may have fed mostly on shellfish rather than large animals.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Kazushige Tanabe and colleagues, 2008 (as Paleocirroteuthis haggarti); moved to Nanaimoteuthis by Shin Ikegami and colleagues, 2026

summary: A large ammonite whose shell was bent back on itself several times like a paperclip, over 1 m long when uncoiled, one of the last ammonites before the end-Cretaceous extinction.
A mayfly whose large, flat larvae are among the commonest fossils in the Jehol lake beds, so typical that they are used to define the Jehol Biota.
A small freshwater bonytongue fish, one of the commonest fossils of the Jehol Biota, often found in mass mortality layers of hundreds.
A crayfish very like living ones of the same genus, preserved complete in the Green River lake beds.

A kalligrammatid lacewing that looked like a butterfly, with eyespots on its wings and a long, tube-like mouth for sipping fluids from the reproductive structures of seed plants, tens of millions of years before true butterflies. The resemblance is convergent; it was not related to butterflies.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Conrad Labandeira, Dong Ren and colleagues, 2016

summary: A tiny insect about 3 mm long with a mix of wasp and bee features, including branched, pollen-catching hairs, described in 2006 as the oldest bee-like insect. Its exact relationship to true bees is debated.

An early, stem-group bee with pollen grains on its legs, showing it had recently visited flowers. Twenty-one tiny beetle larvae trapped with it, five touching it, may have been hitching a ride back to its nest, as some living beetle larvae do with bees.

A tumbling flower beetle carrying 62 grains of eudicot pollen, the group that includes most living flowering plants. Its describers present it as the earliest direct evidence of an insect pollinating flowering plants.

A “hell ant”, one of an extinct group of early ants whose jaws swung upward to pin prey against a horn on the head. Its horn was reinforced with metal. Its describers suggested it might have fed on the blood of other insects; this is speculation.

The first Cretaceous ant described, in 1967, from amber found in seaside cliffs at Cliffwood by Edmund Frey and his wife. It has a mix of wasp and ant features, and showed that ants were already around in the age of dinosaurs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Edward O. Wilson, Frank Carpenter and William Brown, 1967

summary: A stingless bee, a worker of a living group of social bees, the oldest bee clearly belonging to a living group. Older bee-like insects such as Discoscapa are earlier branches. It shows social bees, and the flowers they fed on, were established before the asteroid impact.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Charles Michener and David Grimaldi, 1988 (as Trigona prisca); genus by Michael Engel, 2000

summary: The largest ant known: queens had a wingspan of about 15 cm, as big as a small hummingbird. Giant ants of this group spread across the warm Eocene world, even reaching Wyoming.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Herbert Lutz, 1986 (as Formicium giganteum); genus by Bruce Archibald and colleagues, 2011

species:cetiosaurus-oxoniensis.ageText: About 168 to 166 million years ago (Middle Jurassic, Bathonian)
summary: A long-necked plant-eater about 16 m long, the first sauropod ever named. Richard Owen named the genus in 1841 from huge vertebrae and thought they came from a giant sea-going reptile, hence the name “whale lizard”. Only when John Phillips dug up three skeletons near Bletchingdon, Oxfordshire, in 1869–70 and named this species in 1871 did it become clear it was a land animal.

A fairly complete skeleton found in a quarry near Rutland Water in 1968, the “Rutland dinosaur”, is mounted in Leicester. Cetiosaurus is thought to have made the 220 m trackway at Dewars Farm, the longest known in Europe, though no bones were found with the prints.

facts.label: Name trouble
facts.value: For a century many unrelated sauropod bones were lumped into Cetiosaurus; in 2014 the ICZN fixed C. oxoniensis as the type species

summary: A mallard-sized raptor relative with a swan-like neck making up half the length of its head and body, short, flattened arms and a flat, spoon-shaped snout. Each side of its upper snout tip held 11 closely packed teeth, more than any other known dinosaur, and channels in the snout may have held touch- or pressure-sensitive nerves.

Its describers in 2017 suggested it lived like a merganser, swimming with its arms and catching fish with its long neck. A 2019 study disputed this. In 2022 its close relative Natovenator was found with a flattened, diving-bird-like ribcage, which supports swimming in the group, but a 2024 study found Halszkaraptor’s bite was fast and weak, better suited to insects and other small invertebrates than fish, perhaps caught in dim light with its large eyes. How it lived is still uncertain.

The skeleton was taken from Mongolia by poachers and passed through private collections in Japan and Britain before a fossil dealer, François Escuillié, brought it to scientists in Brussels in 2015. A synchrotron X-ray scan showed it was a genuine single animal, not a forgery, and it was returned to Mongolia. It is named after the Polish palaeontologist Halszka Osmólska and Escuillié.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: About the size of a mallard

facts.label: Known from
facts.value: One skeleton of a roughly one-year-old

summary: A small, long-necked halszkaraptorine, about the size of a small duck, known from a nearly complete skeleton with its skull. Its name means “many-toothed swimming hunter”.

Its ribs angle sharply backwards, giving it a flattened, streamlined body like that of diving birds such as cormorants and penguins. Its describers in 2022 took this as the best evidence yet that halszkaraptorines swam, though it is an inference from body shape, and how well it swam is unknown.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: About the size of a small duck

summary: A tiny raptor relative about 50–70 cm long and under 1 kg, close to adult size, with the enlarged second-toe claw of a dromaeosaur. When it was named in 2007 it was found to be one of the earliest-branching dromaeosaurs, despite living late in the Cretaceous.

Its small size, shared with the earliest troodontids and birds, suggested that the ancestors of birds had already become small before they could fly, rather than shrinking as they took to the air. It was later grouped with Halszkaraptor among the halszkaraptorines. It is named after Mahākāla, a protector deity of Tibetan Buddhism.

species:pycnonemosaurus-nevesi.ageText: About 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous; poorly dated)
summary: A large abelisaurid, the short-snouted, small-armed predators of the southern continents. Its name means “dense forest lizard”, for the forested region where it was found.

It is known from one fragmentary skeleton: five broken teeth, parts of seven tail vertebrae, a hip bone (the pubis), a shin bone and part of the calf bone. It was first estimated at about 7 m long; a 2017 study suggested about 9 m, which would make it one of the largest abelisaurids, but with so few bones the size is uncertain.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos, 2002

species:achillobator-giganticus.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: One of the largest dromaeosaurs, about 4.5–5 m long. Its name combines Achilles, for its large Achilles tendon attachment, with the Mongolian “bator”, hero. No feathers are preserved, but its close relatives had them, so it was almost certainly feathered.

It is known from a partial skeleton found by a Mongolian–Russian expedition in 1989: part of the upper jaw with teeth, vertebrae, a nearly complete hip and leg bones. The hip has an unusually primitive, upright pubis for a dromaeosaur, and some researchers have suggested the skeleton might mix bones from more than one kind of animal. That has not been shown.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Altangerel Perle, Mark Norell and James Clark, 1999

species:albertaceratops-nesmoi.ageText: About 77.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: A centrosaurine horned dinosaur with long brow horns, unusual in a group that mostly had short brow horns and a big nose horn, and a pair of large hooks curving outward from the top of its frill.
Its describer placed it as the earliest-branching centrosaurine. Bones from Montana once referred to it were later assigned to Medusaceratops.

species:avaceratops-lammersi.ageText: About 79 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: A small horned dinosaur whose closest known relative is Nasutoceratops. The type skeleton, of an animal a little over 2 m long, includes much of the limbs and shoulders but only part of the skull.

That skeleton was probably not fully grown: it may be a juvenile or a subadult. A 2010 study argued that it lacks features unique enough to tell it apart, so a larger skull later referred to Avaceratops cannot be firmly assigned. Its size and some of its features may reflect youth rather than a separate species.

facts.label: Growth stage
facts.value: Type specimen probably not fully grown

species:anodontosaurus-lambei.ageText: About 73 to 68 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An ankylosaurid with a wide, pointed tail club, known through the whole span of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation. Its name means “toothless lizard”: the crushed skull it was named from had no teeth preserved.
For decades it was treated as the same animal as Euoplocephalus. Restudy of the skull and tail club in 2009 separated them again.

species:barsboldia-sicinskii.ageText: About 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: A large duck-billed dinosaur known from part of the backbone and hips, with no skull. Its spines along the hips and tail base were very tall, at least four times the height of the vertebrae, and thickened at the tips, which would have given it a ridge along its back.
It was named for the Mongolian palaeontologist Rinchen Barsbold. It was first thought to be a crested lambeosaurine; a 2011 restudy placed it instead as an early saurolophine.

species:kaiwhekea-katiki.ageText: About 70 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: A plesiosaur about 6.5–7 m long, known from a nearly complete skeleton with its skull, the most complete reptile of the dinosaur age found in New Zealand. It is displayed in the Otago Museum in Dunedin.
Its name is Māori for “squid eater”. First described as a cryptoclidid, it is now placed among the aristonectine elasmosaurs, close to Aristonectes.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably small prey such as fish and squid (inferred)

species:metriacanthosaurus-parkeri.ageText: About 160 million years ago (Late Jurassic, early Oxfordian)
summary: A large theropod known only from part of a hip, a leg bone and some back and tail vertebrae, found by W. Parker near Weymouth in the 19th century. Its name means “moderately spined lizard”: its back spines were taller than most theropods’ but lower than those of Altispinax.

The bones were first called Megalosaurus, then Altispinax, before getting their own genus in 1964. It gives its name to the Metriacanthosauridae, relatives of Allosaurus, and is the only named member of that family known from outside Asia.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Alick Walker, 1964 (species by Friedrich von Huene, 1923)

facts.label: Known from
facts.value: Partial hip, leg bone and vertebrae

summary: The only species in its genus and the best-known lemur, with a black-and-white ringed tail. Troops are led by females, and in the morning they sit facing the sun to warm up.
One of about 12 species of Eulemur, the “true lemurs”, which also include the black, crowned and red-bellied lemurs. In many species males and females are coloured differently.
One of about five lesser bamboo lemurs, which live mostly on bamboo shoots, leaves and pith.
One of the rarest primates, surviving in a few patches of southeastern rainforest. It feeds on giant bamboo, including shoots containing enough cyanide to kill animals its size.

One of two ruffed lemurs, with the red ruffed lemur. Large fruit-eaters, they are important pollinators and seed dispersers, and unusually for primates they give birth to litters of two or three young, left in nests.
One of about 25 mouse lemurs, most told apart only by DNA. Madame Berthe’s mouse lemur, about 30 g, is the smallest primate alive.
One of two giant mouse lemurs, with the northern giant mouse lemur. “Giant” only for a mouse lemur: about 300 g. It eats insects, fruit and the sugary secretions of bugs.
It stores fat in its tail and hibernates for up to seven months of the dry season in tree holes, the first tropical primate found to hibernate. There are about nine dwarf lemur species.
A tiny, rarely seen lemur with tufted ears, the only species in its genus. It was known from five museum specimens until it was rediscovered alive in 1989.
One of about four fork-marked lemurs, named for the dark stripe that forks over the head. They feed mostly on tree gum, which they gouge out with specialised teeth.
One of about 26 sportive lemurs, nocturnal leaf-eaters that cling upright to trunks. On a low-energy diet of leaves they spend much of the night resting.
The largest living lemur, up to about 9 kg, with only a stub of a tail. Family groups sing long, wailing songs that carry for kilometres through the rainforest.
One of about nine sifakas, which leap between trunks and, on open ground, bound sideways on their hind legs in a “dance”. Their name echoes their alarm call.
One of about nine woolly lemurs (avahis), the only nocturnal members of their family, eating leaves and living in small pair-bonded families.

A nocturnal lemur that taps on wood with a long, thin, flexible middle finger, listens for grubs, then gnaws in with ever-growing front teeth and hooks them out, filling the niche woodpeckers fill elsewhere. Superstition about it as a bad omen has led to many being killed.
One of two slender lorises, with the grey slender loris of southern India and Sri Lanka: thin-limbed, huge-eyed nocturnal insect hunters that creep slowly up on prey.

One of about nine slow lorises, the only venomous primates: they lick a gland in the arm and mix its secretion with saliva for a painful, sometimes dangerous bite. All species are threatened by the pet trade.

A slow, nocturnal climber with a grip strong enough to hang on for hours. Bony spines on the back of its neck may help defend it, tucked down, against predators. Some researchers split it into three species.
A small, slow-moving relative of the potto that hunts caterpillars, including hairy ones it wipes clean before eating. There is a second, golden angwantibo further south.

species:galago-senegalensis.placeText: Savannas from Senegal to East Africa
summary: A tiny, big-eyed leaper of dry woodland, able to jump several metres. It feeds on insects and tree gum. Galago has about four species.
The largest galago, up to about 1.5 kg, which walks and runs more than it leaps. It is one of two or three greater galagos.
One of the smallest galagos, about 60 g, living in dense tangles of forest undergrowth. The East African dwarf galagos once placed with it now form a separate genus, Paragalago.
One of the East African dwarf galagos, recognised as a separate genus in 2017 after studies of their calls and DNA. Galagos are best told apart by their calls.
One of three squirrel galagos of West-Central African forests, which forage low in the understorey for fallen fruit and insects.
One of two needle-clawed galagos, whose nails end in sharp points that let them cling to smooth trunks while scraping off gum, their main food.

Each of its eyes is about as big as its brain, and it can turn its head almost all the way round. Tarsiers eat only animals: insects, lizards and even small birds. Tarsius has about a dozen species on Sulawesi and nearby islands.
The only species of western tarsier, with the largest eyes relative to its body of any tarsier.
A tiny tarsier of Bohol, Samar, Leyte and Mindanao, the only species in its genus. It communicates partly in ultrasound, too high for humans to hear.
A small monkey with white ear tufts, one of six Atlantic Forest marmosets. Like other marmosets it gouges holes in bark and feeds on the gum that oozes out.
One of about 15 Amazonian marmosets in the genus Mico, several described only since the 1990s.
The smallest monkey, about 100–120 g. It feeds mostly on tree gum and sap, and can turn its head 180 degrees. Some split it into two species.
A tamarin with a white crest of long hair, found only in northwestern Colombia, where most of its forest has been cleared. Saguinus has about 15 species.
One of the saddle-back tamarins, moved to their own genus in 2016. They often travel in mixed groups with other tamarin species.

species:leontopithecus-rosalia.placeText: Atlantic Forest of Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil
summary: A bright orange tamarin with a lion-like mane, one of four lion tamarins. By the 1970s only a few hundred survived; reintroduction of zoo-bred animals and forest protection have raised the wild population to a few thousand.
A black monkey of the marmoset family, the only species in its genus. Unlike marmosets and tamarins it has single babies, not twins.

A gracile capuchin, one of about a dozen species in Cebus. White-faced capuchins rub crushed plants and insects into their fur, perhaps as insect repellent, and some groups use stones to crack shellfish. Central American populations are now a separate species, Cebus imitator.

One of about eight robust capuchins. Its relative the bearded capuchin uses stone hammers and anvils to crack palm nuts, a tradition archaeologists have traced back thousands of years at Serra da Capivara, Brazil.

A small, quick monkey living in troops that can number over a hundred, often following capuchins. Squirrel monkeys have some of the largest brains for their body size among primates. There are about seven species.
The night monkeys (owl monkeys) are the only truly nocturnal monkeys, with very large eyes. Pairs are monogamous and fathers do most of the carrying of the baby. There are about 11 species.

species:pithecia-pithecia.placeText: The Guianas, Venezuela and northern Brazil
summary: Males are black with a striking pale face; females are brown. Sakis eat many unripe fruits and seeds. Pithecia now has about 16 species after a 2014 revision.
A saki with a bushy beard and swollen-looking head. Bearded sakis crack hard unripe fruits with strong canines to eat the seeds inside. There are five species.

species:cacajao-calvus.placeText: Flooded forests of the western Amazon
summary: A short-tailed monkey with a bald, bright red face. The red is a sign of good health, since uakaris infected with malaria turn pale. There are about four uakari species.
Titi monkeys live in pair-bonded families; partners sit side by side with their tails twined together and sing duets. Plecturocebus, split off in 2016, has over 20 species.
Since a 2016 revision, Callicebus covers only the five titi species of Brazil’s Atlantic Forest and nearby dry forests.
A dark titi with a pale collar, one of about six species of Cheracebus, the widow monkeys, split off from other titis in 2016.

Howler monkeys have an enlarged hyoid bone in the throat that amplifies their roars, among the loudest calls of any land animal, carrying several kilometres. Mostly leaf-eaters, they spend much of the day resting. There are about 15 species.

Spider monkeys swing through the canopy using a prehensile tail with a bare, fingerprint-like pad as a fifth limb, and have only a stub of a thumb. They live in groups that split into small parties by day. There are seven species.
The largest New World monkey, one of two muriquis. They are known for peaceful, egalitarian groups that greet each other with hugs. Only small, scattered populations remain.
A thick-furred monkey with a strong prehensile tail. The genus also includes the yellow-tailed woolly monkey of the Peruvian Andes, once thought extinct and rediscovered in 1974.

The “snow monkey”, the most northerly non-human primate, famous for bathing in hot springs in winter. In the 1950s a young female on Kōshima began washing sweet potatoes, a habit that spread through her troop. Macaca has about 23 species from North Africa to Japan, the most widespread primate genus after humans.

species:papio-anubis.placeText: Savannas and woodlands from Mali to Ethiopia and Tanzania
summary: The most widespread of six baboon species, living in large troops with complex social hierarchies. Baboons are mostly ground-living and eat almost anything.

The only primate that lives mainly on grass, plucking blades with nimble fingers while shuffling along on its haunches. A bare red patch on the chest gives it the name “bleeding-heart monkey”. It is the last species of a genus that was widespread in the Pleistocene.

species:mandrillus-sphinx.placeText: Rainforests of Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and Congo
summary: The largest monkey; adult males have red and blue faces and rumps that brighten with rank. Hordes of several hundred have been recorded. Its only relative is the drill.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Males about 25–35 kg; females about 12 kg

species:cercocebus-torquatus.placeText: Coastal forests from Nigeria to Gabon
summary: A mangabey with a red cap and white collar. Cercocebus mangabeys forage on the forest floor and crack hard nuts with powerful jaws. There are about seven species.
A tree-living mangabey, more closely related to baboons than to the ground-living Cercocebus mangabeys, which it resembles by convergence. There are about three to six species.
A monkey of montane forest on Mount Rungwe and in the Udzungwa Mountains, described in 2005, the first new African monkey genus named in more than 80 years. Only about a thousand survive.
A guenon, one of about 20 species of Cercopithecus: colourful, mostly tree-living African monkeys that often form mixed groups with other guenon species. Several species interbreed where they meet.

Vervets give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and each call sends the troop to a different escape: up trees, into bushes or standing to look down. Chlorocebus has six species, including the green monkey and the grivet.

species:erythrocebus-patas.placeText: Savannas from Senegal to East Africa
summary: A long-legged, ground-living monkey of open savanna and the fastest primate, recorded running at about 55 km/h. Recent work splits it into two or three species.

species:allochrocebus-lhoesti.placeText: Montane forests around the Albertine Rift
summary: A dark, ground-foraging monkey with a white beard, one of three mountain monkeys sometimes kept within Cercopithecus.

species:miopithecus-talapoin.placeText: Angola and western Democratic Republic of the Congo
summary: The smallest Old World monkey, about 1 kg, living in large troops in swamp forests along rivers. There is a second species, the Gabon talapoin.

species:allenopithecus-nigroviridis.placeText: Swamp forests of the Congo Basin
summary: A stocky monkey of flooded forests that swims well, helped by partly webbed fingers. It is the only species in its genus.

A black-and-white colobus with a long white mantle and bushy tail. Colobus monkeys have only a tiny stub of a thumb (their name means “docked”) and a multi-chambered stomach for digesting leaves. There are five species.

A red colobus found only on Zanzibar, known for eating charcoal, which may help it digest toxins in the leaves it eats. Red colobus monkeys (about 17 species) are among Africa’s most threatened primates.
The smallest colobus, and the only monkey in which mothers carry newborns in their mouths. It is the only species in its genus.
The Hanuman langur, sacred in Hinduism and common around temples and towns. Grey langurs (about eight species) are leaf-eating monkeys of South Asia.

species:trachypithecus-obscurus.placeText: Malay Peninsula, southern Thailand and Myanmar
summary: A langur with white rings around its eyes, also called the spectacled langur. Its babies are born bright orange and darken over months, as in many lutungs. Trachypithecus has about 20 species.
A deep red leaf monkey of Borneo’s forests. Presbytis, the surilis, has about 17 species in Sundaland, many with striking crests or face markings.
One of the most colourful primates: grey body, maroon “trousers” below the knee, white forearms and a golden face. There are three doucs.

A golden-furred monkey of cold mountain forests, where it survives snowy winters on lichens and bark. Snub-nosed monkeys (five species) live farther north and higher than almost any other non-human primates.

species:nasalis-larvatus.placeText: Mangroves and river forests of Borneo
summary: Adult males have a huge, drooping nose that may amplify calls and attract females. A strong swimmer with partly webbed feet, it lives along rivers and in mangroves. It is the only species in its genus.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Males about 20 kg; females about 10 kg

summary: A short-tailed langur, also called the simakobu, found only on the Mentawai Islands off Sumatra. Hunting and logging have made it one of the most threatened monkeys.

species:hylobates-lar.placeText: Thailand, Malay Peninsula, Myanmar, Laos and northern Sumatra
summary: The white-handed gibbon, a fast brachiator that swings arm over arm and covers up to about 3 m per swing. Mated pairs sing duets each morning. Hylobates has about nine species.
India’s only ape. Hoolocks have three species, including the Skywalker hoolock gibbon described from China in 2017.
The world’s rarest ape, reduced to about ten animals in the 1970s and now about 40, all in one forest reserve on Hainan. Crested gibbons (about seven species) are black males and golden females.
The largest gibbon, with an inflatable throat sac that amplifies its booming duets, heard kilometres away. It is the only species in its genus.

The largest tree-living animal, spending most of its life in the canopy. Orangutans have the slowest life history of any non-human mammal: a mother has a baby only about every 6–8 years. There are three species: Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli, the last described in 2017 and the rarest great ape.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Males about 50–90 kg; females about 30–50 kg

summary: The largest living primate. Gorillas live in family groups led by a silverback male and eat mostly plants. There are two species: the western gorilla and the eastern gorilla, which includes the mountain gorilla, whose numbers have risen thanks to protection.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Males about 140–200 kg; females about 70–90 kg

summary: With the bonobo, our closest living relative: the lineages split roughly 6–7 million years ago. Chimpanzees make and use tools, hunt cooperatively and have local cultural traditions. The genus has two species, the chimpanzee and the bonobo.

species:panthera-tigris.placeText: South and Southeast Asia, the Russian Far East and northeast China
summary: The largest living cat, with males up to about 300 kg in the Russian Far East and India. Tigers once ranged from eastern Turkey and the Caspian Sea to Bali and the Russian Far East; they have lost over 90% of that range, and the Caspian, Javan and Bali tigers are extinct. About 5,500 live in the wild (2023 estimate), around two-thirds of them in India, where numbers have risen since 2006. Panthera, the roaring big cats, also includes the lion, leopard, jaguar and snow leopard.

species:panthera-pardus.placeText: Sub-Saharan Africa and scattered parts of Asia, from Arabia to the Russian Far East
summary: The most widespread wild cat, at home in rainforest, savanna, desert, mountains and even the edges of cities such as Mumbai and Nairobi. It is a stealthy, mostly nocturnal hunter that takes anything from beetles to antelope larger than itself, and often hauls kills up into trees away from lions and hyenas. Black leopards (“black panthers”) are leopards with a gene for dark fur; their rosettes still show in the right light.

Leopards have lost about two-thirds or more of their historic range, vanishing from most of North Africa, the Middle East and much of China. Some forms are close to extinction: about 120 Amur leopards survive on the Russia–China border, and the Arabian leopard is down to perhaps 100–200 animals.

species:panthera-onca.placeText: Mexico to northern Argentina, with occasional visitors to Arizona
summary: The largest cat in the Americas and the third largest in the world, with the most powerful bite for its size of any big cat. Unlike other big cats it often kills by biting through the skull, and it can crack turtle shells. It is a strong swimmer that hunts caimans, capybaras and fish as well as deer and peccaries. Black jaguars, like black leopards, are a dark colour form.

Jaguars once lived from the southwestern United States to central Argentina and Uruguay; they have lost about half of that range, and are gone from Uruguay and El Salvador. A few males still wander into Arizona from Mexico. The Amazon holds most of the remaining population.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Males about 55–100 kg, larger in the Pantanal

species:panthera-uncia.placeText: Mountains of Central and South Asia, from the Himalayas to Mongolia and Siberia
summary: A smoky-grey cat of high, cold mountains, usually between about 3,000 and 5,500 m, with thick fur, broad furry feet that act as snowshoes, and a very long, thick tail it uses for balance and wraps around itself for warmth. It hunts wild sheep and goats such as blue sheep and ibex on steep cliffs. Unlike other Panthera cats it cannot roar.

Its range today is close to its historic range, but it is thinly spread: about 4,000–6,500 remain, threatened by poaching, killing in revenge for livestock losses, and the loss of its wild prey. Its mountain habitat may shrink as the climate warms.

species:panthera-leo.placeText: Sub-Saharan Africa, and Gir forest in Gujarat, India
summary: The only cat that lives in groups: a pride of related females and their cubs, with one or a few males that defend it from other males. Females do most of the hunting, often working together to bring down zebra, wildebeest and buffalo, but males hunt too, especially big prey such as buffalo. Only males grow manes; darker, fuller manes signal a healthier male. Its roar can be heard about 8 km away.

Lions once lived across Africa, the Middle East and India, and in southeastern Europe in ancient times. They have lost over 90% of that range, and their numbers fell by about 40% in just two decades after 1993, to habitat loss, conflict with livestock herders and loss of prey; about 20,000–25,000 survive in the wild. The last Asiatic lions live in and around Gir forest in Gujarat, India, where careful protection has raised their number from perhaps a few dozen in the early 1900s to almost 900 in 2025. The extinct cave lion of Ice Age Eurasia and the American lion were close relatives.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Males about 150–250 kg; females about 110–180 kg

species:neofelis-nebulosa.placeText: Himalayan foothills to southern China and mainland Southeast Asia
summary: A tree-climbing cat with cloud-shaped markings and, for its size, the longest canine teeth of any living cat. It can climb down trunks head-first and hang from branches by its hind feet. The Sunda clouded leopard of Borneo and Sumatra is the second species.

species:acinonyx-jubatus.placeText: Eastern and southern Africa and the Sahara, with a tiny population in Iran; reintroduced to India
summary: The fastest land animal, reaching about 100–110 km/h in short sprints. Its claws only partly retract, gripping like running spikes. Cheetahs have very low genetic diversity, a sign of a population crash in the past. They once lived across most of Africa and from Arabia to India, where they were kept by royalty for hunting; only about 7,000 remain, and the Asiatic cheetah survives only in Iran, with a few dozen or fewer. India’s cheetahs died out by the 1950s, and since 2022 cheetahs from Namibia and South Africa have been released in Kuno National Park.

species:puma-concolor.placeText: From western Canada to southern South America
summary: Also called the puma or mountain lion, it has the largest range of any wild land mammal in the Americas, from the Yukon to Patagonia. It is the largest cat that cannot roar; it purrs and screams instead. The jaguarundi is its closest relative.
A small, long-bodied, short-legged cat with an otter-like look, active by day, and coloured either grey or reddish. It is the only species in its genus, the closest relative of the cougar.

species:lynx-lynx.placeText: Forests from western Europe to the Russian Far East
summary: The largest lynx, with tufted ears, a short tail and big furry feet for snow. It has returned to parts of western Europe through reintroductions. Lynx has four species: Eurasian, Iberian, Canada lynx and bobcat.

species:leptailurus-serval.placeText: Savannas and wetlands of sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A tall, slim cat with the longest legs and largest ears for its size of any cat. It listens for rodents in long grass and catches them with a high pounce, and leaps to snatch birds in flight.

species:caracal-caracal.placeText: Africa, the Middle East and Central and South Asia
summary: A sandy cat with long black ear tufts, famed for leaping straight up to knock birds out of the air. Its genus also includes the African golden cat of the rainforest.
A spotted, mostly nocturnal cat of tropical forests. Leopardus, the small spotted cats of the Americas, has about a dozen species, including the margay, oncilla, kodkod and Geoffroy’s cat.

A thick-furred wild cat with a blunt, ringed tail. The domestic cat descends from its close relative the African wildcat, tamed in the Near East roughly 10,000 years ago. Felis also includes the sand cat, jungle cat and black-footed cat.

species:otocolobus-manul.placeText: Steppes and mountains of Central Asia
summary: A stocky cat with the longest, densest fur of any cat, low-set ears and round pupils, living in cold, dry grasslands and rocky slopes. It is the only species in its genus.

A small spotted cat and one of the most widespread wild cats in Asia. Its genus also includes the fishing cat, which dives for fish, the flat-headed cat and the rusty-spotted cat, one of the smallest cats.

species:pardofelis-marmorata.placeText: Himalayan foothills to Borneo and Sumatra
summary: A small, tree-living cat with a very long, thick tail and a coat patterned like a miniature clouded leopard. It is the only species in its genus.
A medium-sized cat that varies from golden to grey, black or spotted. Its relative, the bay cat of Borneo, is one of the least-known cats.

species:prionodon-linsang.placeText: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java and Borneo
summary: A slim, banded, tree-living hunter with retractable claws. DNA shows the two Asiatic linsangs are the closest living relatives of cats, not civets as long thought. The spotted linsang is the other species.

species:nandinia-binotata.placeText: Rainforests of Central and West Africa
summary: A tree-living omnivore of African forests, eating mostly fruit, and the only species in its family. It branched off before all other living cat-like carnivorans.

species:viverra-zibetha.placeText: Northeast India to southern China and Southeast Asia
summary: A large, grey civet with a black-and-white banded tail and a crest along the back. Viverra has four species, including the critically endangered Malabar civet of southern India.
The largest civet in Africa, a nocturnal omnivore whose musk was harvested for perfume for centuries. It is the only species in its genus.

species:viverricula-indica.placeText: South Asia to southern China and Indonesia
summary: A small, mostly ground-living civet with dark stripes and a ringed tail, common around farmland. It is the only species in its genus.
A slim, spotted, cat-like hunter with a banded tail. In Europe it lives in Iberia and France, probably brought by people long ago from North Africa. Genetta has about 14 species.
A small, slender, spotted, tree-living relative of the genets. Poiana has two species, the other in West Africa.

A common, fruit-loving civet that often lives in roofs and plantations. It eats ripe coffee cherries, and the beans recovered from its droppings are sold as kopi luwak, a trade criticised for keeping civets in cages. Paradoxurus has about three to six species.

species:paguma-larvata.placeText: Himalayas to China, Southeast Asia and Taiwan
summary: A plain-coated civet with a white facial mask. It was linked to the 2003 SARS outbreak, having caught the virus, probably from bats, in wildlife markets. It is the only species in its genus.

A shaggy civet, sometimes called the bearcat, with a prehensile tail, one of only two carnivorans able to grip with the tail (the kinkajou is the other). Its scent is often compared to buttered popcorn. It is the only species in its genus.
A slender, three-striped, tree-living civet that feeds mostly on fruit. It is the only species in its genus.
A rarely seen civet found only on Sulawesi, and the island’s largest native carnivore. It is the only species in its genus.
A ground-foraging civet with bold dark bands across its back, feeding mostly on insects and earthworms. It is the only species in its genus.

species:chrotogale-owstoni.placeText: Northern Vietnam, Laos and southern China
summary: A banded civet that forages for earthworms on forest floors. It is the only species in its genus.
A semi-aquatic civet with webbed feet, long whiskers and nostrils and ears that close underwater, hunting fish and crabs in swamp forests. It is the only species in its genus.
One of the least-known carnivorans, found only in the hills and mountains of northern Borneo. It is the only species in its genus.

Madagascar’s largest native predator, a cat-like hunter with semi-retractable claws and flexible ankles that let it run down trees head-first. Lemurs make up much of its diet. It is the only species in its genus.
A small, spotted, civet-like carnivoran (the fanaloka). Confusingly, its scientific genus is Fossa, while the animal called the fossa is Cryptoprocta. It is the only species in its genus.
A small carnivoran with a narrow snout and tiny cone-shaped teeth, specialised for eating earthworms and snails. It stores fat in its tail for the dry season. A second species lives in the northwest.
A chestnut, mongoose-like carnivoran with a red-and-black ringed tail, active by day. It is the only species in its genus.
A nocturnal, striped carnivoran of eastern rainforest. Its relative, Grandidier’s vontsira, lives only in the dry spiny forest of the southwest.
A small, grey, striped carnivoran that lives in family groups and feeds largely on insect larvae. It is the only species in its genus.
A plain brown carnivoran of lowland rainforest. A second species, Durrell’s vontsira, was described in 2010 from the marshes of Lake Alaotra.

species:herpestes-ichneumon.placeText: Africa, the Middle East and southern Iberia
summary: The largest mongoose in Africa, revered in ancient Egypt. The Asian mongooses once placed in Herpestes, including the famous snake-fighting Indian grey mongoose, are now in Urva. Herpestes has about three species.
The mongoose of Kipling’s “Rikki-Tikki-Tavi”, known for fighting cobras: it relies on speed and thick fur, and is partly resistant to cobra venom. Urva has about ten Asian species.

A small mongoose living in groups of up to about 50, in which sentries stand upright to watch for predators while others forage and helpers babysit the dominant pair’s pups. It is the only species in its genus.
A striped, social mongoose living in packs of 10–40 that raise pups communally, with escorts guarding particular pups. A second species lives in Gambia and West Africa.

Africa’s smallest carnivoran, about 300 g. Groups led by a dominant pair live in termite mounds, and forage alongside hornbills that warn them of birds of prey. A second species lives in the Horn of Africa.
A large, shaggy, dark mongoose of rivers and swamps that hunts crabs and frogs, sometimes smashing shellfish on rocks. It is the only species in its genus.
The largest mongoose, a nocturnal, solitary hunter of insects with a bushy white tail. It is the only species in its genus.
A sandy, bushy-tailed mongoose of open dry country that often shares burrows with meerkats and ground squirrels. It is the only species in its genus.
A grey, nocturnal, insect-eating mongoose of savanna and farmland, named after the hunter Frederick Selous. It is the only species in its genus.
A little-known, nocturnal mongoose of open woodland that eats mainly termites. It is the only species in its genus.
A dark, bushy-tailed mongoose of woodland. Bdeogale has three species, including the black-footed mongoose of Central African rainforests.
A dark mongoose of West African rainforest with long claws for digging earthworms. It was known only from skulls until a live animal was found in 1974. It is the only species in its genus.
A small, dark, long-snouted mongoose that lives in noisy groups on the forest floor. Crossarchus has four species.
One of the least-known mongooses, from savanna–forest edges in central Africa, known from a handful of specimens. It is the only species in its genus.

A powerful hunter as well as a scavenger, killing most of its own food in clans of up to about 80 led by females, who are larger than males. Its jaws crush bone, and its “laugh” is a call of excitement or stress. It is the only living species in its genus; the cave hyena of Ice Age Eurasia was a close relative.

species:hyaena-hyaena.placeText: North and East Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and India
summary: A shaggy, mainly solitary scavenger with a mane that it raises when threatened, ranging from Morocco to India. It is the only living species in its genus.

species:parahyaena-brunnea.placeText: Deserts and dry savannas of southern Africa
summary: A long-haired scavenger of the Kalahari and Namib that also patrols the Skeleton Coast for dead seals and fish. It is the only species in its genus.

A small, striped hyena that eats almost nothing but termites, lapping up hundreds of thousands a night with a long sticky tongue; its cheek teeth are tiny pegs. Two separate populations live in eastern and southern Africa. It is the only species in its genus.

The largest wild dog, hunting in family packs; it once had the largest range of any land mammal besides humans. The domestic dog descends from Ice Age wolves, domesticated at least 15,000 years ago. Canis also includes the coyote, golden jackal, Ethiopian wolf and African golden wolf.
A fox-sized jackal with a dark, silvery saddle. DNA shows the black-backed and side-striped jackals are not close to the golden jackal and wolves, so they were given their own genus in 2017.
The Asian wild dog, a rust-red hunter living in packs that communicate with whistles and can bring down deer much larger than themselves. It is the only species in its genus.

species:lycaon-pictus.placeText: Savannas of eastern and southern Africa
summary: A blotchy-coated hunter with large round ears and only four toes on its front feet. Packs hunt cooperatively and share food with pups and the sick; “sneezes” act as votes on when to set off. Only about 6,000 remain. It is the only species in its genus.

The tallest wild dog, with very long black legs for seeing over tall grass, though it is neither a wolf nor a fox. It eats a lot of fruit, especially the wolf apple. It is the only species in its genus.

species:speothos-venaticus.placeText: Central and South American forests and savannas
summary: A short-legged, stocky dog that hunts in packs, swims well and chases prey into water. It is the only species in its genus.
A grey fox-like dog of savannas and woodlands that eats crabs on floodplains in the wet season, as well as insects, fruit and small animals. It is the only species in its genus.

The largest of the South American foxes, which are not true foxes but form their own branch of the dog family. Lycalopex has six species, including the South American grey fox and the Darwin’s fox of Chiloé.
One of the least-known wild dogs, a shy, short-eared, dark dog of Amazonian rainforest, seen mostly on camera traps. It is the only species in its genus.

A fox-sized dog with a raccoon-like mask, the only canid that hibernates or becomes dormant in cold winters. Released in western Russia for fur, it has spread across much of Europe. The Japanese raccoon dog (tanuki) is the second species.
A small fox with enormous ears for hearing termites and beetles underground. It has more teeth (up to 50) than almost any other placental land mammal. It is the only species in its genus.

species:vulpes-vulpes.placeText: Northern Hemisphere and North Africa; introduced to Australia
summary: The most widespread wild carnivoran, at home from Arctic tundra to city centres. It was introduced to Australia in the 1800s, where it has helped drive many small native mammals to extinction. Vulpes, the true foxes, has about 12 species, including the Arctic fox and the tiny fennec.

species:urocyon-cinereoargenteus.placeText: Southern Canada to northern South America
summary: An ancient branch of the dog family and one of the few canids that regularly climbs trees, using hooked claws. Its relative, the island fox, lives only on the Channel Islands of California and is the size of a house cat.

species:ursus-arctos.placeText: Northern North America, Europe and Asia
summary: One of the largest land carnivorans, including the grizzly and the Kodiak bear. Ursus also includes the polar bear, which evolved from brown bears and can still interbreed with them, and the American and Asian black bears.

species:ursus-maritimus.placeText: Arctic sea ice and coasts of Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Norway and Russia
summary: The largest land carnivore alongside the Kodiak brown bear, with big males weighing about 350–700 kg. It is so tied to the sea that it is legally classed as a marine mammal: it hunts mainly ringed and bearded seals from the sea ice, waiting at breathing holes or stalking seals hauled out on the ice, and can swim for days. One female swam 687 km in nine days. Its fur is not white but made of colourless hairs over black skin; the old idea that the hollow hairs pipe sunlight to the skin like optical fibres has been disproved.

It evolved from brown bears, probably within the last few hundred thousand years (estimates vary), and the two still sometimes interbreed, producing “pizzly” or “grolar” bears. Pregnant females dig snow dens where cubs are born in midwinter, tiny and blind. About 20,000–30,000 live in 19 subpopulations. As the climate warms, sea ice forms later and melts earlier, forcing bears ashore to fast for longer: the Western Hudson Bay population fell from about 1,200 in the 1980s to about 620 in 2021. A small population in southeast Greenland, described in 2022, survives by hunting from floating glacier ice.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Males about 350–700 kg; females about 150–300 kg

species:ailuropoda-melanoleuca.placeText: Mountain bamboo forests of central China
summary: A bear that eats almost nothing but bamboo, helped by a “false thumb” (an enlarged wrist bone) for gripping stems. Protection raised the wild population to about 1,860 in 2014, and its status was improved from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2016. It is the only living species in its genus.

species:tremarctos-ornatus.placeText: The Andes, from Venezuela to Bolivia
summary: South America’s only bear, with pale markings around its eyes, and the last of the short-faced bears, whose giant relatives included Arctodus. It eats mostly plants such as bromeliads and builds platforms in trees. Paddington Bear came from “darkest Peru”.
A shaggy bear that feeds on termites and ants, sucking them up through a gap left by its missing front teeth with mobile lips. Mothers carry cubs on their backs. It is the only species in its genus.
The smallest bear, with a pale crescent on its chest and a very long tongue for getting honey and insects from trees. It is the only species in its genus.

A cat-sized, tree-living relative of skunks and raccoons rather than bears, with a ringed tail and, like the giant panda, a false thumb for holding bamboo. It was called a panda first; the giant panda borrowed the name. Some split it into two species.
The familiar black-and-white skunk, which raises its tail and stamps before spraying musk that can reach about 3 m. Mephitis has two species, with the hooded skunk.
A small, spotted skunk that does a handstand before spraying. Spilogale has about four species.
A skunk with a bare, pig-like snout for rooting out grubs. Hog-nosed skunks (four species) range from the southwestern United States to Patagonia.
Long thought to be badgers, stink badgers are the only skunks outside the Americas. They spray foul secretions like skunks. The Palawan stink badger is the second species.

species:procyon-lotor.placeText: North and Central America; introduced to Europe and Japan
summary: A masked, ringed-tailed omnivore with sensitive, dexterous front paws, thriving in towns and cities. Introduced populations now live across Germany and much of Europe. Procyon has three species, including the crab-eating raccoon of South America.
A long-snouted, ring-tailed raccoon relative. Females and young forage in bands of up to about 30 with tails held upright; adult males live alone. Nasua has two species, with the white-nosed coati.
A small, olive-brown coati of cloud forest and páramo high in the northern Andes. Nasuella has two species.

A slender, nocturnal relative of the raccoon with huge eyes and a long black-and-white ringed tail, an agile climber of cliffs and canyons; miners once kept them to catch mice. Bassariscus has two species, with the cacomistle.
A golden, tree-living fruit-eater with a prehensile tail and a long tongue for nectar and honey, sometimes called the honey bear. It is the only species in its genus.

species:bassaricyon-neblina.placeText: Cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador
summary: Announced in 2013, the first new carnivoran from the Americas in 35 years. A specimen had sat unrecognised in museums for decades, and one even lived in US zoos as an “olingo”. Bassaricyon, the olingos, has four species.

species:mustela-erminea.placeText: Northern Europe and Asia; introduced to New Zealand
summary: A small, slender hunter that turns white in snowy winters (ermine), keeping its black tail tip. Introduced to New Zealand to control rabbits, it now preys on native birds. Mustela also includes the least weasel, the polecat and its domesticated form the ferret, and the European mink.

species:neogale-vison.placeText: North America; escaped farm mink across Europe
summary: A semi-aquatic hunter, farmed for fur. Escapes have established wild populations across Europe, where it threatens water voles and the native European mink. DNA moved the American weasels and minks from Mustela to Neogale in 2021.

species:martes-martes.placeText: Forests of Europe and western Asia
summary: An agile, tree-climbing hunter with a creamy throat patch. Where it has recovered, it seems to reduce numbers of invasive grey squirrels. Martes has about seven species, including the sable and the yellow-throated marten.

species:pekania-pennanti.placeText: Forests of Canada and the northern United States
summary: A large, dark marten relative and one of the few predators that regularly kills porcupines, attacking the face to avoid the quills. It does not eat fish despite its name. It is the only species in its genus.

species:gulo-gulo.placeText: Arctic and subarctic North America and Eurasia
summary: The largest land-dwelling mustelid, powerful enough to drive wolves or bears off a carcass, and a wide-ranging scavenger of snowy wilderness. It is the only species in its genus.
A long-bodied, dark, tree-climbing omnivore that has been seen picking unripe fruit and caching it until it ripens, a sign of planning. It is the only species in its genus.

species:galictis-vittata.placeText: Southern Mexico to Bolivia and Brazil
summary: A low-slung, grey-backed hunter with a black face and belly, outlined in white. Galictis has two species, with the lesser grison.
A little-known, pale, flat-headed weasel of dry grasslands, thought to hunt burrowing rodents such as tuco-tucos. It is the only species in its genus.
The zorilla, a skunk-like African mustelid with bold black-and-white stripes that sprays foul musk in defence. Ictonyx has two species, with the Saharan striped polecat.
A tiny, very long-bodied, striped weasel that hunts rodents in their burrows. It is the only species in its genus.
A strikingly mottled polecat of steppes and deserts that, when threatened, raises its bushy tail and arches its back in warning. It is the only species in its genus.
A black-and-white-faced badger living in clans in large burrow systems, called setts, some used for decades or even centuries. Meles has about four species across Eurasia.

species:arctonyx-collaris.placeText: Northeast India to China and mainland Southeast Asia
summary: A badger with a pink, pig-like snout for rooting in soil. Arctonyx has three species, split in 2008.

species:melogale-moschata.placeText: Southern China, Taiwan and northern Southeast Asia
summary: A small, masked badger with a long tail that eats earthworms and insects and often lives near farms. Melogale has about five species.

species:mellivora-capensis.placeText: Africa, the Middle East and South Asia
summary: A famously tough badger with thick, loose skin that lets it twist round to bite attackers. It digs out bee nests, scorpions and venomous snakes, and is fairly resistant to some snake venoms. It is the only species in its genus.
A flat-bodied digger of prairies that excavates ground squirrels and prairie dogs, and sometimes hunts in partnership with coyotes. It is the only species in its genus.

A river otter that declined badly in the 20th century from pesticide poisoning and has since returned to most of its old range in Britain and elsewhere. Lutra has two species, with the hairy-nosed otter.
A playful, sleek otter of rivers, lakes and coasts that has recovered across much of the United States through reintroductions. Lontra has four species, including the marine otter of Chile and Peru.

species:enhydra-lutris.placeText: North Pacific coasts from Japan to California
summary: The heaviest mustelid and the densest-furred animal, with up to about a million hairs per square inch. Floating on its back, it cracks shellfish on a stone balanced on its chest. By eating sea urchins it protects kelp forests. Hunted almost to extinction for fur, it has partly recovered. It is the only species in its genus.

species:pteronura-brasiliensis.placeText: Rivers of the Amazon, Orinoco and Pantanal
summary: The longest member of the weasel family, up to about 1.7 m, living in noisy family groups that hunt fish together and can drive off caimans. It is the only species in its genus.
The smallest otter, with tiny claws and nimble fingers for feeling for crabs and shellfish. Aonyx also includes the large African clawless otter and the Congo clawless otter.
