species:hydrictis-maculicollis.placeText: Lakes and rivers of sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A slim African otter with creamy spots on its throat, common in Lake Victoria and other clear lakes. It is the only species in its genus.

species:lutrogale-perspicillata.placeText: South and Southeast Asia, with a relict population in Iraq
summary: A large otter with a short, sleek coat, living in family groups; it hunts fish cooperatively and has become a familiar sight in Singapore’s city waterways. It is the only species in its genus.

species:arctocephalus-pusillus.placeText: Coasts of southern Africa and southeastern Australia
summary: The largest fur seal, gathering on rocky coasts in colonies of tens of thousands. Arctocephalus, the southern fur seals, has about eight species.

species:callorhinus-ursinus.placeText: North Pacific; breeds mainly on the Pribilof Islands
summary: A fur seal of the open North Pacific that comes ashore to breed, mostly on Alaska’s Pribilof Islands. Hunted heavily for its thick fur, it was protected by one of the first international wildlife treaties, in 1911. It is the only species in its genus.

species:zalophus-californianus.placeText: Pacific coast from British Columbia to Mexico
summary: The sleek, noisy sea lion of harbours and aquariums. Zalophus has two living species, with the Galápagos sea lion; the Japanese sea lion became extinct in the 1970s.

species:eumetopias-jubatus.placeText: North Pacific coasts from Japan to California
summary: The largest sea lion, with males up to about a tonne. Its western populations crashed after the 1970s, probably partly from changes in the fish it eats. It is the only species in its genus.

species:otaria-flavescens.placeText: Coasts of South America from Peru to Brazil
summary: A thick-maned sea lion. Off Patagonia, killer whales famously beach themselves to grab its pups from the shore. It is the only species in its genus.

species:neophoca-cinerea.placeText: Southern and western coasts of Australia
summary: A sea lion found only in Australia, with an unusual 17–18-month breeding cycle that varies between colonies. It is the only species in its genus.

species:phocarctos-hookeri.placeText: New Zealand’s subantarctic islands and South Island
summary: One of the rarest sea lions, breeding mainly on the Auckland Islands and slowly recolonising mainland New Zealand. It is the only species in its genus.

species:odobenus-rosmarus.placeText: Arctic seas around the North Pole
summary: A huge Arctic pinniped with tusks up to about a metre long, used to haul out onto ice and to fight. It feeds on clams on the seabed, sucking them out of their shells. As sea ice shrinks, walruses gather on beaches in crowds of thousands. It is the only living species in its family.
The common seal of northern coasts, with a dog-like face and V-shaped nostrils. Phoca has two species, with the spotted seal of the North Pacific.

The smallest and most common Arctic seal, which keeps breathing holes open in sea ice and raises pups in snow caves, the main prey of polar bears. Pusa also includes the only freshwater seals: the Baikal seal and the Caspian seal.
A large seal with a long “horse-head” profile. About a third of the world’s grey seals breed around Britain. It is the only species in its genus.
A seal of the pack ice, whose pups are born pure white; the hunting of these “whitecoats” in Canada caused worldwide protests and is now banned. It is the only species in its genus.
A boldly marked seal, dark with pale ribbon-like bands around its neck, hips and flippers, that spends most of the year far out at sea. It is the only species in its genus.

Males inflate a nasal “hood” on their head and blow a red balloon of nasal lining out of one nostril to display. Pups are weaned in about four days, the shortest of any mammal. It is the only species in its genus.
A large Arctic seal with a thick moustache of whiskers for feeling for clams and fish on the seabed. Males sing long, eerie trilling songs under the ice. It is the only species in its genus.

species:monachus-monachus.placeText: Eastern Mediterranean and the Atlantic coast of northwest Africa
summary: One of the rarest seals, now raising pups mostly in sea caves to avoid people. Numbers have slowly increased with protection, especially in Greece and at Cabo Blanco on the Atlantic coast. It is the only species in its genus.
A seal found only around Hawaii, mostly in the northwestern islands, with about 1,600 left. Its relative, the Caribbean monk seal, was declared extinct in 2008, the only seal lost in modern times.

Males have an inflatable trunk-like nose and weigh up to about 2 tonnes. It dives to over 1,500 m. Hunted to perhaps a few dozen animals by the 1890s, it now numbers over 200,000. Mirounga has two species; the southern elephant seal is the largest of all seals.

Probably the most numerous seal in the world, though counts are uncertain. Despite the name it eats almost only krill, sieving them through intricately lobed teeth. It is the only species in its genus.
A long, spotted predator with a huge gape that hunts penguins and other seals, though krill make up much of its diet. It is the only species in its genus.
The southernmost breeding mammal, living under fast ice along Antarctica’s coast and keeping breathing holes open with its teeth. It can dive for over an hour. It is the only species in its genus.
The smallest and least-known Antarctic seal, with very large eyes for hunting squid in dim water. It is the only species in its genus.

The commonest zebra, whose stripes probably deter biting flies. Equus is the only living genus of horses: it includes the wild horse (Przewalski’s horse) and domestic horse, the asses and donkey, and three zebras. The extinct quagga of South Africa was a form of the plains zebra.

facts.label: Species in genus
facts.value: About 7, plus domestic horse and donkey

summary: A dark tapir with a short mane; young tapirs are striped and spotted like watermelons, for camouflage. Tapirus has four or five species: three in the Americas and the black-and-white Malayan tapir in Asia.

The largest rhino, a grass-eater with a wide, square lip. The southern subspecies recovered from about 50 animals around 1900 to about 16,000 today; the northern subspecies has only two females left, both in Kenya. It is the only species in its genus.

A browsing rhino with a pointed, grasping upper lip for leaves and twigs. Poaching cut its numbers from about 65,000 in 1970 to under 2,500 in the 1990s; they have since recovered to about 6,000. It is the only species in its genus.

species:rhinoceros-unicornis.placeText: Grasslands of northeast India and Nepal
summary: A one-horned rhino whose skin forms armour-like folds. Protection, especially in Kaziranga, raised its numbers from about 200 in the early 1900s to over 4,000. Rhinoceros also includes the critically endangered Javan rhino, with fewer than 80 left, all in Ujung Kulon National Park.
The smallest and hairiest rhino, the closest living relative of the extinct woolly rhinoceros. Fewer than 50 survive in a few scattered populations. It is the only species in its genus.

species:camelus-dromedarius.placeText: North Africa, the Middle East and India (domestic); feral in Australia
summary: The one-humped camel, domesticated in Arabia about 3,000 years ago and now only domestic, though hundreds of thousands roam feral in Australia. Its hump stores fat, not water. Camelus also includes the two-humped Bactrian camel and the wild Bactrian camel of the Gobi.
A wild camel of South America, from desert to Patagonian steppe, and the wild ancestor of the domestic llama, bred by Andean peoples for wool and as a pack animal.

species:vicugna-vicugna.placeText: High Andes of Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina
summary: A slender wild camel of the high puna grasslands with some of the finest wool of any animal. Hunted to about 6,000 by the 1960s, it has recovered to over 450,000 under protection and live-shearing schemes. It is the wild ancestor of the alpaca.

species:sus-scrofa.placeText: Europe, Asia and North Africa; introduced widely
summary: One of the most widespread land mammals, and the wild ancestor of the domestic pig, domesticated separately in the Near East and China about 9,000 years ago. Feral pigs now live on every continent except Antarctica. Sus has about eight species, including the Javan warty pig.

A savanna pig with facial “warts” (protective pads), large curved tusks, and the habit of kneeling to graze. It runs with its tail held straight up and reverses into burrows to defend itself with its tusks. The desert warthog is the second species.
A bright orange-red forest pig with a white stripe down its back and long tufted ears. Potamochoerus has two species, with the bushpig of eastern and southern Africa.

species:hylochoerus-meinertzhageni.placeText: Forests of Central, East and West Africa
summary: The largest wild pig, up to about 275 kg, with a broad snout and coarse black hair. It was only described by Western science in 1904. It is the only species in its genus.
A pig whose males have upper tusks that grow up through the top of the snout and curve back towards the forehead. Babyrousa has three or four species on Sulawesi and nearby islands.

The smallest wild pig, about 25 cm tall, living in tall grasslands at the foot of the Himalayas. Thought extinct, it was rediscovered in 1971; a breeding and reintroduction programme has helped it survive. It is the only species in its genus.

species:pecari-tajacu.placeText: Southwestern United States to northern Argentina
summary: The javelina, a pig-like animal with a pale collar that lives in herds and has a scent gland on its back. It is the only species in its genus.
A peccary that roams rainforests in herds of a hundred or more, clacking its teeth when alarmed. It is the only species in its genus.

species:catagonus-wagneri.placeText: The Gran Chaco of Paraguay, Bolivia and Argentina
summary: Known first from fossils, it was described in 1930 from Pleistocene bones and found alive in 1975, a “living fossil”. It is the only living species in its genus.

species:hippopotamus-amphibius.placeText: Rivers and lakes of sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A huge, semi-aquatic grazer that spends the day in water and grazes on land at night. Despite its bulk it can outrun a person over a short distance, and it is among the most dangerous animals in Africa. Its closest living relatives are whales. It is the only living species in its genus.

species:choeropsis-liberiensis.placeText: Rainforests of Liberia and neighbouring countries
summary: A shy, forest-living hippo about a tenth the weight of its big relative, spending less time in water. Only about 2,500 remain. It is the only species in its genus.
The smallest hoofed mammal, about 2 kg, with long tusk-like canines instead of horns. In Malay folklore the mouse-deer, Sang Kancil, is a clever trickster. Tragulus has about six species.
A tiny, spotted chevrotain of Indian forests. Moschiola has three species, two of them in Sri Lanka.

species:hyemoschus-aquaticus.placeText: Rainforest streams of Central and West Africa
summary: An African mouse-deer that hides from predators by diving into streams and staying underwater for minutes at a time. It is the only species in its genus.

The fastest land animal in the Americas, able to run at about 90 km/h and to keep up high speed for kilometres, perhaps an adaptation to extinct American cheetahs. It sheds the outer sheath of its forked horns each year, unlike true antelopes. It is the only species in its family.

The tallest animal, up to about 5.5 m. Its neck has only seven vertebrae, like ours, each very long. A 2016 DNA study split giraffes into four species (northern, southern, reticulated and Masai), a view many now accept.

species:okapia-johnstoni.placeText: Rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
summary: The giraffe’s only living relative, a forest browser with zebra-striped legs and a long, dark tongue that can reach its ears. It was unknown to Western science until 1901. It is the only species in its genus.
An antlerless deer-like animal whose males have long, fang-like upper canines and a musk gland, hunted for centuries for perfume and medicine. Moschus has about seven species.

species:cervus-elaphus.placeText: Europe, North Africa and western Asia
summary: A large deer whose stags roar and clash antlers in the autumn rut; it is Britain’s largest native land mammal. Cervus also includes the North American elk (wapiti) and the sika deer.

species:dama-dama.placeText: Originally Anatolia; introduced across Europe and beyond
summary: A spotted deer with palmate (shovel-shaped) antlers. After the last Ice Age it survived in Anatolia and was spread across Europe by the Romans and later the Normans for deer parks and hunting. Dama has two species, with the Persian fallow deer.

species:axis-axis.placeText: India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka
summary: The spotted deer of Indian forests, which keeps its spots as an adult and often follows langur troops to feed on fruit they drop, while each warns the other of tigers. Axis has about four species, including the hog deer.
A large, dark, shaggy deer of Asian forests and a major prey of tigers. Rusa has four species, including the Javan rusa and the Philippine spotted deer.

species:rucervus-duvaucelii.placeText: Grasslands and swamps of India and Nepal
summary: The swamp deer, whose stags carry antlers with up to twenty points. Its hard-ground subspecies at Kanha in central India was brought back from about 66 animals in 1970. Rucervus has two species, the other being Schomburgk’s deer of Thailand, extinct since the 1930s.

species:elaphurus-davidianus.placeText: Reintroduced to wetlands of eastern China
summary: A marsh deer that became extinct in the wild in China. The last herd, in the Emperor’s hunting park near Beijing, was killed around 1900, but a few had been sent to Europe, and the Duke of Bedford gathered the survivors at Woburn Abbey. Their descendants were returned to China in the 1980s. It is the only species in its genus.

species:panolia-eldii.placeText: Scattered sites in India, Myanmar and Southeast Asia
summary: A deer with bow-shaped antlers. Its Manipur subspecies, the sangai, lives on floating mats of vegetation on Loktak Lake. Panolia has two or three species.

species:muntiacus-reevesi.placeText: Southeast China and Taiwan; introduced to Britain
summary: A small deer with short antlers and tusks that barks when alarmed. Escapees from Woburn Abbey have made it one of the commonest deer in England. Muntjacs (about 12 species) include the Indian muntjac, which has the fewest chromosomes of any mammal: six in females.

species:elaphodus-cephalophus.placeText: Mountain forests of southern China and Myanmar
summary: A small, dark deer with a tuft of black hair on its forehead that almost hides its tiny antlers, and fang-like canines. It is the only species in its genus.

species:hydropotes-inermis.placeText: Korea and eastern China; introduced to England
summary: A deer with no antlers at all; males instead have long, tusk-like canines, earning it the name “vampire deer”. It is the only species in its genus.

A small, graceful deer and Europe’s most numerous. It is one of the few hoofed mammals with delayed implantation: embryos conceived in summer pause their development until winter. Capreolus has two species, with the Siberian roe deer.

species:alces-alces.placeText: Northern forests of North America, Europe and Asia
summary: The largest deer, up to about 2 m at the shoulder, with broad palmate antlers. It wades and even dives in lakes to feed on water plants. In Europe it is called the elk. Some split it into two species.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: Up to about 2 m at the shoulder

species:rangifer-tarandus.placeText: Arctic and subarctic North America, Europe and Asia
summary: Called caribou in North America, the only deer in which both sexes grow antlers. Some herds migrate over 1,000 km a year, among the longest land migrations. Domesticated reindeer are herded by peoples such as the Sámi and Nenets. It is the only species in its genus.

species:odocoileus-virginianus.placeText: Southern Canada to northern South America
summary: The commonest large wild mammal in North America, flashing the white underside of its tail as a warning when it runs. Odocoileus has two species, with the mule deer.

species:mazama-americana.placeText: Rainforests of Central and South America
summary: A small, secretive forest deer with short spike antlers. Brockets are hard to tell apart, and DNA has shown that several “species” are unrelated lookalikes; there are about ten species.

species:hippocamelus-bisulcus.placeText: Southern Andes of Chile and Argentina
summary: The huemul, a stocky mountain deer that appears on Chile’s coat of arms. Fewer than 2,000 remain. Hippocamelus has two species, with the taruca of the central Andes.
The largest South American deer, with partly webbed hooves for walking in marshes such as the Pantanal and Iberá. It is the only species in its genus.
A small deer of open grassland, now much reduced by farming. Males smell strongly of garlic from a gland on the hind feet. It is the only species in its genus.

species:pudu-puda.placeText: Temperate rainforests of southern Chile and Argentina
summary: One of the smallest deer, about 35–40 cm tall, which climbs onto fallen trunks and bends saplings to reach leaves. Pudu has two species, with the even smaller northern pudú.
The largest wild cattle, with bulls up to about 1,500 kg and 2 m at the shoulder. Bos also includes the yak, banteng, the probably extinct kouprey, and domestic cattle, descended from the aurochs.

species:bison-bison.placeText: Parks and reserves of North America
summary: North America’s largest land animal. Tens of millions roamed the plains until commercial hunting cut them to under a thousand by the 1880s; conservation has brought back about half a million, mostly on ranches. Bison has two living species, with the European bison (wisent), which survived only in zoos after 1927 and has been reintroduced.
The wild ancestor of the domestic water buffalo, with huge sweeping horns; fewer than 4,000 survive, mostly in Assam. Bubalus also includes the dwarf anoa of Sulawesi and the tamaraw of Mindoro.
A powerful wild cow with fused horn bases (the boss), living in herds of hundreds. Herds defend members against lions, and it is one of Africa’s “Big Five”. It is the only species in its genus.

species:pseudoryx-nghetinhensis.placeText: Annamite Mountains of Laos and Vietnam
summary: Discovered in 1992 from horns in a hunter’s home, one of the most remarkable large-mammal discoveries of the century. It has never been seen in the wild by a biologist and was last photographed in 2013. It is the only species in its genus.

A tall, white-striped antelope whose males carry spiral horns with up to three twists, up to about 1.8 m along the curve. Tragelaphus, the spiral-horned antelopes, also includes the bongo, nyala, sitatunga and bushbuck.

The second-largest antelope; males reach about 900 kg yet can leap 2.5 m from standing. Their knee joints make a loud clicking sound as they walk. Taurotragus has two species, with the giant eland, the largest antelope.

species:boselaphus-tragocamelus.placeText: India, Nepal and Pakistan; introduced to Texas
summary: Asia’s largest antelope, the “blue bull”, common on farmland in northern India, where it is protected by its sacred association with cows. It is the only species in its genus.
The only living wild mammal with four horns: males have a short front pair as well as the main pair. It is the only species in its genus.

The largest duiker, with a yellow wedge of hair on its back that it raises when alarmed. Duikers are small, hunched forest antelopes that dive into undergrowth (duiker means “diver”); Cephalophus has about 15 species.

species:philantomba-monticola.placeText: Forests of Central, East and southern Africa
summary: One of the smallest antelopes, about 35 cm tall, and one of the most hunted for bushmeat. Philantomba has about three species.
The only duiker of open savanna rather than forest, and one of the most widespread antelopes in Africa. It is the only species in its genus.

species:hippotragus-niger.placeText: Woodlands of eastern and southern Africa
summary: A glossy black antelope with long, backward-curving horns, one of Africa’s most striking. Hippotragus has two living species, with the roan antelope; the bluebuck of South Africa was hunted to extinction around 1800.

A desert antelope with long, straight horns and a bold black-and-white face, able to go for long periods without drinking. Oryx has four species, including the Arabian oryx, the first animal to be moved back from Extinct in the Wild to Vulnerable.

A pale desert antelope with spiral horns and wide hooves for walking on sand, adapted to live almost without drinking. Fewer than 100 may survive in the wild, in Niger. It is the only species in its genus.

A shaggy, cow-like antelope. In the Serengeti–Mara over a million migrate in a great loop each year, following the rains, with mass crossings of crocodile-filled rivers. Connochaetes has two species, with the black wildebeest.
A long-faced, high-shouldered antelope with bracket-shaped horns, one of the fastest antelopes over long distances. Some split it into several species.
A glossy, reddish antelope whose males stand on termite mounds to mark their territories. Damaliscus also includes the bontebok of South Africa, saved from extinction by a few farmers in the 1800s.

Perhaps the rarest antelope, with fewer than 500 left, distinguished by white “spectacles” around its eyes. It is the last survivor of a genus that once lived across Africa. It is the only living species in its genus.

species:kobus-ellipsiprymnus.placeText: Savannas near water in sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A shaggy antelope that never strays far from water, with a white ring on its rump and an oily, musky coat. Kobus also includes the kob, puku and lechwe.
An antelope of tall grass and reedbeds that whistles in alarm and bounds away with a rocking gait. Redunca has three species.

species:pelea-capreolus.placeText: Highlands of South Africa and Lesotho
summary: A woolly, grey antelope of rocky grassland with straight spike horns, found only in South Africa, Lesotho and eSwatini. It is the only species in its genus.

species:aepyceros-melampus.placeText: Savannas of eastern and southern Africa
summary: A graceful, common antelope famous for leaps up to 3 m high and 10 m long. It is unusual in both grazing and browsing. It is the only species in its genus, which branched off early from other antelopes.
An Indian antelope whose males are black and white with long spiral horns. It is one of the fastest land animals over long distances. It is the only species in its genus.

species:gazella-dorcas.placeText: North Africa and the Middle East
summary: A small, pale desert gazelle that can survive without drinking, getting water from plants. Gazella has about ten species across Africa and Asia.

The “tommy”, a small gazelle with a black side stripe, and a favourite prey of cheetahs. When chased it stots, bouncing stiff-legged, perhaps showing predators it is too fit to catch. Eudorcas has about four species.
A large gazelle with long, lyre-shaped horns that can live in dry country without drinking. Nanger has three species, including the dama gazelle of the Sahara, the largest gazelle.

A gazelle-like antelope famous for “pronking”: leaping stiff-legged up to 2 m into the air while lifting a white crest on its back. It is South Africa’s national animal and the only species in its genus.

species:litocranius-walleri.placeText: Dry bush of the Horn of Africa and East Africa
summary: A gazelle with a very long neck that stands upright on its hind legs to browse leaves out of reach of other antelopes. It may never need to drink. It is the only species in its genus.

species:ammodorcas-clarkei.placeText: Ogaden region of Ethiopia and Somalia
summary: A slender, gerenuk-like antelope that runs with its thin tail held straight up. Rarely studied because of conflict in its range. It is the only species in its genus.

species:procapra-gutturosa.placeText: Steppes of Mongolia and northern China
summary: A gazelle of the eastern Mongolian steppe that migrates in herds of tens of thousands, one of the last great migrations of hoofed mammals in Asia. Procapra has three species, including the Tibetan gazelle.

species:saiga-tatarica.placeText: Steppes of Kazakhstan, southern Russia and western Mongolia
summary: A steppe antelope with a bulbous, drooping nose that filters dust in summer and warms air in winter. In 2015 about 200,000 died in three weeks from a bacterial infection, but numbers have since rebounded strongly. It is the only species in its genus.

The chiru, whose extremely fine wool (shahtoosh) was smuggled into luxury shawls, each taking several animals’ wool. Poaching cut its numbers to about 70,000 by the 1990s; protection has brought them back above 150,000. It is the only species in its genus.

species:madoqua-kirkii.placeText: Dry bush of East and southwest Africa
summary: A tiny antelope, about 40 cm tall, named for its alarm call. Pairs mark their territories with dung piles and with tar-like secretions from glands below the eyes. Dik-diks (four species) live in the Horn of Africa and East Africa.
A slender, small antelope of open grassland that lies hidden in the grass and bolts with a whistling snort. It is the only species in its genus.
A small, red-brown antelope of dry savanna that scratches a scrape to bury its dung. Raphicerus has three species, including the grysboks.

species:oreotragus-oreotragus.placeText: Rocky hills of eastern and southern Africa
summary: A small antelope that stands on the tips of its rounded hooves, which grip rock like rubber, letting it bound up near-vertical cliffs. It is the only species in its genus.

species:dorcatragus-megalotis.placeText: Arid hills of Somalia and Djibouti
summary: A small, large-eared antelope of stony desert hills in the Horn of Africa, getting its water from plants. It is the only species in its genus.
The smallest antelope, about 25 cm tall and 2–3 kg, able to leap nearly 3 m. Neotragus has two species, with Bates’s pygmy antelope.

species:nesotragus-moschatus.placeText: Coastal forests of East and southeastern Africa
summary: A tiny, musky-smelling antelope of dense thickets, which freezes to hide and darts away when disturbed. It is the only species in its genus.

A wild goat whose males carry huge, ridged horns up to about 1 m long, able to climb almost vertical dam walls to lick salt. By about 1820 only about 100 survived, in Italy’s Gran Paradiso; every Alpine ibex today descends from them. Capra also includes the wild goat (ancestor of the domestic goat), the markhor and other ibexes.

species:ovis-canadensis.placeText: Rocky Mountains and deserts of western North America
summary: Rams charge each other at about 30 km/h and clash their massive curled horns, with skulls built to absorb the impact. Ovis also includes the mouflon (ancestor of domestic sheep), the argali, the urial and the Dall sheep.

species:ovibos-moschatus.placeText: Arctic Canada and Greenland; reintroduced elsewhere
summary: An Ice Age survivor with a coat of long guard hairs over the finest underwool (qiviut), warmer than sheep’s wool. Threatened by wolves, herds form a defensive ring around their calves. It is the only species in its genus.
A goat-antelope of the Alps and other mountains, with short hooked horns; its soft skin was once used for “shammy” leather. Rupicapra has two species, with the Pyrenean chamois.

species:oreamnos-americanus.placeText: Rocky Mountains and coast ranges of northwestern North America
summary: A white-coated goat-antelope (not a true goat) of high cliffs, with hooves that have hard rims and rubbery pads for grip. It is the only species in its genus.

species:hemitragus-jemlahicus.placeText: The Himalayas; introduced to New Zealand
summary: A shaggy wild goat of steep Himalayan slopes, with a thick mane on males. The Arabian and Nilgiri tahrs, once in the same genus, are now in their own genera, Arabitragus and Nilgiritragus.

species:ammotragus-lervia.placeText: Mountains of North Africa; introduced to Spain and the US
summary: The aoudad, a sandy wild sheep of desert mountains with a long fringe of hair on its throat and front legs. It is the only species in its genus.
The blue sheep, a goat-antelope with traits of both sheep and goats, living on bare high slopes. It is the snow leopard’s main prey. It is the only species in its genus.

species:budorcas-taxicolor.placeText: Eastern Himalayas and mountains of western China
summary: A stocky, golden goat-antelope with a moose-like nose; it may have inspired the legend of the Golden Fleece. It is Bhutan’s national animal. It is the only species in its genus.

species:capricornis-sumatraensis.placeText: Mountains of Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula
summary: A goat-antelope of steep, forested mountains. Capricornis, the serows, has about six species, including the Japanese serow.

species:naemorhedus-goral.placeText: Himalayan foothills of India, Nepal, Bhutan and Pakistan
summary: A small, grey goat-antelope of rugged slopes, sure-footed on rocks. Naemorhedus, the gorals, has about four species.

An Arctic whale that breaks through ice up to about 60 cm thick with its head. It is the longest-lived mammal known: harpoon points from the 1800s found in living whales, and eye-lens dating, suggest some live over 200 years. It is the only species in its genus.

A large baleen whale with white callosities on its head, patches of rough skin colonised by whale lice, whose patterns identify individuals. Eubalaena has three species; the North Atlantic right whale is one of the most endangered whales, with about 370 left.

The smallest baleen whale, about 6 m long, rarely seen at sea. A 2012 study suggested it is the last survivor of the cetotheres, a group thought extinct for 2 million years. It is the only species in its family.

A mottled grey whale that rolls on its side on the seabed to suck up worms and crustaceans from the mud. Eastern Pacific grey whales migrate up to about 20,000 km a year between the Arctic and the lagoons of Baja California, one of the longest mammal migrations. It became extinct in the Atlantic by the 1700s. It is the only species in its family.

The largest animal known to have lived, up to about 30 m and perhaps 150–190 tonnes, eating up to several tonnes of krill a day. Whaling killed about 360,000 in the 20th century, leaving a few thousand; numbers are slowly recovering. Balaenoptera also includes the fin, sei, Bryde’s and minke whales.

A rorqual with very long flippers, famous for breaching and for the long, complex songs of males, which change from year to year and spread between populations. Groups trap fish in nets of bubbles. It is the only species in its genus.

The largest toothed predator, with the largest brain of any animal. It dives to over 2,000 m to hunt squid, including giant squid, and clicks are the loudest sounds made by any animal. The real-life Essex sinking inspired Moby-Dick. It is the only species in its family.
A small, shark-like whale about 3.5 m long, with a false “gill” marking behind its eye. It is seen mostly when stranded. The dwarf sperm whale is the other species.

species:ziphius-cavirostris.placeText: Deep waters of all oceans except the polar seas
summary: The deepest-diving mammal known: one dived to about 3,000 m, and another stayed under for 3 hours 42 minutes. Beaked whales are sensitive to loud naval sonar, which has been linked to mass strandings. It is the only species in its genus.

Males have two tusk-like teeth rising from arched bulges in the lower jaw, often encrusted with barnacles. Mesoplodon is the largest whale genus, with about 16 species; Ramari’s beaked whale was named in 2022, and the spade-toothed whale was first seen whole in 2010.

The largest beaked whale, up to about 12 m. Berardius has three species: Baird’s, Arnoux’s of the Southern Ocean, and Sato’s, described in 2019 and long known to Japanese whalers as the “karasu” (raven).

species:hyperoodon-ampullatus.placeText: Deep waters of the North Atlantic
summary: A beaked whale with a bulging forehead, curious about boats, which made it easy prey for whalers until the 1970s. A small population lives in the Gully, a submarine canyon off Nova Scotia. Hyperoodon has two species, with the southern bottlenose whale.

species:tasmacetus-shepherdi.placeText: Cool waters of the Southern Hemisphere
summary: The only beaked whale with a full set of teeth, about 90 in all. It was known almost only from strandings until filmed alive off New Zealand and Australia in the 2010s. It is the only species in its genus.

Long known only from two skulls, one found on a beach in Australia in 1882 and one in a Somali fertiliser factory. It was first identified alive in the early 2000s. It is the only species in its genus.

A long-beaked river dolphin whose eyes lack lenses, so it is effectively blind and finds its way and food by echolocation in muddy water, swimming on its side. A 2021 study split the Indus river dolphin as a second species.

The boto, the largest river dolphin, which turns pink as it ages (especially males). Its unfused neck vertebrae let it turn its head to weave between tree trunks in flooded forest. Some split it into two or three species.

species:pontoporia-blainvillei.placeText: Coastal waters of Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina
summary: One of the smallest dolphins, with the longest beak for its size of any dolphin. Though it is grouped with river dolphins, it lives in the sea along coasts and estuaries such as the Río de la Plata. Fishing nets drown many each year.

The Yangtze river dolphin, declared “functionally extinct” after a 2006 survey found none; damming, shipping, pollution and illegal electric fishing destroyed it. If gone, it is the first cetacean driven to extinction by humans. It is the only species in its family.

species:monodon-monoceros.placeText: Arctic waters of Canada, Greenland and Russia
summary: The “unicorn of the sea”: males (and a few females) have a tusk up to about 3 m long, a spiralled canine tooth packed with nerve endings. Its tusks were sold in medieval Europe as unicorn horns. It is the only species in its genus.

The white whale, called the “sea canary” for its chirps, whistles and clicks. Unlike most whales it can turn its head, and it changes the shape of its bulbous forehead as it calls. It is the only species in its genus.

species:phocoena-phocoena.placeText: Coastal waters of the North Atlantic, North Pacific and Black Sea
summary: A small, shy porpoise of cool coastal seas, often seen as a small triangular fin. Phocoena also includes the vaquita of Mexico’s Gulf of California, the world’s rarest marine mammal, with only about ten left.

species:neophocaena-phocaenoides.placeText: Coasts of the Indian Ocean and western Pacific
summary: A porpoise without a dorsal fin, living in shallow coastal waters and estuaries. Neophocaena has two species; the narrow-ridged finless porpoise includes the critically endangered Yangtze finless porpoise.
A stocky, black-and-white porpoise, one of the fastest small cetaceans, kicking up a “rooster tail” of spray as it speeds at about 55 km/h. It is the only species in its genus.

The killer whale, the largest dolphin and a top predator found in every ocean. Pods have their own dialects and hunting traditions: some eat only fish, others hunt seals, sharks or even great white sharks and blue whales. Some scientists split it into several species. It is the only species in its genus.

The familiar dolphin of coasts and aquariums. Each dolphin has a signature whistle that works like a name, and some in Shark Bay, Australia, carry sponges on their beaks to protect them while foraging. Tursiops has two or three species.
A fast, sociable dolphin with an hourglass pattern of yellow and grey on its sides, travelling in schools that can number thousands. It is now usually treated as the only species in its genus.
A slender dolphin famous for leaping and spinning up to seven times in the air. Stenella has five species, including the spotted and striped dolphins.

species:sousa-chinensis.placeText: Coastal waters from India to China and northern Australia
summary: A coastal dolphin with a humped back that turns pink as it ages; the pink dolphins of Hong Kong are a local attraction. Sousa has four species.
A small, grey dolphin of the Amazon, related to oceanic dolphins rather than to river dolphins. Sotalia has two species, with the Guiana dolphin of Atlantic coasts.
A dolphin with a long, cone-shaped head without a clear forehead and fine vertical ridges on its teeth. It is the only species in its genus.

species:lagenorhynchus-albirostris.placeText: Cold waters of the North Atlantic
summary: A robust, black-and-white dolphin of the North Atlantic. DNA studies have broken up the old genus Lagenorhynchus, leaving only this species; its former members are now in Leucopleurus and Sagmatias.

species:leucopleurus-acutus.placeText: Cool waters of the North Atlantic
summary: A dolphin with a yellow and white patch along its side, moved to its own genus in 2019. It is the only species in its genus.

species:sagmatias-obliquidens.placeText: Cool waters of the North Pacific
summary: An acrobatic, social dolphin of the North Pacific. Sagmatias holds four species split from Lagenorhynchus in 2019, including the dusky dolphin and the hourglass dolphin of the Southern Ocean.

One of the smallest dolphins, with a rounded fin like a Mickey Mouse ear, found only around New Zealand. Its North Island subspecies, Māui dolphin, numbers only about 50. Cephalorhynchus has four species.

species:lissodelphis-borealis.placeText: Cool waters of the North Pacific
summary: A slender, black dolphin with no dorsal fin at all. Lissodelphis has two species, with the southern right whale dolphin.
A blunt-headed dolphin that turns almost white with age, its skin covered in scars from squid and from other Risso’s dolphins. It is the only species in its genus.
A large, black dolphin with a bulbous head, living in tight-knit pods that sometimes strand together in hundreds. Globicephala has two species, with the short-finned pilot whale.
A large, all-dark dolphin that hunts big fish such as tuna and often shares its catch. It is the only species in its genus.
A small, dark, rarely seen dolphin with a white lip, known to be aggressive in captivity. It is the only species in its genus.
A small, dark, blunt-headed dolphin that travels in herds of hundreds and sometimes mass-strands. It is the only species in its genus.

species:orcaella-brevirostris.placeText: Coasts and rivers of South and Southeast Asia
summary: A round-headed dolphin of coasts, estuaries and three great rivers: the Irrawaddy, Mekong and Mahakam. In Myanmar, fishermen and dolphins have long cooperated to drive fish into nets. Orcaella has two species, with the Australian snubfin dolphin.

A stocky dolphin with a short beak and a dark stripe along its side. It was described in 1956 from a skeleton collected in Borneo in 1895 and not seen alive until the early 1970s. It is the only species in its genus.

species:hydrochoerus-hydrochaeris.placeText: South America east of the Andes
summary: The largest living rodent, up to about 65 kg, a semi-aquatic grazer of rivers, marshes and flooded savannas with webbed toes and eyes, ears and nostrils high on its head. It lives in groups and is famously tolerant of other animals, which often sit on it. Its close relatives include the guinea pig.
Hydrochoerus has two species, with the smaller lesser capybara of Panama, Colombia and Venezuela. Giant extinct relatives such as Josephoartigasia were far larger.

species:castor-canadensis.placeText: Canada, the United States and northern Mexico; introduced to Tierra del Fuego and Finland
summary: The largest rodent in North America, a builder of dams and lodges that turns streams into ponds and wetlands, reshaping whole landscapes. The fur trade almost wiped it out by 1900; it has since recovered across most of its range.

Twenty were released in Tierra del Fuego in 1946 to start a fur trade; their descendants, perhaps 100,000, have felled huge areas of southern beech forest. Its genus has one other species, the Eurasian beaver, which cannot interbreed with it.

Hunted for fur, meat and castoreum (a scent-gland secretion used in medicine and perfume) to about 1,200 animals in eight places by 1900. Protection and reintroductions have brought it back to over a million across Europe and Asia, including Britain, where it had been extinct for about 400 years.
Its dams slow floods, store water in droughts and create wetlands for many other species.

species:rattus-rattus.placeText: Worldwide, especially warm regions; originally South Asia
summary: A slender, agile climber with a long tail, also called the ship rat or roof rat. Originally from South Asia, it spread with people along trade routes and ships to every continent but Antarctica. It carried the fleas that spread plague, though some researchers argue human fleas and lice also spread the Black Death.
On islands it has driven many seabirds, land birds and reptiles to extinction. Rattus has about 65 species.

species:rattus-norvegicus.placeText: Worldwide; originally northern China and Mongolia
summary: The grey, brown or Norway rat, the common large rat of cities, sewers and farms. Despite its name it came from northern China and Mongolia, reaching Europe in the 1700s, where it largely replaced the black rat. It is heavier and a better swimmer than the black rat, and digs burrows rather than climbing.
Its domesticated form is the laboratory rat and the pet “fancy rat”, used in research since the 1800s.

species:sciurus-vulgaris.placeText: Forests of Europe and northern Asia
summary: A tree squirrel with ear tufts that buries seeds and nuts in many small caches, planting new trees from those it forgets. In Britain and Ireland, the introduced grey squirrel has replaced it across much of its range, both by outcompeting it and by carrying squirrelpox, which kills reds but not greys.
Sciurus has about 30 species, including the grey squirrel.

species:sciurus-carolinensis.placeText: Eastern North America; introduced to Britain, Ireland, Italy and South Africa
summary: The eastern grey squirrel, native to the hardwood forests of eastern North America and now common in city parks. Introduced to Britain from the 1870s, it has replaced the native red squirrel over most of England and Wales and is classed there as an invasive species.
Its spread is held back where pine martens have recovered, since martens catch the heavier, ground-feeding greys more easily than reds.

species:oryctolagus-cuniculus.placeText: Native to Spain, Portugal and north-west Africa; introduced across Europe, Australia, New Zealand, Chile, Argentina and many islands
summary: The wild ancestor of every domestic rabbit, a social burrower that lives in warrens. Native to the Iberian Peninsula and north-west Africa, it was spread by the Romans and in the Middle Ages, when rabbits were farmed in walled warrens for meat and fur; it was domesticated in France by around 1500 to 1800.

Twenty-four rabbits released in Victoria in 1859 multiplied into hundreds of millions, stripping vegetation across Australia; the myxoma virus (1950) and rabbit haemorrhagic disease (1995) were released to control them. Introduced rabbits ate Laysan Island bare in the early 1900s, wiping out the Laysan rail, millerbird and honeycreeper.
Ironically, in its native range it is now endangered, hit by those same diseases, and its decline threatens the Iberian lynx and Spanish imperial eagle that depend on it.

species:lepus-europaeus.placeText: Europe, Turkey and western Asia; introduced to South America, Australia and New Zealand
summary: A large, long-legged hare of open farmland and grassland that relies on speed, up to about 70 km/h, rather than burrows. Its young (leverets) are born furred with open eyes in a shallow scrape. In spring, “mad March hares” box: usually a female fending off an over-eager male.
Lepus has about 32 species, including the mountain hare, the Arctic hare, the snowshoe hare, which turns white in winter, and the American jackrabbits, which are hares despite their name.

species:sylvilagus-floridanus.placeText: Eastern and central North America to north-western South America; introduced to Italy
summary: The commonest rabbit of the Americas, named for its white, cotton-ball tail, which it flashes while fleeing. Unlike the European rabbit it does not dig warrens, but hides in thickets and nests in shallow grass-lined hollows. A female can raise several litters a year.
Sylvilagus has about 20 species, the cottontails, including the marsh and swamp rabbits, the desert cottontail and the tapetí of South America.

species:brachylagus-idahoensis.placeText: Sagebrush of the Great Basin, western USA
summary: The smallest rabbit in the world, about 400 g, small enough to sit in a palm. It lives almost only in tall, dense sagebrush, which makes up nearly all of its winter diet, and is one of only two North American rabbits that dig their own burrows.
A small, isolated population in Washington’s Columbia Basin dropped to a few animals in the early 2000s and has been bred in captivity and released again.

species:romerolagus-diazi.placeText: Pine forests and grassland on volcanoes near Mexico City
summary: A tiny, short-eared, nearly tailless rabbit found only on the slopes of a few volcanoes around Mexico City, including Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl, at about 2,800 to 4,250 m. It lives in colonies in dense bunchgrass and, unusually for a rabbit, makes loud, high-pitched calls to warn of danger.
It is one of the most primitive living rabbits, and is threatened by fires, farming and the spread of the city.

species:pentalagus-furnessi.placeText: Amami Ōshima and Tokunoshima, southern Japan
summary: A dark-furred, short-eared, short-legged forest rabbit with long claws for digging, found only on two small islands. It is often called a “living fossil” because it keeps features of ancient rabbits, and it calls to others with high-pitched sounds.

Mongooses released on Amami Ōshima in 1979 to kill venomous habu snakes ate rabbits instead. After a long eradication campaign, the island was declared mongoose-free in 2024 and rabbit numbers have recovered.

species:nesolagus-netscheri.placeText: Mountain forests of the Barisan range, Sumatra, Indonesia
summary: One of the rarest and least-known mammals, a forest rabbit with bold dark stripes and a red rump, seen only a handful of times since the early 1900s, mostly in camera-trap photographs. It is thought to be nocturnal.
Its only relative, the Annamite striped rabbit of Laos and Vietnam, was discovered by scientists only in 1999, from carcasses in a local market.

species:caprolagus-hispidus.placeText: Tall grasslands at the foot of the Himalayas in Nepal, India and Bhutan
summary: Also called the Assam rabbit, a dark, coarse-furred rabbit with small ears that lives in the tall “elephant grass” of the Himalayan foothills. It was thought extinct in the 1950s and 1960s before being found again in 1971.
Burning and clearing of its grassland have left it in scattered patches, mainly in protected areas.

species:bunolagus-monticularis.placeText: Dense shrubs along seasonal rivers in the Karoo, South Africa
summary: One of the world’s most threatened mammals, a rabbit with a dark stripe along its jaw and a woolly brown tail. It lives only in the thin strips of dense bush along the dry riverbeds of the Karoo, where it digs burrows in the soft soil.
Most of this river-bank habitat has been turned into farmland, leaving perhaps a few hundred adults.

species:pronolagus-rupestris.placeText: Rocky hills of southern and eastern Africa
summary: A rabbit (despite the name “hare”) with reddish fur and a bushy, rusty tail that lives among boulders and on rocky slopes, sheltering in crevices by day. It is noisy for a rabbit, screaming when caught.
Pronolagus has four species, the red rock hares, all in southern and eastern Africa.

species:poelagus-marjorita.placeText: Savanna and woodland of central Africa, from Uganda to Chad, and Angola
summary: Also called the Central African rabbit, a short-eared, stiff-furred rabbit of savanna and rocky woodland edges, active at night. It is the only rabbit native to central Africa.
It was once placed in the red rock hare genus; DNA shows it is a separate branch.

species:ochotona-princeps.placeText: Rocky mountain slopes of western North America
summary: A small, round-eared, tailless relative of rabbits that lives on rock slides in the mountains. It does not hibernate; instead it spends the summer gathering grasses and flowers into haypiles under the rocks to eat in winter, and gives a sharp “eep” call when danger is near.

It overheats easily and has vanished from some lower, warmer sites, making it a closely watched sign of climate change. Ochotona has about 34 species, most in Asia, including the plateau pika of Tibet.

species:felis-catus.placeText: Worldwide with people; tamed from the African wildcat in the Near East
summary: The world’s most popular pet, with perhaps 600 million or more cats. Cats descend from the African wildcat, which began living alongside the first farmers in the Near East about 10,000 years ago, probably drawn by mice in grain stores; a cat was buried with a person on Cyprus about 9,500 years ago. Ancient Egypt later revered them.

Pet and feral cats are also among the most damaging introduced predators. They have been linked to at least 60 bird, mammal and reptile extinctions, mostly on islands, such as the Stephens Island wren of New Zealand, and in the USA alone they kill an estimated 1 to 4 billion birds a year.
Some researchers treat the domestic cat as a form of the wildcat, Felis silvestris catus.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Domestic; also feral on every continent but Antarctica

species:canis-familiaris.placeText: Worldwide with people; domesticated from Ice Age wolves
summary: The first domesticated animal, descended from a population of Ice Age grey wolves at least 15,000 years ago, and possibly much earlier; where it happened is still debated. Dogs travelled with people into the Americas and later reached Australia, where they became the dingo about 3,500 years ago.
There are perhaps 700 million to 1 billion dogs, most of them free-roaming village dogs rather than pets, and several hundred breeds, almost all created in the last 200 years.

Dogs have been linked to the extinction of about a dozen species, and the arrival of the dingo may have helped end the thylacine and Tasmanian devil on mainland Australia. Some researchers treat the dog as a form of the wolf, Canis lupus familiaris.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Domestic; also free-roaming and feral (including the dingo)

species:cavia-porcellus.placeText: Domestic worldwide; domesticated in the Andes of South America
summary: Neither from Guinea nor a pig, the guinea pig was domesticated in the Andes at least 5,000 to 7,000 years ago from a wild cavy, and is still raised there for food, as cuy, especially in Peru, Ecuador and Bolivia. Spanish traders brought it to Europe in the 1500s.
It is a close relative of the capybara. Like people, it cannot make its own vitamin C, which made it important in early medical research.

species:mesocricetus-auratus.placeText: Wild only around Aleppo in northern Syria and southern Turkey; domestic worldwide
summary: The Syrian hamster, the classic pet hamster. In the wild it lives alone in deep burrows in farmland, coming out at dusk, and carries food home in its huge cheek pouches.
Almost all pet and laboratory golden hamsters descend from a mother and litter dug up near Aleppo in 1930 by the zoologist Israel Aharoni. The wild population is small and threatened.

species:meriones-unguiculatus.placeText: Steppes and semi-deserts of Mongolia and northern China; domestic worldwide
summary: A sociable desert rodent that lives in family groups in burrows, drums its hind feet to warn of danger and needs very little water. Most pets and laboratory gerbils descend from about 20 pairs caught in Mongolia in 1935.
Meriones has about 17 species, the jirds, from North Africa to China.

species:chinchilla-lanigera.placeText: Rocky slopes of the Andes in northern Chile; domestic worldwide
summary: A rodent with the densest fur of any land animal, with dozens of hairs growing from each follicle, which keeps out cold and parasites; it bathes in dust instead of water. Hunting for fur nearly wiped out wild chinchillas by the early 1900s.
Almost all pet and farmed chinchillas descend from a handful of wild animals taken to the USA in 1923. Only a few small wild colonies survive.

species:mustela-furo.placeText: Domestic worldwide; feral in New Zealand
summary: The domesticated form of the European polecat, kept for at least 2,000 years to hunt rabbits and rats by chasing them out of burrows, called ferreting. It sleeps up to 18 hours a day.
Ferrets, stoats and weasels were released in New Zealand in the 1880s to control introduced rabbits; feral ferrets now prey on native birds such as kiwi.

species:mus-musculus.placeText: Worldwide with people; originally from the Indian subcontinent
summary: Probably the most widespread mammal after humans, it spread from northern India and Pakistan with the first farmers and later on ships to almost everywhere people live. Pet “fancy mice” have been bred in China and Japan for centuries.
The laboratory mouse, the most-used animal in medical research, is a house mouse. On islands, introduced mice can be deadly: on Gough Island in the South Atlantic they eat seabird chicks alive.

species:atelerix-albiventris.placeText: Savannas of West, Central and East Africa
summary: The African pygmy hedgehog of the pet trade, a small hedgehog with only four toes on its hind feet. It eats insects, snails and other small animals, rolls into a spiny ball when threatened, and becomes sluggish in cold or dry seasons.
Atelerix has four species, all in Africa.

A small, green and yellow parrot that roams dry inland Australia in flocks that can number thousands, following rain and seeding grasses. Brought to Britain in 1840 by the naturalist John Gould, it became one of the most popular pet birds, bred in blues, whites and many other colours.
Budgies can learn to mimic speech; one, Puck, was recorded with a vocabulary of over 1,700 words.

The smallest cockatoo, grey with a yellow crest and orange cheek patches, which lives in nomadic flocks in Australia’s interior. It is one of the most popular pet birds, and males often learn to whistle tunes.

species:psittacus-erithacus.placeText: Rainforests of West and Central Africa
summary: A grey parrot with a red tail, famous for its intelligence and gift for speech. Alex, studied by Irene Pepperberg for 30 years, learned to name objects, colours and numbers.

Trapping for the pet trade, with millions of birds exported, and forest loss have caused steep declines; international trade in wild-caught birds was banned in 2016. The Timneh parrot of West Africa is now treated as a separate species.

species:agapornis-roseicollis.placeText: Dry country of Namibia, south-western Angola and north-western South Africa
summary: A small green parrot with a pink face that lives in flocks in dry, rocky country, often nesting inside the huge communal nests of sociable weavers. Lovebirds are named for their close pair bonds and the way pairs sit together preening.
Agapornis has nine species, all from Africa and Madagascar.

species:taeniopygia-castanotis.placeText: Grassland and scrub across most of mainland Australia
summary: A tiny grey finch with an orange beak and, in males, orange cheeks and a striped throat. It lives in flocks in dry country and breeds quickly after rain. Popular as a pet, it is also one of the most-studied birds in science: young males learn their song from their fathers, much as children learn to speak.
The Timor zebra finch of Indonesia’s Lesser Sunda Islands is now usually treated as a separate species.

species:pogona-vitticeps.placeText: Dry woodland and desert of central and eastern Australia
summary: A sturdy lizard with a spiny “beard” under its chin that it puffs out and turns black when threatened or courting. It also waves an arm and bobs its head to signal to others. It eats insects and plants.

Australia has banned the export of its wildlife since the 1960s, so pet bearded dragons come from captive-bred stock. In some, eggs incubated at high temperatures hatch as females even when they are genetically male.

species:eublepharis-macularius.placeText: Dry, rocky grassland of Afghanistan, Pakistan, north-western India and eastern Iran
summary: A spotted, ground-living gecko with movable eyelids and no sticky toe pads, so unlike many geckos it cannot climb walls. It stores fat in its thick tail, which it can shed to escape a predator and regrow.
It is active at night and is one of the most popular pet lizards, bred in many colours and patterns.

species:python-regius.placeText: Savannas and open forests of West and Central Africa
summary: A small, heavy-bodied python, usually under 1.5 m long, named for its habit of curling into a tight ball with its head tucked inside when frightened. It hunts rodents at night, killing them by constriction.
It is the most traded live wild animal from Africa, with tens of thousands exported each year, many from snake farms in Togo, Benin and Ghana.

species:pantherophis-guttatus.placeText: Pine woods, fields and farm buildings of the south-eastern USA
summary: A slender, orange-red rat snake with black-edged blotches, harmless to people, that kills mice and rats by constriction. Its name may come from the maize-like chequered pattern on its belly or from its habit of hunting rodents in corn stores.
It is one of the most popular pet snakes, bred in dozens of colour forms.

species:testudo-hermanni.placeText: Mediterranean Europe, from eastern Spain to the Balkans
summary: A small, yellow-and-black tortoise of Mediterranean scrub and woodland, one of Europe’s few native tortoises. It eats mostly plants, sleeps through the winter and can live for over 70 years.
Fires, farming and collecting for the pet trade have reduced it; it is now protected and pets must be captive-bred.

species:poecilia-reticulata.placeText: Streams of north-eastern South America and the southern Caribbean; introduced worldwide
summary: A small livebearer, giving birth to live young; males are brightly coloured with large tails, females larger and drab. Named after Robert Guppy, who sent specimens from Trinidad in 1866, it is one of the most popular aquarium fish.

Wild guppies in Trinidad are a classic example of evolution: in streams with many predators males are dull, and where predators are few they become bright within a few generations. Guppies released to eat mosquito larvae have harmed native fish in many countries.

species:paracheirodon-innesi.placeText: Blackwater and clearwater streams of the western Amazon basin
summary: A tiny schooling fish with a glowing blue stripe and red tail, which makes it easy for others in the school to see in dark, tea-coloured water. It is one of the best-selling aquarium fish; most are now farmed in Asia.

species:danio-rerio.placeText: Rivers, rice paddies and ponds of northern India, Bangladesh and Nepal
summary: A small, striped minnow and a favourite aquarium fish. It is also one of the most important animals in biology: its embryos are transparent, so scientists can watch organs form, and it can regrow its fins, spinal cord and even parts of its heart.
Genetically modified zebrafish that glow red, green or other colours are sold as pets in some countries.

species:loxodonta-africana.placeText: Savannas and dry woodlands of sub-Saharan Africa, now in scattered populations
summary: The largest living land animal: big males stand up to about 4 m at the shoulder and usually weigh around 6 tonnes. Its huge ears, shaped a little like the map of Africa, help it shed heat. Females and young live in family herds led by the oldest female, the matriarch, while adult males roam alone or in bachelor groups.

Elephants shape the savanna by pushing over trees, digging for water and spreading seeds. Poaching for ivory and loss of land have cut their numbers sharply; Botswana now has the largest population, about 130,000.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Females about 3 t, males about 6 t

species:loxodonta-cyclotis.placeText: Rainforests of Central and West Africa
summary: Smaller than the bush elephant, with rounder ears and straighter, downward-pointing tusks of hard, pinkish ivory. It lives in small family groups in dense rainforest, where it opens paths through the undergrowth and spreads the seeds of many trees, which helps the forest store carbon.

Long treated as a type of African elephant, it was recognised as a separate species by the IUCN in 2021. Its numbers fell by more than 85% over about 30 years, mostly to ivory poaching; Gabon holds most of those left.

species:elephas-maximus.placeText: Forests and grasslands of South and South-east Asia, in scattered populations
summary: Smaller than African elephants, with smaller ears, a rounded back and a single finger-like tip on its trunk. Only some males grow tusks. It has been tamed and worked by people for about 4,000 years, but has never been truly domesticated.

It once lived from Iraq and Syria to the Yangtze in China. Fewer than about 50,000 survive in the wild, squeezed by farms and growing towns. In 2021 a herd in Yunnan, China, became famous worldwide after wandering about 500 km north towards the city of Kunming.

species:dugong-dugon.placeText: Warm, shallow coasts of the Indian Ocean and western Pacific, from East Africa to Vanuatu
summary: The only living member of its family, a sea cow with a whale-like fluked tail and a downturned snout for grazing seagrass on the seabed, leaving feeding trails behind it. It can live for 70 years. Sailors’ stories of mermaids may have been inspired by dugongs and manatees.

Northern Australia holds most of the world’s dugongs. Elsewhere they have declined because of hunting, fishing nets and seagrass loss; in 2022 dugongs were declared functionally extinct in China. Its only recent relative, the giant Steller’s sea cow, was hunted to extinction in the 1760s.

species:trichechus-manatus.placeText: Coasts, rivers and springs from Florida and the Gulf of Mexico through the Caribbean to northern Brazil
summary: A large, slow sea cow with a rounded paddle tail, grazing seagrass and water plants for up to eight hours a day. Like all manatees it keeps growing new molars at the back of its jaws that slowly move forward as the front ones wear out. In winter, Florida manatees gather at warm springs and power-plant outflows.

Christopher Columbus reported seeing three “mermaids” in 1493, noting they were “not half as beautiful as they are painted”; they were probably manatees. Boat strikes are a major threat, and in 2021 more than 1,000 Florida manatees died, many starving after seagrass beds died off.

species:trichechus-inunguis.placeText: Rivers, lakes and flooded forests of the Amazon basin
summary: The smallest manatee and the only one that lives only in fresh water, with smooth, rubbery skin, no nails on its flippers and usually a white patch on its chest. In the dry season, when waters fall, it can fast for months, living off its fat.
Tens of thousands were killed in the mid-1900s for meat and for their tough hides, used to make machine belts and hoses. It is now protected, but is still hunted illegally.

species:trichechus-senegalensis.placeText: Coasts, lagoons and rivers of West and Central Africa, from Senegal to Angola
summary: The least-studied sea cow, very like the West Indian manatee. It lives along coasts and in mangroves and lagoons, and travels far up rivers: it reaches the Niger River in Mali and Niger, hundreds of kilometres from the sea.
It is threatened by hunting, accidental capture in fishing nets and dams that block rivers.

species:procavia-capensis.placeText: Rocky outcrops and cliffs across much of Africa and the Middle East
summary: A stocky, rabbit-sized animal that lives in colonies among rocks, basking in the sun in the morning because it controls its body temperature poorly. Rubbery, sweaty foot pads give it grip on steep rock. Despite looks, its closest living relatives are elephants and sea cows, and its upper incisors grow into small tusks.
It is the “coney” of the Bible. Colonies use the same latrines for thousands of years, building up layers of hardened urine (hyraceum) that preserve pollen and record past climates over 50,000 years.

species:heterohyrax-brucei.placeText: Rocky hills of eastern and southern Africa, from Egypt to South Africa
summary: Also called the bush hyrax, it has a white or yellow spot above each eye and a pale belly. It often shares rock outcrops with the rock hyrax: the two species sleep huddled together and their young play together, but they eat different food, the bush hyrax browsing leaves while the rock hyrax mainly grazes.

species:dendrohyrax-arboreus.placeText: Forests of eastern and southern Africa
summary: A soft-furred hyrax that lives alone in tree holes high in the forest canopy and feeds at night. Its loud, rising series of croaks and shrieks, among the most startling sounds of the African night, can carry for over a kilometre.
Dendrohyrax has four species; one, the Benin tree hyrax, was only recognised in 2021, after scientists noticed its unusual barking calls.

species:orycteropus-afer.placeText: Savannas, grasslands and woodlands across sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A pig-sized, long-eared, night-active digger and the only living member of its order. Its powerful claws break open termite mounds and ant nests, and a long sticky tongue collects tens of thousands of insects in a night. Its name means “earth pig” in Afrikaans. Its teeth have no enamel and are made of fine tubes, and they keep growing throughout its life.

Its burrows are later used as homes by many other animals, from warthogs and hyenas to porcupines, bats and birds. It also eats the fruit of the aardvark cucumber and buries its seeds in its dung, spreading the plant.

species:tenrec-ecaudatus.placeText: Madagascar; introduced to the Comoros, Mauritius, Réunion and the Seychelles
summary: The largest tenrec, a tailless, spiny-haired, hedgehog-like insect-eater up to about 2 kg. It holds the record for the largest litters of any mammal: up to 32 young at once, and females can have up to 29 nipples.
It sleeps through the dry season for months in a burrow. In Madagascar it is hunted for food.

species:setifer-setosus.placeText: Forests, scrub, farmland and towns across Madagascar
summary: A tenrec covered in short, stiff spines that rolls into a ball when threatened, so like a hedgehog that it is a textbook example of convergent evolution: the two are not closely related.

species:echinops-telfairi.placeText: Dry forests and scrub of south-western Madagascar
summary: A small, spiny, hedgehog-like tenrec that climbs well and eats insects. To survive the cool, dry season it hibernates for months, letting its body temperature drop close to that of its surroundings. It is sometimes kept as a pet.

species:hemicentetes-semispinosus.placeText: Rainforests and farmland of eastern Madagascar
summary: A small tenrec striped in black and yellow, with detachable barbed quills. It is the only mammal known to communicate by stridulation: it rubs together special quills on its back to make a high-pitched sound, probably to keep its family group together. It feeds mainly on earthworms.

species:microgale-longicaudata.placeText: Rainforests of eastern and northern Madagascar
summary: A tiny, shrew-like tenrec with a tail more than twice as long as its body, which it can wrap around twigs while climbing. Microgale, the shrew tenrecs, is the largest tenrec genus, with about 22 species, several discovered only since the 1990s.

species:limnogale-mergulus.placeText: Fast-flowing streams of the eastern highlands of Madagascar
summary: The only semi-aquatic tenrec, a small otter-like swimmer with webbed hind feet and a flattened tail that hunts aquatic insect larvae, crayfish and frogs at night. Deforestation that muddies its clear streams is the main threat.

species:potamogale-velox.placeText: Rivers and streams of the rainforests of central Africa
summary: An otter-like insectivore up to about 60 cm long, half of it a flattened tail that it sweeps from side to side to swim. It hunts crabs, fish and frogs at night, finding them with its sensitive whiskers. Despite its name it is not a shrew but a relative of tenrecs.

species:chrysochloris-asiatica.placeText: Sandy and loamy soils of the Western and Northern Cape, South Africa
summary: A small, blind golden mole with iridescent, coppery fur and a leathery nose pad for pushing through soil. Its name “asiatica” is a mistake: early naturalists wrongly thought it came from Siberia.
In 2023 a relative, De Winton’s golden mole, unrecorded for 87 years, was found again by sampling the sand for traces of its DNA.

species:eremitalpa-granti.placeText: Sand dunes of the Namib Desert in Namibia and north-western South Africa
summary: A tiny golden mole that “swims” through loose desert sand rather than digging tunnels, which collapse behind it. Blind, it detects the vibrations of termites and of wind-blown grass hummocks with an enlarged middle-ear bone, and travels several kilometres a night between them.

species:chrysospalax-trevelyani.placeText: Forests of the Eastern Cape, South Africa
summary: The largest golden mole, about 20 cm long and up to 500 g, which forages on the forest floor at night for giant earthworms and millipedes. Its small forest patches are threatened by cattle, firewood collecting and dogs.

species:amblysomus-hottentotus.placeText: Grassland, forest edges and gardens of eastern South Africa, Lesotho and eSwatini
summary: A common golden mole that makes ridges of raised soil across lawns and fields as it tunnels just below the surface for earthworms and insect larvae. Like other golden moles, it can lower its metabolism to save energy in cold weather.

species:rhynchocyon-petersi.placeText: Coastal and mountain forests of Kenya and Tanzania
summary: A squirrel-sized sengi with a long, twitching, trunk-like snout and striking black and red fur, which forages in leaf litter for insects, spiders and worms. Pairs live in territories and build nests of leaves on the forest floor.
Rhynchocyon, the giant sengis, has five species; the grey-faced sengi of Tanzania’s Udzungwa Mountains was only discovered in 2005, first seen on camera traps.

species:elephantulus-rufescens.placeText: Dry savanna and bushland of East Africa
summary: A mouse-sized sengi that keeps a network of cleared trails through its territory and races along them at high speed to escape predators. Pairs mate for life but spend most of their time apart.
Elephantulus has about 10 species. The Somali sengi, unrecorded by scientists for about 50 years, was found alive in Djibouti in 2019 and is now placed in its own genus, Galegeeska.

species:macroscelides-proboscideus.placeText: Semi-desert and dry scrub of Namibia, Botswana and South Africa
summary: A tiny, round-eared sengi of open, dry country that lives in monogamous pairs and saves energy by dropping into torpor on cold nights. Despite its small size it is a close relative of elephants.
Macroscelides has three species; the Etendeka round-eared sengi of Namibia was described in 2014.

species:petrodromus-tetradactylus.placeText: Forests and thickets of central, eastern and southern Africa
summary: A rat-sized sengi with only four toes on its hind feet, which thumps its hind legs on the ground as an alarm signal. It lives in pairs and clears trails through dense undergrowth, foraging mainly for ants and termites.

species:petrosaltator-rozeti.placeText: Rocky, dry country of Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya
summary: The only sengi living north of the Sahara, in rocky scrub and semi-desert. It was long placed in Elephantulus, but DNA showed it is most closely related to the four-toed sengi, and it was given its own genus in 2016.

species:ornithorhynchus-anatinus.placeText: Rivers, streams and lakes of eastern Australia and Tasmania
summary: An egg-laying mammal with a duck-like bill, webbed feet and a beaver-like tail. When the first specimen reached Britain in 1799, some scientists suspected it was a fake stitched together from different animals.

It hunts underwater with its eyes, ears and nostrils closed, finding insect larvae, shrimps and worms with thousands of sensors in its bill that detect the tiny electric fields of their muscles. Males have a venomous spur on each hind ankle, painful enough to disable a dog. The female lays one to three eggs in a burrow and feeds the young milk that seeps from patches of skin, as it has no nipples.
Drought, dams and land clearing have reduced it in many rivers.

species:tachyglossus-aculeatus.placeText: All of Australia, Tasmania and southern New Guinea
summary: A spiny, toothless ant- and termite-eater with a short snout and a long, sticky tongue. It is found almost everywhere in Australia, from snowy mountains to deserts, the most widespread native Australian mammal.

The female lays a single soft-shelled egg directly into a pouch on her belly; the hatchling, called a puggle, stays there until its spines start to grow. It has one of the lowest body temperatures of any mammal, about 32 °C, and can hibernate in cold areas.

species:zaglossus-bruijnii.placeText: Mountain forests of the Bird’s Head region, western New Guinea, Indonesia
summary: The largest monotreme, up to about 16 kg, with a long, down-curved snout for probing soil and leaf litter for earthworms, which it hooks with spines on its tongue. Its spines are short and mostly hidden in thick fur.

It is hunted for food with dogs and is critically endangered. A museum specimen collected in the Kimberley in 1901 suggests long-beaked echidnas may have survived in north-western Australia until about a century ago, long after they were thought to have died out there.

species:zaglossus-bartoni.placeText: Mountain forests of central and eastern New Guinea
summary: Also called Barton’s long-beaked echidna, it lives in the high forests of the central ranges of New Guinea, where it is threatened by hunting and forest clearing. Like its relatives it feeds mainly on earthworms.

species:zaglossus-attenboroughi.placeText: Cyclops Mountains, northern New Guinea, Indonesia
summary: The smallest long-beaked echidna, named after Sir David Attenborough and known for decades from a single specimen collected in 1961. In 2023 an expedition to the steep, rugged Cyclops Mountains finally caught it on camera traps, confirming that it still survives.

species:didelphis-virginiana.placeText: Eastern and central USA, the Pacific coast, Mexico and Central America to Costa Rica
summary: The only marsupial north of Mexico, a cat-sized omnivore with a naked, gripping tail and 50 teeth, more than any other North American land mammal. When badly frightened it may “play possum”, collapsing, drooling and giving off a foul smell for minutes to hours.

Females carry up to about 13 tiny young in the pouch; when they leave it, they ride on her back. It is partly resistant to the venom of rattlesnakes and other pit vipers. It was released in California in the 1890s and has since spread north to Canada.

species:chironectes-minimus.placeText: Streams and rivers from southern Mexico to northern Argentina
summary: Also called the yapok, the only semi-aquatic marsupial, with webbed hind feet and water-repellent fur. It hunts fish, frogs and crayfish at night. Unusually, both sexes have a pouch: the female’s closes with a ring of muscle so her young stay dry underwater, and the male’s protects his scrotum while swimming.

species:monodelphis-domestica.placeText: Dry scrub and forest of eastern and central South America
summary: A small, pouchless opossum that often moves into houses to catch insects and mice, which gives its species name. It is a laboratory animal, and in 2007 it became the first marsupial to have its genome sequenced.

species:caenolestes-fuliginosus.placeText: Cloud forests and páramo of the northern Andes
summary: A small, dark, shrew-like marsupial with a long snout and no pouch that hunts insects and worms in mossy cloud forest and high grassland. Shrew opossums are living relics of a group that was common in South America millions of years ago.

species:dromiciops-gliroides.placeText: Temperate rainforests of southern Chile and Argentina
summary: A tiny, mouse-sized marsupial whose name means “little monkey of the bush”. It hibernates through the cold winter, living off fat stored in its tail. It is the main spreader of the seeds of a mistletoe, which pass through its gut and sprout on the branches where it leaves its droppings.
It is the last of an ancient order more closely related to Australian marsupials than to other American ones.

species:sarcophilus-harrisii.placeText: Tasmania; a small reintroduced population in New South Wales
summary: The largest living meat-eating marsupial, about the size of a small dog, with the strongest bite for its size of any living mammal. It mostly scavenges, crunching through bones, and its screeches over a carcass gave it its name.

Since 1996 a contagious facial cancer, spread by bites, has killed most devils in the wild. Devils vanished from mainland Australia about 3,000 years ago, possibly because of dingoes and people; in 2020 a small group was released at Barrington Tops in New South Wales.

species:dasyurus-viverrinus.placeText: Tasmania; reintroduced to fenced and fox-free sites in mainland south-east Australia
summary: A cat-sized, white-spotted marsupial predator of grassland and forest edge that hunts insects, small mammals and birds at night. It was common around Sydney and Melbourne until the early 1900s, but disease, foxes and cats wiped it out on the mainland by the 1960s.
Dasyurus has six species of quolls; the northern quoll is threatened by poisonous cane toads, which it tries to eat.

A mouse-sized insect-eating marsupial famous for its deadly breeding season: males spend two to three weeks mating frantically, stop eating and sleeping, and their immune systems collapse, so every male dies before his first birthday. Only the females survive to raise the young.

species:planigale-ingrami.placeText: Grassland and woodland of northern Australia
summary: One of the smallest mammals in the world, weighing about 4 g, with a remarkably flat head that lets it squeeze into deep cracks in dry, cracking clay soils to hunt insects and spiders, some nearly as big as itself.

species:myrmecobius-fasciatus.placeText: Eucalyptus woodland of south-western Western Australia; reintroduced to fenced reserves elsewhere
summary: A striped, squirrel-sized marsupial that eats almost nothing but termites, up to 20,000 a day, licked up with a tongue up to 10 cm long. Unusually for a marsupial it is active by day, and the females have no pouch, so their young cling to their teats.
