Once found across southern and central Australia, it was reduced by foxes, cats and land clearing to two small populations by the 1980s. It is the emblem of Western Australia.

species:macrotis-lagotis.placeText: Deserts of the Northern Territory, Western Australia and south-western Queensland
summary: A burrowing desert marsupial with long rabbit-like ears, silky blue-grey fur and a black-and-white tail. It digs spiral burrows up to 2 m deep and eats insects, seeds, bulbs and fungi. Its pouch opens backwards so it does not fill with soil while digging.

It once lived across about 70% of Australia; foxes, cats and rabbits have reduced it to scattered desert areas. In Australia, chocolate Easter Bilbies are sold in place of Easter bunnies to raise money for it.

species:macrotis-leucura.placeText: Sand dunes of the central Australian deserts (extinct)
summary: A smaller, paler relative of the greater bilby with a white-tipped tail, which lived in the sandy deserts of central Australia. Few Europeans ever saw it alive.
The last specimen was collected in 1931; Aboriginal people reported it until the 1950s or 1960s. Foxes, cats and changes in burning practices are thought to have killed it off.

species:perameles-gunnii.placeText: Tasmania, and fox-free islands and fenced reserves in Victoria
summary: A small bandicoot with pale bars across its rump that digs small cone-shaped holes while searching for insects and worms. Foxes and farming wiped it out across Victoria except for one town, and by 2013 it was extinct in the wild on the mainland.
Captive breeding and releases on fox-free islands brought it back, and in 2021 it became the first Australian mammal to be moved from “extinct in the wild” to “endangered”.

facts.label: Status in Victoria
facts.value: Endangered (no longer extinct in the wild)

species:chaeropus-ecaudatus.placeText: Grassland and shrubland of southern Australia (extinct)
summary: A long-legged, rabbit-sized bandicoot that ran on its forefeet’s two hoof-like toes, like a tiny deer or pig, and on hind feet with one large toe. It was the most plant-eating of all bandicoots. In 2019 it was split into two species, with the northern pig-footed bandicoot of the central deserts.
Specimens were collected until about 1901, and Aboriginal people reported it into the 1950s. Foxes, cats and changed fire patterns are blamed for its loss.

species:notoryctes-typhlops.placeText: Sand dunes of the central and western Australian deserts
summary: A blind, earless, golden-furred marsupial that “swims” through sand using huge spade-like claws, the sand filling in behind it, so it leaves no tunnels. Its pouch faces backwards. It is almost identical in shape to the golden moles of Africa, though they are unrelated, a striking case of convergent evolution.
It is rarely seen; most records come from tracks or animals surfacing after rain.

species:phascolarctos-cinereus.placeText: Eucalyptus forests and woodlands of eastern and south-eastern Australia
summary: A tree-living marsupial that eats almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves, which are tough, low in energy and poisonous to most animals; a long gut and special bacteria let it digest them. To save energy it sleeps or rests up to 20 hours a day. Its fingerprints are so like ours that they could confuse a crime scene.

Hunted for fur in the early 1900s, it is now threatened by land clearing, dogs, cars, chlamydia infections and bushfires. In 2022 it was listed as endangered in Queensland, New South Wales and the ACT.

species:vombatus-ursinus.placeText: Forests and heaths of south-eastern Australia and Tasmania
summary: A stocky, powerful burrower that digs tunnels up to 20 m long and can run at up to 40 km/h. Its hard rump plate can block a burrow against predators, and it is famous for producing cube-shaped droppings, which it piles on rocks and logs to mark its territory. Its pouch opens backwards.

species:lasiorhinus-krefftii.placeText: Epping Forest National Park and a second reserve in Queensland
summary: One of the rarest large mammals in the world. By the early 1980s only about 35 survived, in a single patch of Queensland grassland; a predator-proof fence and careful management have brought numbers back to over 300, and a second population was started near St George in 2009.

The largest living marsupial: big males stand about 1.8 m tall and weigh up to about 85 kg. It can hop at over 50 km/h, and its springy tendons make hopping very energy-efficient. Females can carry an embryo on hold, a young in the pouch and an older joey at foot at the same time, each fed different milk from different teats.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Females about 25 kg, males up to about 85 kg

species:macropus-giganteus.placeText: Grassland and open woodland of eastern Australia and Tasmania
summary: A big grey kangaroo of the wetter east, living in mobs that graze at dawn and dusk. Large males box and kick each other to win females. It is one of the most common large animals in Australia, often seen on golf courses and city edges.
Macropus has two species, with the western grey kangaroo.

species:notamacropus-rufogriseus.placeText: Forests and scrub of south-eastern Australia and Tasmania; introduced to New Zealand and Britain
summary: A medium-sized wallaby with a reddish neck and shoulders; the Tasmanian form is called Bennett’s wallaby. Escaped and released animals have formed wild populations in New Zealand, England and Ireland.

species:notamacropus-greyi.placeText: Grassy plains of south-eastern South Australia and western Victoria (extinct)
summary: Said to be the most graceful and fastest of all wallabies, with banded fur and a long tail. It was hunted for sport and fur and lost its grassland to sheep farms and foxes.
By 1924 only a few were left; attempts to move the last group to a reserve failed, and the last known animal, a captive female, died in 1939.

species:setonix-brachyurus.placeText: Rottnest and Bald islands and patches of south-western Western Australia
summary: A cat-sized wallaby with a round face that seems to smile, famous for “quokka selfies” on Rottnest Island. The Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh thought they were giant rats in 1696 and named the island “rat’s nest”.
On the mainland, foxes and land clearing have left only small, scattered groups.

species:dendrolagus-lumholtzi.placeText: Rainforests of the Atherton Tableland, north-eastern Queensland
summary: A kangaroo that has gone back to living in trees, with shorter, stronger legs, curved claws and a long tail for balance. It can leap from branches to the ground from great heights without injury. Tree-kangaroos are the largest tree-living mammals of Australia and New Guinea.

species:bettongia-penicillata.placeText: Small areas of south-western Australia and fenced reserves
summary: The brush-tailed bettong, a small, hopping relative of kangaroos that carries nesting material with its curled tail. It digs up to 100 small holes a night looking for underground fungi (truffles), turning over tonnes of soil a year and spreading fungal spores that trees need.
It recovered strongly after fox control in the 1990s, then crashed again from 2001; it is critically endangered.

species:caloprymnus-campestris.placeText: Gibber plains of north-eastern South Australia and south-western Queensland (extinct)
summary: A small, pale rat-kangaroo of the stony deserts that sheltered in grass-lined nests and could outrun a horse over several kilometres. Known from a few specimens in the 1840s, it was lost for 90 years and then rediscovered in 1931.
It was last seen in 1935, probably wiped out by foxes and cats arriving in its desert home.

The smallest and most primitive living kangaroo relative, about 500 g, active by day. Unlike other kangaroos it moves on all four legs rather than hopping on two, has a first toe on its hind foot, and usually gives birth to twins.

species:trichosurus-vulpecula.placeText: Most of Australia; introduced to New Zealand
summary: A cat-sized, bushy-tailed possum that has adapted well to towns, often living in roofs. In Australia it is protected; in New Zealand, where it was released from the 1830s for a fur trade, about 30 million now damage native forests, eat birds’ eggs and chicks and spread bovine tuberculosis.

A small possum that glides between trees on a skin membrane stretched from its fifth finger to its first toe, travelling 50 m or more in one glide. It feeds on tree sap, gum, nectar and insects, and lives in family groups in tree holes.

A 2020 study split it into three species: this one in the south-east, Krefft’s glider over most of eastern Australia, and the savanna glider in the north. Pet sugar gliders mostly come from New Guinea stock.

species:gymnobelideus-leadbeateri.placeText: Mountain ash forests of the Central Highlands of Victoria
summary: A small, fast-moving possum, like a sugar glider without the gliding membrane, that lives in colonies in hollows of old mountain ash trees. It was thought extinct until rediscovered in 1961. Logging and bushfires, especially in 2009, have destroyed much of its old-growth forest. It is the emblem of Victoria.

species:petauroides-volans.placeText: Tall eucalypt forests of south-eastern Australia
summary: A cat-sized, fluffy-eared glider that eats only eucalyptus leaves and can glide up to 100 m, steering with its long tail. It needs old trees with big hollows to den in.
Bushfires in 2019–20 burned a third of its habitat, and in 2022 it was listed as endangered. Greater gliders are now split into three species.

species:acrobates-pygmaeus.placeText: Forests and woodlands of eastern Australia
summary: The smallest gliding mammal in the world, about the size of a mouse, with a flat tail fringed with stiff hairs like a feather, used to steer. It feeds on nectar, pollen and insects, and special grooved toe pads let it climb smooth surfaces, even glass.

A tiny possum that lives only on nectar and pollen, collected with a long snout and a brush-tipped tongue, especially from banksias and other heathland flowers, which it pollinates. Its teeth are reduced to small pegs. Males produce the largest sperm cells of any mammal.

species:burramys-parvus.placeText: Boulder fields above the snowline in the Australian Alps
summary: The only Australian mammal that lives only in the high mountains, where it hibernates under the snow for up to seven months. It was first described from fossils in 1896 and thought long extinct, until a live one turned up in a ski lodge on Mount Hotham in 1966.
In spring it feasts on Bogong moths that migrate to the mountains; droughts that reduce the moths and warmer winters with less snow threaten it.

The largest penguin, up to about 1.2 m tall, and the only bird that breeds through the Antarctic winter. Males incubate the single egg on their feet for about two months without eating, huddling together against temperatures below −40 °C. It dives deeper than any other bird, to over 500 m. Loss of sea ice is a growing threat.

The second-largest penguin, with orange ear patches, breeding in huge colonies on islands such as South Georgia and the Crozets. Its breeding cycle takes over a year, so pairs raise at most two chicks every three years.

species:pygoscelis-adeliae.placeText: Coasts and pack ice all around Antarctica
summary: A classic black-and-white penguin with a white eye-ring, nesting in colonies on bare rock and building nests of pebbles, which it sometimes steals from neighbours. It was named after the wife of the French explorer Dumont d’Urville.
Named for the thin black line under its chin. Chinstraps have been found to take thousands of “microsleeps” of a few seconds each day while guarding their nests.
A penguin with an orange-red bill and a white patch over each eye, and the fastest-swimming penguin, reaching about 36 km/h. Some recent studies split it into four species.

species:eudyptes-chrysocome.placeText: Islands of southern South America and the southern Indian Ocean
summary: A small crested penguin with spiky yellow eyebrows that hops from rock to rock on steep, wave-battered shores. Some authorities split off an eastern rockhopper as a further species.

species:eudyptes-moseleyi.placeText: Tristan da Cunha, Gough, Amsterdam and St Paul islands
summary: A rockhopper with longer, droopier crest plumes than its southern relative, breeding on a few temperate islands in the South Atlantic and Indian oceans. Its numbers have fallen by more than half since the 1950s.

species:eudyptes-pachyrhynchus.placeText: Southwest coast of New Zealand’s South Island
summary: A crested penguin that nests in dense temperate rainforest and caves along the coast of Fiordland and Stewart Island, unusual for a penguin. Tracking showed some swim thousands of kilometres to feed before moulting.

species:eudyptes-robustus.placeText: The Snares Islands, south of New Zealand
summary: A crested penguin that breeds only on the tiny Snares Islands, under the shade of tree daisies.

species:eudyptes-sclateri.placeText: Bounty and Antipodes islands, New Zealand
summary: The only penguin that can raise its stiff yellow crest. Like other crested penguins it lays two eggs but raises only one chick; the first, smaller egg usually fails.

species:eudyptes-chrysolophus.placeText: Subantarctic islands of the South Atlantic and Indian Ocean
summary: Named by English sailors for its orange crest plumes, after the flamboyant 18th-century “macaroni” fashion. It is probably the most numerous penguin, though numbers have declined.

A crested penguin with a white face that breeds only on Macquarie Island. Some ornithologists treat it as a white-faced form of the macaroni penguin. In the early 1900s hundreds of thousands were boiled down for oil.

species:megadyptes-antipodes.placeText: Southeast New Zealand and its subantarctic islands
summary: The hoiho, one of the rarest penguins, nesting out of sight of other pairs in coastal forest and scrub. Mainland numbers have fallen sharply from disease, warming seas and fishing nets. It is the only living species in its genus.

species:eudyptula-minor.placeText: Coasts of southern Australia and New Zealand
summary: The smallest penguin, about 30 cm tall, and blue-grey rather than black. Every evening at Phillip Island, near Melbourne, crowds watch them parade ashore to their burrows. Australian birds are sometimes split as a separate species.

species:spheniscus-demersus.placeText: Coasts of South Africa and Namibia
summary: The only penguin that breeds in Africa, famous at Boulders Beach near Cape Town. Its braying call gave it the old name “jackass penguin”. Its population has fallen by over 95% in a century, mainly from overfishing of sardines and anchovies, and it was listed as Critically Endangered in 2024.
A banded penguin of the cold, fish-rich Humboldt Current, nesting in burrows dug into guano. Guano mining in the 1800s destroyed much of its nesting habitat.

species:spheniscus-magellanicus.placeText: Coasts of southern South America and the Falklands
summary: A banded penguin nesting in burrows in colonies of hundreds of thousands, such as Punta Tombo in Argentina. Ferdinand Magellan’s crew saw them in 1520. Some migrate north as far as Brazil in winter.

The most northerly penguin; part of its range crosses the equator. It survives in the tropics thanks to cold currents, and pants and shades its feet with its flippers to keep cool. Only a few thousand remain.

The largest living bird, up to about 2.7 m tall and 150 kg, and the fastest on land, running at about 70 km/h on two-toed feet. It lays the largest eggs of any living bird. The legend that ostriches bury their heads in sand is a myth. Its only relative is the Somali ostrich.
Recognised as a separate species in 2014; males have blue-grey necks and legs instead of pink. It prefers bushier country than the common ostrich.
South America’s largest bird, up to about 1.5 m tall. Males build the nest, incubate eggs laid by several females, and raise the chicks alone, fiercely chasing off intruders.
Darwin’s rhea, which Charles Darwin first noticed when he realised the bird he was eating was a different species from the greater rhea. It lives in Patagonian steppe and the high puna of the Andes.

The second-largest living bird, up to about 1.9 m tall, wandering long distances after rain. In the 1932 “Emu War”, soldiers with machine guns failed to stop emus raiding Western Australian wheat farms. Males incubate the dark green eggs for about eight weeks without eating. It is the only living species in its genus.

species:casuarius-casuarius.placeText: Rainforests of New Guinea and northeast Queensland
summary: A tall rainforest bird with a helmet-like casque and blue and red neck. Its dagger-like inner claw can be dangerous, though attacks are rare and usually provoked. It is a key seed disperser, swallowing large fruits whole. Casuarius has three species, with the northern and dwarf cassowaries.

species:casuarius-unappendiculatus.placeText: Lowland forests of northern New Guinea
summary: A large cassowary of swampy lowland forest along the north coast of New Guinea, with a single red wattle at the base of its neck.
The smallest cassowary, living in mountain forests up to about 3,300 m. People in New Guinea have raised captured chicks for feathers and meat for thousands of years.

New Zealand’s national symbol: a hen-sized, nocturnal bird with tiny wings, hair-like feathers and nostrils at the tip of its long bill, which it uses to sniff out worms. Females lay an egg about 20% of their body weight, one of the largest relative to body size of any bird. Stoats kill most chicks where not controlled.

species:apteryx-australis.placeText: South Island and Stewart Island, New Zealand
summary: The tokoeka, the largest kiwi in some populations. On Stewart Island it sometimes forages by day.

species:apteryx-rowi.placeText: Ōkārito forest, South Island, New Zealand
summary: The rarest kiwi, recognised as a species in 2003 and found only in one forest. Its numbers have more than doubled since the 1990s through Operation Nest Egg, which raises chicks safe from stoats.

species:apteryx-haastii.placeText: Mountains of northwest South Island, New Zealand
summary: The largest kiwi, the roroa, living in rugged, snowy mountain country in the northwest of the South Island.

species:apteryx-owenii.placeText: Predator-free islands and sanctuaries in New Zealand
summary: The smallest kiwi. It died out on the mainland; every bird alive today descends from five released on Kapiti Island in the early 1900s. Its numbers have grown from a few hundred to about 2,000 in predator-free sanctuaries.

The national bird of the United States, a fish-eating sea eagle with a white head. The pesticide DDT thinned its eggshells and cut it to about 400 breeding pairs in the lower 48 states by the 1960s; after DDT was banned, it recovered to over 300,000 birds. The family Accipitridae also includes the golden eagle, harpy eagle, hawks, kites and Old World vultures.
A fish hawk that plunges feet-first into water, with a reversible outer toe and spiny foot pads for gripping slippery fish. Like the bald eagle, it declined from DDT and has recovered.

species:vultur-gryphus.placeText: The Andes and Pacific coast of South America
summary: One of the largest flying birds, with a wingspan over 3 m, able to soar for hours on mountain updrafts; one was recorded flying over 170 km while flapping for only 1% of the time. The California condor, its relative, fell to 27 birds in 1987, all taken into captivity; over 500 now live, more than half in the wild.

A long-legged raptor that walks the grasslands and stamps on snakes and lizards with kicks delivered in about 15 milliseconds. Its name may come from its quill-like crest feathers. It is the only species in its family.

The fastest animal on Earth, reaching over 320 km/h in its hunting dive (stoop). After DDT wiped it out from much of North America and Europe, captive breeding brought it back, and it now nests on city skyscrapers and cathedrals.

species:bubo-scandiacus.placeText: Arctic tundra; winters south into Canada, the US and northern Eurasia
summary: A large white owl of the Arctic that hunts by day in the polar summer, mostly lemmings, and nests only in years when lemmings are plentiful. Typical owls (about 230 species) also include the eagle-owls, the tiny elf owl and the burrowing owl.

A pale owl with a heart-shaped face, one of the most widespread land birds. It can catch mice in total darkness by sound alone. Recent checklists split it into several species, such as the American barn owl.

A large red, yellow and blue parrot that gathers at riverbank clay licks, perhaps for the sodium in the clay. Macaws can live for 50 years or more. The family Psittacidae also includes the amazons, conures and the African grey parrot, famous for learning words.

species:cacatua-galerita.placeText: Eastern and northern Australia and New Guinea
summary: A loud white cockatoo with a yellow crest. In Sydney, cockatoos have learned to open wheelie bins to raid rubbish, a skill spreading from suburb to suburb by social learning. The family also includes the galah and the cockatiel.

A flightless, nocturnal parrot, the heaviest in the world, which smells musty-sweet and breeds only in years when rimu trees fruit heavily. It fell to 51 birds in 1995; intensive management on predator-free islands has raised it to about 240.

The smallest bird, about 5–6 cm long and under 2 g, with a nest the size of a thimble and eggs the size of coffee beans. Hummingbirds beat their wings dozens of times a second and have the highest metabolism of any warm-blooded animal.

species:apus-apus.placeText: Breeds across Europe and Asia; winters in Africa
summary: A bird that spends almost its whole life in the air: once it leaves the nest, a young swift may stay airborne for ten months without landing, eating, drinking and sleeping on the wing.

The largest songbird, an intelligent all-black corvid that solves puzzles, plans for the future and plays. The family Corvidae also includes crows (the New Caledonian crow makes hooked tools), magpies, jays and nutcrackers.

species:paradisaea-apoda.placeText: Southwestern New Guinea and the Aru Islands
summary: Males display together in treetop leks, raising cascades of golden plumes. Traders sold skins without legs, so Europeans believed the birds never landed and named it “apoda”, legless. About 45 species of birds-of-paradise are known.

A pheasant-sized songbird with a lyre-shaped tail whose males imitate almost any sound they hear, from other birds to camera shutters and chainsaws. Lyrebirds belong to one of the oldest branches of songbirds.

species:hirundo-rustica.placeText: Breeds across the Northern Hemisphere; winters south
summary: The most widespread swallow, nesting in barns and under bridges and migrating thousands of kilometres between hemispheres each year. Its return has long been taken as a sign of spring.

A red-breasted thrush named by English settlers after the European robin, though the two are not closely related. It is one of the first birds to sing at dawn. Thrushes also include the blackbird and song thrush.

species:erithacus-rubecula.placeText: Europe, western Asia and North Africa
summary: A small, orange-breasted bird that sings through winter and fiercely defends its territory. It often follows gardeners to catch worms they turn up, a habit that may come from following wild boar. The family also includes the nightingale and the wheatears.

species:serinus-canaria.placeText: Canary Islands, Madeira and the Azores
summary: The wild ancestor of the domestic canary, bred for its song since the 1600s. Canaries were once taken down coal mines to warn of poisonous gas. The finch family also includes the Hawaiian honeycreepers, many of which are now extinct.

One of Darwin’s finches. On the island of Daphne Major, Peter and Rosemary Grant measured evolution happening: after a 1977 drought killed off birds that could not crack hard seeds, the next generation had deeper beaks. Darwin’s finches are now known to be tanagers.

A small brown bird that has lived alongside humans since the start of farming, and was introduced to the Americas, Australia and elsewhere in the 1800s. It has declined sharply in many cities for reasons still debated.

species:sturnus-vulgaris.placeText: Europe and western Asia; introduced to North America, Australia and elsewhere
summary: A glossy, speckled songbird and expert mimic, famous for winter murmurations of hundreds of thousands of birds swirling at dusk. About 100 were released in New York’s Central Park in 1890; North America now has over 80 million.

species:mimus-polyglottos.placeText: United States, Mexico and the Caribbean
summary: A grey songbird whose males may learn 200 or more songs, copying other birds, frogs and car alarms, and sing through the night.

species:cardinalis-cardinalis.placeText: Eastern North America to Mexico and Belize
summary: Males are bright red, coloured by pigments from their food. It is the state bird of seven US states, more than any other bird.
The glossy blue-black male builds an avenue of sticks and decorates it with blue objects, from flowers and feathers to bottle tops and pegs, to win females.

species:phoenicopterus-roseus.placeText: Africa, southern Europe, the Middle East and South Asia
summary: The largest flamingo. Flamingos filter shrimp and algae with their heads upside down, and their pink colour comes from carotenoid pigments in that food. They often stand on one leg, which may save energy.

The bird with the largest wingspan, up to about 3.5 m. It glides over the ocean for thousands of kilometres using the wind, and may circle Antarctica several times. Pairs mate for life and raise one chick every two years.

species:ardenna-grisea.placeText: Breeds in New Zealand, Chile and the Falklands; migrates across the oceans
summary: A dark seabird that makes one of the longest migrations known: tracked birds flew about 64,000 km in a year, in a figure-of-eight across the Pacific. In New Zealand its chicks are harvested sustainably by Māori as tītī (muttonbirds).

A huge white pelican that fishes cooperatively, swimming in a horseshoe to herd fish into the shallows before scooping them up in its pouch. The family also includes the Australian pelican, with the longest bill of any bird.

species:balaeniceps-rex.placeText: Swamps of East and Central Africa
summary: A huge grey bird with a clog-shaped bill, standing motionless for long periods before lunging at lungfish and catfish. It can clatter its bill like a machine gun. It is the only species in its family.

A tall heron that stands still at the water’s edge before spearing fish. The family also includes the egrets, once hunted for their plumes for hats, which led to the founding of early bird-protection societies.

species:ciconia-ciconia.placeText: Breeds in Europe and western Asia; winters in Africa
summary: A large black-and-white stork that nests on rooftops and church towers, the stork of the baby-delivering legend. In 1822 one shot in Germany had an African spear through its neck, proving that birds migrate rather than hibernate.

species:threskiornis-aethiopicus.placeText: Sub-Saharan Africa and Iraq; introduced to Europe
summary: Revered in ancient Egypt as a form of the god Thoth; millions were mummified. It has since died out in Egypt. The family also includes the scarlet ibis and the spoonbills.

A tall white crane with a red crown, a symbol of luck and long life in East Asia, famous for its dancing displays. Hokkaido’s population fell to about 30 birds in the 1920s; winter feeding has raised it to over 1,800. The crane family also includes the whooping crane.

species:porphyrio-hochstetteri.placeText: Fiordland and predator-free islands, New Zealand
summary: A large, flightless, blue-green rail thought extinct for half a century until it was rediscovered in 1948 in the Murchison Mountains. About 500 now live in Fiordland and sanctuaries. The rail family has lost many flightless island species to extinction.

The most familiar duck and the ancestor of almost all domestic ducks; males have a glossy green head. The family also includes the swans and geese; the trumpeter and mute swans are among the heaviest flying birds.

species:gallus-gallus.placeText: Forests of South and Southeast Asia
summary: The wild ancestor of the chicken, domesticated in Southeast Asia perhaps 3,500 years ago, probably first around rice and millet fields. There are now over 20 billion chickens, the most numerous bird on Earth. The family also includes pheasants, peafowl, turkeys and quail.

species:leipoa-ocellata.placeText: Dry mallee scrub of southern Australia
summary: The male spends most of the year building and tending a nest mound of sand and rotting leaves up to 5 m wide, checking its temperature with his beak and adding or removing sand to keep the eggs at about 33 °C. Chicks dig themselves out and can fly within a day.

species:dendrocopos-major.placeText: Europe, North Africa and northern Asia
summary: A black, white and red woodpecker that drums on dead branches to claim territory and raids nest boxes for chicks. Woodpeckers’ skulls and tongues are adapted to repeated hammering. The family also includes the ivory-billed woodpecker of the southern US, possibly extinct.
The largest toucan, whose enormous orange bill is light, made of keratin over a honeycomb of bone, and works as a radiator to shed body heat.

species:buceros-bicornis.placeText: India, the Himalayan foothills and Southeast Asia
summary: A huge hornbill with a yellow casque. The female seals herself into a tree hole with mud and droppings and is fed by the male through a slit for months while she raises the chick.

A small, electric-blue kingfisher that dives for fish. Its streamlined bill inspired the nose of Japan’s Shinkansen bullet train, reducing noise from tunnels. The family also includes the laughing kookaburra of Australia.

species:sterna-paradisaea.placeText: Breeds in the Arctic; spends the southern summer in the Antarctic
summary: The bird with the longest migration known, flying from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year, up to about 90,000 km by winding routes, so it sees more daylight than any other animal. The family Laridae also includes the gulls.

A small auk with a striped, colourful bill in the breeding season, nesting in clifftop burrows. It can carry a dozen or more small fish crosswise in its bill. Its relative the great auk was hunted to extinction in 1844.

species:sula-nebouxii.placeText: Pacific coast from Mexico to Peru, and the Galápagos
summary: A seabird whose males show off their bright blue feet in a strutting dance; the brighter the blue, the healthier the bird. Boobies and gannets plunge-dive from up to 30 m.

species:fregata-magnificens.placeText: Tropical Atlantic and eastern Pacific coasts
summary: A black seabird with long, angular wings that can stay aloft for weeks over the ocean, even sleeping in flight. Males inflate a red throat pouch like a balloon to attract females. Frigatebirds steal fish from other seabirds in mid-air.

species:phalacrocorax-carbo.placeText: Coasts and lakes of Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia and eastern North America
summary: A large, black diving bird often seen holding its wings out to dry. In China and Japan, fishermen have trained cormorants to catch fish for over a thousand years. The family also includes the flightless cormorant of the Galápagos.

species:columba-livia.placeText: Wild in Europe, North Africa and Asia; feral pigeons worldwide
summary: The wild ancestor of the domestic and feral pigeon, domesticated thousands of years ago. Homing pigeons, which find their way back over hundreds of kilometres, carried messages in war, and Darwin bred fancy pigeons to study variation. The dodo and the extinct passenger pigeon were relatives.

species:cuculus-canorus.placeText: Breeds across Europe and Asia; winters in Africa and South Asia
summary: A brood parasite: females lay eggs that mimic their hosts’ eggs in the nests of reed warblers, meadow pipits and other birds, and the cuckoo chick pushes its host’s eggs out. Its call names it in many languages.

species:otis-tarda.placeText: Grasslands from Spain to Mongolia and China
summary: One of the heaviest flying birds, with males up to about 18 kg. In spring, males inflate their necks and turn their feathers inside out into a white “foam” display. It was reintroduced to Salisbury Plain in England after dying out there in 1832.

species:tinamus-major.placeText: Rainforests of southern Mexico to the Amazon
summary: A plump, ground-living bird with glossy blue eggs, among the shiniest of any bird’s. Tinamous are related to ostriches and emus and are the only palaeognaths that can fly, though weakly. Males incubate the eggs.

species:gavia-immer.placeText: Northern North America, Greenland and Iceland
summary: A diving bird with haunting wailing and yodelling calls across northern lakes, pictured on Canada’s one-dollar coin, the “loonie”. Its legs are set so far back that it can barely walk on land. In Britain it is called the great northern diver.

A diving bird famous for its elaborate courtship dance, in which pairs mirror each other, shake heads and rise breast to breast holding waterweed. In Victorian Britain it was hunted almost to extinction for its head plumes, prompting the founding of what became the RSPB.

A pinkish bird with a black-and-white barred crest it fans out when excited, named for its “hoop-hoop” call. Nesting females and chicks can squirt foul-smelling secretions to deter predators. It is Israel’s national bird.

species:limosa-lapponica.placeText: Breeds in the Arctic; winters as far as New Zealand and Australia
summary: A long-billed shorebird that makes the longest non-stop flight of any bird: in 2022 a tagged juvenile flew about 13,560 km from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days without landing, eating or drinking.

species:aquila-chrysaetos.placeText: Mountains and open country across North America, Europe, Asia and North Africa
summary: The most widespread large eagle, named for the golden feathers on the back of its head. It hunts hares, marmots, grouse and sometimes young deer, diving at well over 200 km/h. Kazakh and Mongolian eagle hunters still train golden eagles to catch foxes.
It is a national bird of Mexico, Germany, Albania, Kazakhstan and several other countries.

species:aquila-audax.placeText: All of mainland Australia, Tasmania and southern New Guinea
summary: Australia’s largest bird of prey, with a long, diamond-shaped tail and a wingspan that can reach about 2.3 m. It soars for hours over the outback, hunting rabbits, wallabies and lizards and eating roadkill. Pairs sometimes hunt kangaroos together.
It was once shot and poisoned in huge numbers by farmers, but is now protected.

species:harpia-harpyja.placeText: Lowland rainforests from southern Mexico to northern Argentina
summary: One of the most powerful eagles, with a double crest and rear talons up to about 13 cm long, longer than a grizzly bear’s claws. Females, much bigger than males, weigh up to about 9 kg. It hunts sloths and monkeys in the forest canopy, snatching them from branches.
A pair raises one chick every two to three years, so it is hit hard by hunting and forest clearing.

species:pithecophaga-jefferyi.placeText: Rainforests of Mindanao, Luzon, Samar and Leyte, Philippines
summary: One of the largest and rarest eagles, about 1 m long, with a shaggy crest and a huge, arched blue-grey bill. Once called the monkey-eating eagle, it mostly hunts flying lemurs (colugos), civets and other forest animals. It is the national bird of the Philippines.
Only about 400 pairs survive, threatened by logging and hunting; killing one is punished with prison.

species:haliaeetus-pelagicus.placeText: Coasts of the Sea of Okhotsk and Kamchatka; winters south to Hokkaido and Korea
summary: The heaviest eagle in the world, up to about 9 kg, dark brown with white shoulders and tail and an enormous yellow bill. It catches salmon and other big fish; in winter, hundreds gather on the sea ice off Hokkaido.
It is named after the naturalist Georg Steller, who also described Steller’s sea cow.

species:stephanoaetus-coronatus.placeText: Forests of central, eastern and southern Africa
summary: A powerful forest eagle that hunts monkeys and small antelope, killing prey several times its own weight. Damage to the skull of the Taung Child, a 2.8-million-year-old Australopithecus, matches crowned eagle talon marks, suggesting early human relatives were sometimes its prey.

species:polemaetus-bellicosus.placeText: Savannas and open woodland of sub-Saharan Africa
summary: Africa’s largest eagle, with eyesight good enough to spot prey several kilometres away. It hunts guineafowl, hyraxes, monitor lizards and small antelope from a high soar.
Poisoning, power lines and persecution by farmers have caused steep declines, and it was listed as endangered in 2020.

A snake eagle with a bright red face and legs and a tail so short it looks tailless in flight. It spends most of the day gliding low over the savanna, tilting from side to side like a tightrope walker, which gives it its French name. It eats snakes, small mammals and carrion.
It has declined sharply because of poisoned carcasses and was listed as endangered in 2020.

species:circaetus-gallicus.placeText: Southern Europe, North Africa and western and central Asia; winters in the Sahel and India
summary: A large, pale eagle with owl-like yellow eyes that lives almost entirely on snakes, which it catches after hovering and swallows whole, head first. It feeds its chick by letting it pull a snake out of its throat. Thick scales on its legs help protect it from bites.

species:buteo-jamaicensis.placeText: North and Central America and the Caribbean
summary: The commonest large hawk in North America, often seen perched on roadside poles watching for rodents. Its rasping scream is used in films and TV for almost every bird of prey, including bald eagles, whose real calls are thin and twittering.
A red-tailed hawk known as Pale Male nested on a Fifth Avenue apartment building in New York for over 20 years. Buteo has about 30 species, the buzzards and buteo hawks.

species:astur-gentilis.placeText: Forests of Europe, northern Asia and north-western Africa
summary: A powerful forest hawk with short, broad wings and a long tail for twisting between trees at speed to catch pigeons, crows, grouse and squirrels. Females are much larger than males. It has long been flown in falconry.
In 2023 the American goshawk was split off as a separate species, and in 2024 DNA showed goshawks belong in their own genus, Astur, not Accipiter.

species:accipiter-nisus.placeText: Woodland, farmland and towns across Europe and Asia; winters south to Africa and India
summary: A small, fast hawk that ambushes songbirds, often dashing through gardens and along hedges to surprise birds at feeders. Females are almost twice the weight of males and take larger prey, such as pigeons.
Like many birds of prey, it nearly vanished from farmland in the 1960s because of pesticides, and recovered once they were banned.

species:milvus-milvus.placeText: Western and central Europe, especially Germany, France, Spain and Britain
summary: A graceful, reddish raptor with a deeply forked tail that it twists to steer as it drifts over the countryside looking for carrion and small animals. In medieval London kites scavenged in the streets and were protected.

Persecution wiped it out from England and Scotland, leaving a handful of pairs in Wales. Reintroductions from 1989 brought it back, and Britain now has over 6,000 pairs, one of Europe’s greatest bird conservation successes.

species:rostrhamus-sociabilis.placeText: Marshes from Florida and Mexico through Central and South America to Argentina
summary: A kite that eats almost nothing but freshwater apple snails, pulling them from their shells with its slender, deeply hooked bill. It lives in flocks over marshes; the small population in the Florida Everglades is endangered there because of drained wetlands.

species:elanoides-forficatus.placeText: South-eastern USA to Argentina; North American birds winter in South America
summary: A strikingly elegant black-and-white kite with a long, deeply forked tail, which it twists constantly as it swoops over treetops catching flying insects, lizards and frogs, eating them in flight. It even drinks by skimming water like a swallow.
North American birds migrate to South America each winter.

species:elanus-caeruleus.placeText: Africa, southern Iberia and southern Asia
summary: A small, pale grey kite with black shoulders and red eyes that hovers like a kestrel over grassland, dropping onto mice and voles. It has spread through Spain and Portugal and into France in recent decades.

species:circus-aeruginosus.placeText: Reedbeds across Europe and western and central Asia; winters in Africa and South Asia
summary: A long-winged, long-tailed raptor that glides low over reedbeds with its wings raised in a shallow V, dropping onto frogs, small birds and mammals. Like owls, harriers have a ring of stiff feathers round the face that funnels sound to their ears.
In Britain it fell to a single breeding pair in 1971, then recovered to several hundred pairs after pesticides were banned and reedbeds protected.

species:gypaetus-barbatus.placeText: High mountains of southern Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and the Himalayas
summary: Also called the lammergeier, the only animal that lives mainly on bone, which makes up most of its diet. It drops large bones from a height onto rocks to smash them, then swallows the pieces; strong stomach acid dissolves them. Its orange chest comes from rubbing its feathers in iron-rich mud.
It was wiped out in the Alps by about 1913; captive-bred birds released from 1986 now breed there again.

species:neophron-percnopterus.placeText: Southern Europe, Africa, the Middle East and South and Central Asia
summary: A small white vulture with a yellow face, one of the few birds that uses tools: it throws stones at ostrich eggs to crack them open. It also eats carrion, dung and rubbish. It was sacred in ancient Egypt and is the hieroglyph for the letter “a”.
Poisoning, electrocution on power lines and the loss of livestock carcasses have caused steep declines; it is endangered.

species:gyps-rueppelli.placeText: Savannas of the Sahel and East Africa
summary: A large griffon vulture that holds the record for the highest-flying bird: in 1973 one hit an aircraft at about 11,300 m over Côte d’Ivoire. Special haemoglobin in its blood takes up oxygen even in very thin air. Flocks gather in huge numbers at carcasses, following other vultures down.
Its numbers have crashed, mainly because of poisoned carcasses and the trade in vulture parts for traditional medicine.

Once perhaps the most common large bird of prey in the world, with tens of millions in India alone, cleaning up cattle carcasses. In the 1990s and 2000s its numbers fell by more than 99%: vultures were poisoned by diclofenac, a painkiller given to cattle, which causes kidney failure in birds that eat treated carcasses.

Without vultures, rotting carcasses and feral dogs increased, and rabies cases rose. Diclofenac was banned for veterinary use in India, Nepal and Pakistan in 2006, and vultures are being bred in captivity for release.

species:aegypius-monachus.placeText: Mountains and steppes from Spain to Mongolia and China
summary: Also called the Eurasian black vulture, one of the largest flying birds, with a wingspan of up to about 3 m. Its strong bill tears the toughest hide and sinew at carcasses, where other vultures give way to it.
It has recovered in Spain thanks to protection and feeding stations, and has been reintroduced to France.

species:pernis-apivorus.placeText: Forests of Europe and western Asia; winters in tropical Africa
summary: A buzzard-like raptor that specialises in raiding the nests of wasps and bees, digging them out with its feet to eat the larvae and honeycomb. Small, stiff, scale-like feathers on its face protect it from stings.
It migrates to tropical Africa each autumn, with thousands crossing at narrow sea crossings such as Gibraltar and the Bosphorus.

A small falcon that hovers in one spot over roadside verges and fields, head perfectly still, watching for voles. Kestrels can see ultraviolet light, which lets them spot the urine trails voles leave along their runways.

species:falco-rusticolus.placeText: Arctic tundra and coasts around the North Pole
summary: The largest falcon, from almost white to dark grey, which hunts ptarmigan and seabirds across the Arctic. In medieval Europe white gyrfalcons from Greenland and Iceland were the most valuable hunting birds, reserved for kings.

species:caracara-plancus.placeText: Open country from the southern USA to Tierra del Fuego
summary: A long-legged, ground-walking member of the falcon family with a black cap and bare red face, which scavenges carrion and catches small animals on foot. Despite looks, caracaras are true falcons; the crested caracara is the national bird of Mexico in some depictions.

species:phalcoboenus-australis.placeText: Falkland Islands and islands off Tierra del Fuego
summary: A bold, intelligent caracara that lives around seabird and seal colonies on remote islands, scavenging and stealing. Falkland islanders call it the “Johnny rook”. Tests show it is as good at solving puzzles as many parrots and crows.

species:microhierax-caerulescens.placeText: Forest edges of the Himalayan foothills and mainland South-east Asia
summary: One of the smallest birds of prey in the world, about the size of a sparrow, black and white with a chestnut face. It sits on exposed branches and darts out to catch dragonflies, butterflies and small birds.

species:cathartes-aura.placeText: Southern Canada to Tierra del Fuego
summary: A red-headed vulture that soars with wings held in a shallow V, rocking in the wind. Unusually for a bird it has a superb sense of smell and can find a hidden carcass under the forest canopy by the scent of decay; gas companies once used circling vultures to find pipeline leaks.

species:gymnogyps-californianus.placeText: Mountains of California, Arizona, Utah and Baja California
summary: The largest flying land bird in North America, with a wingspan of about 3 m. Lead from bullets in carcasses poisoned it to just 27 birds, and in 1987 the last wild ones were captured for a breeding programme. Released birds have built the population back to over 500, about half flying free.

species:sarcoramphus-papa.placeText: Tropical forests and savannas from southern Mexico to northern Argentina
summary: A white vulture with a startling head of orange, purple, red and yellow bare skin. Its strong bill tears open tough hides that smaller vultures cannot, so they wait for it at carcasses. The Maya portrayed it as a messenger between people and the gods.

species:bubo-virginianus.placeText: Almost all of North America and much of South America
summary: A big, powerful owl with ear tufts and yellow eyes, which takes prey as large as skunks, hares, ospreys and other owls, gripping with a force that needs a lot of strength to open. It nests early, sometimes laying eggs in snow.

species:bubo-bubo.placeText: Mountains, forests and deserts across Europe and Asia
summary: One of the largest owls, with orange eyes and long ear tufts, able to kill foxes, young deer and other birds of prey. Its deep hoot carries several kilometres. Once wiped out from much of western Europe, it has returned to many areas.

species:athene-cunicularia.placeText: Open grassland and deserts of western North America, Florida, Central and South America
summary: A small, long-legged owl that lives in burrows, often ones dug by prairie dogs or tortoises, and is active by day. When threatened in its burrow, young owls make a hiss that sounds like a rattlesnake. Some line their burrows with dung to attract beetles to eat.

species:micrathene-whitneyi.placeText: Deserts of the south-western USA and Mexico
summary: The world’s lightest owl, about 40 g and the size of a sparrow. It nests in old woodpecker holes in giant saguaro cacti and hunts insects and scorpions at night, removing the stings before eating them.

species:strix-nebulosa.placeText: Northern conifer forests of North America and Eurasia
summary: The longest owl, with a huge, round face whose rings of feathers funnel sound to its ears so well that it can hear voles moving under 60 cm of snow and plunge through the snow to catch them. Much of its size is fluffy feathers; it weighs less than a great horned owl.

species:strix-aluco.placeText: Woodland across Europe, North Africa and western Asia
summary: The common owl of European woods and parks, whose calls are the classic “twit-twoo”, actually a female’s sharp “ke-wick” answered by a male’s hoot. Pairs stay in the same territory for life and know every tree in it.

species:ketupa-blakistoni.placeText: River forests of the Russian Far East, north-eastern China and Hokkaido
summary: The largest owl in the world, with a shaggy, ear-tufted head, that wades in icy rivers to catch salmon and trout. It needs old riverside trees big enough to nest in, so it has declined with logging; only a few hundred pairs remain.

species:cygnus-olor.placeText: Europe and central Asia; introduced to North America, South Africa, Japan and Australia
summary: A huge white swan with an orange bill and a black knob, holding its neck in a graceful S-curve. It is not really mute but grunts and hisses, and its wingbeats make a loud throbbing sound. In Britain, unmarked mute swans on open water traditionally belong to the monarch.

An all-black swan with a red bill and white flight feathers that show only when it flies. Europeans believed all swans were white, so “black swan” meant something impossible, until Dutch explorers saw them in Western Australia in 1697. It is the emblem of Western Australia.

species:branta-canadensis.placeText: North America; introduced to Britain, Europe and New Zealand
summary: A large grey-brown goose with a black neck and white chin strap, famous for flying south in noisy V-shaped flocks. Many now live year-round in city parks and on golf courses. Introduced to Britain in the 1600s for the king’s waterfowl collection, it is now common across northern Europe.

A large grey goose with a pink or orange bill, the wild ancestor of most farmyard geese, domesticated in Egypt and Europe thousands of years ago. Konrad Lorenz famously showed that greylag goslings follow and become attached to the first moving thing they see, a process he called imprinting.

species:aix-sponsa.placeText: Wooded swamps and rivers of North America and Cuba
summary: One of the most colourful ducks, the male with a green crest and red eyes. It nests in tree holes, and a day after hatching the ducklings jump from the nest, sometimes 15 m up, to the ground or water below, unharmed. Nest boxes helped it recover from overhunting in the early 1900s.

species:aix-galericulata.placeText: Forested rivers of eastern Asia; introduced to Britain and Europe
summary: The male is one of the most ornate birds in the world, with orange “sails” on his back and orange whiskers. In China, pairs are a symbol of lasting love, given as wedding gifts. Habitat loss has made it rare in China, and escaped birds now form a large wild population in Britain.

species:somateria-mollissima.placeText: Arctic and northern coasts of Europe, Asia and North America
summary: A big sea duck that dives for mussels, swallowing them whole and crushing the shells in its gizzard. Females line their nests with soft down plucked from their breasts; in Iceland and Norway people gently collect this eiderdown from nests to fill duvets.

species:cairina-moschata.placeText: Forested wetlands from Mexico to northern Argentina; domesticated worldwide
summary: A large black duck with white wing patches, wild in tropical American forests, where it nests in tree holes. Native peoples domesticated it long before Europeans arrived; the domestic form, with red, warty facial skin, is now kept worldwide.

species:branta-sandvicensis.placeText: Volcanic slopes and grassland of the Hawaiian islands
summary: The Hawaiian goose, the state bird of Hawaii, descended from Canada geese that reached the islands about 500,000 years ago. It has lost most of the webbing on its feet for walking on lava. Hunting and introduced mongooses cut it to about 30 birds by 1952; captive breeding has brought it back to over 3,000.

species:gallinula-chloropus.placeText: Wetlands across Europe, Asia and Africa
summary: A dark waterbird with a red-and-yellow bill that walks on lily pads with long green toes and jerks its head as it swims. Young from earlier broods often help their parents raise the next one.

species:fulica-atra.placeText: Lakes and ponds across Europe, Asia, North Africa and Australia
summary: A plump black waterbird with a white bill and forehead shield (hence “bald as a coot”). Its toes have scalloped flaps instead of webbing. Coots are aggressive in spring, fighting with their feet, and sometimes kill their own extra chicks.

species:hypotaenidia-owstoni.placeText: Guam (wiped out there) and Cocos Island and Rota, where it has been reintroduced
summary: A flightless rail of the Pacific island of Guam, wiped out in the wild in the 1980s by the brown tree snake, accidentally brought in on cargo after World War II, which ate most of the island’s native birds. The last 21 rails were captured for breeding in 1986.
Released on snake-free Cocos Island, it breeds in the wild again, and in 2019 it became only the second bird ever moved off the “extinct in the wild” list.

species:atlantisia-rogersi.placeText: Inaccessible Island, Tristan da Cunha, South Atlantic
summary: The smallest flightless bird alive, about the size of a chick, which runs mouse-like through tussock grass on one tiny island in the South Atlantic. Its ancestors flew there from South America; with no predators, it lost the power of flight.

species:grus-americana.placeText: Breeds in Wood Buffalo National Park, Canada; winters on the Texas coast
summary: North America’s tallest bird, white with a red crown, named for its loud trumpeting call. By 1941 only about 15 wild birds survived. Protection and captive breeding have raised numbers to over 800; volunteers even taught young cranes a new migration route by leading them with ultralight aircraft.

species:antigone-canadensis.placeText: North America and north-eastern Siberia; winters in the southern USA and Mexico
summary: A tall grey crane with a red cap that dances, leaping and bowing, especially in spring. Each March about half a million gather on the Platte River in Nebraska, one of the great wildlife spectacles. Fossils show sandhill-like cranes have lived in North America for millions of years.

species:balearica-regulorum.placeText: Wetlands and grassland of eastern and southern Africa
summary: A crane with a golden crown of stiff feathers, a bare white face and a red throat pouch, the national bird of Uganda. It is the only crane that roosts in trees. Draining of wetlands and capture for the pet trade have made it endangered.

species:ardea-alba.placeText: Wetlands on every continent except Antarctica
summary: A tall, all-white heron with a yellow bill. In the breeding season it grows long, lacy plumes on its back, which in the late 1800s were in such demand for women’s hats that egrets were shot in huge numbers. Outrage at the slaughter led to the founding of the Audubon Society, and the great egret became its symbol.

species:ardea-herodias.placeText: Wetlands and coasts of North and Central America, the Caribbean and the Galápagos
summary: North America’s largest heron, standing still for long periods in shallow water before stabbing fish, frogs and even gophers with its dagger-like bill. It nests in colonies called heronries high in trees.

species:bubulcus-ibis.placeText: Grassland and farmland worldwide in warm regions
summary: A small, stocky white heron that follows cattle, elephants and tractors to catch the insects they disturb. Originally from Africa and southern Asia, it reached South America on its own around 1877, probably blown across the Atlantic, and has since spread through the Americas and to Australia.

species:nycticorax-nycticorax.placeText: Wetlands on every continent except Australia and Antarctica
summary: A stocky, short-necked heron with red eyes that feeds mainly at dusk and night and roosts in trees by day. It is one of the most widespread herons in the world. Some even use bait, dropping bread or insects on the water to lure fish.

species:botaurus-stellaris.placeText: Reedbeds across Europe and Asia; winters in Africa and southern Asia
summary: A secretive, streaky brown heron that hides in reedbeds, pointing its bill skywards and swaying with the reeds when alarmed. The male’s booming call, like someone blowing over a bottle, can be heard up to 5 km away. It died out in Britain in the 1880s and has since returned.

species:leptoptilos-crumenifer.placeText: Savannas, wetlands and rubbish dumps of sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A huge, bald-headed stork with a pink, dangling throat pouch and one of the largest wingspans of any land bird, up to about 3 m. It eats carrion alongside vultures and scavenges at rubbish dumps and slaughterhouses.

species:jabiru-mycteria.placeText: Wetlands from Mexico to northern Argentina
summary: The tallest flying bird in Central and South America, a white stork with a black head and a bright red band at the base of its neck. It builds huge stick nests in tall trees in the Pantanal and the llanos.

species:eudocimus-ruber.placeText: Mangroves and mudflats of northern South America
summary: A brilliant scarlet ibis that gets its colour from pigments in the crabs and shrimps it eats; young birds are grey-brown. It is the national bird of Trinidad and Tobago, where huge flocks fly in to roost in the Caroni Swamp each evening.

species:platalea-ajaja.placeText: Wetlands from the south-eastern USA to Argentina
summary: A pink wading bird with a flat, spoon-shaped bill that it sweeps from side to side through shallow water, snapping shut on shrimps and fish it touches. Like flamingos, it gets its colour from its food. Plume hunters almost wiped it out in Florida in the 1800s.

species:geronticus-eremita.placeText: Cliffs on the Atlantic coast of Morocco; reintroduced in central Europe
summary: A black ibis with a bald red head and shaggy neck feathers, once common across the Middle East, North Africa and central Europe, where it vanished by the 1600s. The main wild colony now lives near Agadir in Morocco. In Austria and Germany, young birds have been taught to migrate to Italy by following microlight aircraft.

species:phoeniconaias-minor.placeText: Salt lakes of eastern and southern Africa and north-western India
summary: The smallest and most numerous flamingo, with a deep-keeled bill that filters tiny blue-green algae from salty, alkaline lakes, the source of its pink colour. Over a million gather at times on lakes of the East African Rift, and almost all breed at Lake Natron in Tanzania, whose caustic water keeps predators away.

species:larus-argentatus.placeText: Coasts and cities of north-western Europe
summary: The classic grey-backed seaside gull, which now nests on rooftops in many towns and steals chips. Its chicks peck at a red spot on the parent’s bill to make it bring up food, a reflex the scientist Niko Tinbergen studied in famous experiments.

species:rissa-tridactyla.placeText: North Atlantic and North Pacific oceans; nests on sea cliffs
summary: A small, gentle-looking gull of the open ocean, named for its “kitti-waaake” call. It nests on tiny ledges of sheer sea cliffs, gluing nests of mud and seaweed. Kittiwakes have declined steeply where warming seas have reduced the sand eels they feed their chicks.

species:rynchops-niger.placeText: Coasts and rivers of the Americas
summary: A tern-like bird with a unique bill: the lower half is longer than the upper. It flies low over calm water with the lower bill slicing the surface, snapping shut on any fish it touches. Its eyes have cat-like slit pupils to cut glare from water and sand.

A pure white gull with black legs that lives along the edge of the Arctic sea ice all year, scavenging seal carcasses left by polar bears. It nests on remote cliffs and nunataks. Its Canadian population fell by about 70% in 20 years as the ice retreated.

species:scolopax-rusticola.placeText: Damp woodland across Europe and northern Asia
summary: A plump, camouflaged wader of woodland floors that probes for earthworms with its long, flexible-tipped bill. Its eyes are set so far back that it can see all around and above itself. At dusk in spring, males fly “roding” display flights over the treetops.

species:calidris-canutus.placeText: Breeds in the high Arctic; winters on coasts of every continent but Antarctica
summary: A stocky sandpiper with brick-red breeding plumage and one of the longest migrations of any bird, up to 15,000 km each way between the Arctic and southern South America, Africa or Australia. In spring, migrating knots depend on horseshoe crab eggs in Delaware Bay to refuel; overharvesting of crabs caused a steep decline.

species:calidris-pygmaea.placeText: Breeds in Chukotka, Russia; winters on coasts of Bangladesh, Myanmar and South-east Asia
summary: A sparrow-sized sandpiper with a unique spoon-shaped bill tip. It breeds only on coastal tundra in Russia’s far north-east and migrates about 8,000 km to tropical mudflats. Loss of Yellow Sea mudflats and trapping on its wintering grounds cut it to a few hundred pairs; eggs taken for captive rearing have helped it.

species:calidris-pugnax.placeText: Breeds in northern Europe and Siberia; winters in Africa and South Asia
summary: A wader whose breeding males grow huge, colourful neck ruffs and ear tufts and fight in groups called leks to win females. There are three kinds of males: territorial ones, “satellite” males with white ruffs, and rare female-like males that sneak matings.

species:charadrius-vociferus.placeText: North America to north-western South America
summary: A plover with two black breast bands, named for its loud “kill-deer” call. It nests in a simple scrape on gravel, even on flat roofs and car parks. If a predator approaches, the parent pretends to have a broken wing, dragging it along the ground to lure the predator away from the nest.

species:vanellus-vanellus.placeText: Farmland and wet grassland across Europe and Asia
summary: A black-and-white plover with a long wispy crest and green-glossed back, named for its floppy, lapping wingbeats. Its tumbling spring display flights come with a call that gave it the name “peewit”. Changes in farming have caused big declines.

species:haematopus-ostralegus.placeText: Coasts and inland waters of Europe and Asia; winters on coasts south to Africa and India
summary: A noisy, pied wader with a long orange bill and pink legs. Despite its name it rarely eats oysters, but opens mussels and cockles: some birds hammer through the shell, others stab between the two halves to cut the muscle, a technique young birds learn from their parents.

species:recurvirostra-avosetta.placeText: Coastal lagoons and salt lakes of Europe, Africa and Asia
summary: An elegant black-and-white wader with a long, thin, upturned bill that it sweeps from side to side through shallow water to catch small creatures. It returned to breed in Britain in 1947, after a 100-year absence, and became the symbol of the RSPB.

species:phoebastria-immutabilis.placeText: The North Pacific; nests mainly on the north-western Hawaiian Islands
summary: A white-and-dark-grey albatross that ranges across the whole North Pacific. One female, Wisdom, ringed on Midway Atoll in 1956, is the oldest known wild bird and was still laying eggs in her 70s. Chicks often die after their parents feed them floating plastic by mistake.

species:thalassarche-melanophris.placeText: The Southern Ocean; nests mainly on the Falklands, South Georgia and southern Chile
summary: The most widespread albatross, named for the dark eyebrow stripe that gives it a frowning look. Most nest on the Falkland Islands. Many were drowned on longline fishing hooks, but bird-scaring lines on fishing boats have greatly reduced deaths.

species:fulmarus-glacialis.placeText: The North Atlantic and North Pacific oceans
summary: A gull-like seabird of the petrel family with stiff, straight wings and tube-shaped nostrils that help it smell food at sea. When threatened at the nest, it spits a foul-smelling oil that can mat the feathers of attacking birds. Fulmars have spread enormously around Britain in the last 200 years.

species:uria-aalge.placeText: The North Atlantic and North Pacific; nests on sea cliffs
summary: Also called the common guillemot, a penguin-like auk that dives to over 100 m for fish. It nests packed tightly on narrow cliff ledges without any nest; its pear-shaped egg helps stop it rolling off. Chicks jump from the cliffs into the sea before they can fly, and are raised at sea by their fathers.

species:alca-torda.placeText: The North Atlantic; nests on sea cliffs
summary: A black-and-white auk with a deep, blunt, white-striped bill. It is the closest living relative of the great auk, hunted to extinction in 1844. Razorbills can dive to over 100 m, using their wings to “fly” underwater.

species:pelecanus-occidentalis.placeText: Coasts of the Americas from the USA to Chile and Brazil
summary: The only pelican that dives for food, plunging head-first from up to 20 m into the sea and scooping fish into its throat pouch. DDT poisoning wiped it out from Louisiana, the “Pelican State”, by the 1960s; it recovered after DDT was banned.

species:pelecanus-crispus.placeText: Lakes and deltas from south-eastern Europe to Mongolia
summary: One of the heaviest flying birds, up to about 13 kg, with curly feathers on its nape. Drainage of wetlands and persecution made it rare; Lake Prespa in Greece holds the largest colony in the world.

species:morus-bassanus.placeText: The North Atlantic; nests on islands and sea cliffs
summary: The largest seabird of the North Atlantic, white with black wingtips and a yellow head, which dives into the sea from up to 30 m at about 100 km/h, folding its wings at the last moment. Air sacs under its skin cushion the impact. Bass Rock in Scotland, which gave it its scientific name, holds the largest colony in the world.

species:nannopterum-harrisi.placeText: Coasts of Fernandina and Isabela, Galápagos Islands
summary: The only cormorant that cannot fly, with tiny, ragged wings about a third of the length needed. With no land predators and rich feeding close to shore, its ancestors stopped flying; its strong legs make it a powerful diver. Fewer than about 2,000 survive.

species:meleagris-gallopavo.placeText: Forests and clearings of the USA, southern Canada and Mexico
summary: The ancestor of the farmyard turkey, domesticated in Mexico about 2,000 years ago. Wild turkeys are fast fliers over short distances and can run at about 40 km/h. Overhunting almost wiped them out by 1900; reintroductions brought them back to every mainland US state.
Benjamin Franklin praised the turkey as “a much more respectable bird” than the bald eagle.

species:pavo-cristatus.placeText: India and Sri Lanka; kept worldwide
summary: The male, the peacock, raises a fan of up to 200 long, eyed train feathers and shivers them to make them shimmer, a display that troubled Charles Darwin until he realised it was shaped by females choosing mates. It is the national bird of India.

species:phasianus-colchicus.placeText: Native to Asia; introduced across Europe, North America, New Zealand and elsewhere
summary: A long-tailed gamebird, the male with a green head, red face wattles and coppery body. Native to Asia from the Caucasus to Korea, it was brought to Europe perhaps by the Romans and is now one of the most widely introduced birds in the world. Tens of millions are reared and released each year for shooting.

species:lophophorus-impejanus.placeText: High forests and meadows of the Himalayas
summary: A big pheasant whose male glitters in iridescent green, purple, copper and blue, the national bird of Nepal. It digs for roots and insects with its strong bill, even through snow, at up to about 4,500 m.

species:lagopus-muta.placeText: Arctic tundra and high mountains of North America, Europe and Asia
summary: A grouse that turns white in winter and mottled grey-brown in summer to match the snow and rocks. Its feet are covered in feathers like snowshoes, and it burrows into snow to sleep. It is the official bird of Nunavut and the Japanese prefectures of Nagano, Toyama and Gifu.

species:tetrao-urogallus.placeText: Old conifer forests of northern Europe and Siberia, and mountains of central Europe
summary: The largest grouse, the male turkey-sized and black with a fanned tail, which displays at dawn on traditional leks with clicks, pops and a sound like a cork being drawn. In winter it eats almost nothing but pine needles. It died out in Scotland in the 1700s and was reintroduced in 1837, but is again in steep decline.

species:centrocercus-urophasianus.placeText: Sagebrush plains of the western USA and Canada
summary: A large grouse that lives only where sagebrush grows. In spring, males gather on leks before dawn, puffing up white chests, fanning spiky tails and inflating two yellow air sacs that pop like bubbles. It has lost about half its former range to farms, roads and energy development.

species:perdix-perdix.placeText: Farmland and steppe across Europe and western Asia; introduced to North America
summary: A plump, round-bodied partridge with an orange face and a dark horseshoe on its belly that lives in coveys on farmland. It has fallen by over 90% in Britain since the 1950s, as herbicides removed the weeds and insects its chicks need.

species:argusianus-argus.placeText: Lowland rainforest of the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo
summary: A large pheasant whose male has enormously long wing feathers covered in rows of golden “eyes”. On a carefully cleared patch of forest floor, he spreads them into a huge fan around his head to court a female. Darwin used it as an example of sexual selection.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Males up to about 2 m with tail

species:callipepla-californica.placeText: Western USA and Baja California; introduced to Chile, Hawaii and New Zealand
summary: A plump, scaly-bellied quail with a forward-curling black topknot, the state bird of California. Coveys of dozens feed on the ground and run rather than fly, and a sentry keeps watch from a high perch.

species:numida-meleagris.placeText: Savannas and farmland of sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A noisy, polka-dotted gamebird with a bare blue-and-red head topped by a bony casque. Flocks roost in trees and patrol the ground for seeds and insects, including ticks. It was domesticated in Africa and kept by the ancient Greeks and Romans.

species:crax-rubra.placeText: Lowland forests from southern Mexico to western Ecuador
summary: A turkey-sized forest bird; the male is black with a curly crest and a yellow knob on his bill, the female barred brown. It forages on the forest floor for fallen fruit and roosts high in trees. Hunting has made it scarce wherever people live.

species:alectura-lathami.placeText: Rainforests, woodland and suburbs of eastern Australia
summary: A black, red-headed bird whose male rakes together a mound of leaf litter up to 4 m wide, where the rotting leaves incubate the eggs. He tests the heat with his bill and adds or removes litter to keep it at about 33 °C. The chicks dig themselves out and can fly within hours, never meeting their parents.

species:macrocephalon-maleo.placeText: Forests and beaches of Sulawesi, Indonesia
summary: A megapode that buries its huge eggs, five times the size of a hen’s, in sun-warmed beach sand or soil heated by volcanic springs, and leaves them. The chicks hatch fully feathered and able to fly. Egg harvesting has made it endangered.

species:goura-victoria.placeText: Lowland forests of northern New Guinea
summary: One of the largest pigeons, nearly the size of a turkey, blue-grey with a crest of lacy, white-tipped feathers and a deep, booming call. It walks the forest floor eating fallen fruit and seeds. It is hunted for food and its feathers.

species:caloenas-nicobarica.placeText: Small islands from the Nicobar Islands to the Solomon Islands
summary: A pigeon with long, metallic green and copper neck hackles that flies between small islands in flocks. DNA shows it is the closest living relative of the extinct dodo and Rodrigues solitaire, giant flightless pigeons of the Mascarene Islands.

species:zenaida-macroura.placeText: North America, the Caribbean and Central America
summary: A slim, long-tailed dove named for its soft, mournful cooing, and one of the most abundant birds in North America, with perhaps 350 million. Its wings make a sharp whistle on take-off. It is the closest relative of the extinct passenger pigeon among birds still common in North America.

species:didunculus-strigirostris.placeText: Rainforests of Upolu and Savai’i, Samoa
summary: A dark pigeon with a heavy, hooked red bill that has tooth-like notches, used to saw through tough fruit. Its scientific name means “little dodo”. Hunting, forest loss and introduced rats have cut it to perhaps a few hundred birds or fewer; it is the national bird of Samoa.

species:streptopelia-decaocto.placeText: Europe and Asia; spread through North America since the 1980s
summary: A pale dove with a black half-collar that made one of the fastest bird invasions ever recorded. From Turkey and the Balkans it spread across all of Europe in the 20th century, reaching Britain in 1955. Released in the Bahamas in the 1970s, it reached Florida and now lives across most of North America.

species:nestor-notabilis.placeText: Mountains of the South Island of New Zealand
summary: The world’s only alpine parrot, olive-green with orange under its wings, famously curious, playful and destructive: it pulls rubber from cars and opens bags at ski fields. Kea solve puzzles as well as great apes in some tests, and have a call that makes other kea play.
Farmers once paid bounties for them, accusing them of attacking sheep; about 150,000 were killed before they were protected in 1986.

species:psittacula-krameri.placeText: Savannas of Africa and South Asia; feral in cities across Europe and the Middle East
summary: A bright green, long-tailed parakeet with a red bill. Escaped pets have built wild populations in dozens of countries; London alone has tens of thousands, roosting in parks. It is now one of the most widespread introduced parrots in the world.

species:trichoglossus-moluccanus.placeText: Eastern and northern Australia; introduced to Perth and New Zealand
summary: A screeching, rainbow-coloured parrot with a brush-tipped tongue for lapping nectar and pollen from eucalyptus and garden flowers. Huge flocks roost in city trees. In Perth, where it was introduced, it competes with native birds for nest holes.

species:anodorhynchus-hyacinthinus.placeText: Palm savannas of central Brazil, eastern Bolivia and Paraguay
summary: The largest flying parrot, about 1 m long, cobalt blue with yellow skin around its eyes and bill. Its huge bill cracks the hard nuts of palms; in the Pantanal it also eats nuts that have passed undigested through cattle. Trapping for the pet trade made it endangered, but numbers have recovered with protection.

species:cyanopsitta-spixii.placeText: Caatinga dry forest along the Rio São Francisco near Curaçá, Bahia, Brazil
summary: A small, blue macaw, the star of the film Rio, that lived only in creek-side woodland in north-eastern Brazil. Trapping for collectors and habitat loss left a single wild male, which disappeared in 2000, and the species was declared extinct in the wild.
Captive breeding, mostly in Germany, built up a population, and in 2022 the first birds were released back into the wild in Bahia.

facts.label: IUCN status
facts.value: Extinct in the wild (reintroduction under way)

species:myiopsitta-monachus.placeText: Southern South America; feral in cities of North America and Europe
summary: The only parrot that builds its own nest, a huge communal stick structure in trees or on power pylons, with separate rooms for each pair. Escaped pets have founded colonies from Chicago to Barcelona and Madrid.

species:conuropsis-carolinensis.placeText: Forests and riversides of the eastern USA (extinct)
summary: The only parrot native to the eastern USA, green with a yellow-and-orange head, which lived in noisy flocks as far north as the Great Lakes. Farmers shot them as crop pests, collectors took them, and their forests were cleared. Flocks stayed beside wounded birds, so hunters could kill whole flocks.
The last known Carolina parakeet, a male named Incas, died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1918, in the same cage where Martha, the last passenger pigeon, had died four years earlier.

A pink-and-grey cockatoo that lives in big, noisy flocks and has spread across Australia as farms and water troughs opened up the land. In Australian slang, a “galah” is a loudmouthed fool, after its clownish behaviour, such as hanging upside down from power lines in the rain.

species:probosciger-aterrimus.placeText: Rainforests of New Guinea and Cape York, Australia
summary: A large black cockatoo with a huge bill and red cheeks that flush when excited. Males are the only animals other than humans known to make tools for keeping a musical beat: they shape a stick or seed pod and drum it against a hollow tree, each with his own rhythm.

species:archilochus-colubris.placeText: Eastern North America; winters in Central America
summary: The only hummingbird that breeds in eastern North America, the male with a glittering red throat. Weighing about 3 g, many fly non-stop across the Gulf of Mexico, about 800 km, on each migration, nearly doubling their weight in fat beforehand.

species:ensifera-ensifera.placeText: Andean cloud forests from Venezuela to Bolivia
summary: The only bird with a bill longer than the rest of its body. It feeds from long-tubed flowers that other birds cannot reach, such as passionflowers and daturas, and preens with its feet. When perched, it holds its bill pointing up to balance.

species:patagona-gigas.placeText: The Andes from Ecuador to central Chile and Argentina
summary: The largest hummingbird, about the length of a starling and around 20 g, with slow, swift-like wingbeats. In 2024 tracking showed there are two species: a southern one that migrates along the coast and up into the Andes, and a northern, resident one, named Patagona chaski.

species:calypte-anna.placeText: Pacific coast of North America, from British Columbia to Baja California
summary: A hummingbird with a rose-pink throat and crown that has spread north thanks to garden flowers and feeders, now wintering as far as Canada. Males dive from up to 40 m in courtship, pulling out of the dive at over 20 body lengths a second, one of the fastest movements relative to size of any animal; their tail feathers make a loud chirp.

species:chaetura-pelagica.placeText: Eastern North America; winters in the Amazon basin
