summary: A cigar-shaped swift that spends almost all its time in the air, catching insects. It once nested in hollow trees but now mostly uses chimneys, and thousands gather to swirl down into big chimneys at dusk before migrating. Its numbers have fallen as old chimneys are capped.

species:caprimulgus-europaeus.placeText: Heaths and open woods of Europe and western Asia; winters in Africa
summary: A camouflaged, owl-like bird that spends the day motionless on the ground or along a branch, looking like bark. At dusk the male makes a long, mechanical churring song and flies after moths with its huge, bristle-fringed mouth. Its old name “goatsucker” comes from the false belief that it drank milk from goats.

species:phalaenoptilus-nuttallii.placeText: Dry country of western North America and Mexico
summary: A small nightjar named for its “poor-will” call, and the only bird known to hibernate. In winter it can fall into torpor for weeks, its body temperature dropping to about 5 °C. The Hopi people called it hölchko, “the sleeping one”, long before scientists confirmed it in 1946.

species:steatornis-caripensis.placeText: Caves and forests of northern South America and Trinidad
summary: A nightjar relative that roosts and nests in dark caves and flies out at night to eat oily palm fruit. It is one of the few birds that uses echolocation, clicking to find its way in the darkness of caves. Its chicks get so fat that people once boiled them down for oil.

species:podargus-strigoides.placeText: Woodland, scrub and suburbs across Australia
summary: A big-headed, owl-like bird with a wide, frog-like mouth. By day it perches stiffly with its bill pointed up and eyes slitted, looking exactly like a broken branch. At night it drops onto insects, frogs and mice. It is often mistaken for an owl but is related to nightjars.

species:dryocopus-martius.placeText: Mature forests across Europe and northern Asia
summary: A crow-sized woodpecker, black with a red crown, whose large, oval nest holes are later used by owls, ducks, bats and pine martens, making it a key species in old forests. Its loud drumming carries a long way through the forest.

species:melanerpes-formicivorus.placeText: Oak woodland from Oregon to Colombia
summary: A clown-faced woodpecker that lives in family groups and stores acorns in holes it drills in a “granary” tree, sometimes tens of thousands in one tree, each acorn in its own hole. The group defends the granary together and shares breeding.

species:colaptes-auratus.placeText: Woodland and parks across North America to Central America and Cuba
summary: A large, brown, spotted woodpecker that often feeds on the ground, licking up ants with a long, barbed tongue. Eastern birds flash yellow under their wings and western birds red. It sometimes drums on metal chimneys and street lights to make more noise.

species:jynx-torquilla.placeText: Open woodland of Europe and Asia; winters in Africa and South Asia
summary: A cryptic, bark-patterned member of the woodpecker family that does not drill holes but uses existing ones. When threatened in its nest it twists its neck like a snake and hisses, which gave it its name and made it a bird of witchcraft in ancient Greece.

species:ramphastos-sulfuratus.placeText: Tropical forests from southern Mexico to northern Colombia and Venezuela
summary: A toucan with a huge, rainbow-coloured bill in green, orange, red and blue, the national bird of Belize. The bill is light, made of a honeycomb of bone and keratin, and works as a radiator to shed body heat. Flocks of about six travel through the canopy eating fruit.

species:bucorvus-leadbeateri.placeText: Savannas of eastern and southern Africa
summary: A turkey-sized black hornbill with red face and throat skin that walks the savanna in family groups, hunting snakes, tortoises and hares. Its deep, booming calls carry for kilometres. Groups breed only every few years, and only the dominant pair breeds, helped by the others.

species:rhinoplax-vigil.placeText: Lowland rainforests of the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo
summary: A huge hornbill with a solid, ivory-like casque on its bill, which it uses in mid-air head-butting contests. Its loud, hooting call ends in maniacal laughter. Poaching for its casque, carved as “hornbill ivory” and smuggled to China, made it critically endangered.

species:dacelo-novaeguineae.placeText: Eucalyptus woodland of eastern Australia; introduced to the south-west and Tasmania
summary: A giant kingfisher whose loud, laughing chorus at dawn and dusk is one of Australia’s most famous sounds, used in countless jungle films. It rarely eats fish, instead pouncing on lizards, snakes, insects and mice.

species:megaceryle-alcyon.placeText: Rivers and lakes across North America; winters south to northern South America
summary: A shaggy-crested, blue-grey kingfisher with a rattling call that hovers and dives for fish. Unusually among birds, the female is more colourful than the male, with an extra chestnut belly band. Pairs dig nest tunnels up to 2 m long in riverbanks.

species:geococcyx-californianus.placeText: Deserts and scrub of the south-western USA and Mexico
summary: A long-legged ground cuckoo that runs at up to about 30 km/h and kills rattlesnakes, lizards and scorpions, bashing them on rocks. On cold mornings it warms up by exposing a patch of black skin on its back to the sun. It is far less of a clown than its cartoon namesake.

species:ardeotis-kori.placeText: Grassland and savanna of eastern and southern Africa
summary: Perhaps the heaviest bird that can fly, with large males weighing around 13 kg or more. It walks slowly across the savanna eating insects, lizards and seeds, and often has a carmine bee-eater riding on its back to catch insects it disturbs. In courtship, males puff out their white neck feathers like a balloon.

species:coracias-caudatus.placeText: Open woodland and savanna of eastern and southern Africa
summary: A dazzling savanna bird with a lilac breast, turquoise belly and long tail streamers, often seen perched on a dead branch watching for insects and lizards. In courtship, males climb high and then dive, rolling and tumbling, which gave rollers their name.

species:merops-apiaster.placeText: Southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia; winters in Africa
summary: A rainbow-coloured bird that catches bees, wasps and dragonflies in flight, then bashes them on a branch and rubs off the sting before swallowing. Colonies dig nest tunnels in sandy riverbanks. It has spread north with warming summers and now nests occasionally in Britain.

species:pharomachrus-mocinno.placeText: Cloud forests from southern Mexico to western Panama
summary: A shimmering green and crimson trogon whose male grows twin tail streamers up to about 1 m long. Sacred to the Maya and Aztecs, its feathers were worn only by rulers and priests. It is the national bird of Guatemala, whose currency is the quetzal.

A green turaco with a red crest that flashes crimson wings in flight. Turacos are the only birds with true green pigment (turacoverdin) and a red copper-based pigment (turacin); most other green birds are green because of the way light scatters in their feathers. It is the national bird of Angola.

species:opisthocomus-hoazin.placeText: Swamps, oxbow lakes and riverside forests of the Amazon and Orinoco basins
summary: A pheasant-sized bird with a spiky crest and blue face that eats only leaves, which it ferments in a huge crop, like a cow’s rumen, giving it a manure-like smell (it is nicknamed the “stinkbird”). Chicks have two claws on each wing for climbing back up to the nest after dropping into the water to escape predators.

species:pterocles-namaqua.placeText: Deserts and dry grassland of south-western Africa
summary: A pigeon-like desert bird that nests far from water. Males fly to a waterhole, soak their specially structured belly feathers, which hold water like a sponge, and fly back up to 30 km so their chicks can drink from them.

A pale grey, almost flightless bird with a shaggy crest and red-orange bill and legs, found only on New Caledonia. It hunts worms and snails on the forest floor, and has unique nasal flaps that keep soil out of its nostrils. Its barking calls at dawn sound like a dog. Introduced dogs, rats and pigs made it endangered.

species:indicator-indicator.placeText: Savannas and woodland of sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A small bird that eats beeswax and leads people to wild bees’ nests with a chattering call, flying from tree to tree. Honey-hunters such as the Hadza and Yao answer with special calls; when they open the nest, the bird eats the leftover wax. It is one of the few known cooperative partnerships between humans and a wild animal.
Like a cuckoo, it lays its eggs in other birds’ nests, and the chick kills its foster siblings with a hooked bill tip.

A loud, bold flycatcher with a yellow belly and black-and-white striped head, named for its “kis-ka-dee” call. Unlike most flycatchers it eats almost anything, catching fish like a kingfisher and stealing food from other birds.

species:tyrannus-tyrannus.placeText: Breeds across North America; winters in the Amazon
summary: A black-and-white flycatcher that fearlessly attacks hawks, crows and herons that come near its nest, sometimes riding on their backs, which gave kingbirds their scientific name, “tyrant”. In winter it switches from insects to fruit in Amazon forests.

The male is a brilliant scarlet with a dark mask and wings, glowing like a coal as he sings in a fluttering display flight. Several similar species are now recognised across South America and the Galápagos, where one, on San Cristóbal, went extinct in the 1980s.

species:furnarius-rufus.placeText: Open country of southern Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina
summary: A plain, rufous bird that builds a hard, round nest of mud and dung on posts and branches, with a curved inner wall, looking like an old clay bread oven (horno in Spanish). Pairs may take weeks to build one. It is the national bird of Argentina.

species:gymnopithys-leucaspis.placeText: Rainforests from Honduras to the western Amazon
summary: A chestnut-and-white antbird that makes its living following swarms of army ants across the forest floor, catching the insects and spiders that flee from them. It does not eat the ants themselves. Many other birds join the swarms too.

species:machaeropterus-deliciosus.placeText: Cloud forests on the western slope of the Andes in Colombia and Ecuador
summary: A tiny manakin whose male “sings” with his wings: he raises them over his back and shakes them more than 100 times a second, so a ridged feather rubs against a club-shaped one like a violin, making a ringing tone. His wing bones are solid and enlarged to make this possible.

species:rupicola-peruvianus.placeText: Cloud forest ravines of the Andes from Venezuela to Bolivia
summary: The male has a brilliant orange or red disc-shaped crest that hides his bill. Males gather at leks, bowing, jumping and squawking to impress females, who build mud nests on rock faces in ravines. It is the national bird of Peru.

species:procnias-albus.placeText: Mountain forests of the Guiana Shield, Venezuela and northern Brazil
summary: A pure white cotinga with a long, fleshy wattle hanging from its bill. In 2019 its call was measured at about 125 decibels, the loudest bird call ever recorded, louder than a rock concert. Males turn and blast the final note straight at females sitting nearby.

species:setophaga-petechia.placeText: North America to northern South America and the Caribbean
summary: A bright yellow warbler of willow thickets, the male streaked red on the breast, with a sweet “sweet-sweet-I’m-so-sweet” song. When a cowbird lays an egg in its nest, it often builds a new nest floor over the eggs and starts again.

species:setophaga-kirtlandii.placeText: Young jack pine forests of Michigan, Wisconsin and Ontario; winters in the Bahamas
summary: A grey-and-yellow warbler that nests only on the ground under young jack pines that grow after fires. With fire suppression and cowbird nest parasitism, it fell to about 200 singing males in 1974 and 1987. Planting jack pine and trapping cowbirds raised it to over 2,000 pairs, and it was removed from the US endangered list in 2019.

species:setophaga-striata.placeText: Breeds in the northern forests of Alaska and Canada; winters in the Amazon
summary: A tiny warbler weighing about 12 g that makes one of the most extreme migrations of any songbird: each autumn it flies non-stop from north-eastern North America over the Atlantic to the Caribbean or South America, up to about 2,500 km in two to three days, after doubling its weight in fat.

species:agelaius-phoeniceus.placeText: Marshes and fields across North America and Central America
summary: One of the most abundant birds in North America. Males sing a gurgling “konk-la-ree” from cattails, flashing red-and-yellow shoulder patches to defend territories where several females nest. In winter, flocks of millions roost together.

species:icterus-galbula.placeText: Breeds in eastern North America; winters from Mexico to northern South America
summary: A flame-orange and black songbird named after the coat of arms of Lord Baltimore, whose colours matched its feathers; the Baltimore baseball team is named after it. It weaves a hanging, sock-like nest of plant fibres at the tip of a high branch.

A small blackbird that never builds a nest or raises its own young: females lay eggs in the nests of over 200 other species, which raise the cowbird chicks. Originally it followed bison herds across the plains, eating insects they stirred up; forest clearing let it spread east, where it harms rare songbirds.

species:psarocolius-montezuma.placeText: Lowland forests from southern Mexico to central Panama
summary: A large, chestnut blackbird with a bright orange-tipped bill and blue cheeks. Colonies weave up to dozens of long, hanging basket nests, up to about 1.8 m long, from a single isolated tree. The male’s display song ends in a loud, liquid gurgle as he bows forward until he almost falls off the branch.

species:melospiza-melodia.placeText: Most of North America and Mexico
summary: A streaky brown sparrow with one of the most varied songs of any bird: each male has a repertoire of about 8 to 10 song types, and neighbours share and match each other’s songs. Its local forms differ so much that it is a classic example of geographic variation within a species.

species:junco-hyemalis.placeText: Forests across North America; winters across the USA and northern Mexico
summary: A small grey sparrow with a pale bill and white outer tail feathers that it flashes in flight, often called the “snowbird” because it arrives at feeders with winter. Its regional forms look so different that they were once thought to be separate species, and they have become a model for studying how new species form.

species:vireo-olivaceus.placeText: Breeds in eastern North America; winters in the Amazon
summary: A small, olive-green songbird with a red eye that sings short phrases over and over from the treetops all day long. One male was recorded singing more than 22,000 songs in a single day.

species:passerina-ciris.placeText: South-central and south-eastern USA; winters in Mexico, Central America and Cuba
summary: Possibly the most colourful bird in North America: the male has a blue head, red underparts and a lime-green back. It is shy and often hidden in thickets. In Cuba and Mexico it has long been trapped as a cage bird.

A dazzling tanager with an apple-green head, turquoise and violet underparts and a red-and-yellow rump. Small flocks travel through the forest canopy with other birds, eating fruit and insects. Tangara is the largest bird genus in the Americas’ tanager family, with about 50 species.

species:coereba-flaveola.placeText: The Caribbean, southern Mexico and Central America to northern Argentina
summary: A small, yellow-breasted bird with a curved bill that pierces flowers at the base to steal nectar without pollinating them. It is one of the most common birds of the Caribbean and comes readily to sugar bowls on café tables.

One of Darwin’s finches, which lacks a woodpecker’s long tongue, so it uses a cactus spine or twig as a tool to prise insect larvae out of holes in wood, sometimes trimming the tool to the right length. It is one of the few tool-using birds.

species:sialia-sialis.placeText: Open country of eastern North America to Nicaragua
summary: A small thrush, the male bright blue above with a rusty breast, that nests in tree holes. Competition for nest holes with introduced starlings and house sparrows caused a steep decline, reversed by a huge volunteer effort to put up bluebird nest boxes along “bluebird trails”.

species:cyanocitta-cristata.placeText: Forests and towns of eastern and central North America
summary: A noisy, crested blue-and-white jay that buries thousands of acorns each autumn and is thought to have helped oak forests spread north after the Ice Age. It mimics the calls of red-shouldered and red-tailed hawks, perhaps to scare other birds away from food.

species:corvus-moneduloides.placeText: Forests of Grande Terre and Maré, New Caledonia
summary: Perhaps the most skilled tool-maker of any animal besides humans. It cuts and shapes hooked tools from twigs and stepped tools from the barbed edges of pandanus leaves to fish insect larvae out of holes, and in tests it has bent wire into hooks and combined short sticks into longer tools.

species:nucifraga-columbiana.placeText: High conifer forests of the mountains of western North America
summary: A grey-and-black crow of high mountains that buries up to about 30,000 pine seeds each autumn in thousands of separate caches, and remembers where most of them are for up to nine months, even under snow. Forgotten seeds grow into new whitebark pines, which depend on it to spread.

species:drepanis-coccinea.placeText: High mountain forests of Hawaii, Maui and Kauaʻi
summary: A scarlet Hawaiian honeycreeper with a long, sickle-shaped salmon-pink bill for sipping nectar from native lobelias and ʻōhiʻa blossoms. Hawaiian chiefs wore capes made of its feathers. Mosquitoes carrying avian malaria have confined it to high forests, and warming climates are letting them climb higher.
Hawaiian honeycreepers all evolved from one finch that reached the islands about 5 million years ago.

A small finch whose male turns bright yellow with a black cap in summer and dull olive in winter. It nests late in summer, when thistles and other plants have gone to seed, and feeds its chicks almost entirely on seeds. Its flight is a bouncing roller-coaster.

species:prosthemadera-novaeseelandiae.placeText: Forests and gardens throughout New Zealand
summary: A glossy, blue-black honeyeater with a tuft of white feathers at its throat. It has two voice boxes and can sing two notes at once, mixing bell-like notes, clicks, wheezes and sounds too high for people to hear. Tūī can also mimic other birds, telephones and speech.

species:manorina-melanocephala.placeText: Open woodland, parks and suburbs of eastern Australia
summary: A grey honeyeater with a yellow eye patch that lives in large, aggressive colonies which drive almost all other small birds out of their territory. It thrives in the open woodland created by land clearing and suburbs, and is now a serious threat to many other woodland birds.

A striking black-and-yellow honeyeater that wanders long distances following flowering eucalypts. Fewer than about 300 survive. In 2021 scientists found that young males, with too few adults to learn from, were singing the songs of other species instead of their own, and are now teaching them with recordings.

A tiny bird with a cocked tail; breeding males are electric blue and black. Family groups help raise each brood. Females sing a “password” to their eggs, and chicks include it in their begging calls, letting parents spot a cuckoo chick that has not learned it.

species:cicinnurus-respublica.placeText: Hill forests of Waigeo and Batanta, West Papua, Indonesia
summary: A tiny bird-of-paradise whose male has a bare, bright blue crown crossed by black lines, a red back, yellow cape and two curled violet tail wires. He clears a patch of forest floor of leaves and displays there to females. It lives only on two small islands.

species:pteridophora-alberti.placeText: Mountain forests of central New Guinea
summary: A small, black and yellow bird-of-paradise whose male has two head plumes about 40 cm long, twice his body length, decorated with sky-blue, enamel-like flags. During display he bounces on a branch and waves them. Local people use the plumes in headdresses.

species:amblyornis-inornata.placeText: Mountain forests of the Bird’s Head Peninsula, West Papua
summary: A plain brown bird that builds the most elaborate structure of any bird: a hut of sticks up to about 1.5 m wide and 1 m tall around a central pole, with a moss lawn in front decorated with neat piles of flowers, berries, beetle wings and shells, sorted by colour. Each male’s style differs, like a local culture.

species:callaeas-wilsoni.placeText: Forests of the North Island of New Zealand
summary: A blue-grey bird with a black mask and blue wattles at the base of its bill that bounds through branches and glides between trees, rarely flying far. Its haunting, organ-like song is sung as a duet. Predator control has raised it from about 400 pairs in 1999 to over 2,000.

species:heteralocha-acutirostris.placeText: Mountain forests of the southern North Island of New Zealand (extinct)
summary: A glossy black wattlebird with orange wattles and white-tipped tail feathers, famous because male and female had completely different bills: the male’s short and strong for chiselling rotten wood, the female’s long and curved for probing for grubs. Its tail feathers were treasured by Māori chiefs.
Forest clearing, introduced predators and a craze for its feathers, especially after the Duke of York wore one in 1901, drove it to extinction. The last confirmed sighting was in 1907.

New Zealand’s smallest bird, about 6 g, green and almost tailless, that spirals up tree trunks picking insects from the bark. The New Zealand wrens are the oldest surviving branch of the passerines, the order that includes more than half of all birds.

A black-and-yellow nectar-feeding bird of Kauaʻi, the last survivor of the Hawaiian ʻōʻō family. A recording from the 1980s captures the last known male singing his half of a duet to a female that never answered.
Avian malaria spread by introduced mosquitoes, rats and pigs, and hurricanes in 1982 wiped it out; the last one was heard in 1987.

species:gymnorhina-tibicen.placeText: Open country across Australia and southern New Guinea; introduced to New Zealand
summary: A black-and-white bird with one of the most beautiful songs in Australia, a complex, flute-like warbling carol. It is not related to European magpies. In spring some males swoop at people walking or cycling near their nests, and recognise and remember individual faces.

species:rhipidura-leucophrys.placeText: Open country throughout Australia, New Guinea and the Solomon Islands
summary: A bold black-and-white fantail that wags its tail from side to side as it hunts insects on lawns and in fields, and sings through moonlit nights. Despite its small size it chases off eagles, snakes and even dogs that come near its nest. It is not related to true wagtails.

species:parus-major.placeText: Woodland, gardens and parks across Europe and Asia
summary: A boldly marked yellow-and-black tit with a huge range of calls; its “teacher-teacher” song is a sign of spring. Great tits have been studied at Wytham Woods near Oxford since 1947, and were found to be nesting earlier as springs warm. Some have learned to kill and eat roosting bats.

species:cyanistes-caeruleus.placeText: Woodland and gardens of Europe, western Asia and North Africa
summary: A small blue, yellow and white tit and one of the most familiar garden birds in Europe. In 1920s Britain blue tits learned to peck through the foil tops of milk bottles left on doorsteps to drink the cream, and the habit spread rapidly from bird to bird, a famous example of animal culture.

species:poecile-atricapillus.placeText: Forests and towns across northern North America
summary: A tiny, black-capped bird named for its “chick-a-dee-dee-dee” call; the more “dees”, the more dangerous the predator. Each autumn it hides thousands of seeds and remembers where they are, and part of its brain involved in memory grows new cells to help.

species:aegithalos-caudatus.placeText: Woodland and hedges across Europe and Asia
summary: A tiny, round, pink-and-black bird with a tail longer than its body. Pairs build an elastic, domed nest of moss and cobwebs, covered in lichen and lined with up to 2,000 feathers. In winter, families huddle together in a row on a branch to keep warm.

A blue-grey bird that climbs down tree trunks head first, the only European bird to do so regularly. It wedges nuts in bark and hammers them open. It narrows the entrance of its nest hole with mud until only it can squeeze through.

species:troglodytes-troglodytes.placeText: Woodland, gardens and cliffs across Europe, North Africa and Asia
summary: A tiny brown bird with a cocked tail and an astonishingly loud song for its size. Males build several domed nests, and the female chooses one. In cold winters, dozens may roost together in one nest box to keep warm. It is the only member of its American family found in the Old World.

species:campylorhynchus-brunneicapillus.placeText: Deserts of the south-western USA and northern Mexico
summary: The largest wren in the USA, a speckled brown desert bird that builds football-shaped nests in spiny chollas and other cacti, where predators cannot reach. Its harsh, chugging song sounds like a car that will not start. It is the state bird of Arizona.

species:regulus-regulus.placeText: Conifer forests of Europe and Asia
summary: Europe’s smallest bird, about 5–6 g, olive-green with a golden crest. Despite its size it survives Scandinavian winters, and many cross the North Sea each autumn; folklore said they rode on the backs of woodcocks. It feeds almost constantly on tiny insects.

species:phylloscopus-trochilus.placeText: Breeds across northern Europe and Siberia; winters in sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A small, greenish warbler with a sweet, falling song, one of the most abundant summer visitors in northern Europe. Birds from eastern Siberia fly about 12,000 km each way to Africa, an enormous journey for a bird weighing about 9 g.

species:acrocephalus-scirpaceus.placeText: Reedbeds of Europe and western Asia; winters in tropical Africa
summary: A plain brown warbler that weaves a deep, cup-shaped nest around several reed stems. It is one of the main hosts of the common cuckoo, and the drama of reed warblers feeding a giant cuckoo chick many times their size is a classic image of brood parasitism.

species:sylvia-atricapilla.placeText: Woodland and gardens of Europe and western Asia; winters in Africa and southern Europe
summary: A grey warbler with a black cap (brown in females) and a rich, fluting song. Since the 1960s, some blackcaps from central Europe have started migrating north-west to winter in Britain and Ireland, fed by garden bird feeders, instead of south-west to Spain, a new migration route that has evolved within decades.

species:pycnonotus-cafer.placeText: South Asia; introduced to Hawaii, Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and the Middle East
summary: A crested, dark brown bulbul with a red patch under its tail, one of the commonest garden birds in India. Introduced to many Pacific islands, it is listed among the world’s worst invasive species, spreading weeds and eating crops.

species:zosterops-lateralis.placeText: Australia, New Zealand and nearby Pacific islands
summary: A small olive-green bird with a white eye-ring. In 1856 a flock crossed the Tasman Sea from Australia to New Zealand by itself, and silvereyes have since spread across the country, which is why the Māori call them tauhou, “stranger”. White-eyes evolve new species unusually fast when they reach islands.

species:alauda-arvensis.placeText: Farmland and grassland across Europe and Asia
summary: A streaky brown lark famous for its song, poured out continuously for minutes as the male rises almost out of sight and hovers high over fields. It has inspired poems by Shelley and music by Vaughan Williams. Changes to farming have cut its numbers sharply in Europe.

species:motacilla-alba.placeText: Across Europe, Asia and North Africa; winters south to Africa and South Asia
summary: A slim black, white and grey bird that runs across lawns, roads and car parks, constantly wagging its long tail. The British form is called the pied wagtail. In winter, hundreds may roost together in city-centre trees and greenhouses for warmth.

species:lanius-collurio.placeText: Scrub and hedges across Europe and western Asia; winters in southern Africa
summary: A small predatory songbird with a hooked bill and a black bandit mask. It catches beetles, bumblebees, lizards and small birds and impales them on thorns or barbed wire as a “larder”, earning shrikes the name butcherbirds. It vanished as a breeding bird from Britain in the 1990s.

species:bombycilla-garrulus.placeText: Northern forests of Eurasia and North America; winters further south
summary: A plump, crested, pinkish-brown bird with red waxy tips on its wing feathers. In “irruption” years when berries fail in the far north, huge flocks pour south into European and American towns, stripping rowan, cotoneaster and other berry bushes in supermarket car parks.

species:cinclus-cinclus.placeText: Fast-flowing rivers and streams in the mountains and hills of Europe and Asia
summary: A plump brown bird with a white bib that bobs on stones in rushing streams, then walks, dives and swims underwater, using its wings to stay on the bottom while it catches insect larvae. It has dense plumage, extra blood oxygen capacity and a flap that closes its nostrils.

species:prunella-modularis.placeText: Gardens, hedges and woodland edges of Europe and western Asia
summary: A modest, sparrow-like bird with a grey head that shuffles under bushes. Its private life is anything but plain: females often mate with two or more males, and males with several females, and each male helps feed chicks according to how much mating he had.

species:emberiza-citrinella.placeText: Farmland and scrub across Europe and western Siberia; introduced to New Zealand
summary: A bright yellow bunting of hedgerows whose song is often written as “a little bit of bread and no cheese”. Researchers found that British yellowhammers kept 18th-century song dialects that were carried to New Zealand, where they survive even after dying out at home.

species:oriolus-oriolus.placeText: Broadleaf woodland of Europe and western Asia; winters in Africa
summary: The male is a brilliant yellow and black, yet hard to see in the canopy of tall woods, where his fluting “weela-weeoo” song gives him away. It weaves a hammock-like nest slung between twigs in a fork of a branch.

species:dicrurus-adsimilis.placeText: Savannas and woodland of sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A glossy black bird with a deeply forked tail and red eyes. It follows meerkats and pied babblers, giving alarm calls when predators appear. But it also gives false alarm calls, even mimicking the meerkats’ own alarms, so the animals flee and drop their food, which the drongo then steals.

species:pitta-moluccensis.placeText: Breeds in mainland South-east Asia; winters in Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula
summary: A plump, short-tailed ground bird with a black head, green back, shining blue wing patches and red under its tail. It hops on the forest floor, flicking aside leaves to find worms and snails, and calls with a loud, whistled “taew-laew”.

species:ploceus-cucullatus.placeText: Savannas, farmland and villages of sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A noisy, yellow-and-black weaver that nests in big, chattering colonies, often in village trees. The male knots strips of grass and palm leaves into a hanging, kidney-shaped nest, then hangs upside down from it, fluttering to attract a female. If she does not like it, he tears it down and starts again.

species:philetairus-socius.placeText: Dry savanna of Namibia, Botswana and South Africa
summary: A small, sparrow-like weaver that builds the largest nests of any bird: huge thatched apartment blocks of grass in acacia trees or on telephone poles, up to about 7 m long, with over 100 chambers housing several hundred birds. The nests stay cool by day and warm at night, and last for decades.

Probably the most abundant wild bird in the world, with an estimated 1.5 billion adults. Flocks of millions move across Africa following rain and ripening grass seeds, and can strip farmers’ grain fields, so they are poisoned and blown up as a crop pest.

species:nectarinia-famosa.placeText: Mountain fynbos and highland grassland of eastern and southern Africa
summary: The male is a shimmering emerald green with long central tail feathers. Like a hummingbird it feeds on nectar with a long, curved bill, but it usually perches rather than hovers. In South Africa it is a key pollinator of proteas and aloes.

One of the most colourful birds in the world, with a purple breast, yellow belly, green back and a head that can be red, black or yellow. It is popular in aviaries worldwide, but in the wild it fell to a few thousand birds because of changes to fire patterns and grazing in its savanna home.

species:pica-pica.placeText: Open country, farmland and towns across Europe and Asia
summary: A black-and-white crow with a long, iridescent tail. In 2008 magpies were the first non-mammals shown to recognise themselves in a mirror, trying to remove a coloured mark from their own feathers. In folklore they collect shiny objects, but experiments found they are actually wary of them.

species:garrulus-glandarius.placeText: Woodland across Europe, Asia and North Africa
summary: A colourful, pinkish-brown crow with electric-blue wing patches. Each autumn a single jay buries several thousand acorns to eat in winter; the ones it forgets grow into oak trees, making jays important planters of oak woods. Experiments suggest jays plan for future needs and pay attention to what other jays want.

species:turdus-merula.placeText: Europe, North Africa and western Asia; introduced to Australia and New Zealand
summary: A black thrush with a golden-yellow bill (females are brown) and a rich, mellow song heard at dawn and dusk. Originally a shy forest bird, it moved into towns in the 1800s, and city blackbirds now differ genetically from their forest cousins. It is the “blackbird singing in the dead of night” of the Beatles song.

species:turdus-philomelos.placeText: Woodland and gardens across Europe and western Siberia
summary: A brown, speckled thrush that sings each phrase two or three times over, as Robert Browning wrote, “lest you should think he never could recapture the first fine careless rapture”. It smashes snails against a favourite stone, its “anvil”, leaving piles of broken shells.

species:luscinia-megarhynchos.placeText: Thickets and woodland of southern and western Europe and western Asia; winters in tropical Africa
summary: A plain brown bird with one of the most celebrated songs in the world, a rich, varied series of whistles, trills and gurgles, often sung at night. Unpaired males sing at night to attract migrating females, then mostly sing by day once mated. It has inspired poets from Ovid to Keats.

species:oenanthe-oenanthe.placeText: Open, rocky country across the Northern Hemisphere; winters in sub-Saharan Africa
summary: A small grey, black and buff bird with a bold white rump. All the world’s wheatears winter in Africa, even those breeding in Alaska and the Canadian Arctic, so some fly about 30,000 km a year, crossing Asia or the Atlantic, one of the longest migrations of any songbird for its size.

species:carduelis-carduelis.placeText: Europe, North Africa and western Asia; introduced to Australia, New Zealand and South America
summary: A small finch with a red face, black-and-white head and golden wing bars that feeds on thistle and teasel seeds, prising them out with its fine bill. A flock is called a “charm”. It was a popular cage bird for centuries and appears in many Renaissance paintings of the Christ child, and in Carel Fabritius’s The Goldfinch.

species:fringilla-coelebs.placeText: Woodland and gardens across Europe, North Africa and western Asia
summary: One of Europe’s most common birds, the male with a pinkish breast and blue-grey cap. Young chaffinches learn their song from neighbouring males, so local dialects form; its scientific name coelebs, “bachelor”, comes from Linnaeus noticing that only males stayed in Sweden over winter.

species:loxia-curvirostra.placeText: Conifer forests across the Northern Hemisphere
summary: A finch whose bill tips cross over, a tool for prising open pine and spruce cones to extract the seeds with its tongue. Its life follows the cone crop: it can breed even in mid-winter when cones are plentiful, and wanders huge distances when they fail.

species:acridotheres-tristis.placeText: South and Central Asia; introduced across Australia, the Middle East, Africa and Pacific islands
summary: A brown starling with a yellow eye patch and legs, bold and noisy, living around people. It has been introduced to control insects in many places, and is now listed among the world’s worst invasive species: it takes over nest holes from native birds and can destroy their eggs and chicks.

A glossy blue-green starling with a chestnut belly and a white breast band, common around safari lodges. It breeds cooperatively in groups, and helpers raise the young of others; groups living in unpredictable rainfall are more cooperative.

species:passer-montanus.placeText: Europe and Asia; introduced to the USA and Australia
summary: A neat sparrow with a chestnut cap and a black cheek spot. In China in 1958, the Four Pests Campaign set out to kill sparrows for eating grain; so many were killed that insect pests boomed, contributing to the Great Chinese Famine, and the campaign was changed to target bedbugs instead.

species:progne-subis.placeText: Breeds across North America; winters in the Amazon basin
summary: North America’s largest swallow, glossy blue-purple. Native Americans hung hollow gourds for martins to nest in, and in eastern North America they now nest almost entirely in “martin houses” and gourds put up by people. It winters in huge roosts in Brazil.

A broad-snouted crocodylian of swamps, rivers and lakes from North Carolina to Texas. Hunting cut its numbers badly by the 1960s; protection brought it back to over a million and it was taken off the US endangered list in 1987, one of the great conservation recoveries. The temperature of the nest decides whether hatchlings are male or female.

A small alligator, about 1.5–2 m long, that spends winter dormant in burrows. Only a few hundred survive in the wild, but thousands live in breeding centres, and reintroductions have begun. It is one of only two living alligators.
Named for the bony ridge between its eyes like the bridge of a pair of glasses, it is the most widespread and numerous crocodylian in the Americas.
A caiman with the broadest snout of any crocodylian, living in marshes and mangroves from northeast Brazil to northern Argentina. It can survive cold winters further south than most crocodylians.
The caiman of the Pantanal wetlands, where it gathers in crowds of thousands as pools shrink in the dry season. Commercial hunting for skins once took millions; it has recovered under protection.

The largest member of the alligator family, up to about 5 m, and a top predator of the Amazon, taking capybaras, deer and anacondas. It was hunted to about 1% of its former numbers for its dark skin in the 1900s and has since recovered in many areas. It is the only species in its genus.
The smallest crocodylian in the Americas, about 1.2–1.5 m, heavily armoured and living in fast, cool forest streams.
A small, heavily armoured caiman that lives in rainforest streams and often travels far from water over land.

species:crocodylus-niloticus.placeText: Eastern, central and southern Africa and Madagascar
summary: Africa’s largest crocodile, up to about 5.5 m, famous for ambushing wildebeest and zebra at river crossings. It kills more people than any other crocodile. West African populations are now a separate species.

A smaller relative of the Nile crocodile, recognised as a separate species in 2011 after DNA showed it is closer to American crocodiles. It was the sacred crocodile of ancient Egypt; mummified crocodiles from Egyptian tombs include both species.

species:crocodylus-porosus.placeText: Coasts and rivers from India to northern Australia
summary: The largest living reptile, with males over 6 m and about 1,000 kg, and the strongest bite force measured for any living animal. It swims far out to sea, riding currents between islands. Australia’s population has recovered to over 100,000 since hunting was banned in the 1970s.

species:crocodylus-acutus.placeText: Southern Florida, the Caribbean, Central America and northern South America
summary: A slender-snouted crocodile of coasts, mangroves and saline lakes. In southern Florida it lives alongside the American alligator, the only place where the two meet. Its Florida population recovered from a few hundred to over 2,000.

species:crocodylus-intermedius.placeText: Orinoco River basin, Venezuela and Colombia
summary: One of the largest crocodiles, with a long, narrow snout. Hunted almost to extinction for its skin in the early 1900s, only a few hundred breeding adults remain in the wild.

The “freshie”, a slender-snouted fish-eater that is shy of people, much smaller and less dangerous than the saltwater crocodile. It can gallop on land. Introduced cane toads, which are poisonous to eat, have killed many.
A small freshwater crocodile found only in the Philippines and one of the most threatened, with perhaps a hundred adults in the wild. Community-based conservation in northern Luzon has helped it.

species:crocodylus-moreletii.placeText: Gulf of Mexico coast, Yucatán, Belize and Guatemala
summary: A medium-sized crocodile of freshwater marshes and lagoons. Heavily hunted until the 1970s, it has recovered so well under protection that it is now listed as Least Concern.
A freshwater crocodile of swamps and rivers in northern New Guinea. In 2019 crocodiles south of the central mountains were described as a separate species, Hall’s New Guinea crocodile.

Described in 2019, separated from the New Guinea crocodile by the central mountain range and by differences in its skull. It is named after Philip Hall, who studied New Guinea crocodiles in the 1980s.

species:crocodylus-palustris.placeText: India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Nepal and Iran
summary: A broad-snouted crocodile of rivers, lakes and reservoirs, able to walk long distances between water bodies and dig burrows to escape heat. It has been seen balancing sticks on its snout during the egret nesting season, perhaps as a lure for birds collecting nest material.

species:crocodylus-rhombifer.placeText: Zapata Swamp and Isla de la Juventud, Cuba
summary: A small, aggressive, unusually terrestrial crocodile with bright yellow-and-black markings and long legs, found in a tiny area of Cuba. Hybridisation with American crocodiles threatens it.

A freshwater crocodile once common across Southeast Asia and thought nearly extinct in the wild by the 1990s; small wild populations were later found in Cambodia, Laos and Indonesian Borneo. Many thousands live on crocodile farms.
A narrow-snouted, fish-eating crocodile of forest rivers. A 2018 study split the Central African population as a separate species. It is one of Africa’s most threatened crocodiles.
Separated from the West African slender-snouted crocodile in 2018 on the basis of DNA and skull shape, it lives in the rivers and swamps of the Congo Basin and Cameroon.

species:osteolaemus-tetraspis.placeText: Rainforests of West and Central Africa
summary: The smallest crocodile, rarely over 1.5 m, heavily armoured and nocturnal, living in rainforest swamps and pools. In a cave in Gabon, a population living on bats and crickets is turning orange from bat guano. Some split it into two or three species.

species:gavialis-gangeticus.placeText: Rivers of northern India and Nepal
summary: A huge crocodylian with an extremely long, thin snout lined with over 100 teeth for catching fish. Males grow a bulbous knob, the ghara (Hindi for pot), on the snout tip to amplify sounds. Its population crashed to about 200 in the 1970s; captive breeding has helped, and most now live in the Chambal River.

species:tomistoma-schlegelii.placeText: Peat swamps of Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula
summary: Also called the tomistoma, a slender-snouted crocodile of blackwater peat swamps. Long placed with true crocodiles, DNA shows it is the gharial’s closest living relative. Its swamps are being drained for oil palm plantations.

The largest living tortoise, with males over 200 kg and lifespans past 100 years. Each island has its own form, now usually counted as about 13 living species: domed shells on wet islands, and raised “saddleback” shells on dry islands that let tortoises stretch up to reach cactus. Lonesome George, the last Pinta Island tortoise, died in 2012; a female Fernandina tortoise, a species thought extinct for over a century, was found in 2019. Whalers and settlers killed perhaps 100,000–200,000 for food.

One of the two surviving kinds of giant tortoise, with about 100,000 living on remote Aldabra Atoll, more than all Galápagos tortoises together. They have been released on islands off Mauritius to replace extinct Mascarene tortoises as grazers and seed-spreaders. Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise (often counted as part of this species) on Saint Helena, is thought to have hatched around 1832, making him the oldest known land animal.

species:dermochelys-coriacea.placeText: Oceans worldwide, nesting on tropical beaches
summary: The largest living turtle, up to about 2 m long and 500–700 kg; a male stranded in Wales in 1988 weighed 916 kg. It lives on jellyfish, dives deeper than 1,000 m, and keeps its body warmer than the water, letting it feed as far north as Norway and Canada. Many die after swallowing plastic bags that look like jellyfish.

A large sea turtle named for the green colour of its fat, not its shell. Adults are mostly plant-eaters that graze seagrass meadows and seaweed, keeping them healthy like lawnmowers. On some beaches, warming sand now produces almost all female hatchlings, because nest temperature decides sex.

species:caretta-caretta.placeText: Temperate and tropical seas worldwide, including the Mediterranean
summary: A sea turtle with a huge head and crushing jaws for crabs, conchs and other shellfish. Hatchlings from Florida drift for years around the North Atlantic, and those born in Japan cross the whole Pacific to feed off Mexico. Its largest nesting beaches are in Florida and Oman.

species:eretmochelys-imbricata.placeText: Coral reefs of tropical seas worldwide
summary: A reef turtle with a narrow, hawk-like beak for picking sponges out of crevices. Its overlapping shell plates were the “tortoiseshell” of combs and jewellery; millions were killed for it before international trade was banned in 1977, and illegal trade continues.

species:macrochelys-temminckii.placeText: Rivers draining into the Gulf of Mexico, USA
summary: The heaviest freshwater turtle in North America, with males up to about 80 kg. It lies still with its mouth open, wiggling a pink, worm-shaped flap on its tongue to lure fish inside. Turtles from the Suwannee River were split off as a separate species in 2014.

species:chelydra-serpentina.placeText: Southern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico
summary: A pond and river turtle with a long neck and a sharp, fast bite. Its shell is too small to hide in, so on land it defends itself by snapping. It can survive winter under ice for months. Snapping turtles of Central and South America are now treated as separate species.

species:trachemys-scripta.placeText: Mississippi valley and Gulf coast, USA; introduced worldwide
summary: A pond turtle named for the red stripe behind each eye and its habit of sliding off logs into the water. The red-eared slider (the subspecies T. s. elegans) became the most traded pet turtle; released pets now live wild on every continent except Antarctica, and it is listed among the world’s 100 worst invasive species.

A land turtle whose lower shell has a hinge, so it can shut itself completely inside like a box. It can live more than 50 years, with reports of over 100, often within a home range of a few hectares. Collection for the pet trade and road deaths have caused declines.

A side-necked turtle with a flat, triangular head, fringed skin flaps and a rough shell that make it look like a pile of dead leaves. It catches fish by suddenly opening its mouth and throat to suck them in. Turtles from the Orinoco and Rio Negro were described as a second species in 2020.

species:sphenodon-punctatus.placeText: Offshore islands and fenced sanctuaries of New Zealand
summary: The only surviving rhynchocephalian, the last of a group that was widespread in the age of dinosaurs. It looks like a lizard but is not one. It stays active in cool weather that would halt most reptiles, grows slowly and can live over 100 years: Henry, at a New Zealand museum, fathered his first young at about 111. Rats wiped it out on the mainland; it survives on about 30 islands, and since 2005 lives again in the fenced Zealandia sanctuary in Wellington.

species:varanus-komodoensis.placeText: Komodo, Rinca, Flores and nearby islands, Indonesia
summary: The largest living lizard, up to about 3 m and 70 kg, which ambushes deer, pigs and water buffalo. It kills with serrated, iron-coated teeth and a venom from glands in its lower jaw that causes bleeding and shock; the old idea that deadly bacteria in its saliva do the killing has been disproved. Females in zoos have laid fertile eggs without a male. About 3,000 survive in the wild.

species:iguana-iguana.placeText: Mexico to Paraguay; introduced to Florida and the Caribbean
summary: A large, leaf-eating tree lizard, up to about 1.7 m with its tail, that often basks over water and drops into rivers to escape. Like many lizards it has a light-sensing “third eye” on top of its head. Released pets have become an invasive pest in Florida and Puerto Rico.

The only lizard that feeds in the sea, diving for seaweed and sneezing out excess salt from glands near its nose. During El Niño famines adults actually shrink, reabsorbing bone, and grow back when food returns. Darwin called it a “hideous-looking creature”.

species:heloderma-suspectum.placeText: Deserts of the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico
summary: A slow, chunky, pink-and-black venomous lizard that spends most of its life underground and stores fat in its tail. It delivers venom by chewing; bites are very painful but rarely if ever fatal to people. A hormone found in its saliva, exendin-4, became the diabetes drug exenatide in 2005 and helped open the way for today’s GLP-1 drugs.

A large chameleon whose males are vividly coloured in reds, blues, greens or oranges depending on where they come from. A 2015 study of this species showed how chameleons change colour: they adjust a lattice of tiny crystals in their skin that reflects light. A 2021 genetic study suggested it may be several species.

A big, blue-grey gecko with orange spots, named for its loud “to-kay” call. Like many geckos it climbs smooth walls and glass using millions of microscopic hairs on its toes that cling by van der Waals forces, the inspiration for gecko-inspired adhesives. Other well-known geckos include house geckos and the leopard gecko kept as a pet (which belongs to a separate family).

species:chlamydosaurus-kingii.placeText: Northern Australia and southern New Guinea
summary: A tree lizard that, when threatened, opens a huge frill of skin around its neck, gapes and hisses, then runs away upright on its hind legs. The frill and venom-spitting of the Dilophosaurus in Jurassic Park were invented for the film, partly inspired by this lizard; there is no evidence Dilophosaurus had either. Its relatives include the bearded dragon.

A bright green lizard with crests on its head, back and tail, called the “Jesus Christ lizard” because it can sprint across water on its hind legs, slapping the surface with fringed toes. Young ones run farthest; heavy adults soon sink and swim. It is named after the basilisk of legend.

species:phrynosoma-cornutum.placeText: South-central United States and northern Mexico
summary: A flat, spiny lizard, often called a “horned toad”, that eats mostly harvester ants. Cornered by a coyote or dog, it can squirt a stream of foul-tasting blood from its eyes. It has disappeared from much of its range as harvester ants were replaced by invasive fire ants and pesticides. It is the state reptile of Texas.

A stout, short-legged skink that scares off predators by gaping and flashing a broad, bright blue tongue, which also reflects ultraviolet light. It gives birth to live young and is common in suburban gardens, where it eats snails.

The longest snake in the world, with reliable measurements close to 7 m; claims of 10 m or more have never been verified. It is one of very few snakes known to have killed and swallowed adult people, in a handful of documented cases in Indonesia. Its relative the Burmese python has become a major invasive predator in the Florida Everglades.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Usually 3–6 m; record close to 7 m

summary: The heaviest snake alive, with females reaching about 100 kg and over 5 m, far larger than males. It hunts from the water, seizing capybaras, caimans and deer and killing by constriction, which stops blood flow rather than suffocating prey. In 2024 anacondas from the northern part of its range were described as a separate species, the northern green anaconda (Eunectes akayima), a split some scientists dispute; the map shows both.

One of the few animals whose scientific name is the same as its common name. It is usually 2–3 m long and gives birth to live young, unlike pythons, which lay eggs. Experiments on boas in 2015 showed that constriction kills by stopping the prey’s heart and blood flow within seconds to minutes.

species:ophiophagus-hannah.placeText: Northern India to southern China and Indochina
summary: The longest venomous snake, up to about 5.5 m, which feeds mainly on other snakes (its genus name means “snake-eater”). It is the only snake known to build a nest, piling leaves over its eggs and guarding them. It is not a “true cobra” of the genus Naja. In 2024 king cobras were split into four species; this name now covers the northern king cobra.

species:dendroaspis-polylepis.placeText: Savannas of eastern and southern Africa
summary: Africa’s longest venomous snake, usually 2–3 m, named for the inky-black inside of its mouth; its body is grey or olive-brown, not black. Its fast-acting venom was almost always fatal before antivenom. It is among the fastest snakes, but stories of it chasing people at horse speed are myths; it flees when it can.

species:oxyuranus-microlepidotus.placeText: Channel Country of inland eastern Australia
summary: In laboratory tests on mice it has the most toxic venom of any land snake. Yet it lives in remote floodplains, is shy and rarely bites, and no human deaths from it have been recorded. It darkens in winter to absorb more heat, and feeds on native rats.

A venomous sea snake that spends its whole life in the open ocean, drifting in floating debris lines to ambush fish, with a paddle-shaped tail for swimming. It has the widest range of any snake. It cannot drink seawater and survives on rain that briefly sits on the sea surface.

species:crotalus-atrox.placeText: Southwestern United States and northern Mexico
summary: A heavy rattlesnake, up to about 2 m, that warns off large animals with a rattle of loose, interlocking keratin rings. It adds a segment every time it sheds, several times a year, and old segments break off, so counting them does not give its age. Pits on its face sense the body heat of prey. It causes many of the serious snakebites in the United States and northern Mexico.

species:bitis-gabonica.placeText: Rainforests of central and eastern Africa
summary: The heaviest viper, up to about 8 kg, with the longest fangs of any snake, up to about 5 cm. Its geometric pattern makes it almost invisible among dead leaves, where it lies still for days waiting for prey. It is calm and rarely bites people. The West African form is now treated as a separate species, the West African Gaboon viper.

facts.label: Fangs
facts.value: Up to about 5 cm, the longest of any snake

summary: The most widespread reptile in North America, reaching farther north than any other snake on the continent. At Narcisse in Manitoba, tens of thousands emerge from winter dens each spring and form writhing mating balls. Some populations have evolved resistance to the deadly toxin of the newts they eat. Its mild venom is harmless to people.

species:agalychnis-callidryas.placeText: Rainforests from southern Mexico to Colombia
summary: A bright green tree frog that sleeps by day with its blue-and-yellow flanks and red eyes hidden; startled awake, it flashes them to shock predators. It lays eggs on leaves over ponds, and embryos can hatch early and drop into the water if they feel the vibrations of an attacking snake.

Perhaps the most poisonous animal alive: one frog, about 5 cm long, carries enough batrachotoxin to kill about ten people. Emberá people tipped blowgun darts by wiping them on its back. It makes the poison from something in its wild diet, so frogs raised in captivity are harmless.

North America’s largest frog, up to about 20 cm and 750 g, named for the male’s deep, bull-like call. It eats almost anything it can swallow, including other frogs, snakes and ducklings. Spread around the world for frog legs, it is an invasive pest in western North America, Europe, Asia and South America and helped carry the chytrid fungus that has devastated frogs worldwide.

The familiar brown frog of European garden ponds, which gathers in early spring to lay great clumps of frogspawn. It survives farther north than most frogs, beyond the Arctic Circle, and can change its skin shade to match its surroundings.

species:rhinella-marina.placeText: Amazon basin and nearby; introduced to Australia and many islands
summary: A huge toad, up to about 15 cm and over 1 kg, whose glands ooze a poison that kills animals that bite it. In 1935, 102 toads were released in Queensland to control cane beetles, which they did not do; their descendants, now well over 200 million, have spread across northern Australia, killing quolls, goannas and freshwater crocodiles. The toads of Mexico and Central America were split off as a separate species in 2016.

A bright golden toad and a national symbol of Panama, which waves its arms at rivals because rushing streams drown out calls. The chytrid fungus swept through its habitat in the 2000s and it has not been seen in the wild since 2009; it survives in captive breeding programmes awaiting a safe return.

facts.label: IUCN status
facts.value: Critically Endangered (possibly extinct in the wild)

species:conraua-goliath.placeText: Rainforest rivers of Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea
summary: The largest frog alive, with a body up to about 32 cm long and weighing up to about 3 kg. A 2019 study found that adults dig nesting pools beside rivers, shifting rocks up to 2 kg, perhaps explaining their size. It is hunted for food and its rivers are threatened by logging and dams.

A flat, fully aquatic frog with clawed hind toes and no tongue. From the 1930s to the 1960s it was the standard pregnancy test: a woman’s urine injected into a female made her lay eggs if pregnant. It became one of biology’s main laboratory animals (John Gurdon’s cloning of frogs from body cells, which won a 2012 Nobel Prize, used it), and the global trade in it may have helped spread chytrid fungus.

species:paedophryne-amauensis.placeText: Leaf litter of southeastern Papua New Guinea
summary: Described in 2012 at about 7.7 mm long, small enough to sit on a fingernail, and long counted as the smallest known vertebrate. A 2024 study measured Brazil’s flea toad (Brachycephalus pulex) at about 7.1 mm, slightly smaller. It hops among dead leaves on the rainforest floor, eating mites.

A salamander that stays in its larval form all its life, keeping its feathery gills and living in water. It can regrow lost legs, tail, parts of its spinal cord, heart and brain, making it a key animal in regeneration research. Millions live in labs and as pets, but in the wild, pollution, invasive fish and urban growth cut numbers from about 6,000 per square kilometre in 1998 to about 36 in 2014.

species:andrias-davidianus.placeText: Mountain streams of central and southern China
summary: One of the largest amphibians, historically reaching about 1.8 m, though wild ones that big are now unknown. Genetic studies since 2018 show it is several species, and the South China giant salamander (Andrias sligoi) may be the largest of all. Millions are farmed for food, mixing the lineages, while wild populations have nearly vanished. Its relatives are the Japanese giant salamander and the North American hellbender.

species:salamandra-salamandra.placeText: Forests of central and southern Europe
summary: A black-and-yellow salamander whose skin glands make a nerve poison. The old belief that salamanders live in fire probably came from them crawling out of logs thrown on fires. Since about 2010 a fungus from Asia, Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans, has wiped out most fire salamanders in the Netherlands and is spreading in Belgium, Germany and Spain.

Europe’s largest newt, whose males grow a tall, jagged crest in the breeding season. It is strictly protected in Britain and the European Union, so ponds must often be surveyed for it before building work can go ahead. Its skin is warty and secretes a mild poison.

species:proteus-anguinus.placeText: Flooded caves of the Dinaric Alps, Slovenia to Herzegovina
summary: A blind, pale pink cave salamander that keeps its gills for life; olms washed out of caves by floods were once thought to be baby dragons. It can live for about 100 years and go years without eating, and one tracked olm did not move for seven years.

species:siphonops-annulatus.placeText: South America east of the Andes
summary: A legless, burrowing amphibian that looks like a large blue-grey earthworm with white rings. A 2024 study showed that mothers feed their young a milk-like fluid, and the young also peel off and eat their mother’s skin, which regrows. Caecilians have tiny eyes under the skin and smell with sensory tentacles on the face.

species:carcharodon-carcharias.placeText: Cool and warm coastal seas worldwide
summary: The largest predatory fish, up to about 6 m and 2 tonnes, which keeps its body warmer than the sea and hunts seals with ambush rushes from below. The film Jaws (1975) gave it a man-eater image it does not deserve: people are not its prey, and most bites are exploratory. Fishing cut its numbers sharply in the late 1900s. It is not a descendant of megalodon, which belonged to a separate family. Since 2017, orcas off South Africa have killed great whites for their livers, driving them from some hunting grounds.

The largest living fish, commonly 12 m long and reported up to about 18 m. It is a gentle filter-feeder that sieves plankton, fish eggs and small fish, and it lets divers swim alongside it. Each shark’s pattern of spots is unique, letting scientists identify individuals from photographs.

The second-largest fish, up to about 8–10 m, which cruises slowly at the surface with its huge mouth open, filtering plankton. It is a summer visitor off the coasts of Britain and Ireland. Hunted for its liver oil until recent decades, it is now protected in many countries.

A big, striped shark, up to about 5 m, with saw-edged teeth that cut through turtle shells. It eats almost anything: fish, seabirds, sea snakes, dolphins and carrion, and stomachs have held car number plates and tins. After the great white it is responsible for the most recorded bites on people.

species:carcharhinus-leucas.placeText: Warm coasts, estuaries and rivers worldwide
summary: A stocky shark that can live in fresh water as well as the sea. Bull sharks have been found about 4,000 km up the Amazon in Peru, up the Mississippi as far as Illinois, and in Lake Nicaragua. Because it hunts in murky, shallow water near people, it causes many bites.

species:sphyrna-mokarran.placeText: Tropical and warm coastal seas worldwide
summary: The largest hammerhead, up to about 6 m. Its wide, flat head spreads out sensors that detect the electric fields of prey buried in sand, and it uses the head to pin stingrays to the seabed. Overfishing for its fins has made it one of the most threatened sharks.

The longest-lived vertebrate known. A 2016 study dated the eye lenses of Greenland sharks and estimated the oldest at about 390 years, though with a wide margin of error. It grows about 1 cm a year and may not breed until it is around 150. It swims extremely slowly in near-freezing water, yet seals have been found in its stomach, and once the remains of a polar bear.

The largest ray, with a wingspan up to about 7 m, which filters plankton with its huge mouth and somersaults in feeding. It has one of the largest brains for its size of any fish. It breeds very slowly, usually one pup every two to three years, so fishing for its gill plates has hit it hard.

species:petromyzon-marinus.placeText: North Atlantic coasts and rivers; invasive in the Great Lakes
summary: A jawless fish that clamps its sucker mouth onto other fish, rasps through the skin and feeds on blood. It reached the Great Lakes through shipping canals and by the 1950s had helped wipe out their lake trout fisheries; it is now kept down with poisons that target its larvae. In Europe lampreys were a delicacy, and England’s King Henry I was said to have died from eating too many.

species:latimeria-chalumnae.placeText: Deep coastal waters off the Comoros and East Africa
summary: Coelacanths were known only from fossils and thought to have died out with the non-bird dinosaurs, until museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted one in a fishing catch in South Africa in 1938. Most live off the Comoros, resting in caves at 150–250 m. A 2021 study found they can live about 100 years and carry their young for about five years. A second species was found in Indonesia in 1997.

species:neoceratodus-forsteri.placeText: Mary and Burnett rivers, southeastern Queensland
summary: A lungfish with a single lung that gulps air when the water is poor. Fossils of its genus are about 100 million years old. Its genome, sequenced in 2021, has 43 billion letters, about 14 times the human genome; the South American lungfish’s, read in 2024, is twice as large again. “Granddad”, at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium from 1933, lived to over 90.

species:huso-huso.placeText: Caspian and Black Seas and their rivers
summary: One of the largest fish ever caught in fresh water, reported up to about 7 m and over 1,500 kg, and able to live over 100 years. Its eggs are the most expensive caviar. Overfishing and dams that block its spawning rivers have made it critically endangered; nearly all sturgeons are now threatened.

species:atractosteus-spatula.placeText: Rivers of the southern United States and eastern Mexico
summary: A huge, armoured fish, up to about 3 m and 130 kg, with a broad snout full of teeth and scales so hard that Native Americans used them as arrowheads. It can gulp air and survive in warm, stagnant water. Its eggs are poisonous. Gars have changed little in shape since the Cretaceous.

species:amia-calva.placeText: Fresh waters of eastern North America
summary: The last survivor, with one close sister species, of a group of fish that was widespread in the age of dinosaurs. It gulps air into a lung-like swim bladder, survives in stagnant swamps, and males guard the eggs and young. In 2022 bowfins from the north and west were split off as a second species, Amia ocellicauda.

One of the largest freshwater fish, up to about 3 m and 200 kg, also called pirarucu. It must surface to breathe air every 5–20 minutes, and its scales are so tough that piranhas cannot bite through. Overfished by harpoon, it has recovered in Brazilian lakes where local communities count and manage it.

facts.label: Species in genus
facts.value: Several, though their separation is debated

species:clupea-harengus.placeText: North Atlantic, North Sea and Baltic
summary: A small, silvery fish that gathers in schools of millions and has fed Europe for over a thousand years; the herring trade helped make the medieval Hanseatic League rich. Herring make fast clicking sounds by releasing air from the anus, which may help schools keep together at night.

species:salmo-salar.placeText: North Atlantic and the rivers that flow into it
summary: A fish that hatches in rivers, migrates to the ocean, and returns, often to the river it was born in, finding it by smell. Unlike most Pacific salmon, many survive spawning and return again. Millions of tonnes are farmed each year, mostly in Norway, but wild numbers have fallen and it was moved to Near Threatened in 2023. Its relatives include brown trout, rainbow trout and the Pacific salmon.

species:cyprinus-carpio.placeText: Native to the Black and Caspian Sea basins; introduced worldwide
summary: A big, bottom-feeding fish farmed by the Romans and in China for over two thousand years and now one of the most widely farmed fish. Introduced around the world, it muddies water and uproots plants; in parts of Australia’s Murray–Darling rivers it makes up most of the fish by weight. Koi are ornamental carp bred in Japan.

Domesticated in China over a thousand years ago from a dull wild carp, and bred into hundreds of fancy varieties. The idea that goldfish have a three-second memory is a myth: experiments show they remember things for months and can be trained. Goldfish released into lakes grow large and become a damaging invasive species.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Usually 10–20 cm; wild-living ones can pass 40 cm

summary: For centuries one of the world’s most important food fish, which drew European fishing fleets across the Atlantic. Overfishing collapsed the Grand Banks cod off Newfoundland, and Canada closed the fishery in 1992, putting about 40,000 people out of work; numbers there have never fully recovered.

A torpedo-shaped ocean giant, up to about 3 m and 680 kg, that keeps its muscles, eyes and brain warmer than the water and crosses the Atlantic. Heavy fishing for sushi drove it down, but strict quotas let it recover enough to be listed as Least Concern in 2021.

A fast ocean predator that uses its long, flat bill to slash at squid and fish rather than spear them. A special heater organ next to its eyes keeps its eyes and brain warm, sharpening its vision as it dives into cold, dark water by day.

A piranha with razor-sharp interlocking teeth. Its fame for stripping animals to the bone in seconds owes much to Theodore Roosevelt’s 1914 account of a display staged with starved, crowded fish. Piranhas mostly eat fish, insects and carrion, and they school mainly for protection against their own predators.

species:amphiprion-ocellaris.placeText: Coral reefs from the Andaman Sea to northern Australia and Japan
summary: The orange-and-white clownfish of Finding Nemo. It lives among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, protected by a mucus coat. All clownfish start out male; each group is led by one large female, and if she dies the biggest male turns into a female. Demand for pet clownfish rose sharply after the film.

species:takifugu-rubripes.placeText: Northwestern Pacific off Japan, Korea and China
summary: The tiger puffer, prized in Japan as fugu. Its liver and ovaries hold tetrodotoxin, which can kill a person and has no antidote, so in Japan only licensed chefs may prepare it. It puffs up by swallowing water. Its compact genome was sequenced in 2002 to help understand the human one.

A seahorse found from the Mediterranean to the south coast of Britain. As in all seahorses, the female lays her eggs in the male’s pouch, and he carries them until hundreds of tiny seahorses are born. It grips seagrass with its curling tail and sucks up tiny shrimps with its snout.

A huge, flattened fish that looks like a swimming head, up to about 3 m tall from fin tip to fin tip. It eats jellyfish and basks on its side at the surface to warm up after deep dives. A female once held an estimated 300 million eggs, more than any other known vertebrate. The heaviest bony fish recorded, 2,744 kg, was its close relative the bump-head sunfish (Mola alexandrini).

The longest bony fish, reliably measured to about 8 m, a silvery ribbon with a red crest that swims upright in deep water. Oarfish washed ashore probably inspired many sea-serpent tales. In Japan they are said to warn of earthquakes, but a 2019 study found no link.

species:anguilla-anguilla.placeText: Rivers of Europe and North Africa; spawns in the Sargasso Sea
summary: Eels hatch in the Sargasso Sea, drift to Europe as see-through larvae, and spend 5–20 years or more in rivers before swimming thousands of kilometres back to spawn and die. No one has ever seen them spawn. The number of young eels reaching Europe has fallen by over 90% since the 1980s, and smuggling of baby eels to Asia is one of the largest wildlife crimes.

species:electrophorus-electricus.placeText: Amazon and Orinoco basins and the Guianas
summary: Not a true eel but a knifefish, related to catfish and carp. About 80% of its body is filled with electric organs that stun prey and deter attackers. In 2019 electric eels were split into three species; one, Electrophorus voltai, discharges up to 860 volts, the strongest of any animal. It breathes air, and some hunt in groups. The map shows all three species.

species:melanocetus-johnsonii.placeText: Deep waters of tropical and temperate oceans
summary: A fist-sized deep-sea anglerfish, also called the black seadevil, with needle teeth and a glowing lure lit by bacteria. Its stretchy stomach can hold prey larger than itself. In some other deep-sea anglerfish, tiny males fuse permanently to females and live as parasites; in this species the small males stay free-swimming.

species:esox-lucius.placeText: Fresh waters across the Northern Hemisphere
summary: A long, ambush predator that hangs motionless among weeds and lunges at fish, frogs and even ducklings. It lives in lakes and rivers across Europe, northern Asia and North America, one of very few freshwater fish native on all three continents.

species:silurus-glanis.placeText: Central and eastern Europe and western Asia; introduced to western Europe
summary: One of the largest freshwater fish, with fish over 2.7 m caught in Italy’s River Po. Introduced to rivers in Spain, France and Italy, it has learned new hunting tricks: in southern France some lunge out of the water to grab pigeons on the bank.

species:betta-splendens.placeText: Rice paddies and marshes of central Thailand and nearby
summary: The betta, a popular aquarium fish whose males are so aggressive they must be kept apart. It breathes air using its labyrinth organ, letting it live in warm, oxygen-poor puddles. Males build floating bubble nests and guard the eggs. Wild bettas are short-finned and dull; a 2021 genome study suggests they were domesticated in Southeast Asia over a thousand years ago.

species:nautilus-pompilius.placeText: Coral reef slopes of the western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean
summary: The last of the shelled nautiloids, with a coiled shell about 20 cm across divided into chambers. It adjusts the gas and liquid in the chambers to float, spending the day 300 m or more deep on reef slopes and rising at night to scavenge with up to 90 sucker-less tentacles. It can live for over 20 years.

It is often called a living fossil, but only its body plan is ancient: nautiloids go back about 500 million years, while the living nautilus species are much younger. Trade in its shells, sold as ornaments, led to its listing on CITES in 2016.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: “Living fossil” is misleading: its species are young, though its lineage is old

species:architeuthis-dux.placeText: Deep oceans worldwide, except the polar seas
summary: Females reach about 13 m including their two long feeding tentacles, which make up most of that length; males are smaller. Its eyes, up to about 27 cm across, are among the largest of any animal, and help it spot sperm whales, its main predator, in the dark.

Probably the origin of the kraken legend, it was known only from dead and dying specimens until Tsunemi Kubodera and Kyoichi Mori photographed one alive at 900 m off Japan in 2004. The first video of one in the deep sea followed in 2012.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Up to about 13 m including tentacles

summary: The heaviest invertebrate known. A specimen caught by fishers in 2007 weighed about 495 kg. It is shorter than the giant squid but much bulkier, with swivelling hooks on its arms and tentacles as well as suckers.

For a century it was known only from remains, many from the stomachs of sperm whales. In March 2025 a research expedition near the South Sandwich Islands filmed a live one at 600 m for the first time: a see-through juvenile about 30 cm long.

facts.label: First filmed alive
facts.value: 2025, a juvenile near the South Sandwich Islands

species:dosidicus-gigas.placeText: Eastern Pacific, from Chile to Alaska
summary: A powerful, fast-growing squid up to about 1.5 m long and 50 kg, hunting in large groups and flashing red and white as it does, which earned it the name “red devil” in Mexico. It lives only about a year or two.
Since the late 1990s it has spread far north of its old range, reaching California, Canada and Alaska, probably helped by warmer, low-oxygen water and fewer predators.

species:sepia-officinalis.placeText: Northeast Atlantic, the North Sea and the Mediterranean
summary: A broad-bodied relative of squid with a W-shaped pupil and a chalky internal shell, the cuttlebone, which it fills with gas to float and which washes up on beaches. Big males reach about 45 cm.
It changes colour, pattern and skin texture in a fraction of a second to hide or to signal, even though its eyes have only one kind of light sensor and it is thought to be colour-blind.

species:spirula-spirula.placeText: Deep tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide
summary: A small squid relative, about 5 cm long, with a coiled, chambered shell inside its body that keeps it floating head-down in the deep. Its little white shells wash up on beaches worldwide, but the living animal is rarely seen; the first video of one in the wild was made only in 2020, off Australia’s Great Barrier Reef.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: Coiled and chambered, inside the body

species:octopus-vulgaris.placeText: Mediterranean Sea and the eastern Atlantic
