summary: A rocky-shore octopus about 1 m long including its arms, with three hearts, blue blood and most of its neurons in its arms. It solves puzzles, opens jars and escapes tanks, yet lives only one or two years: the female guards her eggs without eating and dies soon after they hatch.
Octopuses once called this species around the world are now known to be several closely related species. In 2022 the United Kingdom recognised octopuses and other cephalopods as sentient in law.

species:enteroctopus-dofleini.placeText: North Pacific, from Japan to California
summary: The largest octopus species. Adults commonly weigh about 15 kg with arms spanning about 4 m; much larger records are doubtful. It hunts crabs, clams and fish in cold coastal waters, and lives three to five years.

species:hapalochlaena-lunulata.placeText: Coral reefs and tide pools of the western Pacific and Indian Ocean
summary: A small octopus, about 10 cm including its arms, that flashes bright blue rings when threatened. Its bite carries tetrodotoxin, made by bacteria living in it, enough to kill a person by stopping their breathing; there is no antidote, but victims survive if kept breathing until the poison wears off.

species:thaumoctopus-mimicus.placeText: Sandy shallows of Indonesia and the western Pacific
summary: An octopus discovered in 1998 off Sulawesi that impersonates other animals, flattening into a flatfish, trailing its arms like a lionfish, or hiding six arms and waving two like a banded sea snake, apparently copying whichever dangerous animal will scare off a threat.

species:amphioctopus-marginatus.placeText: Tropical western Pacific and Indian Ocean
summary: A small octopus that collects discarded coconut shell halves, carries them stacked under its body as it stilt-walks along the sea floor, and assembles them into a shelter. Described in 2009, this was the first tool use recorded in an invertebrate.

facts.label: Known for
facts.value: The first tool use recorded in an invertebrate (2009)

species:vampyroteuthis-infernalis.placeText: Deep tropical and temperate oceans worldwide
summary: A deep-sea cephalopod about 30 cm long, with webbed arms and red eyes. Despite its names, “vampire squid from hell”, it is neither a vampire nor a squid: it is the last of its own group, closer to octopuses, and feeds gently on marine snow, drifting flakes of dead matter, which it gathers on two sticky filaments.
It lives where the water holds very little oxygen, where few predators can follow.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Not a squid, and it does not suck blood

species:argonauta-argo.placeText: Open tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide
summary: An open-ocean octopus whose females make a thin, white, ridged shell with two of their arms, up to about 30 cm across, and use it as an egg case and float, trapping air to stay level. The males are tiny, a few centimetres long.
Its shell gives it the name paper nautilus, but it is an octopus, not a nautilus, and its shell has no chambers.

species:bos-taurus.placeText: Worldwide with people; domesticated from the aurochs
summary: Cattle descend from the aurochs, a huge wild ox that died out in 1627. They were domesticated twice: in the Near East about 10,500 years ago, giving the taurine cattle of Europe, and in the Indus Valley about 8,000 years ago, giving the humped zebu of hot countries, sometimes called Bos indicus.
There are about 1.5 billion cattle, kept for meat, milk, leather and pulling ploughs. The burps of cattle and other livestock are a major source of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.
A bull does not charge because a cape is red: cattle cannot tell red from green, and it is the cape’s movement that provokes it.

facts.label: Domesticated
facts.value: About 10,500 years ago, Near East; zebu about 8,000 years ago, Indus Valley

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Bulls are not angered by red

species:equus-caballus.placeText: Worldwide with people; domesticated on the steppes of western Eurasia
summary: Ancient DNA shows that today’s domestic horses come from the steppes of the lower Volga and Don rivers, in what is now southern Russia, about 4,200 years ago. Within a few centuries, riding and chariots carried them across Eurasia, transforming travel and war.

Earlier horses kept at Botai in Kazakhstan, about 5,500 years ago, turned out to be the ancestors of Przewalski’s horses, not of modern horses. So Przewalski’s horse, often called the last truly wild horse, may instead descend from those early herded horses. Mustangs and brumbies are feral descendants of domestic horses.

facts.label: Domesticated
facts.value: About 4,200 years ago, western Eurasian steppe

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Mustangs are feral, not wild horses

species:equus-asinus.placeText: Worldwide with people; domesticated in East Africa
summary: Donkeys come from the African wild ass, domesticated once, in East Africa, about 7,000 years ago, probably by herders as the Sahara dried out. They became the pack animals that carried goods for early civilisations from Egypt to Mesopotamia.
There are about 50 million donkeys, still vital to farmers and traders in Africa and Asia. Their wild ancestor, the African wild ass, is now critically endangered.

species:sus-domesticus.placeText: Worldwide with people; domesticated from wild boar
summary: Pigs were domesticated from wild boar twice, in eastern Anatolia about 10,500 years ago and in China about 9,000 years ago. Farmers took Near Eastern pigs into Europe, but interbreeding with local wild boar later replaced almost all of their Near Eastern ancestry.
There are nearly a billion pigs, about half of them in China. Despite the saying, pigs hardly sweat at all: they wallow in mud to keep cool and to protect their skin from the sun.

facts.label: Domesticated
facts.value: About 10,500 years ago, Anatolia; about 9,000 years ago, China

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Pigs barely sweat, so they wallow to keep cool

species:ovis-aries.placeText: Worldwide with people; domesticated from the mouflon
summary: Sheep were among the first animals farmed, domesticated from the Asiatic mouflon in the Near East about 10,500 years ago, first for meat, milk and skins. Woolly fleeces that keep growing came later, about 5,000 years ago; wild sheep moult a short coat each year.
There are about 1.3 billion sheep. The Soay sheep of the remote St Kilda islands in Scotland are a feral breed close to the early domestic sheep of Europe.

species:capra-hircus.placeText: Worldwide with people; domesticated from the wild goat
summary: Goats were domesticated from the wild goat, or bezoar ibex, in the Zagros Mountains of Iran and in Anatolia about 10,500 years ago. Hardy and able to browse on almost anything leafy, they thrive where cattle cannot.

There are over a billion goats. Feral goats strip islands of plants; a project on the Galápagos removed about 140,000 from Isabela and nearby islands by 2006 to save the giant tortoises’ habitat. And no, they do not eat tin cans.

facts.label: Domesticated
facts.value: About 10,500 years ago, Zagros Mountains and Anatolia

species:gallus-gallus-domesticus.placeText: Worldwide with people; domesticated from the red junglefowl
summary: The most numerous bird on Earth, with over 20 billion alive at any time. Chickens come from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia, domesticated perhaps 3,500 years ago, probably around rice and millet fields, and at first kept more for cockfighting and ceremonies than for food.

Like all birds, chickens are living dinosaurs. They are often called the closest living relatives of T. rex, after a 2008 study of proteins from a T. rex bone, but every bird is equally closely related to it: the chicken is no closer than a sparrow or an ostrich.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: No closer to T. rex than any other bird

species:lama-glama.placeText: The Andes, and farms worldwide; domesticated from the guanaco
summary: The pack animal of the Andes, domesticated from the guanaco in the highlands of Peru about 4,000 to 7,000 years ago. Llama caravans carried goods across the Inca Empire, and their dung was burned for fuel and used to grow crops at high altitude.
A llama will carry only about a quarter of its body weight, and lies down and refuses to move if overloaded.

facts.label: Load
facts.value: About a quarter of its body weight

species:vicugna-pacos.placeText: The Andes, and farms worldwide; domesticated from the vicuña
summary: Kept for its soft, warm fleece rather than as a pack animal. For a long time alpacas were thought to come from the guanaco, like llamas, but DNA studies since 2001 show they were domesticated from the smaller, wild vicuña, so they are now placed in the vicuña’s genus.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Not a small llama: it comes from the vicuña

species:bubalus-bubalis.placeText: South and Southeast Asia, and farms worldwide
summary: About 200 million water buffalo are kept, mostly in Asia, for ploughing rice paddies, milk and meat. There are two kinds, domesticated separately from the wild water buffalo: river buffalo in South Asia about 5,000 years ago, and swamp buffalo in China and Southeast Asia about 4,000 years ago. Buffalo milk makes true mozzarella di bufala.

facts.label: Domesticated
facts.value: About 5,000 years ago, South Asia; about 4,000 years ago, East Asia

species:bos-grunniens.placeText: The Tibetan Plateau and the high mountains of Central Asia
summary: A shaggy ox domesticated from the wild yak on the Tibetan Plateau about 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, which let people live year-round above 4,000 m. Yaks give milk, meat, wool, leather and dung for fuel, and carry loads over high passes. Its name means “grunting ox”, from its grunting call.

facts.label: Domesticated
facts.value: About 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, Tibetan Plateau

species:camelus-bactrianus.placeText: The steppes and deserts of Central Asia
summary: The two-humped camel of Central Asia, domesticated about 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, which carried goods along the Silk Road through deserts that are scorching in summer and far below freezing in winter.
Its humps store fat, not water. The wild Bactrian camel of the Gobi is a separate species, not its ancestor, and is critically endangered.

facts.label: Domesticated
facts.value: About 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, Central Asia

species:apis-mellifera.placeText: Native to Europe, Africa and the Near East; kept worldwide
summary: A social bee living in colonies of tens of thousands, led by a single queen. People have taken honey from wild nests for at least 9,000 years and kept bees in hives for over 4,000. Three-quarters of the world’s main food crops benefit from animal pollinators such as bees.
A worker bee dies after stinging a mammal only because her barbed sting catches in thick skin and tears away; she can sting other insects and survive.

facts.label: Colony
facts.value: Tens of thousands of bees, one queen

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Bees die after stinging only when the sting gets stuck

summary: A stegosaur with exceptionally long tail spikes, the longest of any stegosaur known. Charles Gilmore named it in 1914 as a species of Stegosaurus, Stegosaurus longispinus, from a partial skeleton found near Alcova, Wyoming. Most of those bones were later lost.

In 2016 it was given its own genus. It probably belongs to the dacentrurines, the group of the Portuguese Miragaia and the European Dacentrurus, and some researchers have suggested it could even be a species of Miragaia.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Charles Gilmore, 1914 (as Stegosaurus longispinus); own genus 2016

species:ardetosaurus-viator.ageText: About 155 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Kimmeridgian)
species:ardetosaurus-viator.placeText: Big Horn Basin, northern Wyoming, USA
summary: A whip-tailed diplodocine sauropod, a relative of Diplodocus and Barosaurus, named in 2024 from a partial skeleton with neck, back and tail bones, hips and part of a hind leg.

Its bones had a long journey: dug up in 1993, they were shipped to Switzerland, then Germany, where they were damaged in a museum fire, and finally the Netherlands, where they are now kept. Its species name, viator, means “traveller”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Casper van der Linden and colleagues, 2024

species:coelurus-fragilis.ageText: About 155 to 152 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A small, lightly built predatory dinosaur, about 2 to 2.5 m long, known from one partial skeleton. Its name means “hollow tail”, after its thin-walled, hollow tail bones. Othniel Marsh named it in 1879, during his “Bone Wars” rivalry with Edward Cope.

Its name gave rise to Coelurosauria, the great group of theropods that includes tyrannosaurs, raptors and birds, yet Coelurus itself was poorly understood for a century and often confused with its contemporary Ornitholestes. It is now known to be an early coelurosaur, perhaps a distant relative of tyrannosaurs.

related.note: Its Morrison contemporary, long confused with it.

species:cteniogenys-antiquus.ageText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
species:cteniogenys-antiquus.placeText: Como Bluff, Wyoming, USA (also Britain and Portugal)
summary: A small, lizard-sized choristodere, one of the earliest members of this group of aquatic reptiles that later produced the long-snouted, crocodile-like Champsosaurus. It was found at Como Bluff in 1881 and named in 1928 by Charles Gilmore. Similar remains are known from the Middle Jurassic of Britain and the Late Jurassic of Portugal.

A freshwater turtle of the pleurosternids, an extinct group of side-necked-looking but not side-necked turtles common in Jurassic rivers and ponds. Its name honours the Dinosaur National Monument visitor centre, near where it was found.

species:uluops-uluops.ageText: About 150 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Tithonian)
summary: A freshwater turtle known from a single skull. It was first described as a baenid, a group common in the Cretaceous, but newer studies place it at the base of the pleurosternids, alongside Dinochelys.

species:dryolestes-priscus.ageText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
species:dryolestes-priscus.placeText: Como Bluff, Wyoming, USA; also Portugal
summary: A tiny, shrew-like mammal with sharp, many-cusped cheek teeth, named by Othniel Marsh in 1878. Its name means “oak robber”. Dryolestes gives its name to the dryolestids, small insect-eaters that were among the commonest mammals of the Jurassic. It is also known from the Alcobaça Formation of Portugal.

species:laolestes-eminens.ageText: About 152 to 135 million years ago (Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous)
species:laolestes-eminens.placeText: Wyoming, USA; also Portugal and England
summary: A small dryolestid mammal, a relative of Dryolestes, known from jaws and teeth. Besides the Morrison Formation it is known from the Late Jurassic of Portugal and the Early Cretaceous Wadhurst Clay of England.

species:priacodon-ferox.ageText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
species:priacodon-ferox.placeText: Como Bluff, Wyoming, and Fruita, Colorado, USA; also Portugal
summary: A small triconodont mammal, with three sharp cusps in a row on each cheek tooth, suited to slicing up insects and perhaps small vertebrates. Four species are known, from the Morrison Formation and from the Alcobaça Formation of Portugal.

A large, plant-eating relative of the tuatara of New Zealand. Its jaws were packed with broad, closely set teeth for grinding vegetation, and its name means “packed teeth”. It belongs to the eilenodontines, a group of herbivorous rhynchocephalians that lasted into the Late Cretaceous of South America.

related.note: A much smaller tuatara relative from the same rocks.

species:opisthiamimus-gregori.placeText: Big Horn Basin, northern Wyoming, USA
summary: A tiny relative of the tuatara, known from a nearly complete skeleton. Its skull was only about 2 cm long and its body about 8.5 cm from snout to vent, about the size of a small lizard. Named in 2022, it would have looked much like a miniature tuatara, and probably ate insects and other small invertebrates.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: David DeMar, Marc Jones and Matthew Carrano, 2022

facts.label: Size
facts.value: About 8.5 cm snout to vent, perhaps 16 cm with tail

species:paramacellodus-oweni.ageText: About 155 to 140 million years ago (Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous)
species:paramacellodus-oweni.placeText: Como Bluff, Wyoming, and Dinosaur National Monument, Utah, USA; also England, France and Portugal
summary: A small lizard from one of the earliest lizard radiations, the paramacellodids, which spread across the northern continents in the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous. They were armoured with small bony plates in the skin and were probably distant relatives of skinks. The type species was named from the Purbeck Group of Dorset, England; the Morrison material probably belongs to the same or a close species.

species:enigmacursor-mollyborthwickae.ageText: About 155 to 148 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A small, fast-running plant-eating dinosaur, about 1 m long and knee-high to an adult human, named in 2025 from a three-dimensionally preserved partial skeleton. Its name means “puzzle runner”, after the long confusion over the small two-legged plant-eaters of the Morrison Formation.

It was found by a commercial company between 2021 and 2022, bought by the Natural History Museum in London in 2024, and is now on display there. Its describers found it most closely related to Yandusaurus from China.

related.note: Another small Morrison plant-eater.

species:nanosaurus-agilis.ageText: About 155 to 148 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A small, two-legged plant-eating dinosaur, about 1.5 to 2 m long, one of the commonest small dinosaurs of the Morrison Formation. Othniel Marsh named it in 1877 from a few bones. Its name means “dwarf lizard”.

Its history is tangled: over a century, Marsh and Peter Galton named several other small plant-eaters from the same rocks, Othnielia, Othnielosaurus and Drinker, which are now all treated as Nanosaurus. Once called a “hypsilophodont”, it is now seen as an early neornithischian. Burrow-like structures with young Nanosaurus skeletons suggest it may have dug burrows.
species:nanosaurus-agilis.akaNote: Othnielosaurus, Othnielia and Drinker were all once separate genera; they are now treated as Nanosaurus.

species:enneabatrachus-hechti.placeText: Como Bluff, Wyoming, and Dinosaur National Monument, Utah, USA
summary: One of the earliest true frogs from North America, known only from a hip bone a few millimetres long found in Quarry 9 at Como Bluff, and another specimen from Dinosaur National Monument. Its name means “Quarry nine frog”. Alive, it weighed only a few grams. Indeterminate remains of the genus are known from Morocco.

species:rhadinosteus-parvus.ageText: About 155 to 151 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Kimmeridgian)
species:rhadinosteus-parvus.placeText: Rainbow Park, Dinosaur National Monument, Utah, USA
summary: A small frog known from several slabs with multiple partial skeletons. It was probably a pipoid, related to today’s tongueless frogs and perhaps to the Mexican burrowing toad. Its name means “long slender bone”.

A small, long-legged land-dwelling crocodile relative, under 1 m long, with a short face and a pair of large, canine-like teeth in its lower jaw. It belonged to the shartegosuchids, a group otherwise known from Asia, and was a fast four-legged hunter on land rather than a river ambusher. It was known as the “Fruita form” until it was named in 2011.

A small, slender-limbed early crocodile relative, about 1 m long, one of the “sphenosuchians”, long-legged, fast-running land animals unlike any living crocodile. It was named in 1877 as a species of the dinosaur Nanosaurus and moved to its own genus in 1881.
Macelognathus, from the same rocks, may be the same animal; if so, Hallopus is the older name.

related.note: Perhaps the same animal.

species:macelognathus-vagans.placeText: Como Bluff, Wyoming, and Fruita, Colorado, USA
summary: A long-legged early crocodile relative with a toothless, beak-like tip to its lower jaw, a striking case of convergence with the beaked caenagnathid dinosaurs. Othniel Marsh named it in 1884 from a jaw he thought belonged to a turtle; it was later called a dinosaur, and only new bones from Fruita, described in 2005, showed it was a “sphenosuchian” crocodylomorph. It may be the same animal as Hallopus.

related.note: Perhaps the same animal.

summary: A tiny, about 20 cm long, long-legged land crocodile relative known from one skeleton found during road building at Dinosaur National Monument; it may have been a juvenile. Two rows of wide bony plates ran down its back. It is the most primitive crocodyliform of the Morrison Formation and probably ate insects and small animals.

species:galeamopus-hayi.ageText: About 155 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Kimmeridgian)
summary: A diplodocine sauropod, close to Diplodocus, known from one of the best diplodocid skeletons ever found, with its skull. It was found near Sheridan, Wyoming, in 1902 and named Diplodocus hayi in 1924; a 2015 study of diplodocid relationships showed it was distinct and gave it its own genus. A second species, Galeamopus pabsti, was named in 2017.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: William Holland, 1924 (as Diplodocus hayi); genus by Emanuel Tschopp and colleagues, 2015

summary: A relatively small sauropod, perhaps about 15 m long, found in southern Montana in 1999 and 2000 and named in 2004. It is now usually placed with the dicraeosaurids, short-necked relatives of the diplodocids best known from South America and Africa, which would make it the only one known from North America.
Its name comes from the Crow language, suuwassa, “the first thunder heard in spring”, a nod to the “thunder lizard” nickname of sauropods; the fossil was found on ancestral Crow land.

species:maraapunisaurus-fragillimus.placeText: Garden Park, near Cañon City, Colorado, USA
summary: A sauropod known only from one enormous partial backbone, found in 1877 and named by Edward Cope as Amphicoelias fragillimus. The bone was lost soon after, and survives only in Cope’s description and drawing. Taken at face value, the vertebra stood about 1.5 m tall even as preserved, and early estimates made it the longest animal ever, up to 58 m and 150 tonnes.

Those numbers are speculation. Some researchers suspect a typo in Cope’s measurements; others accept a giant. A 2018 study by Kenneth Carpenter interpreted it as a rebbachisaurid, a relative of Nigersaurus, and estimated a still enormous but more modest 30 to 35 m. Its new name comes from the Southern Ute word maraapuni, “huge”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Edward Cope, 1878 (as Amphicoelias fragillimus); genus by Kenneth Carpenter, 2018

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Very uncertain: about 30–35 m (2018 estimate); older estimates up to 58 m

species:mymoorapelta-maysi.ageText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
species:mymoorapelta-maysi.placeText: Mygatt-Moore Quarry, Mesa County, Colorado, USA
summary: A small, early armoured dinosaur, perhaps about 3 m long, the first Jurassic ankylosaur named from North America. Its name combines those of the Mygatt and Moore families, who found the quarry in 1981, with pelta, “shield”. More than 160 of its bones and armour pieces are known, and one hip bone bears bite marks.
It is usually placed among the nodosaurids or close to them, together with Gargoyleosaurus from Wyoming.

A short-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about 2.5 m, found in 1992 by a team digging up a Stegosaurus. Its species name means “unhoped-for”, because the researchers were hoping for a dinosaur, not a pterosaur. It is known from a neck bone, an upper arm bone and a few finger and foot bones, and may be closely related to, or even the same as, Mesadactylus.

A small pterosaur from the Dry Mesa Quarry. Its type specimen is a set of fused hip vertebrae so bird-like that it was at first thought to belong to a bird; its species name means “bird hip”. Wing and leg bones referred to it look like those of a short-tailed pterodactyloid, but some researchers think the hip bones came from a different pterosaur, perhaps an anurognathid.

The first pterosaur named from the Jurassic of North America, by Othniel Marsh in 1878 (first as a species of Pterodactylus). It is based on a single partial wing bone from the hand, and is usually treated as a doubtful name for an indeterminate short-tailed pterosaur. Its name means “skin finger”.

A partial skeleton described in 2002 as a long-tailed pterosaur. In 2007 its identity was questioned, and it was called an indeterminate reptile, but newer preparation of the bones suggests it really is a pterosaur. Its exact relationships remain uncertain.

species:morrolepis-schaefferi.ageText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A primitive ray-finned fish about 20 cm long, one of the coccolepidids, late survivors of the “palaeoniscoid” fish that dominated Palaeozoic waters. It swam in the rivers and lakes of the Morrison plains. Related species are known from the earliest Cretaceous of England and the Jurassic of Kazakhstan.

A filter-feeding ctenochasmatid pterosaur known from a crushed partial skeleton of a young animal, without its skull but with a complete wing and both legs. Traces of its soft wing membrane survive, including fibres that stiffened the wing, and possible webbing between its toes.
A long-necked ctenochasmatid pterosaur, one of the bristle-toothed filter feeders, known from a partial skeleton without a skull. Its name means “kite finger”. Its wingspan was perhaps 2.5 m.
The first pterosaur described from the Jehol Biota, in 1997, from wings and legs without a skull. It is placed with the filter-feeding ctenochasmatids, relatives of the South American Pterodaustro.
A ctenochasmatid pterosaur with a long, low skull lined with many fine teeth for sieving small prey from the water. Its partial skeleton preserves traces of soft tissue on the head.

One of the largest pterosaurs of the Jehol Biota, with a skull about 95 cm long, long, slender jaws with fine teeth and a low crest at the back of the head. Its wingspan was first estimated at about 7 m, but estimates for pterosaurs known mainly from skulls are very uncertain.
A very small pterodactyloid pterosaur, known from a young individual with traces of its wing membranes and body fuzz. Some researchers think it is a juvenile of another Jehol pterosaur.
A boreopterid pterosaur with a long, low skull and jaws lined with long, needle-like, interlocking teeth, probably for catching fish. Its wingspan was about 4 m.

species:hongshanornis-longicresta.ageText: About 125 to 122 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A small, long-legged early relative of modern birds, perhaps a wader, with a toothless beak. Its fossils preserve feathers, and a ridge of feathers on its head inspired its species name, “long crest”. It gives its name to the hongshanornithids.

An early long-tailed bird, a relative of Jeholornis, known from one complete but juvenile skeleton. Its jaws had no teeth, so it lost them independently of modern birds. Its long arms suggest it could fly.

related.note: A close relative.

summary: A sparrow-sized bird known from one incomplete skeleton. It was first thought to be an early relative of modern birds, but a 2012 restudy showed it was an enantiornithine, one of the “opposite birds”.

A tiny juvenile bird-like dinosaur, about 8 cm long, with a short tail of unfused vertebrae, between the long tails of early birds and the stubby tails of later ones; its name means “intermediate bird”. Some researchers have suggested it is closer to the scansoriopterygids than to birds.

species:kayrasaurus-changliensis.ageText: About 126 to 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: The largest therizinosaur known from the Jehol Biota, about 3.6 m long and 117 to 274 kg, named in 2026 from a nearly complete but very flattened skeleton with its skull. Like other therizinosaurs it had a toothless beak at the front of its jaws; behind it, its small teeth were unusually closely packed.

related.note: A smaller Yixian therizinosaur.

summary: An early ostrich-dinosaur, with a toothless beak at the tip of its jaws but still a few teeth further back, found preserved in a “death pose” with its head thrown back. Small stones in its belly were probably gizzard stones for grinding plant food.
A small troodontid with a wavy-edged snout bone, which gives it its name, “wavy nose”, and unusually large teeth for a troodontid (“big-toothed”). It was a relative of Sinovenator and Mei.

A small feathered theropod known only from its arms, shoulders and a few ribs, with feather traces. Its hands were long, with a very long third finger, which gives its species name “long hand”; it may have been a scansoriopterygid-like climber or a dromaeosaurid relative.

A dromaeosaurid about 1.65 m long known from a nearly complete skeleton with feathers. Its arms were short for a raptor, yet they carried large wings of fully formed, vaned feathers like those of birds, and it had long tail feathers too. It was probably too heavy to fly, so its wings were likely used for display, brooding or balance.

species:zhongjianosaurus-yangi.ageText: About 125 to 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: The smallest known microraptorine, a relative of Microraptor, and one of the smallest non-bird dinosaurs. It is known from a partial skeleton and shows that several kinds of small raptors lived side by side in the Jehol forests.

related.note: Its larger relative.

summary: A small lizard known from eight fossils, several with skin outlines preserved. Its species name, “spiny tail”, refers to the spiky scales on its tail. It is one of eight lizards named from the Yixian Formation.

A gliding lizard, known from one complete skeleton with skin impressions. Eight long ribs on each side supported a membrane of skin, like the “wings” of today’s Draco lizards of Southeast Asia, which it could spread to glide between trees. Its name means “flying dragon”. The skeleton may be a juvenile.

An early relative of modern birds with small teeth and a fan of tail feathers, known from a skeleton with feathers. Despite its name, which refers to the Yixian Formation, it was found in the slightly younger Jiufotang Formation. The fan-shaped tail shows that modern-style tail feathers for steering in flight had already evolved.

A pigeon-sized diving bird, first known from a single leg found in 1981 near Yumen, Gansu, and later from dozens of skeletons with webbed feet. It probably dived for food in lakes, like a grebe or loon. It is one of the oldest members of the Ornithurae, the group that includes modern birds.
An early relative of modern birds known from a partial skeleton with backbone, ribs, hips and upper legs. Named in 1993, it was one of the first birds described from the Jehol Biota.

An enantiornithine, one of the “opposite birds”, closely related to the long-snouted Longipteryx. It was first described with a hooked, hawk-like beak, but the specimen is badly preserved; restudy suggests it had a normal, toothed, long snout like its relatives.

related.note: A close relative.

summary: A sparrow-sized enantiornithine with teeth and clawed fingers, one of the first “opposite birds” found in China, named in 1992. Several other species once placed in Cathayornis have since been moved to other genera or treated as doubtful.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Zhou Zhonghe, Jin Fan and Zhang Jiangyong, 1992

species:chromeornis-funkyi.ageText: About 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: A long-snouted enantiornithine named in 2025, found with a mass of small stones in its throat. These were probably not gizzard stones; the researchers suggest the bird swallowed them because it was ill, and died trying to bring them back up.

species:imparavis-attenboroughi.ageText: About 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: An enantiornithine bird named in 2024 from a well-preserved skeleton. Its name means “odd bird”, for its unusual mix of features, and its species name honours the naturalist Sir David Attenborough.

species:plumadraco-bankoorum.ageText: About 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: A bohaiornithid enantiornithine named in 2026 from a complete skeleton with soft tissues, including a pair of long, ribbon-like tail plumes, probably for display.

species:changzhousaurus-sinensis.ageText: About 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: A very small feathered dinosaur, only 34 cm long, named in 2026 from a nearly complete skeleton with feather traces. It had large wings on its arms, smaller “wings” of long feathers on its legs, like Microraptor, and a fan of long plumes at the end of its tail. Exactly where it fits among birds and raptors is unclear.

A small, slender microraptorine raptor, a relative of Microraptor, known from parts of the skull, arms and legs. Its name means “graceful thief”. It comes from the Lujiatun beds at the base of the Yixian Formation.

species:norellraptor-barsboldi.ageText: About 125 to 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A microraptorine raptor named in 2026 from a single complete skeleton with feather impressions. Its name honours the palaeontologists Mark Norell and Rinchen Barsbold.

species:similicaudipteryx-yixianensis.ageText: About 124 to 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A caudipterid oviraptorosaur, a relative of Caudipteryx. Two juvenile specimens of different ages show that its feathers changed as it grew: young ones had ribbon-like feathers, while older ones had normal vaned feathers, evidence of moulting through a dinosaur’s life.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: He Tao, Wang Xiaolin and Zhou Zhonghe, 2008

related.note: Its close relative.

species:liaoningosaurus-paradoxus.ageText: About 125 to 119 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A very small armoured dinosaur known from more than 20 juvenile specimens, the smallest about 34 cm long. It had a bony shell over its belly, unusual for an ankylosaur. One specimen has fish remains in its gut, and its sharp teeth and claws led its describers to suggest, speculatively, that it ate fish and spent time in water, which would be unique among ornithischians.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Xu Xing, Wang Xiaolin and You Hailu, 2001

summary: A crocodile-like choristodere, one of the long-snouted aquatic reptiles that hunted fish in the Jehol lakes alongside the long-necked Hyphalosaurus. It is known from a partial skeleton.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Gao Chunling, Lü Junchang and colleagues, 2005

related.note: A long-necked choristodere from the same lakes.

species:dongoconodon-platycauda.ageText: About 125 to 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A triconodont mammal named in 2026 from a nearly complete skeleton. Signs of webbed hands and a flattened tail suggest it was semi-aquatic, swimming like a small otter or platypus. Unusually for a mammal, it replaced its teeth many times through its life.
A ctenochasmatid pterosaur with a long, low, sword-shaped skull, which gives its name, “sword-shaped head”. Like its relatives it probably sieved small prey from shallow water.

A fish-eating pterosaur with long, curved, interlocking front teeth and a tall crest rising from the top of its skull. Its name means “ghost dragon hunter”. It is an anhanguerid, related to Anhanguera of Brazil, and a coprolite (fossil dropping) with fish bones was found with it.
A toothless chaoyangopterid pterosaur, a relative of the giant azhdarchids, with a tall, narrow skull and a crest along the top. Like other azhdarchoids it may have stalked prey on the ground.

species:adamanasuchus-eisenhardtae.ageText: About 222 to 216 million years ago (Late Triassic)
species:adamanasuchus-eisenhardtae.placeText: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA
summary: An aetosaur, one of the armoured, pig-snouted plant-eating relatives of crocodiles, known from bony armour plates. The Adamana locality in Petrified Forest National Park, after which it is named, also names the Adamanian, one of the time units used to date Late Triassic land faunas.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Spencer Lucas, Adrian Hunt and Justin Spielmann, 2007

summary: An aetosaur with large, curved spikes on the armour plates along its sides. It was first named as a species of Desmatosuchus, then given the genus name Heliocanthus, which turned out to be already in use for a fish, so it was renamed Rioarribasuchus in 2007, after Rio Arriba County, New Mexico.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Kate Zeigler, Andrew Heckert and Spencer Lucas, 2003 (as Desmatosuchus chamaensis)

related.note: Its original genus.

species:avicranium-renestoi.ageText: About 213 to 203 million years ago (Late Triassic)
species:avicranium-renestoi.placeText: Coelophysis Quarry, Ghost Ranch, New Mexico, USA
summary: A drepanosaur, one of the strange tree-climbing reptiles with grasping feet and prehensile tails, known from a three-dimensional skull. The skull is remarkably bird-like, with large eyes, a domed braincase and a narrow, toothless beak-like snout, which gives it its name, “bird skull”.

related.note: A fellow drepanosaur.

species:drepanosaurus-unguicaudatus.ageText: About 215 to 205 million years ago (Late Triassic)
species:drepanosaurus-unguicaudatus.placeText: Northern Italy; also New Mexico and Arizona, USA
summary: A tree-dwelling reptile with a chameleon-like body, a prehensile tail ending in a claw, and a single enormous claw on each hand, on a forearm unlike any other animal’s. Its name means “sickle lizard”. It probably used the giant claws to hook into bark and tear it open for insects, like an anteater or pangolin, and the tail to grip branches.
It was first found in the Zorzino Limestone of northern Italy; arms of Drepanosaurus are also known from the Chinle Formation in New Mexico.

species:chinlea-sorenseni.ageText: About 225 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: A freshwater coelacanth of the mawsoniids, the family of the later giant Mawsonia, living in the rivers of the Chinle Formation, after which it is named. “Chinle” comes from a Navajo word meaning “flowing out”, for where water flows out of Canyon de Chelly.

species:chinlestegophis-jenkinsi.ageText: About 221 to 206 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: A tiny temnospondyl amphibian known from two partial skulls. Its describers proposed in 2017 that it was an early relative of caecilians, the legless burrowing amphibians alive today; if so, caecilians would be the last surviving temnospondyls. This idea is debated.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Jason Pardo, Bryan Small and Adam Huttenlocker, 2017

species:crosbysaurus-harrisae.ageText: About 220 to 205 million years ago (Late Triassic)
species:crosbysaurus-harrisae.placeText: Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Utah and North Carolina, USA
summary: An animal known only from leaf-shaped teeth. It was named in 2004 as an early ornithischian dinosaur, but after the skeleton of Revueltosaurus showed that such teeth could belong to crocodile relatives, Crosbysaurus was reinterpreted as an archosauromorph reptile of uncertain type.

related.note: Another “dinosaur” known from teeth that turned out not to be one.

species:eosphorosuchus-lacrimosa.ageText: About 205 million years ago (Late Triassic, Rhaetian)
summary: An early crocodylomorph named in 2026 from a partial skull and skeleton. It had an unusually short snout built for a strong bite. One of its toe bones is swollen where it was bitten on the foot; the injury healed before it died.

species:eotephradactylus-mcintireae.ageText: About 209 million years ago (Late Triassic, late Norian)
species:eotephradactylus-mcintireae.placeText: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA
summary: One of the oldest pterosaurs from North America, named in 2025 from part of a lower jaw, teeth and perhaps a wing bone, found in 2011 in a bonebed full of fish, turtles and early mammal relatives. Its teeth are worn as if from crunching fish. Its name means “ash-winged dawn goddess”, after the volcanic ash in the rocks.

A silesaurid, one of the slender, long-legged close relatives of dinosaurs (or, in some studies, very early ornithischians), with a deeper, stronger skull than its relatives and teeth well suited to eating plants. It comes from the northernmost outcrops of the Chinle Formation.

species:ptychotherates-bucculentus.ageText: About 210 to 205 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: An early predatory dinosaur named in 2026 from a partial skull with the deepest snout of any Triassic dinosaur. It belongs with Chindesaurus, Daemonosaurus and Tawa in a group related to Herrerasaurus.

species:sonselasuchus-cedrus.ageText: About 215 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
species:sonselasuchus-cedrus.placeText: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA
summary: A shuvosaurid, one of the toothless, beaked, two-legged crocodile relatives that looked remarkably like ostrich dinosaurs, named in 2026 from a bonebed with at least 36 individuals.

related.note: A related shuvosaurid.

species:abrictosaurus-consors.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
species:abrictosaurus-consors.placeText: Qacha’s Nek, Lesotho, and Eastern Cape, South Africa
summary: A small heterodontosaurid, about 1.2 m long and under 45 kg, one of the most primitive of these little two-legged plant-eaters. One skull has tusk-like canine teeth and the other does not, which may be a difference between males and females. Its name means “wakeful lizard”, a nod to Richard Thulborn’s idea, now rejected, that heterodontosaurs slept through dry seasons.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Richard Thulborn, 1974 (as Lycorhinus consors); genus by James Hopson, 1975

related.note: A close relative.

species:lycorhinus-angustidens.ageText: About 195 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Sinemurian)
summary: A heterodontosaurid known from a partial jaw, first described in 1924 as a cynodont because of its canine-like tusk; its name means “wolf snout”. The original jaw has degraded, and only one tooth and an impression of the rest survive, so whether it is the same animal as Heterodontosaurus is debated.

species:pegomastax-africana.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A cat-sized heterodontosaurid with a parrot-like beak and short, sharp, tusk-like canines, known from a skull found in 1966 and 1967 but only named in 2012 by Paul Sereno, who suggested it might have had a coat of porcupine-like bristles, as seen in its relative Tianyulong. Its name means “strong jaw”.

species:eocursor-parvus.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic; once thought Late Triassic)
summary: A small, fast two-legged plant-eater about 1 m long, one of the most completely known early ornithischians, with large hands. Its name means “dawn runner”. It was first thought to be Late Triassic, about 210 million years old, but the dating of its rocks is uncertain and it is now usually placed in the Early Jurassic.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Richard Butler, Roger Smith and David Norman, 2007

species:blikanasaurus-cromptoni.ageText: About 215 to 205 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: A heavily built early sauropodomorph known only from a hind leg, with short, stout foot bones. It was once thought to be one of the earliest sauropods; newer studies place it among the sauropodomorphs leading towards them, perhaps a close relative of Melanorosaurus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Peter Galton and Jacques van Heerden, 1985

species:melanorosaurus-readi.ageText: About 215 to 205 million years ago (Late Triassic)
species:melanorosaurus-readi.placeText: Thaba ’Nyama (Black Mountain), Eastern Cape, South Africa
summary: A large early sauropodomorph, perhaps about 8 m long, with massive, heavy limb bones like those of true sauropods, which suggest it walked mostly on all fours. It was probably an omnivore. Its name means “Black Mountain lizard”.

species:pulanesaura-eocollum.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: An early relative of sauropods, named in 2015 from at least two individuals. Its describers argued it was a four-legged browser that fed low down, unlike its contemporaries, and that this low-browsing lifestyle came before the long necks of later sauropods. Its name means “rain lizard” and “dawn neck”.

species:litargosuchus-leptorhynchus.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A small, slender, long-legged early crocodile relative with a narrow snout, one of the “sphenosuchians”. Its name means “fast-running crocodile”.

species:tritylodon-longaevus.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A plant-eating cynodont, a very close relative of mammals, with gnawing front teeth like a rodent’s and broad cheek teeth with three rows of cusps for grinding, which give it its name, “three-knobbed tooth”. Richard Owen named it in 1884, and it was long thought to be a mammal.

species:chiniquodon-theotonicus.ageText: About 236 to 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
species:chiniquodon-theotonicus.placeText: Argentina and Brazil; also Namibia and Madagascar
summary: A meat-eating cynodont, a close relative of the ancestors of mammals, about the size of a fox. A 2026 study estimated adults at about 12 kg and suggested, speculatively, that it gave birth to live young, unlike the egg-laying assumed for all cynodonts.

species:dinodontosaurus-brevirostris.ageText: About 240 to 230 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: A large, beaked, plant-eating dicynodont with a skull up to 40 cm long and a pair of tusks. It was one of the most common large plant-eaters of its time in South America; one site in Brazil preserves a group of youngsters together, evidence of herding.

species:gracilisuchus-stipanicicorum.ageText: About 236 to 234 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: A tiny, lightly built crocodile-line archosaur about 30 cm long, once thought to be a dinosaur relative because it could probably run on two legs. It is now placed among the suchians, near the ancestry of crocodylomorphs.

species:luperosuchus-fractus.ageText: About 237 million years ago (late Middle or early Late Triassic)
summary: One of the largest predators of the Chañares Formation, a loricatan, one of the big crocodile-line hunters once called “rauisuchians”, related to Prestosuchus and Saurosuchus. It is known mainly from a skull. Its name means “vexing crocodile”.

species:anteavis-crurilongus.ageText: About 230 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: One of the earliest theropod dinosaurs, named in 2025 from a partial skeleton and skull. Its long shins give it its species name, “long legs”, and its genus name means “before birds”.

A large shuvosaurid, a toothless, two-legged crocodile relative that looked like an ostrich dinosaur, with a thigh bone 47 cm long, which suggests it was very large, perhaps about 9 m long (a rough estimate). Its species name means “long neck”.

One of the largest Triassic predatory dinosaurs, a relative of Coelophysis, and the best known Triassic theropod from Europe. Its two partial skeletons suggest about 5 m, but they seem to be young animals; fragments suggest adults may have reached 7 to 9 m.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Friedrich von Huene, 1934 (as Halticosaurus liliensterni); genus by Samuel Welles, 1984

species:ruehleia-bedheimensis.ageText: About 216 to 208 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: An early sauropodomorph known from one nearly complete skeleton found in 1952, long thought to be a Plateosaurus. Peter Galton named it in 2001 after the palaeontologist Hugo Rühle von Lilienstern.
A tritylodontid, a plant-eating close relative of mammals, very like Kayentatherium from the same rocks but smaller, with different teeth.

related.note: Its larger relative.

species:eopneumatosuchus-colberti.placeText: Near the Grand Canyon, Arizona, USA
summary: An early crocodyliform known from the back of a skull with unusually large air spaces in the bones, which give it its name, “dawn air-filled crocodile”. Like other early crocodyliforms it was probably a small land animal.

A small predatory dinosaur known from a partial hind leg and hip of a young animal, named in 2010. It was described as a tetanuran; some researchers think it may instead be a young coelophysoid, a relative of Coelophysis.

A crow-sized feathered dinosaur, related to Anchiornis, with a bony crest along its snout. Microscopic pigment structures (melanosomes) in its neck feathers are flat and arranged like those that make iridescent colours in hummingbird feathers, so it probably had shimmering, rainbow-like plumage on its head and neck. Its name means “rainbow with a big crest” in Mandarin.
It also had the oldest known asymmetrical feathers, in its tail, a feature later used in flight by birds.

related.note: A close relative from the same rocks.

species:pulaosaurus-qinglong.ageText: About 165 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: A small two-legged plant-eating dinosaur named in 2025 from a nearly complete skeleton with its skull and impressions of soft tissue. Remarkably, it preserves parts of its voice box (larynx), one of very few non-bird dinosaurs to do so; its structure suggests it may have made bird-like calls. It is the first neornithischian named from the Yanliao Biota.

A gliding mammal relative, a euharamiyid, with a furry skin membrane stretched between its limbs like a modern flying squirrel. It probably glided between trees and ate seeds and other plant parts, grinding them between molars that worked like a double mortar and pestle, which gives its species name. Its name means “glider tooth”.

species:archaeoistiodactylus-linglongtae.ageText: About 165 to 160 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A small pterosaur known from a partial skeleton. It was first described as an early relative of the Cretaceous istiodactylids, which gave it its name, but later study showed it was a wukongopterid, perhaps even a specimen of Darwinopterus.

related.note: It may belong to Darwinopterus.

species:changchengopterus-pani.ageText: About 165 to 160 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A small long-tailed pterosaur known from a skeleton without a skull. It was named in 2009; later studies suggest it may be a wukongopterid, a relative of Darwinopterus.

species:fenghuangopterus-lii.ageText: About 165 to 160 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A long-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about 1 m, known from a nearly complete skeleton with its skull. It belongs to the scaphognathines, relatives of Scaphognathus of the Solnhofen limestone. Its name means “phoenix wing”, after Phoenix Mountain near Chaoyang.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Lü Junchang, Fucha Xiaohui and Chen Jinmin, 2010

species:qinglongopterus-guoi.ageText: About 165 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: A small long-tailed pterosaur known from a nearly complete skeleton. It is a rhamphorhynchine, very close to Rhamphorhynchus of the much younger Solnhofen limestone, showing that this group was already widespread in the Middle Jurassic.

species:agilisaurus-louderbacki.ageText: About 168 to 164 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A small, two-legged plant-eating dinosaur about 1.2 to 1.7 m long and about 40 kg, known from one of the most complete small ornithischian skeletons from the Jurassic, found in 1984 during construction of the Zigong Dinosaur Museum. Its name means “agile lizard”. Its leaf-shaped teeth had wavy enamel, a feature once thought unique to hadrosaurs.

species:hexinlusaurus-multidens.ageText: About 170 to 165 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A small two-legged plant-eater, about 1.8 m long, first named as a species of Yandusaurus in 1983 and given its own genus in 2005, named after the palaeontologist He Xinlu. Its species name means “many teeth”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: He Xinlu and Cai Kaiji, 1983 (as Yandusaurus multidens); genus by Paul Barrett and colleagues, 2005

species:yandusaurus-hongheensis.ageText: About 168 to 162 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A small two-legged plant-eating dinosaur about 1.5 m long, named in 1979 from a partial skeleton found near Zigong, a city known as Yandu, the “salt capital”, for its ancient salt wells. The 2025 Morrison dinosaur Enigmacursor was found to be its closest relative.

related.note: Its closest known relative, from North America.

species:abrosaurus-dongpoi.ageText: About 168 to 164 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A small, early macronarian sauropod, no more than about 9 m long, with a boxy skull topped by a tall bony arch around the nostrils, a little like a small Camarasaurus. Its skull has large openings separated by thin struts, which gives it its name, “delicate lizard”. Its species name honours the 11th-century Sichuanese poet Su Dongpo.

species:xuanhanosaurus-qilixiaensis.ageText: About 166 million years ago (Middle Jurassic, Bathonian)
summary: A predatory dinosaur, perhaps about 4.5 m long, known from a partial skeleton with strong arms. Dong Zhiming, who named it, suggested it might have walked on all fours, but this is now rejected. It is an early tetanuran, perhaps an early allosauroid.

species:kaijiangosaurus-lini.ageText: About 168 to 164 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A medium-sized predatory dinosaur known from neck vertebrae and some limb bones. It may be the same animal as Gasosaurus from the same rocks.

related.note: Perhaps the same animal.

species:angustinaripterus-longicephalus.ageText: About 168 to 164 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A long-tailed pterosaur known from a long skull with narrow nostrils, which give it its name, and long, interlocking fang-like teeth for catching fish. Its wingspan was perhaps about 1.6 m.

species:bashanosaurus-primitivus.ageText: About 168 million years ago (Middle Jurassic, Bathonian)
summary: One of the oldest and most primitive stegosaurs, named in 2022 from three partial skeletons. It was a small stegosaur, perhaps about 2.8 m long, with plates and spines along its back like its relative Huayangosaurus.

related.note: A close relative from the same rocks.

summary: A slender stegosaur about 4 m long, known from a partial skeleton without a skull; it may have been a young animal. It was the first stegosaur described from China, by Yang Zhongjian in 1959.

A stegosaur known from a partial skeleton found in 1983, with back plates and a large shoulder spine like that of Gigantspinosaurus. Its description in 1994 was little known outside China for many years.

related.note: Another stegosaur with big shoulder spines.

summary: A small sauropod known only from a partial juvenile skeleton. It has been compared to Bellusaurus, and some researchers think it may simply be a young mamenchisaurid.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Ye Yong, Gao Yuhui and Jiang Shan, 2005

species:bellusaurus-sui.ageText: About 162 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Oxfordian)
summary: A small sauropod known from the bones of at least 17 juveniles, each about 4.8 m long, found together in one quarry, perhaps a herd drowned in a flood. It was once thought to be a relative of Camarasaurus; a 2018 restudy placed it close to the neosauropods.
A sauropod, probably a mamenchisaurid, named in 1937 by Yang Zhongjian from a partial skeleton found by the Sino-Swedish Expedition of the 1920s and 1930s. It was perhaps about 12 m long.

One of the earliest ceratopsians, about the size of a spaniel, with a sculpted, wrinkled surface to its skull bones. It lived alongside Yinlong, another early ceratopsian, showing that the horned dinosaurs had already split into different lines by the Late Jurassic.

related.note: Another early ceratopsian from the same rocks.

species:junggarsuchus-sloani.ageText: About 163 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: A long-legged, running early crocodile relative about 1 m long, one of the “sphenosuchians”. A second, more complete skull described in 2022 showed it had a strongly built, rigid skull, a step towards the skull of modern crocodiles, even though it lived on land and walked upright.

species:kryptodrakon-progenitor.ageText: About 163 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: The oldest known pterodactyloid, the group of short-tailed pterosaurs that later produced the giants. It is known from a partial skeleton with a wingspan of about 1.5 m. Its name means “hidden dragon”, a nod to the film Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, parts of which were filmed nearby. It lived inland, near rivers, suggesting pterodactyloids first evolved away from the sea.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Brian Andres, James Clark and Xu Xing, 2014

species:sericipterus-wucaiwanensis.ageText: About 162 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Oxfordian)
summary: A large long-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about 1.7 m, long fang-like teeth and a crest on its snout. Its name means “silk wing”, after the Silk Road that passed through Xinjiang.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Brian Andres, James Clark and Xu Xing, 2010

species:avimimus-portentosus.ageText: About 72 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, long-legged oviraptorosaur about 1.5 m long with a short, toothless, bird-like beak, named “bird mimic” for its many bird-like features. Sergei Kurzanov, who named it in 1981, thought a ridge on its forearm anchored feathers, one of the first such suggestions for a non-bird dinosaur; feathered oviraptorosaurs found since make that very likely. A bonebed in the Nemegt Formation suggests it lived in flocks.

species:breviceratops-kozlowskii.ageText: About 72 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, hornless protoceratopsid known from several young individuals, first named as a species of Protoceratops in 1975. Its name means “short horned face”. Some researchers suspect it is a juvenile of Bagaceratops.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska, 1975 (as Protoceratops kozlowskii); genus by Sergei Kurzanov, 1990

summary: A rat-sized multituberculate, one of the rodent-like mammals that thrived alongside the dinosaurs. A study of its ankle found a spur like the venomous spur of a male platypus, so some early mammals may have been venomous (an idea that is still speculative).

species:nemegtbaatar-gobiensis.ageText: About 76 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small multituberculate mammal known from skulls, named after the Nemegt Valley and Ulaanbaatar. Studies of its braincase suggest it had a keen sense of smell.

species:ceratonykus-oculatus.ageText: About 72 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small alvarezsaurid, one of the bird-like dinosaurs with stubby, single-clawed arms, perhaps for breaking into insect nests. It is known from a fragmentary skeleton with part of the skull. Its describers suggested alvarezsaurs might not be theropods at all, a view that has not been accepted.

species:gobipteryx-minuta.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A toothless enantiornithine, one of the “opposite birds”, known from skulls. Embryos found in eggs nearby, perhaps of Gobipteryx, were well developed with wing feathers, suggesting chicks could fly or run soon after hatching.

species:quaesitosaurus-orientalis.ageText: About 72 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A titanosaur known only from a long, low, horse-like skull with peg-like teeth at the front, much like a Diplodocus skull. It is a relative of Nemegtosaurus, also known only from its skull, and may even be the same animal. Its name means “extraordinary lizard”.

species:tylocephale-gilmorei.ageText: About 72 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A dome-headed dinosaur known from a partial skull found in 1971 by a Polish–Mongolian expedition. Its dome was tall and narrow, perhaps the tallest of any pachycephalosaur. Its name means “swollen head”.

species:zaraapelta-nomadis.ageText: About 72 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An ankylosaurid known from a single skull with an unusual pattern of bony knobs and ridges around the eyes and horns at the back of the head. Its name means “hedgehog shield”. It was closely related to Tarchia.

A small predatory dinosaur, perhaps 3 to 4 m long, known from a jaw, hips and leg bones. Its name means “small predator” in Mongolian. It is probably an early tyrannosauroid, though one study suggested the bones came from more than one kind of animal.

A slender troodontid known from leg and foot bones. Its name comes from the borogoves, creatures in Lewis Carroll’s poem “Jabberwocky”. Its second toe claw was straighter than that of other troodontids.

species:gurilynia-nessovi.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A fairly large enantiornithine, one of the “opposite birds”, known from fragments of the shoulder and wing. Its species name honours the Russian palaeontologist Lev Nessov.

A bony-tongued fish, a relative of today’s arowanas and arapaima, and the only fish known from the Nemegt Formation. Several fairly complete skeletons are known. It was named in 2022; before that its remains were thought to belong to another genus.
A small, flightless diving bird, a hesperornithine, known from a single vertebra. Unlike its sea-going relatives, it lived inland, in the rivers and estuaries of the Nemegt.

An alvarezsaurid named in 2025 from a partial skeleton with the most complete arm known from any parvicursorine. Like its relatives it had one huge claw on each short, sturdy arm, and some unusual bones in its hand; its name means “grasping claw”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Alexander Averianov, Alexey Lopatin and Atuchin, 2025

species:duonychus-tsogtbaatari.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A therizinosaur with only two fingers on each hand instead of the usual three, named in 2025. One of its huge curved claws still has its horny sheath preserved, which made the claw noticeably longer and more curved than the bone alone. The claws were probably used to pull branches towards its mouth.

species:enigmosaurus-mongoliensis.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A therizinosaur known mainly from a well-preserved hip with the broad, backward-turned pubis typical of these pot-bellied plant-eaters. Its name means “enigma lizard”, because when it was named, therizinosaurs were a puzzle whose relationships no one understood.

species:erlikosaurus-andrewsi.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A therizinosaur, about 3.5 m long, known from one of the few complete therizinosaur skulls, with a toothless beak at the front of its jaws and small leaf-shaped teeth behind. CT scans of its braincase showed keen senses of smell, hearing and balance. It is named after Erlik, a god of death in Mongolian mythology.

related.note: A larger relative from the same rocks.

species:segnosaurus-galbinensis.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A large therizinosaur, perhaps 6 to 7 m long, known from several partial skeletons found in the 1970s. Its strange mix of features (a beaked, toothed jaw, broad hips and four-toed feet) puzzled scientists for decades; it was variously thought to be a fish-eater, a prosauropod relative or a link between groups, and gave its name to the old group “segnosaurs”. It is now known to be a plant-eating relative of birds. Its name means “slow lizard”.

species:erketu-ellisoni.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A sauropod with one of the longest necks for its body size of any dinosaur. Its neck vertebrae are extremely long; the neck may have been around 8 m, perhaps half its total length. It is a somphospondylan, a relative of the titanosaurs, and is named after Erketü, a creator god in Mongolian mythology.

species:garudimimus-brevipes.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An ostrich-dinosaur about 3.5 m long, with shorter legs than its later relatives, which gives its species name, “short foot”. It was once restored with a small horn on its head, but that was a misplaced skull bone. It is named after Garuda, the bird-like creature of Hindu and Buddhist mythology.

species:graciliceratops-mongoliensis.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, slender neoceratopsian about 1 m long, known from a juvenile skeleton with a small frill. It may have been able to run on two legs. Its name means “slender horned face”.

A mid-sized tyrannosauroid, about 4 m long and roughly 750 kg, named in 2025 from two partial skeletons found in 1972 and 1973 and first thought to belong to Alectrosaurus. Its name means “dragon prince”: its describers found it to be one of the closest relatives of the giant tyrannosaurids, and suggested their ancestors crossed from Asia to North America and back.
A small zhelestid mammal, from a group of early placental-line mammals with teeth suited to a mixed diet, named in 2025 from a partial lower jaw.

species:talarurus-plicatospineus.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An ankylosaurid about 5 to 6 m long, with a tail club, known from several partial skeletons first found in 1948 by a Soviet expedition. Its name means “wicker tail”, after the basket-like lattice of bony tendons that stiffened its tail.

species:tsagantegia-longicranialis.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An ankylosaurid known from a skull with an unusually long snout and flat armour plates on its face, unlike other ankylosaurs.

species:minotaurasaurus-ramachandrani.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An ankylosaurid with backward-curving horns on its skull, which inspired its name, “Minotaur lizard”. The skull was sold to a private collector and is suspected to have been exported illegally from Mongolia. Some researchers think it is the same animal as Tarchia.

species:udanoceratops-tschizhovi.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: The largest leptoceratopsid, perhaps 4 m long, with a deep, heavy skull and a low frill. It is one of the few leptoceratopsids from Asia; most lived in North America.
A small, short-headed crocodile relative known from fragmentary remains, too incomplete to place precisely within the crocodylomorphs.

species:gilmoreosaurus-mongoliensis.ageText: About 96 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A duck-billed dinosaur relative about 6 to 8 m long, a hadrosauroid close to the true hadrosaurids, from bonebeds found by the American Museum of Natural History in 1923. Its bones are among the dinosaur bones in which tumours have been found. It is named after the palaeontologist Charles Gilmore.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Charles Gilmore, 1933 (as Mandschurosaurus mongoliensis); genus by Michael Brett-Surman, 1979

species:sonidosaurus-saihangaobiensis.ageText: About 90 to 85 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small titanosaur about 9 m long, found in 2001. It is named after the Sonid region of Inner Mongolia.

species:parahesperornis-alexi.ageText: About 85 to 82 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A flightless, toothed diving bird, smaller than its relative Hesperornis, known from one of the most complete hesperornithine skeletons, with its skull. It swam with its feet in the shallows of the Western Interior Seaway, hunting fish.

The oldest known chasmosaurine, the long-frilled branch of the horned dinosaurs that later produced Triceratops. It is known from parts of the frill and horns; its frill had a scalloped edge and its brow horns were probably fairly large. Its species name, tyrannus, means “tyrant”.

species:lokiceratops-rangiformis.ageText: About 78 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: A centrosaurine horned dinosaur, about 6.7 m long and 4.9 tonnes, with no nose horn but a pair of huge, curved, blade-like spikes at the back of its frill, the largest frill spikes of any ceratopsid. Its name comes from the Norse god Loki and his curved blades, and rangiformis means “reindeer-shaped”, for its antler-like spikes.

It was found on private land in 2019, bought by a Danish museum and named in 2024. Four other horned dinosaurs are known from the same layers, more than from any other place, suggesting that their elaborate frills helped each species recognise its own kind.

A horned dinosaur known only from a pair of brow horn cores and part of the back of a skull, named by Othniel Marsh in 1888. It is too incomplete to tell apart from its relatives and is treated as a doubtful name. Even so, it is important: the whole horned-dinosaur group, Ceratopsia, and the family Ceratopsidae are named after it.

species:monoclonius-crassus.ageText: About 77 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: One of the first horned dinosaurs named, by Edward Cope in 1876, from frill and other bones. For decades many centrosaurine skulls were called Monoclonius, and it was often shown in old books as a single-horned dinosaur. Its type fossils come from young animals and cannot be told apart from Centrosaurus or its relatives, so it is now treated as a doubtful name.

related.note: Probably the same as, or close to, Centrosaurus.

summary: One of the first dinosaurs named from North America, by Joseph Leidy in 1856, from a handful of teeth that later turned out to be a mix of duck-billed and horned dinosaur teeth. For about 80 years “Trachodon” was the standard name for duck-billed dinosaurs in museums and books, including the famous “Trachodon mummy”, now Edmontosaurus. Today it is treated as a doubtful name.

related.note: The “Trachodon mummy” is now Edmontosaurus.

summary: A tyrannosaurid named by Joseph Leidy in 1868 from front teeth that lack serrations. Many later tyrannosaur fossils were lumped into it, but the teeth probably belong to young tyrannosaurids such as Daspletosaurus or Gorgosaurus, and it is generally treated as a doubtful name.

species:cryodrakon-boreas.ageText: About 77 to 74 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A giant azhdarchid pterosaur, a relative of Quetzalcoatlus. Its bones were found from 1972 onwards and long called Quetzalcoatlus, until a 2019 study named them Cryodrakon, the “frozen dragon”, after Canada’s cold climate today. Its wingspan was about 5 m in a young individual, and a large neck bone suggests adults reached perhaps 10 m. It probably stalked prey on the ground like a giant stork.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: David Hone, Michael Habib and François Therrien, 2019

facts.label: Wingspan
facts.value: About 5 m (young); adults perhaps up to 10 m

related.note: Its giant relative from Texas.

summary: An elasmosaurid plesiosaur, one of the long-necked marine reptiles, found in river deposits far up the coastal plain rather than in the sea. Its name means “river swimmer”. It and other plesiosaur fossils from the same rocks show these animals regularly swam up rivers from the Western Interior Seaway, perhaps to feed.

species:panoplosaurus-mirus.ageText: About 76 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A nodosaurid, an armoured dinosaur without a tail club, about 5 to 7 m long, with a broad, heavily armoured head and bony plates over its neck and back. Its name means “well-armoured lizard”. It lived alongside the similar Edmontonia and is one of its closest relatives.

related.note: A close relative from the same rocks.

summary: A small ostrich-dinosaur known from a partial skeleton found in 1934 and once thought to be Struthiomimus. It was renamed in 2016; its name means “ratite prophet”, because its build foreshadowed today’s flightless ratite birds such as the ostrich.

species:richardoestesia-gilmorei.ageText: About 77 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:richardoestesia-gilmorei.placeText: Alberta, Canada, and the western USA
summary: A small predatory dinosaur known from jaws and many teeth. The teeth are tiny, straight and very finely serrated, and some researchers have suggested it ate fish. It is now mostly used as a name for a type of tooth, and the teeth called Richardoestesia may come from several different animals. It is named after the palaeontologist Richard Estes.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Philip Currie, Keith Rigby and Robert Sloan, 1990

summary: A centrosaurine horned dinosaur with a crown of small spikes around the edge of its frill, which gives it its name, “crown lizard”. It is known from two bonebeds with many individuals, found by Philip Currie, and was first named as a species of Centrosaurus in 2005.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Michael Ryan and Anthony Russell, 2005 (as Centrosaurus brinkmani); genus 2012

species:wendiceratops-pinhornensis.placeText: Pinhorn Grazing Reserve, southern Alberta, Canada
summary: An early centrosaurine horned dinosaur, about 6 m long, with forward-curling hooks on its frill. It was found in 2010 by fossil hunter Wendy Sloboda, after whom it is named, and its bonebed contained at least four individuals. It suggests that a nose horn evolved early in the group.

species:tromerosaurus-solumons.ageText: About 78 to 76 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: A tyrannosaurid named in 2026 from at least three partial skulls and skeletons, one from the Oldman Formation once thought to be Daspletosaurus, and two from the Dinosaur Park Formation once assigned to another tyrannosaur. It belongs to the albertosaurines, the more lightly built tyrannosaurids.
A small leptoceratopsid, about 2.5 m long, known from a skeleton almost 80% complete. It had a beak and a tiny frill, and could probably walk on two legs or four. Its name means “cherry face”.
An ankylosaurid with a tail club, known from a partial skull and skeleton. Its name comes from the Blackfoot word for “large stone”. Some researchers think it may be the same animal as Scolosaurus.
A small azhdarchoid pterosaur with a wingspan of about 2.5 m, known from a partial skeleton found inland. It was first described as an azhdarchid, but may belong to another group of azhdarchoids.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Kevin Padian, Armand de Ricqlès and Jack Horner, 1995

summary: Known from three bones of an elbow, Piksi was described in 2002 as a large, chicken-like ground bird; its name means “strange-elbowed big bird”, from the Blackfoot piksi, “chicken”. A 2012 restudy showed the bones most likely belonged to a small pterosaur instead.

species:brontotholus-harmoni.ageText: About 76 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: A dome-headed dinosaur named in 2025 from several partial domes found in Montana and Alberta. Its name means “thunder dome”.

A chicken-sized alvarezsaurid, the oldest known from North America, known from arm and leg bones of several individuals, most from a bonebed dominated by Albertosaurus. Its short, powerful arms were made for digging, but too short for burrowing, so it probably broke into termite nests in rotting wood.

A slender ostrich-dinosaur, about 135 kg, whose name means “emu mimic”. It had large eyes and long legs and was once thought to be one of the fastest dinosaurs. Many researchers treat it as the same animal as Ornithomimus edmontonicus; others keep it separate.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: William Parks, 1926 (as Struthiomimus brevitertius); genus by Dale Russell, 1972

related.note: Perhaps the same animal.

species:alaskacephale-gangloffi.ageText: About 70 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:alaskacephale-gangloffi.placeText: Colville River, North Slope, Alaska, USA
summary: An Arctic dome-headed dinosaur known from a single skull bone with two rows of bony knobs, found in 1999. It lived well north of the Arctic Circle, through months of winter darkness. It was a close relative of Pachycephalosaurus.

species:camurodon-borealis.ageText: About 72 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A multituberculate, one of the rodent-like mammals that lived alongside dinosaurs in the Arctic, named in 2026 from four teeth.

species:infernogallus-jamesi.ageText: About 67 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A turkey-sized caenagnathid, a toothless, beaked relative of Anzu and the oviraptors, weighing about 11 kg, named in 2026 from a partial skull and skeleton and bones from many Hell Creek sites. Its name means “chicken from hell”, a nod to Anzu’s nickname; the species honours James William Boyd, grandfather of one of its describers.

Its jaw muscles were arranged in a way seen in no other non-bird dinosaur but matched by living fruit-eating parrots, so its describers argue it was the first known dinosaur specialised for eating fruit. This is worked out from the shape of its skull alone: no fruit, seeds or stomach contents have been found with it.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably fruit, judged from parrot-like jaw muscles (not direct evidence)

related.note: Its larger relative, the original “chicken from hell”.

species:platytholus-clemensi.ageText: About 67 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A medium-sized dome-headed dinosaur named in 2023 from a partial skull with an unusually flat-topped dome. It lived alongside the smaller Sphaerotholus and the larger Pachycephalosaurus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Jack Horner, Mark Goodwin and David Evans, 2023

species:protungulatum-donnae.ageText: About 66 to 64 million years ago (end of the Cretaceous to early Paleocene)
summary: A small, rat-sized mammal, perhaps one of the earliest placental mammals and an early relative of hoofed mammals; its name means “first ungulate”. It may have lived just before the asteroid impact, though some of its fossils may have been reworked into older rocks from just after it. A 2013 study suggested it was the earliest placental, but this is debated.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Robert Sloan and Leigh Van Valen, 1965

summary: The first horned dinosaur known from more than teeth, named by Edward Cope in 1872 from hips, back vertebrae and ribs; its name means “great wonder”, and it was thought to be the largest land animal then known. It is probably Triceratops, but the bones cannot prove it, so it is treated as a doubtful name. A famous 1897 painting by Charles Knight showed it with a spiky Styracosaurus-like frill.

related.note: Probably the same animal.

species:nedoceratops-hatcheri.ageText: About 67 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A horned dinosaur known from a single skull with no nose horn and a frill with unusual holes. It was first named Diceratops (“two-horned face”) in 1905, but that name was taken. Whether it is a distinct animal, a Triceratops with injuries or old-age changes, or a growth stage linking Triceratops and Torosaurus is still debated.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Richard Lull, 1905 (as Diceratops hatcheri); renamed by Andrey Ukrainsky, 2007

related.note: Perhaps the same animal.

species:nanocuris-improvida.ageText: About 68 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:nanocuris-improvida.placeText: Saskatchewan, Canada; Wyoming and Montana, USA
