summary: A small, meat-eating mammal with slicing teeth like a tiny cat’s. First thought to be a placental relative, it is now known to be a deltatheroidan, an early relative of marsupials, and one of the last of its group in North America before the asteroid impact.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Richard Fox, Craig Scott and Harold Bryant, 2007

summary: A bird known from a shoulder bone, named by Othniel Marsh in 1892. Its relationships have been debated; it is now usually placed among early ornithurine birds, outside the modern groups. Similar bones are known from Alberta.
A hesperornithine, a toothed diving bird, known from scrappy remains found in river deposits, showing that some of these sea birds lived in fresh water. Its name means “river bird”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Andrzej Elżanowski, Gregory Paul and Thomas Stidham, 2001

species:angulomastacator-daviesi.placeText: Big Bend National Park, Texas, USA
summary: A crested duck-billed dinosaur (lambeosaurine) known from a single upper jaw bone with an unusual sharp downward bend. Its name means “bend chewer”, referring both to the jaw and to the Big Bend region where it was found.

A toothed sea bird known from fused hip vertebrae, named by Othniel Marsh in 1873. For a century other bones, actually from Ichthyornis, were wrongly put with it, which gave it a false reputation as a tern-like bird. It is now known only from its type specimen and is a close relative of Ichthyornis.

related.note: A close relative.

species:claosaurus-agilis.ageText: About 87 to 82 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A primitive duck-billed dinosaur relative, about 3.5 m long, known from a partial skeleton found by Othniel Marsh in 1871 in sea chalk; its carcass must have floated out to sea. Its name means “broken lizard”, after the jumbled position of its bones. It is one of the oldest hadrosauroids from North America.

species:niobrarasaurus-coleii.ageText: About 87 to 82 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A nodosaurid armoured dinosaur, about 5 to 6.5 m long, found in 1930 in chalk laid down far out in the Western Interior Seaway, hundreds of kilometres from land. Its body must have drifted out to sea, perhaps bloated, before sinking. It was probably a close relative of Nodosaurus.

species:hierosaurus-sternbergii.ageText: About 87 to 82 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A nodosaurid known from armour plates found by Charles H. Sternberg in 1908 in sea chalk. It is usually treated as a doubtful name, though it may be the same animal as Niobrarasaurus.
A slender, eel-like marine fish with a long snout, one of the dercetids, relatives of today’s lizardfish, with rows of bony scutes along its body. Only two specimens are known.

A mysterious marine ray-finned fish known from one poorly preserved specimen, so hard to classify that it was given its own family and order. Some researchers think it is a late-surviving member of a group otherwise known from older rocks.

species:alnashetri-cerropoliciensis.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A tiny, slender alvarezsauroid, an early relative of the stubby-armed termite-eaters, known first from leg bones and later from a much more complete skeleton with a skull. Its name means “slender thighs” in the local Tehuelche language.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Peter Makovicky, Sebastián Apesteguía and Federico Gianechini, 2012

species:antusuchus-rionegrinus.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A small peirosaurid, a land-dwelling crocodile relative, named in 2026. Its skull was only 11.5 cm long, about half the size of the next smallest peirosaurid. Its blade-like, serrated teeth show it was a meat-eater, and two individuals found close together hint that it may have lived in groups.

species:avitabatrachus-uliana.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A frog related to today’s clawed frogs and Surinam toads (pipids), aquatic frogs that live in Africa and South America, a distribution that dates back to when the two continents were joined.

species:campananeyen-fragilissimus.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A rebbachisaurid sauropod, a broad-mouthed relative of Nigersaurus, named in 2024 from a fragmentary skeleton. Its species name, “most fragile”, refers to the delicate, air-filled bones of its backbone.

species:rayososaurus-agrioensis.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A rebbachisaurid sauropod named by José Bonaparte in 1996 from a shoulder blade, thigh bone and shin. Limaysaurus was once placed in Rayososaurus as a second species.

related.note: Once considered a species of Rayososaurus.

species:jakapil-kaniukura.ageText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A small, early armoured dinosaur about 1.5 m long that probably walked on two legs, with rows of bony plates on its back and a short, deep jaw with leaf-shaped teeth. Named in 2022, it showed that primitive two-legged thyreophorans, like the Early Jurassic Scutellosaurus, survived into the Cretaceous in South America. Its name means “shield bearer” in the Puelche language.

related.note: A much older two-legged armoured dinosaur.

species:gualicho-shinyae.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A predatory dinosaur about 6 to 7 m long with tiny, two-fingered arms, much like a tyrannosaur’s, though it was not related to them. It probably belongs to an unusual group, perhaps with Deltadromeus of North Africa. Its name comes from Gualichu, a spirit of the Tehuelche people, because the dig was plagued by bad luck; its species name honours Akiko Shinya, who found it.

species:taurovenator-violantei.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A large carcharodontosaurid, a relative of Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus, first known from a single skull bone above the eye, which gives it its name, “bull hunter”. Later finds added more of its skeleton. It may be the same animal as Mapusaurus.

related.note: Perhaps the same animal.

species:tralkasaurus-cuyi.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A medium-sized abelisaurid, about 4 m long, named in 2020 from part of a skull and skeleton. Its name means “thunder lizard” in Mapuche. It shows that small and medium abelisaurids lived alongside the giant carcharodontosaurids.

species:bustingorrytitan-shiva.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A huge titanosaur named in 2023 from a partial skeleton, comparable in size to Argentinosaurus and Patagotitan. Its species name refers to Shiva, the Hindu god of destruction, and the genus honours the Bustingorry family, who owned the land where it was found.

related.note: Another giant titanosaur from the same rocks.

species:chucarosaurus-diripienda.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A large titanosaur named in 2023 from limb and hip bones. Its long, slender limbs suggest it was more lightly built than Argentinosaurus. Its name means “indomitable reptile”, and its species name, “to be plundered”, refers to fossil thieves who damaged the site.

species:chubutisaurus-insignis.ageText: About 103 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A large sauropod, perhaps about 18 to 23 m long (estimates vary), a somphospondylan, an early relative of the titanosaurs. It was found in 1961 by a farmer, and teeth of a large predator were found among its bones.

species:genyodectes-serus.ageText: About 112 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A predatory dinosaur known from the front of a snout with long, blade-like teeth, named in 1901, the first theropod named from Argentina. A 2004 restudy showed it was very like Ceratosaurus, a rare Cretaceous member of that family.

species:amargatitanis-macni.ageText: About 129 to 123 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A sauropod known from part of a hind leg, hip and two vertebrae, found by José Bonaparte in 1983. It was first thought to be a titanosaur, but newer studies show it was a dicraeosaurid, a relative of Amargasaurus from the same rocks.

species:ligabueino-andesi.ageText: About 129 to 123 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A tiny noasaurid theropod known from a fragmentary juvenile skeleton about 70 to 80 cm long. It is named after the Italian doctor and explorer Giancarlo Ligabue, who funded the expedition.

species:neuquensaurus-australis.ageText: About 83 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, armoured saltasaurine titanosaur, about 7 to 9 m long, closely related to Saltasaurus, with bony plates in its skin. Richard Lydekker described it in 1893 as a species of Titanosaurus, making it one of the first titanosaurs known from Argentina.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Richard Lydekker, 1893 (as Titanosaurus australis); genus by Jaime Powell, 1992

species:laplatasaurus-araukanicus.ageText: About 80 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A titanosaur named in 1929 by Friedrich von Huene. Many bones from Argentina, India and elsewhere were once lumped into it, but only its type specimen is now accepted. It is named after La Plata, home of the museum where it is kept.

species:chadititan-calvoi.ageText: About 80 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: A small, slender-limbed rinconsaurian titanosaur named in 2025 from several partial skeletons. Its name means “titan of the salt”.

species:patagopelta-cristata.ageText: About 72 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small armoured dinosaur, perhaps 2 to 3 m long, named in 2022 from teeth, bones and armour, with a crest-like ridge on its neck armour. First described as a nodosaurid, it is now thought to be a parankylosaur, a relative of Stegouros and Kunbarrasaurus, the southern group of ankylosaurs.

related.note: A parankylosaur relative from Chile.

species:quilmesaurus-curriei.ageText: About 72 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An abelisaurid known from a thigh bone and shin, probably a close relative of Carnotaurus. Its name honours the Quilmes people, who resisted Spanish conquest, and its species name the palaeontologist Philip Currie.

species:ferugliotherium-windhauseni.ageText: About 72 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small mammal known from teeth and jaw fragments, first thought to be a multituberculate. It is now placed with the gondwanatheres, a mysterious group of grinding-toothed mammals of the southern continents.

A large land-dwelling crocodile relative, about 3.5 m long and 250 kg, named in 2025 from a well-preserved skull and skeleton. It was a peirosaurid with a broad, powerful skull and large conical teeth, an apex predator that could probably tackle medium-sized dinosaurs. Its species name means “fierce”.
An unenlagiine, a long-snouted southern raptor relative, named in 2026 from fragmentary remains, one of the southernmost of its group.

A platypus relative known from a single lower molar on a piece of jaw, named in 2023, the oldest platypus-family fossil from South America and one of only a few Cretaceous monotremes known outside Australia. It is estimated at about 1.6 kg.

A tuatara relative known from a fragment of a tooth-bearing jaw, named in 2024 as a member of the same subfamily as the living tuatara. Later researchers questioned which bone it is, and how close it is to the tuatara.
A very large titanosaur, perhaps 20 to 28 m long, known from a huge forelimb described by Richard Lydekker in 1893. Its name means “silver lizard”, after Argentina, “land of silver”.

species:patagoniaemys-gasparinae.ageText: About 72 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A large stem turtle with an oval, pitted shell, a relative of the horned meiolaniid turtles. A second species was named in 2026.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Juliana Sterli and Marcelo de la Fuente, 2011

summary: A small mammal known from one blade-like lower premolar with eight cusps, about 4 mm long. It may be a multituberculate, which would make it one of very few from South America, but this is uncertain.

species:orretherium-tsalkin.ageText: About 74 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:orretherium-tsalkin.placeText: Valle del Río de las Chinas, Magallanes, Chile
summary: A small mammal of about 1.3 kg, a mesungulatid, one of the meridiolestidans, a southern group distantly related to marsupials and placentals. It is known from a jaw with five teeth, which gives its name, “five-tooth beast”, partly from the Aónikenk language.

species:yeutherium-pressor.ageText: About 74 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small meridiolestidan mammal, a reigitheriid, named in 2025 from teeth and jaw fragments.

species:cladosictis-patagonica.ageText: About 21 to 15 million years ago (Early to Middle Miocene)
summary: A long-bodied, otter- or weasel-like meat-eating marsupial relative, a sparassodont, about 80 cm long. It probably hunted small animals along rivers. Its name means “branch weasel”.

A horse-like litoptern about 1.2 m long that walked on three toes, the middle one much larger, just as early horses did, even though it was not related to horses, a classic example of convergent evolution in South America’s native hoofed mammals.

species:eocardia-montana.ageText: About 17.5 to 16 million years ago (Early to Middle Miocene)
summary: A rodent about 30 cm long, an early relative of guinea pigs and capybaras (cavioids), with ever-growing cheek teeth for grinding grass.

species:necrolestes-patagonensis.ageText: About 21 to 17.5 million years ago (Early Miocene)
summary: A small burrowing mammal with an upturned snout and digging forelimbs, like a mole. Its name means “grave robber”, for its burrowing. A 2012 study showed it was the last surviving meridiolestidan, a group that otherwise died out with the dinosaurs, outliving them by some 45 million years.

species:pachyrukhos-moyani.ageText: About 21 to 15 million years ago (Early to Middle Miocene)
summary: A small, rabbit-like notoungulate, about 30 cm long, with long hind legs for hopping and ever-growing teeth, one of South America’s native hoofed mammals that took on the role of hares.

species:waptia-fieldensis.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A shrimp-like swimming arthropod about 6.65 cm long, with a large two-part shell over its front half and a tail ending in two flaps. Some specimens carry clusters of eggs under the shell, with embryos inside, one of the oldest direct records of an animal caring for its young. It is one of the commonest animals of the Burgess Shale, and is named after Mount Wapta and Mount Field, which overlook the quarry.

species:canadaspis-perfecta.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A bivalved arthropod about 5 cm long, with a two-part shell over its head and front body, that walked on the sea floor and probably stirred up mud to find food. It is one of the commonest Burgess Shale animals. Its name means “shield of Canada”; related forms are known from China.

species:odaraia-alata.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A swimming arthropod enclosed in a tube-like shell, with huge eyes and a tail with three fins like an aircraft tail. It probably swam upside down, filtering food from the water with its many legs.

species:balhuticaris-voltae.placeText: Marble Canyon, Kootenay National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: One of the largest animals of the Cambrian, up to about 24.5 cm long, a bivalved arthropod with more than 100 body segments and a wide, butterfly-shaped shell. It was named in 2022 and shows that giant size evolved in several kinds of arthropod soon after they appeared.

species:burgessia-bella.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A small arthropod about 1 to 2 cm long, with a round, see-through head shield, a long spine-like tail and branching guts visible through the shield. More than 1,700 specimens are known. Its relationships among the arthropods are uncertain.

species:helmetia-expansa.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A flat, oval arthropod up to about 20 cm long, a soft-shelled relative of the trilobites, with a pair of small spines at the front of its head.

species:cambroraster-falcatus.placeText: Marble Canyon, Kootenay National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A radiodont, a relative of Anomalocaris, up to about 30 cm long, with an enormous horseshoe-shaped head shield that made it look like the Millennium Falcon from Star Wars, which inspired its species name. Its front claws were fringed with comb-like spines, and it probably raked through the sea-floor mud for small animals. Hundreds of specimens were found, and it was named in 2019.

species:aysheaia-pedunculata.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A soft-bodied “worm with legs”, a lobopodian 1 to 6 cm long, with ten pairs of stubby, clawed legs and spiny grasping limbs at the front. It is often found with sponges, so it may have lived on them and eaten them. It looks much like a velvet worm and is a relative of arthropods.

species:ovatiovermis-cribratus.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A lobopodian that probably stood on its hind legs, anchored to the sea floor or a sponge, while its long, spiny front legs filtered food from the water, like a living sieve. Its name means “egg-shaped worm” and “sieve”. It was named in 2017.

species:entothyreos-synnaustrus.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A lobopodian named in 2024 whose legs were hardened with stiff, plate-like coverings, much like those of arthropods. It shows that tough, jointed-looking limbs began to evolve in lobopodians before true arthropods appeared.

species:nectocaris-pteryx.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A flattened, kite-shaped swimming animal about 5 cm long, with fins along its body, a pair of stalked eyes and long tentacles at the front. In 2010 it was proposed as an early cephalopod, a squid relative, but that idea has been widely rejected; newer work suggests it may be related to arrow worms. What it really was is still debated.

species:banffia-constricta.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A soft-bodied animal up to about 12 cm long, split by a twisted waist into a front and a back half. It is usually placed with the vetulicolians, puzzling Cambrian animals that may be early relatives of chordates. Named after Banff, Alberta.

species:eldonia-ludwigi.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A disc-shaped, jellyfish-like animal up to about 10 cm across, with a coiled gut visible inside. Walcott first thought it was a sea cucumber. It is now placed with the cambroernids, an extinct group perhaps related to echinoderms and acorn worms, and probably floated or lay on the sea floor. Related species occur in China and Siberia.

species:echmatocrinus-brachiatus.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A cone-shaped animal attached to the sea floor, with a crown of seven to ten feathery tentacles, covered in small mineral plates. It was first described as the oldest crinoid (sea lily), but it has also been interpreted as an octocoral, a soft coral; what it was is still debated. About 20 specimens are known.

species:burgessomedusa-phasmiformis.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: The oldest definite swimming jellyfish, named in 2023 from 182 specimens. Its bell was up to 20 cm tall, ringed by about 90 short tentacles, and it was probably a predator. It shows that jellyfish with the familiar swimming stage already existed more than 500 million years ago.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Justin Moon, Jean-Bernard Caron and Joseph Moysiuk, 2023

species:takakkawia-lineata.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A small sponge about 4 cm tall, with four flanges made of rows of star-shaped spicules running up its body. It is named after Takakkaw Falls in Yoho National Park.

species:acanthotretella-spinosa.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A small brachiopod (lamp shell) with a thin, soft shell bristling with long, hair-like spines, and a fleshy stalk that anchored it to the sea floor. Such soft details are almost never preserved in brachiopods.

species:oikozetetes-seilacheri.placeText: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A halkieriid known only from its two cap-shaped shells, one from each end of the body. Its relative Halkieria was a slug-like animal covered in small scales with a shell at each end; such animals may be early relatives of molluscs, brachiopods or annelid worms.

species:ursactis-comosa.placeText: Tokumm Creek, Kootenay National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: A bristly sea worm (polychaete), the most abundant Cambrian polychaete known, named in 2023. Most specimens come from the Tokumm Creek locality of the Burgess Shale.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Hiroki Osawa, Jean-Bernard Caron and Robert Gaines, 2023

summary: Only the second definite opabiniid, after the five-eyed Opabinia of the Burgess Shale, named in 2022 from a specimen long kept in a museum drawer. It had a long, flexible snout ending in a grasping claw, like Opabinia.

One of the earliest known vertebrates, a tiny, eel-shaped jawless fish only a few centimetres long, with eyes and nostrils on its head. With Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia, it shows that animals with backbones were already swimming in Cambrian seas 518 million years ago.

species:shankouclava-anningense.placeText: Shankou, Anning, near Kunming, Yunnan, China
summary: One of the oldest possible tunicates (sea squirts), small bag-shaped animals that live attached to the sea floor and filter water. Tunicates are the closest living relatives of vertebrates.
A radiodont, a relative of Anomalocaris, named in 2022 from a nearly complete young individual about 15 cm long and separate claws. Its name means “innovation crab”.

Known only from huge, tooth-lined mouth rings up to about 13 cm across, Omnidens (“all tooth”) may have been one of the largest animals of the early Cambrian, perhaps over 1.5 m long (a speculative estimate). Its mouth is like that of the gilled lobopodian Pambdelurion, suggesting it was a giant relative of it.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Hou Xianguang, Jan Bergström and Yang Jie, 2006

summary: One of the most primitive known arthropods, named in 2022. It had both swimming flaps, like radiodonts, and simple legs, showing how the jointed legs of arthropods evolved from the flaps of their ancestors.
A flat, trilobite-like arthropod whose head shield and body plates were fused into a single shield, with grooves marking about 19 segments.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Hou Xianguang, Lars Ramsköld and Jan Bergström, 1991

summary: A small, flat, many-segmented arthropod known from about 15 specimens.

A tiny lobopodian, a worm with stubby legs and a row of hard plates along its back. In 2022 traces of its brain and nerves were found preserved, showing a simple brain that helped explain how the brains of arthropods evolved.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Hou Xianguang, Lars Ramsköld and Jan Bergström, 1991

summary: A redlichiid trilobite, one of the earliest groups of trilobites, found in rocks just above the Chengjiang Biota.
A tiny early chelicerate, a distant relative of horseshoe crabs, sea scorpions and spiders, named in 2024. It was very common in the Fezouata seas, as its species name suggests.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Lorenzo Lustri, Pierre Gueriau and Allison Daley, 2024

summary: The largest known vertebrate of the Silurian, an early bony fish perhaps about 1 m long, with blunt, crushing teeth for eating shellfish or armoured fish. Its name means “big mouth”. It showed that big jawed predators existed before the Devonian, earlier than thought.
An early bony fish covered in thick, interlocking scales, related to Guiyu, one of the earliest well-preserved bony fishes. Its fossils show the scale and fin patterns of the first bony fishes.

A ptyctodont, a small, chimaera-like armoured fish with crushing tooth plates for shellfish, preserved in three dimensions. Ptyctodonts are among the placoderms that showed internal fertilisation: one of their relatives from Gogo, Materpiscis, preserves an embryo inside its mother.

An armoured predatory fish, a close relative of the giant Dunkleosteus, about 1 m long, with bony cutting blades for jaws. The Gogo fossils of this species are so well preserved that its skull and shoulder armour can be studied in three dimensions.

A rhizodont, a large predatory lobe-finned fish related to the ancestors of four-legged animals. Its pectoral fins had bones like a wrist and finger-like rays, an early step towards limbs, and young specimens show the fins could flex and push against the river bottom.

A flat, bottom-dwelling armoured fish, a phyllolepid, with leaf-like plates covering its head and body and tiny eyes. It lived in fresh water; the genus was among the last placoderms, dying out at the end of the Devonian. This species comes from Red Hill.

species:holoptychius-nobilissimus.ageText: About 383 to 359 million years ago (Late Devonian)
species:holoptychius-nobilissimus.placeText: Scotland; also found worldwide, including Pennsylvania, USA
summary: A large, predatory lobe-finned fish up to about 1 m or more long, covered in thick, wrinkled, rounded scales. It belongs to the porolepiforms, relatives of the lungfish, and is one of the most widespread Late Devonian fishes, known from North America, Europe and South America; many lived in rivers.

species:belantsea-montana.placeText: Bear Gulch, Fergus County, Montana, USA
summary: A petalodont, a relative of chimaeras, with a tall, flattened, disc-like body and big fins, more like a reef fish than a shark. It probably nibbled sponges and other food from the sea floor with its petal-shaped teeth. It is named after a legendary ancestor of the Crow people.

species:squatinactis-caudispinatus.placeText: Bear Gulch, Fergus County, Montana, USA
summary: A flattened, ray-like shark with broad, wing-like pectoral fins, which probably lay on the sea floor like today’s angel sharks.

species:stethacanthus-altonensis.ageText: About 370 to 299 million years ago (Late Devonian to Carboniferous)
species:stethacanthus-altonensis.placeText: Illinois and Montana, USA; also Europe, Asia and Australia
summary: A shark-like fish up to about 2 m long, famous for the “ironing board”: a flat-topped, brush-like spine on the back of males, covered in small tooth-like denticles, as was a patch on top of the head. It was probably a display feature for attracting mates or threatening rivals.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Orestes St. John and Amos Worthen, 1875 (as Physonemus altonensis); genus by John Newberry, 1889

species:caridosuctor-populosum.placeText: Bear Gulch, Fergus County, Montana, USA
summary: A marine coelacanth about 22 cm long, the largest and most common coelacanth of Bear Gulch. Its name means “shrimp sucker”, after its probable diet.

species:syllipsimopodi-bideni.placeText: Bear Gulch, Fergus County, Montana, USA
summary: A small, squid-like animal about 12 cm long with ten arms, two longer than the others, and suckers. When named in 2022 it was presented as the oldest relative of octopuses and vampire squid, pushing their origin back 82 million years, but later researchers argued it is a more distant relative of squids and octopuses. Its species name honours US President Joe Biden.

species:comptonatus-chasei.ageText: About 126 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
species:comptonatus-chasei.placeText: Compton Bay, Isle of Wight, England
summary: A bulky iguanodontian plant-eater, perhaps about 6 m long, named in 2024 from a partial skeleton found in 2013 by the late fossil collector Nick Chase, after whom it is named. Its name means “the Compton thunderer”. It shows that more kinds of large ornithopods lived on the Isle of Wight than once thought.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Jeremy Lockwood, David Martill and Susannah Maidment, 2024

species:istiorachis-macarthurae.ageText: About 126 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: An iguanodontian with very tall spines on its back vertebrae, which would have formed a low sail or ridge along its back, perhaps for display. Its name means “sail spine”; its species name honours the sailor Dame Ellen MacArthur. It was named in 2025.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Jeremy Lockwood, David Martill and Susannah Maidment, 2025

species:vectiraptor-greeni.ageText: About 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: A large raptor, perhaps about 2.5 to 3 m long, known from back vertebrae and part of the hip, named in 2021, the first dromaeosaurid named from the Isle of Wight. Its name means “Isle of Wight thief”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Nicholas Longrich, David Martill and Brian Jacobs, 2021

species:ornithodesmus-cluniculus.ageText: About 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: A small raptor known from a single bird-like hip bone. Harry Seeley named it in 1887 thinking it was a bird; it was later called a pterosaur, and the pterosaur bones once lumped with it are now Istiodactylus. Since 1993 it has been recognised as a dromaeosaurid dinosaur.

Known from a thickened skull roof with two small domes, Yaverlandia was long cited as the oldest dome-headed dinosaur (pachycephalosaur). Restudy in 2011 showed it was not a pachycephalosaur but probably a small theropod; a second skull described later raises the possibility that it was not a dinosaur at all. Its identity remains uncertain.

species:aerodactylus-scolopaciceps.ageText: About 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic, early Tithonian)
summary: A small, long-snouted, short-tailed pterosaur, split from Pterodactylus in 2014 and named after the Pokémon Aerodactyl. Some researchers think its specimens are just young or varied Pterodactylus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Hermann von Meyer, 1860 (as Pterodactylus scolopaciceps); genus by Steven Vidovic and David Martill, 2014

species:bellubrunnus-rothgaengeri.ageText: About 152 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Kimmeridgian)
summary: A small long-tailed pterosaur known from a complete skeleton of a juvenile with a wingspan of about 30 cm. Unusually, its wingtips curved forwards rather than backwards. Its name means “the beautiful one of Brunn”, after the quarry where it was found.

species:alligatorellus-beaumonti.ageText: About 152 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
species:alligatorellus-beaumonti.placeText: Cerin, France, and Kelheim, Bavaria, Germany
summary: A tiny crocodile relative, about 20 cm long, an atoposaurid with two rows of bony plates down its back. A skeleton from the Solnhofen limestone at Kelheim was probably washed into a lagoon, where it was buried with sea lilies.

species:thrissops-formosus.ageText: About 155 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A fast, streamlined predatory fish up to about 90 cm long with a deeply forked tail, an early relative of the giant Cretaceous “bulldog fish” Xiphactinus. Some specimens contain the fish they ate.

species:allothrissops-mesogaster.ageText: About 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic, early Tithonian)
summary: A primitive “bulldog fish” (ichthyodectiform), one of the earliest members of the group that later produced Xiphactinus.

species:ainia-armata.ageText: About 152 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Kimmeridgian)
summary: A predatory ray-finned fish, a distant relative of today’s bowfin, long known as Callopterus, a name that turned out to be already in use. It is closer to Caturus.

species:ischyodus-quenstedti.ageText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A chimaera (ratfish), a relative of sharks, about 1.5 m long, with a long whip-like tail and crushing tooth plates for shellfish. Ischyodus is the most long-lived chimaera genus, with more than 39 species over 140 million years, but almost all are known only from tooth plates; this Jurassic species is known from whole skeletons.

species:clausocaris-lithographica.ageText: About 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic, early Tithonian)
summary: A thylacocephalan, a strange extinct arthropod whose body was hidden inside a large, flattened shell, with huge eyes at the front and three pairs of long grasping limbs for catching prey. It was probably an ambush predator in open water.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Paul Oppenheim, 1888 (as Clausia); renamed by Hans Polz, 1989

species:suevoleviathan-disinteger.ageText: About 183 to 181 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: A large, primitive ichthyosaur, about 4 m long, with an unusually broad front flipper. Its name means “Swabian leviathan”.

species:hydrorion-brachypterygius.ageText: About 183 to 181 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: A small long-necked plesiosaur, known from several skeletons, first named as a species of Plesiosaurus and then Microcleidus. Its name means “water hunter”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Friedrich von Huene, 1923 (species); genus by Frank Großmann, 2007

species:microcleidus-homalospondylus.ageText: About 183 to 181 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
species:microcleidus-homalospondylus.placeText: Whitby, Yorkshire, England; also Germany, Luxembourg and France
summary: A plesiosaur with a very long neck of about 40 vertebrae and a short tail, about 3 to 5 m long. It probably fed on small fish and squid. Its species are known from England, France, Luxembourg and the Posidonia Shale of Germany.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Richard Owen, 1865 (as Plesiosaurus homalospondylus); genus by David Watson, 1909

species:plesionectes-longicollum.ageText: About 183 to 181 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: An early long-necked plesiosaur named in 2025 from a nearly complete skeleton. It is one of the oldest plesiosaurs from the Toarcian, and its name means “near swimmer”.

species:mystriosaurus-laurillardi.ageText: About 183 to 181 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: A teleosaurid, a long-snouted sea crocodile relative, more than 4 m long. Long lumped into “Steneosaurus”, it was shown in 2019 to be a separate genus.

One of the earliest sauropods, known only from a shin and ankle found in sea rocks; its body must have washed out to sea. The bone was thought to belong to a plesiosaur until Rupert Wild recognised it as a sauropod in the 1970s. It is on display at the Urweltmuseum Hauff in Holzmaden.

species:leptolepis-coryphaenoides.ageText: About 183 to 165 million years ago (Early to Middle Jurassic)
species:leptolepis-coryphaenoides.placeText: Germany, England and elsewhere in Europe
summary: A small, herring-like schooling fish, one of the commonest fish of the Early Jurassic seas of Europe and an early relative of today’s teleosts, the group that includes most living fish. It was food for ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and larger fish.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Heinrich Bronn, 1830 (as Cyprinus coryphaenoides); genus by Louis Agassiz, 1832

summary: A cryptoclidid plesiosaur, a long-necked marine reptile, known from Svalbard; the genus is also known from England. Its skeletons from the Slottsmøya site were among the finds that made Svalbard famous for Jurassic marine reptiles.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Persson, 1962 (as Tricleidus svalbardensis); moved to Colymbosaurus in 2012

species:kimmerosaurus-langhami.ageText: About 152 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
species:kimmerosaurus-langhami.placeText: Kimmeridge, Dorset, England; also Svalbard, Norway
summary: A cryptoclidid plesiosaur known from a skull with many fine, needle-like teeth, probably for catching small prey. Its name means “lizard from Kimmeridge”.

species:cetiosauriscus-stewarti.ageText: About 166 to 164 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A sauropod about 15 m long, known from a partial skeleton found in a clay pit in 1898, laid down in the sea; its carcass drifted out from land. Once thought to be a diplodocid relative, it is now seen as a more primitive eusauropod.

species:tyrannoneustes-lythrodectikos.ageText: About 165 million years ago (Middle Jurassic, Callovian)
summary: A metriorhynchid, a fully sea-going crocodile relative with flippers and a tail fin, with a wide gape and serrated teeth, one of the earliest of the big-prey hunters among them. Its name means “blood-biting tyrant swimmer”.

species:dracopelta-zbyszewskii.ageText: About 152 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: An early armoured dinosaur, perhaps about 2 to 3 m long, known from part of a rib cage with armour plates. Its name means “dragon shield”. It is one of the oldest ankylosaurs from Europe.

species:losillasaurus-giganteus.ageText: About 152 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A turiasaur, one of the large, broad-toothed sauropods of Late Jurassic Iberia, related to Turiasaurus. It is known from a partial skeleton found near Losilla in Valencia.

species:europejara-olcadesorum.ageText: About 126 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: The oldest known tapejarid, a toothless, crested pterosaur, and the first from Europe, named in 2012 from a skull and jaw. It had a tall crest on its lower jaw and a long one on its snout, and may have eaten fruit or seeds, as some think its relatives did.

species:crusafontia-cuencana.ageText: About 126 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: A tiny dryolestid mammal, perhaps about 10 cm long, known from teeth and a jaw, named after the Spanish palaeontologist Miquel Crusafont.

species:phalarodon-fraasi.ageText: About 247 to 242 million years ago (Middle Triassic)
species:phalarodon-fraasi.placeText: Monte San Giorgio, Switzerland and Italy; also Nevada, Svalbard and China
summary: A mixosaurid, a small early ichthyosaur, with blunt, crushing back teeth for eating hard-shelled prey. Its history is tangled: species have been moved in and out of it and Mixosaurus, and Contectopalatus is now treated as the same animal.
An early ichthyosaur known from an incomplete skull with teeth on the roof of its mouth. It is named after the Swedish palaeontologist Carl Wiman.

species:ampelosaurus-atacis.ageText: About 71.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, early Maastrichtian)
summary: A titanosaur about 15 m long, with bony plates and spikes set in its skin. It is known from hundreds of bones from Bellevue, in the Aude valley, among vineyards, which gives its name, “vine lizard”. It was one of the European island sauropods, though not a dwarf.

A large toothed bird, an ichthyornithine about 1.5 kg, among the last toothed birds before the asteroid impact. Its skull bones showed a movable palate like that of modern birds, which was thought to have evolved only in the group of ducks and chickens. Its name refers to Janus, the two-faced Roman god, for its mix of old and modern features.

species:janenschia-robusta.ageText: About 155 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A large sauropod known from legs and feet, once thought to be one of the earliest titanosaurs. It is now usually seen as a more primitive macronarian, perhaps related to Camarasaurus. It is named after Werner Janensch, who led the German Tendaguru expedition.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Eberhard Fraas, 1908 (as Gigantosaurus robustus); genus by Rupert Wild, 1991

species:tendaguria-tanzaniensis.ageText: About 155 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A sauropod known from two unusually low back vertebrae, now usually placed among the turiasaurs, like Turiasaurus of Spain.

species:veterupristisaurus-milneri.ageText: About 155 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A large predatory dinosaur, perhaps 8.5 to 10 m long, known from tail vertebrae, one of the oldest carcharodontosaurids, the family of the later giants Giganotosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus.
Known only from teeth, Ostafrikasaurus may be the oldest known spinosaurid, the fish-eating family of Spinosaurus, though some researchers think the teeth could belong to another kind of theropod.

species:tendaguripterus-recki.ageText: About 155 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A small pterosaur known only from part of a lower jaw with short, cone-shaped teeth, probably a relative of the dsungaripterids, which crushed shellfish.

species:aegisuchus-witmeri.ageText: About 98 to 93 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A giant, flat-headed crocodile relative known from the back of its skull, nicknamed “ShieldCroc” for a raised, shield-like area on the skull that may have been covered in blood vessels for display or temperature control. Estimates of its length, 15 to 22 m, are very uncertain because so little is known; it may have been much smaller.

related.note: Its close relative from Egypt.

species:kemkemia-auditorei.ageText: About 98 to 93 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: Known from one tail vertebra, Kemkemia was first described in 2009 as a large theropod dinosaur, but is now thought to be a crocodile relative.
A large, flat-headed crocodile relative named by Ernst Stromer in 1933. Its fossils were destroyed in the bombing of Munich in 1944, along with his Spinosaurus.
A small, short-snouted land crocodile relative, a notosuchian, named by Ernst Stromer in 1914 from a skull destroyed in 1944.

A huge crocodile relative with a long, flat, duck-like snout, about 2 m long, and a toothless lower jaw, perhaps with a throat pouch for scooping up small prey, perhaps around 10 m long (a rough estimate). Its only skull was destroyed in 1944; its relative Laganosuchus helps show what it looked like.
A small land crocodile relative about 70 cm long with a broad, flat, duck-like snout, nicknamed “DuckCroc”. It probably poked about on land and in shallow water for frogs, fish and grubs.

A large abelisaurid known from a lower jaw and teeth, found in phosphate mines that were then on the sea floor; its body washed out to sea. It was one of the last big predatory dinosaurs of Africa before the asteroid impact.

species:azhdarcho-lancicollis.ageText: About 92 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: The pterosaur that gave its name to the azhdarchids, the family of the giant Quetzalcoatlus. It was smaller, with a wingspan of perhaps 4.5 m, and is known from fragments including its very long neck vertebrae. Its name comes from Azhdarkho, a dragon in Persian legend.

species:itemirus-medullaris.ageText: About 92 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A dromaeosaurid known from a braincase, which shows good senses of balance and hearing. It was first described as a tyrannosaur relative.

species:aidachar-paludalis.ageText: About 95 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:aidachar-paludalis.placeText: Kyzylkum Desert, Uzbekistan; also North Africa
summary: A freshwater “bulldog fish” (ichthyodectiform), a relative of Xiphactinus that lived in rivers. It is named after Aydahar, a dragon of Kazakh legend.
An enantiornithine, one of the “opposite birds”, known from a single piece of shoulder bone. It was one of several birds living in the Bissekty river delta.

species:indosuchus-raptorius.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An abelisaurid about 7 m long and 1.2 tonnes, with a flat-topped skull bearing a crest. It was named in 1932, and despite its name (“Indian crocodile”) it is a dinosaur. It lived alongside Rajasaurus.

species:vorona-berivotrensis.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A bird known from leg bones, probably of one individual; its name is the Malagasy word for “bird”. It is an early relative of modern birds, outside the modern groups.

species:sahonachelys-mailakavava.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small side-necked turtle known from an almost complete skeleton, named in 2021. Its narrow, pointed snout suggests it fed by suction, sucking in small prey, unlike its relatives. Its name means “frog turtle”, after the frog-like look of its skull.

species:lufengosaurus-huenei.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A long-necked plant-eating dinosaur about 6 to 9 m long, a massospondylid related to Massospondylus of South Africa. In 1958 it became the first complete dinosaur skeleton mounted in China, and it was celebrated on a postage stamp. In 2017 scientists reported traces of collagen protein preserved inside one of its ribs, about 195 million years old.

species:xingxiulong-chengi.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A long-necked plant-eater about 4 to 5 m long that walked on two legs but had a sturdy, sauropod-like hip with four fused vertebrae, an early step towards the bodies of giant sauropods. It is named after the Xingxiu Bridge, an old bridge in Lufeng.

species:lishulong-wangi.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A large early sauropodiform, a relative of the ancestors of sauropods, named in 2024 from a skull and neck. Its name means “chestnut tree dragon”, after the village where it was found.

species:sinosaurus-triassicus.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A crested predatory dinosaur about 5.5 m long, with a pair of thin crests on its head like those of Dilophosaurus. A skull found in 1987 was described as a Chinese species of Dilophosaurus, but it is now included in Sinosaurus. Despite its name (“triassicus”), it lived in the Early Jurassic.

related.note: A crested relative from North America.

species:eshanosaurus-deguchiianus.ageText: About 201 to 199 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: Known from a single lower jaw with leaf-shaped teeth, Eshanosaurus was described in 2001 as the oldest therizinosaur, which would also make it the oldest coelurosaur by tens of millions of years. Many researchers think the jaw more likely belonged to an early sauropodomorph, so its identity remains debated.

A tiny mammal relative with a skull only 12 mm long and a weight of about 2 grams, as small as a paper clip. Its large braincase and its middle-ear bones, already separate from its jaw, are mammal-like, and it is one of the closest relatives of true mammals.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Luo Zhe-Xi, Alfred Crompton and Sun Ai-Lin, 2001

summary: An early mammal relative with a jaw joint like that of mammals. Unlike mammals, though, it kept replacing its teeth throughout life and kept growing, like a reptile.

species:bienotherium-yunnanense.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: The largest tritylodontid of the Lufeng Formation, a plant-eating cynodont with rodent-like gnawing front teeth and grinding cheek teeth for tough plants. It is named after Bian Meinian, who discovered it.
A small, slender, long-legged early crocodile relative, a “sphenosuchian”, known from several skeletons. Its inner ear suggests it had keen hearing, and it was probably a fast, active land predator.

species:dianchungosaurus-lufengensis.ageText: About 195 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: Named in 1982 as a heterodontosaurid dinosaur, Dianchungosaurus was shown in 2005 to be a crocodile relative, a mesoeucrocodylian, based on jaw fragments.

species:staurikosaurus-pricei.ageText: About 233 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: One of the earliest known dinosaurs, a slender, two-legged predator about 2 m long, a relative of Herrerasaurus. It was found in 1936 and named in 1970; its name means “Southern Cross lizard”, after the constellation seen in the southern sky. Teyuwasu, named from leg bones in 1999, is probably the same animal.

related.note: A larger relative from Argentina.

species:gnathovorax-cabreirai.ageText: About 233 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
species:gnathovorax-cabreirai.placeText: São João do Polêsine, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: A herrerasaurid predator about 3 m long, known from one of the best herrerasaurid skeletons ever found, nearly complete with its skull. Its name means “jaw glutton”. CT scans of its braincase showed large areas for balance and smell.

species:buriolestes-schultzi.ageText: About 233 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
species:buriolestes-schultzi.placeText: São João do Polêsine, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: One of the earliest sauropodomorphs, the group that later produced the giant sauropods, yet it was only about 1.5 m long and had sharp, curved, serrated teeth: it was a meat-eater, showing that the ancestors of the giant plant-eaters were small predators.

species:nhandumirim-waldsangae.ageText: About 233 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A small early dinosaur known from a young individual, now thought to be a saturnaliid sauropodomorph, a relative of Saturnalia. Its name means “small rhea” in the Tupi language.

species:venetoraptor-gassenae.placeText: Vale Vêneto, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: A lagerpetid, one of the closest relatives of pterosaurs, with a parrot-like beak and long fingers ending in big, sickle-shaped claws, perhaps for climbing or grasping. Named in 2023, it showed that this group was far more varied than once thought.

species:prestosuchus-chiniquensis.ageText: About 240 to 235 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
species:prestosuchus-chiniquensis.placeText: Chiniquá, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: One of the largest early crocodile-line predators, a loricatan perhaps 6 to 7 m long, with a huge, deep skull and long, serrated teeth. It was the top predator of its time in southern Brazil, preying on dicynodonts like Dinodontosaurus. Several large skeletons are known.

species:protuberum-cabralense.ageText: About 240 to 235 million years ago (Middle Triassic)
summary: One of the largest Triassic cynodonts, a plant-eating traversodontid whose ribs, back and hips were covered in bony knobs, which give it its name. What the knobs were for is unknown.

species:brasinorhynchus-mariantensis.ageText: About 240 to 235 million years ago (Middle Triassic)
summary: A rhynchosaur, one of the stocky, beaked, plant-eating reptiles that were among the commonest animals of the Triassic.

species:isodapedon-varzealis.ageText: About 233 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A hyperodapedontine rhynchosaur, a relative of the very common Hyperodapedon, named in 2026 from a partial skull.

related.note: A close relative.

species:itaguyra-occulta.ageText: About 233 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A silesaurid, one of the slender relatives (or earliest members) of ornithischian dinosaurs, named in 2025 from two hip bones. Its name means “stone bird”.

species:amanasaurus-nesbitti.ageText: About 233 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A silesaurid known from two thigh bones, named in 2024. Its name means “rain lizard”.

species:parvosuchus-aurelioi.ageText: About 237 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: A small, slender crocodile-line predator about 1 m long, a gracilisuchid, named in 2024 from a skull and partial skeleton. It may have walked on two legs.

species:tainrakuasuchus-bellator.ageText: About 240 to 235 million years ago (Middle Triassic)
summary: A poposauroid, a long-necked crocodile-line predator about 2.4 m long, named in 2025 from part of a jaw, vertebrae and hips.

Once thought to be a very early dinosaur, Spondylosoma, named in 1942 from scattered bones, is now known to be an aphanosaur, one of the earliest members of the bird-line archosaurs, outside the dinosaurs.

species:barberenasuchus-brasiliensis.ageText: About 237 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: An archosauriform reptile known from a poorly preserved skull. It was described as an early crocodylomorph, later called a “rauisuchian”; its true relationships are uncertain.
A tiny procolophonoid, a stocky, lizard-like early reptile, named in 2026 from a very small skull of a young animal.
A small archosauriform named in 2026, perhaps related to Euparkeria of South Africa, a group otherwise unknown from South America.
A proterochampsid, one of the long-snouted, crocodile-like archosauriforms of Triassic South America, known from a hind leg.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Rodrigo Müller, Maurício Garcia and Fonseca, 2022

species:unaysaurus-tolentinoi.ageText: About 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
species:unaysaurus-tolentinoi.placeText: Agudo, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: An early long-necked plant-eater about 2.5 m long, found in 1998 and announced in 2004. It is closely related to Plateosaurus of Germany, showing how easily dinosaurs could spread across Pangaea. Its name comes from the Tupi word for “black water”.

species:macrocollum-itaquii.ageText: About 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
species:macrocollum-itaquii.placeText: Agudo, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: The oldest known long-necked dinosaur, about 3.5 m long, known from three complete skeletons found together, which hints that early sauropodomorphs may have lived in groups. Its name means “long neck”.

species:sacisaurus-agudoensis.ageText: About 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
species:sacisaurus-agudoensis.placeText: Agudo, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: A silesaurid with a toothless, beak-like tip to its lower jaw. Of the dozens of bones found, 35 thigh bones were all from the right leg, so it was named after the Saci, a one-legged trickster of Brazilian folklore.

species:brasilodon-quadrangularis.ageText: About 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
species:brasilodon-quadrangularis.placeText: Faxinal do Soturno, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: A shrew-sized, insect-eating cynodont about 20 cm long, one of the closest relatives of mammals of its time. A 2022 study found it replaced its teeth only once, as mammals do, making it the oldest animal with this mammal-like trait. Brasilitherium is now considered the same animal.

species:clevosaurus-brasiliensis.placeText: Faxinal do Soturno, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: A small, lizard-like tuatara relative. Clevosaurus was one of the most widespread reptiles of the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic, with species found on every continent except Australia and Antarctica, including five from cave fills in southwest England and Wales. This species is from Brazil.

species:riojasaurus-incertus.ageText: About 220 to 213 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: A large, heavily built long-necked plant-eater about 6.6 m long, with thick limbs and probably a four-legged gait. Named by José Bonaparte in 1969, it was one of the biggest animals of its time in South America.

species:lessemsaurus-sauropoides.ageText: About 220 to 213 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: One of the largest Triassic dinosaurs, perhaps about 9 m long and several tonnes, with tall-spined vertebrae. It belongs to the lessemsaurids, a group of giant early sauropodomorphs that reached sauropod-like size before true sauropods evolved. It is named after the dinosaur writer Don Lessem.

species:coloradisaurus-brevis.ageText: About 220 to 213 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: A massospondylid sauropodomorph, a relative of Massospondylus and Lufengosaurus, known from a skull and a second skeleton. It was first named Coloradia, but that name was already in use for a moth.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: José Bonaparte, 1979 (as Coloradia brevis); renamed by Peter Galton, 1990

species:zupaysaurus-rougieri.ageText: About 220 to 213 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: An early predatory dinosaur about 4 m long, known from a skull and partial skeleton. It was once restored with paired crests like Dilophosaurus, but later study questioned them. Its name means “devil lizard”, from the Quechua word zupay.

species:fasolasuchus-tenax.ageText: About 220 to 213 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: One of the largest land predators of the Triassic, a loricatan (“rauisuchian”) perhaps 8 to 10 m long, larger than any meat-eating dinosaur of its time. It was one of the last of its kind before the end-Triassic extinction.

species:riojasuchus-tenuisceps.ageText: About 220 to 213 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: An ornithosuchid, a crocodile-line archosaur that could walk on two legs, with a hooked snout and a curious gap in its teeth. It is one of the youngest and most complete members of its family; its skull suggests it may have been a scavenger.

species:neoaetosauroides-engaeus.ageText: About 220 to 213 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: A primitive aetosaur, an armoured crocodile relative, the first found in the Los Colorados Formation. Wear on its teeth suggests it may have eaten insects and other small animals rather than plants.

species:hemiprotosuchus-leali.ageText: About 220 to 213 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: One of the oldest crocodyliforms, a small, short-snouted, land-dwelling protosuchid with armour plates along its back.

species:patagosaurus-fariasi.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: One of the best known early sauropods, about 15 to 16 m long, known from several skeletons including juveniles. It was a relative of Cetiosaurus of England.

species:piatnitzkysaurus-floresi.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: A lightly built predatory dinosaur over 4 m long, an early tetanuran, perhaps related to the megalosaurs. It is named after the geologist Alejandro Piatnitzky.

species:volkheimeria-chubutensis.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: A small early sauropod known from a partial skeleton, named after the palaeobotanist Wolfgang Volkheimer. It lived alongside Patagosaurus.

species:asfaltomylos-patagonicus.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: A tiny australosphenidan mammal, known from a jaw with teeth. Australosphenidans were southern mammals with complex, crushing molars, and may include the ancestors of the platypus and echidnas.

species:henosferus-molus.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: A small australosphenidan mammal known from jaws, a relative of Asfaltomylos. Grooves on its jaw suggest it still had small extra jaw bones, not yet moved into the ear as in later mammals.

species:argentoconodon-fariasorum.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: A small triconodont mammal, first known from a single tooth. Its thigh bone suggests it may have glided, like its close relative Volaticotherium from China.

species:condorchelys-antiqua.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: The oldest Jurassic turtle from South America, a stem turtle that could not pull its head into its shell, known from shell and skull pieces.

species:notobatrachus-degiustoi.ageText: About 179 to 168 million years ago (Early to Middle Jurassic)
summary: The most completely known Jurassic frog, from many skeletons, some with traces of skin. It looked much like a modern frog, though with a few primitive features, such as ribs.

species:tapinocephalus-atherstonei.ageText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: A huge, barrel-bodied plant-eating dinocephalian, perhaps about 3 m long and up to 1.5 tonnes, with an extremely thick, domed skull, probably used in head-butting contests like those of its relative Moschops. It gives its name to the Tapinocephalus Assemblage Zone. Its name means “low head”.

related.note: A close relative.

species:jonkeria-truculenta.ageText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: A large dinocephalian, perhaps about 4 m long, with a long, low skull and big canine teeth. It was probably an omnivore or plant-eater, a relative of the giant Titanosuchus.

species:eodicynodon-oosthuizeni.ageText: About 267 to 265 million years ago (middle Permian)
species:eodicynodon-oosthuizeni.placeText: Prince Albert, Western Cape, South Africa
summary: The oldest and most primitive known dicynodont, a small plant-eater with a short beak and tusks, from the lowest Beaufort Group rocks, the Eodicynodon Assemblage Zone, just below the Tapinocephalus zone. Dicynodonts went on to become the most common plant-eaters of the late Permian and Triassic.

species:robertia-broomiana.ageText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: A small, early dicynodont with a beak, tusks and a few small teeth, named in honour of the palaeontologist Robert Broom, who described many Karoo animals.

species:brachyprosopus-broomi.ageText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: A small, short-faced dicynodont from the Abrahamskraal Formation. Chelydontops, named in 1975, is now thought to be the same animal.

species:colobodectes-cluveri.ageText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: A small, early dicynodont from the Abrahamskraal Formation, known from skulls. Its name honours the palaeontologist Michael Cluver.

species:anomocephalus-africanus.ageText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: A primitive anomodont, an early relative of the dicynodonts, that still had a full set of teeth in both jaws rather than a beak. Its closest relative is Tiarajudens of Brazil.

related.note: Its closest relative.

species:bullacephalus-jacksoni.ageText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: A burnetiid biarmosuchian, a primitive therapsid with bony bumps and bosses on its skull, known from a nearly complete skull and jaw. Its name means “bubble head”.

species:elliotsmithia-longiceps.ageText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: A small varanopid, a monitor-lizard-like early synapsid, the only “pelycosaur” known from Gondwana. Only two specimens are known. Its species name means “long head”.

species:eriphostoma-microdon.ageText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: One of the oldest and smallest gorgonopsians, the sabre-toothed predators that later became the top hunters of the late Permian. In the middle Permian, gorgonopsians were still small and lived in the shadow of the dinocephalians.

species:rhinesuchus-whaitsi.ageText: About 265 to 255 million years ago (middle to late Permian)
summary: A large temnospondyl amphibian with a flat, triangular skull, a crocodile-like ambush predator of Permian rivers and pools. Its name means “rasp crocodile”, for the ridged surface of its skull bones.

species:endothiodon-bathystoma.ageText: About 260 to 255 million years ago (late Permian)
species:endothiodon-bathystoma.placeText: South Africa; also Brazil, Tanzania, Zambia, Mozambique and India
summary: A medium to large dicynodont with a long beak and rows of teeth set inside the edge of the upper jaw, which gives its name, “inside tooth”. It was widespread across southern Pangaea and gives its name to the Endothiodon Assemblage Zone.
A medium-sized dicynodont with a keeled beak, so common that a layer of the Karoo is named after it, the Tropidostoma Assemblage Zone.

A dicynodont with a bulbous, knobbly snout, named in 2017; its name means “bulbous reptile”, and its species name, “leaf razor”, refers to its sharp beak. The name is also a nod to the Pokémon Bulbasaur. It is an early relative of the giant Triassic Lisowicia.

species:pristerognathus-polyodon.ageText: About 260 to 257 million years ago (middle to late Permian)
summary: A dog-sized therocephalian predator with a long snout and large canines. It was one of the predators that took over after the middle Permian extinction, and lent its name to a former Karoo zone, the Pristerognathus Assemblage Zone.

species:lycosuchus-vanderrieti.ageText: About 260 to 257 million years ago (middle to late Permian)
summary: An early therocephalian predator with two pairs of functional canine teeth on each side, a unique feature that seems to have been a way of always having a working canine while one was being replaced. Its name means “wolf crocodile”.

species:charassognathus-gracilis.ageText: About 260 to 257 million years ago (middle to late Permian)
species:charassognathus-gracilis.placeText: Near Fraserburg, Northern Cape, South Africa
summary: One of the earliest and most primitive cynodonts, the group that later gave rise to mammals, known from a small skull and skeleton described in 2007. Its name means “notched jaw”.

species:herpetoskylax-hopsoni.ageText: About 260 to 257 million years ago (middle to late Permian)
summary: A biarmosuchian, a primitive therapsid predator, whose name, “reptile puppy”, mixes reptile and mammal words, reflecting the mix of features in early mammal relatives.

species:aulacephalodon-bainii.ageText: About 258 to 253 million years ago (late Permian)
summary: A medium-sized, stout plant-eating dicynodont with a broad, bossed snout and tusks, one of the commonest large plant-eaters of the late Permian Karoo. Its name means “furrow-head tooth”.

species:pristerodon-mackayi.ageText: About 258 to 253 million years ago (late Permian)
species:pristerodon-mackayi.placeText: South Africa; also Zambia and India
summary: A small, common dicynodont with a beak and a row of small cheek teeth. Many other names given to Karoo fossils are now thought to belong to it.

species:cistecephaloides-boonstrai.ageText: About 258 to 255 million years ago (late Permian)
summary: A small, burrowing dicynodont related to Cistecephalus, with a broad, flat head and strong forelimbs for digging.

related.note: A close relative.

species:compsodon-helmoedi.ageText: About 258 to 255 million years ago (late Permian)
summary: A small emydopoid dicynodont, a relative of the burrowing Cistecephalus, from the Balfour Formation of South Africa and the Madumabisa Mudstone of Zambia.

species:aelurosaurus-felinus.ageText: About 259 to 252 million years ago (late Permian)
summary: A small gorgonopsian, about the size of a fox, with sabre-like canines. Richard Owen named it “cat lizard” in 1881 because its skull reminded him of a cat’s.

species:daptocephalus-leoniceps.ageText: About 255 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
summary: A large dicynodont, a close relative of Dicynodon, that gives its name to the last Permian layer of the Karoo, the Daptocephalus Assemblage Zone. A second species is known from Tanzania and Zambia.

species:pelanomodon-moschops.ageText: About 255 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
summary: A tuskless, broad-snouted dicynodont, a relative of Aulacephalodon. It died out in the end-Permian extinction.

species:dinogorgon-rubidgei.ageText: About 255 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
summary: A large rubidgeine gorgonopsian, one of the sabre-toothed top predators of the last Permian Karoo, with a broad, heavy skull and huge canines. Its name means “terrible gorgon”, and it honours the Rubidge family of Karoo fossil collectors.

related.note: A close relative.

species:theriognathus-microps.ageText: About 255 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
species:theriognathus-microps.placeText: South Africa; also Zambia and Tanzania
summary: A whaitsiid therocephalian with a long, narrow snout, small eyes and large canines but few back teeth. It may have hunted at night or in burrows, perhaps eating small animals.

species:cynosaurus-suppostus.ageText: About 255 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
summary: A small, early cynodont, a distant relative of mammals, first named Cynosuchus by Richard Owen in 1876. Its name means “dog lizard”.

species:milleretta-rubidgei.ageText: About 255 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
summary: A small, lizard-like early reptile about 60 cm long, a millerettid. It had an opening in the side of its skull and may have had an eardrum able to hear airborne sounds.

species:owenetta-rubidgei.ageText: About 257 to 251 million years ago (late Permian to earliest Triassic)
summary: A small, stocky, lizard-like procolophonian reptile, one of the few of its group known from the Permian. Its relatives survived the end-Permian extinction and thrived in the Triassic.
A small, lightly built therocephalian, about 20 cm long, that probably hunted insects. It lived just after the end-Permian extinction, among the survivors. Its name means “hedgehog lizard”.

species:coletta-seca.placeText: Cradock District, Eastern Cape, South Africa
summary: A small, early procolophonid reptile known from a skull, from just after the end-Permian extinction.

species:bauria-cynops.ageText: About 248 to 242 million years ago (Early to Middle Triassic)
summary: A late therocephalian that, unusually, had broad, overlapping cheek teeth for grinding plants, a feature otherwise seen in plant-eating cynodonts. It also had a bony palate separating its mouth from its nose, like mammals, which evolved independently.

species:microgomphodon-oligocynus.ageText: About 248 to 242 million years ago (Early to Middle Triassic)
summary: A small bauriid therocephalian, a relative of Bauria, with grinding cheek teeth for a plant diet.

species:trirachodon-kannemeyeri.ageText: About 248 to 242 million years ago (Early to Middle Triassic)
summary: A small cynodont with three-ridged cheek teeth. A burrow complex found in South Africa held about 20 individuals of different ages, showing that these mammal relatives lived in family groups underground.

species:bolotridon-frerensis.ageText: About 248 to 242 million years ago (Early to Middle Triassic)
summary: A cynodont originally named Tribolodon, a name already taken by a fish; its new name, given in 1977, is an anagram of the old one.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Harry Seeley, 1895 (as Tribolodon frerensis); renamed by Brian Coad, 1977

species:impidens-hancoxi.ageText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic)
summary: A large, wolf-sized cynodont named in 2024 from fossils found in Antarctica and South Africa. It was probably the top predator of the cool, high-latitude forests of southern Gondwana, and was one of the largest meat-eating cynodonts.
An early rhynchosaur, one of the beaked, plant-eating reptiles, known from a skull. Its name means “dawn Hyperodapedon-lizard”.
An erythrosuchid, a big-headed predatory relative of archosaurs, a species named in 2014 and honouring Nelson Mandela by his clan name, Madiba. The genus is also known from Russia.

related.note: A larger relative.

species:laidleria-gracilis.ageText: About 248 to 242 million years ago (Early to Middle Triassic)
summary: A small, flat-headed temnospondyl amphibian, known from one species, which gives its name to the family Laidleriidae.

species:pampaphoneus-biccai.ageText: About 268 to 265 million years ago (middle Permian)
species:pampaphoneus-biccai.placeText: São Gabriel, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: A large predatory anteosaurid dinocephalian, perhaps 3 m long and 400 kg, the top predator of its time in South America, with large canines and incisors. A second, more complete skull described in 2025 confirmed its size.

related.note: A relative from South Africa.

summary: A plant-eating anomodont with long, sabre-like canine teeth, probably for display or defence, not hunting. It also had leaf-shaped back teeth that met to slice plants, one of the earliest examples of such tooth-on-tooth chewing.

species:rastodon-procurvidens.ageText: About 266 to 259 million years ago (middle Permian)
summary: A small dicynodont with forward-curving tusks, unique among dicynodonts, and one of the few middle Permian dicynodonts known from outside Africa.

species:australerpeton-cosgriffi.ageText: About 260 million years ago (middle to late Permian)
summary: A long-snouted temnospondyl amphibian, a rhinesuchid with a gharial-like skull, probably a fish-eater in lakes and rivers.

species:bageherpeton-longignathus.placeText: Near Bagé, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: A long-jawed archegosaurid temnospondyl known from a lower jaw, a crocodile-like fish-eater. It is named after the nearby city of Bagé.
A xenacanth, a freshwater shark with a long spine on its head and an eel-like tail fin. The genus lived from the Carboniferous into the Permian; this species was described from Brazil in 2017.

species:baurusuchus-pachecoi.ageText: About 85 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A dog-like, land-dwelling crocodile relative up to about 3.5 m long and over 100 kg, with long, upright legs, a tall, narrow skull and big, blade-like teeth. It was one of the top predators of Late Cretaceous Brazil, filling a role taken elsewhere by meat-eating dinosaurs.

species:aplestosuchus-sordidus.ageText: About 85 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A baurusuchid known from a nearly complete skeleton with the remains of another crocodile relative, a smaller sphagesaurid, preserved inside its belly: direct evidence that these predatory notosuchians ate other notosuchians. Its name means “greedy crocodile”.

species:caipirasuchus-paulistanus.ageText: About 85 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A sphagesaurid, a plant-eating land crocodile relative with complex cheek teeth that sheared past each other as its jaw moved back and forth, a way of chewing more like a mammal’s than a crocodile’s.

species:montealtosuchus-arrudacamposi.ageText: About 85 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A peirosaurid, a land crocodile relative about 1.7 m long, known from a nearly complete skull and skeleton found in 2004 near Monte Alto.

species:adamantinasuchus-navae.ageText: About 85 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small notosuchian with a short skull and teeth suited to an omnivorous diet, known from one fossil collected by William Nava, after whom it is named.

species:brasileosaurus-pachecoi.ageText: About 85 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small notosuchian crocodile relative named in 1931 by Friedrich von Huene from fossils found by the engineer Joviano Pacheco.

species:epoidesuchus-tavaresae.ageText: About 85 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An itasuchid notosuchian named in 2024, with long, slender jaws that suggest it lived partly in water, catching fish, unlike most of its land-living relatives.

species:gondwanatitan-faustoi.ageText: About 85 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A medium-sized titanosaur, perhaps 7 to 8 m long, closely related to Aeolosaurus of Argentina, with slender limbs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Alexander Kellner and Sergio de Azevedo, 1999

species:tametara-mirim.ageText: About 85 to 80 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, early snake named in 2026 from a three-dimensional, articulated skull and skeleton, one of very few Mesozoic snakes preserved this well, alongside Najash and Dinilysia.

related.note: Another well-preserved early snake.

species:navaornis-hestiae.ageText: About 85 to 80 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An enantiornithine bird named in 2024 from a beautifully preserved, uncrushed skull. Its toothless beak and enlarged brain were surprisingly modern, showing that some “opposite birds” had evolved brains and skulls like those of modern birds independently.

species:trigonosaurus-pricei.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: A saltasaurid titanosaur known from two partial skeletons found by Llewellyn Ivor Price, after whom it is named. Its name comes from Triângulo Mineiro, the region of Minas Gerais where it was found.

species:uberabasuchus-terrificus.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: A large peirosaurid, a land crocodile relative perhaps about 2.5 to 3 m long, with a tall skull and round-sectioned teeth suited to crushing bites. It was probably a terrestrial predator in a dry landscape.

species:itasuchus-jesuinoi.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: An itasuchid notosuchian with a long snout, first described by Llewellyn Ivor Price in 1955. It probably lived partly in water.

species:labidiosuchus-amicum.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: A small notosuchian with a bizarre lower jaw shaped like a Y and teeth of very different shapes, perhaps for an omnivorous diet.

species:galgadraco-zephyrius.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: The first pterosaur named from the Bauru Group, an azhdarchid known from a piece of the tip of its upper beak, named in 2025.

species:brasileodactylus-araripensis.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A fish-eating anhanguerian pterosaur with long, curved, interlocking front teeth. Cearadactylus, a skull once restored upside down and made famous by Michael Crichton’s novel Jurassic Park, is now considered the same animal.
species:brasileodactylus-araripensis.akaNote: Cearadactylus, famous from the novel Jurassic Park and once restored with its snout upside down, is now thought to be the same animal.

species:maaradactylus-kellneri.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: An anhanguerid pterosaur with a crest on its snout and many interlocking teeth, named in 2014. Its name refers to Maara, a princess of a local legend of the Araripe.

species:unwindia-trigonus.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A pterosaur known from a partial skull with a crest along the top, named in 2011 after the pterosaur researcher David Unwin.

species:aratasaurus-museunacionali.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A small, early coelurosaur known from a partial right leg, a juvenile perhaps about 3 m long. Its species name honours Brazil’s National Museum, which was devastated by fire in 2018; the specimen survived.

species:bakiribu-waridza.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: Named in 2025 from the jaws of two individuals preserved in a regurgitalite, a lump of vomit perhaps coughed up by a spinosaur. The jaws were described as those of a filter-feeding pterosaur like Pterodaustro, with closely packed, comb-like teeth; other researchers have since suggested they may belong to a different animal, so its identity is debated.

species:santanachelys-gaffneyi.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: One of the oldest known sea turtles, about 20 cm long, a protostegid, an early relative of the giant Archelon. Its skull has large openings around the eyes, perhaps for salt glands like those modern sea turtles use to get rid of excess salt.

species:cearachelys-placidoi.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
