summary: A side-necked turtle of the bothremydids, a group that included freshwater and coastal turtles.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Eugene Gaffney, Diógenes Campos and Ren Hirayama, 2001

species:araripichthys-castilhoi.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A deep-bodied, disc-shaped marine fish with long fins, one of the commonest fish in the Araripe concretions. The genus is also known from Morocco, Mexico and Venezuela.

species:epachthosaurus-sciuttoi.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:epachthosaurus-sciuttoi.placeText: Golfo San Jorge Basin, Chubut, Argentina
summary: A titanosaur known from a nearly complete, articulated skeleton without a skull, one of the most complete early titanosaurs. Its name means “heavy lizard”.

species:sarmientosaurus-musacchioi.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A titanosaur known from one of the most complete titanosaur skulls ever found, with a braincase that could be CT-scanned. It had large eyes and probably held its head pointing downwards, feeding on low plants.

species:xenotarsosaurus-bonapartei.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:xenotarsosaurus-bonapartei.placeText: Golfo San Jorge Basin, Chubut, Argentina
summary: An abelisaurid, perhaps about 5 m long, known from back vertebrae and a leg whose ankle bones were fused to the shin, an unusual feature that gives its name, “strange ankle lizard”.

species:aniksosaurus-darwini.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:aniksosaurus-darwini.placeText: Golfo San Jorge Basin, Chubut, Argentina
summary: A small, two-legged predatory dinosaur about 2 m long, known from several individuals. It was found on 21 September 1995, the first day of spring in the Southern Hemisphere, which gives its name, “spring lizard”; its species name honours Charles Darwin, who visited Patagonia on the Beagle.

species:notohypsilophodon-comodorensis.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:notohypsilophodon-comodorensis.placeText: Golfo San Jorge Basin, Chubut, Argentina
summary: A small, two-legged plant-eating ornithopod known from a partial skeleton, once called the only “hypsilophodont” from South America; it is now seen as an early ornithopod, perhaps an elasmarian.

species:campylodoniscus-ameghinoi.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:campylodoniscus-ameghinoi.placeText: Golfo San Jorge Basin, Chubut, Argentina
summary: A titanosaur known from part of an upper jaw with teeth, named by Friedrich von Huene in 1929 as Campylodon, a name that was already in use, so it was renamed in 1961.

species:bonitasaura-salgadoi.ageText: About 86 to 83 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
species:bonitasaura-salgadoi.placeText: La Bonita quarry, Río Negro, Argentina
summary: A titanosaur with a square, sharp-edged lower jaw that may have carried a horny, guillotine-like sheath for cropping plants, an adaptation unknown in other titanosaurs when it was described.

species:inawentu-oslatus.ageText: About 86 to 83 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
summary: A titanosaur named in 2024 from a partial skeleton with its skull. Its square jaw resembles those of the rebbachisaurids, which disappeared earlier, suggesting it took over their low-browsing role. Its name means “imitator”.

species:yeneen-houssayi.ageText: About 86 to 83 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
summary: A titanosaur named in 2026 from a partial skeleton, showing how many kinds of titanosaurs lived together in the Bajo de la Carpa.

species:neuquensuchus-universitas.ageText: About 86 to 83 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
species:neuquensuchus-universitas.placeText: Universidad Nacional del Comahue, Neuquén, Argentina
summary: A small crocodile relative found on the campus of the Universidad Nacional del Comahue in the city of Neuquén, which gives its species name. Its long limbs suggest an upright, land-living animal.

species:microsuchus-schilleri.ageText: About 86 to 83 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
summary: A small notosuchian crocodile relative named in 1928, known from limited remains.

species:cynodontosuchus-rothi.ageText: About 86 to 83 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A baurusuchid, a predatory land crocodile relative with big, dog-like canine teeth, named in 1896 by Arthur Smith Woodward, one of the first notosuchians known.

species:antarctosaurus-wichmannianus.ageText: About 80 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A titanosaur with a square-jawed skull, named in 1929 by Friedrich von Huene. Despite its name, “southern lizard”, it is not from Antarctica. Bones from several animals may have been mixed in its type specimen. A second species, A. giganteus, is known from enormous thigh bones over 2.3 m long and may have been one of the largest dinosaurs, though it may belong to a different genus.

species:pyrotherium-romeroi.ageText: About 29 to 24 million years ago (late Oligocene)
summary: A large, elephant-like South American hoofed mammal, perhaps about 3 m long, with tusks and probably a short trunk, though it was not related to elephants. Its name means “fire beast”, because its first fossils came from old volcanic ash.

species:leontinia-gaudryi.ageText: About 29 to 24 million years ago (late Oligocene)
summary: A large, rhinoceros-like notoungulate, the most common animal in the late Oligocene rocks where it is found.

species:rhynchippus-equinus.ageText: About 29 to 24 million years ago (late Oligocene)
species:rhynchippus-equinus.placeText: Patagonia, Argentina; also Bolivia and Brazil
summary: A sheep-sized notohippid notoungulate with high-crowned teeth for grazing, once thought to be related to horses; its name means “beaked horse”.

species:cramauchenia-normalis.ageText: About 29 to 18 million years ago (late Oligocene to early Miocene)
summary: An early macraucheniid litoptern, a relative of the long-necked Macrauchenia. Its name is an anagram of Macrauchenia.

species:andrewsornis-abbotti.ageText: About 29 to 24 million years ago (late Oligocene)
summary: A medium-sized terror bird, a flightless predatory phorusrhacid, known mainly from a skull.

species:madtsoia-bai.ageText: About 45 to 38 million years ago (middle Eocene)
summary: A giant constrictor-like snake, estimated at about 9 to 10 m long, from the madtsoiids, an ancient group that survived in Australia until about 50,000 years ago. Other species of Madtsoia are known from Brazil, India and Madagascar.

species:eocaiman-cavernensis.ageText: About 45 to 38 million years ago (middle Eocene)
summary: One of the earliest caimans, a primitive member of the caiman group, with species from the early Paleocene to the Miocene of Argentina, Brazil and Colombia.

species:pentaceratops-sternbergii.ageText: About 75 to 73 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
species:pentaceratops-sternbergii.placeText: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: A large chasmosaurine horned dinosaur about 6 to 7 m long, with one of the largest skulls of any land animal, up to about 2.3 m including its huge frill. Its name means “five-horned face”: besides the nose horn and two brow horns, it had pointed cheek bones that stuck out sideways. About a dozen skulls and skeletons are known.
It was found in 1921 by Charles H. Sternberg, after whom it is named. One giant specimen was later made its own genus, Titanoceratops, a decision still debated.

species:bisticeratops-froeseorum.ageText: About 75 to 73 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
summary: A chasmosaurine horned dinosaur known from a nearly complete skull with short brow horns, named in 2022. It is a close relative of Pentaceratops.

related.note: A close relative.

species:kritosaurus-navajovius.ageText: About 74 to 73 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:kritosaurus-navajovius.placeText: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: A duck-billed dinosaur without a hollow crest, known from an incomplete skull found by Barnum Brown in 1904. Its snout was broken and wrongly restored, and later finds of relatives showed it probably had a raised arch over the nose, the famous “Roman nose” of its tribe, the kritosaurins. Its name means “separated lizard”, often mistranslated as “noble lizard”.

species:ahshislesaurus-wimani.ageText: About 75 to 73 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
species:ahshislesaurus-wimani.placeText: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: A kritosaurin duck-billed dinosaur named in 2025 from a partial skull and neck found in 1916. It had a small bump over its snout rather than a crest, and had long been argued over as a possible specimen of Kritosaurus.

species:naashoibitosaurus-ostromi.placeText: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: A kritosaurin duck-billed dinosaur known from a partial skeleton with a skull. It was first described as a specimen of Kritosaurus. Its name comes from the Navajo word for “creek”.

species:nodocephalosaurus-kirtlandensis.ageText: About 73.5 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:nodocephalosaurus-kirtlandensis.placeText: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: An ankylosaurid known from a partial skull covered in rounded bony knobs, which gives its name, “knob-headed lizard”. It seems to be closer to Asian ankylosaurids than to those of Alberta and Montana.

species:velafrons-coahuilensis.ageText: About 73.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
summary: A crested duck-billed dinosaur (lambeosaurine) known from a mostly complete skull of a juvenile with a bony crest on its forehead, which gives its name, “sailed forehead”.

species:tlatolophus-galorum.ageText: About 73.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
summary: A crested duck-billed dinosaur related to Parasaurolophus, with a tall, curved, hollow crest probably used to make loud sounds. Its name means “word crest”, combining the Nahuatl word tlahtolli, “word”, with the shape of the speech scrolls in Aztec drawings, which its crest resembles.

related.note: A close relative.

species:coahuilasaurus-lipani.ageText: About 73.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
summary: A kritosaurin duck-billed dinosaur named in 2024 from jaw tips and skull fragments. Its species name honours the Lipan Apache people of the region.

species:mexidracon-longimanus.ageText: About 73.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
summary: An ostrich-dinosaur named in 2025 from a partial skeleton with unusually long arms, as its species name, “long hand”, says. Its name means “Mexican dragon”.

species:xenovenator-espinosai.ageText: About 73.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
species:xenovenator-espinosai.placeText: Coahuila, Mexico; perhaps also New Mexico, USA
summary: A troodontid named in 2026 from skull fragments with an unusually thick, rough, swollen top of the head, unlike any other troodontid; it may have been used for display or head-butting.

species:plotosaurus-bennisoni.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
species:plotosaurus-bennisoni.placeText: Panoche Hills, Fresno County, California, USA
summary: One of the most advanced swimming mosasaurs, about 5 to 6 m long, with a streamlined body, narrow flippers, a tail fluke and large eyes, converging on the shape of ichthyosaurs and dolphins. Some specimens preserve scales. It was first named Kolposaurus, but that name was already used for a nothosaur.

species:plesiotylosaurus-crassidens.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
species:plesiotylosaurus-crassidens.placeText: Panoche Hills, Fresno County, California, USA
summary: A large mosasaur with thick, strong teeth, a relative of Mosasaurus and Prognathodon despite a name meaning “near Tylosaurus”.

species:hydrotherosaurus-alexandrae.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
species:hydrotherosaurus-alexandrae.placeText: Panoche Hills, Fresno County, California, USA
summary: An elasmosaur, a very long-necked plesiosaur about 8 m long, known from a nearly complete skeleton with stomach stones. It is named after Annie Montague Alexander, the founder of the University of California Museum of Paleontology.

species:aphrosaurus-furlongi.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
species:aphrosaurus-furlongi.placeText: Panoche Hills, Fresno County, California, USA
summary: An elasmosaur known from skeletons found by a rancher in 1939. It is sometimes considered a doubtful name.

species:augustynolophus-morrisi.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
species:augustynolophus-morrisi.placeText: Panoche Hills, Fresno County, California, USA
summary: A duck-billed dinosaur related to Saurolophus, one of the last non-bird dinosaurs, found in sea rocks after its body drifted offshore. It was first described as a species of Saurolophus. In 2017 it became California’s official state dinosaur.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Albert Prieto-Márquez and Jonathan Wagner, 2013 (as Saurolophus morrisi); genus 2014

species:megacephalosaurus-eulerti.ageText: About 94 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Turonian)
summary: A short-necked pliosaur with the largest skull of any plesiosaur from North America, up to 1.75 m long, and an estimated body length of about 6 to 9 m. Its long snout and evenly sized teeth suggest it ate fairly small prey.

species:brachauchenius-lucasi.ageText: About 94 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Turonian)
summary: One of the last pliosaurs, a short-necked marine reptile perhaps about 9 m long, with a big skull and strong teeth. Its name means “short neck”. After it, pliosaurs disappeared and mosasaurs took over as the top predators of the seas.

species:bananogmius-aratus.ageText: About 95 to 84 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A large, deep-bodied marine fish, a plethodid, related to today’s bony-tongued fish, common in the Western Interior Seaway and the proto-North Sea.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Originally Anogmius aratus; renamed by Gilbert Whitley, 1940

species:taeniolabis-taoensis.ageText: About 65.5 to 65 million years ago (early Paleocene)
summary: The largest multituberculate, a rodent-like mammal about the size of a beaver, up to about 30 kg, with gnawing front teeth. It appeared within about 700,000 years of the asteroid impact, as plant-eating mammals grew rapidly in size in the newly empty world.

species:carsioptychus-coarctatus.ageText: About 65.9 to 65 million years ago (early Paleocene)
summary: A pig-sized, plant-eating periptychid mammal, perhaps about 9 kg, one of the first mammals to grow large after the asteroid impact. CT scans show a small brain with a good sense of smell.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Edward Cope, 1882 (as Periptychus coarctatus); genus by George Gaylord Simpson, 1936

species:mandrasuchus-milleri.ageText: About 66 to 65 million years ago (earliest Paleocene)
summary: The oldest confirmed alligatorine, the alligator branch, named in 2026 from Corral Bluffs. It lived within the first million years after the asteroid impact, showing that crocodilians recovered quickly.

A brachiosaurid sauropod known from four skulls, two of them complete, among the very few complete sauropod skulls from North America. It was found at Dinosaur National Monument and named after Abydos, the Egyptian city that held the head of the god Osiris. Its species name honours the sauropod expert John McIntosh.

A sauropod whose hip bone had an enormous blade for muscles, giving it proportionally the largest thigh muscles of any known sauropod; its name means “thunder thighs”. Its describers suggested it might have kicked predators or moved over rough ground.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Michael Taylor, Mathew Wedel and Richard Cifelli, 2011

species:venenosaurus-dicrocei.ageText: About 125 to 120 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
species:venenosaurus-dicrocei.placeText: Poison Strip, Grand County, Utah, USA
summary: A sauropod, a relative of the titanosaurs, found in 1998 by a museum volunteer, Anthony DiCroce. Its name means “poison lizard”, after the Poison Strip Member where it was found.

species:animantarx-ramaljonesi.ageText: About 99 to 96 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A nodosaurid armoured dinosaur whose skeleton was discovered by a radiation detector: the bones were slightly radioactive, and the team found them by scanning the ground before digging. Its name means “living citadel”.
A large, heavily built iguanodont, perhaps about 9 m long, known from a partial skeleton. Its name means “colossal iguana”.

species:nedcolbertia-justinhofmanni.ageText: About 135 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Valanginian)
summary: A small predatory dinosaur, perhaps 3 m long, known from three partial skeletons. It is named after the palaeontologist Edwin “Ned” Colbert.
A medium-sized raptor known from vertebrae and part of a leg. Its name is the Ute word for “coyote”, a predator of similar size.

A chipmunk-sized mammal with digging forelimbs and simple, peg-like teeth, built like a tiny armadillo or aardvark. It probably dug into termite nests, a lifestyle that evolved independently in later mammals.

A small, bird-like troodontid about 1 m long, nicknamed “Lori”, found in 2001 and named in 2019. It is one of the oldest troodontids from North America and probably lived on the ground in wetlands, as it shows no adaptations for flight.

A sauropod known from two neck vertebrae collected by the German Tendaguru expedition in 1909. It was first thought to be a diplodocid, but newer studies suggest it was a titanosauriform. Its species name honours Boheti bin Amrani, the expedition’s chief collector.

species:gilmoremys-lancensis.ageText: About 67 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:gilmoremys-lancensis.placeText: Montana, North Dakota and Wyoming, USA
summary: A softshell turtle, related to today’s softshells, with a flat, leathery shell, a long neck and a snorkel-like snout for breathing while hidden in mud.

species:cimexomys-minor.ageText: About 67 to 64 million years ago (end of the Cretaceous to early Paleocene)
summary: A small multituberculate, a rodent-like mammal that lived with the last dinosaurs and survived the asteroid impact into the Paleocene.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Robert Sloan and Leigh Van Valen, 1965

species:castorocauda-lutrasimilis.ageText: About 166 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: A swimming mammal relative with a flat, scaly, beaver-like tail and otter-like teeth, probably for catching fish, preserved with its fur. At 500 to 800 g it is the largest Jurassic mammaliaform known, and the oldest with a fur coat and adaptations for water. Its discovery in 2006 showed that Mesozoic mammals were far more varied than once thought.

species:volaticotherium-antiquum.ageText: About 166 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: One of the earliest gliding mammals, known from a skeleton with a furry membrane stretched between its legs, like a flying squirrel. It probably ate insects. Its name means “ancient gliding beast”.

related.note: An older relative that may also have glided.

species:scansoriopteryx-heilmanni.ageText: About 166 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: A sparrow-sized juvenile scansoriopterygid with feet adapted for climbing and an extremely long third finger, which in its relatives Yi and Ambopteryx supported a bat-like wing membrane. Its name means “climbing wing”. It was described in 2002, the same year as Epidendrosaurus, which is probably the same animal.

related.note: A relative with membranous wings.

species:epidexipteryx-hui.ageText: About 166 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: A pigeon-sized scansoriopterygid with four long, ribbon-like tail feathers, the earliest known ornamental feathers, used for display rather than flight. Its body was covered in fuzz and it had large front teeth. Its name means “display feather”.

A small scansoriopterygid, about 32 cm long and 306 g, preserved with feathers and a bat-like membrane on its arms, the second dinosaur found with such wings after Yi. Its stomach held gizzard stones and bone fragments. Its name means “both wings”.

related.note: Its closest relative.

species:pedopenna-daohugouensis.ageText: About 166 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: Known only from a foot and leg with long, vaned feathers on the foot, Pedopenna (“foot feather”) was a small feathered dinosaur that probably had leg “wings” like Anchiornis and Microraptor, and may be older than Archaeopteryx.

species:pterorhynchus-wellnhoferi.ageText: About 166 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: A long-tailed pterosaur with a wingspan of about 85 cm and a tall head crest made of soft tissue, preserved with traces of its body fuzz (pycnofibres). It is named after the pterosaur expert Peter Wellnhofer.

species:beishanlong-grandis.ageText: About 120 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: A giant ostrich-dinosaur, perhaps about 7 to 8 m long and over 600 kg, the second largest known after Deinocheirus. Its bones show it was not yet fully grown.

species:auroraceratops-rugosus.ageText: About 120 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: A small, two-legged early neoceratopsian about 1.3 m long with a short, wide face and wrinkled skull bones, known from many specimens. Its name means “dawn horned face”, partly honouring Dawn Dodson, wife of one of its describers.

species:brevidentavis-zhangi.ageText: About 120 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: An early relative of modern birds with short, stubby teeth, named in 2021 from a partial skull, one of several toothed ornithuromorphs from the Changma lake.

species:meemannavis-ductrix.ageText: About 120 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: An early toothed relative of modern birds, named in 2021 after the palaeontologist Zhang Mee-mann, a pioneer of Chinese fossil fish research.

species:yunnanosaurus-huangi.ageText: About 199 to 183 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A large long-necked plant-eater, up to about 13 m long in its larger species, that could walk on two or four legs. Its spoon-shaped, self-sharpening teeth wore against each other like those of sauropods, though it evolved them independently. It is known from more than 20 skeletons, some with skulls.

species:chinshakiangosaurus-chunghoensis.ageText: About 195 to 180 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: An early sauropod known from a fragmentary skeleton with a lower jaw, one of very few early sauropods with skull bones. Its jaw suggests it had fleshy cheeks.

species:yimenosaurus-youngi.ageText: About 195 to 180 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A long-necked plant-eater about 9 m long, known from a partial skull and skeleton, named in honour of the Chinese palaeontologist Yang Zhongjian (C. C. Young).

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Bai Ziqi, Yang Jie and Wang Guohui, 1990

species:yuxisaurus-kopchicki.ageText: About 195 to 180 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: An early armoured dinosaur, a relative of Scelidosaurus, named in 2022 from a partial skeleton and many armour plates. It is the first definite early thyreophoran from Asia, showing these animals had spread across Pangaea.

species:amurosaurus-riabinini.ageText: About 67 to 66 million years ago (latest Cretaceous)
summary: A crested duck-billed dinosaur (lambeosaurine) about 8 m long, the best-known dinosaur from Russia, known from hundreds of bones from a single huge bonebed. Sahaliyania, from the Chinese side of the Amur River, is now thought to be the same animal.

species:kerberosaurus-manakini.ageText: About 67 to 66 million years ago (latest Cretaceous)
summary: A flat-headed duck-billed dinosaur related to Saurolophus and Prosaurolophus, known from skull bones in the same bonebed as Amurosaurus. It is named after Kerberos, the three-headed dog guarding the underworld in Greek myth.

species:dinocephalosaurus-orientalis.ageText: About 244 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A sea-going reptile about 5 m long with an extremely long, snake-like neck made of 32 vertebrae, longer than its body and tail combined, used for ambushing fish. A fossil found with an embryo inside showed it gave birth to live young, the first evidence of live birth in this group of archosauromorphs.

species:atopodentatus-unicus.ageText: About 244 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A plant-eating marine reptile about 3 m long with a hammer-shaped head: a wide, T-shaped mouth lined with chisel-like teeth at the front and many needle-like teeth behind. It probably scraped algae off the sea floor and filtered it through its teeth. Its first skull was crushed and was reconstructed with a strange zipper-like mouth until better skulls were found in 2016.

species:qianosuchus-mixtus.ageText: About 244 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A crocodile-line archosaur over 3 m long with a deep, paddle-like tail, the only known Triassic archosaur adapted to life at sea, perhaps living like a saltwater crocodile. It is a poposauroid, related to the two-legged Effigia and the sailed Arizonasaurus.

species:austronaga-minuta.ageText: About 244 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A small, long-necked aquatic reptile, a relative of Dinocephalosaurus, named in 2023 from a complete skeleton with remains of its digestive tract preserved.

species:gracilicollum-latens.ageText: About 244 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A small, slender-necked archosauromorph reptile named in 2023 from a skull and partial neck, probably a relative of the long-necked tanysaurs.

species:youngolepis-praecursor.ageText: About 415 to 410 million years ago (Early Devonian)
summary: An early lobe-finned fish on the lineage leading to lungfishes, known from beautifully preserved skulls. Its braincase played a key part in debates about how lungfishes and four-legged animals are related.

species:achoania-jarviki.ageText: About 415 to 410 million years ago (Early Devonian)
summary: An early bony fish known from a skull. It was first thought to be a lobe-finned fish, but later studies suggest it may sit just outside both main groups of bony fishes.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Zhu Min, Yu Xiaobo and Per Ahlberg, 2001

species:yunnanolepis-chii.ageText: About 415 to 395 million years ago (Early to Middle Devonian)
summary: A primitive antiarch, a small armoured placoderm fish with jointed, arm-like pectoral fins encased in bone, that grubbed about on the sea floor.

A small arthropod with five eyes and a pair of grasping front limbs like those of Anomalocaris, but a segmented body with jointed legs like a true arthropod. Described in 2020, it is a “missing link” between radiodonts and arthropods. It is named after the qilin, a mythical chimera-like creature.
A vetulicolian, a puzzling Cambrian animal with a front half with gill-like openings and a segmented, tail-like back half. Vetulicolians may be early relatives of chordates.
A vetulicolian with a large front body bearing a row of gill pouches and a jointed back half. Xidazoon, named the same year, is the same animal.

A large early tyrannosauroid, perhaps about 9 m long, known from a partial skull and skeleton. Despite its size, comparable to later tyrannosaurids, it was probably a proceratosaurid, a relative of crested early tyrannosaurs like Guanlong, and may be close to Yutyrannus.

related.note: A large feathered relative.

summary: An early bird with a dinosaur-like skull and a very long scapula and foot bones, named in 2023 from a complete skeleton. It sits between Archaeopteryx-like birds and later, more modern birds.
One of the earliest and most primitive eutherians, the group that includes placental mammals, named in 2023. It was a tiny, shrew-like animal.

related.note: Another early eutherian from the Jehol Biota.

summary: A toothless chaoyangopterid pterosaur named in 2023 from an almost complete skeleton. Its name means “beautiful flying dragon”, and its species name, youhao, means “friendship”, marking a collaboration between Chinese and Brazilian scientists.
A pterosaur known from a lower jaw with 36 slender, evenly spaced teeth angled forward at its tip, probably for catching fish. It is named after Pangu, the creator in Chinese myth.

species:linheraptor-exquisitus.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A Velociraptor-like raptor under 2 m long known from one nearly complete, beautifully preserved skeleton. Some researchers think it is the same animal as Tsaagan of Mongolia.

species:linhenykus-monodactylus.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A tiny alvarezsaurid, the only known non-bird dinosaur with just one finger on each hand: a single stout claw for digging into insect nests.

species:philovenator-curriei.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small troodontid known from a hind leg, first thought to be a young Saurornithoides. Its name means “love hunter”, and its species name honours the palaeontologist Philip Currie.

species:gobiosuchus-kielanae.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, heavily armoured land crocodile relative, covered in bony plates, that lived among the dunes of the Gobi.

species:zosuchus-davidsonae.ageText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, primitive crocodyliform related to Gobiosuchus, named after the fossil preparator Amy Davidson.

species:tanius-sinensis.ageText: About 75 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A hadrosauroid, a duck-billed dinosaur relative, perhaps about 7 m long, named in 1929 by Carl Wiman. It honours the Chinese geologist Tan Xichou, who found it.
A toothless pterosaur with a long, low skull and no crest, which gives its name to the chaoyangopterids, relatives of the giant azhdarchids.
A small toothless pterosaur, first described as an early azhdarchid and now thought to be a chaoyangopterid. Its name means “dawn Azhdarcho”.
A toothless chaoyangopterid pterosaur with a pointed beak, named after Jilin University, whose researchers described it.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Dong Zhiming, Sun Yuewu and Wu Shaoyuan, 2003

summary: An istiodactylid pterosaur with short, blade-like, interlocking teeth at the front of a broad, rounded snout, probably for slicing chunks from carcasses or prey.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Wang Xiaolin, Diógenes Campos, Zhou Zhonghe and Alexander Kellner, 2008

summary: An istiodactylid pterosaur known from a short lower jaw with a few small teeth at the tip.
An istiodactylid pterosaur known from a skull and partial skeleton, closely related to Liaoxipterus and Istiodactylus.
A large fish-eating anhanguerid pterosaur with a low crest on its snout and very long front teeth, up to about 7 cm, among the largest of any pterosaur. Its wingspan was perhaps about 5 m.

A sparrow-sized enantiornithine, one of the “opposite birds”, described in 1992 as one of the first Cretaceous birds from China. It mixed primitive features, like teeth and clawed fingers, with a modern-style short tail and perching feet.
An early bird with a short, deep, toothless beak, named in 2002. It is very like Sapeornis and many researchers think it is the same animal.

related.note: Probably the same animal.

summary: A large, short-armed raptor about 1.6 m long, known from an almost complete skeleton. Its arms were too short for flight or gliding, unlike its small relatives such as Microraptor.

species:xiongguanlong-baimoensis.ageText: About 125 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A mid-sized tyrannosauroid, perhaps about 4 to 5 m long, with a long, narrow snout. It is an intermediate between small early tyrannosauroids and the later giants.
A small iguanodont known from a young individual about 4.5 m long. Its name means “horse dragon”, for its long, horse-like skull, and its species name “shield tooth” for its teeth.
A turiasaur, one of the broad-toothed sauropods otherwise known from Europe, known from thousands of jumbled bones from a single bonebed near Moab, showing these sauropods reached North America.

A rabbit-sized mammal relative known from a well-preserved skull, one of the haramiyidans, a group otherwise known mainly from Africa and Asia. Its tiny eyes and large smell centres suggest it was nocturnal. Its species name means “yellow cat” in the Ute language.

species:fona-herzogae.ageText: About 99 to 96 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, two-legged plant-eater named in 2024 from several skeletons and skulls, an early relative of Thescelosaurus. Its bones suggest it may have dug burrows.

species:iani-smithi.ageText: About 99 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A plant-eating ornithopod about 3.7 m long named in 2023 from a partial skeleton with skull. It belongs to the rhabdodontomorphs, a group otherwise known mainly from Europe. Its name comes from Janus, the two-faced Roman god of change, because it lived during a time of great change in North American faunas.

species:cedarpelta-bilbeyhallorum.ageText: About 98 to 94 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: A large, early ankylosaurid, perhaps about 5 to 7 m long, known from many jumbled bones. Its skull was not fused like those of later ankylosaurs, so its bones could be studied separately.
An early predatory dinosaur with a short skull and large, forward-pointing, buck-tooth fangs, which give its species name, “buck-toothed”. It is a relative of Herrerasaurus and Tawa.
An erpetosuchid, a crocodile-line archosaur with heavy bony armour plates along its back, about 1 to 2 m long.

species:prozostrodon-brasiliensis.ageText: About 233 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A cat-sized cynodont close to the ancestors of mammals, with a skull about 6.7 cm long, probably a predator of small reptiles.

species:plateosauravus-cullingworthi.ageText: About 215 to 205 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: An early long-necked plant-eater first named as a species of Plateosaurus in 1924. Its name means “grandfather of Plateosaurus”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Sidney Haughton, 1924 (as Plateosaurus cullingworthi); genus by Friedrich von Huene, 1932

species:sphenosuchus-acutus.ageText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: A small, long-legged early crocodile relative known from a superbly preserved skull, which gives its name to the “sphenosuchians”. Studies of its skull, especially by Alick Walker, were key to understanding how crocodiles and birds are related.
A small, short-snouted, heavily armoured early crocodyliform about 1 m long, a protosuchid. It probably lived on land but its limbs and tail suggest it could swim.
The oldest known goniopholidid-like crocodile relative, with a flat, crocodile-shaped skull, probably a semi-aquatic hunter.
One of the oldest turtles from North America, an early stem turtle that could not yet pull its head into its shell.
A massopodan sauropodomorph named in 2022 from a skeleton long thought to be a Plateosaurus, kept in the University of Tübingen collection.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Omar Regalado Fernández and Ingmar Werneburg, 2022

summary: A tree-dwelling haramiyidan with long fingers and toes and a grasping tail, perhaps a squirrel-like climber that ate seeds and fruit.
A small stegosaur, about 3 to 4 m long, with thick, spike-like plates and perhaps two or three pairs of tail spikes.

species:datousaurus-bashanensis.ageText: About 168 to 164 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A sauropod about 14 m long with a deep, heavy skull and a fairly short neck. Its name means “chieftain lizard”, and is also a pun on da tou, “big head” in Chinese.

species:protognathosaurus-oxyodon.ageText: About 168 to 164 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: A sauropod known only from part of a lower jaw with teeth.

species:zigongosaurus-fuxiensis.ageText: About 165 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
summary: A long-necked mamenchisaurid sauropod. Because Chinese Jurassic sauropods are poorly understood, it has been placed in Omeisaurus or Mamenchisaurus by some researchers.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Hou Lianhai, Zhou Shiwu and Chao Xijin, 1976

species:klamelisaurus-gobiensis.ageText: About 162 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
species:klamelisaurus-gobiensis.placeText: Kelameili Mountains, Junggar Basin, Xinjiang, China
summary: A mamenchisaurid sauropod about 17 m long, known from a partial skeleton found in 1982 near an abandoned mine.

species:aoniraptor-libertatem.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A megaraptoran, a lightly built predator related to Megaraptor, known from tail vertebrae and other bones. It may be the same animal as Gualicho.

species:sidersaura-marae.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: One of the largest rebbachisaurids, perhaps about 20 m long, named in 2024 from four individuals. Its name means “star lizard”, after the star-shaped ends of its tail vertebrae.

species:astigmasaura-genuflexa.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A rebbachisaurid sauropod named in 2025 from an incomplete, articulated skeleton found with its legs folded beneath it.

species:patagosphenos-watuku.ageText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: A tuatara relative, a large sphenodontian named in 2019, related to the living tuatara’s ancestors.

species:thapunngaka-shawi.ageText: About 105 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian)
summary: The largest pterosaur known from Australia, with a wingspan estimated at about 7 m, known from a lower jaw with a bony crest and sockets for about 40 teeth. Its name means “spear mouth” in the Wanamara language.

species:aussiedraco-molnari.ageText: About 105 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian)
summary: A toothed pterosaur known from a lower jaw, now placed with the targaryendraconians, a group named after the dragon-riding Targaryens of Game of Thrones.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Alexander Kellner, Taissa Rodrigues and Fabiana Costa, 2011

species:mythunga-camara.ageText: About 105 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian)
summary: An anhanguerid pterosaur known from a partial skull, a close relative of Ferrodraco from Winton.

species:nanantius-eos.ageText: About 105 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian)
summary: A small enantiornithine bird known from a shin bone found in the stomach area of an ichthyosaur, probably its last meal. Until 2026 it was the only named Cretaceous bird from Australia.

species:tenuicruris-piscanexum.ageText: About 105 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian)
summary: An enantiornithine bird named in 2026 from a single slender leg bone, the second Mesozoic bird named from Australia.

Australia’s largest known dinosaur, a giant titanosaur relative perhaps 25 to 30 m long, nicknamed “Cooper” after Cooper Creek. Found in 2007 and named in 2021, its bones were 3D-scanned so they could be compared with others without moving the heavy fossils.

An anhanguerid pterosaur with crests on the tips of its jaws and a wingspan of about 4 m, known from the most complete pterosaur skull found in Australia, preserved in ironstone, which gives its name, “iron dragon”.

A crocodile relative about 2.5 m long found with the bones of a young ornithopod dinosaur inside its belly, the first direct evidence of a crocodile eating a dinosaur in Australia. Its species name means “dinosaur killer”.

An ankylosaurid about 6 m long, known from a complete skull and tail club with skin and armour still in place. It is named after Zuul, the monster in the film Ghostbusters, and its species name means “destroyer of shins”, after the tail club. Damaged armour on its sides suggests ankylosaurs fought each other with their clubs.

A chasmosaurine horned dinosaur nicknamed “Judith”, with sideways-pointing brow horns and curled spikes on its frill. Its forelimb shows a long-lasting infection in the elbow joint, a painful injury it lived with for years.
A centrosaurine horned dinosaur with two long, forward-curving spikes on its frill. Its name means “bent sword horned face”, and its species name refers to Cronus, who in Greek myth used a sickle.

A caenagnathid, a toothless, beaked relative of oviraptors, known from a skeleton whose arm bones bear quill knobs, the attachment points for large feathers, showing it had wing-like arms for display.

species:ojoceratops-fowleri.ageText: About 69 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:ojoceratops-fowleri.placeText: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: A chasmosaurine horned dinosaur known from frill bones, very like Triceratops; some researchers think it is the same animal.

related.note: Perhaps the same animal.

species:glyptodontopelta-mimus.ageText: About 69 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:glyptodontopelta-mimus.placeText: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: A nodosaurid known from armour plates fused into a shield over its hips, like the shell of a glyptodont, the giant armadillo relative, which gives it its name.

species:navajodactylus-boerei.placeText: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: A pterosaur known from a wing bone, probably an azhdarchid.

species:eoneophron-infernalis.ageText: About 67 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A caenagnathid about the size of a large wolf, named in 2024 from a hind leg, smaller than Anzu and larger than Infernogallus. Its name means “dawn Neophron”, after the Egyptian vulture.

species:jaculinykus-yaruui.ageText: About 72 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An alvarezsaurid named in 2023 from a nearly complete skeleton with its skull, found curled up in a bird-like sleeping posture. It had one large finger and a tiny second one.

species:harenadraco-prima.ageText: About 72 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: The first troodontid from the Barun Goyot Formation, named in 2024 from a fragmentary skeleton. Its name means “sand dragon”.
A small caenagnathid, a beaked relative of oviraptors, known from feet whose ankle bones were fused, which gives its name, “foot-sole lizard”.

A small oviraptorid with a thick lower jaw built for crushing, perhaps for eating seeds or shellfish. It is not closely related to the other Nemegt oviraptorids, suggesting different diets kept them apart.

species:gobiazhdarcho-tsogtbaatari.ageText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An azhdarchid pterosaur, a relative of Quetzalcoatlus, named in 2025 from three neck vertebrae. It lived alongside the larger azhdarchid Tsogtopteryx.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Rodrigo Pêgas, Zhou Xuanyu and Yoshitsugu Kobayashi, 2025

summary: A small, heavily armoured gobiosuchid crocodile relative; its name means “hedgehog crocodile”, after its spiky armour.

species:ulughbegsaurus-uzbekistanensis.ageText: About 92 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A carcharodontosaurid about 7.5 to 8 m long and about a tonne, known from an upper jaw bone. It was the top predator of its time in Central Asia, before tyrannosaurids took over that role.

species:kizylkumavis-cretacea.ageText: About 92 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An enantiornithine bird known from part of an arm bone.

species:asiatyrannus-xui.ageText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, deep-snouted tyrannosaurine, perhaps 3.5 to 4 m long, named in 2024. It lived alongside the long-snouted Qianzhousaurus, showing that tyrannosaurs of different sizes and shapes shared the same habitats.

related.note: A long-snouted tyrannosaur from the same rocks.

species:tongtianlong-limosus.ageText: About 72 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An oviraptorid found by construction workers in 2015, preserved face down in mudstone with its arms and head raised, as if it died struggling to free itself from mud. Its species name means “muddy”.

species:jiangxisaurus-ganzhouensis.ageText: About 72 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: An oviraptorid similar to Heyuannia, with strongly curved claws and a slender lower jaw, one of several oviraptorids from the egg-rich rocks around Ganzhou.
One of the oldest ostrich-dinosaurs, named in 2023. Its brain shape and some other features resemble those of tyrannosaurs, which gives its name, “tyrant mimic”.

A small atoposaurid crocodile relative named in 2024 from three individuals with a complete skull. Its tall, narrow skull and land-adapted limbs suggest it hunted on land, a little like a monitor lizard, which gives its name.

An armoured dinosaur named in 2023 from a skeleton long thought to be Polacanthus, the first new ankylosaur from the Isle of Wight in over 100 years. Its species name honours the palaeontologist Paul Barrett.
A small, fast-running plant-eater named in 2024 from a juvenile skeleton, a close relative of Hypsilophodon. Its name means “Isle of Wight runner”.

species:paludohadros-proudlovii.ageText: About 129 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: A hadrosauroid, a relative of the duck-billed dinosaurs, named in 2026 from a partial skull and skeleton. Its name means “marsh hadrosaur”.
A dryomorph ornithopod, a relative of Dryosaurus and Camptosaurus, named in 2024 from arm and leg bones. Its name means “western claw”.
A gnathosaurine pterosaur, a relative of Gnathosaurus from Solnhofen, named in 2023 from parts of the upper jaw with teeth and neck vertebrae.
A crocodile relative with an extremely long, narrow, tube-like snout like a gharial’s, for catching fish.
A small, early iguanodontian known from isolated bones, first described as a species of the English Valdosaurus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Peter Galton and Philippe Taquet, 1982 (as Valdosaurus nigeriensis); genus by Galton, 2009

species:fortignathus-felixi.ageText: About 97 to 93 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A long-snouted crocodile relative known from three incomplete lower jaws.
A crocodile relative, perhaps a notosuchian, known from skull bones with teeth of different sizes.

species:kelumapusaura-machi.ageText: About 72 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A saurolophine duck-billed dinosaur named in 2022 from a bonebed with several individuals. Its name means “red earth lizard” in Mapuche.

A carnotaurine abelisaurid about 5 m long, named in 2024 from a young skeleton found in the same rocks as Carnotaurus. Unlike Carnotaurus it lacked horns, showing that two different abelisaurids lived together.
An abelisaurid named in 2022 after a Tehuelche god, known from vertebrae and limb bones.

species:rinconsaurus-caudamirus.ageText: About 86 to 83 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:rinconsaurus-caudamirus.placeText: Rincón de los Sauces, Neuquén, Argentina
summary: A slender titanosaur about 11 m long known from three partial skeletons, with unusual tail vertebrae, which give its species name, “wonderful tail”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Jorge Calvo and Bernardo González Riga, 2003

summary: A hadrosauroid, a duck-billed dinosaur relative about 4 m long, named in 2023 from bones of several individuals. Its ancestors seem to have reached South America separately from the true hadrosaurids. Its name means “similar to a wild duck” in the Aónikenk language.

species:barbosania-gracilirostris.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A crestless, slender-snouted toothed pterosaur known from a nearly complete skeleton, now placed with the targaryendraconians.

species:caririsuchus-camposi.ageText: About 115 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: An itasuchid crocodile relative known from bones in the Araripe concretions.
An ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur about 4.5 m long, one of the youngest from the Slottsmøya site, from just after the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.
A small leptocleidid plesiosaur about 2.6 m long, known from a nearly complete skeleton found in the oil sands mines. It is named after the palaeontologist Elizabeth Nicholls.
An unusually long-necked polycotylid plesiosaur named in 2022. Its name means “snake-crocodile face”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Scott Persons, Hallie Street and Kelley, 2022

summary: A vetulicolian, one of the puzzling Cambrian animals with a bulky front half and a segmented, tail-like back half, probably early relatives of chordates. It was the first vetulicolian found in Australia, and its back half shows a rod-like structure that may be a notochord.

species:skeemella-clavula.placeText: House Range and Drum Mountains, Utah, USA
summary: A long, segmented vetulicolian, an early possible chordate relative, found in the rocks just above the Wheeler Shale and in the Marjum Formation. Its back half is unusually long, with many segments.
A phacopid trilobite, related to the trilobites with large, many-lensed eyes, found in the shallow coastal sandstones that also hold some of the earliest fish.

species:buffalopterus-pustulosus.placeText: Near Buffalo, New York, USA, and Ontario, Canada
summary: A sea scorpion about 30 cm long with a strange round, bulb-like tail spine instead of the usual pointed one. It was first thought to reach about 1 m, but later study shrank that estimate.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: About 30 cm (older estimates of 1 m are too big)

summary: A close relative of Tiktaalik named in 2022, found near the same site. Its front fins were built for swimming, not for propping itself up, so it seems to have gone back to a fully watery life while its relatives were moving towards land.

related.note: Its close relative from the same rocks.

summary: An armoured arthrodire fish, a smaller relative of Dunkleosteus from the same seas.

species:bolosaurus-striatus.ageText: About 295 to 280 million years ago (early Permian)
summary: A small early reptile with bulbous, overlapping cheek teeth that worked together to chop plants, one of the first land animals specialised for chewing plant food. Bolosaurids are also known from Russia, and its relative Eudibamus from Germany may have run on its hind legs.

One of the oldest known monotremes, the egg-laying mammal group of the platypus and echidnas, known from four tiny lower jaws. The animal was perhaps about 10 cm long. Its jaw has a large canal for nerves, like the platypus’s, which may mean it already had an electricity-sensing bill, although this is debated.

species:zhyrasuchus-angustifrons.ageText: About 92 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A crocodile relative known only from a few skull bones. It may have been an early true crocodile, but the fossils are too poor to be sure; it may even be the same as Tadzhikosuchus.

species:albertochampsa-langstoni.ageText: About 76 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small, early relative of alligators and caimans, known from a skull only about 21 cm long. It was rare compared with the common crocodilian Leidyosuchus.
A small to medium-sized relative of alligators, with a skull about 20 cm long and large, rounded crushing teeth at the back of its jaws, perhaps for shellfish or turtles.

One of the largest enantiornithine birds, about the size of a turkey vulture, known from a partial skeleton. Its arm bones carry quill knobs like a modern bird’s, showing that “opposite birds” had evolved advanced flight.
A side-necked turtle known from a nearly complete skull, the first fossil turtle skull from Madagascar older than the last few thousand years.

species:bonnerichthys-gladius.ageText: About 87 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A giant filter-feeding fish at least 5 m long, a relative of the even bigger Jurassic Leedsichthys. For over a century its bones were misidentified; it was recognised as a plankton-eater only in 2010, showing that big filter-feeding fish lived alongside the plesiosaurs and mosasaurs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Edward Drinker Cope, 1873 (as Portheus gladius); genus by Friedman and colleagues, 2010

species:anthracosuchus-balrogus.placeText: Cerrejón coal mine, La Guajira, Colombia
summary: A dyrosaurid crocodile relative with an unusually short, blunt snout and thick bony armour, which probably hunted turtles and fish in the rivers of the Cerrejón rainforest. Its species name comes from the Balrog, the fire monster in The Lord of the Rings, and its genus name means “coal crocodile”.

species:asineops-squamifrons.ageText: About 52 to 49 million years ago (early Eocene)
summary: A puzzling freshwater fish with no close living relatives, the only member of its own family. Its name means “donkey face”. It was common in ancient Lake Gosiute but very rare at Fossil Lake.
An early catfish about 20 to 28 cm long, in a family of its own. Like living catfish it had barbels for feeling for food and sharp spines on its front fins for defence.

species:tsoabichi-greenriverensis.ageText: About 52 to 49 million years ago (early Eocene)
summary: A small early caiman, about 1 m long, whose skeletons sometimes keep outlines of the skin and scales. Its name means “monster” in Shoshone. It shows caimans, now found only in Central and South America, once reached North America.

species:calciavis-grandei.ageText: About 52 to 49 million years ago (early Eocene)
summary: A lithornithid, a chicken-sized flying relative of ostriches, emus and tinamous, preserved with skin and feathers. Some researchers think it belongs in Lithornis.

species:gallinuloides-wyomingensis.ageText: About 52 to 49 million years ago (early Eocene)
summary: One of the oldest known relatives of chickens, pheasants and turkeys, known from a skeleton found in 1900. It was an early offshoot of the galliform line.

species:limnofregata-azygosternon.ageText: About 52 to 49 million years ago (early Eocene)
summary: An early frigatebird known from several complete skeletons, some with feather outlines. Unlike living frigatebirds, which soar over oceans, it lived around a freshwater lake, which gives its name, “freshwater frigatebird”. Its beak was shorter and less hooked.

species:protorohippus-venticolum.ageText: About 52 to 50 million years ago (early Eocene)
summary: A small early horse with four toes on its front feet and three on its back feet. Some researchers include it in Eohippus. A complete skeleton from the Green River Formation is one of the best early horse fossils.

A fox-sized, chevrotain-like hoofed mammal that is one of the closest known relatives of whales. Its ear bone has the special shape found only in whales, and its thick, heavy bones suggest it waded in water to escape predators, much as the African mouse-deer does today.

facts.label: Found in
facts.value: The Subathu Formation of Kashmir, the same age as the Kuldana Formation

species:sarkastodon-mongoliensis.ageText: About 45 to 40 million years ago (middle Eocene)
summary: One of the largest oxyaenids, an extinct group of meat-eating mammals not closely related to today’s carnivores. It was perhaps about 3 m long, with heavy, blunt teeth suited to crushing bones or tough food. Body weight estimates vary widely, from a few hundred kilograms up to about 800 kg.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Perhaps several hundred kg; estimates up to about 800 kg are uncertain

species:moeritherium-lyonsi.ageText: About 37 to 35 million years ago (late Eocene)
summary: A pig-sized early relative of elephants with short legs and a long body, probably living partly in water like a hippo. It had no trunk, though its upper lip may have been flexible, and its second incisors were slightly enlarged, the start of tusks.

species:phiomia-serridens.ageText: About 35 to 30 million years ago (late Eocene to early Oligocene)
summary: An early elephant relative about 1.4 to 1.7 m tall at the shoulder, with short tusks in both jaws and probably a short trunk. It was once thought to be the same as Palaeomastodon.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Charles William Andrews and Hugh Beadnell, 1902

summary: A hyaenodont, an extinct kind of meat-eating mammal, weighing about 18 to 36 kg, named after the Egyptian cat goddess Bastet. It was first described as a species of Pterodon.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Patricia Holroyd, 1999 (as Pterodon syrtos); genus by Borths and colleagues, 2016

species:hyracodon-nebraskensis.ageText: About 34 to 28 million years ago (late Eocene to Oligocene)
summary: A hornless, pony-sized rhino relative with long, slim legs built for running, one of the “running rhinos”. It was related to the giant Paraceratherium of Asia.
A cat-sized early ruminant related to today’s chevrotains, with long, slender legs and no tusk-like canines. It is one of the most common fossils of the Big Badlands, and probably lived in herds.

A tiny primate known from a few teeth. It was first described in 2001 as a dwarf lemur, which would have meant lemurs evolved in Asia. Later study showed it was an adapiform instead, so it no longer upsets the story of lemurs evolving in Africa and Madagascar.

species:paraptenodytes-antarcticus.ageText: About 20 to 16 million years ago (early Miocene)
summary: A fossil penguin between a Magellanic penguin and an emperor penguin in size, known from a partial skeleton. It belongs to an extinct side branch, not the ancestors of living penguins.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Florentino Ameghino, 1891 (species by Moreno and Mercerat)

summary: A long-legged horse of the open grasslands, with one toe per foot in some individuals and three in others. It was once thought to be the ancestor of modern horses, but its curved teeth and skull hollows show it was a side branch.

species:hesperogavialis-cruxenti.ageText: About 10 to 7 million years ago (late Miocene)
summary: A long-snouted gharial relative, one of the best-known gryposuchine gharials of South America, though the back of its skull is still unknown.

species:ikanogavialis-gameroi.ageText: About 10 to 7 million years ago (late Miocene)
summary: A gharial relative that lived along the coast, perhaps the most sea-going of the South American gryposuchines. A similar animal, possibly the same genus, has been reported from much younger rocks on Woodlark Island, Papua New Guinea.

A sea-going gharial relative about 4.3 m long that lived along the Pacific coast alongside the larger Piscogavialis. Its skull suggests a generalist diet. Falling sea levels and cooling seas probably caused its extinction.

species:procariama-simplex.ageText: About 7 to 4 million years ago (late Miocene to Pliocene)
summary: The largest member of the psilopterines, the smallest kind of terror bird, related to the living seriemas. It was a fast-running ground predator.

species:nyasasaurus-parringtoni.ageText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic; exact age debated)
summary: Perhaps the earliest known dinosaur, or the closest relative of dinosaurs, known from an upper arm bone and some vertebrae. Its bone tissue shows fast growth like early dinosaurs. It may have been about 2 to 3 m long, including a long tail (estimate).

If the Manda Beds are truly Anisian, it lived about 10 million years before the oldest certain dinosaurs from South America. Both its exact place in the family tree and the age of the rocks are still debated.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Sterling Nesbitt and colleagues, 2013 (first described by Alan Charig in 1956)

facts.label: Length
facts.value: Perhaps 2–3 m (estimate from very few bones)

species:teleocrater-rhadinus.ageText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic; exact age debated)
summary: A long-necked, four-legged meat-eater about 2 to 3 m long, an aphanosaur, one of the earliest relatives of dinosaurs and pterosaurs. Its ankle joints were crocodile-like, showing that the first members of the bird line did not look like dinosaurs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Sterling Nesbitt and colleagues, 2017 (named informally by Alan Charig in 1956)

species:asilisaurus-kongwe.ageText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic; exact age debated)
summary: A silesaurid about 1 to 3 m long, a slender, four-legged plant-eater with a beak-like tip to its lower jaw, known from many individuals. Its name means “ancestor lizard” in Swahili.
It shows the dinosaur line had already split into several groups by the Middle Triassic. Some recent studies place silesaurids as early ornithischians, others as close relatives of dinosaurs.

species:mandasuchus-tanyauchen.ageText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic; exact age debated)
summary: A four-legged, crocodile-line predator with a long neck, a loricatan related to the later rauisuchids and crocodiles. It was first mentioned by Alan Charig in 1956 but only formally named in 2018.

species:mambawakale-ruhuhu.ageText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic; exact age debated)
summary: A large crocodile-line predator known from a skull and partial skeleton found in 1963. It was informally called “Pallisteria” for almost 60 years before being named in 2022. Its name means “ancient crocodile” in Swahili.

species:hypselorhachis-mirabilis.ageText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic; exact age debated)
summary: A crocodile-line reptile known only from one vertebra with a very tall, thin spine, probably part of a sail along its back, like its relative Ctenosauriscus.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Richard Butler and colleagues, 2009 (name first used by Alan Charig)

species:aleodon-brachyrhamphus.ageText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic; exact age debated)
summary: A short-snouted cynodont related to the ancestors of mammals, with grinding cheek teeth for a partly plant-based diet. A second species has been found in Brazil, and it is also known from Namibia.

species:yarasuchus-deccanensis.ageText: About 247 to 242 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A four-legged aphanosaur, an early relative of dinosaurs and pterosaurs, with a long neck and tall spines on its back. Its name means “red crocodile” in Telugu. It was first thought to be a crocodile-line rauisuchian; it is now grouped with Teleocrater.

related.note: A close relative from Tanzania.

species:wadiasaurus-indicus.ageText: About 247 to 242 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A large, beaked plant-eating dicynodont found in bonebeds with many individuals, suggesting it lived in herds. It is the only kannemeyeriid known for certain from India.

species:bharitalasuchus-tapani.ageText: About 247 to 242 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: One of the last erythrosuchids, the big-headed top predators of the Early and Middle Triassic. Its name means “Indian crocodile”, and the species honours Tapan Roy Chowdhury.

species:scleromochlus-taylori.ageText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, late Carnian)
species:scleromochlus-taylori.placeText: Near Elgin and Lossiemouth, Moray, Scotland
summary: A tiny archosaur under 20 cm long with long hind legs. For a century it was debated whether it was a hopping animal close to dinosaurs or to pterosaurs.

A 2022 study used CT scans of the natural moulds to rebuild its skeleton and found it was a close relative of the lagerpetids, the group thought to be closest to pterosaurs. It was a ground-living animal, not a glider.

species:saltopus-elginensis.ageText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, late Carnian)
species:saltopus-elginensis.placeText: Near Elgin and Lossiemouth, Moray, Scotland
summary: A very small, two-legged dinosauriform, perhaps chicken-sized, known from one poorly preserved skeleton. It was once called a dinosaur; a 2011 restudy found it was a close relative of dinosaurs instead.

species:ornithosuchus-woodwardi.ageText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, late Carnian)
species:ornithosuchus-woodwardi.placeText: Near Elgin and Lossiemouth, Moray, Scotland
summary: A crocodile-line predator perhaps 2 to 4 m long that could walk on two or four legs. It was once thought to be the ancestor of big meat-eating dinosaurs like Allosaurus.
Myth-buster: it is now known to be on the crocodile side of the archosaur family tree, and its resemblance to dinosaurs is convergent.

species:erpetosuchus-granti.ageText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, late Carnian)
species:erpetosuchus-granti.placeText: Near Elgin and Lossiemouth, Moray, Scotland
summary: A small, armoured crocodile-line archosaur with a short skull and few teeth. Similar fossils from Connecticut show its relatives also lived in North America. It was once thought to be close to crocodiles, but its position is now uncertain.

species:leptopleuron-lacertinum.ageText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, late Carnian)
species:leptopleuron-lacertinum.placeText: Near Elgin and Lossiemouth, Moray, Scotland
summary: A stocky, lizard-like procolophonid with spiky cheek bones and blunt teeth, perhaps for eating tough plants or insects. Named in 1851, it was the first Elgin reptile to be described and was also called Telerpeton.

species:brachyrhinodon-taylori.ageText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, late Carnian)
species:brachyrhinodon-taylori.placeText: Near Elgin and Lossiemouth, Moray, Scotland
summary: A small, short-snouted relative of the tuatara, a clevosaurid, with sharp teeth fused to the jaw.

species:dongusuchus-efremovi.ageText: About 245 to 240 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: An aphanosaur, an early relative of dinosaurs and pterosaurs, known only from slender thigh bones. Its species name honours Ivan Efremov, palaeontologist and science-fiction writer.

species:uralosaurus-magnus.ageText: About 245 to 240 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A big-headed erythrosuchid predator, first named as a species of the African Erythrosuchus in 1980 and given its own genus in 1995.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Vitaly Ochev, 1980 (as Erythrosuchus magnus); genus by Andrey Sennikov, 1995

species:sarmatosuchus-otschevi.ageText: About 245 to 240 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: An early archosauriform, a distant cousin of the first archosaurs, known from one partial skull and skeleton. It was first placed with Proterosuchus but is now thought to be more advanced.

species:rabidosaurus-cristatus.ageText: About 245 to 240 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A medium-sized, beaked plant-eating kannemeyeriid dicynodont. Its name means “furious lizard”, despite it being a plant-eater.

species:uralokannemeyeria-vjuschkovi.ageText: About 245 to 240 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: A large kannemeyeriiform dicynodont, a heavy, beaked plant-eater, named after the Urals and its resemblance to the South African Kannemeyeria.

species:shuvosaurus-inexpectatus.ageText: About 220 to 215 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
species:shuvosaurus-inexpectatus.placeText: Post Quarry, near Post, Texas, USA
summary: A toothless, beaked, two-legged animal about 2 to 3 m long that looked remarkably like an ostrich dinosaur. When its skull was described in 1993 it was thought to be an early ornithomimid.
Myth-buster: the discovery of its close relative Effigia in New Mexico showed it was on the crocodile side of the family tree, one of the most striking cases of convergent evolution with dinosaurs.
species:shuvosaurus-inexpectatus.akaNote: Chatterjeea elegans, named in 1995 from skeletons in the same quarry, turned out to be the body of Shuvosaurus.

related.note: Its close relative, whose skeleton revealed what Shuvosaurus was.

species:protoavis-texensis.ageText: About 220 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
species:protoavis-texensis.placeText: Post Quarry, near Post, Texas, USA
summary: A famous and highly controversial fossil described in 1991 as a bird 75 million years older than Archaeopteryx.

Myth-buster: almost all palaeontologists now think the bones are a jumble from several different animals, including a drepanosaur and small dinosaurs or other reptiles. It is not accepted as evidence of Triassic birds.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Doubtful; probably a mix of several animals (chimera)

species:adelobasileus-cromptoni.ageText: About 225 to 220 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: A small mammal relative known from the back of a skull about 1.5 cm long. The shape of its inner ear housing places it very near the common ancestor of all mammals. Its name means “obscure king”.

species:gojirasaurus-quayi.ageText: About 215 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: A coelophysoid theropod named after Godzilla (Gojira in Japanese), originally estimated at about 5.5 m long, which would make it one of the largest Triassic predatory dinosaurs.

Caution: later study found that some of its bones belong to other animals, and the rest may come from a young individual of an already-known coelophysoid. Many researchers treat it as a doubtful name.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Doubtful; partly a mix of bones from different animals

species:lucasuchus-hunti.ageText: About 215 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
species:lucasuchus-hunti.placeText: Revuelto Creek, Quay County, New Mexico, USA
summary: A desmatosuchine aetosaur, a plant-eating armoured crocodile-line reptile with long horn-like spikes on its sides, named after the palaeontologist Spencer Lucas.

species:sierritasuchus-macalpini.ageText: About 225 to 220 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: A small desmatosuchine aetosaur known from a young skeleton found in 1939 and long filed as Desmatosuchus. It was named as its own genus in 2008.

species:tecovasuchus-chatterjeei.ageText: About 225 to 215 million years ago (Late Triassic)
species:tecovasuchus-chatterjeei.placeText: Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, USA
summary: A typothoracine aetosaur known mostly from its distinctive armour plates, found in the Dockum and the Chinle.

species:leptosuchus-crosbiensis.ageText: About 225 to 215 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: A long-snouted phytosaur, a crocodile-like reptile not closely related to true crocodiles, common in the lower Dockum and Chinle. Its classification has a complicated history, with several species moved in and out.

species:redondasaurus-gregorii.ageText: About 210 to 202 million years ago (Late Triassic)
summary: One of the last and most advanced phytosaurs, with eye sockets raised above the skull roof. Some researchers treat it as a species of Machaeroprosopus rather than a separate genus.

species:angistorhinus-grandis.ageText: About 232 to 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A large, early phytosaur with a narrow snout, one of the first phytosaurs to be named from North America.

species:ahvaytum-bahndooiveche.ageText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A chicken-sized early dinosaur known from a few leg bones, probably an early sauropodomorph. It is the oldest named dinosaur from the northern supercontinent Laurasia, about the same age as the earliest dinosaurs of South America. Its name means “dinosaur from long ago” in the Eastern Shoshone language.

species:beesiiwo-cooowuse.ageText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A hyperodapedontine rhynchosaur, a beaked plant-eating reptile, known from four jaw pieces. Its name means “big lizard” in the Arapaho language.

species:efraasia-minor.ageText: About 215 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: A lightly built early long-necked dinosaur, perhaps up to about 6 m long, related to Plateosaurus. It is named after Eberhard Fraas, who collected the first specimens.
Its bones were first split between three species in three different genera; in 2003 they were shown to be one animal at different growth stages.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Friedrich von Huene, 1908 (as Teratosaurus minor); genus by Peter Galton, 1973

species:procompsognathus-triassicus.ageText: About 215 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: A small, lightly built predatory dinosaur about 1 m long, known from one poorly preserved skeleton. Later study suggested its skull may come from a small crocodile relative instead.
It became famous as the “compy” in Michael Crichton’s novel Jurassic Park, where it was shown as a tiny venomous scavenger. There is no evidence it was venomous.

species:teratosaurus-suevicus.ageText: About 215 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: A large rauisuchid, a four-legged crocodile-line predator perhaps about 6 m long, known from an upper jaw with big, serrated teeth.

Myth-buster: for over a century it was pictured as one of the first big meat-eating dinosaurs, because its jaw was paired with the skeleton of a plant-eating sauropodomorph. In 1985 the two were shown to belong to different animals.

species:saltoposuchus-connectens.ageText: About 215 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: A small, slim, long-tailed early crocodile relative that ran on long legs, often wrongly shown in old books as an ancestor of the dinosaurs. All known specimens are young individuals. The British Terrestrisuchus may be the same animal.

species:hovasaurus-boulei.ageText: About 255 to 249 million years ago (latest Permian to earliest Triassic)
summary: A small swimming reptile with a very long, flattened tail for sculling. Many skeletons have small pebbles in the belly, probably swallowed as ballast to help it stay under water. It survived the end-Permian extinction and is one of the commonest fossils of the Sakamena.

species:claudiosaurus-germaini.ageText: About 258 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
summary: A slender, long-necked reptile about 60 cm long that probably lived partly in water. It was once suggested to be an ancestor of plesiosaurs and other marine reptiles; that idea is no longer widely accepted.

species:thadeosaurus-colcanapi.ageText: About 258 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
summary: A small, lizard-like tangasaurid reptile, a land-living relative of Hovasaurus, known from several natural moulds.

species:triadobatrachus-massinoti.ageText: About 251 to 249 million years ago (earliest Triassic)
summary: The oldest known member of the frog line, about 10 cm long, a famous transitional fossil. Its skull was already frog-like, but it had a long body with many vertebrae and a short tail.
It probably swam by kicking its hind legs but could not jump like modern frogs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Jean Piveteau, 1936 (as Protobatrachus); renamed by Oskar Kuhn, 1962

species:mahavisaurus-dentatus.ageText: About 251 to 249 million years ago (earliest Triassic)
summary: A rhytidosteid temnospondyl, a flat-headed amphibian, known from a nearly complete skull from just after the end-Permian extinction.

species:moghreberia-nmachouensis.ageText: About 235 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A large placeriine dicynodont, a heavy, beaked plant-eater, related to Placerias from Arizona. Its name comes from the Arabic name for Morocco, al-Maghrib.

species:almasaurus-habbazi.ageText: About 235 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: A latiscopid temnospondyl, a large flat-headed amphibian, known from several skulls.
A chigutisaurid temnospondyl, a big amphibian with a broad, flat head. Its name means “monstrous head”. Other species are known from the Ischigualasto Formation.

species:andescynodon-mendozensis.ageText: About 240 to 230 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: One of the earliest traversodontids, plant-eating cynodonts with broad grinding cheek teeth. It is also known from the older Cerro de las Cabras Formation.
An archosauriform known from a partial skeleton with armour plates. It was first described as a proterosuchid, but its exact relationships are unclear.

species:guaibasaurus-candelariensis.ageText: About 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, early Norian)
species:guaibasaurus-candelariensis.placeText: Candelária, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: An early saurischian dinosaur about 2 to 3 m long. Most studies place it as an early sauropodomorph, a distant relative of the giant sauropods, though some have suggested it was a theropod.

species:faxinalipterus-minimus.ageText: About 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, early Norian)
species:faxinalipterus-minimus.placeText: Faxinal do Soturno, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: A tiny animal described in 2010 as one of the oldest pterosaurs.
Myth-buster: a 2022 restudy found its bones belong to a lagerpetid, a ground-living relative of pterosaurs, not a flying pterosaur.

species:cargninia-enigmatica.ageText: About 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, early Norian)
species:cargninia-enigmatica.placeText: Faxinal do Soturno, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: A small lepidosauromorph, an early relative of lizards and tuataras, known from two partial lower jaws with small peg-like teeth. Its species name means “enigmatic”.

species:eoabelisaurus-mefi.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: The oldest known abelisauroid, about 6 m long, from a nearly complete skeleton. It already had the short arms of later abelisaurids like Carnotaurus, about 100 million years earlier.

species:allkaruen-koi.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: A pterosaur known from a skull and braincase so well preserved that the shape of its brain could be studied. Its name means “ancient brain” in the Tehuelche language.

species:melkamter-pateko.ageText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: The oldest known monofenestratan pterosaur, from the group that includes Pterodactylus and the later giant pterosaurs, known from a partial skull. Its name means “winged lizard” in Tehuelche.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Alexandra Fernandes, Diego Pol and Oliver Rauhut, 2024

species:funcusvermis-gilmorei.placeText: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA
summary: The oldest known caecilian relative, a small burrowing amphibian. Unlike living caecilians, which are legless, it still had small legs. Its name means “funky worm”, after the funk music played in the lab while the fossils were sorted.

species:acaenasuchus-geoffreyi.placeText: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA
summary: A small, spiky, armoured crocodile-line reptile close to the desmatosuchine aetosaurs. It was once thought to be a juvenile Desmatosuchus, but later study treats it as its own animal.

species:cretalamna-appendiculata.ageText: About 100 to 46 million years ago (Late Cretaceous to Eocene)
species:cretalamna-appendiculata.placeText: Worldwide; first described from the English Chalk
summary: A mackerel shark, perhaps about 2 to 3 m long (estimates vary), known mostly from teeth found worldwide. It is thought to be the ancestor of the otodontid line that led to the giant megalodon. The name now covers several closely related species.

facts.label: Named
