facts.value: Louis Agassiz, 1835 (as Lamna appendiculata); genus by Glikman, 1958

species:berycopsis-elegans.ageText: About 100 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A deep-bodied spiny-finned fish, usually placed with the beardfishes, a small group that still lives in deep seas today. Relatives are known from Germany and Lebanon.

species:aulolepis-typus.ageText: About 97 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small sea fish, one of the early spiny-finned fishes, from the English Chalk and its German equivalent.

species:lonchodraco-giganteus.ageText: About 95 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A toothed pterosaur with a blade-like crest under the tips of its jaws, known from jaw pieces found in the Kent chalk in the 1840s. It was first called Pterodactylus giganteus, one of the first pterosaurs named from Britain.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: James Bowerbank, 1846 (as Pterodactylus giganteus); genus by Taissa Rodrigues and Alexander Kellner, 2013

species:gallardosaurus-iturraldei.ageText: About 160 to 157 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Oxfordian)
species:gallardosaurus-iturraldei.placeText: Viñales, Pinar del Río, western Cuba
summary: A pliosaur, a short-necked, big-headed marine reptile, known from a skull and neck vertebrae. It is very close to Peloneustes from the Oxford Clay of England, showing pliosaurs swam through the Caribbean Seaway.

species:vinialesaurus-caroli.ageText: About 160 to 157 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Oxfordian)
species:vinialesaurus-caroli.placeText: Viñales, Pinar del Río, western Cuba
summary: A long-necked cryptoclidid plesiosaur known from the front of a skull and the first neck vertebrae. It was first named as a kind of Cryptoclidus in 1949 and got its own genus in 2002.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Carlos de la Torre and Luis Rojas, 1949; genus by Zulma Gasparini and colleagues, 2002

species:cacibupteryx-caribensis.ageText: About 160 to 157 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Oxfordian)
species:cacibupteryx-caribensis.placeText: Viñales, Pinar del Río, western Cuba
summary: A long-tailed rhamphorhynchid pterosaur known from a partial skull, one of the few Jurassic pterosaurs from the Americas.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Zulma Gasparini, Marta Fernández and Marcelo de la Fuente, 2004

species:nesodactylus-hesperius.ageText: About 160 to 157 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Oxfordian)
species:nesodactylus-hesperius.placeText: Viñales, Pinar del Río, western Cuba
summary: A long-tailed rhamphorhynchid pterosaur known from a partial skeleton found in a limestone nodule in 1918 and named in 1969. Its name means “island finger”.

species:notoemys-oxfordiensis.ageText: About 160 to 157 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Oxfordian)
species:notoemys-oxfordiensis.placeText: Viñales, Pinar del Río, western Cuba
summary: An early side-necked turtle, a platychelyid, one of the oldest relatives of the side-necked turtles that live in South America, Africa and Australia today. Other Notoemys species come from Argentina and Colombia.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Marcelo de la Fuente and Manuel Iturralde-Vinent, 2001 (as Caribemys)

species:notoemys-oxfordiensis.akaNote: First named Caribemys oxfordiensis in 2001 and later moved to Notoemys.

species:eupodophis-descouensi.ageText: About 98 to 94 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: An 85 cm sea snake with two tiny hind legs about 2 cm long, a famous “snake with legs”. In 2011 X-ray imaging revealed a second leg hidden inside the rock, showing it had knees, ankles and shin bones.
Its legs were probably useless leftovers from its lizard ancestors, not a stage on the way to growing legs.

species:aphanizocnemus-libanensis.ageText: About 98 to 94 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: A small sea-going lizard about 30 cm long, half of it a flattened tail for swimming, with paddle-like hands and feet. It is usually placed with the dolichosaurs, close to snakes and mosasaurs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Cristiano Dal Sasso and Giovanni Pinna, 1997

species:pontosaurus-kornhuberi.ageText: About 98 to 94 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: A long-bodied swimming lizard, a dolichosaur related to mosasaurs and snakes. The first species was found on the island of Hvar in Croatia; this one, from Lebanon, is known from a beautiful complete skeleton with traces of soft tissue.

species:anguillavus-quadripinnis.ageText: About 98 to 94 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: One of the earliest eels, about 20 cm long. Unlike modern eels it still had small pelvic fins, which gives its species name, “four fins”. Its name means “eel ancestor”.

species:charitopsis-spinosus.ageText: About 98 to 94 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: A small sea fish related to the living beaked salmon, Gonorynchus.

species:microtuban-altivolans.ageText: About 98 to 94 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: A small, toothless azhdarchoid pterosaur known from a partial skeleton with unusually short wing fingers. It was found in rocks laid down far from shore, suggesting it could fly long distances over the sea.

species:pannoniasaurus-inexpectatus.ageText: About 86 to 84 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
summary: A mosasaur up to about 6 m long that lived in rivers and lakes, not the sea, the first freshwater mosasaur known. Its species name means “unexpected”. It was probably the top predator in Iharkút’s waters.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: László Makádi, Michael Caldwell and Attila Ősi, 2012

species:ajkaceratops-kozmai.ageText: About 86 to 84 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
summary: A small, parrot-beaked dinosaur described in 2010 as the first ceratopsian from Europe, related to Asian forms that may have reached Europe by island-hopping.
Later studies questioned whether it was a ceratopsian at all, but more complete skull material described in 2026 supports its placement as one.

species:bakonydraco-galaczi.ageText: About 86 to 84 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
summary: A toothless azhdarchoid pterosaur with a wingspan of perhaps about 3.5 m, known from a complete lower jaw and many other jaw pieces. It may have eaten fruit or small prey.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Attila Ősi, David Weishampel and Coralia Jianu, 2005

species:leaellynasaura-amicagraphica.ageText: About 115 to 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A small, two-legged plant-eater with one of the longest tails relative to its body of any dinosaur, about three times its body length, perhaps wrapped around itself for warmth.

It lived inside the Antarctic Circle. Its large eye sockets and brain’s vision centres have been suggested to help it see during the long polar winter, though this is debated. It is named after Leaellyn Rich, daughter of its discoverers.

An early monotreme known from one upper arm bone, which is strong like an echidna’s and suggests it dug. Its name means “cold digger”, and its species name honours the Cadbury company, which supported the dig.

species:steropodon-galmani.ageText: About 100 to 96 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
species:steropodon-galmani.placeText: Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, Australia
summary: A platypus-like monotreme known from a jaw with three teeth, preserved as opal. Described in 1985, it was the first Mesozoic mammal found in Australia, and with a jaw about 3 cm long it was large for a mammal of its time.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Michael Archer, Tim Flannery, Alex Ritchie and Ralph Molnar, 1985

species:opalios-splendens.ageText: About 100 to 96 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
species:opalios-splendens.placeText: Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, Australia
summary: A monotreme named in 2024 from a piece of opalised jaw, one of three new monotremes named that year from Lightning Ridge, showing early egg-laying mammals were surprisingly varied.

species:weewarrasaurus-pobeni.ageText: About 100 to 96 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
species:weewarrasaurus-pobeni.placeText: Wee Warra opal field, Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, Australia
summary: A small, dog-sized ornithopod known from a jaw preserved in opal. It was found in a bag of rough opal bought by Mike Poben, who gave it to scientists; it is named after him and the Wee Warra opal field.

species:tupandactylus-imperator.ageText: About 115 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: A tapejarid pterosaur with an enormous sail-like head crest many times taller than its skull, supported by bony rods. A 2022 study of an almost complete specimen found two kinds of fuzzy filaments, including branched ones like simple feathers, with pigment granules.
A second, smaller-crested species, T. navigans, may be the other sex of the same species.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Diógenes Campos and Alexander Kellner, 1997 (as Tapejara imperator); genus 2007

related.note: Its smaller relative from the Romualdo Formation.

species:arthurdactylus-conandoylei.ageText: About 115 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: A fish-eating ornithocheirid pterosaur with a wingspan of about 4.5 m, known from a skeleton without its skull. It is named after Arthur Conan Doyle, whose novel The Lost World has pterosaurs living on a South American plateau.

species:ludodactylus-sibbicki.ageText: About 115 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: An anhanguerid pterosaur with both teeth and a Pteranodon-like crest at the back of its head, a combination seen on many toy pterosaurs but unknown in real ones until it was found, which gives its name, “toy finger”. The only skull has a plant leaf caught in its jaws.

species:lacusovagus-magnificens.ageText: About 115 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: A large toothless chaoyangopterid pterosaur with a wide skull and a wingspan perhaps over 4 m, much larger than its Chinese relatives. Its name means “lake wanderer”.

species:tetrapodophis-amplectus.ageText: About 115 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: A small, long-bodied reptile with four tiny limbs, about 20 cm long, described in 2015 as a four-legged snake.

Caution: later study argued it is a dolichosaur, a swimming lizard related to mosasaurs, rather than a snake. The only specimen is in a private collection in Germany, and the circumstances of its export from Brazil are controversial, which has limited further research.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: David Martill, Helmut Tischlinger and Nicholas Longrich, 2015

species:plesiosuchus-manselii.ageText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A large metriorhynchid sea crocodile, perhaps around 6 to 7 m long, with a short, deep skull and big, serrated teeth for hunting large prey, including other marine reptiles. It had flippers and a fish-like tail fin.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: John Hulke, 1870 (as Steneosaurus manselii); genus by Richard Owen, 1884

species:torvoneustes-carpenteri.ageText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A metriorhynchid sea crocodile with blunt, rounded teeth, perhaps for crushing hard-shelled prey such as turtles and ammonites. It was moved between three genera before getting its own in 2010. Its name means “savage swimmer”.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Wilkinson and colleagues, 2008 (as Dakosaurus carpenteri); genus by Marco Andrade and colleagues, 2010

species:haestasaurus-becklesii.ageText: About 140 to 135 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A macronarian sauropod known from a forearm found in 1852 with a patch of fossil skin of small, six-sided scales, the first dinosaur skin ever found. Long filed under Pelorosaurus, it got its own genus in 2015, named after Haesta, the chief whose people gave Hastings its name.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Gideon Mantell, 1852 (as Pelorosaurus becklesii); genus by Paul Upchurch, Philip Mannion and Michael Taylor, 2015

species:valdosaurus-canaliculatus.ageText: About 137 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
species:valdosaurus-canaliculatus.placeText: Isle of Wight and the Weald, England
summary: A fast-running, two-legged dryosaurid plant-eater about 1.2 m long or more, related to Dryosaurus of the Morrison Formation. Its bones were first thought to belong to Hypsilophodon, then Camptosaurus and then Dryosaurus before it got its own genus.

species:ornimegalonyx-oteroi.ageText: Late Pleistocene, perhaps until about 10,000 years ago
summary: One of the largest owls that ever lived, standing about 1 m tall and perhaps weighing around 9 kg (estimates vary), with long, powerful legs. Its short wings and heavy legs suggest it could barely fly, if at all, and hunted on the ground, running down prey like a giant roadrunner.

It probably preyed on giant hutias, large rodents of the Caribbean, and perhaps young ground sloths. Like many Caribbean animals, it disappeared around the end of the Ice Age or soon after; when exactly, and whether people played a part, is uncertain.

related.note: A living owl of similar build, though far smaller.

summary: A flat, armoured amphibian about 74 cm long, named in 2026 from two nearly complete skeletons found in rocks laid down in the open sea, dozens of kilometres from land. It may be the first amphibian known to have lived its whole life in salt water.

Strontium in its bones matches Triassic seawater, which suggests it grew up drinking it. Its describers think it lay on the sea floor and sucked in passing prey. Living amphibians cannot cope with salt water, so outside scientists have called the find potentially revolutionary; the marine lifestyle is an interpretation of two specimens and may be tested by further finds.

facts.label: Relatives
facts.value: Gerrothorax pulcherrimus, from freshwater rocks in Germany and Greenland

species:rinconraptor-pipoae.ageText: About 86 to 83 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
species:rinconraptor-pipoae.placeText: Cerro Overo, near Rincón de los Sauces, Neuquén, Argentina
summary: A megaraptorid, one of the long-armed, big-clawed predators of Cretaceous South America and Australia, named in 2026. It was about 7 metres long, an estimate from comparing its vertebrae with better-known relatives, and is known from parts of the backbone, a humerus and a tibia.
Its bones were first spotted in 2016 and dug up in 2019. The genus is named after Rincón de los Sauces, and the species honours Laura Pipo, a researcher on the 2019 dig who died in 2020.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: Reports give about 86 or about 83 million years ago

species:longisquama-insignis.ageText: About 230 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: A small reptile from lakeside forests of the Madygen Formation, known from one poorly preserved skeleton and several impressions. It is famous for a row of long, flat structures along its back, which gave it its name, “long scales”.

In the 1990s and 2000s some claimed the back structures were feathers and that Longisquama was close to the ancestry of birds. A 2012 restudy found they are skin appendages, not feathers, and it is now regarded as a diapsid reptile of uncertain position with no bearing on bird origins.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Not a feathered bird ancestor: its back crest is made of skin

summary: A cow-sized oreodont, one of a family of sheep- to cow-sized grazing and browsing mammals found only in North America, common in the John Day fossil beds of Oregon. Oreodonts are often compared with pigs or sheep, but they were their own branch of even-toed hoofed mammals.

Its name is uncertain: a 2014 restudy found no clear differences between Eporeodon and Eucrotaphus from the same rocks, and recommended merging them, though it is not yet known whether they are one species (perhaps males and females) or two living side by side.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: About the size of a cow

facts.label: Name
facts.value: May be the same animal as Eucrotaphus (under study)

species:sharovipteryx-mirabilis.ageText: About 230 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: A small reptile about 20 cm long with very long hind legs and a skin membrane stretched between them and the tail, making it one of the oldest known gliders. It probably glided with its hind legs spread, steering with smaller flaps at the front, though the front of the body is poorly preserved.

It is known from a single skeleton. It was once suggested to be a pterosaur ancestor, but it is now usually placed among archosauromorphs near the long-necked tanystropheids, and is not close to pterosaurs.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Sharov, 1971, as Podopteryx; renamed in 1981 because that name was taken

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Not a pterosaur ancestor: its wings were on its back legs

species:madysaurus-sharovi.ageText: About 230 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: A small cynodont, a member of the group that includes the ancestors of mammals, and the only synapsid known from Madygen. It is known from a skull and skeleton, and its exact place among cynodonts is debated.

species:madygenerpeton-pustulatus.ageText: About 230 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: A chroniosuchian, one of a group of crocodile-like, armoured four-legged animals with bony plates along the back, that probably lurked in water like a crocodile. Chroniosuchians are often called amphibians, but they sit near the split between amphibians and the line leading to reptiles, and their exact position is debated.

species:triassurus-sixtelae.ageText: About 230 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: A tiny salamander known from two larvae. A 2020 restudy found it is a stem salamander, an early relative of all living salamanders, which makes it one of the oldest salamanders known and pushes their record back into the Triassic.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Ivakhnenko, 1978; restudied by Schoch and colleagues, 2020

summary: A small, three-toed horse that browsed on leaves, with longer legs and a longer face than earlier horses. It is the only Miohippus species that can be recognised in the Turtle Cove fossils.

Horse evolution is often drawn as a straight line from small to large, but Miohippus lived alongside its close relative Mesohippus for millions of years, and later horses branched out in many directions; only one branch leads to living horses.

facts.label: Toes
facts.value: Three on each foot, the middle one largest

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Horse evolution was a bush, not a ladder

summary: An early rhino with a pair of small horns side by side at the tip of its nose, rather than one behind the other as in living rhinos. The paired horns are thought to have been carried by males.

facts.label: Horns
facts.value: Two, side by side on the nose

species:pogonodon-davisi.placeText: John Day Basin, Oregon, and the Great Plains, USA
summary: A large sabre-toothed nimravid, one of the “false sabre-toothed cats”. Nimravids look like cats, but grew their sabres and cat-like shape separately from true cats. It is known from the Turtle Cove and Kimberly members of the John Day Formation and from the White River rocks of the Great Plains.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Not a true cat, though it looked like one

summary: An early dog of the extinct subfamily Hesperocyoninae, and one of the most common dogs found in the John Day Formation. It had a long body and fairly short legs, more like a mongoose or civet than a modern dog.
A short-faced, strong-jawed hesperocyonine dog, one of the first dogs built for a diet mostly of meat. Several skulls are known from the Turtle Cove Member.

species:archaeocyon-pavidus.placeText: John Day Basin, Oregon, and the Great Plains, USA
summary: A small, fox-sized dog, one of the earliest borophagines. Later members of that group grew into the large “bone-crushing dogs” of the Miocene, but Archaeocyon itself was a small generalist.
A large shastasaurid ichthyosaur several metres long and the most common ichthyosaur of the Guanling biota, known from many complete skeletons. It had a long, toothed snout and long, narrow flippers.
Some researchers have treated it as a species of the Californian Shastasaurus, but most studies now keep it as its own genus.
A giant shastasaurid ichthyosaur with a short, toothless snout, which some researchers think it used to suck in prey such as squid-like animals, an unusual way of feeding for an ichthyosaur.
A 2011 study renamed it Shastasaurus liangae, but a 2013 study of more skeletons argued it is a separate genus, and the question is not settled.

A small ichthyosaur, a few metres long, more closely related to the dolphin-shaped ichthyosaurs of the Jurassic than to the giant shastasaurids it lived with. Its name comes from Qian, an old name for Guizhou.
A thalattosaur several metres long with a long, narrow snout and a long, flattened tail for swimming, known from complete skeletons. Its species name comes from the Huangguoshu waterfall nearby.
A thalattosaur with a long, pointed upper jaw that stuck out well beyond the lower jaw, like a built-in spear. Its name comes from Xinpu, the village at the centre of the Guanling fossil beds.

A placodont, a turtle-like sea reptile with a broad, armoured body and flat, crushing teeth for cracking shellfish. Placodonts looked like turtles but were relatives of plesiosaurs, and the likeness is convergent.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Not a turtle: a turtle-shaped relative of plesiosaurs

summary: A placodont covered in a mosaic of many small bony plates, forming a shell over its back. Its name means “pebble turtle”, but like all placodonts it was not a turtle.

species:ammonitritor-scientiacivium.ageText: About 249 million years ago (Early Triassic, Olenekian)
summary: A sea reptile named in 2026 from the first three-dimensionally preserved omphalosaur skull, with part of its neck. Omphalosaurs had batteries of rounded teeth for crushing hard-shelled prey, and its name means “ammonite grinder”, after the shelled relatives of squid it probably ate.

It was found in 2010 by Felix Saludes on an expedition led by Luc Ebbo, and the species name means “of citizen scientists”, honouring the amateurs who found and helped describe it. Its describers place omphalosaurs among early ichthyosaur relatives, but at least one researcher argues they are not related to ichthyosaurs; how closely is still debated.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Martin Sander, Luc Ebbo and colleagues, 2026 (Biological Reviews)

facts.label: Known from
facts.value: A skull without its braincase and palate, and part of the neck

summary: A small early relative of ichthyosaurs, about a metre long, with rounded back teeth for crushing shellfish. Strictly it sits just outside true ichthyosaurs, among the wider group of ichthyopterygians. The bonebed it comes from is called the Grippia level after it.
A trematosaur, an amphibian with an extremely long, narrow snout like a gharial’s, built for snapping up fish. Trematosaurs were among the few amphibians that could live in salty coastal seas.

species:ctenosuchus-tenuidens.ageText: About 167 million years ago (Middle Jurassic, Bathonian)
summary: A long, narrow-snouted crocodile relative named in 2026 from two partial skeletons. Its teeth are unlike those of any relative: very thin, about ten times taller than wide, and packed closely, with more than 40 on each side of the upper jaw. Its name means “comb crocodile with thin teeth”.

It belongs to the teleosaurids, a family of the thalattosuchians, which are usually thought of as sea crocodiles. Ctenosuchus, though, lived in rivers or lakes, and is the only freshwater teleosauroid known from the southern continents. It probably caught small fish and shrimp-like prey. Its describers mention that the comb of teeth might even have strained food from the water, but they call this a tentative idea.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Imran and colleagues, 2026 (Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology)

facts.label: Teeth
facts.value: More than 40 needle-thin teeth on each side of the upper jaw

facts.label: Habitat
facts.value: Freshwater, unusual for its sea-going family

facts.label: Speculative
facts.value: Filter feeding is a tentative suggestion, not established

species:cameroceras-trentonense.ageText: About 456 to 450 million years ago (Late Ordovician)
summary: A straight-shelled nautiloid, a relative of the living nautilus, from the Ordovician seas of North America. Like other endocerids it had a long, cone-shaped shell with a thick siphuncle, a tube running its length that helped control buoyancy.

It is often said to have been 9 to 11 m long, the giant of its seas. That figure comes from a second-hand report of a shell destroyed in the field before anyone collected or photographed it. The largest orthocone actually known is Endoceras giganteum, estimated at about 5.7 m.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: The 9 to 11 m length is not supported by any specimen

species:endoceras-giganteum.ageText: About 470 to 445 million years ago (Middle to Late Ordovician)
summary: The longest shelled cephalopod known. Its largest specimen is about 3 m long even with the narrow end missing, and a 2015 study estimated the complete shell at about 5.7 m.

Endocerids like it were among the top predators of the Ordovician seas, though how they hunted is debated: a long, heavy shell suggests a slow animal that may have drifted after small prey rather than chasing big ones.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: About 5.7 m (estimated from a 3 m incomplete shell)

summary: The orthocone the whole group is named after, a slender, straight-shelled nautiloid from the Ordovician limestones of Sweden and the Baltic. Its name means “straight horn”.

The polished black “Orthoceras” sold in rock shops and as ornaments almost all come from Morocco and are Devonian, some 80 million years younger. They belong to several other orthocone genera, and the name is a trade label rather than an identification.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Polished Moroccan “Orthoceras” are other, younger orthocones

species:isotelus-gigas.ageText: About 456 to 450 million years ago (Late Ordovician)
species:isotelus-gigas.placeText: New York, USA, and Ontario, Canada
summary: A large, smooth, broad trilobite that ploughed the sea floor of Ordovician North America. Its relatives include Isotelus rex from Manitoba, at over 70 cm the largest complete trilobite known. Isotelus is the state fossil of Ohio.

species:ceraurus-pleurexanthemus.ageText: About 456 to 450 million years ago (Late Ordovician)
species:ceraurus-pleurexanthemus.placeText: New York, USA, and Ontario, Canada
summary: A spiny trilobite with long backward-pointing spines at its tail and the corners of its head. Specimens from the Walcott–Rust Quarry in New York, studied by Charles Walcott in the 1870s, were among the first trilobites found with their legs and gills preserved.

A small crocodile, probably under 2 m long, that lived mostly on land on New Caledonia, an island with no other large predators. Its back teeth were blunt, suited to crushing hard-shelled prey such as snails and crabs. It was the first species of Mekosuchus named, and its name means “unexpected”, as no crocodiles were known from the island.

It is one of the last mekosuchines, a group of crocodiles found only in Australia and the Pacific that included land-hunting forms such as Quinkana. Its youngest bones are around 3,000 years old, close to when people first arrived, but whether people caused its disappearance is not settled.

facts.label: Diet
facts.value: Probably snails, crabs and other hard-shelled prey

related.note: An older relative from the Miocene of Australia.

summary: A giant flightless ground bird about 1.7 m long and around 30 kg, with a deep, bony-crested bill, the largest bird known from New Caledonia. It is a distant relative of megapodes and chickens.

When named in 1980 it was thought to be a relative of emus and other ratites; better fossils later showed it belongs with the fowl-like birds. Bones from the Pindai Caves gave the first radiocarbon dates for it, showing it survived until people arrived about 3,000 years ago, and its bones in their settlements suggest it was hunted.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: First thought to be a ratite; it was a fowl-like bird

summary: An elephant relative that shrank on Flores. The later form, Stegodon florensis insularis, found at Liang Bua, was much smaller than its mainland ancestors, a case of island dwarfism like Homo floresiensis itself. Stegodons were not true elephants but a related branch with ridged, roof-like molars.

It was the largest animal on Flores and probably the main prey of Komodo dragons. It vanished about 50,000 years ago, at the same time as Homo floresiensis; whether hunting played a part is not known.

A huge stork, about 1.8 m tall and around 16 kg, so heavy-boned it may have been unable to fly, related to today’s marabou storks. Named in 2010 from bones in Liang Bua, it probably scavenged Stegodon carcasses and caught small animals. Stories that it hunted Homo floresiensis are speculation.

facts.label: Speculative
facts.value: That it preyed on Homo floresiensis

summary: An early member of our genus with a brain of about 500–700 cm³, larger than Australopithecus but about half ours, and long arms suited to climbing. Louis Leakey and colleagues named it in 1964 from Olduvai fossils; its name means “handy man”, because it was thought to have made the Oldowan stone tools found with it.

Whether it really belongs in Homo is debated: some researchers place it in Australopithecus, and stone tools are now known from before it, so it was probably not the first toolmaker. At Olduvai it lived alongside Paranthropus boisei.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Louis Leakey, Phillip Tobias and John Napier, 1964

summary: A giant buffalo relative named from Olduvai Gorge, with very long, curved horns. It grazed the East African grasslands alongside early humans. Some studies suggest it was more closely related to wild cattle (Bos) than to the living African buffalo.

A large, two-horned rhino of the forests and woodlands of Pleistocene Europe and Asia, the warm-climate counterpart of the woolly rhino. It browsed on leaves and shrubs, and thrived in interglacials such as the one when Neanderthals lived at Krapina. Neanderthals hunted it at several sites.

A large crocodile, about 5 to 6 m long, comparable to a big Nile crocodile, with a pair of small horns at the back of its skull. It lurked in the lake and rivers of Olduvai about 1.84 million years ago, where early humans came to drink.

Its name means “man-eating crocodile”, because hominin bones from the same layers, a foot and a leg, carry crocodile tooth marks. As one of its describers put it, “I can’t guarantee these crocodiles were killing people, but they were certainly biting them.”

facts.label: Evidence
facts.value: Crocodile tooth marks on hominin foot and leg bones

species:theropithecus-oswaldi.ageText: About 3.5 to 0.4 million years ago (Pliocene to Pleistocene)
species:theropithecus-oswaldi.placeText: East, southern and northern Africa, and as far as Spain and India
summary: A giant relative of today’s gelada, the grass-eating baboon of Ethiopia, and one of the largest monkeys known: one estimate puts a big male at about 72 kg, several times a gelada’s weight. Like the gelada it mostly grazed, picking grass blades and roots with nimble fingers.

It lived across Africa alongside early humans for millions of years and is found with them at Olduvai and Swartkrans. At one Kenyan site many young giant geladas seem to have been butchered with stone tools, and hunting by people may have helped end it, though that is debated.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: Perhaps about 72 kg for a large male (one estimate)

related.note: Its living relative, the gelada of Ethiopia.

species:megantereon-whitei.ageText: About 3 to 1 million years ago (Pliocene to Pleistocene)
summary: A sabre-toothed cat about the size of a jaguar, with long, flattened upper canines and powerful forelimbs for pinning prey. Carbon isotopes suggest it, along with leopards, hunted the hominins of the Cradle of Humankind.
African Megantereon are usually called M. whitei, but some researchers include them in the Eurasian species M. cultridens.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: About the size of a jaguar

species:dinofelis-barlowi.ageText: About 3 to 1.5 million years ago (Pliocene to Pleistocene)
summary: A big, leopard- to jaguar-sized cat with short, flattened sabre-like canines, between true sabre-tooths and modern big cats in build. It was long blamed for killing the hominins of the South African caves, earning the name “hominid hunter”, but carbon isotopes suggest it mostly ate grazing animals such as antelope, and no tooth marks on hominin bones can be pinned on it.
At Swartkrans its fossils are identified only as Dinofelis; D. barlowi is the species named from the nearby Sterkfontein cave.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Not the hominin hunter it was once thought to be

species:chasmaporthetes-nitidula.ageText: About 3 to 1 million years ago (Pliocene to Pleistocene)
summary: A long-legged, cheetah-like hyena built for running down prey rather than crushing bones like today’s spotted hyena. Its genus is the only hyena known to have reached the Americas, crossing from Asia during the Ice Age.

The oldest known proboscidean, a fox-sized animal of perhaps 5 kg, known from jaws and teeth. Living only about 6 million years after the dinosaurs died out, it already had the start of the enlarged incisors that would become tusks. The whole elephant family began as small animals like this in Africa.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: About the size of a fox

summary: A small early proboscidean about 60 cm long and around 15 kg, named after the phosphate beds where it was found. It had no trunk or tusks, but details of its skull and teeth already place it on the elephant line.

One of the first large proboscideans, heavily built, with two pairs of short tusks: a pair in the upper jaw and a pair in the lower jaw. It was a side branch rather than an ancestor of elephants, showing that big size evolved more than once early in the group.

The gomphothere the group is named after, an elephant-sized proboscidean with four tusks: a long, downward-curving pair in the upper jaw and a shorter, straight pair jutting from its long lower jaw. Gomphotherium spread out of Africa about 18 million years ago, when Africa and Eurasia joined, and reached North America too.

A proboscidean with extremely long, straight upper tusks, up to about 3 m, and no lower tusks, living in the forests of Pliocene Europe. Its tusks were so long relative to its body that it probably held its head high. It is sometimes placed in its own family rather than with the gomphotheres.

species:cuvieronius-hyodon.ageText: About 5 million to 13,000 years ago (Pliocene to Pleistocene)
species:cuvieronius-hyodon.placeText: Southern North America, Central America and the Andes
summary: A gomphothere with tusks that twisted in a spiral, which crossed into South America and lived high in the Andes. At El Fin del Mundo in Mexico, Clovis hunters killed and butchered Cuvieronius about 13,400 years ago, showing that people hunted gomphotheres as well as mammoths.

The commonest South American gomphothere, found from the lowlands of Argentina and Brazil to the coast of Ecuador. It reached South America when the continents joined, and survived until early people arrived, who hunted it. It is not a mastodon, despite its name, which means “southern mastodon”.

A shovel-tusker whose long lower jaw ended in a pair of broad, flat tusks side by side, forming a wide scoop. It was long pictured shovelling up water plants, but wear on its tusks suggests it used them, together with its trunk, to cut and strip tougher vegetation, more like a scythe.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Probably cut vegetation rather than scooping water plants

species:amebelodon-fricki.ageText: About 9 to 6 million years ago (late Miocene)
summary: A North American shovel-tusker with long, flattened lower tusks, roaming the grasslands and river valleys of the Great Plains. Shovel-tuskers like it were among the commonest large mammals of Miocene North America.

species:stegodon-zdanskyi.ageText: About 3 to 1 million years ago (Pliocene to Pleistocene)
summary: One of the largest proboscideans ever, a giant stegodon of northern China with long, sweeping tusks. A famous mounted skeleton from Gansu shows an animal taller than an African elephant. It is the full-sized kind of animal from which island stegodons shrank.
A stegodon with tusks over 3 m long, set so close together that its trunk probably had to hang to one side or rest on top of them. It was named after Ganesha, the elephant-headed Hindu god.

species:stegodon-insignis.ageText: About 3 to 1 million years ago (Pliocene to Pleistocene)
summary: The species the genus was first described from, found in the Siwalik Hills. Its name, Stegodon, means “roofed tooth”, from the low, ridged crests of its molars, which look like the roof of a house.

The commonest stegodon of Pleistocene southern China and Southeast Asia, so typical of its time that its fauna is called the “Stegodon–Ailuropoda” fauna, after it and the giant panda. It lived alongside Homo erectus, giant pandas, giant tapirs and orangutans, and survived late into the last Ice Age.
An African stegodon from the Pliocene of Uganda and the Congo basin, showing that stegodons lived in Africa as well as Asia before dying out there as true elephants spread.

species:primelephas-gomphotheroides.ageText: About 7 to 5 million years ago (late Miocene)
summary: An early elephant from about the time the lines leading to African elephants, Asian elephants and mammoths split apart, and a likely ancestor of all three. Its name means “first elephant”, and it still had small tusks in its lower jaw as well as its upper, a leftover from gomphothere ancestors.

A straight-tusked elephant of Pleistocene India, known from the Narmada valley. It may have been the largest land mammal that ever lived: a 2015 estimate from an incomplete leg bone suggested about 22 tonnes, larger than Paraceratherium, but that rests on fragmentary fossils and is uncertain.

facts.label: Speculative
facts.value: Perhaps about 22 tonnes, from a partial leg bone

summary: One of the smallest elephants ever: adults stood about 90 cm at the shoulder and weighed around 300 kg, about 2% of the weight of their ancestor, the straight-tusked elephant, which reached the islands from mainland Europe. Spinagallo Cave held over 100 of them.

It has been suggested that ancient Greeks finding dwarf elephant skulls, with their single large nasal opening in the middle, imagined one-eyed giants, the Cyclops. This is an appealing idea but cannot be proved.

facts.label: Speculative
facts.value: That its skulls inspired the Cyclops myth

related.note: Its full-sized ancestor, the straight-tusked elephant of Europe.

species:mammuthus-meridionalis.ageText: About 2.5 to 0.8 million years ago (Early Pleistocene)
summary: An early mammoth of the forests and parklands of Europe and Asia, about 4 m tall at the shoulder and with little or no woolly coat. It was the ancestor of the steppe mammoth, which in turn gave rise to the woolly mammoth in Eurasia and the Columbian mammoth in North America.

related.note: Its descendant, by way of the steppe mammoth.

summary: A mammoth that shrank on the Channel Islands off California, standing about 1.2 to 2.1 m at the shoulder, half the height of its ancestor, the Columbian mammoth, which swam a few kilometres across when sea levels were low. It died out about 13,000 years ago, as rising seas shrank its island and around the time people arrived.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: About 1.2 to 2.1 m at the shoulder

related.note: Its full-sized ancestor, the Columbian mammoth.

species:micropachycephalosaurus-hongtuya.ageText: About 75 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: A small plant-eating dinosaur, probably under a metre long, with the longest name of any dinosaur: 23 letters in the genus alone. It is known only from scrappy remains, parts of the jaws, skull, hips and legs, found on a cliff near Laiyang.

Its name means “small thick-headed lizard”, because Dong Zhiming described it in 1978 as a tiny pachycephalosaur, one of the dome-headed dinosaurs. Later studies found nothing to link it to them, and a 2011 analysis placed it instead as an early ceratopsian, a distant relative of Triceratops, though its fossils are so incomplete that this is still debated. PaleoDex places it with both groups, among the fringe-headed dinosaurs, rather than in either.

It lived long after ceratopsians and pachycephalosaurs went their separate ways in the Jurassic, so it is not a link from the time they split; if it is not an early ceratopsian, it may be a late survivor of a branch close to that split.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Despite its name, probably not a pachycephalosaur

related.note: An early ceratopsian, if it belongs with the horned dinosaurs.
A pachycephalosaur, the group it was first placed in.

species:stenopelix-valdensis.ageText: About 145 to 140 million years ago (earliest Cretaceous)
summary: A small, two-legged plant-eater, about 1.5 m long, known from a single skeleton found in 1855 and preserved only as a natural mould in sandstone, with no skull. It has been called a pachycephalosaur, a ceratopsian and something in between.

A 2009 study found it fits with the fringe-headed dinosaurs but could not place it in either group, while a 2011 analysis found it to be an early ceratopsian close to Yinlong. Like Micropachycephalosaurus, PaleoDex places it with both groups.

facts.label: Known from
facts.value: A single headless skeleton, as a mould in sandstone

related.note: Another fringe-headed dinosaur that cannot be placed in either group.

summary: The oldest definite pachycephalosaur, named in 2025, at least 15 million years older than any other. The skeleton is small, under 1 m long, and bone growth rings show it was a juvenile, yet it already had a full skull dome, without the knobs and spikes of later dome-heads.
It is also the most complete early pachycephalosaur: it preserves the first known dome-head hands and a cluster of gastroliths, stomach stones it swallowed to help grind plants.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Tsogtbaatar Chinzorig, Lindsay Zanno and colleagues, 2025 (Nature)

summary: One of the oldest ceratopsians, a small, two-legged plant-eater with a parrot-like beak and the rostral bone at the tip of its upper jaw that marks all ceratopsians. Found in 1976 and formally named in 1999, it showed that horned dinosaurs began in the Jurassic, long before their big frilled descendants.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Zhao Xijin, Cheng Zhengwu and Xu Xing, 1999

related.note: Another Late Jurassic ceratopsian from China.

species:altirhinus-kurzanovi.ageText: About 115 to 105 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A large iguanodont, about 8 m long, with a tall, arched bump on its snout, perhaps for display, calls or a better sense of smell. It had a thumb spike like Iguanodon and grazed on low plants with a broad beak. It was found by Soviet and Mongolian expeditions in 1981.

species:shamosaurus-scutatus.ageText: About 115 to 105 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: An early ankylosaurid, an armoured dinosaur from before the family evolved its famous tail clubs. It had a long, narrow snout and a back covered in bony plates.

species:choyrodon-barsboldi.ageText: About 115 to 105 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: An early relative of the duck-billed dinosaurs, named in 2018 from several individuals of different ages. Its snout shows an early stage in the evolution of the hadrosaurs’ broad bill.

species:khurendukhosaurus-orlovi.ageText: About 115 to 105 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A long-necked choristodere, a freshwater reptile unrelated to lizards or crocodiles that caught fish in lakes with a small head on a long neck, somewhat like a miniature plesiosaur.

species:tchoiria-namsarai.ageText: About 115 to 105 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: A crocodile-like choristodere with a long snout, which hunted fish in the lakes of Early Cretaceous Mongolia. It looked like a gharial, but choristoderes are an old, separate branch of reptiles that evolved the same shape for the same way of life.

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Not a crocodile, though it looked like one

species:xuanhuaceratops-niei.ageText: About 152 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: A small, early ceratopsian from the Tuchengzi (Houcheng) rocks of Hebei, a close relative of Chaoyangsaurus; together they form a family of the earliest horned-dinosaur relatives. Its bones, with those of Chaoyangsaurus and an unnamed sauropod, are the only dinosaur skeletons known from these rocks, which are better known for footprints.

related.note: Its closest known relative, from the same rocks.

species:pholidosaurus-schaumburgensis.ageText: About 145 to 140 million years ago (earliest Cretaceous)
summary: A long-snouted crocodile relative that hunted fish in the lagoons and deltas of early Cretaceous Germany. It gave its name to the pholidosaurs, a family that later produced giants such as Sarcosuchus.

species:tylosaurus-rex.placeText: Texas and the Western Interior Seaway, USA
summary: One of the largest mosasaurs known, up to about 13 m long, named in 2026 from a skeleton found in Texas in 1979 and now on display at the Perot Museum in Dallas. Unlike Tylosaurus proriger, it had serrated teeth, edged like steak knives for slicing big prey.

Its describers re-examined tylosaur fossils in more than a dozen museums and found that several famous giants long counted as Tylosaurus proriger, including the “Bunker” specimen in Kansas and “Sophie” at Yale, belong to this new species. Mosasaurs were giant sea-going lizards, closer to snakes and monitor lizards than to dinosaurs; its name nods to the other T. rex.

facts.label: Named
facts.value: Amelia Zietlow, Michael Polcyn and Ron Tykoski, 2026

facts.label: Teeth
facts.value: Serrated, unlike those of Tylosaurus proriger

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: A sea lizard, not a dinosaur

related.note: Its close relative; several of its largest specimens were reassigned to T. rex.

event:apollo-11.title: Apollo 11 Moon landing
event:apollo-11.placeText: Tranquility Base, Sea of Tranquillity (Mare Tranquillitatis), the Moon
summary: On 20 July 1969 the Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquillity, a broad, flat plain of ancient lava on the Moon’s near side. Neil Armstrong radioed: “Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.”
About six and a half hours later Armstrong became the first person to step onto the Moon, followed by Buzz Aldrin. Michael Collins stayed in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia.

The astronauts left a laser retroreflector on the surface, and it is still in use. Timing laser pulses bounced off it is how scientists measure the Moon drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year, the rate PaleoDex uses for the Earth–Moon distance.

facts.label: Crew
facts.value: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins

facts.label: On the surface
facts.value: 21 hours 36 minutes, about 2½ hours of it outside

facts.label: Samples returned
facts.value: 21.5 kg of lunar rock and soil

facts.label: Footprints
facts.value: Laid 21 July 1969; with no wind or rain on the Moon, they should last for millions of years unless disturbed

trackmakers.note: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin left the first footprints on another world.

image.caption: Buzz Aldrin on the Moon, photographed by Neil Armstrong, whose reflection shows in the visor.

event:hell-creek.title: Hell Creek Formation
event:hell-creek.dateText: About 68 to 66 million years ago (latest Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
event:hell-creek.placeText: Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota and Wyoming, USA
summary: The Hell Creek Formation is a layer of sandstones and mudstones laid down by rivers on a warm, humid coastal lowland in the last two million years of the Cretaceous. Rivers flowing east from the young Rocky Mountains spread sand and mud across floodplains, swamps and forests.

It records the final dinosaur ecosystems before the asteroid impact. Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops are its most famous residents, alongside Edmontosaurus, Ankylosaurus, Pachycephalosaurus, crocodilians, turtles, early mammals and flowering plants.
The formation ends at the impact. In places the thin boundary clay, rich in iridium from the asteroid, sits right at its top, and the layers above it (the Fort Union Formation) are Paleocene.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: The first T. rex skeleton (1902) and “Sue” (1990)

points.label: Hell Creek
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, 66 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Freshwater mussels
invertebrates.text: Hell Creek’s rivers were lined with beds of freshwater mussels (unionids), relatives of today’s river mussels. Their thick, often ridged shells are common fossils in old channel sands, and many kinds lived side by side, from smooth, rounded shells to heavily sculptured ones such as Plesielliptio and Proparreysia. Like modern mussels they filtered the water and needed clean, flowing rivers.

invertebrates.title: Leaf miners and leaf chewers
invertebrates.text: The insects themselves are rarely preserved, but fossil leaves from Hell Creek are covered in their work: holes and bitten edges from chewers, galls, and winding tunnels left by leaf-mining larvae. Many of these feeding marks were made by specialists tied to one kind of plant, and many disappear at the asteroid impact, showing how hard the extinction hit insects and plants together.

event:lance.title: Lance Formation
event:lance.dateText: About 69 to 66 million years ago (latest Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
event:lance.placeText: Eastern Wyoming, with outcrops in South Dakota, USA
summary: The Lance Formation is a set of river sandstones, mudstones and thin coals in eastern Wyoming, named after Lance Creek in Niobrara County. Like Hell Creek, its near neighbour and twin, it was laid down by rivers on a warm, humid coastal lowland in the last few million years of the Cretaceous.

It is one of the classic dinosaur rock units of North America. In 1889–1892 the collector John Bell Hatcher dug dozens of Triceratops skulls from it, and in 1908 the Sternberg family found the famous Edmontosaurus “mummy” with skin impressions preserved over much of its body. Its rich small fossils include early mammals, lizards, snakes, salamanders and fish.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Niobrara County, Wyoming, and nearby South Dakota

points.label: Lance
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 67 million years ago

event:scollard.title: Scollard Formation
event:scollard.dateText: About 67 to 63 million years ago; its lower part is latest Cretaceous, its upper part Paleocene
event:scollard.placeText: Red Deer River valley, central Alberta, Canada
summary: The Scollard Formation is a set of river sandstones, mudstones and coal seams exposed along the Red Deer River valley in central Alberta. It spans the end of the Cretaceous: dinosaurs are found in its lower part, and the boundary clay from the asteroid impact lies within it, below coal seams laid down in the Paleocene.
Its latest-Cretaceous rocks hold the northernmost part of the same world as Hell Creek, with Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops and Ankylosaurus living on a cooler, wetter floodplain.

facts.label: Famous for
facts.value: The K–Pg boundary and the last dinosaurs of Canada

points.label: Scollard
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 66.5 million years ago

event:frenchman.title: Frenchman Formation
event:frenchman.dateText: About 67 to 66 million years ago (latest Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
event:frenchman.placeText: Frenchman River valley, southwestern Saskatchewan, Canada
summary: The Frenchman Formation is a set of river sandstones and mudstones in southwestern Saskatchewan, around the Frenchman River valley near Eastend. It was laid down by rivers in the last million years or so of the Cretaceous, at the same time as Hell Creek further south.
It is best known for “Scotty”, a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton found in 1991 that is thought to be the heaviest T. rex known. Triceratops and other Hell Creek dinosaurs are found here too.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Frenchman River valley, near Eastend, Saskatchewan

points.label: Frenchman
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 66.5 million years ago

event:ojo-alamo.title: Ojo Alamo Formation
event:ojo-alamo.dateText: Latest Cretaceous to earliest Paleocene; its dinosaur-bearing Naashoibito Member is latest Cretaceous (Maastrichtian)
event:ojo-alamo.placeText: San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: The Ojo Alamo Formation is a set of river sandstones and mudstones in the San Juan Basin of northwestern New Mexico, named after Ojo Alamo (“cottonwood spring”). Its lower part, the Naashoibito Member, was laid down by rivers crossing a warm floodplain near the end of the Cretaceous, in the southern part of the western North American landmass.

The Naashoibito Member preserves one of the southernmost latest-Cretaceous dinosaur faunas in North America, including Tyrannosaurus rex and the giant long-necked titanosaur Alamosaurus, which is named after the formation.
Above it, the Kimbeto Member was deposited by rivers after the asteroid impact, in the earliest Paleocene.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: San Juan Basin, northwestern New Mexico

points.label: Ojo Alamo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 68 million years ago

event:nemegt.title: Nemegt Formation
event:nemegt.dateText: About 70 million years ago (latest Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
event:nemegt.placeText: Nemegt Basin, Gobi Desert, southern Mongolia
summary: The Nemegt Formation is a set of river sandstones and mudstones in the Gobi Desert of southern Mongolia. Unlike the dune deposits beneath it, it was laid down in a wetter time, by rivers winding across floodplains dotted with lakes and woodland.

It holds one of the richest latest-Cretaceous dinosaur faunas in Asia: the tyrannosaurids Tarbosaurus and Alioramus, the duck-billed Saurolophus, the long-armed Deinocheirus and Therizinosaurus, armoured Tarchia, long-necked titanosaurs, and many small feathered dinosaurs, alongside turtles and crocodile relatives.
Soviet expeditions in the 1940s and the Polish–Mongolian expeditions of the 1960s and 70s made it famous, and it is still one of the world’s great dinosaur hunting grounds.

points.label: Nemegt
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 70 million years ago

event:chengjiang.title: Chengjiang biota (Maotianshan Shale)
summary: Fine mud washed into a shallow sea buried whole communities of early Cambrian animals so quickly that their soft bodies, guts, eyes and even nerves were preserved. It is one of the best windows on the Cambrian explosion, when most of the major animal groups appear in the fossil record within a few tens of millions of years.

Among the arthropods, sponges, worms and strange armoured lobopodians are the oldest known vertebrates: small, fish-shaped animals with a head, gill pouches and zig-zag muscle blocks, the earliest members of the group that would one day include us.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Maotianshan hill, near Chengjiang, Yunnan, China

points.label: Chengjiang
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 518 million years ago

event:burgess-shale.title: Burgess Shale
event:burgess-shale.dateText: About 508 million years ago (middle Cambrian, Wuliuan)
event:burgess-shale.placeText: Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
summary: Mudflows tumbling down the foot of a great underwater cliff, the Cathedral Escarpment, buried sea-floor animals in a dark, oxygen-poor basin, preserving their soft parts as thin films in the shale. Charles Walcott found the site in 1909 and collected over 65,000 fossils.

The Burgess Shale made the Cambrian explosion famous. Its strange animals, such as five-eyed Opabinia and spiny Hallucigenia, showed how varied early animal life was. It also holds Metaspriggina, one of the earliest vertebrates, and Pikaia, a close cousin of the vertebrates.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Walcott Quarry, Mount Stephen and nearby, Yoho National Park

points.label: Burgess Shale
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 508 million years ago

event:harding-sandstone.title: Harding Sandstone
event:harding-sandstone.dateText: About 457 to 453 million years ago (Late Ordovician, Sandbian)
summary: Sand laid down along a shallow, tidal coastline of a warm sea that covered much of North America. Broken bits of bony armour, washed together in the sands, belong to some of the earliest vertebrates known from abundant remains.

Charles Walcott described them in 1892, and for decades they were the oldest known fish. They were jawless, covered in plates and scales of bone and dentine, the same hard tissues that make up our teeth.

points.label: Harding
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 455 million years ago

event:soom-shale.title: Soom Shale
event:soom-shale.dateText: About 444 million years ago (latest Ordovician, Hirnantian)
event:soom-shale.placeText: Cederberg mountains, Western Cape, South Africa
summary: Laid down in a cold, still sea at the end of the Ordovician glaciation, when ice sheets covered much of the southern supercontinent Gondwana, then lying over the South Pole. The bottom water had almost no oxygen, so nothing disturbed the dead, and their soft parts were preserved in clay minerals.

It records life just after the first wave of the end-Ordovician mass extinction. Its most famous fossils are conodonts with their soft bodies preserved, showing that these tiny teeth, common in rocks all over the world, belonged to eel-like early vertebrates.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: A cold sea near the South Pole, just after the ice age peaked

points.label: Soom Shale
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 444 million years ago

event:kuanti.title: Kuanti Formation
event:kuanti.dateText: About 425 to 422 million years ago (late Silurian, Ludlow)
summary: Limestones and shales from a shallow, tropical sea on the South China block, then an island continent near the equator. The rocks hold the Xiaoxiang fauna, the oldest group of well-preserved jawed fish, and they have changed what is known about how jaws and bony skeletons evolved.

Here are Guiyu, the oldest complete bony fish, and Entelognathus, an armoured placoderm with the same jaw bones that bony fish (and so humans) have, suggesting our jaws evolved from those of armoured fish.

facts.label: Fauna
facts.value: The Xiaoxiang fauna, studied by Zhu Min and colleagues

points.label: Kuanti
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 423 million years ago

event:gogo.title: Gogo Formation
event:gogo.dateText: About 384 to 378 million years ago (Late Devonian, Frasnian)
summary: A great tropical barrier reef, built by sponges, corals and microbes, once fringed this part of Australia. Fish living in its deep inter-reef basins sank into oxygen-poor mud, and limy nodules formed around them, preserving them in three dimensions, often with their muscles, nerves, blood vessels and even unborn young.

Gogo fish are dissolved out of their nodules in weak acid, giving perfect, uncrushed skeletons. They include Materpiscis, a placoderm mother with an embryo still attached by its umbilical cord, the oldest known live birth.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Gogo Station, near Fitzroy Crossing, Western Australia

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Basins between the reefs of the Canning Basin

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: The oldest known live birth (Materpiscis), and fossil hearts

points.label: Gogo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 380 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Reef builders
invertebrates.text: The reef itself was built mainly by stromatoporoids, extinct sponges that grew in layered mounds, together with microbial mats and tabulate and rugose corals. Devonian reefs were among the largest ever, before the Late Devonian extinction wiped most of them out.

invertebrates.title: Ammonoids
invertebrates.text: Coiled, shelled relatives of squid, ancestors of the ammonites. Goniatites such as Manticoceras swam above the reef basins.

event:fram.title: Fram Formation
event:fram.dateText: About 377 to 374 million years ago (Late Devonian, Frasnian)
summary: Today an Arctic island; 375 million years ago a warm, tropical floodplain of shallow, meandering streams near the equator. Neil Shubin, Ted Daeschler and Farish Jenkins went looking for rocks of exactly this age and setting to find a fish on its way to becoming a land animal.
After four summers of searching they found Tiktaalik in 2004: a fish with a flat head, a neck, lungs as well as gills, and sturdy fins with wrist-like bones, able to prop itself up in the shallows.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Red and grey sandstone and siltstone

points.label: Fram
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 375 million years ago

event:britta-dal.title: Britta Dal Formation
event:britta-dal.dateText: About 366 to 362 million years ago (Late Devonian, Famennian)
summary: River sands and muds from a warm, seasonally dry basin near the equator, part of the Old Red Sandstone continent. They hold two of the earliest four-limbed vertebrates known from good skeletons.

Acanthostega had legs with eight fingers but still breathed with gills and probably never left the water. Ichthyostega, found by Swedish and Danish expeditions in the 1930s, had a stronger skeleton and may have hauled itself across land like a seal.

points.label: Britta Dal
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 364 million years ago

event:cleveland-shale.title: Cleveland Shale
event:cleveland-shale.dateText: About 361 to 359 million years ago (latest Devonian, Famennian)
summary: Black mud from the floor of a warm inland sea with little oxygen near the bottom, part of the Ohio Shale. It is famous for big Devonian fish, many found in the 1800s when roads and railways were cut through the shale around Cleveland.

The top predator was Dunkleosteus, a huge armoured placoderm with self-sharpening bony blades for jaws. Some of the earliest well-preserved sharks, such as Cladoselache, lived alongside it, sometimes with their last meals still in their stomachs.

points.label: Cleveland Shale
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 360 million years ago

event:east-kirkton.title: East Kirkton Limestone
event:east-kirkton.dateText: About 336 to 334 million years ago (early Carboniferous, Viséan)
summary: A lake fed by hot springs in a landscape of volcanoes and forests near the equator. Animals that fell or washed into its mineral-rich water were preserved in layers of limestone, giving a rare look at life on land early in the Carboniferous.

The quarry, found by the fossil collector Stan Wood in 1984, holds some of the oldest land-living vertebrates: early amphibians and Westlothiana, an animal close to the ancestry of reptiles and mammals, alongside giant scorpions and sea scorpions.

points.label: East Kirkton
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 335 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Sea scorpions
invertebrates.text: Hibbertopterus, a giant eurypterid that raked through mud with blade-like legs. Trackways show it could also walk across land.

event:joggins.title: Joggins Formation
event:joggins.dateText: About 318 to 314 million years ago (Pennsylvanian, Bashkirian)
event:joggins.placeText: Bay of Fundy, Nova Scotia, Canada
summary: The “coal age” rainforest preserved in the sea cliffs of the Bay of Fundy. Again and again, forests of giant club-mosses, Lepidodendron and Sigillaria, were drowned by floods and buried in mud, leaving their trunks standing upright in the rock.

When the trees rotted, their hollow stumps became traps. Inside them geologists Charles Lyell and William Dawson found in 1852 the bones of small animals, including Hylonomus, the oldest known reptile and one of the first animals to lay eggs with a shell on land.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Sandstone, mudstone and coal, with upright fossil trees

points.label: Joggins
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 316 million years ago

event:mazon-creek.title: Mazon Creek (Francis Creek Shale)
event:mazon-creek.dateText: About 311 to 307 million years ago (Pennsylvanian, Moscovian)
event:mazon-creek.placeText: Grundy and Will counties, Illinois, USA
summary: A great river delta spreading into a shallow sea near the equator, with coal swamps behind it. Plants and animals, from jellyfish to insects, were washed into the mud and quickly sealed inside ironstone nodules, which split open to reveal them.

Most were found in the spoil heaps of strip mines in the 20th century, where hundreds of thousands of nodules were collected, many by amateurs. The fossils include sharks, early amphibians, insects, horseshoe crabs and the mysterious Tully monster.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Around Braidwood and the Mazon River, Illinois

facts.label: Famous find
facts.value: The Tully monster, Illinois’s state fossil

points.label: Mazon Creek
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 309 million years ago

event:commentry.title: Commentry coal basin
event:commentry.dateText: About 302 to 299 million years ago (late Carboniferous, Gzhelian)
summary: A small coal basin in the middle of the Variscan mountains, where lakes and swamps sat among tree-ferns, horsetails and seed plants near the equator. Its mines produced coal from the 1800s, and with it one of the richest collections of Carboniferous insects ever found.

Its fame rests on the giant griffinfly Meganeura, described by Charles Brongniart from Commentry in 1884. Insects were the first animals to fly, about 100 million years before pterosaurs, and in the late Carboniferous some grew larger than at any time since.

points.label: Commentry
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 300 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Six-winged insects
invertebrates.text: Palaeodictyopterans such as Stenodictya had a small extra pair of winglets in front of their four wings and beak-like mouthparts for sucking plant juices. They were common in the Carboniferous and died out in the Permian.

event:texas-red-beds.title: Texas Red Beds
event:texas-red-beds.dateText: About 295 to 273 million years ago (early Permian)
summary: Red mudstones and sandstones from river floodplains and ponds on the edge of Pangaea, near the equator, with a climate growing drier and more seasonal. The red colour comes from iron oxide, a sign the land often dried out.

Collected since Edward Drinker Cope’s time in the 1870s, the red beds are the best record of early Permian life on land: sail-backed synapsids (relatives of mammals) such as Dimetrodon and Edaphosaurus, the big amphibian Eryops, and boomerang-headed Diplocaulus.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Archer, Baylor, Wichita and nearby counties, Texas

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Red mudstone and sandstone (Wichita and Clear Fork groups)

facts.label: Collectors
facts.value: Edward Drinker Cope, Charles Sternberg, Alfred Romer

points.label: Texas Red Beds
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 285 million years ago

event:muschelkalk.title: Muschelkalk
event:muschelkalk.dateText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic)
event:muschelkalk.placeText: Central and southern Germany, with outcrops in France, Poland and the Netherlands
summary: Limestones and marls from the Germanic Basin, a warm, shallow sea that flooded central Europe in the Middle Triassic, when the world was recovering from the end-Permian mass extinction. Its name means “shell limestone”, from the masses of shells it contains; it is the middle of the three layers that gave the Triassic its name.

Its sea held some of the first big marine reptiles: the seal-like nothosaurs, shell-crushing placodonts and early ichthyosaurs, hunting fish and the coiled ammonite Ceratites among meadows of sea lilies.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Franconia, Thuringia, Baden-Württemberg and other parts of Germany

facts.label: Name
facts.value: German for “shell limestone”; the middle part of the three-part Triassic

points.label: Muschelkalk
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 241 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Ceratites
invertebrates.text: The ammonite Ceratites, whose shells, with frilly suture lines, are among the best-known fossils of the Muschelkalk and are used to divide its layers.

invertebrates.title: Sea lilies
invertebrates.text: Encrinus liliiformis, a sea lily whose broken stems make up whole beds of “trochite limestone”.

invertebrates.title: Shells
invertebrates.text: Countless bivalves, brachiopods and snails, the shells that give the rock its name.

groupNotes.title: Other marine reptiles
groupNotes.text: Early ichthyosaurs, the long-necked Tanystropheus, the plesiosaur forerunner Pistosaurus and other nothosaurs such as Cymatosaurus.

groupNotes.title: Fish
groupNotes.text: Ray-finned fish such as Colobodus and Saurichthys, and early sharks.

event:el-mers.title: El Mers Group
event:el-mers.dateText: About 168 to 164 million years ago (Middle Jurassic, Bathonian to Callovian)
summary: Mudstones, sandstones and limestones from a coast in what is now the Middle Atlas mountains, where rivers met a shallow sea. Most of its fossils are shellfish, but it has also produced two of the most important early armoured dinosaurs.

Adratiklit is one of the oldest stegosaurs known, and Spicomellus, with its spiked bony collar, is the oldest known ankylosaur. Together they show that both armoured groups were already distinct, and already strange, in the Middle Jurassic.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Mudstone, sandstone and limestone (El Mers I, II and III Formations)

points.label: El Mers
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 166 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Ammonites
invertebrates.text: Ammonites such as Clydoniceras and Morphoceras, used to date the rocks.

invertebrates.title: Shellfish
invertebrates.text: Oysters and other bivalves, brachiopods and tiny ostracods.

event:karoo-lystrosaurus.title: Lystrosaurus Assemblage Zone, Karoo
event:karoo-lystrosaurus.dateText: About 252.5 to 249 million years ago (across the end-Permian extinction into the Early Triassic)
event:karoo-lystrosaurus.placeText: Karoo Basin, Free State and Eastern Cape, South Africa
summary: The Karoo Basin holds an almost unbroken record of life on land through the end-Permian extinction, the worst in Earth’s history. Near Bethulie the rocks change from the grey-green mudstones of Permian floodplains to red beds laid down by braided rivers in a hotter, drier world.

In the layers just after the extinction one animal dominates: Lystrosaurus, a pig-sized, tusked plant-eater that survived and spread across Pangaea. With it are some of the first archosaur relatives, the line that would lead to crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds, and early cynodonts on the line to mammals.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Around Bethulie and the Katberg mountains, South Africa

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Mudstone and sandstone (Palingkloof Member and Katberg Formation)

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Floodplains of rivers draining a high-latitude part of Pangaea

points.label: Karoo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 251 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Burrows
invertebrates.text: Burrowing invertebrates, known mostly from their tunnels.

event:monte-san-giorgio.title: Monte San Giorgio (Besano Formation)
event:monte-san-giorgio.dateText: About 243 to 239 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian–Ladinian)
event:monte-san-giorgio.placeText: Monte San Giorgio, Ticino, Switzerland, and Lombardy, Italy
summary: A tropical lagoon basin on the edge of the Tethys Ocean, sheltered by reefs, with stagnant, oxygen-poor water at the bottom. Fish and marine reptiles that sank into it were preserved whole in thin layers of black shale and dolomite.

It is the best record of Middle Triassic sea life, from soon after the end-Permian extinction, when reptiles were taking to the sea for the first time: early ichthyosaurs, nothosaurs and the absurdly long-necked Tanystropheus, along with thousands of fish.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Monte San Giorgio, on the Swiss–Italian border above Lake Lugano

points.label: Monte San Giorgio
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 242 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Ammonoids
invertebrates.text: Ceratitid ammonoids, the group that recovered after the end-Permian extinction, such as Ceratites relatives used to date the layers here.

event:ischigualasto.title: Ischigualasto Formation
event:ischigualasto.dateText: About 231.5 to 226 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
event:ischigualasto.placeText: Valle de la Luna, San Juan Province, Argentina
summary: The “Valley of the Moon”: badlands of river sandstones and mudstones, with layers of volcanic ash that can be dated precisely. In the Late Triassic this was a warm, seasonally wet river valley in the south-west of Pangaea.

It holds some of the oldest known dinosaurs. They were still small or uncommon here: most animals were plant-eating rhynchosaurs, dicynodonts and cynodonts, and the dinosaurs’ rise to dominance was still to come.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Ischigualasto Provincial Park, San Juan, Argentina

facts.label: Status
facts.value: UNESCO World Heritage Site with Talampaya (2000)

points.label: Ischigualasto
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 230 million years ago

event:chinle.title: Chinle Formation
event:chinle.dateText: About 227 to 205 million years ago (Late Triassic)
event:chinle.placeText: Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Colorado, USA
summary: Colourful mudstones and sandstones laid down by great rivers flowing across south-western North America, then near the equator. The trunks of conifers carried by these rivers became the agate logs of Petrified Forest National Park.

At Ghost Ranch in New Mexico, a single bed holds hundreds of skeletons of the early dinosaur Coelophysis, perhaps killed together by a flood. Elsewhere crocodile-like phytosaurs, armoured aetosaurs, the big predator Postosuchus and the dicynodont Placerias show that crocodile relatives, not dinosaurs, still ruled.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Ghost Ranch (New Mexico), Petrified Forest (Arizona) and nearby

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Mudstone, sandstone and conglomerate in reds, purples and greys

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: The Coelophysis quarry at Ghost Ranch (1947), petrified forests

points.label: Chinle
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 212 million years ago

event:lyme-regis.title: Blue Lias and Charmouth Mudstone (Jurassic Coast)
event:lyme-regis.dateText: About 201 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Hettangian–Sinemurian)
event:lyme-regis.placeText: Lyme Regis and Charmouth, Dorset, England
summary: Alternating limestone and shale from the floor of a warm, shallow sea that covered much of Europe early in the Jurassic. The cliffs around Lyme Regis are still crumbling, and every winter storm exposes new fossils.

Here, in the early 1800s, Mary Anning and her family found the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be recognised, the first complete plesiosaur and the first British pterosaur. Her finds helped show that whole worlds of animals had lived and died out before humans.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Limestone and shale (Blue Lias), mudstone (Charmouth Mudstone)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Part of the Jurassic Coast UNESCO World Heritage Site (2001)

points.label: Lyme Regis
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 196 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Belemnites
invertebrates.text: Squid-like animals with a bullet-shaped internal shell. Mary Anning found fossil ink sacs in them, and the dried ink could still be used to draw with.

event:waterloo-mudstone.title: Waterloo Mudstone Formation
event:waterloo-mudstone.dateText: About 200 to 195 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Hettangian–Sinemurian)
summary: Grey mudstones from the floor of a shallow sea, exposed on the coast of Islandmagee. They hold ammonites and marine reptiles, and also the only dinosaur bones ever found on the island of Ireland.

The two bones were collected by the late schoolteacher and amateur collector Roger Byrne and given to the Ulster Museum. In 2020 a study using 3D scans confirmed they came from two very different dinosaurs: a dense, heavy thigh bone from Scelidosaurus, an early armoured plant-eater, and a slender, thin-walled shin bone from a two-legged meat-eater similar to Sarcosaurus. Both carcasses must have drifted out to sea before sinking.

points.label: Islandmagee
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 198 million years ago

event:posidonia-shale.title: Posidonia Shale
event:posidonia-shale.dateText: About 183.5 to 181.5 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: Black, oily shale from a shallow sea whose bottom water lost its oxygen during the Toarcian oceanic anoxic event, a period of global warming triggered by volcanic eruptions. With no scavengers on the sea floor, carcasses lay undisturbed.

The quarries around Holzmaden are famous for ichthyosaurs preserved with their skin outlines, showing their dorsal fins and tail flukes, and for mothers that died while giving birth, proving ichthyosaurs bore live young.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Holzmaden and Ohmden, near Stuttgart, Germany

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: The flat clam once called Posidonia (now Bositra)

points.label: Posidonia Shale
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 183 million years ago

event:great-oolite.title: Great Oolite Group
event:great-oolite.dateText: About 168 to 165 million years ago (Middle Jurassic, Bathonian)
summary: Pale limestones made of tiny sand-grain spheres (ooids), laid down in a warm, shallow tropical sea dotted with low islands. The Cotswolds’ honey-coloured building stone comes from these rocks.

Bones washed in from the islands include two important theropods: Megalosaurus, from the Stonesfield Slate near Oxford, the first dinosaur ever named, and Proceratosaurus, one of the oldest known tyrannosaurs, found while digging a reservoir at Minchinhampton.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: The Cotswolds, from Bath to Oxfordshire

points.label: Great Oolite
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 167 million years ago

event:shishugou.title: Shishugou Formation
event:shishugou.dateText: About 164 to 158 million years ago (Middle–Late Jurassic)
summary: Red and green mudstones from a warm, seasonally wet floodplain with volcanoes nearby. Its most remarkable fossils come from “death pits”: footprints of giant sauropods, a metre or more deep, filled with soft volcanic mud that trapped smaller animals one on top of another.
The pits at Wucaiwan gave up the early tyrannosaur Guanlong and the strange beaked ceratosaur Limusaurus. Giant sauropods such as Mamenchisaurus and the big predator Sinraptor roamed the same plains.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Mudstone and sandstone with volcanic ash

points.label: Shishugou
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 160 million years ago
