event:morrison.title: Morrison Formation
event:morrison.dateText: About 156 to 147 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Kimmeridgian–Tithonian)
event:morrison.placeText: Western USA, from Montana to New Mexico
summary: Mudstones and sandstones laid down by rivers and lakes across a vast, seasonally dry plain east of a young mountain range. Gallery forests of conifers, ginkgos and tree ferns lined the rivers, with ferns and horsetails on the open floodplains.

It is the classic home of the giant dinosaurs: long-necked sauropods such as Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, Brontosaurus, Brachiosaurus and Camarasaurus, plated Stegosaurus, and the predators Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus. Its quarries were the battleground of the 1870s–1890s “Bone Wars” between Othniel Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Dinosaur National Monument (Utah), Como Bluff (Wyoming) and across the West

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: The Bone Wars; the Carnegie Quarry wall at Dinosaur National Monument

points.label: Morrison
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 151 million years ago

event:solnhofen.title: Solnhofen Limestone
event:solnhofen.dateText: About 151.5 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Tithonian)
summary: Fine, flat-bedded limestone from salty, oxygen-poor lagoons behind reefs and islands at the edge of the Tethys Sea. Animals that fell, flew or were washed in were buried in soft lime mud and preserved in extraordinary detail, down to feathers and wing membranes.

Quarried for centuries as lithographic printing stone, it has yielded about a dozen skeletons of Archaeopteryx, found from 1861, two years after Darwin’s On the Origin of Species, alongside small dinosaurs, pterosaurs, fish, insects and horseshoe crabs.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Solnhofen, Eichstätt and nearby quarries, Bavaria

points.label: Solnhofen
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 151 million years ago

event:catskill.title: Catskill Formation (Red Hill)
event:catskill.dateText: About 366 to 362 million years ago (Late Devonian, Famennian)
event:catskill.placeText: Red Hill, Clinton County, Pennsylvania, USA
summary: Red sandstones and mudstones from a vast river delta spreading west from the young Acadian mountains, across a warm, tropical lowland with some of the first forests of Archaeopteris trees. A road cut at Red Hill exposes one of the richest Late Devonian sites in the world.
Its streams and pools held early tetrapods such as Hynerpeton, armoured placoderms, sharks, lungfish and the giant predatory lobe-finned fish Hyneria.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Red Hill road cut, near Hyner, Pennsylvania

points.label: Red Hill
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 364 million years ago

event:irati.title: Irati Formation
event:irati.dateText: About 280 to 278 million years ago (early Permian)
summary: Dark shales and limestones from a huge, shallow, salty inland sea in the middle of Gondwana. It is the home of Mesosaurus, the first reptile to return to the water.

The same Mesosaurus is found in South Africa’s Whitehill Formation, across the Atlantic. A small freshwater reptile could not have swum an ocean, so it was one of the first pieces of evidence, used by Alfred Wegener, that the continents had once been joined.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: São Mateus do Sul, Paraná, and nearby, Brazil

facts.label: Same age as
facts.value: The Whitehill Formation of South Africa and Namibia

points.label: Irati
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 279 million years ago

event:phosphoria.title: Phosphoria Formation
event:phosphoria.dateText: About 280 to 270 million years ago (early–middle Permian)
event:phosphoria.placeText: South-eastern Idaho, Wyoming and Utah, USA
summary: Phosphate-rich mudstones from a sea on the western edge of Pangaea, where cold, nutrient-rich water welled up from the deep, feeding plankton and the animals that ate them. The phosphate is mined today for fertiliser.
The mines have yielded many tooth-whorls of Helicoprion, the “buzz-saw shark”, including a 2013 CT-scanned specimen with its jaws that finally showed how the spiral of teeth fitted in its mouth.

points.label: Phosphoria
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 275 million years ago

event:karoo-tapinocephalus.title: Tapinocephalus Assemblage Zone, Karoo
event:karoo-tapinocephalus.dateText: About 265 to 260 million years ago (middle Permian)
event:karoo-tapinocephalus.placeText: Beaufort West and Prince Albert, Western Cape, South Africa
summary: Mudstones from wide, cool floodplains in southern Gondwana. The middle Permian Karoo was ruled by dinocephalians, big, heavy-headed synapsids, both plant-eaters such as Moschops, which butted heads, and huge predators such as Anteosaurus.
Most of them disappeared in an extinction at the end of the middle Permian, about 260 million years ago, making way for gorgonopsians and dicynodonts.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Great Karoo, around Beaufort West, South Africa

points.label: Tapinocephalus zone
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 263 million years ago

event:kupferschiefer.title: Kupferschiefer
event:kupferschiefer.dateText: About 259 to 257 million years ago (late Permian, Wuchiapingian)
summary: A thin, black, copper-rich shale from the floor of the Zechstein Sea, a shallow, salty inland sea that flooded a basin in the hot, desert interior of Pangaea. Mined for copper since the Middle Ages, it is full of beautifully preserved fish.
Reptiles washed in from the shores, including Coelurosauravus, the first vertebrate to glide, on skin wings held out on rod-like bones from its body.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Mansfeld, Richelsdorf and elsewhere in central Germany

points.label: Kupferschiefer
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 258 million years ago

event:karoo-cistecephalus.title: Cistecephalus Assemblage Zone, Karoo
event:karoo-cistecephalus.dateText: About 258 to 255 million years ago (late Permian)
event:karoo-cistecephalus.placeText: Nieu-Bethesda and Graaff-Reinet, Eastern Cape, South Africa
summary: Floodplain mudstones from the late Permian Karoo, a seasonal landscape of meandering rivers. The commonest animals were small burrowing dicynodonts such as Diictodon, whose corkscrew burrows are found with their makers still curled inside.
The top predators were the gorgonopsians, sabre-toothed synapsids such as Gorgonops.

points.label: Cistecephalus zone
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 256 million years ago

event:sokolki.title: Sokolki fauna (Salarevo Formation)
event:sokolki.dateText: About 255 to 253 million years ago (late Permian)
event:sokolki.placeText: Northern Dvina River, Arkhangelsk Oblast, Russia
summary: River sands and muds from a dry, seasonal landscape in the east of Pangaea. Vladimir Amalitzky dug a riverbank here from 1899 and found whole skeletons in hard lenses of sandstone, one of the best records of late Permian life.
It holds the biggest gorgonopsian, Inostrancevia, and the armoured pareiasaur Scutosaurus, its likely prey, from a few million years before the end-Permian extinction.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Sokolki, on the Northern Dvina, Russia

points.label: Sokolki
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 254 million years ago

event:trossingen.title: Trossingen Formation
event:trossingen.dateText: About 214 to 204 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian–Rhaetian)
event:trossingen.placeText: Trossingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany, and Frick, Switzerland
summary: Red and grey mudstones from a hot, seasonally dry plain in the middle of Pangaea. Herds of Plateosaurus, one of the first big dinosaurs, lived here, and many skeletons are found mired upright in what was once soft mud.
Digs at Trossingen in the 1910s–1930s and at Frick in Switzerland have produced dozens of complete skeletons, making Plateosaurus one of the best-known dinosaurs.

points.label: Trossingen
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 210 million years ago

event:kayenta.title: Kayenta Formation
event:kayenta.dateText: About 196 to 183 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
event:kayenta.placeText: Northern Arizona and southern Utah, USA
summary: Rivers winding between growing sand seas in western North America, early in the Jurassic. Its red sandstones form cliffs across the Colorado Plateau, and Navajo land near Tuba City yielded the first Dilophosaurus in 1940.
Dilophosaurus was the top predator. With it lived the small armoured dinosaur Scutellosaurus, the early sauropodomorph Sarahsaurus, and tritylodonts, close relatives of mammals.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Navajo Nation near Tuba City (Arizona), and southern Utah

points.label: Kayenta
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 190 million years ago

event:hanson.title: Hanson Formation
event:hanson.dateText: About 190 to 186 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: Volcanic ash and river sediments from a forested valley in southern Gondwana. Antarctica was then at about the same high latitude, but the world was warm and ice-free, with long dark winters and forests of conifers and seed ferns.
Found 4,000 m up a mountain about 650 km from the South Pole, it gave Antarctica its first named dinosaur, the crested predator Cryolophosaurus.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Mount Kirkpatrick, Antarctica, about 4,000 m up

points.label: Hanson
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 188 million years ago

event:oxford-clay.title: Oxford Clay Formation
event:oxford-clay.dateText: About 166 to 161 million years ago (Middle–Late Jurassic, Callovian)
event:oxford-clay.placeText: Peterborough and the English Midlands, England
summary: Grey clay from the floor of a warm, shallow sea that covered much of England. Brick pits around Peterborough dug it up by the million tonnes from the late 1800s, and the workers turned up skeleton after skeleton of marine reptiles.
Its sea held the big pliosaur Liopleurodon, long-necked plesiosaurs, ichthyosaurs, sea crocodiles and the largest bony fish ever, Leedsichthys.

facts.label: Collected by
facts.value: Alfred and Charles Leeds, from the 1860s

points.label: Oxford Clay
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 163 million years ago

event:tiaojishan.title: Tiaojishan Formation
event:tiaojishan.dateText: About 161 to 158 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Oxfordian)
summary: Lakes in forested, volcanic hills, preserving animals in fine detail, part of the Yanliao Biota, about 35 million years older than the Yixian.

Its small feathered dinosaurs show that feathers and wings were tried out in many ways before birds: four-winged Anchiornis, whose colours have been worked out from its fossil feathers, and Yi, with bat-like wings of skin.

points.label: Tiaojishan
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 160 million years ago

event:langenberg.title: Langenberg Quarry (Süntel Formation)
event:langenberg.dateText: About 155 to 153 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Kimmeridgian)
event:langenberg.placeText: Oker, near Goslar, Lower Saxony, Germany
summary: Limestones from a shallow tropical sea dotted with islands, which covered much of Europe in the Late Jurassic. Bones of dinosaurs living on one of the islands washed into the sea.
Isolated on a small island, Europasaurus evolved into a dwarf sauropod only about 6 m long, an example of “island dwarfism” like the dwarf elephants of the Ice Age Mediterranean.

points.label: Langenberg
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 154 million years ago

event:tendaguru.title: Tendaguru Formation
event:tendaguru.dateText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: Coastal plains and tidal flats on the shore of a young sea between Africa and Madagascar, with a seasonal climate. Dinosaurs here were close cousins of those of the Morrison Formation in North America.

German expeditions from 1909 to 1913 employed hundreds of local workers and carried 250 tonnes of bones to the coast on foot. Among them was Giraffatitan, whose mounted skeleton in Berlin is the tallest in the world.

points.label: Tendaguru
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 152 million years ago

event:lourinha.title: Lourinhã Formation
event:lourinha.dateText: About 153 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
event:lourinha.placeText: Lourinhã and the coast north of Lisbon, Portugal
summary: River sands and floodplain muds on the edge of the newly opening North Atlantic, when Iberia was an island close to North America. Its dinosaurs are close relatives of those of the Morrison.

The sea cliffs around Lourinhã have yielded giant sauropods such as Lusotitan, the huge predator Torvosaurus, the long-necked stegosaur Miragaia, and nests of Lourinhanosaurus eggs with embryos. Lusotitan was one of the stars of Walking with Dinosaurs (2025).

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Coastal cliffs from Peniche to Torres Vedras, Portugal

points.label: Lourinhã
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 150 million years ago

event:agardhfjellet.title: Agardhfjellet Formation (Slottsmøya)
event:agardhfjellet.dateText: About 150 to 147 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Tithonian)
summary: Black shale from a cool sea at high northern latitudes, with methane seeps on the sea floor. Expeditions from the University of Oslo from 2004 found dozens of marine reptile skeletons on the slopes of Spitsbergen.
The most famous is the giant pliosaur Pliosaurus funkei, nicknamed “Predator X” before it had a scientific name. Plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs swam in the same sea.

points.label: Svalbard
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 148 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Clams at seeps
invertebrates.text: Clams and other animals around methane seeps.

event:yellow-cat.title: Cedar Mountain Formation (Yellow Cat Member)
event:yellow-cat.dateText: About 139 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
event:yellow-cat.placeText: Near Arches National Park, eastern Utah, USA
summary: Mudstones from a seasonally dry floodplain crossed by rivers, with lakes and springs. Some beds hold bonebeds where many animals died together, including one block holding a dozen or more Utahraptors of all ages, apparently trapped in quicksand.
Its dinosaurs fill a gap between the Jurassic giants of the Morrison and the later Cretaceous: the giant raptor Utahraptor, the early therizinosaur Falcarius and the spiky ankylosaur Gastonia.

points.label: Yellow Cat
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 132 million years ago

event:wessex.title: Wessex Formation
event:wessex.dateText: About 130 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: Red and green mudstones from a broad, warm floodplain with meandering rivers, ponds and seasonal wildfires. Plant debris swept together by floods left “plant debris beds” full of bones, which wash out of the island’s south-west coast cliffs every winter.

The Isle of Wight is one of the richest dinosaur sites in Europe. Its residents included the early tyrannosaur Eotyrannus, the allosaur relative Neovenator, the iguanodont Mantellisaurus, the armoured Polacanthus and the small, fast Hypsilophodon.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Brighstone Bay to Compton Bay, Isle of Wight

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Red and green mudstone with plant debris beds

points.label: Wessex
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 127 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Insects
invertebrates.text: Insects in amber and in fine mud.

event:yixian.title: Yixian Formation
event:yixian.dateText: About 126 to 122 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: Lakes in a forested, volcanic landscape, with a cool climate. Again and again, eruptions blanketed the area in fine ash and poisonous gas, and animals were buried in the lake muds in exquisite detail, down to feathers, fur, skin and stomach contents. It is part of the Jehol Biota.

The Yixian changed our picture of dinosaurs. In 1996 Sinosauropteryx became the first non-bird dinosaur found with feathers, and since then dozens of feathered dinosaurs, early birds, mammals, pterosaurs, insects and flowering plants have come from these rocks.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Sihetun, Lujiatun and nearby, western Liaoning

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Lake shales, sandstones and volcanic ash

points.label: Yixian
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 125 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Early pollinators
invertebrates.text: Long-snouted scorpionflies such as Jeholopsyche, and kalligrammatid lacewings, which looked like butterflies with eyespots on their wings, sipped nectar-like fluids from seed plants long before butterflies existed.

event:kem-kem.title: Kem Kem Group
event:kem-kem.dateText: About 100 to 95 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: The red escarpments of the Kem Kem hold the remains of a vast river system flowing north into the Tethys Sea, full of giant fish: coelacanths, lungfish and huge sawskates.

Strangely, almost all its large animals were predators: Spinosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, Deltadromeus and big crocodiles. Much of the food chain was built on fish. Part of this imbalance may come from bones from different times and places being mixed together in the river deposits.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Red sandstone and mudstone (Gara Sbaa and Douira formations)

points.label: Kem Kem
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 97 million years ago

event:mussentuchit.title: Cedar Mountain Formation (Mussentuchit Member)
event:mussentuchit.dateText: About 99 to 95.5 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous)
summary: Grey mudstones from a wet, swampy coastal plain on the western shore of the young Western Interior Seaway, rich in volcanic ash that can be dated precisely.
It records a turning point in North America: giant allosaur relatives such as Siats were the top predators, and the tyrannosaurs, still small, were just arriving from Asia, as shown by Moros.

points.label: Mussentuchit
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 97 million years ago

event:bissekty.title: Bissekty Formation
event:bissekty.dateText: About 92 to 89.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Turonian)
summary: Sands laid down by rivers near the coast of a shallow sea in Central Asia. Bones are mostly found as single pieces, collected over decades by Soviet and later international expeditions, but together they show a rich mix of dinosaurs, mammals, crocodiles, turtles and sharks.
Its dinosaurs come from a poorly known time, and they include Timurlengia, a horse-sized tyrannosaur with an advanced brain and ears, showing these features evolved before tyrannosaurs became giants.

facts.label: Explored by
facts.value: Lev Nessov from the 1970s; later the URBAC expeditions

points.label: Bissekty
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 91 million years ago

event:niobrara.title: Niobrara Formation (Smoky Hill Chalk)
event:niobrara.dateText: About 87 to 82 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Coniacian–Campanian)
summary: Chalk made of the shells of tiny plankton, settled on the floor of the Western Interior Seaway, a warm sea that split North America in two. Kansas then lay in the middle of the sea, hundreds of kilometres from shore.

The chalk is famous for its sea monsters: giant mosasaurs, the huge predatory fish Xiphactinus, sharks, flightless diving birds and the big pterosaur Pteranodon, which soared over the waves. Fossil collectors such as Charles Sternberg worked its badlands from the 1870s.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Gove, Logan and Trego counties, Kansas

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: Xiphactinus with a whole fish in its stomach (“fish within a fish”)

points.label: Niobrara
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 85 million years ago

event:wahweap.title: Wahweap Formation
event:wahweap.dateText: About 81.5 to 79 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: Sandstones and mudstones from rivers flowing east across the coastal plain of Laramidia, the western island continent of North America, towards the Western Interior Seaway.
Its dinosaurs are older relatives of the better-known ones of the Kaiparowits above: the early tyrannosaurine Lythronax, the horned Diabloceratops and the crestless hadrosaur Acristavus.

points.label: Wahweap
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 80 million years ago

event:oldman.title: Oldman Formation
event:oldman.dateText: About 77.5 to 76.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: River sands and floodplain muds from a time when the coast of the Western Interior Seaway had pulled back east, leaving a drier, upland plain. It lies just below the Dinosaur Park Formation.

It is the home of Daspletosaurus torosus, the heavily built tyrannosaur on the line towards T. rex, and the duck-billed Brachylophosaurus. At Devil’s Coulee, nests of hadrosaur eggs with embryos were found in 1987.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Southern Alberta, including Devil’s Coulee near Warner

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: The type skeleton of Daspletosaurus; dinosaur egg nests

points.label: Oldman
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 77 million years ago

event:demopolis.title: Demopolis Chalk
event:demopolis.dateText: About 79.5 to 74.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: Chalk from the floor of a warm sea covering what is now the southern United States, off the coast of Appalachia, the eastern island continent of North America.

Mostly it holds sea creatures, mosasaurs, turtles, sharks and fish. But now and then the carcass of a land animal drifted out to sea, and one such carcass is the best skeleton of an eastern tyrannosaur, Appalachiosaurus.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: The “Black Belt” of Alabama and Mississippi

points.label: Demopolis
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 77 million years ago

event:dinosaur-park.title: Dinosaur Park Formation
event:dinosaur-park.dateText: About 76.5 to 74.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: Sands and muds from a warm, wet coastal plain crossed by rivers, near the edge of the Western Interior Seaway. Forests of conifers and flowering plants grew along the channels, and floods buried huge herds in bonebeds.

It may be the richest dinosaur site in the world: more than 50 kinds have been found, over 150 complete skeletons are in museums, and new ones erode out of the badlands every year. Hadrosaurs and horned dinosaurs lived here in great variety, hunted by Gorgosaurus and Daspletosaurus.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Dinosaur Provincial Park, near Brooks, Alberta

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: Huge horned dinosaur bonebeds; a hadrosaur with preserved skin

points.label: Dinosaur Park
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 76 million years ago

event:kaiparowits.title: Kaiparowits Formation
event:kaiparowits.dateText: About 76.6 to 74.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: Mudstones from a wet, humid floodplain with rivers, swamps and lakes, about 100 km from the shore of the Western Interior Seaway. It is the same age as the Dinosaur Park Formation in Canada, but its dinosaurs are different.

That difference suggests the dinosaurs of Laramidia lived in separate northern and southern provinces. The Kaiparowits has its own tyrannosaur, Teratophoneus, and spectacular horned dinosaurs such as Kosmoceratops.

points.label: Kaiparowits
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 76 million years ago

event:djadochta.title: Djadochta Formation
event:djadochta.dateText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: A dry landscape of sand dunes and oases in Late Cretaceous Asia. Animals were buried alive when dunes collapsed or sandstorms struck, so many skeletons are found complete, some in the poses in which they died.

Roy Chapman Andrews’ expeditions found the first dinosaur egg nests here in 1923, along with Velociraptor, Protoceratops and Oviraptor. In 1971 a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops were found locked together in combat, buried as they fought.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Bayanzag (Flaming Cliffs) and Tugrikin Shire, Mongolia

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: The first dinosaur egg nests (1923); the “Fighting Dinosaurs” (1971)

points.label: Djadochta
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 73 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Insect burrows
invertebrates.text: Burrowing insects, known from their pupal chambers.

event:hall-lake.title: Hall Lake Formation
event:hall-lake.dateText: About 73.5 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
summary: River deposits in southern New Mexico, near the southern end of Laramidia. Its fossils were collected in the 1980s and studied decades later.

They include a partial Tyrannosaurus skull named in 2024 as a separate, older species, T. mcraeensis, and the horned dinosaur Sierraceratops, suggesting the giants of the latest Cretaceous may have come from the south.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Near Elephant Butte Reservoir, New Mexico

points.label: Hall Lake
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 73 million years ago

event:horseshoe-canyon.title: Horseshoe Canyon Formation
event:horseshoe-canyon.dateText: About 74 to 67 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian–Maastrichtian)
summary: Coal-bearing mudstones and sandstones from a cool, wet coastal plain of swamps, bogs and rivers, as the Western Interior Seaway rose and fell nearby. The badlands of the Red Deer River valley around Drumheller are cut into these rocks.

Its top predator was Albertosaurus. In 1910 Barnum Brown found a bonebed with at least 26 Albertosaurus of all ages, a sign that they may have lived in groups. Duck-billed Edmontosaurus and Hypacrosaurus, horned Anchiceratops and Pachyrhinosaurus, and ostrich-like Ornithomimus lived alongside it.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Red Deer River valley, Drumheller, Alberta

points.label: Horseshoe Canyon
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 71 million years ago

event:nanxiong.title: Nanxiong Formation
event:nanxiong.dateText: About 72 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: Red beds from a warm, seasonally dry inland basin in southern China. Thousands of dinosaur eggs have been found here, many by construction workers in the fast-growing city of Ganzhou.
Oviraptorosaurs were especially varied: at least seven kinds lived in the basin. The long-snouted tyrannosaur Qianzhousaurus, “Pinocchio rex”, also lived here.

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: Thousands of dinosaur eggs; many oviraptorosaurs

points.label: Nanxiong
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 69 million years ago

event:new-egypt.title: New Egypt Formation
event:new-egypt.dateText: About 68 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: Greensand from a shallow sea off the coast of Appalachia, the eastern island continent of North America. Marl pits in these sands were dug for fertiliser in the 1800s, and the diggers turned up mosasaurs, turtles, crocodiles and, occasionally, dinosaurs washed out to sea.
In 1866 a quarry near Barnsboro produced Dryptosaurus, an eastern tyrannosaur. Edward Drinker Cope described it as leaping on its prey, an image later painted by Charles Knight.

points.label: New Egypt
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 67 million years ago

event:allaru.title: Allaru Mudstone
event:allaru.dateText: About 104 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, late Albian)
event:allaru.placeText: Around Richmond and Hughenden, north-central Queensland, Australia
summary: Grey mudstone from the floor of the Eromanga Sea, the shallow inland sea that covered much of eastern Australia. It lies above the Toolebuc Formation and below the Mackunda Formation, and records the sea at its widest before it began to dry up.

Its fossils are mostly sea creatures: the ichthyosaur Platypterygius, the small sea turtle Notochelone, long-necked plesiosaurs, big predatory fish such as Cooyoo, ammonites and crabs. Dinosaurs whose bodies floated out to sea are found too, among them Australia’s first named sauropod, Austrosaurus, and the small armoured Kunbarrasaurus, the most complete dinosaur skeleton known from Australia.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Around Richmond and Hughenden, north-central Queensland

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Blue-grey marine mudstone with thin sandstone and siltstone

points.label: Allaru
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 102 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Ammonites
invertebrates.text: Coiled ammonites such as Beudanticeras and Goodhallites, and heteromorphs with open, hooked shells such as Labeceras and Myloceras.

invertebrates.title: An early octopus relative
invertebrates.text: Eromangateuthis, a squid-like animal with an internal shell, an early relative of octopuses.

invertebrates.title: Crabs, corals and bivalves
invertebrates.text: The crab Torynomma, the coral Mckenziephyllia, and bivalves such as Inoceramus and Aucellina, plus belemnites.

groupNotes.title: Plesiosaurs
groupNotes.text: Bones of long-necked elasmosaurid plesiosaurs.

groupNotes.title: Other fish
groupNotes.text: Pachyrhizodus, a fast predatory fish with fang-like teeth; the beaked Richmondichthys; and Flindersichthys.

groupNotes.title: Another ornithopod
groupNotes.text: Bones that may belong to Muttaburrasaurus, known from the Mackunda Formation above.

event:mackunda.title: Mackunda Formation
event:mackunda.dateText: About 104 to 96 million years ago (late Early to early Late Cretaceous; dating debated)
summary: Sandstones and mudstones laid down along the shores of the Eromanga Sea, a shallow inland sea that once covered much of eastern Australia, as it was drying up and giving way to the river plains of the Winton Formation above.
It was long dated to about 104 to 102 million years ago, but a 2026 study of tiny zircon crystals from the Muttaburrasaurus site gave about 96 million years, though with a wide margin of error.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Sandstone, siltstone and mudstone of a shrinking inland sea

points.label: Mackunda
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 99 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Heteromorph ammonites
invertebrates.text: Labeceras and Myloceras, ammonites whose shells grew in open hooks and loose spirals rather than tight coils.

invertebrates.title: Bivalves
invertebrates.text: Clams and scallop relatives, including giant flat Inoceramus, Aucellina and Maccoyella, living on the muddy sea floor.

invertebrates.title: Belemnites and sea snails
invertebrates.text: Belemnites (squid-like animals with bullet-shaped inner shells) and sea snails such as Euspira and Anchura.

groupNotes.title: Mackerel sharks
groupNotes.text: Teeth of lamniform sharks, relatives of today’s great white and mako, from the inland sea.

groupNotes.title: Another ornithopod
groupNotes.text: Bones of a second, unnamed large plant-eating ornithopod, perhaps related to Iguanodon.

event:wonthaggi.title: Wonthaggi Formation
event:wonthaggi.dateText: About 135 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
event:wonthaggi.placeText: Coast of Gippsland, Victoria, Australia (Flat Rocks, San Remo, Kilcunda)
summary: River sands, silts and coal laid down in a rift valley that was slowly pulling Australia away from Antarctica. At the time it lay at about 77°S, deep inside the Antarctic Circle, with months of winter darkness. The rocks preserve frost-heaved mounds, ice-wedge cracks and frozen bogs, signs that the ground froze and perhaps held permafrost.

Its fossils, mostly small bones and teeth, have been dug from the shore platforms since 1994 by the “Dinosaur Dreaming” project and its volunteers. They include the last known temnospondyl, Koolasuchus, small two-legged plant-eating dinosaurs, megaraptoran teeth and some of the oldest mammals known from Australia.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 125 million years ago at Flat Rocks

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Shore platforms near Inverloch and San Remo, Victoria

points.label: Wonthaggi
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 126 million years ago

event:clearwater.title: Clearwater Formation
event:clearwater.dateText: About 113 to 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, late Aptian)
event:clearwater.placeText: Suncor Millennium Mine, near Fort McMurray, Alberta, Canada
summary: Dark marine mudstones and sands laid down on the floor of the Boreal Sea, an arm of the Arctic Ocean that reached deep into what is now western Canada. They lie above the oil sands of northern Alberta and are dug through by the giant open-pit mines there, where machine operators have found marine reptiles, ammonites and, once, a dinosaur.

That dinosaur, the nodosaur Borealopelta, is one of the best-preserved dinosaurs ever found: its body was carried out to sea, sank on its back and was buried so quickly that its armour, skin and stomach contents survived in three dimensions.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Oil sands mines near Fort McMurray, Alberta

points.label: Clearwater
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 112 million years ago

event:weald-clay.title: Weald Clay (Smokejacks Pit)
event:weald-clay.dateText: About 131 to 126 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: Clays and silts from a broad, swampy river plain with lagoons and lakes, part of the Wealden of southern England, then a warm, seasonal lowland.

In 1983 the amateur collector William Walker found a huge claw in Smokejacks clay pit. It belonged to Baryonyx, the first spinosaur known from a good skeleton. Fish scales in its stomach showed for the first time that spinosaurs ate fish; a young iguanodont was in there too.

points.label: Weald Clay
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 129 million years ago

event:las-hoyas.title: Las Hoyas (La Huérguina Formation)
event:las-hoyas.dateText: About 127 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: Fine limestones from a subtropical wetland of shallow lakes and marshes, where microbial mats sealed in dead animals and preserved skin, feathers and soft tissue.
It holds the humped predator Concavenator, the many-toothed ostrich dinosaur Pelecanimimus, early birds, crocodiles, frogs and salamanders, and thousands of fish and insects.

points.label: Las Hoyas
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 126 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Insects
invertebrates.text: Insects, including dragonflies and water bugs.

event:bernissart.title: Sainte-Barbe Clays (Bernissart)
event:bernissart.dateText: About 127 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: Clays that filled a sinkhole in older coal-bearing rocks, at the edge of a Wealden swamp. In 1878 coal miners 322 m underground broke into the clay and found skeletons: at least 38 Iguanodon, the first complete dinosaur skeletons ever found.

They were dug out over three years, mounted standing upright like kangaroos and displayed in Brussels, where they still stand. Whether a herd died together or carcasses collected over time is still debated.

points.label: Bernissart
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 126 million years ago

event:la-amarga.title: La Amarga Formation
event:la-amarga.dateText: About 129 to 122 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: River and lake sediments from a seasonally dry part of Patagonia, early in the Cretaceous, when South America was still joined to Africa.
It is the home of Amargasaurus, the sauropod with two rows of tall spines down its neck, alongside other sauropods, small abelisaurs and early mammals.

points.label: La Amarga
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 126 million years ago

event:jiufotang.title: Jiufotang Formation
event:jiufotang.dateText: About 122 to 119 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: Lake shales from the later part of the Jehol Biota, deposited just after the Yixian in the same volcanic, forested landscape.
It is famous for Microraptor, the four-winged, crow-sized dinosaur whose glossy black feathers have been reconstructed from fossil pigment, and for long-tailed early birds such as Jeholornis.

points.label: Jiufotang
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 120 million years ago

event:elrhaz.title: Elrhaz Formation (Gadoufaoua)
event:elrhaz.dateText: About 125 to 112 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian–Albian)
summary: Today a remote stretch of the Sahara; in the Early Cretaceous a lush floodplain of big rivers near the equator, with forests and swamps. Whole skeletons weather out of the sand at Gadoufaoua.

Expeditions by Philippe Taquet from the 1960s and Paul Sereno from the 1990s found the giant crocodile Sarcosuchus, the sail-backed Ouranosaurus, the fish-eating spinosaur Suchomimus and the vacuum-cleaner sauropod Nigersaurus.

points.label: Gadoufaoua
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 115 million years ago

event:cloverly.title: Cloverly Formation
event:cloverly.dateText: About 115 to 108 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian–Albian)
summary: Mudstones from a seasonally wet floodplain in western North America, with rivers flowing towards an advancing sea.

In 1964 John Ostrom found Deinonychus here, a fast, agile, sickle-clawed predator. It overturned the idea of dinosaurs as slow, cold-blooded giants, launched the “Dinosaur Renaissance” and became the model for the raptors of Jurassic Park. Its teeth are often found with Tenontosaurus skeletons, its likely prey.

points.label: Cloverly
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 112 million years ago

event:antlers.title: Antlers Formation
event:antlers.dateText: About 115 to 108 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian–Albian)
event:antlers.placeText: South-eastern Oklahoma and north Texas, USA
summary: Sands and muds from a humid coastal plain on the edge of a warm sea spreading across Texas. Its rivers and swamps were home to some of the biggest dinosaurs of their time in North America.
The top predator was Acrocanthosaurus, with a tall ridge along its back, hunting giant sauropods such as Sauroposeidon and the plant-eater Tenontosaurus, alongside Deinonychus.

points.label: Antlers
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 112 million years ago

event:romualdo.title: Romualdo Formation (Santana Group)
event:romualdo.dateText: About 113 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian)
summary: A coastal lagoon in the gap opening between South America and Africa as the South Atlantic formed. Animals were sealed inside limestone nodules so quickly that muscles, gills and even stomach contents are preserved in 3D.
It is one of the richest pterosaur sites in the world, from big-crested fish-eaters to toothless tapejarids, and also has the spinosaur Irritator, coelacanths and thousands of fish.

points.label: Santana
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 111 million years ago

event:toolebuc.title: Toolebuc Formation
event:toolebuc.dateText: About 105 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian)
summary: Limestones from the Eromanga Sea, a cold, shallow inland sea that covered much of central Australia, then far to the south near the Antarctic Circle.
Its top predator was the giant pliosaur Kronosaurus, alongside ichthyosaurs, long-necked plesiosaurs, turtles and fish. Kronosaurus Korner museum in Richmond displays them.

points.label: Toolebuc
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 103 million years ago

event:cerro-barcino.title: Cerro Barcino Formation
event:cerro-barcino.dateText: About 103 to 100 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian)
summary: River sediments in Patagonia. In 2012 a farm worker at La Flecha ranch spotted a giant thigh bone, and the dig that followed found the bones of six individuals of Patagotitan, one of the largest animals ever to walk the Earth.
Teeth of the big predator Tyrannotitan were found among them.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: La Flecha ranch, near Trelew, Chubut

points.label: Cerro Barcino
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 101 million years ago

event:candeleros.title: Candeleros Formation
event:candeleros.dateText: About 111 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, early Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: Red sandstones from rivers and dunes in a seasonally dry Patagonia. In 1993 Rubén Carolini, a car mechanic and amateur fossil hunter, found the skeleton of Giganotosaurus, one of the largest meat-eating dinosaurs.
Its world also had rebbachisaurid and titanosaur sauropods, the small raptor-like Buitreraptor, abelisaurs, and Najash, a snake with back legs.

It was long dated to the Cenomanian, about 100 to 97 million years ago, early in the Late Cretaceous. In 2026 Ignacio Maniel and colleagues dated zircon crystals from volcanic ash beds and found it is older, from the early Albian of the Early Cretaceous, about 111 million years ago.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 111 million years ago (re-dated in 2026; once thought about 98)

facts.label: Museum
facts.value: Museo Municipal Ernesto Bachmann, El Chocón

points.label: Candeleros
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 111 million years ago

event:bahariya.title: Bahariya Formation
event:bahariya.dateText: About 99 to 94 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: A tropical coast of tidal flats and mangrove-like swamps on the southern shore of the Tethys Sea. Ernst Stromer collected here from 1911 and found the first Spinosaurus, Aegyptosaurus and a big carcharodontosaur (renamed Tameryraptor in 2025); his fossils were destroyed in a bombing raid on Munich in 1944.
An American team returned in 2000 and found the giant titanosaur Paralititan, buried in what was once a mangrove swamp.

facts.label: Explored by
facts.value: Ernst Stromer and Richard Markgraf (1911–1914); Joshua Smith and colleagues (2000)

points.label: Bahariya
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 97 million years ago

event:echkar.title: Echkar Formation
event:echkar.dateText: About 97 to 93 million years ago (early Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: River deposits in what is now the Sahara, the same age as the Kem Kem and Bahariya. It holds a strange mix of crocodile relatives, from the boar-tusked Kaprosuchus to the duck-faced Laganosuchus.
Its dinosaurs include the short-snouted abelisaur Rugops and a second species of Carcharodontosaurus.

points.label: Echkar
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 95 million years ago

event:huincul.title: Huincul Formation
event:huincul.dateText: About 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Albian; re-dated in 2026)
summary: Sandstones from braided rivers in a seasonally dry Patagonia. In 1987 a rancher found what he thought was a petrified log: it was a leg bone of Argentinosaurus, perhaps the largest land animal ever.
Its predators included Mapusaurus, found in a bonebed with at least seven individuals, the huge Meraxes, and the abelisaur Skorpiovenator.

It was long thought to be early Late Cretaceous, about 97 to 93 million years old. A 2026 study dating zircon crystals in a volcanic ash bed found it is older, from the Albian of the Early Cretaceous, about 106 million years ago.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 106 million years ago (re-dated in 2026; once thought about 95)

facts.label: Museum
facts.value: Museo Municipal Carmen Funes, Plaza Huincul

points.label: Huincul
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 106 million years ago

event:iren-dabasu.title: Iren Dabasu Formation
event:iren-dabasu.dateText: About 95 to 86 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: River sands from a seasonally dry plain in Inner Mongolia, first explored by the American Museum’s Central Asiatic Expeditions in the 1920s.

In 2005, while filming a documentary, palaeontologist Xu Xing found a thigh bone he thought belonged to a tyrannosaur. It was from Gigantoraptor, a giant, beaked oviraptorosaur the size of a tyrannosaur.

points.label: Iren Dabasu
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 92 million years ago

event:dorotea.title: Dorotea Formation
event:dorotea.dateText: About 75 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian to early Maastrichtian)
summary: Sandstones and mudstones from coastal plains and shallow seas at the southern tip of South America, which was then still close to Antarctica. Expeditions to Cerro Guido, near Torres del Paine, have found one of the richest Late Cretaceous faunas of the far south.
Alongside the armoured Stegouros lived the duck-billed dinosaur relative Gonkoken, titanosaurs, early mammals, plesiosaurs and sharks, with ammonites in the nearby sea.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Cerro Guido, near Torres del Paine, Magallanes, Chile

points.label: Dorotea
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 73 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Ammonites and bivalves
invertebrates.text: Ammonites such as Pachydiscus and Gunnarites, and trigoniid bivalves.

groupNotes.title: Gonkoken
groupNotes.text: Gonkoken nanoi, named in 2023, a duck-billed dinosaur relative whose ancestors reached South America from the north.

groupNotes.title: Early mammals
groupNotes.text: Magallanodon, a gondwanathere, and Orretherium, a meridiolestidan, both from groups found only on the southern continents.

groupNotes.title: Sea reptiles and sharks
groupNotes.text: The plesiosaur Aristonectes, side-necked turtles, and sharks such as Carcharias and Serratolamna.

event:aguja.title: Aguja Formation
event:aguja.dateText: About 82 to 76 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
event:aguja.placeText: Big Bend National Park, Texas, USA
summary: Coastal swamps, lagoons and river mouths on the western shore of the Western Interior Seaway, at the southern end of Laramidia.

Its most famous resident is Deinosuchus, a giant alligator relative that ambushed dinosaurs at the water’s edge: big dinosaur bones from the area carry its tooth marks. Horned dinosaurs, hadrosaurs and turtles lived in the swamps with it.

points.label: Aguja
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 79 million years ago

event:pierre-shale.title: Pierre Shale
event:pierre-shale.dateText: About 81 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian–Maastrichtian)
event:pierre-shale.placeText: South Dakota, Kansas and across the Great Plains, USA
summary: Dark mud from the floor of the Western Interior Seaway, laid down after the Niobrara chalk as the sea grew deeper and cooler. It covers much of the Great Plains.
Its sea held the largest turtle ever, Archelon, the long-necked plesiosaur Elasmosaurus, which Cope famously reconstructed with its head on the end of its tail, and big mosasaurs.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: South Dakota, Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, Montana

points.label: Pierre Shale
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 76 million years ago

event:cerro-fortaleza.title: Cerro Fortaleza Formation
event:cerro-fortaleza.dateText: About 77 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian–Maastrichtian; dating debated)
summary: River sediments in southern Patagonia, laid down in a forested floodplain. A river burst its banks and buried two giant titanosaurs in quickly settling mud, preserving most of their skeletons.
They were found in 2005 and named Dreadnoughtus, one of the most complete giant sauropods known.

Older papers call these rocks the Pari Aike Formation, and under that name they yielded the giant titanosaur Puertasaurus, the plant-eater Talenkauen and the megaraptorid Orkoraptor. Their exact age is still debated.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Near Lago Cardiel, Santa Cruz, Argentina

points.label: Cerro Fortaleza
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 75 million years ago

event:gres-a-reptiles.title: Argiles et Grès à Reptiles Formation
event:gres-a-reptiles.dateText: About 72 to 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian–early Maastrichtian)
summary: Red clays and sandstones from rivers on one of the islands of the European archipelago that lay in the Tethys Sea at the end of the Cretaceous. Dinosaur eggs are so common in the area that whole nesting grounds are known.
Its dinosaurs include the raptor Pyroraptor, the small plant-eater Rhabdodon and titanosaurs.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Around Aix-en-Provence and the Arc Basin, France

points.label: Provence
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 71 million years ago

event:la-colonia.title: La Colonia Formation
event:la-colonia.dateText: About 72 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: Estuaries, tidal flats and coastal plains along a shallow sea that flooded Patagonia at the end of the Cretaceous.
In 1984 José Bonaparte’s team found a nearly complete skeleton of Carnotaurus here, with skin impressions covering much of its body. Plesiosaurs, turtles and early mammals are also found.

points.label: La Colonia
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 70 million years ago

event:prince-creek.title: Prince Creek Formation
event:prince-creek.dateText: About 72 to 68 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, early Maastrichtian)
event:prince-creek.placeText: Colville River, North Slope, Alaska, USA
summary: River sediments from a coastal plain at about 80° north, closer to the pole than today. Dinosaurs here lived through months of winter darkness, cold and occasional snow, in forests of conifers and flowering shrubs.

They included herds of Pachyrhinosaurus and the duck-billed Ugrunaaluk, the small tyrannosaur Nanuqsaurus and troodontids. Babies found here show dinosaurs nested in the Arctic rather than migrating away.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Bluffs along the Colville River, Alaska

points.label: Prince Creek
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 69 million years ago

event:hateg.title: Hațeg Basin
event:hateg.dateText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: In the latest Cretaceous Hațeg was an island in the Tethys Sea. In 1895 Ilona Nopcsa found bones on her family estate, and her brother, Baron Franz Nopcsa, noticed the dinosaurs were unusually small. He proposed island dwarfism to explain it, the first time the idea was applied to dinosaurs.
On the island lived dwarf titanosaurs and hadrosaurs, a strange stocky raptor-like dinosaur, Balaur, and above all the giant azhdarchid Hatzegopteryx, probably the top predator.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Hațeg Country UNESCO Global Geopark, Romania

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Sânpetru and Densuș-Ciula formations: river sandstone and mudstone

points.label: Hațeg
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 68 million years ago

event:maevarano.title: Maevarano Formation
event:maevarano.dateText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: Rivers crossing a hot, seasonally dry plain on the island of Madagascar, already cut off from India and Africa. Debris flows in the wet season buried animals, preserving many complete skeletons.
Its fauna was unique: the cannibal abelisaur Majungasaurus, the titanosaur Rapetosaurus, the buck-toothed Masiakasaurus, a giant frog, a pug-nosed plant-eating crocodile and strange mammals.

facts.label: Explored by
facts.value: The Mahajanga Basin Project, led by David Krause, from 1993

points.label: Maevarano
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 68 million years ago

event:maungataniwha.title: Maungataniwha Sandstone (Mangahouanga)
event:maungataniwha.dateText: About 72 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
event:maungataniwha.placeText: Mangahouanga Stream, Hawke’s Bay, New Zealand
summary: Shallow sea sands off the coast of Zealandia, the mostly sunken continent that had just split from Gondwana, then far to the south. Joan Wiffen, an amateur collector, found New Zealand’s first dinosaur bones here in the 1970s.
It is best known for marine reptiles: the long-necked elasmosaur Tuarangisaurus and mosasaurs.

points.label: Mangahouanga
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 69 million years ago

event:wangshi.title: Wangshi Group (Zhucheng)
event:wangshi.dateText: About 73 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
summary: River and floodplain deposits in eastern China. A single quarry at Kugou in Zhucheng holds one of the largest dinosaur bonebeds in the world, with more than 7,600 bones, mostly of the giant duck-billed Shantungosaurus.
Among them were the horned dinosaur Sinoceratops, the only true ceratopsid known from Asia, and the big tyrannosaur Zhuchengtyrannus.

points.label: Zhucheng
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 72 million years ago

event:lameta.title: Lameta Formation
event:lameta.dateText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
event:lameta.placeText: Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat, India
summary: River and lake sediments laid down on India as it drifted north across the Indian Ocean, between the first eruptions of the Deccan Traps, one of the biggest volcanic outpourings in Earth’s history.
Titanosaurs nested here by the thousand, and the horned abelisaur Rajasaurus probably hunted them. One nest holds an egg-eating snake, Sanajeh, coiled around a titanosaur egg and a hatchling.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Jabalpur (Madhya Pradesh), and Kheda and Balasinor (Gujarat)

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Limestone and sandstone, between Deccan lava flows

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: Titanosaurus, the first titanosaur named (1877); Balasinor nesting grounds

points.label: Lameta
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 67 million years ago

event:ouled-abdoun.title: Ouled Abdoun Basin phosphates
event:ouled-abdoun.dateText: About 72 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: Phosphate beds from a warm, shallow sea over north-west Africa, rich in nutrients and life. Phosphate mining around Khouribga has turned up vast numbers of fossils from the last few million years before the asteroid.
Its sea was full of mosasaurs, from the huge, scarred Thalassotitan to shell-crushers, along with plesiosaurs, sharks, sea turtles, and pterosaurs flying overhead.

points.label: Ouled Abdoun
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 67 million years ago

event:maastricht.title: Maastricht Formation
event:maastricht.dateText: About 68 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Maastrichtian)
summary: Soft yellow limestone from a warm, shallow sea that covered the Low Countries, quarried in tunnels under St Pietersberg hill for centuries. It gave its name to the last stage of the Cretaceous, the Maastrichtian.
In about 1780 quarrymen found a huge jaw. The French army seized it in 1795, and it helped Georges Cuvier show that animals could go extinct. In 1822 it was named Mosasaurus, “lizard of the Meuse”.

points.label: Maastricht
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 67 million years ago

event:javelina.title: Javelina Formation
event:javelina.dateText: About 69 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Maastrichtian)
event:javelina.placeText: Big Bend National Park, Texas, USA
summary: River sediments from an inland floodplain in southern Laramidia, far from the coast, with forests and seasonal rivers. Its giant sauropod Alamosaurus shows that sauropods returned to North America from the south late in the Cretaceous.
In 1971 a student, Douglas Lawson, found the wing bones of Quetzalcoatlus here, one of the largest flying animals ever.

points.label: Javelina
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 67 million years ago

event:lopez-de-bertodano.title: López de Bertodano Formation
event:lopez-de-bertodano.dateText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: Muddy sands from a cool, shallow sea along the Antarctic Peninsula, then covered in forests. Its layers run right through the asteroid impact, recording the extinction near the South Pole.
It holds Vegavis, one of the oldest members of the modern bird groups, a relative of ducks and geese, and its sea held long-necked elasmosaurs and mosasaurs.

points.label: Seymour Island
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 67 million years ago

event:green-river.title: Green River Formation (Fossil Butte)
event:green-river.dateText: About 53 to 48 million years ago (early Eocene)
summary: Fine, layered limestones from large lakes in the warm, subtropical early Eocene, the warmest time of the last 66 million years. Fossil Lake in Wyoming, the smallest of them, has given millions of perfectly preserved fish, along with bats, birds, crocodiles, turtles, insects and palm leaves.
The thin layers (varves) record single seasons. Fish are so common that some slabs hold hundreds that died together, perhaps in algal blooms or when the lake turned over.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 52 million years ago (Fossil Butte Member)

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Fossil Butte National Monument, near Kemmerer, Wyoming

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Finely layered limestone and oil shale

facts.label: Famous finds
facts.value: Millions of Knightia; the oldest complete bats

points.label: Green River
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 52 million years ago

event:messel.title: Messel Pit
event:messel.dateText: About 48 to 47 million years ago (middle Eocene)
summary: A deep crater lake (maar) formed by a volcanic explosion, surrounded by subtropical forest. Its still, stagnant depths, perhaps poisoned at times by volcanic gas, preserved animals in oil shale with fur, feathers, skin outlines, stomach contents and even the shimmering colours of beetles.

Mined for oil shale and nearly turned into a rubbish dump, Messel was saved and became Germany’s first natural World Heritage Site. It shows an early world of mammals: tiny horses, early primates, bats, anteater-like animals and giant flightless birds.

points.label: Messel
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 48 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Jewel beetles
invertebrates.text: Messel’s jewel beetles and leaf beetles still shine green, blue and bronze after 47 million years. Their colours come from microscopic layers in their shells that reflect light, not from pigments, so they have survived fossilisation.

groupNotes.title: Bats
groupNotes.text: At least seven kinds of bat hunted over the Messel lake, among the earliest bats anywhere: Palaeochiropteryx, Archaeonycteris, Hassianycteris and Tachypteron. Their stomach contents show different species took different insects, and Hassianycteris was one of the largest bats of its time.

groupNotes.title: Rodents
groupNotes.text: Early rodents such as Ailuravus, a squirrel-like animal about 90 cm long including its bushy tail, and the smaller Masillamys climbed in the forest around the lake.

event:riversleigh.title: Riversleigh
event:riversleigh.dateText: About 25 to 12 million years ago (late Oligocene to middle Miocene)
event:riversleigh.placeText: Boodjamulla (Lawn Hill) National Park, north-west Queensland, Australia
summary: Limestone pools, caves and springs in a lush rainforest that once covered much of Australia, before the continent dried out. Lime-rich water preserved bones in three dimensions, and they are freed from the rock with acid.

Riversleigh has more than 350 kinds of extinct animal, a record of Australia’s strange mammals: early relatives of the thylacine, marsupial lions, giant platypuses, tree-climbing diprotodontids, blade-toothed kangaroos and small land-living crocodiles.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 25 to 12 million years ago (and younger)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: UNESCO World Heritage Site, with Naracoorte (1994)

points.label: Riversleigh
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 15 million years ago

groupNotes.title: Bats
groupNotes.text: The Riversleigh caves hold dozens of kinds of fossil bat, especially leaf-nosed bats such as Brachipposideros, which roosted in the caves in great colonies.

event:ashfall.title: Ashfall Fossil Beds
summary: About 12 million years ago a supervolcano in what is now Idaho, part of the Yellowstone hotspot, erupted, and ash drifted over 1,000 km to the grasslands of Nebraska. Animals gathered at a waterhole breathed the fine glassy dust and died over weeks, birds first, then small mammals, horses, and finally rhinos.

Their skeletons lie complete where they fell, buried in deep ash: a “Pompeii of prehistoric animals”. Some rhino mothers have calves beside them, some have their last meal of grass seeds in their mouths.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Ashfall Fossil Beds State Historical Park, near Royal, Nebraska

points.label: Ashfall
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 12 million years ago

groupNotes.title: Rodents
groupNotes.text: Small rodents.

event:hadar.title: Hadar Formation
summary: Sediments from a lake and the rivers feeding it in the Afar rift, surrounded by woodland and grassland. Volcanic ash layers between them give precise dates.

On 24 November 1974, Donald Johanson and Tom Gray found “Lucy”, a 40% complete skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis, 3.2 million years old. She walked upright on two legs but had a brain the size of a chimpanzee’s. A year later the team found the “First Family”, at least 13 individuals together.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Hadar, on the Awash River, Ethiopia

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Part of the Lower Valley of the Awash UNESCO site (1980)

points.label: Hadar
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 3.2 million years ago

event:la-brea.title: La Brea Tar Pits
event:la-brea.placeText: Hancock Park, Los Angeles, California, USA
summary: Natural asphalt has been seeping up here for tens of thousands of years. Animals that stepped into the sticky pools were trapped, and their struggles drew in predators and scavengers that were trapped in turn. That is why predators outnumber their prey here by about nine to one.
More than 3.5 million fossils have come out of the asphalt, from mammoths, sabre-toothed cats and dire wolves to insects and pollen. Excavation still goes on in the middle of Los Angeles.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Hancock Park, Wilshire Boulevard, Los Angeles

facts.label: Fossils
facts.value: More than 3.5 million, including over 2,000 sabre-toothed cats

points.label: La Brea
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 20,000 years ago

invertebrates.title: Leafcutter bees
invertebrates.text: Two nests of leafcutter bees, Megachile gentilis, were found in the asphalt with the pupae still inside their leaf-wrapped cells, 23,000 to 40,000 years old. The species still lives in California today.

invertebrates.title: Petroleum flies
invertebrates.text: The larvae of the petroleum fly, Helaeomyia petrolei, live in the tar pits today, swimming in the oil and eating insects that get stuck. They are one of very few animals that can survive in crude oil.

groupNotes.title: Rodents
groupNotes.text: Ground squirrels, pocket gophers, wood rats and mice.

event:naredi.title: Naredi Formation
event:naredi.placeText: Panandhro lignite mine, Kutch, Gujarat, India
summary: Coastal swamp and lagoon deposits from a time when India was an island continent just meeting Asia, and the world was far warmer than today. Its lignite (brown coal) is mined at Panandhro, where workers turned up the backbone of Vasuki, one of the largest snakes ever.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Panandhro lignite mine, Kutch, Gujarat, India

points.label: Naredi
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 47 million years ago

event:cerrejon.title: Cerrejón Formation
summary: The oldest known rainforest in South America, a hot, wet coastal swamp forest a few million years after the dinosaurs died out. Its peat became the coal of the vast Cerrejón open-pit mine, where the fossils are found.
In a world hotter than today, cold-blooded animals grew huge: Titanoboa, one of the two largest snakes known, lived here with giant turtles and crocodile relatives.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Cerrejón coal mine, La Guajira, Colombia

points.label: Cerrejón
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 59 million years ago

event:willwood.title: Willwood Formation
event:willwood.dateText: About 56 to 52 million years ago (earliest Eocene)
summary: Red-banded floodplain mudstones laid down during the hottest time of the last 66 million years, the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum and the warm early Eocene. Subtropical forests reached far north, and new groups of mammals, including the first horses and primates, spread across the northern continents.
The giant flightless bird Gastornis walked these forests alongside tiny horses and the hippo-like Coryphodon.

points.label: Willwood
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 54 million years ago

groupNotes.title: Rodents
groupNotes.text: Squirrel-like early rodents such as Paramys were common. Rodents had reached North America shortly before, near the end of the Paleocene.

event:kuldana.title: Kuldana Formation
event:kuldana.dateText: About 50 to 47 million years ago (early–middle Eocene)
summary: Red river and coastal sediments on the shore of the shrinking Tethys Sea, as India pushed into Asia. Here the ancestors of whales took their first steps into the water.
It holds Pakicetus, a wolf-sized land animal with a whale’s ear, and Ambulocetus, the “walking, swimming whale”, built like a crocodile.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Kohat District and the Kala Chitta Hills, Pakistan

points.label: Kuldana
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 48 million years ago

event:irdin-manha.title: Irdin Manha Formation
event:irdin-manha.dateText: About 45 to 40 million years ago (middle Eocene)
summary: River sediments from a warm plain in Inner Mongolia, explored by the American Museum’s Central Asiatic Expeditions. In 1923 Kan Chuen-pao found a single huge skull here: Andrewsarchus.
Other mammals included early tapirs and rhino relatives, brontotheres and the horned uintathere Gobiatherium.

points.label: Irdin Manha
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 42 million years ago

event:wadi-al-hitan.title: Wadi Al-Hitan (Valley of the Whales)
event:wadi-al-hitan.dateText: About 41 to 37 million years ago (late Eocene)
summary: A shallow, warm bay of the Tethys Sea, with mangroves along the shore. Hundreds of whale skeletons weather out of the desert here, many with tiny back legs, showing the last steps of whales’ move to the sea.
Basilosaurus, the top predator, hunted the smaller whale Dorudon: juvenile Dorudon skulls carry its bite marks.

points.label: Wadi Al-Hitan
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 39 million years ago

event:bugti.title: Bugti Hills (Chitarwata Formation)
summary: River sediments from a coastal plain on the edge of the Indian subcontinent. Guy Pilgrim found giant bones here in the early 1900s belonging to Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal ever.
It lived alongside early elephant relatives, crocodiles, and the ancestors of many of Asia’s mammals.

points.label: Bugti Hills
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 25 million years ago

event:agate.title: Agate Fossil Beds
event:agate.dateText: About 22 to 20 million years ago (early Miocene)
summary: A waterhole on a dry grassland plain. During droughts animals crowded around the last water and died in great numbers, leaving a bonebed packed with thousands of skeletons of small rhinos.
The “hell pig” Daeodon, clawed Moropus, gazelle-like camels and burrowing beavers lived here. The beavers’ spiral burrows, “Devil’s corkscrews”, puzzled scientists for decades.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Agate Fossil Beds National Monument, Nebraska

points.label: Agate
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 21 million years ago

event:santa-cruz.title: Santa Cruz Formation
event:santa-cruz.dateText: About 18 to 16 million years ago (early Miocene)
event:santa-cruz.placeText: Atlantic coast of Santa Cruz Province, Patagonia, Argentina
summary: Patagonia in the warm early Miocene, a mix of forest and open woodland. South America was then an island continent, and its animals had evolved in isolation: marsupial-like predators, strange hoofed mammals, glyptodonts and ground sloths, monkeys and giant flightless “terror birds”.
Carlos and Florentino Ameghino collected here in the 1880s, and the sea cliffs are still yielding complete skeletons.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Coastal cliffs from Río Gallegos to Monte León, Argentina

points.label: Santa Cruz
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 17 million years ago

groupNotes.title: Rodents
groupNotes.text: Early caviomorph rodents, relatives of guinea pigs and chinchillas, were common, among them Perimys and Eocardia. Their ancestors had reached South America from Africa, probably by rafting, around 40 million years ago.

event:eppelsheim.title: Eppelsheim Formation (Dinotheriensande)
event:eppelsheim.dateText: About 10.5 to 9 million years ago (late Miocene)
summary: Sands laid down by a river, the ancestor of the Rhine, flowing through warm, wooded country in the late Miocene. Its fossils were described from the 1820s, making it one of the first famous mammal sites.
It is named after Deinotherium, the giant elephant relative with downward-curving tusks, found here first, along with three-toed horses, chalicotheres and early apes.

points.label: Eppelsheim
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 10 million years ago

event:pisco.title: Pisco Formation
event:pisco.dateText: About 10 to 5 million years ago (late Miocene)
summary: Diatom-rich sediments from a cold, nutrient-rich coastal sea off Peru, now uplifted into the driest desert on Earth. Hundreds of whale skeletons lie exposed on the desert floor.
Its sea held the giant shark megalodon and the giant sperm whale Livyatan, both able to hunt whales, along with seals, aquatic sloths that grazed seagrass, penguins and sea birds.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Cerro Colorado and Cerro los Quesos, Ica, Peru

points.label: Pisco
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 9 million years ago

event:andalhuala.title: Andalhuala Formation
event:andalhuala.dateText: About 7.5 to 3 million years ago (late Miocene to Pliocene)
summary: River sediments in the foothills of the rising Andes, in a drying, open landscape of grassland and scrub. South America was still an island, just before the land bridge with North America formed.
The sabre-toothed metatherian Thylacosmilus hunted here, and the giant teratorn Argentavis, the heaviest flying bird ever, soared overhead.

points.label: Andalhuala
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 6 million years ago

event:chongzuo-caves.title: Chongzuo caves
event:chongzuo-caves.dateText: About 2 million to 215,000 years ago (Early–Middle Pleistocene)
summary: Limestone caves in the karst hills of southern China, then surrounded by dense subtropical forest. Porcupines carried bones into the caves to gnaw, leaving thousands of teeth of forest animals.

Among them are teeth and jaws of Gigantopithecus, the largest ape ever. A 2024 study of 22 caves found it died out between 295,000 and 215,000 years ago, as the forests became more seasonal and its diet failed.

points.label: Chongzuo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 400,000 years ago

event:two-medicine.title: Two Medicine Formation
event:two-medicine.dateText: About 81 to 74 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
event:two-medicine.placeText: Choteau and Glacier County, Montana, USA
summary: Upland river plains between the rising Rocky Mountains and the Western Interior Seaway, with a seasonal, fairly dry climate and volcanoes to the west.

In 1978 Jack Horner and Bob Makela found nests of baby duck-billed dinosaurs at “Egg Mountain” near Choteau, the first evidence that some dinosaurs cared for their young in colonies. The same rocks hold horned dinosaurs, tyrannosaurs and small feathered theropods.
Egg clutches at Egg Mountain were first credited to the small plant-eater Orodromeus. Embryos inside them later showed they were laid by a troodontid, and the Orodromeus bones nearby may be its prey.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Egg Mountain near Choteau, and the Blackfeet Reservation, Montana

points.label: Two Medicine
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 76 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Dung beetles in dinosaur dung
invertebrates.text: Fossil dung from the Two Medicine, packed with chewed conifer wood and probably left by Maiasaura, is riddled with backfilled burrows like those dung beetles make today. They are among the oldest evidence of dung beetles, and of a food web linking dinosaurs, beetles and conifers.

event:ruseifa.title: Ruseifa phosphates
event:ruseifa.dateText: About 72 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: Phosphate beds from a warm, shallow sea along the southern shore of the Tethys, part of the same belt of phosphate deposits that runs to Morocco. Mining here since the 1930s has turned up fish, sharks and marine reptiles.
In 1943 a railway worker found an unusually long, hollow bone, later recognised as the neck vertebra of a giant azhdarchid pterosaur, Arambourgiania, one of the first giant pterosaurs known.

Sharks are the commonest fossils. Marine reptiles include the mosasaurs Prognathodon, Globidens (with crushing teeth for shellfish) and Halisaurus, along with long-necked plesiosaurs, sea turtles and crocodile relatives, most known from scattered bones and teeth.

points.label: Ruseifa
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 70 million years ago

event:collon-cura.title: Collón Curá Formation
event:collon-cura.dateText: About 16 to 14 million years ago (Middle Miocene)
summary: Volcanic ash and river deposits laid down on the plains of northern Patagonia as the Andes rose to the west, under a climate that was turning drier and more open.
A high-school student, Guillermo Aguirre-Zabala, found a huge bird skull near Comallo. It was named Kelenken in 2007 and is the largest bird skull known.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Río Negro and Neuquén provinces, Argentina

points.label: Collón Curá
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 15 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Fossil bee nests
invertebrates.text: Fossil brood cells of ground-nesting bees (Celliforma) are common in the old soils, showing dry woodland and scrub.

groupNotes.title: Rodents
groupNotes.text: Caviomorph rodents, including early relatives of guinea pigs and maras, were common.

event:allen.title: Allen Formation
event:allen.dateText: About 72 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian to Maastrichtian)
event:allen.placeText: Salitral Moreno and Bajo de Santa Rosa, Río Negro, Argentina
summary: Coastal plains, lagoons and salt flats along the edge of a shallow sea that flooded into Patagonia at the end of the Cretaceous.

It holds titanosaurs and their eggs, duck-billed dinosaurs that had reached South America from the north, the alvarezsaurid Bonapartenykus with eggs, and the unusual raptor Austroraptor. Plesiosaurs swam in the nearby sea.
One hadrosaur name from here, Willinakaqe, is now considered too poorly founded to use; some of its bones were moved to Bonapartesaurus.

points.label: Allen
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 70 million years ago

event:santa-fe-river.title: Santa Fe River sites
event:santa-fe-river.dateText: About 2.6 to 2 million years ago (Early Pleistocene)
event:santa-fe-river.placeText: Gilchrist and Columbia counties, Florida, USA
summary: Fossils washed out of older beds into the bed of the Santa Fe River, where divers and collectors recover them. Bones of different ages are mixed together here, so they have to be dated individually.

Animals from South America that had crossed into North America, among them the glyptodont Glyptotherium, the pampathere Holmesina, ground sloths and the terror bird Titanis, lived alongside native horses, tapirs and peccaries.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 2.6 to 2.3 million years ago for most of the fauna; one Titanis bone dated to about 2 million

points.label: Santa Fe River
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 2.3 million years ago

event:chapadmalal.title: Chapadmalal sea cliffs
event:chapadmalal.dateText: About 3.7 to 3 million years ago (Pliocene, Chapadmalalan age)
event:chapadmalal.placeText: Mar del Plata, Buenos Aires province, Argentina
summary: Wind-blown silts and old soils of the Pampas, exposed in the sea cliffs south of Mar del Plata. They give their name to the Chapadmalalan age of the South American land-mammal timescale.
In 2010 the most complete terror bird skeleton yet found, Llallawavis, came out of the cliffs here. The giant raccoon relative Chapalmalania was named from these cliffs too.
Several glyptodont species were once named from here. Restudy found some were not separate at all: one supposed species, “Paraglyptodon” chapadmalensis, turned out to be a young Glyptodon.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Sea cliffs between Mar del Plata and Miramar, Argentina

points.label: Chapadmalal
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 3.5 million years ago

groupNotes.title: Rodents
groupNotes.text: Many caviomorph rodents lived on the Pliocene pampas, among them an early mara, Dolichotis chapalmalense.

event:farak.title: Farak Formation
event:farak.dateText: About 100 to 95 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
event:farak.placeText: Jenguebi and Iguidi, central Niger (map position approximate)
summary: River deposits laid down far inland, roughly 500 to 1,000 km from the nearest coast of the time. Most spinosaurid fossils elsewhere come from rocks near the sea, so finding them here shows they also lived along rivers deep inside the continent.
Paul Sereno’s teams collected here in 2000, 2019 and 2022. The finds include Spinosaurus mirabilis, named in 2026, as well as carcharodontosaurid and sauropod remains that have not yet been named.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 95 million years ago (some studies say about 100 to 97 million)

points.label: Farak
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 96 million years ago

event:enciso.title: Enciso Group
event:enciso.dateText: About 125 to 119 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian to Aptian)
summary: Lakes and wetlands in the Cameros Basin of northern Spain. La Rioja is known for thousands of dinosaur footprints in these rocks, and bones are found here too.
A spinosaurid skeleton found near Igea in the 2000s, first thought to be Baryonyx, was named Riojavenatrix in 2024.

points.label: Enciso
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 121 million years ago

event:arcillas-de-morella.title: Arcillas de Morella Formation
event:arcillas-de-morella.dateText: About 127 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
event:arcillas-de-morella.placeText: Morella, Cinctorres and Vallibona, Castellón, Spain
summary: Coastal plains, deltas and marshes in eastern Spain, with iguanodonts, sauropods, ankylosaurs and several kinds of spinosaurid.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Red and grey clays with sandstone

points.label: Morella
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 126 million years ago

event:papo-seco.title: Papo Seco Formation
event:papo-seco.dateText: About 129 to 127 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, early Barremian)
summary: Coastal lagoons and mudflats now exposed in the sea cliffs near Cabo Espichel. A spinosaurid skeleton excavated here, first described as Baryonyx in 2011, was named Iberospinus in 2022.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Sea cliffs near Cabo Espichel, Portugal

points.label: Papo Seco
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 128 million years ago

event:camarillas.title: Camarillas Formation
event:camarillas.dateText: About 129 to 126 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Barremian)
summary: River channels and floodplains in the Maestrazgo Basin of Teruel. Camarillasaurus, named in 2014 from a partial skeleton, was first thought to be a ceratosaur but was later shown to be a spinosaurid.

points.label: Camarillas
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 127 million years ago

event:gres-superieurs.title: Grès supérieurs Formation
