event:gres-superieurs.dateText: About 125 to 105 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian to Albian)
summary: Red river sandstones in southern Laos, first explored for dinosaurs by the French geologist Josué-Heilmann Hoffet in the 1930s. They are the same age as the Khok Kruat Formation of Thailand, and hold the sauropod Tangvayosaurus, iguanodonts, the spinosaurid Ichthyovenator and dinosaur footprints.

points.label: Grès supérieurs
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 118 million years ago

event:alcantara.title: Alcântara Formation
event:alcantara.dateText: About 100 to 95 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: Coastal and estuary deposits on Cajual Island, where bonebeds wash out along the shore. Its fauna is strikingly like that of the Kem Kem in Morocco, from the same time, when South America and Africa had only just separated.

points.label: Alcântara
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 97 million years ago

event:sao-khua.title: Sao Khua Formation
event:sao-khua.dateText: About 133 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: River deposits of the Khorat Plateau in northeastern Thailand, the richest dinosaur rocks in Southeast Asia, with sauropods, theropods, crocodile relatives and the first spinosaurid teeth reported from Asia.

points.label: Sao Khua
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 128 million years ago

event:kitadani.title: Kitadani Formation
event:kitadani.dateText: About 125 to 115 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: River and lake deposits at the Kitadani quarry in Katsuyama, Japan’s richest dinosaur site, worked by the Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum since 1989. Several dinosaurs named from here, such as Fukuiraptor and Fukuisaurus, carry the prefecture’s name.

points.label: Kitadani
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 120 million years ago

event:winton.title: Winton Formation
event:winton.dateText: About 98 to 93 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian to Turonian)
summary: Forested river plains in what is now outback Queensland, then far to the south, near the Antarctic Circle. Australia was still joined to Antarctica.
At the “Matilda” site near Winton, the predator Australovenator and the sauropod Diamantinasaurus were found together in 2006.

Lark Quarry preserves thousands of footprints of small two-legged dinosaurs. They were long described as a stampede of small dinosaurs fleeing a large predator. A 2013 restudy argued instead that many were made by small plant-eaters swimming or wading across a river over days or weeks, and that the big “predator” tracks may belong to a large plant-eater. The original researchers disagree, so the site’s story is still debated.

points.label: Winton
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 95 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Bivalves, snails and insects
invertebrates.text: Freshwater bivalves and snails, and insects.

event:portezuelo.title: Portezuelo Formation
event:portezuelo.dateText: About 91 to 88 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Turonian to Coniacian)
summary: River sandstones of the Neuquén Basin. Megaraptor, the namesake of the megaraptorans, was named from here in 1998, along with giant sauropods and the long-legged theropod Unenlagia.

points.label: Portezuelo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 90 million years ago

event:sierra-barrosa.title: Sierra Barrosa Formation
event:sierra-barrosa.dateText: About 89 to 86 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Coniacian)
summary: River deposits in the Neuquén Basin that yielded Murusraptor, found in a canyon wall and one of the few megaraptorans with part of its skull preserved.

points.label: Sierra Barrosa
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 88 million years ago

event:bajo-de-la-carpa.title: Bajo de la Carpa Formation
event:bajo-de-la-carpa.dateText: About 86 to 83 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
summary: Sandy river and dune deposits around Neuquén city and Añelo, known for small crocodile relatives, snakes and birds, as well as the megaraptorans Tratayenia and Rinconraptor, and the raptor-like Diuqin.

points.label: Bajo de la Carpa
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 85 million years ago

event:anacleto.title: Anacleto Formation
event:anacleto.dateText: About 85 to 79 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian to Campanian)
event:anacleto.placeText: Southern Mendoza and Neuquén, Argentina (map position approximate)
summary: River and floodplain deposits of the Neuquén Basin. At Auca Mahuevo, found in 1997, thousands of titanosaur eggs were laid in nesting grounds used again and again; many contain embryos, some with traces of skin. The abelisaurid Aucasaurus was found at the same site. The air-boned megaraptoran Aerosteon comes from these rocks in Mendoza.

points.label: Anacleto
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 82 million years ago

event:chorrillo.title: Chorrillo Formation
event:chorrillo.dateText: About 72 to 68 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
event:chorrillo.placeText: Estancia La Anita, near El Calafate, Santa Cruz, Argentina
summary: Coastal river plains in southernmost Patagonia, near a sea that was flooding in from the Atlantic. It has yielded the giant megaraptorid Maip, titanosaurs, early mammals, frogs and the sauropod Nullotitan.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Near El Calafate, Santa Cruz, Argentina

points.label: Chorrillo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 69 million years ago

event:colhue-huapi.title: Lago Colhué Huapi Formation
event:colhue-huapi.dateText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: River deposits from the last few million years before the asteroid impact, in central Patagonia, with titanosaurs, hadrosaurs, turtles, crocodile relatives and the megaraptorid Joaquinraptor.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: South of Lago Colhué Huapi, Chubut, Argentina

points.label: Colhué Huapi
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 68 million years ago

event:bear-gulch.title: Bear Gulch Limestone
event:bear-gulch.dateText: About 320 to 316 million years ago (Carboniferous, Serpukhovian)
summary: A warm, shallow tropical bay whose quiet, low-oxygen bottom preserved fish whole, often with their colour patterns and soft outlines.

It is best known for its sharks and their relatives, many strange: males with spines or claspers on their heads, and some of the earliest ratfish relatives. Richard Lund collected here for decades from the 1960s.

points.label: Bear Gulch
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 318 million years ago

event:miguasha.title: Escuminac Formation (Miguasha)
event:miguasha.dateText: About 383 to 378 million years ago (Late Devonian, Frasnian)
summary: An estuary on the edge of the Old Red Sandstone continent, now cliffs on the Gaspé Peninsula. It has yielded thousands of fish, from armoured jawless fish to lobe-finned fish close to the first tetrapods.
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, chosen as the best record of the “Age of Fishes”. In 2020 a complete Elpistostege from here showed bones in its fin arranged like the fingers of a hand.

points.label: Miguasha
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 380 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Scorpions
invertebrates.text: Rare scorpions washed into the estuary, a reminder that arthropods had colonised the land by then.

event:urumaco.title: Urumaco Formation
event:urumaco.dateText: About 10 to 6 million years ago (Late Miocene; dating debated)
summary: Swamps, rivers, estuaries and coastal lagoons on the northern edge of South America, where a large river system once drained into the Caribbean.
It is famous for giants: the turtle Stupendemys, with a shell over 2 m long; the caiman Purussaurus; several big gharials; and some of the largest rodents ever.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Sandstone, mudstone, coal and shelly limestone

points.label: Urumaco
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 8 million years ago

groupNotes.title: Giant rodents
groupNotes.text: Phoberomys pattersoni, a relative of the pacarana, was one of the largest rodents ever, estimated at several hundred kilograms. A second giant rodent, Neoepiblema, lived here too.

event:oehningen.title: Öhningen quarries
event:oehningen.placeText: Öhningen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany, by Lake Constance
summary: Fine limestones from a lake in a volcanic region, quarried since the Middle Ages and rich in fossil leaves, insects and fish.

In 1726 Johann Jakob Scheuchzer described a skeleton from here as “Homo diluvii testis”, a man who had witnessed and drowned in the biblical Flood. In 1811 Georges Cuvier uncovered its forelimbs and showed it was a giant salamander.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Öhningen, on the shore of Lake Constance, Germany

points.label: Öhningen
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 13 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Insects
invertebrates.text: Hundreds of kinds of fossil insects, studied by Oswald Heer in the 19th century, among the first large fossil insect faunas described.

event:karoo-cynognathus.title: Karoo Basin: Cynognathus Assemblage Zone
event:karoo-cynognathus.dateText: About 247 to 242 million years ago (Early to Middle Triassic)
event:karoo-cynognathus.placeText: Burgersdorp and Aliwal North, Eastern Cape, South Africa
summary: River plains of southern Pangaea a few million years after the end-Permian extinction, as life recovered. The rocks are named after the dog-sized predator Cynognathus.
They hold large cynodonts and dicynodonts, the giant early archosaur relative Erythrosuchus and the small, agile Euparkeria, close to the ancestor of crocodiles and dinosaurs.

points.label: Cynognathus Zone
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 245 million years ago

event:chanares.title: Chañares Formation
event:chanares.dateText: About 236 to 234 million years ago (Late Triassic, early Carnian)
summary: River plains buried by volcanic ash, which preserved concretions full of small animals. Alfred Romer’s expeditions in the 1960s found them.

It holds some of the closest relatives of the first dinosaurs and pterosaurs, small, long-legged animals living a few million years before the first true dinosaurs, alongside cynodonts and early crocodile-line reptiles.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Near Talampaya National Park, La Rioja, Argentina

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Volcanic tuff and mudstone with concretions

points.label: Chañares
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 235 million years ago

event:upper-shaximiao.title: Upper Shaximiao Formation
event:upper-shaximiao.dateText: About 163 to 157 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
event:upper-shaximiao.placeText: Sichuan Basin, around Zigong and Chongqing, China
summary: Red mudstones and sandstones laid down by rivers and lakes across the Sichuan Basin, a warm, seasonally dry lowland in the Late Jurassic. It lies above the Lower Shaximiao Formation of Dashanpu and holds the next chapter of Sichuan’s dinosaur story.

Its dinosaurs echo those of North America’s Morrison Formation: long-necked mamenchisaurids, plated stegosaurs such as Tuojiangosaurus, Chungkingosaurus and the giant-spined Gigantspinosaurus, and the big allosaur relative Yangchuanosaurus. Many are displayed at the Zigong Dinosaur Museum.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Zigong, Chongqing and elsewhere in the Sichuan Basin

points.label: Upper Shaximiao
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 160 million years ago

groupNotes.title: Mamenchisaurus
groupNotes.text: Very long-necked sauropods such as Mamenchisaurus hochuanensis and M. constructus, the first Mamenchisaurus ever found.

groupNotes.title: More stegosaurs
groupNotes.text: The small Chungkingosaurus, one of several stegosaurs that lived here at the same time.

groupNotes.title: Others
groupNotes.text: Crocodile relatives, turtles, fish and plesiosaurs from the rivers and lakes.

event:elliot.title: Elliot Formation
event:elliot.dateText: About 215 to 190 million years ago (Late Triassic to Early Jurassic)
event:elliot.placeText: Free State and Eastern Cape, South Africa, and Lesotho
summary: Red river plains in southern Pangaea that span the end-Triassic extinction and became drier over time. They record early dinosaurs, early mammals and their relatives.
At Golden Gate Highlands National Park, nesting grounds of Massospondylus with clutches of eggs, some with embryos, are among the oldest dinosaur nesting sites known.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Golden Gate Highlands, South Africa, and Lesotho

points.label: Elliot
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 200 million years ago

event:dashanpu.title: Lower Shaximiao Formation (Dashanpu)
event:dashanpu.dateText: About 170 to 165 million years ago (Middle Jurassic)
summary: Lakes and river plains in the Sichuan Basin. The Dashanpu quarry, found in the 1970s during building work for a gas field, yielded thousands of bones, and the Zigong Dinosaur Museum now stands over it.
It holds one of the best Middle Jurassic dinosaur faunas: the club-tailed sauropod Shunosaurus, the long-necked Omeisaurus, the early stegosaur Huayangosaurus and the predator Gasosaurus.

points.label: Dashanpu
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 168 million years ago

event:white-river.title: White River Group (Big Badlands)
event:white-river.dateText: About 34 to 30 million years ago (Late Eocene to Early Oligocene)
event:white-river.placeText: Badlands National Park, South Dakota, and Nebraska, USA
summary: Floodplains and wooded river valleys of the Great Plains as the world cooled and dried at the end of the Eocene, changing forests into more open woodland.

Fossils from these badlands, sent east from the 1840s and described by Joseph Leidy, were among the first fossil mammals studied in North America. Oreodonts, early horses, rhinos, camels, sabre-toothed nimravids, hyaenodonts and the last giant brontotheres lived here.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Volcanic-ash-rich mudstone and siltstone (Chadron and Brule Formations)

points.label: White River
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 32 million years ago

groupNotes.title: Rodents
groupNotes.text: Beavers, squirrel relatives and other early rodents were common.

event:jebel-qatrani.title: Jebel Qatrani Formation (Fayum)
event:jebel-qatrani.dateText: About 34 to 29.5 million years ago (Late Eocene to Early Oligocene)
summary: Tropical river forests and swamps near the shore of the Tethys, in what is now Egyptian desert, with fossil tree trunks still lying in the sand.
It is the best record of Africa’s mammals before Africa joined Eurasia, including early relatives of monkeys and apes, early elephants and the horned Arsinoitherium.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: North of Lake Qarun, Fayum, Egypt

points.label: Fayum
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 31 million years ago

event:sirius-passet.title: Sirius Passet
summary: A muddy sea floor at the edge of a deeper basin, now one of the most remote fossil sites on Earth, reached only by short summer expeditions. It is about the same age as Chengjiang.
It preserves soft-bodied animals from the first burst of the Cambrian explosion, including armoured slug-like animals, early arthropod relatives and giant predatory worms.

points.label: Sirius Passet
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 518 million years ago

event:emu-bay.title: Emu Bay Shale
summary: A shallow sea floor beside an active fault scarp. It is famous for exceptionally preserved eyes and guts of early arthropods.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Emu Bay, Kangaroo Island, South Australia

points.label: Emu Bay
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 514 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Anomalocaris eyes
invertebrates.text: Isolated compound eyes described in 2011, each with more than 16,000 lenses, are thought to belong to Anomalocaris. They show this early top predator had eyesight as sharp as many living insects.

invertebrates.title: Other arthropods
invertebrates.text: Isoxys and other small swimming arthropods.

event:wheeler-shale.title: Wheeler Shale
summary: A deep, quiet sea floor at the edge of the North American continent. Commercial quarries here produce more trilobites than anywhere else, and rarer layers hold soft-bodied animals like those of the Burgess Shale.

points.label: Wheeler
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 507 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Radiodonts
invertebrates.text: Radiodonts, relatives of Anomalocaris, including filter-feeding and sediment-sifting kinds, are known from their frontal appendages and occasional whole bodies.

event:fezouata.title: Fezouata Biota
event:fezouata.dateText: About 480 to 477 million years ago (Early Ordovician)
summary: Muddy sea floors in a cold, high-latitude sea near the South Pole, now in the Anti-Atlas of Morocco. Found by a local collector, they showed that many Burgess Shale-type animals survived into the Ordovician alongside newer groups.

points.label: Fezouata
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 478 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Marrellomorphs and early horseshoe crab relatives
invertebrates.text: Large marrellomorphs with long, swept-back spines, relatives of the Burgess Shale lace crab, and early relatives of horseshoe crabs.

event:anzaldo.title: Anzaldo Formation
event:anzaldo.dateText: About 465 to 455 million years ago (Middle to Late Ordovician)
summary: A shallow sea near the coast of Gondwana where early jawless fish were buried in large numbers, among the oldest well-preserved vertebrates.

points.label: Anzaldo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 460 million years ago

event:beechers.title: Beecher’s Trilobite Bed
summary: A thin layer of dark shale in the Frankfort Shale where trilobites were replaced by the mineral pyrite (fool’s gold), preserving their legs and antennae. Charles Beecher studied them in the 1890s.

points.label: Beecher’s Bed
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 450 million years ago

event:herefordshire.title: Herefordshire Lagerstätte
summary: Small sea-floor animals buried by volcanic ash and preserved in three dimensions inside hard nodules. They are studied by grinding a nodule away a fraction of a millimetre at a time, photographing each layer and rebuilding the animal on a computer.

points.label: Herefordshire
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 430 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Molluscs, worms and starfish relatives
invertebrates.text: Molluscs, worms, sponges and starfish relatives, all a few millimetres to centimetres long.

event:bertie.title: Bertie Group (Bertie Waterlime)
event:bertie.placeText: Western New York, USA, and Ontario, Canada
summary: A salty, shallow lagoon where sea scorpions gathered and died in huge numbers, perhaps when they came to moult or mate.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Near Buffalo, New York, and southern Ontario

points.label: Bertie
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 420 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Other arthropods
invertebrates.text: Small crustaceans and horseshoe crab relatives.

event:rhynie.title: Rhynie Chert
summary: Hot springs, like those of Yellowstone, flooded a marshy landscape with silica-rich water that turned plants and small animals into stone in fine detail. It is the best record of one of the first ecosystems on land.
The plants are tiny and simple, without leaves or roots, and the animals are all arthropods: mites, springtails, spider relatives, harvestmen and centipedes.

points.label: Rhynie
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 407 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Trigonotarbids and mites
invertebrates.text: Trigonotarbids (extinct spider relatives), mites and small freshwater crustaceans.

event:hunsruck.title: Hunsrück Slate
event:hunsruck.dateText: About 407 to 400 million years ago (Early Devonian)
summary: Roofing slate mined since the Middle Ages, in which sea animals were replaced by pyrite. X-ray images reveal soft tissues inside the slabs, and the slate quarries have yielded thousands of starfish and brittle stars.

points.label: Hunsrück
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 405 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Starfish and brittle stars
invertebrates.text: Many kinds of starfish and brittle stars, often preserved whole.

invertebrates.title: Crinoids and arthropods
invertebrates.text: Sea lilies (crinoids), trilobites and other arthropods.

event:achanarras.title: Achanarras Fish Bed
summary: The bottom of Lake Orcadie, a huge lake in the Old Red Sandstone continent. Repeated mass deaths of fish, perhaps when the water stagnated, left layers full of complete fish.
The Scottish stonemason and writer Hugh Miller described many of these fish in the 19th century in “The Old Red Sandstone”.

points.label: Achanarras
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 390 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Small crustaceans
invertebrates.text: Small crustaceans; invertebrates are rare in these lake beds.

event:barun-goyot.title: Barun Goyot Formation
event:barun-goyot.dateText: About 72 to 71 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, early Maastrichtian; dating debated)
event:barun-goyot.placeText: Khulsan and Hermiin Tsav, Ömnögovi, Mongolia
summary: Sand dunes and dry plains with seasonal lakes, between the dune fields of the Djadochta and the wetter river plains of the Nemegt. Polish–Mongolian expeditions of the 1960s and 70s worked it from Khulsan, its type locality.
The small horned dinosaur Bagaceratops is the commonest fossil, alongside ankylosaurs, oviraptorids, pachycephalosaurs, lizards and many small mammals.

points.label: Barun Goyot
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 72 million years ago

event:kachin.title: Kachin amber (Burmese amber)
event:kachin.dateText: About 99 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, earliest Cenomanian)
summary: Resin from coastal tropical forests, now amber, that trapped thousands of kinds of insects, spiders, plants and even small vertebrates, including feathered dinosaur tails, birds and frogs. It records the time when flowering plants were spreading and insects that visit flowers were evolving with them.

The amber comes from mines in a conflict zone. Because mining profits may fund armed groups, the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology called in 2020 and 2021 for a halt to publishing fossils from it, especially material obtained after 2017. Other researchers disagree with a blanket ban, so this remains debated.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 99 million years ago (dated from volcanic ash in the amber beds)

facts.label: Ethics
facts.value: Publication moratorium called for by the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology (2020, 2021)

points.label: Kachin amber
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 99 million years ago

event:raritan.title: Raritan amber (New Jersey)
event:raritan.dateText: About 94 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Turonian)
event:raritan.placeText: Cliffwood and Sayreville, New Jersey, USA
summary: Amber from conifer forests on the Atlantic coastal plain, found in clay pits and seaside cliffs. It contains some of the earliest ants, early flower-visiting insects and tiny flowers themselves.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Middlesex and Monmouth counties, New Jersey

points.label: Raritan amber
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 92 million years ago

event:kinkora.title: Kinkora amber (New Jersey)
event:kinkora.dateText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
event:kinkora.placeText: Kinkora, Burlington County, New Jersey, USA
summary: A small amount of amber collected near Kinkora in the 1920s or 1930s from Maastrichtian sediments, best known for a single stingless bee. Its exact source bed is not known, and its Cretaceous age was once doubted but later supported.

points.label: Kinkora amber
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 68 million years ago

event:nanaimo.title: Nanaimo Group
event:nanaimo.dateText: About 86 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian to Campanian)
event:nanaimo.placeText: Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada
summary: Sea-floor and coastal deposits of the North Pacific, rich in ammonites, crabs, clams and marine reptiles. Large fossil octopus jaws from here and from Hokkaido, Japan, have been used to estimate the sizes of giant Cretaceous octopuses.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: East coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia

points.label: Nanaimo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 80 million years ago

event:zachelmie.title: Zachełmie tetrapod trackways
event:zachelmie.dateText: About 395 million years ago (Middle Devonian, Eifelian)
event:zachelmie.placeText: Zachełmie quarry, Holy Cross Mountains, Poland
summary: Footprints and trackways of four-legged animals on what was a tidal flat or lagoon shore, some from animals perhaps up to 2.5–3 m long.

Described in 2010, they are about 18 million years older than the oldest tetrapod skeletons and older than fish-like relatives such as Tiktaalik. They suggest the first tetrapods evolved earlier than their bones show, and lived alongside those relatives for millions of years.

facts.label: Found
facts.value: Described by Grzegorz Niedźwiedzki and colleagues, 2010

points.label: Zachełmie
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 395 million years ago

event:plagne.title: Plagne sauropod trackway
event:plagne.dateText: About 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Tithonian)
summary: A trail of giant sauropod footprints on what was a tidal flat, found by two amateur naturalists in 2009. Prints are up to about 1.2–1.5 m across, and the trackway runs for about 155 m, one of the longest sauropod trackways known.

points.label: Plagne
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 150 million years ago

event:walmadany.title: Walmadany dinosaur tracks
event:walmadany.dateText: About 140 to 127 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
event:walmadany.placeText: Dampier Peninsula, near Broome, Western Australia
summary: Thousands of footprints along about 25 km of coastline, made by at least 21 kinds of dinosaur, among the most varied dinosaur track sites in the world. One sauropod print is about 1.7 m long, the largest dinosaur footprint known.

The tracks are part of a song cycle of the Goolarabooloo people, telling of the journey of an ancestral being, Marala. Their scientific study in 2017 followed a campaign that helped stop a gas plant being built on the site.

facts.label: Trackmakers
facts.value: Sauropods, theropods, ornithopods and armoured dinosaurs; species unknown

points.label: Walmadany
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 133 million years ago

event:paluxy.title: Paluxy River tracks (Dinosaur Valley State Park)
event:paluxy.dateText: About 113 to 110 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: Sauropod and theropod footprints in limestone of the Paluxy River bed, on what was a muddy coastal plain. In the 1930s Roland T. Bird excavated a famous stretch where a large theropod’s tracks run alongside those of a herd of sauropods; whether it was following them is debated.

From the 1930s some claimed that giant human footprints lay beside the dinosaur tracks. They turned out to be elongated dinosaur prints, erosion marks and carvings, and even most creationists abandoned the claim after studies in the 1970s and 80s.

facts.label: “Man tracks”
facts.value: Debunked: dinosaur tracks, erosion and carvings

points.label: Paluxy
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 112 million years ago

trackmakers.note: The large three-toed tracks match the size and age of Acrocanthosaurus, the only big theropod known from these rocks.
The sauropod tracks have been linked to Sauroposeidon, but no bones are found with them.

event:lark-quarry.title: Lark Quarry dinosaur trackways
event:lark-quarry.dateText: About 95 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: More than 3,000 footprints of small two-legged dinosaurs, now under a protective building. They were long described as a stampede of small dinosaurs fleeing a large predator. A 2013 restudy argued that many were made by small plant-eaters swimming or wading across a river over days or weeks, and that the big “predator” tracks may belong to a large plant-eater. The original researchers disagree.

facts.label: Trackmakers
facts.value: Small ornithopods and perhaps theropods; the large tracks are debated

points.label: Lark Quarry
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 95 million years ago

event:cal-orcko.title: Cal Orck’o
event:cal-orcko.dateText: About 68 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: A limestone wall in a cement quarry, tilted almost upright by the rise of the Andes, covered in thousands of dinosaur footprints made on the muddy shore of a lake or lagoon. Titanosaurs, theropods and armoured dinosaurs crossed it near the end of the Cretaceous.

facts.label: Trackmakers
facts.value: Titanosaurs, theropods and ankylosaurs; species unknown

points.label: Cal Orck’o
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 68 million years ago

event:laetoli.title: Laetoli footprints
summary: Footprints pressed into wet volcanic ash, then hardened and buried, including a trail of at least two or three hominins walking upright with a human-like stride. They were found by Mary Leakey’s team in 1976–78, along with tracks of many other animals.
They show that upright walking evolved long before large brains. A 2021 study argued that a second set of prints at another part of the site was made by a different, unknown hominin.

points.label: Laetoli
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 3.66 million years ago

trackmakers.note: The only hominin known from Laetoli at that time; its fossils are found in the same beds.

event:happisburgh.title: Happisburgh footprints
summary: About 150 footprints, a dozen clearly preserved, of a small group of adults and children on an estuary mudflat, exposed by waves on the beach in May 2013 and recorded in photographs before the sea washed them away within two weeks. They are the oldest known human footprints outside Africa.

facts.label: Trackmaker
facts.value: Probably Homo antecessor, though no bones have been found at the site

facts.label: Today
facts.value: Destroyed by the sea in 2013; known from photographs and 3D models

points.label: Happisburgh
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 900,000 years ago

event:white-sands.title: White Sands footprints
event:white-sands.placeText: White Sands National Park, New Mexico, USA
summary: Thousands of footprints on the shore of an ancient lake, made by people, many of them children and teenagers, along with mammoths, giant ground sloths, camels and wolf-like canids. Some trackways seem to show people and sloths interacting.

Dated in 2021 from seeds and confirmed in 2023 with pollen and quartz, they show that people were in North America during the height of the last Ice Age, thousands of years earlier than long thought. Some researchers still question the dates.

facts.label: Dating
facts.value: Seeds (2021), confirmed by conifer pollen and quartz (2023)

points.label: White Sands
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 22,000 years ago

trackmakers.note: Modern humans, the oldest firm evidence of people in the Americas if the dates hold.

event:valentia.title: Valentia Island tetrapod trackway
event:valentia.dateText: About 385 million years ago (late Middle Devonian)
summary: A trail of about 150 prints left by a four-legged animal crossing a river floodplain, found in 1992 by geology student Iwan Stössel. It is one of the oldest records of vertebrates walking.

The age comes from a dated volcanic ash in the same rocks. A few researchers have questioned whether every mark was made by a tetrapod rather than a fish or by water, but most accept it as a tetrapod trackway.

points.label: Valentia
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 385 million years ago

event:manakacha.title: Grand Canyon Manakacha trackway
event:manakacha.placeText: Bright Angel Trail, Grand Canyon, Arizona, USA
summary: Two trails of footprints on a boulder that fell beside the Bright Angel Trail, spotted by geologist Allan Krill in 2016 and described in 2020. They are the oldest vertebrate tracks known from the Grand Canyon.

The prints show a lateral-sequence walk, with legs on one side moving one after the other, as in living dogs and cats. The maker was an early reptile-like amniote or synapsid. Younger rocks in the canyon, such as the Coconino Sandstone, hold many Permian trackways.

facts.label: Found
facts.value: Allan Krill, 2016; described by Stephen Rowland and colleagues, 2020

points.label: Manakacha
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 313 million years ago

event:bromacker.title: Bromacker trackways
summary: A quarry where both footprints and skeletons of the same upland animals are found, which lets scientists match tracks to their makers, something rarely possible.

A 2015 study used the skeleton of the diadectid Orobates to show that one kind of track, Ichniotherium sphaerodactylum, matches its feet; another, Ichniotherium cottae, matches the related Diadectes found here.

facts.label: Trackmakers
facts.value: Diadectids such as Orobates and Diadectes absitus, early reptiles and synapsids

points.label: Bromacker
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 290 million years ago

event:robledo.title: Prehistoric Trackways National Monument
event:robledo.dateText: About 285 to 280 million years ago (Early Permian)
event:robledo.placeText: Robledo Mountains, near Las Cruces, New Mexico, USA
summary: Thousands of tracks of amphibians, reptiles, synapsids and insects on a tidal flat, from long before the dinosaurs. Amateur palaeontologist Jerry MacDonald found and collected many of them from 1987, and the area became a national monument in 2009.

points.label: Robledo Mountains
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 283 million years ago

trackmakers.note: The track type Dimetropus is thought to have been made by sphenacodont synapsids like Dimetrodon, which lived in the region; the exact species is unknown.

event:hildburghausen.title: Chirotherium tracks of Hildburghausen
event:hildburghausen.dateText: About 247 to 243 million years ago (Early to Middle Triassic)
summary: Hand-shaped prints found in sandstone quarries in 1833, described in 1834 and named Chirotherium (“hand beast”) in 1835. Early guesses for the maker included a bear, an ape or a giant marsupial; Richard Owen later suggested a giant amphibian.

The puzzle lasted more than a century. In 1965 Bernard Krebs showed that the feet of the Triassic archosaur Ticinosuchus fit the prints, and similar reptiles such as Arizonasaurus are also candidates. The outer “thumb” is actually the fifth toe.

facts.label: Found
facts.value: 1833; named Chirotherium by Johann Kaup in 1835

points.label: Hildburghausen
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 245 million years ago

trackmakers.note: Its feet match the prints closely, but it lived a little later and farther south; a close relative probably made them.

event:rocky-hill.title: Dinosaur State Park tracks
summary: About 2,000 footprints uncovered in 1966 by bulldozer operator Edward McCarthy while digging for a state building. About 500 are now under a dome, one of the largest dinosaur track displays in North America.
The tracks are Eubrontes, three-toed prints of a large theropod walking along a lake in a rift valley that formed as Pangaea split. Eubrontes is Connecticut’s state fossil.

points.label: Rocky Hill
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 200 million years ago

trackmakers.note: Eubrontes tracks are often linked to a Dilophosaurus-sized theropod, but no bones are found with them and Dilophosaurus itself is known only from Arizona.

event:st-george.title: St. George Dinosaur Discovery Site
event:st-george.placeText: Johnson Farm, St. George, Utah, USA
summary: Found in 2000 by Sheldon Johnson while levelling land, on the shore of an ancient lake. Besides walking tracks there are rare swim traces, where dinosaurs scraped the bottom with their claws, and marks of resting theropods.

points.label: St. George
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 199 million years ago

trackmakers.note: The large theropod tracks fit an animal like Dilophosaurus, known from slightly younger rocks nearby.

event:pedreira-galinha.title: Pedreira do Galinha sauropod trackways
event:pedreira-galinha.placeText: Serra de Aire, near Fátima, Portugal
summary: Sauropod trackways in an old limestone quarry, now a natural monument. Two trails run for about 142 and 147 m, among the longest sauropod trackways known, and show clear hand and foot prints of a type named Polyonyx gomesi.

points.label: Galinha
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 175 million years ago

event:skye-tracks.title: Isle of Skye dinosaur tracks
event:skye-tracks.placeText: Brothers’ Point, Isle of Skye, Scotland
summary: Tracks of sauropods, theropods and ornithopods on what was a shallow lagoon shore, from a time with few dinosaur bones anywhere in the world. A 2020 study reported Deltapodus, a track type thought to be made by stegosaurs.

facts.label: Trackmakers
facts.value: Sauropods, theropods, ornithopods and probably stegosaurs; species unknown

points.label: Skye
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 170 million years ago

event:dewars-farm.title: Dewars Farm Quarry trackways (“Dinosaur Highway”)
event:dewars-farm.dateText: About 166 million years ago (Middle Jurassic, Bathonian)
summary: Hundreds of footprints on what was a shallow tropical lagoon shore, uncovered in a working limestone quarry after worker Gary Johnson noticed odd bumps in the clay. A first dig in 2024, announced in January 2025, exposed five trackways, the longest more than 150 m: four of sauropods and one of a large theropod whose path crosses theirs.

A second dig in summer 2025, announced in October 2025 by the Oxford University Museum of Natural History and the University of Birmingham, followed one sauropod trail for about 220 m from first to last exposed print, nearly 100 footprints each close to a metre long. It is the longest sauropod trackway known in Europe, longer than Plagne in France (about 155 m), and may be the longest known anywhere. It may extend further still under unquarried rock.

facts.label: Found
facts.value: Gary Johnson, quarry worker; dug 2024 and 2025

points.label: Dewars Farm
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 166 million years ago

trackmakers.note: The researchers think the sauropod tracks were made by Cetiosaurus, the sauropod known from bones of the same age in Oxfordshire. No bones were found with the tracks, and some palaeontologists think naming the maker goes too far.
The only large theropod known from rocks of this age in the region; Megalosaurus was first named from nearby Stonesfield.

event:purgatoire.title: Purgatoire River tracksite
summary: More than 1,300 footprints on the shore of an ancient lake, the largest dinosaur track site in North America. Several sauropod trackways run side by side in the same direction, one of the first pieces of evidence that sauropods moved in groups.

points.label: Purgatoire
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 150 million years ago

trackmakers.note: The large theropod tracks fit Allosaurus, the most common big predator in the Morrison Formation.

event:courtedoux.title: Courtedoux tracksites
summary: Thousands of footprints in more than 280 trackways, found from 2002 during construction of the A16 motorway and recorded before the road was built. Sauropods and theropods walked across tidal flats on islands in a shallow tropical sea.

points.label: Courtedoux
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 152 million years ago

event:crayssac.title: Crayssac pterosaur tracks (“Pterosaur Beach”)
event:crayssac.dateText: About 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic, early Tithonian)
summary: A lagoon shore crossed by pterosaurs, crocodile relatives, turtles and small dinosaurs. A 2009 study described a trackway showing a pterosaur landing: two foot drags as it touched down, a hop, then the hands coming down as it walked off on all fours.

points.label: Crayssac
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 150 million years ago

event:munchehagen.title: Münchehagen tracksite
event:munchehagen.dateText: About 140 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Berriasian)
summary: Sauropod and ornithopod trackways in sandstone of a coastal plain, protected under a hall at the Dinosaurier-Park Münchehagen. Some sauropod trails are among the best preserved in Europe.

facts.label: Trackmakers
facts.value: Sauropods, iguanodontians and theropods; species unknown

points.label: Münchehagen
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 140 million years ago

event:sousa.title: Valley of the Dinosaurs, Sousa
event:sousa.dateText: About 140 to 125 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: Footprints of theropods, sauropods and ornithopods in the Rio do Peixe basin, a rift valley that formed as South America and Africa pulled apart. Tracks have been known here since the 1920s, and dozens of sites are now recorded, the richest in Brazil.

facts.label: Trackmakers
facts.value: Theropods, sauropods and ornithopods; species unknown

points.label: Sousa
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 133 million years ago

event:peace-river.title: Peace River Canyon tracks
event:peace-river.placeText: Near Hudson’s Hope, British Columbia, Canada
summary: Charles M. Sternberg recorded dinosaur tracks here in 1930, the first studied in western Canada. Ornithopods, theropods and armoured dinosaurs walked across coastal swamps that later became coal.
Many tracks were cast or removed before most of the canyon was flooded by a dam reservoir. Others have since been found near Tumbler Ridge.

points.label: Peace River
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 115 million years ago

event:dinosaur-ridge.title: Dinosaur Ridge tracks
event:dinosaur-ridge.dateText: About 100 million years ago (Early to Late Cretaceous)
summary: Hundreds of footprints exposed in 1937 when a road was cut across the ridge, made on the muddy shore of the advancing Western Interior Seaway. Most are of iguanodont-like ornithopods, with theropod tracks and crocodile traces too.

points.label: Dinosaur Ridge
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 100 million years ago

event:el-chocon-tracks.title: Villa El Chocón tracks
event:el-chocon-tracks.dateText: About 97 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
event:el-chocon-tracks.placeText: Shore of Lake Ezequiel Ramos Mexía, Neuquén, Argentina
summary: Large three-toed theropod prints and sauropod tracks on the lakeshore near the town where Giganotosaurus was found, exposed when the reservoir level drops.

points.label: El Chocón tracks
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 97 million years ago

trackmakers.note: Big theropod tracks in the same formation as Giganotosaurus; the match is size and age only.

event:uhangri.title: Uhangri pterosaur and dinosaur tracks
event:uhangri.dateText: About 81 to 79 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: Lake-shore tracks of dinosaurs, birds and pterosaurs. The pterosaur prints, named Haenamichnus in 2002, are the largest known, and one trail about 7.3 m long was the longest pterosaur trackway known when described. They were probably made by a giant azhdarchid.

points.label: Uhangri
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 80 million years ago

event:denali-tracks.title: Denali dinosaur tracks
summary: Thousands of tracks found since 2005 in a park with almost no dinosaur bones, from a polar forest with dark winters. Hadrosaurs of all ages left prints, from young to adult, suggesting herds; there are also theropod, therizinosaur, bird and pterosaur tracks.

points.label: Denali
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 70 million years ago

event:fumanya.title: Fumanya titanosaur tracks
event:fumanya.dateText: About 67 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: Nearly 3,000 footprints in more than 50 trackways, exposed on the steep walls of old coal mines in the Pyrenees. They are the largest Late Cretaceous sauropod track site in Europe, left by wide-gauge titanosaurs crossing a coastal mudflat shortly before the end of the age of dinosaurs.

points.label: Fumanya
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 67 million years ago

event:trachilos.title: Trachilos footprints
event:trachilos.dateText: Disputed: about 6 million years ago (latest Miocene), or perhaps much younger
summary: Prints on an old beach surface that the 2017 describers said show a human-like foot, with a big toe in line with the others. If so, a hominin-like animal walked in Europe more than 5.6 million years ago.

Every part of this is disputed: some researchers say the rocks are about 3 million years old, and others that the marks are not footprints at all, or were made by another animal. It is listed here with that caveat.

facts.label: Laid
facts.value: About 6.05 million years ago (2021 estimate); others argue about 3 million

points.label: Trachilos
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 6.05 million years ago

event:ileret.title: Ileret footprints
event:ileret.dateText: About 1.53 to 1.51 million years ago (Early Pleistocene)
event:ileret.placeText: Ileret, east of Lake Turkana, Kenya
summary: Hominin footprints in two layers of lake-side sediment, described in 2009. They show an essentially modern foot, with an arch, a big toe in line and a modern stride, and later finds at the site show groups walking together.

A 2024 study found a second kind of footprint on the same surface, with a more ape-like, splayed big toe, probably made by Paranthropus boisei. The two species crossed the same lakeshore within hours or days of each other, the first direct evidence of two hominin species sharing ground.

facts.label: Trackmakers
facts.value: Probably Homo erectus (also called Homo ergaster) and Paranthropus boisei

points.label: Ileret
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 1.52 million years ago

trackmakers.note: The modern-looking footprints, from their size, shape and age.
A second footprint type, described in 2024, probably made by Paranthropus boisei alongside Homo erectus.

event:matalascanas.title: Matalascañas footprints
summary: Human footprints exposed by storms on a beach near Doñana. First dated to about 106,000 years, they were redated in 2022 to about 296,000 years, so the makers were early members of the Neanderthal lineage rather than classic Neanderthals.

points.label: Matalascañas
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 296,000 years ago

trackmakers.note: At this age the makers belonged to the Neanderthal lineage, but may predate Neanderthals as usually defined.

event:langebaan.title: Langebaan footprints (“Eve’s footprints”)
event:langebaan.placeText: Langebaan Lagoon, Western Cape, South Africa
summary: Three footprints of a modern human walking down a wet dune, found in 1995 by David Roberts and described with Lee Berger in 1997. They were among the oldest known footprints of our species. The “Eve” nickname is popular, not scientific: there is no way to tell the walker’s sex.

facts.label: Today
facts.value: Removed to the Iziko South African Museum, Cape Town

points.label: Langebaan
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 117,000 years ago

trackmakers.note: A modern human; the foot shape and age leave no other candidate in southern Africa.

event:le-rozel.title: Le Rozel footprints
summary: Some 257 footprints in coastal dune sand, excavated from 2012 and published in 2019, along with stone tools. Most were made by children and teenagers, giving a rare look at the make-up of a Neanderthal group.

facts.label: Prints
facts.value: 257, the largest Neanderthal footprint collection known

points.label: Le Rozel
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 80,000 years ago

trackmakers.note: Neanderthals were the only humans in western Europe at this time, and their tools are found in the same layers.

event:willandra.title: Willandra Lakes footprints
event:willandra.placeText: Mungo National Park, New South Wales, Australia
summary: More than 700 footprints of men, women and children, the largest set of Ice Age human footprints known when found. Mary Pappin Jr., a Mutthi Mutthi woman, spotted them in 2003. One trail appears to show a person running fast, and one a one-legged man walking with a stick.

points.label: Willandra
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 21,000 years ago

trackmakers.note: Aboriginal Australians, ancestors of the people of the Willandra Lakes today.

event:engare-sero.title: Engare Sero footprints
event:engare-sero.dateText: Between about 19,000 and 6,000 years ago (most likely 12,000 to 10,000)
summary: More than 400 human footprints in volcanic mudflow from the nearby volcano Ol Doinyo Lengai, the largest collection of human footprints in Africa. A 2020 study suggested one group was mostly women walking together, with a few men and children passing.

points.label: Engare Sero
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 11,000 years ago

trackmakers.note: Modern humans.

event:pehuen-co.title: Pehuen-Có megafauna tracks
summary: Footprints of giant ground sloths, Macrauchenia, mastodon-like gomphotheres, giant armadillo relatives, camelids and birds on an old mudflat, exposed on a beach after a storm in 1986 and found by Teresa Manera. Eleven kinds of mammal track and four of birds are recorded. The site is now a provincial reserve.

facts.label: Laid
facts.value: About 12,000 radiocarbon years ago (roughly 14,000 calendar years)

points.label: Pehuen-Có
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 14,000 years ago

trackmakers.note: The largest sloth tracks match Megatherium, the giant ground sloth of the Pampas.
Three-toed tracks named Macrauchenichnus match the feet of Macrauchenia.

event:formby.title: Formby Point footprints
event:formby.dateText: About 8,000 to 4,500 years ago (Mesolithic to Neolithic)
summary: Footprints of people, red and roe deer, aurochs and cranes in mud layers that wash out of the beach and are destroyed by the next tides. Local teacher Gordon Roberts recorded thousands of them over more than 25 years.

points.label: Formby
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 7,000 years ago

trackmakers.note: Mesolithic and Neolithic people, including children, perhaps hunting and gathering on the mudflats.
Large cloven-hoofed prints match the extinct wild ox.

event:acahualinca.title: Footprints of Acahualinca
summary: Footprints of 15 or 16 people walking towards Lake Managua across fresh volcanic ash, found in the 1870s and now in a site museum. Early estimates put them at 5,000 years or more; dating of the ash from an eruption of Masaya places them at about 2,100 years. Animal tracks cross the human ones at a different time.

points.label: Acahualinca
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 2,000 years ago

trackmakers.note: Ancient Nicaraguans.

event:bayan-shireh.title: Bayan Shireh Formation
event:bayan-shireh.dateText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian–Turonian; dating debated)
event:bayan-shireh.placeText: Bayan Shireh, Burkhant and nearby, Dornogovi, Mongolia
summary: River and lake deposits in the eastern Gobi, laid down when the region was wetter than the later dune fields of the Djadochta.
It is the home of the therizinosaurs Segnosaurus and Erlikosaurus, the ostrich dinosaur Garudimimus, the ankylosaur Talarurus and the large dromaeosaur Achillobator.

points.label: Bayan Shireh
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 92 million years ago

event:judith-river.title: Judith River Formation
event:judith-river.dateText: About 79 to 75 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Campanian)
summary: Rivers and swamps on a coastal plain beside the Western Interior Seaway. In 1855 Ferdinand Hayden collected teeth here that Joseph Leidy named in 1856, among the first dinosaurs described from North America, including Troodon, Trachodon and Deinodon.
Later finds include the duck-billed Brachylophosaurus, horned dinosaurs such as Medusaceratops and Avaceratops, crocodylians, turtles and early mammals.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Missouri River Breaks and nearby, Montana

points.label: Judith River
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 77 million years ago

event:katiki.title: Katiki Formation
event:katiki.dateText: About 70 to 69 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
event:katiki.placeText: Shag Point, coastal Otago, New Zealand
summary: Grey siltstone laid down in a cold, high-latitude sea off the newly separated landmass of Zealandia. It holds plesiosaurs, including the nearly complete Kaiwhekea, as well as concretions with other marine reptile bones.

points.label: Katiki
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 70 million years ago

event:cachoeira-bom-jardim.title: Cachoeira do Bom Jardim Formation
event:cachoeira-bom-jardim.dateText: About 70 million years ago (Late Cretaceous; poorly dated)
summary: Red conglomeratic sandstones of the Bauru Group in central Brazil, laid down by rivers. Its fossils are scarce and the rocks are hard to date closely. The large abelisaurid Pycnonemosaurus comes from here.

points.label: Cachoeira do Bom Jardim
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 70 million years ago

event:lufeng.title: Lufeng Formation
event:lufeng.dateText: About 200 to 190 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Hettangian–Sinemurian)
summary: Purple and dark red mudstones and siltstones from rivers and lakes in a warm, seasonally dry basin in southwestern China. Since Yang Zhongjian (C. C. Young) began digging here in 1938, it has become one of the richest early dinosaur sites in Asia.

Its fossils include the long-necked plant-eaters Lufengosaurus and Yunnanosaurus, the crested predator Sinosaurus, and some of the closest relatives of mammals: the tiny Hadrocodium, the tritylodontids and Sinoconodon. In 2017 collagen proteins were found preserved inside a Lufengosaurus rib, among the oldest such traces known.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Purple and red mudstone and siltstone

points.label: Lufeng
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 195 million years ago

event:santa-maria.title: Santa Maria Formation
event:santa-maria.dateText: About 240 to 228 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
event:santa-maria.placeText: Around Santa Maria, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: Red mudstones from river floodplains and lakes in southern Brazil, in what was then the heart of Pangaea. Its lower layers are full of big plant-eating dicynodonts and the giant predator Prestosuchus; its upper layers, about 233 million years old, hold some of the oldest dinosaurs known.

Those dinosaurs include the predatory herrerasaurs Staurikosaurus and Gnathovorax and the small, early sauropodomorphs Buriolestes and Saturnalia. They lived among far more common rhynchosaurs, cynodonts and crocodile-line reptiles.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Around Santa Maria and Candelária, Rio Grande do Sul

points.label: Santa Maria
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 233 million years ago

event:caturrita.title: Caturrita Formation
event:caturrita.dateText: About 225 million years ago (Late Triassic, early Norian)
event:caturrita.placeText: Agudo and Faxinal do Soturno, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
summary: River sands and silts that lie above the Santa Maria Formation, a little younger. Its dinosaurs are early long-necked plant-eaters such as Unaysaurus and Macrocollum, alongside the silesaurid Sacisaurus.
It is also famous for tiny, shrew-sized cynodonts such as Brasilodon, among the closest relatives of mammals of their time.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Agudo and Faxinal do Soturno, Rio Grande do Sul

points.label: Caturrita
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 225 million years ago

event:los-colorados.title: Los Colorados Formation
event:los-colorados.dateText: About 220 to 213 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: Red river and lake beds up to 600 m thick that lie on top of the Ischigualasto Formation, in what is now Talampaya National Park. They record the time when dinosaurs were taking over from the crocodile-line reptiles.

José Bonaparte collected many of its fossils in the 1960s and 70s: the large long-necked plant-eaters Riojasaurus and Lessemsaurus, the predator Zupaysaurus, and late “rauisuchians” such as the huge Fasolasuchus.

points.label: Los Colorados
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 216 million years ago

event:canadon-asfalto.title: Cañadón Asfalto Formation
event:canadon-asfalto.dateText: About 179 to 177 million years ago (Early Jurassic, Toarcian)
summary: Lake and river beds with volcanic ash in a rift valley that was opening in Patagonia. It is one of the few places in the world with good dinosaur fossils from the late Early Jurassic.

Its animals include the sauropod Patagosaurus, the predators Piatnitzkysaurus and Condorraptor, early turtles, frogs and some of the earliest southern mammals, including the australosphenidans, distant relatives of the platypus.

facts.label: Rocks

event:karoo-endothiodon.title: Endothiodon and Tropidostoma assemblage zones, Karoo
event:karoo-endothiodon.dateText: About 260 to 257 million years ago (end of the middle Permian to early late Permian)
event:karoo-endothiodon.placeText: Fraserburg and Beaufort West, Western and Northern Cape, South Africa
summary: River and floodplain mudstones of the lower Teekloof Formation, laid down just after the extinction that ended the middle Permian and wiped out the giant dinocephalians. Life recovered with new kinds of dicynodonts, such as the tusked Endothiodon and Tropidostoma, and the first cynodonts, the group that would one day give rise to mammals.

points.label: Karoo (Endothiodon)
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 259 million years ago

event:karoo-daptocephalus.title: Daptocephalus Assemblage Zone, Karoo
event:karoo-daptocephalus.dateText: About 255 to 252 million years ago (latest Permian)
event:karoo-daptocephalus.placeText: Graaff-Reinet and the Lootsberg Pass, Eastern Cape, South Africa
summary: The last layers of Permian life in the Karoo, from the Balfour Formation, formerly called the Dicynodon Assemblage Zone. They record a rich world of dicynodonts, sabre-toothed gorgonopsians and therocephalians just before the end-Permian extinction, the worst mass extinction in Earth’s history.
Most of these animals vanish at its top, replaced by the Lystrosaurus-dominated world of the earliest Triassic.

points.label: Karoo (Daptocephalus)

event:rio-do-rasto.title: Rio do Rasto Formation
event:rio-do-rasto.dateText: About 268 to 255 million years ago (middle to late Permian)
event:rio-do-rasto.placeText: Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil
summary: Red and green mudstones and sandstones from lakes, deltas and rivers that filled the Paraná Basin as an inland sea dried up. It is Brazil’s richest Permian fossil site.
Its animals include the predatory dinocephalian Pampaphoneus, the sabre-toothed plant-eater Tiarajudens, dicynodonts, long-snouted temnospondyl amphibians and freshwater sharks.

facts.label: Where today

event:adamantina.title: Adamantina Formation (Bauru Group)
event:adamantina.dateText: About 85 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous; dating debated)
event:adamantina.placeText: Western São Paulo State and Minas Gerais, Brazil
summary: Red sandstones from rivers and dunes in a hot, semi-arid inland basin. Its most common fossils are notosuchians, land-dwelling crocodile relatives that filled roles taken elsewhere by mammals and small dinosaurs: dog-like predators such as Baurusuchus, and plant-eaters with chewing teeth such as Caipirasuchus.
Titanosaurs, small theropods, frogs, turtles, snakes and early birds lived alongside them. Its age is debated: estimates range from the Santonian to the Maastrichtian.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Western São Paulo State, around Monte Alto and Presidente Prudente

facts.value: Museu de Paleontologia de Monte Alto

event:serra-da-galga.title: Serra da Galga Formation (Bauru Group)
event:serra-da-galga.dateText: About 70 to 66 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian)
summary: River sands and gravels near Uberaba, once part of the Marília Formation. Since the 1940s Llewellyn Ivor Price dug here, and the village of Peirópolis now has a dinosaur museum and research centre.
Its fossils include titanosaurs such as Trigonosaurus, predatory notosuchians like Uberabasuchus, and the first pterosaur from the Bauru Group.

facts.label: Museum
facts.value: Centro de Pesquisas Paleontológicas Llewellyn Ivor Price, Peirópolis

event:bajo-barreal.title: Bajo Barreal Formation
event:bajo-barreal.dateText: About 96 to 89 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian–Turonian)
event:bajo-barreal.placeText: Golfo San Jorge Basin, Chubut, Argentina
summary: River sandstones and volcanic ash in southern Chubut, studied by Rubén Martínez and his team from the Universidad Nacional de la Patagonia. Its dinosaurs include titanosaurs such as Epachthosaurus and Sarmientosaurus, the abelisaurid Xenotarsosaurus and the small ornithopod Notohypsilophodon.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Around Lago Colhué Huapi and Sarmiento, Chubut

event:sarmiento.title: Sarmiento Formation
event:sarmiento.dateText: About 45 to 18 million years ago (middle Eocene to early Miocene)
event:sarmiento.placeText: Gran Barranca and Cabeza Blanca, Chubut, Argentina
summary: Layers of wind-blown volcanic ash, loess and river deposits, exposed at the great cliff of Gran Barranca by Lake Colhué Huapi. They span about 25 million years and record how Patagonia dried out and grasslands spread as the world cooled.

Its fossil mammals, first studied by the Ameghino brothers in the 1890s, define several of South America’s land-mammal ages, including the Deseadan of the late Oligocene: notoungulates, litopterns, the elephant-like Pyrotherium, early rodents and primates, and terror birds.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Gran Barranca, south of Lake Colhué Huapi, Chubut

event:kirtland.title: Kirtland and Fruitland formations
event:kirtland.dateText: About 76 to 73 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
event:kirtland.placeText: Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness, San Juan Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: Coal swamps, river channels and floodplains on the coastal plain west of the Western Interior Seaway, now eroded into the badlands of the Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness. Charles H. Sternberg and others collected here from the 1920s.

Its dinosaurs include the five-horned Pentaceratops and its relatives, the tyrannosaur Bistahieversor, the duck-bill Parasaurolophus cyrtocristatus, kritosaurin hadrosaurs and armoured ankylosaurs. They were part of a southern fauna that was surprisingly different from that of Alberta and Montana at the same time.

points.label: Kirtland

event:cerro-del-pueblo.title: Cerro del Pueblo Formation
event:cerro-del-pueblo.dateText: About 73.5 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, late Campanian)
event:cerro-del-pueblo.placeText: Rincón Colorado and General Cepeda, Coahuila, Mexico
summary: Coastal deltas, lagoons and estuaries on the shore of the Gulf of Mexico, near Saltillo. It is the richest dinosaur site in Mexico.

Its fossils include crested duck-bills such as Velafrons and the trumpet-crested Tlatolophus, the horned Coahuilaceratops, ostrich dinosaurs, troodontids and tyrannosaurs, along with turtles, crocodiles and ammonites from the nearby sea.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Around General Cepeda and Rincón Colorado, Coahuila

points.label: Cerro del Pueblo

event:moreno.title: Moreno Formation
event:moreno.dateText: About 70 to 64 million years ago (latest Cretaceous to earliest Paleocene)
event:moreno.placeText: Panoche Hills, Fresno County, California, USA
summary: Marine shales laid down in the Pacific off the coast of California. Ranchers and University of California teams found many marine reptiles here from the 1930s: the streamlined mosasaur Plotosaurus, elasmosaurs and other plesiosaurs.
A duck-billed dinosaur, Augustynolophus, whose body drifted out to sea, is California’s state dinosaur.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 70 to 66 million years ago (its upper part is Paleocene)

event:greenhorn-carlile.title: Greenhorn Limestone and Carlile Shale
event:greenhorn-carlile.dateText: About 95 to 90 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian–Turonian)
event:greenhorn-carlile.placeText: Kansas, Colorado and the Great Plains, USA
summary: Chalky limestones and shales from the floor of the Western Interior Seaway when it was at its deepest and widest. Its predators were giant pliosaurs, the short-necked plesiosaurs such as Brachauchenius and Megacephalosaurus, along with big sharks and fish.

points.label: Greenhorn–Carlile
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 93 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Ammonites and clams
invertebrates.text: Ammonites such as Collignoniceras and giant flat inoceramid clams, among the commonest fossils of these seas.

event:denver.title: Denver Formation (Corral Bluffs)
event:denver.dateText: About 68 to 64 million years ago (latest Cretaceous to earliest Paleocene)
event:denver.placeText: Corral Bluffs, Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA
summary: River deposits of the Denver Basin that span the asteroid impact. At Corral Bluffs, concretions hold some of the best skulls of mammals from the first million years after the dinosaurs died, together with fossil leaves and pollen, showing how forests and mammals recovered step by step.
Within about 300,000 years of the impact, mammals had grown from rat-sized to as big as a pig, such as Carsioptychus, and within 700,000 years Taeniolabis reached about 30 kg.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 66 to 65 million years ago at Corral Bluffs

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Corral Bluffs, east of Colorado Springs

event:cedar-mountain-middle.title: Cedar Mountain Formation (Poison Strip and Ruby Ranch members)
event:cedar-mountain-middle.dateText: About 125 to 104 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian–Albian)
summary: The middle part of the Cedar Mountain Formation, between the older Yellow Cat Member and the younger Mussentuchit Member: river sands and floodplain muds with ancient soils, laid down as the land was slowly drying.
Its dinosaurs include sauropods such as Venenosaurus, Brontomerus and the brachiosaurid Abydosaurus, whose skulls are some of the few complete sauropod skulls from North America.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Around Moab and Dinosaur National Monument, Utah

event:daohugou.title: Daohugou Beds (Haifanggou Formation)
event:daohugou.dateText: About 166 to 160 million years ago (Middle to Late Jurassic)
event:daohugou.placeText: Daohugou, Ningcheng County, Inner Mongolia, China
summary: Fine lake shales with volcanic ash, part of the Yanliao Biota, slightly older than or the same age as the Tiaojishan Formation. They preserve fur, feathers, wing membranes and insects in exquisite detail.

Its animals include the strange scansoriopterygids, small feathered dinosaurs with long fingers, the otter-like Castorocauda, the gliding mammal Volaticotherium, long-tailed pterosaurs, salamanders and thousands of insects.

points.label: Daohugou
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 164 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Insects
invertebrates.text: Thousands of insects, including scorpionflies, lacewings, mayflies and early fleas, and spiders.

event:xiagou.title: Xiagou Formation and Xinminpu Group
event:xiagou.dateText: About 120 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
event:xiagou.placeText: Changma Basin and Mazongshan, Gansu, China
summary: Lake shales and river beds in the Gansu corridor, west of the Jehol Biota and a little younger. The Changma lake beds hold hundreds of early birds, including the diving Gansus, while nearby river beds at Mazongshan have dinosaurs such as Auroraceratops and the giant ostrich-dinosaur Beishanlong.

event:fengjiahe.title: Fengjiahe Formation
event:fengjiahe.dateText: About 195 to 180 million years ago (Early Jurassic)
summary: Red river and lake beds in central Yunnan, a little younger than or the same age as the Lufeng Formation. Its dinosaurs include long-necked plant-eaters such as Yunnanosaurus and Chinshakiangosaurus, and Yuxisaurus, the first early armoured dinosaur from Asia.

facts.label: Where today

event:tsagayan.dateText: About 67 to 66 million years ago (latest Cretaceous, late Maastrichtian)
event:tsagayan.placeText: Blagoveshchensk, Amur Region, Russia, and Heilongjiang, China
summary: River deposits on both sides of the Amur River, on the Russia–China border, from the last moments before the asteroid impact. Huge bonebeds near Blagoveshchensk are packed with the jumbled bones of duck-billed dinosaurs, such as the crested Amurosaurus and the flat-headed Kerberosaurus.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Blagoveshchensk, Russia, and Jiayin, Heilongjiang, China

event:guanling.title: Guanling Formation (Luoping and Panxian biotas)
event:guanling.dateText: About 245 to 243 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
event:guanling.placeText: Luoping, Yunnan, and Panxian, Guizhou, China
summary: Fine limestones from shallow, oxygen-poor sea basins in southern China, laid down about 8 million years after the end-Permian extinction. They preserve one of the earliest diverse marine ecosystems after the extinction, with thousands of fish, crustaceans and marine reptiles.

Its animals include the long-necked Dinocephalosaurus, which gave birth to live young, the filter-feeding Atopodentatus, early ichthyosaurs, nothosaurs and the sea-going crocodile relative Qianosuchus.

points.label: Guanling
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 244 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Crustaceans and others
invertebrates.text: Shrimp-like decapods, horseshoe crabs, sea lilies, bivalves and ammonoids.

event:xitun.title: Xitun Formation
event:xitun.dateText: About 415 to 410 million years ago (Early Devonian, Lochkovian)
summary: Shallow coastal sea and estuary deposits near Qujing that hold some of the oldest and most important early bony fishes, including early relatives of lungfishes and lobe-finned fishes, along with jawless galeaspids and armoured antiarch placoderms.

event:manda.title: Manda Beds
event:manda.dateText: About 247 to 237 million years ago (Middle Triassic; exact age debated)
summary: River sandstones and mudstones in the Ruhuhu Basin, close to Lake Nyasa (Lake Malawi). They hold some of the oldest relatives of dinosaurs and pterosaurs, including Nyasasaurus, perhaps the earliest dinosaur, and Teleocrater.

Many of its animals were first studied by Alan Charig in his 1956 thesis but were only formally named 50 to 65 years later. They are usually dated to the Anisian, about 245 million years ago, although some researchers think the beds are younger, which matters for how early dinosaurs appeared.

facts.label: Age

event:lossiemouth.title: Lossiemouth Sandstone (Elgin Reptiles)
event:lossiemouth.dateText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, late Carnian)
event:lossiemouth.placeText: Near Elgin and Lossiemouth, Moray, Scotland
summary: Yellow desert sandstone laid down by wind-blown dunes up to about 20 m tall. The bones rotted away long ago, leaving hollow moulds in the rock, so the animals are studied from casts and, today, from CT scans.

The “Elgin Reptiles” have been studied since the 1850s. They include the tiny pterosaur relative Scleromochlus, the dinosaur relative Saltopus, the crocodile-line Ornithosuchus and the procolophonid Leptopleuron.

event:donguz.title: Donguz Formation
event:donguz.dateText: About 245 to 240 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: River deposits along the Donguz and Berdyanka rivers in the southern Urals, also called the Eryosuchus fauna after its most common animal, the big flat-headed amphibian Eryosuchus.
It holds large kannemeyeriid dicynodonts, the erythrosuchid Uralosaurus, the early archosauriform Sarmatosuchus and the dinosaur-line archosaur Dongusuchus.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 243 million years ago (Anisian, perhaps early Ladinian)

event:dockum.placeText: West Texas and eastern New Mexico, USA
summary: Red river and lake rocks of the Texas and New Mexico plains, the eastern twin of the Chinle Formation. Its layers, from the older Tecovas Formation to the younger Bull Canyon, Cooper Canyon and Redonda formations, record about 20 million years of Late Triassic life.
Its animals include phytosaurs, armoured aetosaurs, the beaked, two-legged Shuvosaurus, the early mammal relative Adelobasileus and the controversial “first bird” Protoavis.

facts.value: About 228 to 205 million years ago (Carnian to Rhaetian)

event:popo-agie.dateText: About 232 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: Red and purple river mudstones of the Chugwater Group in central Wyoming. In 2025 it gave the oldest named dinosaur from the northern supercontinent Laurasia, Ahvaytum.
Recent work has been done together with the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho tribes of the Wind River Reservation, and several new animals have names in their languages.

event:lowenstein.title: Löwenstein Formation (Stubensandstein)
event:lowenstein.dateText: About 215 to 210 million years ago (Late Triassic, Norian)
summary: River sandstones of southern Germany, long quarried as “Stubensandstein”, a sand used to scour wooden floors. It is a little older than the Trossingen Formation, which holds the famous Plateosaurus herds.
Its fossils include the early long-necked dinosaur Efraasia, the small predatory dinosaur Procompsognathus, the large crocodile-line predator Teratosaurus, phytosaurs, aetosaurs and early turtles.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 215 to 210 million years ago (middle Norian)

event:sakamena.title: Sakamena Group
event:sakamena.dateText: About 258 to 249 million years ago (latest Permian to earliest Triassic)
summary: Lake and river rocks laid down in a rift valley as Madagascar began to pull away from Africa. The Lower Sakamena Formation is latest Permian; the Middle Sakamena Formation is earliest Triassic, so the group spans the great end-Permian extinction.
Its fossils, often preserved as natural moulds in nodules, include swimming diapsid reptiles like Hovasaurus and Claudiosaurus and the oldest known frog relative, Triadobatrachus.

event:argana.title: Timezgadiouine Formation (Argana Group)
event:argana.dateText: About 235 to 228 million years ago (Late Triassic, Carnian)
summary: Red river and lake rocks in the Argana valley of the High Atlas. The fossil-rich layer, known as T5, holds big flat-headed amphibians, phytosaurs, the giant dicynodont Moghreberia and lungfish.
It formed in one of the rift valleys that later opened into the Atlantic Ocean, and its animals are very like those of the same age in eastern North America.

points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 232 million years ago

event:cacheuta.title: Cacheuta Formation
summary: Dark lake shales in the Cuyo Basin near Mendoza, rich in fish, insects and plants. The same shales are the source rock for much of Mendoza’s oil.
Its four-legged animals include the big-headed amphibian Pelorocephalus, the cynodont Andescynodon and the archosauriform Cuyosuchus.

points.label: Cacheuta

event:yerrapalli.title: Yerrapalli Formation
event:yerrapalli.dateText: About 247 to 242 million years ago (Middle Triassic, Anisian)
summary: Red river mudstones in the Pranhita–Godavari valley of central India, with a fauna very like that of the Manda Beds in Tanzania.
It holds the herding dicynodont Wadiasaurus, the erythrosuchid Bharitalasuchus, the dinosaur-line archosaur Yarasuchus, big amphibians and lungfish.

points.label: Yerrapalli
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 244 million years ago

event:chalk.title: Chalk Group (English Chalk)
event:chalk.dateText: About 100 to 72 million years ago (Late Cretaceous)
event:chalk.placeText: South-east England, including the White Cliffs of Dover and the Sussex Downs
summary: Thick white limestone built from the tiny chalk plates of countless planktonic algae (coccolithophores) that settled on the floor of a warm, clear shelf sea when sea levels were very high. The White Cliffs of Dover are its best-known exposure.

Victorian quarrymen found fish, sharks, turtles, ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs, mosasaurs and pterosaurs. Its fish, such as the beardfish relative Berycopsis and the mackerel shark Cretalamna, are often preserved in three dimensions.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 100 to 72 million years ago (Cenomanian to Campanian)

facts.label: Where today

invertebrates.title: Sea life
invertebrates.text: Sea urchins such as Micraster, belemnites, ammonites, inoceramid clams, sponges and brachiopods are common; flint nodules formed from sponge silica.

event:jagua.title: Jagua Formation
event:jagua.dateText: About 160 to 157 million years ago (Late Jurassic, Oxfordian)
event:jagua.placeText: Viñales, Pinar del Río, western Cuba
summary: Dark limestones and shales with nodules, laid down in the young Caribbean Seaway, which opened as North and South America pulled apart and for the first time linked the Pacific with the young Atlantic.

Its marine reptiles, such as the pliosaur Gallardosaurus and the plesiosaur Vinialesaurus, are close relatives of those in the Oxford Clay of England, showing animals swam through the new seaway between Europe and the Pacific.

facts.value: Marine limestone, shale and fossil-bearing nodules

event:sannine.title: Sannine Formation (Lebanese fish beds)
event:sannine.dateText: About 98 to 94 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
summary: Finely layered limestones from quiet sea basins on the edge of the Tethys Ocean, famous for exquisitely preserved fish, which have been collected since at least the Middle Ages.
Besides thousands of fish, sharks, rays, octopuses and shrimps, it holds early snakes with legs, like Eupodophis, swimming lizards related to mosasaurs and snakes, and pterosaurs.

invertebrates.title: Shrimps and octopuses

event:csehbanya.title: Csehbánya Formation (Iharkút)
event:csehbanya.dateText: About 86 to 84 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Santonian)
summary: River and floodplain deposits uncovered in an open-cast bauxite mine at Iharkút, found in 2000 by Attila Ősi. At the time, Hungary was part of an island in the European archipelago of the Tethys Ocean.

It is one of the richest Late Cretaceous sites in Europe, with the nodosaur Hungarosaurus, the ornithopod Mochlodon, the possible ceratopsian Ajkaceratops, the pterosaur Bakonydraco, the freshwater mosasaur Pannoniasaurus, crocodiles, turtles, lizards, frogs and fish.

facts.value: River channel sandstones and floodplain clays
