event:eumeralla.title: Eumeralla Formation (Dinosaur Cove)
event:eumeralla.dateText: About 115 to 106 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: River deposits from a rift valley between Australia and Antarctica, when this region lay inside the Antarctic Circle. Animals lived through weeks of winter darkness, with cool temperatures and probably seasonal frost.

At Dinosaur Cove, volunteers tunnelled into sea cliffs to dig out the fossils. Its animals include small, big-eyed ornithopods like Leaellynasaura, small theropods, early mammals, turtles and lungfish.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 110 million years ago (late Aptian to Albian)

points.label: Eumeralla
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 110 million years ago

event:griman-creek.title: Griman Creek Formation (Lightning Ridge)
event:griman-creek.dateText: About 100 to 96 million years ago (Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian)
event:griman-creek.placeText: Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, Australia
summary: Coastal river and floodplain deposits near the edge of the inland Eromanga Sea. Many of its bones and teeth have been turned into precious opal, and they are found by opal miners rather than palaeontologists.

It has the richest early monotreme fauna anywhere, including Steropodon, Kollikodon and Opalios, along with small ornithopods, the theropod “Lightning Claw”, turtles, crocodiles, lungfish and the ornithopod Fostoria.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Lightning Ridge opal fields, New South Wales

points.label: Griman Creek
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 98 million years ago

event:crato.title: Crato Formation (Santana Group)
event:crato.dateText: About 115 to 113 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Aptian)
summary: Finely layered limestone from a salty lake or lagoon, quarried as paving stone around Nova Olinda and Santana do Cariri. It lies just below the Romualdo Formation, whose nodules hold 3D fossils.

It is one of the world’s great fossil sites for insects, and also preserves feathered birds, pterosaurs with crests and soft tissues, frogs, lizards, the four-legged snake-like Tetrapodophis and huge numbers of the small fish Dastilbe.
Many Crato fossils have been illegally exported from Brazil, and some important specimens have been returned in recent years.

points.label: Crato
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 114 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Insects and spiders
invertebrates.text: Hundreds of species of insects, including dragonflies, cockroaches, crickets and mayflies, and spiders and scorpions.

event:kimmeridge-clay.title: Kimmeridge Clay Formation
event:kimmeridge-clay.dateText: About 155 to 150 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
summary: Dark, oily mudstones laid down in a warm, quiet sea; the rock is the main source of North Sea oil. Its seas were ruled by giant pliosaurs, such as the huge skull found at Kimmeridge Bay in 2023.
It also holds ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs, metriorhynchid sea crocodiles, sharks, fish and pterosaurs, many collected by Steve Etches and shown in the Etches Collection museum at Kimmeridge.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 157 to 145 million years ago (Kimmeridgian to early Tithonian)

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Jurassic Coast of Dorset, and inland to Yorkshire

points.label: Kimmeridge Clay
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 152 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Ammonites
invertebrates.text: Ammonites, often crushed flat, and oysters and other shellfish.

event:hastings.title: Hastings Beds (Wealden Group)
event:hastings.dateText: About 142 to 133 million years ago (Early Cretaceous, Berriasian–Valanginian)
event:hastings.placeText: Hastings and the Weald of Sussex and Kent, England
summary: River sands and clays laid down on a wide floodplain, the older part of the Wealden. Some of the first dinosaur fossils ever studied, including bones collected by Gideon Mantell in the 1820s and 1830s, came from these rocks.
Its animals include iguanodonts, the dryosaurid Valdosaurus, armoured dinosaurs, sauropods like Haestasaurus, crocodiles, turtles and early mammals.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Hastings, Tunbridge Wells and the High Weald

points.label: Hastings
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 137 million years ago

event:marmarth-trex.title: Marmarth T. rex trackway
event:marmarth-trex.placeText: Near Marmarth, North Dakota, USA (Hell Creek Formation)
summary: Four three-toed footprints spanning about 7 metres, with a stride of about 4 metres, described in 2026 as the first known trackway of an adult T. rex. Science teacher and museum volunteer Kent Hups spotted it in July 2025 in the Badlands, on land run by the U.S. Forest Service.

The prints are heavily weathered, so the walking speed worked out from them, about 6 to 7 km/h, is approximate. Researchers from the Denver Museum of Nature & Science and Liverpool John Moores University call it “likely attributable” to an adult T. rex; some prints were lifted out by helicopter for display in Denver.

facts.label: Found
facts.value: Kent Hups, 2025; described in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, 2026

points.label: T. rex tracks
points.jumpLabel: Where the tracks were laid, about 67 million years ago

trackmakers.note: Its size and shape fit an adult T. rex, the only giant meat-eater known from these rocks.

event:madygen.title: Madygen Formation
event:madygen.dateText: About 240 to 227 million years ago (Middle to Late Triassic)
summary: Lake and river deposits from a valley in the Triassic mountains of Central Asia, one of the richest Triassic lake fossil sites in the world. Fine mud preserved plants, tens of thousands of insects and some very strange reptiles.

Its reptiles include the crested Longisquama and the glider Sharovipteryx, alongside the small cynodont Madysaurus, the armoured amphibian-like Madygenerpeton, the early salamander Triassurus, lungfish, the long-snouted fish Saurichthys and hybodont sharks, known mostly from their egg cases.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 232 million years ago (dates vary between studies)

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Near Madygen village, Batken region, Kyrgyzstan

points.label: Madygen
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 232 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Insects
invertebrates.text: Over 20,000 insects have been collected, including the giant cricket-relatives called titanopterans, such as Gigatitan, some of the largest insects of their time, plus early beetles, cockroaches and dragonfly relatives.

event:john-day.title: John Day Formation
event:john-day.dateText: About 39 to 18 million years ago (late Eocene to early Miocene)
event:john-day.placeText: John Day Fossil Beds National Monument, Oregon, USA
summary: Layer upon layer of volcanic ash from the young Cascade volcanoes, weathered into the red, green and buff hills of central Oregon. Most of its fossils come from the Turtle Cove Member, about 30 to 25 million years old, which has given more than a hundred kinds of mammals.

Turtle Cove animals include oreodonts such as Eporeodon, the three-toed horse Miohippus, the two-horned rhino Diceratherium, sabre-toothed nimravids such as Pogonodon and Dinictis, early dogs including Mesocyon, Enhydrocyon and Archaeocyon, and the tiny mouse-deer Hypertragulus, the most common fossil there.
Over its 20 million years the region dried out and woodland gave way to more open country, so its layers record mammals adapting to a cooling, drying climate.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: Turtle Cove Member about 30 to 25 million years ago

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Sheep Rock, Painted Hills and nearby, central Oregon

facts.label: Visit
facts.value: Thomas Condon Paleontology Center, Sheep Rock Unit

points.label: John Day
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 29 million years ago

event:xiaowa.title: Xiaowa Formation (Guanling biota)
event:xiaowa.dateText: About 237 to 235 million years ago (Late Triassic, early Carnian)
summary: Dark limestone and marl from an oxygen-poor sea basin, famous for whole skeletons of marine reptiles and great colonies of sea lilies. Earlier papers call these rocks the Wayao Member of the Falang Formation. Not to be confused with the older Guanling Formation of Luoping and Panxian.

Its animals include large shastasaurid ichthyosaurs (Guizhouichthyosaurus, Guanlingsaurus) and the smaller Qianichthyosaurus, the thalattosaurs Anshunsaurus and Xinpusaurus, armoured placodonts such as Sinocyamodus and Psephochelys, and, described in 2026, the sea-going amphibian Gerrothorax maritimus.

points.label: Xiaowa
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 237 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Sea lilies on driftwood
invertebrates.text: Colonies of the crinoid Traumatocrinus, with stems over 11 metres long, hung from floating logs: the first sea lilies known to have lived drifting at sea. Ammonoids and bivalves are common too.

event:vikinghogda.title: Vikinghøgda Formation
event:vikinghogda.dateText: About 251 to 247 million years ago (Early Triassic)
event:vikinghogda.placeText: Central Spitsbergen, Svalbard, Norway (map position approximate)
summary: Dark shale and siltstone from a sea on the northern edge of Pangaea, laid down only a few million years after the end-Permian extinction. Its bonebeds show how quickly reptiles took to the sea and refilled the oceans after the extinction.

Its animals include the early ichthyosaur relative Grippia, the shell-crushing omphalosaur Ammonitritor, large ichthyosaurs such as Cymbospondylus, the long-snouted amphibian Aphaneramma, and many fish, including Saurichthys, coelacanths, lungfish and hybodont sharks.

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Dark shale and siltstone with bonebeds

points.label: Vikinghøgda
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 249 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Ammonoids
invertebrates.text: Ammonoids are common and are used to date the layers; they were likely food for the shell-crushing reptiles.

event:anoual.title: Anoual Formation
event:anoual.dateText: About 168 to 166 million years ago (Middle Jurassic, Bathonian)
event:anoual.placeText: Talsint–Anoual area, Figuig province, eastern Morocco (map position approximate)
summary: Red mudstones with thin limestone beds, laid down by rivers, lakes and floodplains in the High Atlas. It is one of the few places in Africa with land and freshwater animals from the Middle Jurassic.

At Guelb el Ahmar, washing and sieving the rock has turned up at least 29 kinds of small animals, including the first Middle Jurassic mammals known from Africa, along with amphibians, lizard relatives, crocodile relatives and pterosaur teeth. Most are known from teeth and scraps and have not yet been named. The narrow-snouted Ctenosuchus, named in 2026, is the best-preserved animal found so far.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Near Talsint and Anoual, eastern Morocco

points.label: Anoual
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 167 million years ago

event:trenton.title: Trenton Group
event:trenton.dateText: About 456 to 450 million years ago (Late Ordovician)
event:trenton.placeText: Trenton Falls and the Mohawk Valley, New York, USA, and southern Ontario, Canada
summary: Layers of limestone and shale from a warm, shallow tropical sea that covered eastern North America, then lying south of the equator. They are packed with shells, sea lilies, bryozoans and trilobites.

Its trilobites include the big, smooth Isotelus and the spiny Ceraurus, which at the Walcott–Rust Quarry is preserved with its legs. Straight-shelled nautiloids such as Cameroceras hunted in the same sea.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Central New York and southern Ontario

points.label: Trenton
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 453 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Sea floor life
invertebrates.text: Brachiopods, bryozoans, sea lilies, snails and corals.

event:orthoceratite-limestone.title: Orthoceratite Limestone
event:orthoceratite-limestone.dateText: About 475 to 465 million years ago (Early to Middle Ordovician)
summary: Red and grey limestone laid down very slowly on the floor of a cool sea over the ancient continent of Baltica, named for the orthocone shells that crowd its surfaces. It has been quarried for centuries, and polished slabs pave old floors and churches across Scandinavia.
At Kinnekulle the same limestone holds dozens of fossil meteorites, debris from a collision in the asteroid belt about 466 million years ago that showered the Earth for millions of years.

points.label: Orthoceratite
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 470 million years ago

invertebrates.title: Trilobites
invertebrates.text: Asaphid trilobites such as Megistaspis, with brachiopods and other shells.

event:pindai.title: Pindai Caves
event:pindai.placeText: Népoui Peninsula, north-west coast of Grande Terre, New Caledonia
summary: Six caves in raised coral limestone at the tip of the Népoui Peninsula, holding the richest fossil deposits found on New Caledonia’s main island, along with traces of the first people to settle there, who arrived about 3,000 years ago.

Its bones come from the island’s lost animals: the land crocodile Mekosuchus, the giant horned turtle Meiolania, the giant ground bird Sylviornis, and at least 20 other birds now extinct there, including a flightless swamphen, a larger relative of the kagu, pigeons and owls. Some occur in the same layers as people, but problems with dating mean how far humans caused these extinctions is still debated.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 3,000 years ago (the time of human arrival)

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Cave deposits in raised coral limestone

points.label: Pindai
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 3,000 years ago

event:rising-star.title: Rising Star Cave
event:rising-star.placeText: Cradle of Humankind, near Johannesburg, South Africa
summary: A cave system in the dolomite hills of the Cradle of Humankind, a World Heritage Site rich in human ancestors. In 2013 cavers squeezed through an 18 cm-wide gap into the Dinaledi Chamber and found its floor covered in bones; thousands of pieces from at least 15 individuals of a new species, Homo naledi, have been recovered from it and the nearby Lesedi Chamber.
Almost all the bones belong to Homo naledi, with hardly any other animals. How they got there, through passages so tight that only slim cavers can reach them, is still debated.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Cradle of Humankind, Gauteng, South Africa

facts.label: Visit
facts.value: The chambers are closed; Maropeng visitor centre tells the story

points.label: Rising Star
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 300,000 years ago

event:liang-bua.title: Liang Bua
event:liang-bua.dateText: About 190,000 to 50,000 years ago for the Homo floresiensis layers (Pleistocene)
summary: A large limestone cave in the hills of western Flores, “cool cave” in the local Manggarai language, where Homo floresiensis was found in 2003. Its layers hold an island fauna shaped by isolation: dwarfed elephant relatives, giant rats the size of rabbits, Komodo dragons, a giant stork and a vulture.

Homo floresiensis, the dwarf Stegodon, the giant stork and the vulture all disappear from the cave at about the same time, about 50,000 years ago, a little after modern humans reached the region. Carcasses of Stegodon probably fed a whole guild of scavengers: vultures, giant storks, crows, Komodo dragons and perhaps Homo floresiensis too.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: About 100,000 to 60,000 years ago for the skeletons

points.label: Liang Bua
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 100,000 years ago

event:olduvai.title: Olduvai Gorge
event:olduvai.dateText: About 1.9 to 1.2 million years ago for Beds I and II (Pleistocene)
summary: A gorge cut through the layers of an old lake basin on the edge of the Serengeti, where Louis and Mary Leakey worked for decades. Mary Leakey found the robust skull of Paranthropus boisei here in 1959, and the gorge gave its name to the Oldowan, the oldest widespread stone-tool industry.

Paranthropus boisei and Homo habilis lived here together in Bed I, about 1.85 million years ago. Homo erectus appears higher up, in Bed II, alongside Paranthropus but no longer Homo habilis. They shared the lakeshore with elephants, giant buffalo, pigs, horses, antelopes, crocodiles and big cats, as the land became more open grassland over time.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: Bed I about 1.85 to 1.7 million years ago; Bed II about 1.7 to 1.2 million

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Northern Tanzania, between Ngorongoro and the Serengeti

facts.label: Rocks
facts.value: Lake and river sediments and volcanic ash

facts.label: Visit
facts.value: Olduvai Gorge museum and visitor centre

points.label: Olduvai
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 1.8 million years ago

event:swartkrans.title: Swartkrans
event:swartkrans.placeText: Cradle of Humankind, near Johannesburg, South Africa
summary: A cave in the Cradle of Humankind with the largest collection of Paranthropus robustus fossils, and the first site where Paranthropus and early Homo were found together, showing they lived at the same time.

Bob Brain’s work here, in his book The Hunters or the Hunted?, showed that many of the hominins were prey rather than hunters: a young Paranthropus skull has two holes matching a leopard’s canines. Leopards, lions, spotted hyenas, the giant hunting hyena Chasmaporthetes and the sabre-toothed cats Megantereon and Dinofelis all lived here; carbon isotopes suggest leopards and Megantereon, rather than Dinofelis, were the main hominin hunters.

facts.label: Where today
facts.value: Cradle of Humankind, Gauteng, South Africa

facts.label: Myth
facts.value: Its hominins were mostly hunted, not hunters

points.label: Swartkrans
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 1.8 million years ago

event:krapina.title: Krapina
summary: A rock shelter above the Krapinica stream that has given about 900 Neanderthal bones from at least 70 individuals, one of the largest Neanderthal collections anywhere, excavated by Dragutin Gorjanović-Kramberger from 1899.

It dates from the warm last interglacial, when Europe was about as warm as today. Its 25 kinds of mammals are led by small, warm-period cave bears, beavers, Merck’s rhinos and big wild cattle; some bones carry cut marks and burning from Neanderthal butchery.

facts.label: Visit
facts.value: Krapina Neanderthal Museum, beside the site

points.label: Krapina
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 125,000 years ago

event:harbin.title: Harbin (Songhua River)
summary: River deposits of the Songhua River at Harbin in north-east China. A worker is said to have found the Harbin skull here in 1933 while building a bridge and hid it in a well for decades; it was named Homo longi, “Dragon Man”, in 2021. Its exact find spot is unknown, so its age, at least 146,000 years, comes from sediment stuck in its nasal cavity.
Harbin’s Pleistocene deposits come from a cold steppe, home to woolly mammoths, giant deer, Przewalski’s horses, elk, bison and brown bears.

points.label: Harbin
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 150,000 years ago

event:ouled-abdoun-paleogene.title: Ouled Abdoun Basin (Paleocene–Eocene)
event:ouled-abdoun-paleogene.dateText: About 61 to 54 million years ago (Paleocene to early Eocene)
summary: The upper layers of Morocco’s great phosphate beds, laid down in a shallow sea soon after the dinosaurs’ extinction. Mixed in with countless sharks’ teeth and fish are the bones of land mammals washed out to sea, among them the oldest known proboscideans, the group that would give rise to elephants.

points.label: Ouled Abdoun
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 58 million years ago

event:siwaliks.title: Upper Siwaliks
event:siwaliks.dateText: About 3.6 to 0.6 million years ago (Pliocene to Pleistocene)
event:siwaliks.placeText: Siwalik Hills, northern India and Pakistan
summary: River sediments shed from the rising Himalayas, forming the foothills of northern India and Pakistan. Hugh Falconer and Proby Cautley collected huge numbers of fossils here in the 1830s, among them several Stegodon species, early elephants, hippos, giraffe relatives such as Sivatherium, and big cats.

points.label: Siwaliks
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 2 million years ago

event:tunggur.title: Tunggur Formation
event:tunggur.dateText: About 13.8 to 11.6 million years ago (middle Miocene)
event:tunggur.placeText: Tunggur tableland, Inner Mongolia, China (map position approximate)
summary: Lake and river deposits on the Mongolian plateau, explored by the American Museum of Natural History’s Central Asiatic Expeditions in the 1920s. Its “Platybelodon quarry” held a mass of shovel-tuskers, along with horses, rhinos and other mammals of a warmer, wetter middle Miocene Asia.

points.label: Tunggur
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 13 million years ago

event:spinagallo.title: Spinagallo Cave
summary: A cave in south-eastern Sicily that held the bones of over 100 dwarf elephants, Palaeoloxodon falconeri, of all ages, from newborns to adults, making it one of the best records of an island dwarf anywhere. Giant dormice and swans lived on the island with them.

points.label: Spinagallo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 350,000 years ago

event:santa-rosa-island.title: Santa Rosa Island
event:santa-rosa-island.placeText: Channel Islands National Park, California, USA
summary: In the Ice Age, when sea levels were lower, the northern Channel Islands were joined into one island, Santarosae, only a few kilometres off the coast. Columbian mammoths swam across and shrank into pygmy mammoths. The island also holds Arlington Springs Man, about 13,000 years old, among the oldest human remains in North America, from around the time the pygmy mammoths vanished.

facts.label: Visit
facts.value: By boat, Channel Islands National Park

points.label: Santa Rosa
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 20,000 years ago

event:el-fin-del-mundo.title: El Fin del Mundo
event:el-fin-del-mundo.dateText: About 13,400 years ago (end of the Pleistocene)
summary: An archaeological site in the Sonoran Desert where Clovis hunters killed and butchered at least two gomphotheres, Cuvieronius, about 13,400 years ago. Clovis spear points lay among the bones. It is one of the oldest Clovis sites, and the only one with gomphotheres rather than mammoths or mastodons.

points.label: Fin del Mundo
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 13,000 years ago

event:tuchengzi.title: Tuchengzi Formation
event:tuchengzi.dateText: About 152 to 145 million years ago (Late Jurassic)
event:tuchengzi.placeText: Chaoyang, Liaoning, and northern Hebei, China
summary: Red sandstones and conglomerates laid down by rivers and wind in a dry basin at the very end of the Jurassic, below the famous Jehol beds. Its bones are rare: the only dinosaur skeletons are the early ceratopsians Chaoyangsaurus and Xuanhuaceratops and an unnamed brachiosaurid sauropod. Far commoner are footprints, including those of small meat-eaters (Grallator). It records the time between the Jurassic Daohugou animals and the Early Cretaceous Jehol biota.

points.label: Tuchengzi
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 150 million years ago

event:khuren-dukh.title: Khuren Dukh Formation
event:khuren-dukh.dateText: About 115 to 105 million years ago (Early Cretaceous)
summary: Lake and river deposits in the eastern Gobi, older than the famous Late Cretaceous beds of Mongolia. In 2025 it gave Zavacephale, the oldest definite pachycephalosaur. It lived alongside the arched-nosed iguanodont Altirhinus, the early duck-bill relative Choyrodon, the armoured Shamosaurus, Psittacosaurus, and two kinds of choristodere in the lakes.

points.label: Khuren Dukh
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 108 million years ago

event:obernkirchen.title: Obernkirchen Sandstone
event:obernkirchen.dateText: About 145 to 140 million years ago (earliest Cretaceous)
event:obernkirchen.placeText: Bückeberg hills near Obernkirchen, Lower Saxony, Germany
summary: Fine sandstone from the coastal plains and deltas of north-west Germany at the start of the Cretaceous, quarried for centuries as a prized building stone. Its surfaces are crossed by thousands of footprints of iguanodonts, meat-eaters and ankylosaurs, with tracks of a swimming turtle and a pterosaur. Its few skeletons include the puzzling plant-eater Stenopelix, found in 1855, and the long-snouted crocodile relative Pholidosaurus. Many old track sites have been lost as quarrying has declined.

points.label: Obernkirchen
points.jumpLabel: Where it formed, about 142 million years ago
